**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 1 (part 1 of 5):**

**Sūrat al-An'ām (the chapter of Cattle)**

6. As Abu 'Ubayd, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tabarani also narrated from him that it was revealed at night in Mecca all at once. Abu al-Shaykh narrated the report of its being revealed all at once from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, traced back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Al-Nahhas, in his book *al-Nasikh* (On Abrogation), narrated from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) that it is Meccan except for three verses, which were revealed in Medina: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ up to the completion of the three verses. Ibn Rahawayh, in his *Musnad* (a collection of hadith arranged by the names of the narrators) and elsewhere, narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab that it is Meccan except for two verses: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ and what follows it. Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from al-Kalbi and Sufyan, who said: "The whole of Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca except for two verses revealed in Medina, concerning a man of the Jews, and he is the one who said: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human﴾," and the verse continues. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Juhayfa: "The whole of Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca except for ﴿Even if We had sent down the angels to them﴾," which is Medinan.

[p. 76]

Others said: "All of it is Meccan except six verses: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ up to the completion of three verses, and ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ up to the end of the last three." The number of its verses is one hundred and sixty-five according to the Kufans, one hundred and sixty-six according to the Basrans and Syrians, and one hundred and sixty-seven according to the Hijazis. Many reports have been transmitted about its virtue. Al-Hakim narrated it and declared it authentic; al-Bayhaqi narrated it in *al-Shu'ab* (The Branches of Faith); and al-Isma'ili narrated it in his *Mu'jam* (dictionary of narrators), from Jabir, who said: "When Surat al-An'am was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) glorified God, and then he said, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Seventy thousand angels escorted this chapter, filling the horizon.'" The report of the angels escorting it was narrated by a group of hadith scholars. However, some of them narrated that the escorts were seventy thousand, some narrated that they were fewer, and some narrated that they were more. Al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays the dawn prayer in congregation, sits in his place of prayer, and recites the first three verses of Surat al-An'am, God will assign to him seventy angels who glorify God and seek forgiveness for him until the Day of Resurrection."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Habib ibn Muhammad al-'Abid, who said: "Whoever recites the first three verses of al-An'am, up to His words ﴿that you earn﴾, God will send to him seventy thousand angels who will supplicate for him until the Day of Resurrection, and he will have the like of their deeds. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will admit him to Paradise, give him to drink from the Salsabil, bathe him in al-Kawthar, and say: 'I am your Lord in truth, and you are My servant.'" There are other reports of this kind. Most of them in this regard are weak, and some are fabricated, as is not hidden from one who examines them. Perhaps the reports about this surah having been revealed all at once are also of this kind.

The Imam (al-Razi) reported that people agree that it was revealed all at once. Then he raised an objection: how is it possible to say, at each verse of it, that the cause of its revelation was such-and-such a matter, given that they say this? The claim that what the speaker meant is that no verses of another surah were revealed between the times of the revelation of its verses is not supported by the apparent meaning; rather, there are reports that explicitly contradict it. The claim that it was revealed twice, once in a block and once piecemeal, contradicts the apparent meaning and has no evidence.

What supports what we have pointed out about the weakness of the reports on its revelation all at once is what Ibn al-Salah said in his *Fatawa* (legal opinions): "The hadith transmitted regarding its being revealed all at once, we have narrated it through the chain of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, but we have not found a sound chain for it, and what contradicts it has been narrated." End of quotation. From this it is known, contrary to the Imam's claim, that people agree on its being revealed all at once. So reflect.

As for the connection between it and the end of al-Ma'idah, according to what some scholars have said: this surah opens with praise (*al-hamd*), and that one closes with the judgment of the matter, and these two are mutually implied, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿They will be judged with truth, and it will be said: Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said regarding the connection: when He, exalted is He, mentioned at the end of al-Ma'idah ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾ in summary, this surah opens by explaining that and detailing it. He, glorified is He, begins by mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth, and adds that He made the darknesses and the light, which is part of what is contained in *wa-mā fīhinna* (and whatever is in them). Then He mentions that He created the human species and decreed for it a term, and set for it another term for the resurrection, and that He, majestic is His majesty, is the originator of generations, one generation after another. Then He said: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, etc., thereby establishing for Him the dominion of all that is contained in a place. Then He, mighty is the One who speaks, said: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾, thereby establishing that He, majestic and exalted, possesses all that is contained in time. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the creation of all animals, including beasts and birds, then the creation of sleep, wakefulness, and death. Then, in the course of the surah, He, mighty and majestic, greatly emphasized origination and creation with respect to what is in them: the two luminaries and the stars, the splitting of the dawn, the splitting of the grain and the date-stone, the sending down of water, the bringing forth of plants and fruits of various kinds, the producing of gardens, trellised and untrellised, and other things in which there is detail of what is in them. He, peace be upon him, also mentioned another aspect of the connection, which is that when He, glorified is He, mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that God has made lawful for you﴾, etc., and then, after it, He, majestic is His majesty, mentioned ﴿God did not appoint any bahira (a slit-eared she-camel)﴾, etc., informing about the unbelievers that they forbade things that God had provided for them, fabricating against God, and the purpose of that was to warn the believers not to forbid any of those things lest they resemble the unbelievers in their conduct. Since that mention was brief, He, majestic is His majesty, brought this surah to explain the state of the unbelievers in their conduct, presenting it in the clearest manner and the most complete form. Then He argued with them about it, established proofs for its falsehood, opposed them, contradicted them, and so on, with what the narrative contains. Thus this surah is an explanation of what that surah contained of that, in summary, and in detail, expansion, completion and elaboration. It begins with the mention of creation and dominion, because the Creator and the Owner is the One who has disposal over His dominion and His creatures, by permitting, forbidding, prohibiting and making lawful; therefore He, glorified is He, must not be challenged regarding His disposal of His dominion.

This surah also has a connection on one side with al-Fatihah, by explaining the summary of His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾; and with al-Baqarah, by explaining the summary of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He who created you and those before you﴾, and His saying, mighty is His name: ﴿He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾; and with Al 'Imran, from the aspect of its detailing His saying, majestic and exalted: ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾, etc.; and with al-Nisa', from the aspect of what it contains about the beginning of creation and the condemnation of what they forbade to their wives and the killing of daughters; and with al-Ma'idah, in terms of its including foods of various kinds.

It may be said: since the axis of this surah revolves around establishing the Creator and the proofs of monotheism, to the extent that Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini said: "In Surat al-An'am are all the foundations of monotheism," it corresponds to that surah in that it contains the refutation of the divinity of 'Isa, peace be upon him, the rebuke of the unbelievers for their corrupt belief, and their false fabrication. Furthermore, since His blessings, glorified and exalted is He, are of a kind that exceeds enumeration, and no bounds of counting can encompass them, yet they return in summary to bringing into being and sustaining in the first creation, and bringing into being and sustaining in the final creation; and in al-Fatihah, which is the Mother of the Book, reference is made to all of them; in al-An'am, to the first bringing into being; in al-Kahf, to the first sustaining; in Saba', to the second bringing into being; and in Fatir, to the second sustaining. These five surahs begin with praise.

Among the subtleties is that He, glorified and exalted is He, placed in each quarter of His Noble and Glorious Book a surah beginning with praise. The One who speaks, mighty is He, said: (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful) ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾.

*Al-hamd lillāh* is either a declarative sentence (*jumlah khabariyyah*) or an imperative/performative sentence (*jumlah insha'iyyah*). Some scholars preferred the first, because taking it as performative involves removing the utterance from its literal meaning without necessity, and because, if it were performative, it would entail that the quality of being praiseworthy did not exist before the praiser praised, since performative utterance coincides in existence with its meaning. Others preferred the second, because if the sentence "praise belongs to God" were a declaration, it would follow that the one who says "praise belongs to God" could not be called a *ḥāmid* (praiser), since linguistically no derived noun is formed for the one reporting something from the object of his report; thus one does not say of someone who says "Zayd has standing" that he is *qā'im* (standing). The consequent is false, so the antecedent is false. This does not follow if the sentence is performative, because from a performative utterance a derived noun of agency is formed as a description of the speaker, so one says of someone who says "I sold" that he is *bā'i'* (seller).

It was objected that this does not apply to every performative utterance; otherwise one would say of someone who said "he struck" that he is *ḍārib* (striker), and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And mothers suckle their children﴾, yet He is not called *mur'ia* (nurser). Rather, this only applies when the performative utterance is a state of the speaker, as in the formulae of contracts; and then there is no difference between it and the declarative in what has been mentioned. What the researchers hold is that both interpretations are permissible for this sentence, and they answered the objection that follows from it. Yet the declarative interpretation is preferred here, because the surah was revealed to explain monotheism and to restrain the unbelievers, and conveying its content in declarative form suits the context, whereas making it an expression of praise does not suit it. It was also said that taking it as declarative here is so that what follows it, and the subsequent *thumma* (then), can be coordinated with it. Whoever takes it as performative and does not permit coordinating a performative with a declarative makes the coordination with the relative clause or with the performative sentence, and makes the coordinated element an expression of astonishment and wonder. The distance of this from the apparent meaning and its artificiality are not hidden.

In making praise depend first on the proper name and then, second, on the attribute with which He, glorified and exalted is He, has described Himself, there is an alert to the realization of two entitlements: the realization of His entitlement, majestic and mighty is He, to praise by reason of His essence, and the realization of His entitlement, glorified and exalted is He, by reason of the blessing indicated by what is in the relative clause that functions as the attribute. According to some, the meaning of His essential entitlement, glorified and exalted is He, is His being entitled, majestic and exalted is He, to praise by reason of all His attributes and actions, and this is the meaning of their saying that He, exalted is He, deserves worship for His essence. Whoever denied this denied the validity of directing veneration and worship to the essence as such.

Al-Alusi's commentary, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 6, verse 1 (part 2 of 5):

The Imam has stated explicitly, in his commentary on the Ishara (allusion), when mentioning the stations of the gnostics (al-'arifin), that people in worship fall into three classes. The first, which is the most perfect and most noble, are those who worship Him, glorified and exalted is He, for His essence itself, and for nothing else. The second, which comes next to the first in perfection, are those who worship Him for one of His attributes, namely that He, exalted is He, is deserving of worship. The third, which is the last of the ranks of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), are those who worship Him so that their souls may be perfected in their connection to Him. The conception of glorifying the Essence as such is not problematic, because, as al-Shihab said, were that to occur at the outset, before rationally apprehending the aspects of perfection, it would be problematic. But after knowing the One Praised, majestic is His majesty, by the marks of beauty, and conceiving Him with the utmost attributes of perfection, there is nothing strange in His being turned to in glorification and praise, mighty is His affair, once more, setting aside everything other than the Essence, after ascending through the degrees of contemplation. For this reason the people of the outward (ahl al-zahir) said: "His attributes do not increase knowledge, but they are a pleasure we have mentioned." So what of the gnostics who are immersed in the seas of gnosis (al-'irfan), and they are the people, the entire people?

As for what al-Salakuti verified, and what we followed in al-Fatiha, it is that the essential deservingness (al-istihqaq al-dhati) is that in which no particularity of an attribute is taken into account, even collectively, not that in which the pure Essence is deserving of it. For the deservingness of praise is only for the beautiful, and it is called essential because the Essence is taken into account in it without considering the particularity of an attribute, or because the indication of the name of the Essence is upon it, or because, since it is not ascribed to a particular attribute of the specific attributes, it is ascribed to the Essence.

Some of the later verifiers mentioned a discussion on this point, in which he refuted, in what he held, many of the eminent scholars.

Its summary is that the preposition lam in (lillah) is for general particularity (mutlaq al-ikhtisas), not for specific restrictive particularity (al-ikhtisas al-qasri) in determination. The evidence is that they said of phrases like lahu al-hamd that the fronting (taqdim) is for restrictive particularity. So if the preposition lam also conveyed it, there would be no difference between al-hamdu lillah and lahu al-hamd except that the second is more emphatic in conveying restriction. What is explicitly stated is the distinction that one of them conveys restriction and the other does not. Particularities come in various modes, and the determination of some of them is left to the reason (illah) upon which the ruling is based, which is the praiseworthy cause and other contextual indicators. So when you see the ruling is based on His attributes specific to Him, glorified and exalted is He, it is necessary that praise be restricted to Him, and the ruling founded on the cause is taken as restrictive, so that the effect matches its cause. Moreover, if the attributes specific to Him, mighty and majestic is He, are such as indicate that He, mighty is His affair, bestows favours on His servants, then it is necessary that praise be a right of God, exalted is He, obligatory upon His servants, glorified is He, so the ruling founded on the cause is taken as implying deservingness, for correspondence as well. And if the ruling is not founded on anything, or the consideration of the cause upon which the ruling is based is set aside, then what is established in the ruling is only the lowest degree of particularity, namely that His being worthy of praise is bare of restriction and deservingness.

What I have pointed to is supported by the differing expressions of the Allama al-Baydawi in explaining the meanings of the sentences of praise, and by the fact that what is meant by deservingness (al-istijab), which some grammarians made one of the meanings of lam, is what is equivalent to general particularity as he established it, not the meaning he alluded to. Accordingly, the sense of the sentence al-hamdu lillah in our present context is that He, exalted is He, is truly worthy of praise, and there is no indication in it, considered in itself, apart from the praiseworthy cause that is the reason for the ruling, of restricting the reality of praise to Him, glorified is He, nor of its reaching the limit of deservingness. Yes, in placing the ruling upon what is within the scope of the attribute there is an indication that praise is a right of God, exalted is He, obligatory upon His servants, specifically His, mighty is His affair, restricted to Him, glorified is He, since placing the ruling upon the attribute, as they said, indicates by its explicit content the causality of the attribute for the ruling, and by its implicit content the negation of the ruling for whom the attribute is negated.

Then he said: In sum, the sentence "al-hamdu lillah" is a claim and a signified meaning (mudda'an wa madlul).

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: "Who created" etc. is evidence and a cause. There is no praise here except one praise, justified by what is within the scope of the attribute, not a praise justified by the Essence that combines all attributes, or by the pure Essence first, as has been said, and by the attribute second, so that it would be like two praises according to the two causes. For the word Allah is a proper name, and it has no signification of the attributes by any of the three kinds of signification. How, then, could it be praised for it and be a cause for the deservingness of praise? For this reason, the ruling of deservingness of praise hardly occurs except when justified by clear matters indicating His glorious attributes and His beautiful acts, and the name of the Essence is not relied upon alone, except in the glorifications and praises of the believers, but not in the argument against the deniers, which is what we are concerned to explain. Also, what the pure Essence, as such, entails: what use is it in arguing against a people most of whom do not see or hear, who are only like cattle, nay, they are further astray?

As for what is said: the phrase "al-hamdu lillah" was used with the name of the Essence that combines all attributes, and it was not said "to the Knowing" or "to the Powerful" or other names indicating majesty or honour, lest it be supposed that praise is restricted to one attribute rather than another, that is a statement built upon what you have seen to be its corruption, namely that the Essence is praiseworthy for itself.

It may also be said: mention of the name of the Essence is only because the idolaters being argued against, the ignorant, do not know Him, exalted is He, and do not mention Him among themselves or in argument except by His name, the Knowing, glorified is He, not by attributes, as is shown by the fact that their answers are reported with the mention of that noble name in most questions, except in a few cases where their answer was without the name of the Essence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will surely say: "The Mighty, the Knowing created them"﴾. Some have held that this is a necessary implication of what they say, and what it indicates in summary is placed in its stead. Thus it is as if they said: "Allah", as He reports of them in several places. Then it is as if it were said: the God whom they know and mention by this name is the One deserving of praise, because He is the creator of the heavens and the earth, and because He is such-and-such. And when you know that the Essence is not fit to be praised for itself, and that what is truly worthy of being praised is the attributes, and that what praise is grounded upon in every place is some of the attributes according to what the context requires, not all the attributes, you know that whoever claims that praise is grounded on some attributes rather than others implies that the entitlement to praise is restricted to one attribute rather than another, which would lead him into the very predicament he fled from, as is not hidden.

The truth, then, is that what is praised for is the attribute upon which the entitlement to praise is grounded, and that singling out some attributes so that the entitlement to praise is grounded upon them in some situations is only by the requirement of that context. If you say: what is the view on praise considered with respect to the pure Essence, or with respect to its combining all attributes, as has been said, is there a basis for it or not? I say: either the pure Essence being praised for itself, and likewise the Essence being praised for combining all attributes, in situations like those we are in, has no basis.

As for what they mentioned in explaining the prefaces of some books, that praise is considered with respect to the Essence combining all attributes, perhaps its origin is that praise, when it implies a beautiful attribute fit to ground the ruling of entitlement to praise and to be praised for it, then where no such attribute is mentioned with it, and no indicator points to it, but rather the Essence possessing all beautiful attributes is mentioned alone, the consideration of a beautiful attribute there is established by implication. Then, since singling out one of these considerations over the others would entail preference without a preponderant reason, it must be that all beautiful attributes are considered together, so that praise is by consideration of all of them. Where a beautiful attribute fit to be praised for is mentioned with it, and a context clearly indicates it, that consideration is dispensed with, because recourse to it was out of necessity, and there is no necessity then, as is not hidden. Whoever has not been guided to the difference between what occurs in the Noble Qur'an for purposes and what occurs in the prefaces of books merely for blessing, nor to the difference between what has its praiseworthy cause stated explicitly or indicated by a clear context and what is not so, has mounted the back of a blind course and stumbled like a blind camel, mixing up the requirements of some contexts with others, not knowing on what nobility the speech of God, exalted is He, rests, and the speech of others goes in what valley.

In brief: the ordering of the ruling contained in the sentence "al-hamdu lillah" here upon the attribute specific to Him, glorified is He, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth, and what is conjoined to it, conveys restrictive particularity in the manner already mentioned. This is indicated by the words of the Allama al-Baydawi in his commentary on this verse, for one who reflects carefully. However, what he mentioned, may God have mercy on him, at the beginning of Saba' regarding the difference between "al-hamdu lillah alladhi lahu ma fi al-samawat wa ma fi al-ard" and "lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah," whose gist is that the sentence "lahu al-hamd" was brought with the fronting of the relative clause in order to convey restriction, because the bestowal of the blessings of the Hereafter is particular to Him, exalted is He. By contrast, the sentence "al-hamdu lillah alladhi lahu" etc. was not brought with the fronting of the relative clause, so as not to convey restriction, because the bestowal of blessing is not absolutely particular to Him, exalted is He, such that no other has any part in it, since it may come through an intermediary, and so that intermediary deserves praise in a certain kind of deservingness by reason of his mediation. For the gist of what he mentioned in that surah is that there is no restriction in the sentence "al-hamdu lillah alladhi lahu" etc., unlike the sentence "lahu al-hamd." And the gist of what he indicated in this passage, and likewise in al-Fatiha, is that the sentence "al-hamdu lillah," when ordered upon attributes specific to Him, such as the creating and the making mentioned, also conveys restriction. The only remaining question is that the method of conveying restriction in the two cases differs: in one the fronting of the relative clause, and in the other the notion of causality. So reflect upon this, and may God, exalted is He, take charge of your guidance.

He, glorified is He, used the plural for the heavens and the singular for the earth, although, according to the many texts, the earth is also plural. The harmony between words is among the embellishments of speech, so when someone uses the dual of two opposites or the like, they should use the plural for the other as well. For this reason Abu Nuwas was criticized for his saying:

"And as for you, know that among us there is a word, when you have completed lifespans and provision,"

where he used the plural in one place and the singular in another, though the plural was used for a reason that justified departing from that principle, namely to indicate their difference in nobility. He used the plural for the nobler, showing care for all its individuals, and the singular for the less noble. The nobility of the heaven is because it is the place of the sanctified angels, on their differing ranks, and the direction of supplication, and the ascent of pure spirits, and because of its greatness and its encompassing of the earth, according to the view that it is spherical, which some of us hold, and the greatness of God's signs in it, and because God, exalted is He, has never been disobeyed in it at all, and in it is the Garden, which is the abode of the beloved ones, and for other reasons. As for the earth, although it is the abode of obligation and the place of the prophets, peace be upon them, that is only for conveying the message and gathering what makes them fit for standing in the presence of holiness, since it is not a place of permanence. The creation of the prophets' bodies from it, and their burial in it, together with the fact that their spirits, which are the source of nobility, are not from it and are not buried in it, does not indicate

[p. 82]

...over more than its nobility. As for whether it indicates its superiority, that hardly stands uncontested. Likewise, that Allah the Exalted described some of its parts as blessed does not indicate more than what we have mentioned. Because of this same nobility, it was also placed before the earth in mention. It has been said that the plural "heavens" and the singular "earth" are because the heaven functions as the agent (fa'il) and the earth functions as the receptive substrate (qabil). Had the heaven been singular, the effects would be alike, and that would disrupt the interests of this world. As for the earth, it is receptive, and a single receptive substrate suffices for reception.

The summary of this is that the difference in effects indicates the multiplicity of the heavens by rational proof, while the earth, although it is multiple, has no rational proof for its multiplicity. Therefore He used the plural for the heavens and not for the earth.

It has been objected that this reasoning may, in fact, imply the opposite. Some have said that there is no real multiplicity in the earth, which is why it was not made plural. As for the multiplicity mentioned in some reports, such as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever usurps a span of land unjustly, it will be hung around his neck from the seven earths," it is to be understood as multiplicity in terms of the seven climes (aqalim). Likewise, what Abu al-Shaykh and al-Tirmidhi reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what this is? This is an earth. Do you know what is beneath it?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Another earth, and between them is a distance of five hundred years," until he counted seven earths, between each two earths being five hundred years. The word "beneath" (tahtiyyah) does not contradict this, for the earth, like the heaven, is spherical, and it may be said of a thing that after the last it is beneath it. The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "between them five hundred years" means that the arc from one of the heavens directly above the first clime, and the beginning of the next, is five hundred years. There is no doubt that this may exceed this amount, and numbers are often intended for multiplicity rather than a precise quantity.

Allah the Exalted's saying ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ is to be understood as the likeness in number seven as found in the climes, not as real multiplicity. It is not hidden that this is an over-elaboration to which nothing has led except attributing inability to the power of Allah, and that He, glory be to Him, is incapable of creating seven earths in accordance with what the apparent text states, which came from the presence of the most eloquent of those who ever spoke in Arabic, and who removed, by the pure sweetness of his noble speech, the thirst of every obstructed one. Interpreting the likeness in the verse as the likeness that the proponent of this view claims is also contrary to the apparent meaning.

Perhaps, if Allah wills, the occasion will lead to the completion of the discussion on this point. Some verifying scholars have mentioned, regarding the reason for placing the heavens before the earth, that it is due to the precedence of the creation of the heavens over the creation of the earth. It is not hidden that this is a view held by some of them.

From al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may Allah sanctify his secret, it is reported that the creation of the outermost sphere (al-muhaddad) precedes the creation of the earth, and the creation of the remaining spheres comes after the creation of the earth. Some discussion on this point has already passed. The specific mention of the creation of the earth is because it encompasses the totality of the upper and lower effects and the general manifest and hidden blessings, the greatest of which is the blessing of existence, which is sufficient to make the praise of Him, the Exalted, obligatory upon every existent. How much more so, then, are the various kinds of outward and inward blessings that branch from it, upon which the interests of the servants in this life and the Hereafter depend.

By "creation" (khalq) is meant origination and bringing into being, that is, He brought the heavens and the earth into existence and produced them in the state in which they are, containing signs for those who reflect.

﴿And made the darknesses and the light﴾ is conjoined to ﴿created the heavens﴾, and it is included with it in the sense of indicating the cause of praise, even though it follows from it, because their making is preceded by the creation of their place of origin and their locus, as has been said. The making (ja'l), as the Shaykh al-Islam said, is origination and innovation, like creation, except that it is specific to existential origination (takwini), and it carries the sense of determination and arrangement. This applies to it generally, as in the verse, and to the legislative (tashri'i) as well, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Allah did not ordain any bahirah﴾. In any case, it indicates the connection of its object with something else, such that there is in it, or for it, or from it, or similar, a connection that permits some adverbial expression to come between them, whether it is a free (laghw) or a fixed (mustaqarr) adverbial, but not in the sense that it is the principal element of the statement, rather a qualifier of it.

[p. 83]

It has been said that the difference between making and creating is that creating carries the sense of determination, while making carries the sense of inclusion, meaning that it is derived from something else as if it were within it. That is why the origination of light and darkness was expressed by "making", to indicate that they do not subsist by themselves, as the Dualists (al-Thanawiyyah) claimed.

It has been objected that the Dualists maintain that light and darkness are two eternal, corporeal bodies that hear and see, the first being the creator of good and the second the creator of evil. Therefore they are not in the true, customary sense, so their corrupt claim is refuted by this alone. Also, the refutation is achieved by their being originated, regardless of what is implied in the concept of making, and had He used "creating" instead, the purpose would have been achieved. Furthermore, the transitive making with a single object, as is the case here, does not require that it be not self-subsistent. Do you not see His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And made for you from the hides of cattle houses﴾ and ﴿And placed between them a barrier﴾, and so on. This has been answered with something that is not free from scrutiny.

He used the plural for "darknesses" and the singular for "light" so that the contrast would be fitting with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾, or for the reason we mentioned in al-Baqarah.

It has also been said that the reason is that "darkness" means misguidance, which is multiple, and "light" means guidance, which is single. The multiplicity and unity are indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the [other] ways, lest they separate you from His way.﴾

Several have chosen to understand "darkness" and "light" here as the two sensible realities, although in the Noble Book they come to mean guidance and misguidance, and this reading has a valid basis here too, because the original principle is to take the word in its literal sense. This is possible, and it is supported by what fits and suits it, as it is apparently demanded by being paired with the heavens and the earth.

It is reported from Qatadah that the intended meaning of the two is Paradise and Hellfire, but its remoteness is not hidden. Among the scholars there is a long discussion and extensive investigation regarding light and darkness, to the extent that they have composed treatises on this matter, and they have left no statement for any speaker to add.

Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned that light is a quality which in itself is a perfection for the transparent insofar as it is transparent, or it is the quality by which seeing does not depend on seeing something else. He also mentioned that some people claim it is small bodies that separate from the luminous source and connect to what is illuminated, and this is false. Firstly, because their being lights is either identical with their being bodies, or it is distinct from it. The first is false, because the concept of luminosity differs from the concept of corporeality, which is why one can conceive of a dark body but cannot conceive of a dark light. If it is said that they are bodies carrying that quality, which separate from the luminous source and connect to what is illuminated, this too is false, because those bodies described by those qualities are either perceptible or not. If the first, then light would not be perceptible. If the second, they would be covering what is beneath them, and it would necessarily follow that the more they gather, the more they cover, but the matter is the opposite. Secondly, because if the ray were a body, its natural motion would be in one direction only, but light falls upon every body in every direction. Thirdly, because if light enters through a window and then we suddenly seal it, those luminous parts either remain or do not. If they remain, either they remain in the house or they leave. If it is said that they left through the window before sealing, that is impossible. If it is said that they ceased to exist, that too is false, for how can it be judged that a body, when it intervened between two bodies, ceased to exist? Therefore they remain in the house, and there is no doubt that their luminosity has departed from them. This is what we say: that the facing of the illuminated is the cause of the coming into being of that quality, and if this is established in some bodies, it is established in all. Fourthly, because when the sun rises above the horizon, the whole face of the earth becomes visible at once, and it is far-fetched that those parts should transfer from the fourth heaven to the face of the earth in that subtle moment, especially since piercing the sphere is impossible according to them.

The opponent argued that the ray is moving, and everything moving is a body, so the ray is a body. (The minor premise is established in three ways.) The first: the ray descends from its source, and what descends is moving by necessity. The second: it moves and travels by the motion of the luminous source. The third: it sometimes is reflected from what it meets to something else, and reflection is motion.

The answer: their saying "the ray descends" is false, otherwise we would see it in the middle of the distance. Rather, the ray arises in the facing receptive substrate at once, and because its arising is from something high, it was imagined that it descends. As for the claim of movement, it is answered that the shadow moves though it is not a body. Therefore the truth is that it is a quality that arises in the facing substrate, and when the facing ceases from it and moves to another receptive substrate, the light vanishes from the first and arises in that other. The same applies to reflection, for the intervening body is a condition for the ray to arise from the luminous source in that body.

Then, those who said it is a quality disagreed. Some claimed it is merely the manifestation of color, and they claimed that absolute manifestation is light, and absolute concealment is darkness, and what lies between the two is shade, whose degrees vary according to degrees of nearness and distance from the two extremes. They elaborated at length in establishing this, to no useful benefit. It is not impossible that light is an existential quality additional to the essence of color, as the following points indicate.

First: the manifestation of color indicates the renewal of a matter. It is either the color itself, or a non-relational attribute, or a relational attribute. The first is false, because it must be either that light is taken as the renewal of color or the renewed color. The first implies that a thing is illuminated only at the moment of its renewal, and the second implies that light is the color itself, so their saying "light is the manifestation of color" would have no meaning. If they make light a positive quality additional to the essence of color and call it "manifestation," the dispute becomes merely verbal. If they claim that this manifestation is the renewal of a relational state, that is false, because light is a non-relational matter and cannot be explained by a relational state.

Second: white may be luminous and bright, and so may black, for light belongs to both. If the luminosity of each were its very essence, it would follow that light would be partly contrary to part of itself, which is impossible, since light is opposed only by darkness.

Third: color can exist without light, as black may be non-luminous, and light can exist without color, like water and crystal when they are in darkness and light falls on them alone, for then their light is seen. That is light and not color. Since each of them exists without the other, there must be a difference between them.

The fourth point: a luminous body sometimes reflects light alone onto other things, and sometimes reflects both light and color. This happens when it is strong in both. If light were the manifestation of color, it would be impossible for light to lend another body a plain sheen (*bareeq sadhaj*). The claim that this sheen is the manifestation of the color of the receiving body faces the objection: why, when the reflecting body's color and light are intense, do they hide the color of the body receiving the reflection, nullify it, and give it their own color, along with other evidence?

The Imam (al-Razi) distinguished between *nur* (light), *daw'* (radiance), *shu'a'* (ray) and *bareeq* (sheen) as follows. When bodies become actually visible and illuminated, that visibility is a stable quality (*kayfiyya*) present in them and spread over them, without its being said that it is black, white, red or yellow. The other is *lam'an* (gleam), which ripples over bodies and conceals their color, as if something were flowing out of them. Each of these two kinds is either from the thing's own essence or from something else. Visibility belonging to a thing from its own essence, as with the sun and fire, is called *daw'*. Visibility belonging to a thing from something else is called *nur*. The ripple belonging to a thing from its own essence, as with the sun, is called *shu'a'*. That which belongs to a thing from something else, as with a mirror, is called *bareeq*.

You have already had the discussion of the distinction between *nur* and *daw'* in Surat al-Baqara, and likewise the discussion of darkness (*zulma*) and its relation to light. The well-known view is that between them there is the opposition of privation and possession (*taqabul al-'adam wa al-malaka*). For this reason darkness is mentioned before light in the noble verse.

[p. 84]

They have stated explicitly that privation precedes possession.

The verification of this, as some verifiers have stated, is that when two things are opposed, one of which is existential only, then if the opposition is considered with respect to a receptive subject for the existential matter, either according to its individual, its species, or its near or remote genus, they are privation (*'adam*) and possession (*malaka*) in the real sense. Or if it is considered with respect to the time in which the attainment is possible, they are privation and possession in the common (*mashhur*) sense. If neither of these is considered, they are negation and affirmation (*salb wa ijab*).

So privation in the common sense for blindness and sight is the absence of the existential thing, such as the capacity to see, together with what arises from the preparing matter for its reception at the time when it is proper for it to be so, as has been verified in the wisdom of the eye and its commentaries. When it is established that every receptive subject for an existential matter, at the beginning of its receptivity and preparedness, is characterized by that privation before the existence of that matter actually occurs, it becomes clear that every possession is preceded by its privation, because the existence of that quality in potentiality precedes its existence in actuality.

Mir Zahid Jan (*al-Mawla Mirzajan*) said: In the opposition of privation and possession, it is necessary that the concept of the privative include that the subject is receptive of the existential. It is not sufficient to relate the receptive subject to the existential without taking into the concept of the privative that the subject is receptive of it. That is why they have explicitly stated that the opposition of privation and existence is the opposition of affirmation and negation.

In *al-Shifa'* [Ibn Sina] said: Blindness is the actual absence of sight together with its potential existence, and this is something that must be included in its common meaning. End of quote. With this, some doubts that have occurred to some reflecting on this matter are dispelled.

It has been said regarding the precedence of the privation of possession over existence: the privation of possession is a specific privation, and absolute privation is included within it, and absolute privation precedes existence in all created beings.

For this reason the Imam said: He mentioned the darknesses before the light because the non-existence of created things precedes their existence, as is found in a hadith narrated by Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "God, exalted is He, created the creation in darkness, then sprinkled upon them of His light; and in another version, then cast upon them of His light. Whoever is struck by His light is guided, and whoever misses it goes astray. For this reason the pen dried up over what is to be."

Upon this, darkness in the report means non-existence, and light means existence. The context of the hadith does not fit this, and the apparent meaning is what has been said: darkness is the absence of guidance and the darkness of nature, and light is guidance. Among the theologians (*mutakallimun*) there is one who claimed that darkness is an accident (*'arad*) opposed to light, and he argued for this from this verse. He did not realize that privation of possession, like blindness, is not pure non-existence such that *ja'l* (making, conferring) cannot relate to it. The verification of this, as has been said, is that *ja'l* here does not mean creation and bringing into existence, but rather the inclusion of one thing in another and making it subsist in it, like the container subsisting in the vessel or the attribute in the qualified. Non-existence belongs to the second kind, so *ja'l* may validly be connected to it even though it is not an existing entity. In *al-Tawali'* it is stated that a renewed non-existence may be by the act of an agent, just as a newly arising existence is. Understand this, and may God Most High guide you.

﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ [6:1]

- The verb *ya'dilun* here may be from *al-'adl* in the sense of *al-'udul* (turning away), or from it in the sense of *al-taswiya* (equalizing). *Al-kufr* may mean *al-shirk* (association, the opposite of faith) or *kufran al-ni'ma* (ingratitude for blessings). The particle *ba'* may be connected to *kafaru* or to *ya'dilun*. In all these possibilities the sentence is either an imperative of disapproval (*insha' al-isti'bad*) or a declarative sentence coming to report the abomination of their state. It is either conjoined to the sentence *al-hamdu lillah* (praise belongs to God), as an imperative or a declarative, or to His word *khalaqa* (He created), which is the relative clause of *alladhi*, or to *al-zulumat*, the object of *ja'ala*. The possibilities thus rise to sixty-four, arising from multiplying sixteen by four: the possibilities of the conjoined sentence being four, namely the possibilities of the sentence it is conjoined to. If other well-known considerations are taken into account, the possibilities reach four thousand and more. But we have no great need for this consideration. What many verifiers have chosen from among these possibilities is that the sentence is conjoined to the sentence of praise, with *al-'adl* meaning *al-'udul*, that is, turning away. The preposition is connected to *kafaru*, and it is from *al-kufr* in the sense of association or ingratitude. A noun is understood after the preposition. The meaning is: God, exalted is He, is worthy of praise for the great blessings He created, which He bestowed upon the elite and the common. Then those who associated others with Him, or who disbelieved His blessings, turn away and so are ungrateful for His blessings. And it may be conjoined to the relative clause, with *al-'adl* meaning equalizing, the preposition connected to it, and *al-kufr* in one of its two meanings.

The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, created these great blessings and mighty creations, which include everything other than Him. Then these disbelievers, or these deniers of the blessings, make others equal to Him, those who have no power over these things and who are in the grip of His disposition and the cradle of His nurture.

*Thumma* (then) is for the disapproval of what those who disbelieved did, or for rebuke on account of it, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. Abu Hayyan took it to indicate mere temporal sequence. Although this is valid here, considering that every extended period admits sequence with respect to its beginning and immediacy with respect to its end, as the grammarians have verified, what was mentioned is more suitable to the context. The subtle reason for placing "their Lord" in the place of the pronoun referring to Him, on the assumption of emphasizing the matter of disapproval, and the reason for connecting the preposition to *ya'dilun* on one possibility and to *kafaru* on the other, is that when it is from *al-'adl* in the sense of equalizing, it requires the preposition *ba'* to be connected to it, unlike when it is from *al-'adl* in the sense of turning away. In that case it is apparent that the preposition is connected to what precedes it. What the verifier al-Taftazani said to me, that there is no specifier for either of the two readings of *bi-rabbihim ya'dilun* in favor of one of the two conjunctions, may be answered: the reason for specifying each reading as it has been specified is the coherence of the verse's arrangement in that case, and the evident strong relevance between what is conjoined with *thumma* of disapproval and what it is conjoined to. For if it is said in the first case, for example, that God, exalted is He, deserved all praises from His servants, it is understood that turning away from Him and turning away from praising Him, glory be to Him, is in the extreme of disapproval. It is therefore fitting to say: "Then those who disbelieved in their Lord turn away from Him, so they do not praise Him and do not even turn a glance toward Him." It is not fitting to say: "They make others equal to Him," since this was not previously mentioned explicitly, and by a stronger inference it negates equalizing. And if it is said for example in the second case: "He made His affair the creation of these great bodies, which none is able to do," it is fitting in disapproval to say: "Then those who disbelieved make others equal to Him, what has no power over anything," not that they do not praise Him and turn away from Him.

Some verifiers said: If the meaning is according to the first reading, that praise and commendation are due to the Benefactor with these comprehensive blessings that encompass all nations, how could the disbelievers and polytheists, who are immersed in the seas of His goodness, turn away from Him? And according to the second reading, known for His power to create these great creations, which include everything other than Him, from the elite and the common, how could these disbelievers, or these deniers of the blessings, make others equal to Him while they are in His grip? So the specification in the first case is that it is not hidden that it is disapproved for a servant to turn away from his master and the patron of his blessings toward someone else, unlike making equal, since the Benefactor may be equaled by another who does good to others. In the second case, that making equal to Him is disapproved is something hardly conceivable, unlike turning away from Him, which may be conceived because the one who turns away may be ignorant of his due. Turning away does not contradict lack of knowledge, whereas making equal does, since one does not make two things equal that one does not know in any way at all. So reflect.

Some have objected to the conjunction with the relative clause, that there is no reason to append what has no bearing on deserving praise to the one who deserves it, and then make the whole a relative clause in a context requiring that the relative clause be praiseworthy. It was answered that the statement, on that assumption, indicates the exaltedness of His station, the generality of His goodness to the deserving and others, since He bestows such glorious blessings upon one who does not praise Him and associates others with Him, may He be exalted. This contains a glorification indicating the perfection of deserving. It may also be said that the placement of this conjoined sentence in the position of the one praised is by way of the glorification derived from denying its content: it is as if it were said, "Praise belongs to God, may His majesty be far above being equaled to anything." But it is not hidden that what is praised must, according to the well-known view, be a beautiful voluntary act, and what was mentioned is not so. Therefore interpretation is necessary.

Shaykh al-Islam (al-Bayḍawi) mentioned in objection to the said conjunction that what is included in the string of the relative clause, which indicates the grounds for His praise, must have some role in that indication in general. There is no doubt that their disbelief is entirely unrelated to this, and claiming that it has a role in it because it indicates perfect generosity is as if it were said: "Praise belongs to God who bestowed such great blessings on one who does not praise Him." This is an affectation the composition does not support and an inversion the context refuses. How not, since the context of the noble text, as the verses make clear, is to rebuke the disbelievers by explaining the extreme of their wrongdoing toward Him, glory be to Him, together with the utmost of His goodness toward them. It is not an explanation of His goodness toward them together with the extreme of their wrongdoing toward Him, mighty and majestic, as the above claim would require. With this it becomes clear that there is no way to make the conjoined sentence among the companions of the sentence it is conjoined to, since the rule for a relative clause is that it should not be intended for its own sake. So what do you suppose about its companions? You have understood that the conjoined sentence is the one for which the speech was brought. End quote.

Page 87 is marked in the original text as "[Page 87]".

It has been objected to this that, on this reading, it is undoubtedly intended as "Praise belongs to God, who has bestowed these great blessings upon those who do not praise Him." There is no artificiality in this, given its eloquence. The claim that there is an inversion (ta'kis, reversal of the intended order) is not accepted, since the context is one of praise, as the sentence opening with it indicates, and what follows is a different statement. A requirement of one context is not abandoned for the sake of another context's requirement, since every context has its own mode of speech.

It has also been objected, from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, that this is not valid, because the clause lacks a connecting pronoun (rabt) linking it to the relative clause (al-sila). The reply is that this is possible only if it comes out in the manner of the expression "Abu Sa'id, I narrated from al-Khudri," where the noun is placed in the position of the pronoun. The sense would then be: "Then those who disbelieved in Him swerve (ya'dilun)." However, this is so rare that it cannot be used as a basis for analogy, and it is not fitting to interpret the Book of God in such a manner when it can be interpreted in the correct and eloquent way.

It was answered that the weakness of this in linking the relative clause does not necessarily entail its weakness in what is coordinated to it, for a great deal is tolerated in the follower (al-tabi') that is not tolerated elsewhere. The statement that this coordination (ataf) does not require a connecting pronoun is strange, because none of the grammarians has said that what is coordinated to a relative clause by "thumma" (then) may be free of a connecting pronoun. The most that they mention is that it is a subtle point (nukta) for linking by means of the noun.

Shaykh al-Islam objected to the possibility that "al-'adl" means "swerving" (al-'udul), with the censure directed at them for not praising Him. He said: their disbelief in Him, Exalted is He, especially considering His lordship (rububiyya), is far more grievous and a greater crime than their swerving from praising Him, Glorified is He. Thus making the lesser of the two evils the principal element of the speech, intended for information, while bringing the greater of them out as a subordinate restrictive phrase (qayd mafrugh minhu), is something that has no standing in sound speech, let alone in the revealed composition (al-nazm al-tanzili).

It was answered that, since the context is one of praise, it was fitting to censure them for that, so the objection of the Shaykh does not arise. He (may God sanctify his secret) mentioned an interpretation of the verse and claimed that it is the one truly worthy of the grandeur of the revelation, and al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) criticised it in this regard. Perhaps the matter is simpler than that.

What the scholars' statements clearly indicate is that the complement (sila) of "ya'dilun," when it is from "al-'adl" in the sense of "swerving," is left unstated so that the denunciation falls on the act itself. They only postulated an object for it when it is from "al-'adl" in the sense of "equating," so they said "other than Him" or "the idols," because it is not fitting to deny "equating" in the absence of its object, unlike denying "swerving."

It has been examined as follows: mere swerving, without consideration of its object, is not objectionable. Do you not see that swerving from falsehood is not objected to? Therefore, the apparent sense is that its object is intended, but it was omitted for the sake of the verse-ending (al-fasila, the rhyming final word). Just as the placing of "bi-rabbihim" (with their Lord) before its verb, on the possibility that it is linked to what comes after it, is for this reason, and it may also be for emphasis (li'l-ihtimam).

Some of the researchers (al-muhaqqiqin) said: although this may appear at first sight to be a valid objection, upon investigation it is not. This is because swerving, although it has two forms, one blameworthy, which is swerving from the truth to falsehood, and one praiseworthy, which is swerving from falsehood to the truth, nevertheless the swerving characteristic of the disbelievers does not admit of the second. Therefore its specification is not in need of postulating an object, and treating it as intransitive (manzilatu al-lazim) is more eloquent upon reflection. This contrasts with "equating," which is among the relations (al-nisab) that cannot be conceived without an object, which is why they postulated one. From this it is known that treating a verb as intransitive, which is common among them, occurs or is appropriate only in what is not of the category of relations.

Ibn al-Duraysi, in Fada'il al-Qur'an, and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others, related from Ka'b who said: The Torah was opened with: ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve in their Lord swerve﴾, and it was concluded with: ﴿Praise belongs to God, who has not taken a son﴾, up to His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿and magnify Him with magnification﴾.

[Page 88 begins mid-passage]

﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence that opens a new statement but continues the thread) brought to explain their denial of resurrection. Although the address may validly be general, here it is specifically directed at ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, as the address that follows indicates. Thus there is a shift of address (*iltifat*, a change from third person to second person). The purpose is to increase the rebuke and reproach. Mentioning their creation in particular, among the other proofs for the truth of resurrection, is significant, even though what precedes is among its clearest proofs, because the proof from the self (*dalil al-anfus*) is closer to the observer than the proof from the horizons (*dalil al-afaq*) mentioned in the preceding verse. The meaning of creating those addressed from clay is that He began by creating them from it, since it is the first material, as it is the origin of Adam, peace be upon him, who is the origin of all humanity. Glorified is He, who did not attribute the creation to Adam, peace be upon him, although he was in reality the one created from it. This suffices for the purpose for which the statement is made, namely to clarify the method of analogy (*minhaj al-qiyas*) and to emphasise the removal of doubt and confusion. It has also been said regarding the justification for their creation from it: man is created from the seed and the menstrual blood, and these two are derived from nourishment that originates from the earth, either directly or indirectly.

Al-Mahdawi said regarding this: every human being is created originally from clay, based on the report: "There is no child born except that some of the dust of its grave is sprinkled upon its sperm." There is something in the heart about this, and the hadith, if authentic, contains some kind of figurative usage (*tajawwuz*). It has also been said that the statement involves an elision of a noun in the genitive construction (*hadhf mudaf*), meaning: He created your fathers. In any case, there is in it, from the clarity of the indication of the perfection of His power, may His majesty be exalted, over resurrection, what is not hidden. For whoever is capable of bringing to life what has never tasted the scent of life at all, is capable of bringing to life what has accompanied it for a period, with even clearer power.

﴿Then He decreed a term﴾, meaning: He determined and wrote, ﴿a term﴾, meaning a specific limit of time for death. The *thumma* (then) denotes sequence in mention, not in time, so that the decree precedes the creation. It has also been said: the apparent meaning is sequence in time. The determination and writing mean that which the angels know and record, as occurred in the hadith of the two *Sahihs*: "Indeed, the creation of one of you is gathered in his mother's belly for forty days as a drop, then he is a clot for a similar period, then he is a lump of flesh for a similar period, then an angel is sent to him, and he breathes the soul into him, and he is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his term, his deeds, and whether he is wretched or happy."

﴿And there is a specified term﴾, meaning a specific limit for resurrection from the graves. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the beginning with it is valid because it is specified by the description, or because it occurs in the position of detail. ﴿With Him﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*), and its indefiniteness (*tanwin*) is for the magnification of its status and the grandeur of its matter. The adverbial phrase has been placed before its predicate, although the common practice with an indefinite noun about which the predicate is stated is that it must be placed after it, in fulfilment of the right of magnification, since what is intended by this is worthy of being placed first. So the meaning is: and a term, that is, a term known solely to Him, glorified and exalted, which no one besides Him can know the time of its arrival, neither in general nor in detail. This differs from the term of death, for it is known in general, based on the manifestation of its signs or on what is customary in human actions.

It has been said: the purpose of informing about this, or of restricting it to being with Him, glorified and exalted, is that it belongs to the five unseen matters that none knows but Allah, exalted is He. The first (term) also, although none knows it before it occurs except Him, as He said: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, yet we know it for those whose deaths we have witnessed and whose birth and death dates we have recorded, so we know it, whether what is meant is the final end of the period or its entirety, when it was and how long its duration was.

Some have gone to the view that the first term is what lies between creation and death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection. This was narrated by al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatadah and al-Dahhak, and was chosen by al-Zajjaj. It was also narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "He decreed a term from his birth to his death, and a specified term with Him from death to resurrection, whose appointed time no one knows but Him, glorified is He. So if the man is righteous and maintains the ties of kinship, Allah, exalted is He, increases for him in the term of life from the term of death to resurrection; and if he is not righteous and does not maintain ties of kinship, Allah, exalted is He, diminishes him from the term of life and adds to the term of death." This is based on His saying: ﴿No one is granted long life nor is his life shortened except that it is in a Book﴾. On this view, the meaning of the term not changing is that its end does not change. It has also been said: the first term is the period in which the people of this world live until they die, and the second term is the term of the Hereafter, which has no end. This is attributed to Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, and was chosen by al-Jubba'i.

It is not hidden how remote it is to apply the term to a period without end. It was reported from Abu Muslim that the first term is the term of those who have passed, and the second is the term of those who remain and those who will come. It has also been said: the first is sleep, and the second is death. This was narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Tabarsi supported it with His saying: ﴿And He sends the other (soul) until a specified term﴾. It is not hidden how remote this is, because although sleep is the brother of death, it is not known that it is called a term, even though it is called death. It has also been said: both terms are for death, and each person has two terms: a term that He writes, which accepts increase and decrease, and this is what is meant by "lifespan" in the report: "Indeed, maintaining ties of kinship increases lifespan," and similar reports. ﴿And a specified term with Him﴾, glorified and exalted, does not accept change, and no one besides Him knows it, may His majesty be exalted. Many people have said that what is meant by the increase mentioned in reports other than the report of increase is increase in blessing and success in obedience. It has also been said that what is meant is the length of life through the continuance of a good reputation, as they say: "The mention of a young man is his second lifespan." Al-Shihab weakened this. It has also been said: the two terms are one, and the sense is: "And this is a specified term," so it is the predicate of an elided subject, and ﴿with Him﴾ is a predicate after a predicate, or is related to ﴿specified﴾. This is the most remote of the views.

﴿Then you doubt﴾.

2

[Note: I have omitted nothing; the last portion below continues on the next page.]

[Page 89 begins]

Meaning: you doubt about resurrection, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Khalid ibn Ma'dan. According to al-Raghib, *miyah* (doubt, *mirya*) is hesitation between two opposites, and the request for evidence is derived from *muraa al-dar'* (milking the udder), when one strokes it to draw out milk. The suitability of its use for doubt lies in the fact that doubt is a cause for extracting knowledge, which is like pure milk from between dung and blood. It has been said: *imtira'* means denial; it has also been said it means disputation. In any case, the meaning is to express amazement at their doubting the occurrence of resurrection and its realisation in itself, while they witness within themselves evidences that completely cut off the basis of this. For whoever is able to bring life and what follows from it into a matter that is not at all prepared for any of that, is clearer in power to bring it into a matter that has prepared for it and accompanied it for a period. From this it becomes known that a portion of those earlier aspects does not suit the course of the noble arrangement, and that directing the amazement at doubting according to the first interpretation is inappropriate, since those addressed are firmly certain that resurrection does not occur, and insist on denying and rejecting it, as many verses indicate. This is to show that their certainty in that is at the highest degree of amazement and disapproval.

Some researchers have mentioned that the first verse is evidence for monotheism (*tawhid*), just as this one is evidence for resurrection. The reasoning is that it indicates that praise and exaltation are not fitting for anything other than Him, mighty and majestic, because He is the Benefactor and there is none other than Him. It necessarily follows that there is no worshipped one and no god besides Him, by way of priority. Some have claimed that it does not indicate this except by considering the argument of mutual exclusion (*burhan al-tamanu'*, the proof by mutual impossibility of rivals), for if one sets that aside, it indicates no more than the existence of the Creator. The source of this is the restriction of the term "evidence" to rational demonstration or to its premises from which its figures are composed, and this is not necessarily so. Some people also made the first verse evidence for resurrection, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it﴾. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

[Page 89 ends]

[p. 90]

His saying, Exalted and Most High, ﴿And He is Allah﴾ is a sentence made up of a subject (mubtada'), which refers back to Him, Exalted is He, as the majority of scholars said, and a predicate (khabar), and it is conjoined to what precedes it. It is brought to show that the rulings of His divinity extend to all created beings, and that His knowledge encompasses the details of the states of the servants and their deeds, which lead to recompense. This follows the allusion, within what has already been mentioned, to the reality of the Return. The predication (haml) is evidently beneficial if what comes after is taken into account. Otherwise it is in the manner of the line: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."

His saying, Exalted and Most High, ﴿in the heavens and in the earth﴾ is, as it has been said, connected to the descriptive meaning contained in the glorious Name, as in your saying, "He is Hatim in Tayy," meaning "the generous one."

The meaning considered here may be the one derived from the root of the noble Name, namely "the One worshipped," or the attributes of perfection for which the Name is well known. However, in this context it is taken in the sense required by the restrictive construction (al-tarkib al-hasri) that defines both ends of the predication, which indicates Oneness and sole possession of divinity. Or it is taken in the sense universally agreed upon, that this Name is applied to Him alone. So it is as if it were said: "And He is the One worshipped in them," or "And He is the Owner, the Disposer and the Governor in them, according to what the will requires, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom," or "And He is the One who is singled out for divinity in them," or "And He is the One who is called Allah in them, to whom nothing is associated in this Name." The meaning of all this is merely the consideration of one of the meanings mentioned within that glorious Name. Such a meaning suffices for the dependence of the prepositional phrase (ta'alluq al-jarr). It does not mean that the word Allah is taken in its linguistic meaning, or in the sense of "Owner," "Disposer," or "Unique," nor that the verb is supposed to be "said."

On every one of these estimations, the objection is averted that the adverbial phrase (zarf) cannot depend on the Name of Allah, Exalted is He, because it is a fixed noun (jumud), nor on "being" (ka'in), because then it would be an adverb of place for Allah, Exalted and Most High, who is transcendent above place and time. Some people permitted its dependence on "being" (ka'in) as a second predicate after a predicate, and the statement would then be in the figure of speech of eloquent comparison (al-tashbih al-baligh), or metonymy (kinaya) according to the view of those who did not require the permissibility of the literal meaning, or a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), in which the state arising from the encompassing of His knowledge, Exalted and Most High, of the heavens and the earth and what is in them is likened to the state of a seer who is established in a place and looks at it and what is in it. The common element between them is the presence of that thing before him.

It has also been permitted that it be a metonymy by a figurative sense (majaz mursal), by using it for a necessary concomitant of its meaning, which is evident. It has also been permitted that it be a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah bil-kinaya), by likening Him, Glorious is His Name, to one who is established in a place and attributing to Him one of its necessary concomitants, namely His knowledge of it, as it were, within it. This is not at all of the forbidden kind of comparison. On this reading, His saying, Exalted and Most High, ﴿He knows your secret and your public﴾ means: what you conceal and what you declare of sayings, or of sayings and deeds together, as an explanation of the intended meaning and a confirmation of what is understood from the statement. Restricting His knowledge, Exalted is He, to what was mentioned, even though it includes all who are in the heavens and their companions, is because the noble text is directed toward describing the state of those addressed. Likewise, it may be considered an explanation if the attribute of perfection for which the glorious Name is known is taken into account, when the prepositional phrase depends on it, as you know. For taking into account His complete ownership and complete disposal, as has been explained, necessarily entails taking into account His all-encompassing knowledge.

On the other estimations, there is no room, as has been said, for making it an explanation, because the knowledge mentioned is not included in the concept of being worshipped, nor in the restriction of the application of the Name to Him, Exalted is He. Likewise, the concept of the one singled out for divinity. So how could this be an explanation of that? Considering knowledge within what the One singled out for divinity applies to does not suffice for it to be explanatory. It has been said, regarding its explanatory function on the estimation of considering the One singled out for divinity: the restriction of divinity to the sense of governing creation, and whoever is alone in governing all the affairs of someone, must know all of them so that governing them is complete for him. Therefore, the consideration of the One singled out for divinity necessarily entails the consideration of His all-encompassing knowledge, Exalted is He, in the manner already established in the consideration of His Name, Glorious is His Name, regarding complete ownership and complete disposal in the aforementioned way.

From this it becomes known that the objection is averted which was raised against the possibility that the preceding prepositional phrase depends on the consideration of the One singled out for divinity, namely that singularity in divinity is a matter having no connection to a place. So there is no sense in making it dependent on a place, let alone on all places. For the governing of creation is among the things connected to what is within the space of the prepositional phrase, and likewise to what is in it. This was answered by objecting to the explanation of divinity in the aforementioned sense. Perhaps the sentence on those estimations is a third predicate. Many scholars have permitted that a sentence be a predicate following a singular predicate, and some have made it so without restriction. The indication of the intended meaning of the adverbial sentence in this case is rational, namely that everyone knows that He, Sanctified and Exalted, is transcendent above what the outward sense of place would require. This is like His saying, Exalted and Most High, ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾, since it was not followed by anything explaining it.

It has also been permitted that it be a new independent statement, which is a grammatical resumption (istinaf nahwi), and many scholars preferred this because it is free of artificiality. Or it is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), for which a hypothetical question must be assumed. It has been said that the sentence is the predicate of "He," and the glorious Name is an appositive (badal) of it, and the adverbial phrase depends on "He knows" (ya'lamu). It suffices for that that the thing known is in what has been mentioned, and it does not require that the knower be in it, lest this entail His being in a place, which is impossible for Him, Exalted and Most High. This, as has been said, is like your saying, "I shot the game in the sacred precinct (haram)," which is true when you are outside it while the game is inside it.

Some verifying scholars (al-mudaqqiqin) quoted from the Imam al-Tamartashi in "al-Iman" that when an adverbial phrase is mentioned after a verb that has a doer, as when you say, "If you struck in the house or in the mosque," if both the doer and the object are in it, the matter is clear. If the doer is in it but not the object, or vice versa, then if the verb is one whose effect appears on the object, such as striking, killing or wounding, what is considered is that the object is in it. If it is one whose effect does not appear on the object, such as insulting, what is considered is that the doer is in it. For this reason some jurists said: if you insult him in the mosque, or shoot at him, then such-and-such applies. The condition for the oath being broken is that the doer is in it. But if he says, "If you strike him in the mosque, or wound him, or kill him, or shoot him, then such-and-such," the condition is that the object is in it. A distinction was made between the two verbs of shooting: the one that takes "to" (ila) and the one that takes the object directly.
