The former is the sending of an arrow from a bow with intention, which has no visible effect on the locus and does not depend on the arrival of the doer's act. The latter is the sending of an arrow or something similar in such a way that it reaches the target and affects it. For this reason each of them is classed in a separate category. On this basis, what we are dealing with becomes problematic, because knowledge has no visible effect on the known. It would then be necessary that the statement be of the kind "If you insult him in the mosque," and that would lead to an impossibility. But if knowledge here is a metaphor for recompense, and recompense is something whose effect appears on the object, then the statement is of the kind "If you strike him in the mosque," and it suffices that the object be in it without the doer. There is in this a matter of reversal. Moreover, that the object here, namely the secret and the public of those addressed, be in the heavens has no basis.

[p. 91]

The claim that the meaning in that case is "He knows your souls that have departed, which are in the heavens, and your souls that are attached to your bodies, which are on the earth," is a forced interpretation and a departure from the outward sense. Furthermore, the address would then be to the believers, whereas previously it was to the disbelievers, so the connection and coherence are lost. Similar to this is the claim of generalizing the address so that it includes the angels. And it is evident that their secret and their public are in the heavens.

It has been answered that it is possible that the placing of the secret and the public of those addressed within them is to widen the scope and to depict that He, Exalted and Most High, is not absent from His knowledge of anything in any place whatsoever, not that they are also in the heavens. It has been said that what is meant by the secret is what was hidden from them of the wonders of the kingdom and the mysteries of the dominion, which they have not perceived, and by the public what appeared to them of the heavens and the earth. The attribution of the secret and the public to the pronoun of those addressed is metaphorical. This is not a satisfactory answer, as is not hidden.

Some have permitted that the prepositional phrase depends on the verbal noun (masdar) by way of contention (tanazu'), and this was objected to on the grounds that the complement of a verbal noun may not precede it, and that contention would also entail the contention with the complement preceding. It was answered that some permit contention even with the complement preceding, and others say that it is permissible for the adverb to precede the verbal noun because they allow more latitude with it than with other things. It is reported from Ibn Hisham that he said: the preceding of the complement of a verbal noun is prohibited only when it is considered as a verb with a verbal particle, and this case is not like that, so it is not among what they prohibited. Our master Sadr al-Din said: the dependence of the prepositional phrase on a later verbal noun is refuted by its dependence on "god" (ilah) in His saying, Exalted and Most High, ﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god﴾, although "ilah" is a verbal noun, and many have explicitly stated its dependence on it. If it is interpreted as an adjective, like "the one worshipped," then let "secret" and "public" be interpreted as "hidden" and "apparent."

From Abu Ali al-Farisi it is reported that he made "He" (huwa) a pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and "Allah" a subject whose predicate is what follows, and the whole sentence is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter, meaning: the matter and the affair is that, ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾.

3

That is, what you do to bring about benefit or to repel harm, of the deeds acquired by the hearts and the limbs, secretly and openly. The specifying of this by mention, although it is included in what preceded on the estimation of generalizing the secret and the public, is to show the complete concern for it, because it is the axis of the wheel of recompense. This is the secret in the repetition of "He knows." Some people distinguished between the two conjoined clauses by making knowledge here an expression for its recompense, and leaving it in its meaning that is understood from what preceded. The interpretation of the acquired (al-muktasab) as the recompense of deeds, the rewards and punishments, is not evident. Likewise, interpreting the secret and the public as what has occurred, and the acquired as what has not yet occurred.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 4:**

﴿And never does a sign come to them from the signs of their Lord﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins without grammatical connection to what precedes it), brought to explain their disbelief in the signs of God, Exalted is He, and their complete turning away from them. This follows the explanation of their disbelief in God, Exalted is He, their turning away from some of the signs of Oneness (tawhid), their doubt concerning the Resurrection, and their turning away from some of its proofs. Turning away from addressing them indicates that their earlier aversion has reached a point that demands they not be addressed with speech at all, but rather be passed over entirely. Enumerating their transgressions against others serves as blame for them and as a denunciation of their condition.

So (ma) is a negation particle, and the present-tense form is used to narrate a past state, as the scholar al-Bayḍawi indicated, and how excellent is his expression, or to indicate continuous, renewed persistence. The first (min) is an extra particle used for comprehensiveness (istighraq) or for emphasizing it. The second (min) is partitive (tab'id), and it is connected to a omitted genitive or nominative element that functions as a qualifier of "sign." Ibn al-Ḥajib took it to be explanatory (tabyin), because if it were partitive, it would contradict the first (min) being comprehensive, since a sign that encompasses all is not a part of the signs. It has been answered that the comprehensiveness here applies to a sign characterized by coming, so although it is comprehensive, it is a part of all the signs. However, his statement afterwards is not free from scrutiny.

The attribution of the signs to the Lord, who is attributed to their pronoun, serves to magnify their status, which in turn implies the enormity of what they have dared to do against them.

Page 92

What is meant by them is either the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyya) or the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyya), which include miracles and other wonders of created things. According to the first meaning, "coming" means descending. According to the second, it means appearing, as has been said. It is understood from the words of some researchers that it is in all cases used in the sense of appearing, employing it for its necessary implication, which is arrival, a meaning that applies only to bodies, metaphorically and not as a metonymy, as has been said.

The sum of the meaning according to the first view is: no sign from the Qur'anic signs of great significance descends to them, among which are those verses that speak of the marvels of God's wondrous creation, Exalted is His majesty, which indicate that the rules of His divinity apply to all existing things and that His knowledge encompasses all the states and deeds of the servants, which would necessitate that they turn to them and believe in them, **except that they are turning away from them**.

﴿Except that they were turning away from them﴾

4

That is: not attending to them and not paying heed to them. According to the second view: no sign appears to them from the created signs, among which are the sublime matters of His glorious affairs, Glorified and Exalted is He, which testify to His Oneness, Mighty and Majestic is He, **except that they were leaving off proper reflection upon them**, which would lead to belief in their Creator. The origin of i'rad (turning away) is turning the face away from some perceptible thing. Its use for disregarding or abandoning reflection is a metaphor, as some researchers have established. Shaykh al-Islam interpreted turning away, in the first sense, as being in the manner of denial and mockery. And ('an) is connected to mu'ridin (turning away). The fronting (of the preposition) is for preserving the rhyme (fawasil).

The clause after "except" is, as al-Karkhi said, in the accusative position, as a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the object of "comes" or from its subject qualified by the description, as has been said, and it contains a pronoun referring to each of them. Its preference over "they turned away from them," as occurred in a similar form in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And if they see any sign, they turn away from it﴾ (7:146), serves to indicate their continuous persistence in turning away, in accordance with the continuous arrival of the signs.

In the statement there is an indication of the extent of their immersion in misguidance, since it informs that their turning away from the signs that come to them is, as the word *lamma* in His saying, Exalted is He, makes clear, that the coming (of the signs)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 5:

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them﴾. The truth here is a reference to the Qur'an, which they turned away from when they turned away from each and every one of its verses. He expressed it this way to show the full monstrousness of what they did to it. The fa' (the particle "fa", "so") is, on the assumption that the "verses" meant are the revealed verses (al-ayat al-tanziliyya), as is most apparent according to what our master Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) established, for the sake of ordering what follows upon what precedes. This is not on the basis that the denial is different from the turning away in reality, such that it follows it or results from it. Rather, it is on the basis that the denial specifies the turning away in reality, and the ordering follows the conceptual difference, since the concept of denying the truth is more heinous than the aforementioned turning away, as it is something whose occurrence from anyone is unimaginable.

For this reason, it is presented in the form of a clear necessary consequence of absurdity, and it is ordered upon it by the fa' to show the utmost extent of its absurdity. Then this was qualified by it being without reflection, rather at the moment of coming, to emphasize the heinousness of their abominable act. On the assumption that the verses meant are the cosmic verses (al-ayat al-takwiniyya), the fa' enters upon the answer of a deleted conditional clause. The meaning on the first reading is: since they turned away from those verses at the time of their coming, they have denied what no sane person could possibly deny at all, without reflecting on its state and outcome and considering what it contains of the evidences that necessitate its verification. On the second reading: if they were turning away from the verses at the time of their coming, there is no wonder in that, for they have done something far greater than them, which is even greater than turning away, in that they denied the truth, which is the greatest of the verses.

Abu Hayyan (in al-Bahr al-Muhit) chose that the fa' is causal (sababiyya), and what follows it is caused by what precedes it. It was also permitted that it be causal in the sense that what follows it is the cause of what precedes it. Al-Radi said: "The causal fa' may sometimes have the meaning of the causal lam, and that is when what follows it is the cause of what precedes it, such as the Exalted's saying: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾." Many then called it the fa' of causation (al-fa' al-ta'liliyya). Does it then indicate sequence (tartib) or not? Al-Radi did not state anything about that. The words of some indicate that it is also for sequence and succession (ta'aqqub).

[p. 93]

It was objected that the cause is prior to the effect and does not follow it. The author of al-Tawdih (Sadr al-Shari'a) strained to justify this by saying that what comes after the fa' is a cause with regard to an effect, and its entry by the fa' is with regard to its being an effect, not with regard to its being a cause. This was refuted by saying that this does not hold in every context. In al-Talwih, the closer view is what the scholars mentioned: that it enters upon causes only in consideration of their continuity, so that it lags behind the beginning of the judgment. In Sharh al-Miftah by al-Sharif (al-Jurjani), he said: "If you say: how is it conceivable that the cause is ordered upon the effect? I say: insofar as mentioning the effect requires mentioning the cause." End of quote. On this basis, the ordering appears here in an unrestricted way. But the apparent meaning of the words of the grammarians and others is that this fa' is specific to occurring after an imperative, such as: "Honour Zayd, for he is your father," and "Worship God, for worship is the truth," and so on. Therefore, the first aspect is preferable. The fa' is not an explanatory fa' (fa' fasiha), as some have imagined from the statement of the Allama al-Baydawi in explaining the meaning of the verse: "As if it was said: since they were turning away from all the verses, they denied the Qur'an." This is because the explanatory fa' is not assumed as the answer of "lamma" (when), since its past answer does not take the fa' in the eloquent usage. So how could a meaning that requires its absence be assumed for the fa'? Rather, al-Baydawi's purpose is only to state the resulting meaning, and for this reason he dropped the fa'. Yes, it has been said: this meaning is something that the revelation should be exalted above, but there is room for reflection in this.

Some verifiers have stated that the matter of ordering applies in the verse whether the word "ayah" means proof, miracle, or the Qur'anic verse, because the turning away and the denial are different in it. As for the fa' in the Exalted's saying: ﴿So they will soon receive the news of what they used to mock﴾, it is also for ordering, based on the fact that what preceded, being a great matter, requires the threat to be ordered upon it. It has been said: (yastahzi'un, "they mock") is an announcement that what preceded was accompanied by mockery.

Abu Hayyan used it as evidence that there is a deleted conjoined element in the speech, meaning: "so they denied the truth and mocked it." It is not hidden that this is something for which there is no necessity. The "ma" (what) is a reference to the aforementioned truth, and it was expressed this way to amplify its matter by its vagueness, and to give the reason for the judgment by what is in the relative clause. Al-anba' (the news) is the plural of naba', which is the report whose impact is great. What is meant by the news of the Qur'an that comes to them, whose meaning is realised among them and whose threats' signs become manifest to them, is its informing them of what will happen to them in this world, such as killing, captivity, expulsion, and similar immediate punishments. It has also been said: what is meant is what includes that and the punishments that will befall them in the Hereafter, such as the fire and the like. It has also been said: what is meant by the "news" is what contains the punishments of the Hereafter, or the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. The apparent meaning of the verses that follow favours the first.

Some verifiers have stated that the construction of "anba'" (news) is explanatory (idafa bayaniyya), and this is an acceptable possibility. The claim that it is an interpolation, and that the meaning is "there will become manifest to them what they mocked of the threat contained in it, or of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), or the like," has no basis, since there is no reason for its interpolation. In al-Bahr: the denial was restricted to "the truth" here, and the deferment was with "sawfa" (soon). In al-Shu'ara' (verse 6), it is: "So they have denied, so there will come to them," without restricting the denial and without the deferment by the sin (sin, the particle of near future). This is because al-An'am was revealed before al-Shu'ara', so the wording was fully stated in it, and it was omitted from al-Shu'ara', though it is intended, by referring to the first. The omission was suited to brevity in the deferment particle, so the sin was used.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 6:

﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that resumes the discourse) brought to specify what is meant by what preceded. It was also said that it begins a rebuke of them by offering them sincere counsel, but the first view is more apparent. The seeing (ru'ya) is cognitive ('irfaniyya, knowing by recognition), and it was said to be visual (basariyya), meaning in their travels, but this is not valid. On both views, it requires a single object. The word "kam" (how many), whether interrogative or declarative (khabariyya), is suspending the verb from acting on it (mu'allaqa 'an al-'amal), indicating multiplicity, and it together with what follows it in its clause takes the place of the verb's object. It is in the accusative governed by "ahlakna" (We destroyed) as its object. It refers to persons.

[Page 94]

It was said that the seeing is knowledge ('ilmiyya), requiring two objects, and the clause serves in place of both. "Min qarn" (from a generation) is a specifier (tamyiz) of "kam," on the basis that it refers to the people of an era of eras, called so because they are joined (iqtiran) for a period of time, so it is from "qaranta" (you joined). The length of that period has been disputed. It was said: a hundred and twenty years; it was said: a hundred; it was said: eighty; it was said: seventy; it was said: years; it was said: thirty; it was said: twenty; it was said: the average length of life among the people of each era. Since this has no fixed measure that defines it, al-Zajjaj said: it refers to the people of an era in which there is a prophet or someone outstanding in knowledge, according to the customary practice of God Most High. It may be taken as a hundred years, because it has been reported that God Most High appoints for this community, at the head of every hundred years, one who renews for it the affairs of its religion.

It was also said: it is a term for a span of time, on which opinions differ in the same manner as previously mentioned. Some have chosen that it is literal both for the specified time and for its people. What is meant here is the people, without the burden of positing an elided noun or resorting to metaphorical extension.

Some have permitted that "kam" be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) governed by "ahlakna," in the sense of "destruction" (ihlak), or as an adverb of time in the sense of "periods," but this is far-fetched. The first "min" is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya), connected to "ahlakna." The interrogative hamza is for denial, to affirm the seeing. The meaning is: Did these deniers, who mock, not know, through observing the remnants and the widespread reports, how many nations We destroyed before their creation or before their time, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot, and their like? The speech therefore involves an elided noun, with the noun's modifier put in its place.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We established them on the earth﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: what was their condition? Abu al-Baqa said that it occupies a position in the genitive as a qualifier of "qarn," because clauses following indefinite nouns are qualifiers, since they need specification. The pronoun is plural in view of the meaning of "qarn." Mawlana Shaykh al-Islam criticized this, saying that its magnifying tanwin (tanwin al-tafkhim) makes qualification unnecessary, and furthermore, that with its implication that its content and the content of the four clauses conjoined to it are taken for granted and not intended by the context of the discourse, this leads to a disruption of the noble composition. How could it not, since the meaning then would be: Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, described as being such and such, and [did they not see] Our destruction of them for their sins, and that it was clearly corrupt? End of quotation. It is not hidden that the magnifying tanwin does not preclude description, and indefinite nouns in which this occurs are more than can be counted. As for what he mentioned afterwards, al-Shihab said that it is an oversight on his part or inattention to their commentary, with their words: "So We destroyed them," etc., to be mentioned later: "That did not avail them anything."

Establishing a thing on the earth, as it has been said, means making it firmly settled in it, and since that requires making the earth its place of settlement, both usages have been rejected. It was said at one time: "He established him in the earth," and from this is His saying: ﴿We had established them in that wherein We have not established you﴾. At another time: "He established for him in the earth," and from this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, until each of the two has been treated as the other. From this also is His saying: ﴿what We have not established for you﴾, after what preceded it, as if it were said in the first case: "We established for them," and in the second: "What We have not established you."

In al-Taj: "If you say makkantuhu and makkanta lahu, it is like nasahtahu and nasahta lahu." Abu Ali said: the lam is superfluous, like "radifa lakum" (it followed you). The discourse of al-Raghib in his Mufradat supports this. Some researchers mentioned that "makkanahu" is more eloquent than "makkana lahu." For this reason, the former was assigned to the earlier peoples and the latter to the later peoples. The "ma" is either a relative pronoun qualifying an elided noun, whose implied meaning is the establishment that We grant to you, or an indefinite noun described by a qualifier, meaning an establishment that We did not grant to it. On both, it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and the returning pronoun in the relative clause or qualifier is elided. It was said that it is a direct object (maf'ul bihi), because what is meant by establishment is granting, as is indicated by what has been reported from Qatada, meaning: We gave them what they used to establish themselves with, of kinds of disposal, what We did not give you. It was said that it is a verbal noun of time (masdariyya zarfiyya), meaning the period of your not being established, but its remoteness is not hidden.

The address is to the disbelievers. It was said: to all people. It was said: to the believers, but the first is apparent. The shift (iltifat, change of grammatical person) is because, in addressing them directly with their weak condition, there is a rebuke that is not hidden. It was said: it is so that the referent of the two pronouns becomes clear and is not confused from the start. This is a point about iltifat that the experts in rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) did not take notice of.

﴿And We sent down the sky﴾, meaning the rain, as reported from Harun al-Taymi, and it is also attributed to Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. It was said: the clouds, and using it in this sense is a sent metaphor (majaz mursal). It was said: it is literal, in the sense of canopy, and the metaphor is in attributing the sending to it, because what is sent is the water of rain and it is its source. In this there is hyperbole that is not hidden. Sending (irsal) and sending down (inzal), as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), are close in meaning, because its derivation is from "risl," the milk that comes down from the udder in succession. ﴿upon them in abundance﴾, meaning copious, pouring down much. It is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha) that is used equally for masculine and feminine. It is a circumstantial state (hal) of "the sky," and the adverbial phrase is connected to "We sent."

﴿And We made the rivers﴾, meaning We made them flow from beneath them, that is, from beneath their dwellings. What is meant is that they lived in plenty and abundance, among rivers and fruits. The clause is in the position of the second object of "We made." He did not say: "We caused the rivers to flow," as He said: "We sent down the sky," to indicate that it is subjugated and continually flowing, not because a river cannot be other than flowing, so that the speech would be useless. Since the arrangement then looks to it being from beneath them, the benefit is evident. Had what was mentioned been correct, it would not have occurred in the noble composition as in His saying: ﴿flowing beneath them rivers﴾. He inclined to the view that "ja'l" (making) means creating and originating, which is specific to Him, exalted is He, and for this reason He changed the style. On this view, the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state of the object. What is meant, as has been said, by enumerating those great blessings poured upon them after mentioning their establishment, is not to show the greatness of their offense in denying them and their deserving of the most severe punishments, but to show their possession of all the means of attaining their aims and the foundations of security from hardships and perils, and that this did not avail them anything. The statement that this did not avail them is what most exegetes indicate.

[Page 95]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We destroyed them for their sins﴾. The "fa" is for sequence (ta'qib). It was said: it is a "fasiha" (a "fa" that expresses a condition implied by what precedes), and the meaning is: "So they disbelieved, and We destroyed them," but the first has been preferred. The "ba'" is causal, meaning: We destroyed every generation of those generations by reason of the sins that pertain to them, such as denying the messengers, peace be upon them. "Anshana" (We brought into being) means We originated. ﴿after them﴾, meaning after their destruction through that cause, ﴿another generation﴾.

6

- as a substitute for those who were destroyed. This is an explanation, because God Most High is not too great for Him to destroy a generation and leave His lands empty of them, for He, majestic is His majesty, is able to bring into being in their place others to populate the lands through them. It is therefore like a completion of what precedes, similar to His saying: ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾. In it is an indication that they were uprooted from their origin, and none of their offspring remained, since He made others and they came after them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 7:**

﴿Had We sent down to you a written scripture on paper﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence that begins a new point), introduced by way of shifting the mode of address (*talwin al-khitab*, moving between second and third person) to show how stubborn they were in obstinacy (*mukabara*) and the false statements that follow from it, after the description of their condition in other respects.

It is reported from al-Kalbi and others that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya and Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, when they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, we will not believe you until you bring us a book from Allah, the Exalted, and with it four angels who testify that it is from Allah, the Exalted, and that you are His messenger."

"Kitab" (the written scripture) and the prepositional phrase after it are connected to an omitted element that functions as an adjective for it, or the phrase is connected to it directly. It has been said that if "kitab" is treated as a noun, like *imam*, then the prepositional phrase is in the position of an adjective to it. If it is treated as a verbal noun (*masdar*) meaning "the written," then the phrase is connected to it.

Page 96

It is also permitted that the phrase be connected to "nazzalna" (We sent down), and there is discussion of this after. "Al-qirtas" (paper), with a kasra or a damma on the qaf, both of which are read, is an arabicized form (*mu'arrab*) of *kurrasa* (notebook), as has been said. Among those who explicitly stated that it is not Arabic is al-Jawaliqi. It has also been said that it is a homonym (*mushtarak*) meaning "paper," and it is reported from Qatada that it means "the page." In the Qamus it is stated: "al-qirtas" has a qaf that may take three vowels, as in *ja'far* and *dirham*, and it means "kaghad" (paper). Al-Shihab said: it is specific to what is written, or it is more general than that and includes other things.

0 – ﴿So they touched it﴾, i.e., the scripture or the paper. "Al-lams," as al-Jawhari said, is touching with the hand. Allah's words ﴿with their hands﴾ are for added specification and to remove the possibility of the metaphorical usage found in His words ﴿and we have touched the heaven﴾, i.e., we investigated it. It has also been said that it is more general than touching with the hand. Al-Raghib said: *al-mass* is perceiving with the surface of the skin, as is *al-lams*. By restricting it to this, the possibility of metaphor is also removed.

It has been said that it was restricted in this way because the perception of contact involves all the limbs, while the hand has a special property in perception that the other limbs do not have. As for the metaphorical use of touching to mean investigating, this is not removed by it, since there is no distance in that being meant by their own direct investigation. Rather, it is removed because the literal meaning is more suitable to the context. But this is not correct, as is not hidden. It has also been said that the mention of the hands is to indicate that the touching was with both hands, and the benefit of this is not clear. The specification of touching is because sight precedes it where there is no obstacle, and because forgery does not occur in it, so they cannot say, if they abandon obstinacy and stubbornness: ﴿Our eyes have only been dazzled﴾.

It was objected that touching here only removes the possibility that what was seen was imagined, but it does not establish that it came down from the heaven.

It was answered that when visual perception of the descent is supported by tactile perception of the place where it landed, the intellect's immediate judgment of the thing seen is certain, admitting no contradiction. After that, nothing remains except pure obstinacy. Moreover, its occurrence there without anyone touching it is sufficient as a miracle, as is not hidden.

Ibn al-Munir said: the apparent purpose of adding "with their hands" is to confirm the reading as near, i.e., they read it, and it was with their hands, not far from them, as they would not have believed otherwise.

Allah's words ﴿the ones who disbelieved would have said﴾ are the answer to "law" (if), according to the most eloquent view, in which the affirmative answer is joined with the lam. The intended meaning is "they would have said," out of obstinacy and opposition to the truth. He placed the relative pronoun in place of the personal pronoun only to specify their attribute of disbelief, which is in the clause that follows it. As has been said, the disbelief that is not expiated is an appropriate position for it, also in terms of its linguistic meaning. It is also permitted that the intended people are a known group of disbelievers, and then the discussion of "the placing" becomes a placed matter. The "in" (not) in His, the Glorified's, words ﴿this is not﴾, i.e., the scripture, is a negative particle, meaning: this is not ﴿anything but a manifest sorcery﴾.

7

- That is, the evident fact that it is sorcery.

﴿And they say, "Why has no angel been sent down to him?"﴾ The apparent sense is that this is a resumed statement (isti'naf) explaining their rejection of his prophethood, peter-by-peter, in a way that is even more explicit than the first. It has also been said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the response clause of (law) ("if"), and that what is permitted in the later parts is permitted in the earlier ones. It has been objected that this hideous claim is not something that could be expected to issue from them even on the supposition that the Book mentioned was sent down, but is rather one of their established falsehoods and fabricated superstitions, which they use as a pretext whenever their stratagems run out and their excuses fail them. It has been answered that there is no improbability in supposing that this statement would issue from them on the supposition of that sending down, because it is something that throws the stubborn disbeliever into utter bewilderment, so that he does not know what to answer or what to hold on to. The word (lawla) here is for urging (tahdid), and what is meant by it is reproach for not bringing an angel who would be witnessed alongside him, so that, in their assumption, doubt would be removed.

Abu al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited his people to Islam and spoke to them and conveyed to them, as has reached me, and Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaldah, 'Abdah ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, Ibn Abi Khalaf ibn Wahb, and al-'As ibn Wa'il ibn Hisham said to him: 'If only an angel had been made to accompany you, O Muhammad, to speak to the people on your behalf and be seen
[Page 97]
with you.' Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed His saying: ﴿And they say, 'Why has no angel been sent down?'﴾ etc." That is, "Why was an angel not sent down to him, who would accompany him, speak to the people on his behalf, and inform them that he is a messenger from his Lord, exalted is He, to them?" Perhaps this is similar to what Allah, exalted is He, related of them in His saying: ﴿Why has no angel been sent down to him so that he might be a warner along with him?﴾ Since the basis of this proposal rests on two things, the sending down of an angel in his own form and his being made to accompany the Prophet (ﷺ), speaking to the people on his behalf and warning them, it has been answered that this is something that hardly exists, because it combines two contraries: sending down an angel in his own form requires that he not be made a speaker and a warner, and making him a speaker and a warner requires that he not be sent down in his own form. The first has been indicated by His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down an angel,﴾ in his true form, so that they witnessed him with their own eyes: ﴿the matter would have been decided,﴾ that is, the matter of their destruction would have been completed through their witnessing him, because of the great terror of the sight, together with their weakness of faculties and lack of fitness.

It has been said that all the prophets, peace be upon them, and they are the ones they are, saw the angel only in human form, and none of them saw him in his own form except the Prophet (ﷺ), who saw him thus twice: once on earth at Jiyad, and once in the heavens. It is not hidden that this requires transmission from authentic reports. What is authentically transmitted in the narration of al-Tirmidhi from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, is that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Jibril, peace be upon him, twice, as mentioned, in his original form. But there is no indication in it that any of his brother prophets other than him, peace be upon him, did not see him thus. This has not been reported, as Ibn Hajar said, and how excellent he is as a memorizer in such matters, from the books of narrations. As for the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing, and likewise the seeing of other prophets besides Jibril, peace be upon him, in the original form, it is permissible without doubt, and the apparent sense of the reports is that it has also occurred for our Prophet, peace be upon him. As for the occurrence of the seeing of all the other prophets, peace be upon them, I have found nothing on it either affirming or denying. And the non-occurrence of Jibril's seeing, even if it were authentic, does not indicate the non-seeing of others, since the forms of the angels are not all like his form, peace be upon him, in greatness. The report of the two disputants and the guests of Abraham, Lot and David, peace be upon them, does not indicate more than that these prophets saw the angels in the form of human beings, and that does not entail that they did not see them except thus. Otherwise it would entail, for example, that the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing of Jibril in the form of Dihyah ibn Khalifah al-Kalbi, may Allah be pleased with him, meant that he (ﷺ) saw them only in human form, and that is contrary to what the reports imply. The first verb in the response is constructed in the active voice, ascribed to the "we" of majesty, though in the question it was passive, to magnify the matter and cultivate awe; and the second is constructed in the passive, to follow the customs of majesty. And the word (thumma) "then" in His saying: ﴿then they would not be reprieved﴾

8

means: they would not be given respite after its being sent down and their witnessing it for the blink of an eye, let alone that they would receive any word from it or remove, by their claim, any doubt through it. It is to draw attention to the great distance between the two matters: the decision of the matter and the absence of reprieve, for the sudden arrival of severity is more severe than severity itself. It has also been said that it is an indication that they would have a respite in which they could reflect.

It has been objected that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then they would not be reprieved﴾ is coordinated with His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ("would have been decided"), and that there is no respite for reflection after the decision of the matter.

It has been said, regarding the cause of their destruction on the supposition of the sending down of the angel as they proposed: when they witnessed him, having come down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his original form, that is a sign than which nothing is clearer, and then they did not believe, there would be no escape from their destruction, for the custom of Allah, exalted is He, has run thus concerning those before them who disbelieved after the sending down of what they had proposed. This has been reported from Qatadah. It has also been said that the choice, which is the basis of obligation, is removed upon its descent, because this is a compelling sign. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾, and so their destruction is necessary, lest their existence remain empty of wisdom, since they were created only to be tested by obligation, and that remains with compulsion. In this there is the point that it contradicts the principles of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah), and it can only be made consistent with the principles of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and those are weaker than a spider's web. Even so, it is not free of difficulties, as will not be hidden from one who investigates. Some eminent scholars have mentioned that this aspect contradicts what precedes it, because what precedes indicates the continuation of choice, and that they would not believe if they witnessed the angel having come down, while the indication of this is the negation and removal of choice, and that their faith would be faith of despair.

Ibn al-Munir said: It is not fitting to make the cause of their being swiftly destroyed the clarity of the sign in the descent of the angel, for that may be understood to mean that the signs which obliged them to believe are less clear than the descent of the angel, and the matter is not so. Therefore the correct view, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best, is that the cause of hastening their punishment on the supposition of the descent of the angel and their not believing is that they proposed what the obligation of faith depends upon, since what the obligation depends upon is the miracle insofar as it is a miracle, not a particular miracle. So when they were answered according to their proposal and it did not benefit them, they were then in a state of utter firmness in obstinacy, which is suitable for not being given a respite. Perhaps the view on which we have relied is the better one, and it has been reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. The objection to it, that ﴿they would not be reprieved﴾ indicates their being annihilated (ihlak) and not their destruction (halak) through seeing the angel, is dispelled by what we have pointed to, as is not hidden, and it is not an artificiality for which the words of the Interpreter of the Qur'an should be abandoned. The second has been indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, on the basis that the first pronoun refers to the warner who speaks to the people on his behalf, which is understood from the implication of the speech by means of the context, peace be upon him, and the second pronoun refers to the angel, not to what the first referred to. That is: "And if We had made the warner whose sending down you proposed an angel, We would have made that angel a man," because they could not witness the angel in his original form. The choice of (rajulan) "a man" over (bashaRan) "a human" signifies, as has been said, that the making is by way of representation and not by way of changing the reality, and specifies what the representation is made by. And there is in it an implication, as 'Isam al-Din and others said, that a messenger would not be a woman, and that is agreed upon; the disagreement is only about her prophethood.

The deviation from (And if We had sent him down as an angel) to what is in the sublime arrangement is known in its secret from what preceded in clarifying the intended meaning. It has been said: the deviation is to preserve correspondence (mushakalah) with what follows. Shaykh al-Islam explained why the first pronoun was not made to refer to the angel mentioned before, by reversing the order of the two objects, and saying: "And if We had made him a warner, We would have made him a man," with the intended meaning understood from it as well, namely to establish that the basis for presenting the first making in the context of supposition and assumption, and the basis for its entailing the second, is only the angelhood of the warner, not the warnerhood of the angel. That is because the making by its nature requires that its first object be the subject and its second the predicate, since it has the meaning of "to cause to become," transferred from "became," which enters upon the subject and predicate. There is no doubt that the locus of the benefit and the basis of necessity between the two sides of the conditional sentence is the predicate of the antecedent, not its subject. So since (law) is a counterfactual particle, it is intended to show the negation of the first making because it entails the undesirable outcome, which is the second making. It was necessary to make the basis of entailment in the first a second object without fail. For this reason its counterpart was made likewise in the second making, to display the complete contrariety between them, which necessitates the negation of the consequent. It is not without beauty. And more than one scholar permitted that...

(Page 99)

Regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Had We made him [an angel]﴾ and so on: it is the answer to a second demand. This is because the disbelievers made two demands. The first was that an angel descend to the Messenger of God ﷺ in his original form, so that the people could see him with their own eyes. The second was that an angel descend to the people and be sent to them in place of a human messenger. They used to say, "Why was an angel not sent down to Muhammad ﷺ so that he might be a warner along with him?" They also said, ﴿This is only a human being like you﴾ and ﴿If God had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾. So the first of their statements was answered by His words, exalted is He, ﴿Had We sent down an angel﴾ and so on, and their last statement was answered by what has been mentioned. Thus the pronoun in (ja'alnahu, "We made him") refers to the Messenger who was sent down to the people. It is not hidden that making this an answer to a different demand is not evident from the noble wording, and there is no reason for it at all.

Some scholars took it to be another answer, and made the pronoun refer to the sought-after thing. This was objected to on the grounds that the sought-after thing is also an angel, and there is no sense in our saying, "Had We made the angel an angel," unless it is said that the meaning is: "Had We made his angelhood an angel." This was countered by saying that the sought-after thing is the descending one who accompanies the Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. In that case there is no difficulty in the statement, except that the necessity of making the descending angel a man in order to make him an angel, as is the implication of the second verse, contradicts the necessity of their destruction upon seeing him, as is the implication of the first verse. This is because the second depends on the absence of the first, since its basis is that he descends in his own form and not in the form of a man. Therefore the verse must be an answer to a different demand, not another answer to the first demand, so that no contradiction arises.

It was answered that, on the assumption that it is another answer, it is an answer by way of supposition. The meaning is: "Had We sent him down as they demanded, they would have been destroyed. And if we assume that they are not destroyed, he must still be depicted as a man, because they cannot bear to see him in his true form. Then the sending would be pointless and without benefit." You know that what we have relied upon, which is related from the scholar of the Ummah (Ibn Abbas), is free from such objections. Yes, some learned scholars raised a problem: it is established among the logicians (ahl al-mizan) that the truth of the converse follows from the truth of the original proposition. On this basis, the falsity of the consequent entails the falsity of the antecedent. Here, the converse of the true proposition, "Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man," is not true, since "Had We made him a man, We would have made him an angel" is not so. There is no doubt about its non-realization, for God has made him a man and has not made him an angel. The answer is that what the logicians stated is a technical convention, and it is not necessary that the rule of the logicians agree with the rule of the language speakers. This is not accepted, for it has been established that that rule does not contradict the rule of the language, and that it is something on which there is no disagreement.

This was answered after the introduction of a preliminary point, namely that the conditional (law) has two usages. The linguistic usage, in which it indicates the absence of the second because of the absence of the first, as in "Had you come to me, I would have honored you." The meaning of such a proposition is the report that something did not come about because another thing did not come about. The conventional usage, which the logicians have adopted among themselves. They made it one of the particles of connection, either necessary (lazimi) or coincidental (ittifaqi). The truth of the proposition in which it occurs consists in the correspondence of the judgment of necessity with reality, and its falsity in the lack of that correspondence. They judge it to be false if there is no necessary connection between the two parts, even when both parts are realized. The linguists have also used it in this sense, either by homonymy or by metaphor, as one says, "Had Zayd been in the town, someone would have seen him." And in some reports: "Had al-Khidr been alive, he would have visited me." It is clear that the aim is to infer absence from absence, not to indicate that the absence of the second is the cause of the absence of the first. They have also counted among this usage, "Had there been in them [heaven and earth] gods other than God, they would have been corrupted."

These two usages were confused for Ibn al-Hajib, to the extent that he said what he said. He held that the statement of the objector, "the converse of the true proposition..." etc., if it means that the true proposition is the one taken according to the first usage, then we do not grant that its converse is what was mentioned. For the converse of "Had you come to me, I would have honored you" is not "Had I honored you, you would have come to me." This would only be so if the judgment in this usage were a connection between the condition and the consequent. But that is not the case. Rather, the proposition is the consequent clause, and the condition is a qualifier of it, as al-Sakkaki explicitly stated. Furthermore, some of the imams of tafsir said that the meaning of the verse, ﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him [appear] in the form of a man﴾, and that the aim is to show the collapse of their purpose in their saying, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?" That is, the descent of an angel would not benefit them, because they, being what they are, cannot see an angel in the form he actually has, unless He makes him appear in the form of a human being at some stage of descent, so that a certain affinity arises between them and him, and they then see him. In that case the verse is far from being examined for the converse of its proposition, or for how it fares in truth and falsehood. For it was not put forward to show the necessity of the second making from the first making, so that absence might be inferred from absence or presence from presence. Thus the relation of this inquiry to the verse is like the relation of fish to the fishmonger. If he means that the true proposition is the one taken according to the conventional logical usage, then it is granted that its converse must be true if the original is true. But we do not grant that its converse is false here on that assumption. For if it is supposed that the necessity of making him a man for the first making holds universally under all suppositions, then the necessity of making him an angel for making him a man holds under some states and suppositions. This is the necessity established in their rules. Moreover, his statement, "God has made him a man and has not made him an angel," is not fitting from one like him, for it is an inference from the absence of the consequent, while the antecedent exists, to the invalidity of the necessity. It is like someone saying: "If we say that if Zayd neighs, he is an animal, the converse does not hold, which may be: If Zayd is an animal, he neighs, since he does not neigh in fact." The source of this is the supposition that the absence of realization of one or both parts contradicts the necessity.

You know that the truth of the necessity does not depend on the realization of both parts, nor on the realization of the antecedent. End. Al-Ala'i (Mawla al-Ala'i) examined this. First, that the proposition is the consequent clause, with the condition being a qualifier of it, is a statement mentioned by some Arabic grammarians and refuted by al-Sayyid al-Sanad, who established the agreement of both groups that the sentence is the whole. In that case, how can the answer be built on that?

Second, the objector did not infer from the absence of the consequent, while the antecedent exists, the invalidity of the necessity, as is not hidden to whoever looks carefully at his expression. The correct formulation is: the most common use of "law" among the grammarians is for two meanings. The first is what the respondent mentioned, namely the absence of the second because of the absence of the first. The second is indicating that the consequent is necessarily existent at all times in the speaker's intention. This occurs when the condition is considered unlikely to necessitate that consequent, and its negation is more suitable and fitting to necessitate that consequent. Then the consequent necessarily continues to exist under the supposition of both the existence and non-existence of the condition, as in the saying: "Excellent is the servant Suhayb; had he not feared God, he would not have disobeyed Him." The researchers have explicitly stated that the verse is either of the first kind, i.e., "Had We made him a companion for you, an angel that they might see, or made the Messenger sent to them an angel, We would have made that angel in the form of a man. But We did not make that angel in the form of a man, because We did not make the companion or the Messenger sent to them an angel." Or it is of the second kind, i.e., "Had We made the Messenger an angel, he would have been in the form of a man. How much more so if he were a human being?" Each of the two does not accept the mentioned converse, and there is no third. So there is no difficulty. Reflect on this. The inquiry, after this, needs an extended discussion, and had we extended it, it would have wearied the readers.

﴿And We would have confused them as they confuse [themselves]﴾

9

Some have taken it to be the answer to an omitted clause, meaning: "And had We made him a man, We would have confused..." etc. The apparent reason for this is the repetition of the lam of the answer, for it requires its independence, and that there is no necessary connection between the sending of an angel and confusing them, since it is not a cause of it, but rather the reverse. It may also be an conjunction to the answer of the mentioned "law," and there is no harm in conjoining the necessary consequence of the answer to it. The point of repeating the lam is that the necessary consequence of a thing has the rank of the thing itself. So it is as if it were a cloak. The word labs (confusion, "wearing") originally means covering with a garment, and it is also applied to preventing the mind from grasping a thing by something that is like a covering for it. It is said: "I labisat al-amr 'ala al-qawm, albisuhu," when I made it ambiguous and problematic for them. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "It is said labistu 'alayhi al-amr," when I mixed it up for him until he did not know its direction. That is, "We would have confused them, by making him appear as a man, [in matters] which they would have confused for themselves at that time, by saying to him, 'You are only a human being and not an angel.' And if he were to prove his angelhood by means of a miracle such as the Qur'an or the like, they would have denied him, just as they denied Muhammad ﷺ." The attribution of the confusion to Him, exalted is He, is either because it occurs by His creation, exalted is He, or because it is a necessary consequence of making him a man.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "We would have confused them, at that time, with what they confuse upon themselves right now, in denying the Prophet ﷺ and attributing his clear signs to magic." The word ma ("what") according to what al-Kashshaf chose for the first view is a relative pronoun. According to the second view, it may be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), which is the more apparent, because the omission of the comparison is consistent in expressions like "I struck the strike of the prince." It may also be a relative pronoun, i.e., "like that which they confuse." The object of "yalbisuna" (they confuse) in both cases is "upon themselves." It is understood from al-Zajjaj's words that it is "upon their weak ones," where he said: "They used to confuse their weak ones about the matter of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, saying, 'This is only a human being like you.' So He, exalted is He, informed that if We had made the one sent to them an angel, We would have shown them him in the form of a man. Then they would be confused about it, just as their weak ones were confused by it."

Ibn Muhaysin read (wa labbasna) with one lam (lam). Al-Zuhri read ﴿wa lalabasna﴾ with shaddah (emphasis). Here, al-Imam al-Razi mentioned, in explaining the wisdom of making the angel, if sent down, in the form of a human being, several points. First, that a kind is more inclined toward its own kind. Second, that humans cannot bear to see an angel. Third, that the angels' acts of obedience are strong, so they would look down on human acts of obedience, and perhaps would not excuse them for committing sins. Fourth, that prophethood is a bounty from God, so He chooses for it whomever He wills among His servants, whether he be an angel or a human being.

It is not hidden that the third point is refuted by this: it is only valid if the reality of the angel supposed to descend is transformed into the reality of a human being. This, besides being a change of realities, contradicts what is understood from the books of the imams of tafsir, that the transformation is formal, not real. Also, the fourth point does not show why it is a wisdom to depict the angel in the form of a human being.

As for al-Ala'i's statement: "Perhaps its wisdom is that the figure who is supposed to be a prophet, since he comprises two aspects, the human in form and the angelic in reality, is not far from being evidence that prophethood is a bounty from God, which He grants to whomever He wills among His servants, whether he be an angel like this figure with respect to his reality, or a human like him with respect to his form." This is among things whose face of acceptability does not shine forth.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 10:

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked﴾: a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he suffers from his people, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Abu Jahl and their like. That is, you are not the first messenger whom his people mocked. How many a messenger of exalted rank was treated thus! The tanwin here is for glorification and multiplicity. The "min" is a beginning particle (min ibtida'iyyah) connected to a omitted element that functions as a qualifier of "rusul" (messengers). The speech is elliptical, with an omitted modifying noun. The opening of the sentence with the oath and the particle of confirmation contains an emphasis that is not hidden. That this consolation is only of this degree has been missed by some scholars, though it is evident. You may also say: the consolation is by this verse and what follows it, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So there befell those who mocked them what they had been mocking at﴾,

because it implies that whoever mocks the messengers is punished. It is as if God, glorified and exalted, promised His messenger (may God's blessings and peace be upon him) the punishment of whoever mocks him, peace be upon him, if they persist in that.

(Ḥāqa) means "encompassed," as narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and preferred by al-Zajjaj. al-Farra' explained it as "the consequence of his affair returned upon him." It was also said: "alighted" (ḥalla), which al-Ṭabarsi preferred. It was also said: "descended" (nazala). This is close to the previous meaning. Its meaning revolves around encompassing and comprehensiveness, and it is hardly used except in a context of harm, as in the verse:

"He trampled the strong horses over the fortress of their homes,
and the striking of a sword encompassed them."

Al-Raghib said: its origin is "ḥaqqa," and one of the two doubled letters was replaced by a weak letter, like "taẓannantu" and "taẓannaytu." Or it is like "dhamma" and "dhāma." The known usage in the language is what al-Zajjaj preferred.

al-Azhari said: Abu Ishaq took (ḥāqa) to mean "encompassed," and it seems he took its root from "al-ḥawq" with a ḍamma, which is what surrounds the glans of the penis with its edges. It may also be pronounced with a fatḥa, as in al-Qamus. One of the meanings of "al-ḥawq" with a fatḥa is considered to be encompassing. Also in the same work: "ḥāqa bihi yaḥīqu ḥayqan, ḥuyūqan, wa ḥayaqānan" (with the letter yā' vowelled with fatḥa) means "encompassed him," like "aḥāqa." Also: "the sword ḥāka"; "the matter ḥāqa them" meaning it adhered to them, became obligatory upon them, and descended. God "aḥāqa their plotting" (made it befall them). The "ḥayq" is what encompasses a person of a hateful thing he has done. Its apparent meaning is that (ḥāqa) is from the yā' root, and this is the view of most lexicographers, which contradicts the apparent sense of al-Azhari's statement that it is from the wāw root.

"Minhum" is connected to "sakhirū" with the resumptive pronoun. It is said: "sakhirū minhu" and "sakhirū bihi," just as "hazi'a minhu" and "hazi'a bihi"; the two are identical in meaning and usage. It was also said: "al-sukhriyyah" and "al-istihza'" have the same meaning, but the first may be transitive with "min" and "bi." In al-Durr al-Masun it is said: one says only "istahza'a bihi," and it is not transitive with "min." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the pronoun refers to the mockers, and in that case the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the subject pronoun in "sakhirū." This was rejected on the grounds that the meaning would then be "so there befell those who mocked, being among the mockers," and this circumstantial clause would have no benefit, since it is understood from "sakhirū." It was answered that this is based on the premise that mocking and scoffing are the same, which is not necessarily so. Perhaps whoever made the pronoun refer to the mockers would take "istihza'" to mean "seeking mockery," so its clarification is valid and there is no repetition in the wording. Al-Raghib says: "al-istihza'" is seeking mockery, though it may be used to express engaging in mockery, just as "al-istijabah" (response) is seeking an answer, though it may take the place of an answer.

It was permitted that the pronoun refers to the nations of the messengers, and this was attributed to al-Ḥawfi. Abu Hayyan rejected it on the grounds that it requires a pronoun referring to something not mentioned. It was answered that it is in effect something mentioned. "Bi-alladhina" is connected to "ḥāqa," and its being placed before its subject, which is "mā" (what), is to hasten to explain that evil reaches them. "Mā" is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah), with the pronoun "bihi" referring to the Messenger who is included among the messengers; or a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with the pronoun referring to it, and the speech is elliptical with an omitted noun, meaning: "so there encompassed them the consequence of their mocking," or "the consequence of that at which they were mocking." It may be said: there is no need to posit an omitted noun, and the speech involves the use of the cause to denote the effect, because what encompasses them is the punishment or the like, not the mocking nor the thing mocked, but this has been placed in its position for emphasis.

It was also said: the intended meaning of "that at which they were mocking" is the punishment with which the messengers used to warn them, so there is no need for the earlier figurative usage or the omission. This was preferred by the Imam al-Wahidi. The objection to this, that there is no indication that the thing mocked is the punishment, and that the context points to the messengers, peace be upon them, being the ones mocked, is answered by saying that mocking the messengers, peace be upon them, necessarily entails mocking what they brought, and what they threatened their people with when it descends; and such a thing, being evident, does not need an indicator.

Some people claimed that "ḥāqa bihim" is a metonymy (kināyah) for their destruction, and that ascribing it to what it is ascribed to is a rational figurative usage (majāz ʿaqlī), of the kind found in: "my right over so-and-so brought me to your city." For it is known from the doctrine of the People of Truth that the one who destroys is none but God, the Exalted, so ascribing it to other than Him is only figurative. You know that "ḥayq" is encompassment, and attributing it to the punishment is, without doubt, literal, and there is no need to interpret it as destruction or to resort to rational figurative usage. Perhaps the intention of those who interpreted it thus was to explain the result of the statement and the sum of its meaning. Indeed,

[Page 103]

if we say that encompassment applies only to bodies and not to meanings, then it is necessary to resort to some figurative extension in the speech when attributing it to the punishment; but not in the manner that this claim mentioned, as is not hidden. As for the plural in "kānū yastahziʾūn" (they were mocking), what has passed many times regarding its like applies. "Bihi" is connected to what follows it. Its placement before its verb is for the sake of observing the verse-endings (fawāṣil).

ِ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of those who denied."﴾

Verse 11

This is an address to the master of those addressed (ﷺ), to warn his people and remind them of the conditions of the earlier nations and what befell them because of their evil deeds, as a caution against what they are upon, insofar as it resembles those deeds. In this there is also a completion of consolation for him (peace be upon him), through the subtle assurance it contains that there will befall them the like of what befell their predecessors. Allah, glorified and exalted, has fulfilled this in a fulfilment clearer than the sun on the Day of Badr. By "observation" is meant reflection (tafakkur), and it has been said: observation by sight; al-Tabarsi combined the two, on the basis of the view that such a combination is permissible. "How" (kayfa) is either the predicate placed before "kana" (was) or a circumstantial term (hal), and the verb is complete (tammah). "Consequence" (al-'aqibah) is the eventual outcome of a thing, and it is a verbal noun like al-'afiyah. The expression "those who denied" rather than "those who mocked" has been said to indicate that the outcome of one who denied, when it is such, then how much more so the outcome of one who combined denial with mockery. It has been objected that the definite article in "al-mukadhdhibin" is for a specific reference, namely those who mocked, so they would be combining both matters; yet mocking what they brought necessarily entails denying it. It is not hidden that the intent of the speaker is that, although those people combined both matters, there is in referring to them by this title here what is not hidden of an indication to the gravity of what befell them. It has also been said that placing "those who denied" in the position of "those who mocked" is to establish that denial is the basis of what befell them, so that the hearers would refrain from it, not from mockery alone, while denial remains in its state, on the assumption that it is the basis in that matter. The command to observe is conjoined to the command to travel by "then" (thumma). It has been said that this is to signal a difference between the two, even though each of the two commands is obligatory, because the first only requires the second, as in your saying: "Perform ablution, then pray." It has also been said that it signals the difference because the first permits travel on the earth for trade and other benefits, and the second enjoins reflection upon the traces of those who perished; and there is no doubt in the great distance between the obligatory and the permissible. It has been objected, as al-Shihab said, that sound taste rejects this, because it introduces an extraneous matter, namely the explanation of the permissibility of travel for trade, between the report about the condition of those who mock and what is appropriate to it and connected to it of the command to take heed from their traces; and this clearly disrupts eloquence. This was answered by the claim that, although this appears at first glance, it does not arise, since it is not extraneous at that point: the intent is their abandonment, leaving them to themselves in turning away from the truth by busying themselves with the affairs of their worldly life, like His saying, exalted is He: "and that they may enjoy themselves" (wa-liyatamatta'u). This is the summary of what has been said: that the speech is a metaphor for abandonment and leaving alone, and that such a matter is extremely displeasing, as when you say to one who has resolved upon a matter leading to great harm, after you have exhausted your advice to him without success: "Leave it to you, do what you wish," for you do not intend by that the actual matter; how could you, since one who commands something wills it, while you are intensely averse and grieved? Rather, it is as if you said to him: since you have refused advice, you are fit to be told: do what you wish. It is not hidden that understanding this from the verse is far-fetched. Al-Zamakhshari distinguished between this verse and his saying in Surah al-Naml: "Say: Travel through the earth and observe," by taking the command to travel here as the permission mentioned just above, and taking the command to travel there as travel for the sake of observation. For this reason the conjunction in that verse is with "fa" (then/so). Some others considered the matter in a way other than what we have indicated. It has also been mentioned that the verification is that He, glorified, said here "then observe" (thumma unzuru), and in other places "fa-unzuru," because the context here requires "thumma" rather than it in those other places. This is because of the preceding saying of His, exalted, in the matter at hand: "Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth," together with His, glorified and exalted, saying: "and We produced after them another generation." The first indicates that the destroyed were many groups, and the second indicates that those brought into being after them are also many; so their command to travel is a call to them to know this, and the intent is thereby the investigation of the lands and the dwellings of the corrupt, despite their multitude, so that they may see the traces in one abode after another. This requires a long time and duration, which prevents the immediacy that "fa" requires; and "thumma" is not so in the other places. End of quotation. And this is not free from disquiet.

Several scholars chose that the travel here is one unified act, but it is an extended matter, so observation is conjoined to it with "fa" at times, considering its end, and with "thumma" at other times, considering its beginning; and this is the case with every extended action.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke and reproach to them: ﴿To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ — of the rational and non-rational beings alike; that is, to whom belong all existents, in creation, ownership and disposal?

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Say: "To Allah."﴾ is an affirmation of the answer on their behalf, or a compelling of them to acknowledge that the whole belongs to Him, glorified and exalted is He. In it there is an indication that the answer has become so evident that no denier can deny it and no repeller can repel it, for the questioner's ordering the answer is only appropriate, as the Imam (al-Razi) said, when the answer is of that kind. It has been said: in it there is also an indication that they were slow to answer, although the answer was fixed, since they were being refuted. Ala' al-Milla (Isam al-Din al-Isfara'ini) mentioned that His saying, glorified and exalted is He: "Say: To whom..." etc. means the command to seek this inquiry and to turn towards attaining it; and His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: "To Allah."﴾ means: when you seek and your reflection leads you to the truth, then acknowledge it and do not deny it. This is guidance to the path of monotheism in actions, after the guidance to monotheism in divinity, namely avoiding the state of the deniers.

In this there is an indication of the connection (of this verse with what precedes), and what will come shortly, God willing, will make clear the excellent reason for it. The prepositional phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "It is for Allah, exalted be His state," or "That belongs to Allah, exalted be His state."

﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ is an independent sentence, falling under the command, proclaiming the all-encompassing scope of His mercy, mighty and majestic is He, for all creatures, following the statement of the all-encompassing scope of His ownership and power, glorified and exalted is He, over everything, which justifies the sending down of punishment upon the deniers. It is brought to declare that He, exalted is He, is compassionate towards the servants, does not hasten punishment upon them, and accepts repentance from them. What preceded and what followed of the rulings of wrath is nothing but from the ill choice of the servants due to their eternal ill preparedness, not from the requirements of His essence, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ The meaning of "He prescribed mercy for Himself" — exalted is His state — is its obligation by way of bounty and benevolence upon His holy essence itself, not through the mediation of anything. It has also been said: it is what al-Shaykhan and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah the Exalted had decreed the creation, He wrote a book which He placed with Him above the Throne: 'Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath.'" And in the narration of Ibn Mardawayh: "Allah the Exalted wrote a book with His hand for Himself before He created the heavens and the earth, and placed it beneath His Throne, in which: 'My mercy precedes My wrath.'" — and other reports. The meaning of the precedence and dominance of mercy in them is that it is more ancient in its attachment to the creatures and more extensive in reaching them, together with its being one of the requirements of the essence which bestows good.

In the Sharh Muslim of Imam al-Nawawi: The scholars said: the wrath of Allah the Exalted and His good pleasure both return to the meaning of will. So His will for reward for the obedient, and benefit for the servant, is called good pleasure and mercy; and His will for the punishment of the disobedient and their abandonment is called wrath. His will, glorified and exalted is He, is an eternal attribute by which He wills. They said: what is meant by precedence and dominance here is the abundance of mercy and its comprehensiveness, as one says: generosity and courage dominated so-and-so when they became abundant in him. End. And it returns to what we have said. The summary of the matter in this is that precedence and dominance are in the attachments, not in the essential attribute itself, for prior precedence of one attribute over another in Him, exalted is He, would imply the origination of what is preceded; likewise abundance and scarcity between two attributes would imply that origination. Mercy may also mean that by which one shows mercy, and in this sense it is characterised by plurality, descent and the like. In accordance with this is explained what Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted, on the day He created the heavens and the earth, created one hundred mercies, each mercy being the extent of what lies between the heavens and the earth. He placed among them one mercy on the earth, by which the mother inclines towards her child, and the beasts and birds are compassionate to one another. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will complete them with this mercy."

And ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr: "Allah the Exalted has one hundred mercies, of which He sent down one mercy to the people of the world, by which the jinn and mankind, the bird of the sky, the fish of the water, the beasts of the earth and its insects, and what is between the air, show mercy to one another; and He stored ninety-nine mercies with Himself. Then, when the Day of Resurrection comes, He will gather the mercy that He had sent down to the people of the world, and join it to what is with Him, and place it in the hearts of the people of Paradise and upon the people of Paradise." And other reports.

The mercy in the verse is intended to encompass both abodes, together with the generality of its objects. As for what is narrated from al-Kalbi, that the meaning is: He made mercy obligatory upon Himself for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), by not punishing them when they deny as He punished those before them from the bygone nations and past generations, but rather delaying them until the Day of Resurrection — this was not intended except to show what suits the occasion among the particulars of that general. In expressing the Essence by "self" there is a refutation of those who claim that the word "self" is not applied to Allah, the Exalted, even if the Essence is meant, except by way of mushakala (figurative correspondence); and the consideration of a presumed mushakala is not evident, as the evident is otherwise.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾ — the answer to the oath is omitted; it occupies, as Abu al-Baqa' said, the place of "kataba" (He prescribed). The sentence is a grammatical resumptive (isti'naf nahwi) brought as a threat upon their polytheism and their heedlessness of reflection. It has been said: it is explanatory (bayani), as if it were said: "And what is that mercy?" So it was said: "He will surely gather you..." etc., for were it not for the fear of the Resurrection and punishment, there would be chaos and disorder, order would cease, and confusion would abound. It was objected to this that what was mentioned appears only if they were acknowledging the resurrection, and they are not — so there is nothing.

Some of the verifiers also said: it is a strained interpretation, and the answer is only directed by considering that the threat entails abstention from prohibitions, which entails mercy. It has been said: the suitability of what is in the verse as an answer is by considering that the meaning is: "He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection, and will not hasten punishment upon you now for your denial," as the al-Kalbi indicated. It has been said: the oath and its answer are in the place of accusative as a substitute for "mercy," a substitution of part. The grammarians have mentioned that a clause may be substituted for a singular noun, though they did not address the types of substitution in this.
