The prepositional phrase is said to be attached to an omitted verb, that is: "He will surely gather you in the graves, raised up, unto a day..." etc., on the basis that resurrection here means sending forth, which is transitive with "ila" (to) and requires no implied verb. It was objected that resurrection occurs toward a place, not toward a time, unless by "the Day of Resurrection" is meant its occurrence in its time. It has been said: it is attached to the mentioned verb, and the meaning is a gathering that contains the sense of driving and compulsion, as if it were said: "He will raise you, drive you, and compel you unto the Day of Resurrection," that is, unto its reckoning. It has been said: it is attached to the verb, and "ila" is in the sense of "fi" (in), as in the saying of the poet:

"Do not leave me with threats, as though I were among the people, smeared with pitch, mangy."

Some denied that "ila" comes in the sense of "fi" in their speech; and even if that were correct, it would be permissible to say "Zayd ila al-Kufa" meaning "in al-Kufa." They interpreted the verse by implying a word such as "mudafan" (added), "mubghadan" (hated), or "makrihan" (disliked). It was answered that this objection applies only if it is said that using "ila" in the sense of "fi" is a regular analogy, and perhaps the one who affirms the usage does not say this; and resorting to implication is contrary to the original, while resorting to the view that "ila" means "fi," even if not regularly, is easier than that. It has been said: it means "li" (for); it has been said: it is superfluous, and the address is to the disbelievers, as is apparent from the context. It has been said: it is general to them and to the believers, after being specific to the disbelievers, meaning: "He will surely gather you, O people, unto the Day of Resurrection."

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ — that is, it is not fitting for anyone to doubt it, because of the clarity of its proofs and the brilliance of its evidences, some of which have preceded. The sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Day," and the pronoun in the genitive refers to it. It is permissible that it be an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, with the pronoun referring to it, meaning: "a gathering with no doubt in it." It was also permitted that it be an emphasis of what precedes it, as they said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾.

﴿Those who have lost themselves﴾ — by squandering their capital, which is the original nature (fitra), sound intellect, the proximate readiness arising from witnessing the Messenger (ﷺ), hearing revelation, and other traces of mercy. As for the position of the relative pronoun, it has been said: it is in the accusative as a dispraise, or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "You are those who..." and it is a detached epithet (na't maqta'). It is not necessary that every detached epithet be valid to follow as an epithet; rather the sense of description suffices for it. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Woe to every backbiter, slanderer﴾ ﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾; how the "alladhi" was detached there despite its invalidity as an epithet of the indefinite noun — so it is not objected that detachment occurs only in an epithet, and the pronoun is described. It has been said: it is a substitute from the pronoun, a substitution of part from whole, with an implied pronoun, or it is a predicate of an omitted subject by way of detachment, also as substitution. Detachment is not restricted to epithets. Perhaps they did not make it accusative by an implied verb, or a predicate of an omitted subject, without need for what was mentioned, because they hold that bare implication does not convey dispraise or praise except with detachment. Al-Akhfash preferred substitution, and Abu al-Baqa' criticised this, saying it is remote, because the pronouns of the speaker and addressee are not substituted from, for their clarity is utmost, while other than them is inferior in that respect. It has been said: it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿so they do not believe﴾.

21

The "fa" (so) indicates that their not believing and their persistence in disbelief is caused by their losing themselves, for the nullification of the intellect through following the senses, illusion, and absorption in imitation led them to persist in disbelief and refrain from faith. In the Kashshaf: If you say, how can their not believing be caused by their loss, when the matter is the reverse? I say: its meaning is: those who lost themselves in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, because they chose disbelief; so they do not believe.

The summary of this is: those whom Allah has judged to be lost because they chose disbelief — so they do not believe. The judgment of loss precedes non-belief, because it is concomitant with knowledge of choosing disbelief, not with its actual occurrence; so the causing of non-belief from this aspect is valid. You know that this question is dissolved by taking the loss in the sense we have mentioned, and this is perhaps better than what is in the Kashshaf, for it contains a certain disquiet. The sentence, as many have said, is a concluding clause (tadhyil) brought from His side, exalted is He, to censure their state, and is not included under the command.

It has been said: on the supposition of a fresh start, the apparent reading is to conjoin the sentence to ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, so the disjunction requires positing a question, as if it were said: "Why then do the disbelievers doubt it?" And it was answered that their losing themselves became a cause of non-belief. It was also permitted, on that supposition, that the sentence be circumstantial, and that, as you see, is far-fetched.

* * *

**صفحة 107**

This is the allusive (ishara) interpretation of the verses. ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾: the "heavens" are the heavens of the world of spirits, and the "earth" is the earth of the world of bodies. It is said that the spirit is the heaven of the heart, because the rain of inspiration (ilham) descends from it, and the heart is its earth, because in it grow the blossoms of wisdom and the light of knowledge. ﴿And made the darknesses﴾: that is, He brought into being, in the world of bodies, the darknesses of the levels, which are the shadowy veils of the Holy Essence (al-Dhat al-Muqaddas). And He brought into being, in the world of spirits, the light of knowledge and perception. It is also said that the darknesses are idle thoughts and false impulses, and the light is inspiration. Some have said: the darknesses are the deeds of the body, and the light is the states of the heart. Then, after all this has become manifest, ﴿those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals [to Him]﴾: they take others as equal to Him, and they associate with Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, one who is equal to Him in existence, while He is God, who has no equal in all His attributes. ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾: this is the clay of the prime matter (al-madda al-hayuliyya, hyle). ﴿Then He decreed a term﴾: that is, a specific limit of time, which when the seeker reaches it on his way to his Lord, glory be to Him and exalted is He, he is annihilated (fana') therein, mighty is His majesty. ﴿And a term specified with Him﴾: this is the subsistence after annihilation (baqa' ba'd al-fana'). It has been said that the first term is that which the readiness (isti'dad) naturally requires, according to the individual essence, and it is called the natural term of the person with regard to his particular temperament and his specific composition, without consideration of any temporal accident. It is indefinite (nukkira) because it belongs to the rulings of the prior decree, which is the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab), and it is universal, free of particularizations, since its locus is the first holy spirit. The second term is the determined temporal term, which occurs when the conditions are gathered and the impediments removed, and it is recorded in the book of the celestial soul, which is the Tablet of Destiny (lawh al-qadar). ﴿Then you﴾, after you have come to know this, ﴿doubt﴾ and are uncertain about His disposal of you as He wills. ﴿And He is God in the heavens and in the earth﴾: that is, His divinity (uluhiyya) is the same with respect to the upper and the lower worlds. ﴿He knows your secret﴾ in the world of spirits, which is the world of the unseen (ghayb), ﴿and your open [deeds]﴾ in the world of bodies, which is the world of witness (shahada). ﴿And He knows what you earn﴾ in both of them, of knowledge, movements, stillnesses and other things, and He will recompense you according to them. It has also been said: the meaning is that He knows the wandering of your spirits in the heaven in search of the mines of joys, and the turning of your forms on the earth in search of the means to witness Him, and He knows what you obtain thereby. ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord﴾, the inner ones (anfusiyya) and the outer ones (afaqiyya), ﴿but they turn away from it﴾, because of their poor choice and the blindness of their eyes to witnessing the radiant lights of God on the pages of existence. They said, because of the weakness of their certainty: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ so that we might see him and our doubt would be removed. ﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾: that is, the matter of their destruction, since they lack the capacity to bear witnessing him. ﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, so that they could witness him. ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾: that is, whatever is in the two worlds. ﴿Say: To God﴾, by bringing into being and by annihilating. ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾.

My master, the Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, said: The mercy of God, exalted is He, is general, and it is the blessing of bounty (ni'mat al-imtinan) which is received without merit. It is the meaning intended in His words, exalted is He: ﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them﴾. To it the word "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) in the basmala alludes, specifically, and it is the obligatory mercy intended by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So I shall prescribe it for those who fear God﴾. To it the word "the Most Compassionate" (al-Rahim) in the basmala alludes. His discourse, may God sanctify his secret, in the Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya) indicates that what is in the verse is the specific mercy, while the context requires that it is the general mercy.

He, may God sanctify his secret, also mentioned, in the course of discussing mercy and the saying of God, mighty is His majesty, on the Day of Resurrection: "The angels have interceded, the prophets have interceded, and the believers have interceded, and there remains the Most Merciful of the merciful," that the mercy of God, exalted is He, has preceded His wrath, as is in the report. So it is in front of the wrath, and the wrath of God, exalted is He, continues to run its course in vengeance upon the servants until it reaches the end of its reach, and then finds that mercy has preceded it, and so it takes hold of the servant who is the object of wrath, and it is spread over him, and the judgment returns to it concerning him. The distance that the wrath traverses is between "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" in the basmala and "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" that comes after "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds." So "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds" is the distance, its beginning and its end being what you have known. That is the very measure of the distance, because in it appear both ease and hardship. For this reason praise, which is thanksgiving, is in it, and it is not restricted to ease or to hardship, so that it encompasses both. The Law says, in praise for ease: "Praise belongs to God, the Bestower, the Bounteous," and it says, in praise for hardship: "Praise belongs to God in every state." So "Praise belongs to God" has come in both ease and hardship, and for this reason it is the very measure of the distance. No one in the Hereafter fails to praise God, exalted is He, and to hope for His mercy and fear His punishment, and to find it sweet. So God, exalted is He, placed after "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds" the "Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Thus the world lies between them, with what it contains of the praiseworthy and the blameworthy. This is similar to what came in the sura "Did We not expand [your breast]" (Alam Nashrah), and it is a wondrous reminder from Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, to His servants, so that hope and longing for the mercy of God, exalted is He, may grow strong in them.

And if you turn even the slightest turn, you will know that there is no trace of the traces of severity except that it is embroidered with the mercy of God, exalted is He. Rather, there is no fortune or misfortune except that it has come forth from the risings of the spheres of the mercy, which pour its heavy showers upon the receptive things according to their receptivities. And among what shows the precedence of mercy is that every existing thing is preceded by the attachment of the will to bringing it into being and bringing it forth from the realm of non-existence, which is the source of every deficiency. There is no doubt that this is a mercy, just as there is no doubt that it precedes. Yes, mercy in some respects divides into two kinds: a pure mercy, which is not mixed with any vengeance, like the bliss of Paradise, and it rises from the constellations of His name, glory be to Him, the Most Compassionate. And because the Prophet (ﷺ) loves for his community to enter Paradise and dislikes for them the Fire, the Real, mighty is His name, called him "Compassionate" in His words, glory be to Him and exalted is He: ﴿He grieves at what distresses you, ardently concerned for you, and to the believers gentle and merciful﴾. And a mercy that may be mixed with vengeance, like disciplining a child with beating out of mercy for him, and like drinking a bitter, unpleasant medicine. This rises from the horizons of His name, mighty is His name, "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman). Perhaps this general mercy is what is intended in His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds﴾. Then know that the precedence of mercy over wrath apparently requires the precedence of the manifestations of beauty over the manifestations of majesty, because mercy belongs to beauty and wrath belongs to majesty.

Our master, Shaykh 'Abd al-Karim al-Jili, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that majesty is prior to beauty. For there has come in a hadith: "Greatness is My waist-wrap and magnificence is My cloak." And nothing is closer to a person than a cloak and a waist-wrap. Then he said: This does not contradict His saying, glory be to Him: "My mercy has preceded My wrath," because the preceding mercy is only on the condition of generality, and generality belongs to majesty. It has been claimed that a single beautiful attribute, when it fulfills its perfection in manifestation or comes close to it, is called majesty, because of the strength of the manifestation of the authority of beauty. Thus the concept of mercy belongs to beauty, but its generality and its reaching its end is majesty. You know that if precedence is explained by the meaning that al-Nawawi transmitted from the scholars earlier, namely abundance and comprehensiveness, then it is something whose realization in mercy is beyond doubt, for in every wrath there is mercy, but in every mercy there is not necessarily wrath, as is not hidden from one who investigates carefully.

In sum, in the mercy of God, glory be to Him, there is an expectation of the utmost hope, so much so that Iblis hopes for it on the Day of Resurrection, as some reports indicate. And the people most favored with it, God willing, are this community. We ask God, exalted is He, to grant us and you the greatest share of it. ﴿He will surely gather you for a Day of Resurrection﴾, the lesser or the greater, ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ in reality, even if those veiled do not perceive it, ﴿those who have lost their souls﴾ by destroying them in the appetites and the transient pleasures, so they have been veiled from the lasting, luminous realities, and have exchanged them for the transient, shadowy sensible things. ﴿So they do not believe﴾ because of this. We ask God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, for pardon and well-being in religion, in this world and in the Hereafter.

﴿And to Him﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to (lillāh, "to Allah"), so it falls under (qul, "say"), as a second argument against the polytheists. Many scholars held this view.

Abū Ḥayyān said: The apparent meaning is that it is a resumed statement (istiʾnāf, a new sentence) and is not included under the command. That is, "and to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, alone."

[Page 109]

﴿whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾: that is, the two specified times. (Mā) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). (Sakana) may come from al-suknā (dwelling, residence), in which case the statement includes both what moves and what is still, without any need for an implied element. Its construction with (fī, "in") with reference to time, although the proper use of (fī) is for place, is due to likening the settledness in time to the settledness in place. It is also permitted that there is a figurative correspondence (mushākala, a stylistic pairing of words) in an implied sense, since the meaning of "to Allah is whatever is in the heavens and the earth" is "whatever dwells and settles in them." The intended meaning is "and to Him belongs whatever they contain."

Or (sakana) may come from al-sukūn (stillness), the opposite of movement, as has been said. In the statement there is an elision (iktifāʾ, omitting one of two opposites), as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾. The full sense is "whatever dwells and moves in them." Stillness is mentioned without its opposite and not vice versa, because stillness is more common in existence, and the end of every moving thing is stillness, as has been said: "When your winds blow, seize them, for every fluttering thing has a stillness." Also, stillness is usually a blessing, since it is rest, whereas movement is not so. This was rebutted: there is no basis for mentioning stillness alone without movement in a context of extension, description and showing the perfection of dominion and control. It was answered that this omitted element is virtually present, being quickly understood from the mention of its opposite. The context calls for mentioning it, and it calls for the generality of changes and affairs occurring in the night and the day. When it is maintained that stillness together with its quickly understood opposite is a metonymy (kināya) for all of that, it suits the context.

It has also been said: "whatever dwells" includes all created beings, since none of them is free from the attribute of stillness, even the moving thing while it appears to be moving. This is based on what has been verified in its proper place, that the differences in movements are by speed and slowness, due to the fewness or abundance of the intervening pauses. The detailed discussion of the meaning of movement and stillness and the explanation of the well-known categories of movement is extensive and should be sought in its proper place.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: that is, the one who is most thorough in hearing every thing heard, so He hears the inner thoughts of everything that dwells in the two dwellings (the night and the day).

31

That is, the one who is most thorough in knowledge of every known thing from the various kinds. The sentence is brought to explain the comprehensiveness of His hearing and knowledge, exalted is He, after explaining the comprehensiveness of His power, majestic is His affair. Or it is a warning concerning their sayings and deeds, and that is why hearing and knowledge are specifically mentioned. It may be that this sentence is part of what is said (in the command to say), and it may be part of what Allah, exalted is He, says.

[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 6, verse 14]

﴿Say﴾ to the polytheists, after rebuking them for what preceded: ﴿Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?﴾ This is a denial of taking other than Allah Most High as a protector, not a denial of taking a protector in general. For this reason the first object was placed first and the interrogative *hamzah* (the question particle *alif*) was given priority. A similar construction is ﴿Do you bid me to worship other than Allah?﴾. The "protector" (*waliyy*) here means the one worshipped, because the verse is a response to those who called on him (ﷺ). It has been said that the people of Makkah said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: "O Muhammad, you have abandoned the religion of your people. We know that nothing has moved you to this except poverty. Return, and we will gather wealth from our possessions for you until you become one of our wealthiest." So this verse was revealed. It has been objected that the polytheist did not single out worship for other than Allah Most High, so the rebuttal would only fit if it were said: "Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?" It is answered that whoever associates another with Allah Most High does not take Allah Most High as an object of worship, because the worship of Him, glory be to Him, cannot be combined with the worship of another, as it has been said:

*"If your friend befriends one whom you oppose, then he has become your enemy, and speech has ended."*

It has also been said that *waliyy* means "helper," as is one of its well-known meanings. From the denial of taking other than Allah Most High as a helper it is understood, *a fortiori*, that one does not take him as an object of worship. According to what has been said, the statement may be of the type that departs from the apparent sense, intending pure sincere counsel so that it is more readily accepted, as in His saying, Most High: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who created me, and to whom you will be returned?﴾

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, its Innovator (*mubdi'uhā*), as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.
[page 110]
Abu Ubaydah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari also transmitted from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I did not know what *Fatir al-Samawat wal-Ard* meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said, '*Ana fatartuhā*' ('I originated it'), meaning '*ana ibtada'tuhā*' ('I began it')."

*Fatir* is a qualifier (*na't*) of the Name of Allah (*al-Jalalah*), emphasising the denial. It is valid for it to be a qualifier of a definite noun, because the participle here has the sense of the past tense, whether the words are God's own speech from the outset or are reported from the Messenger (ﷺ). This is because what matters is the time of the judgment, not the time of the utterance. That the past sense is intended is shown by the fact that al-Zuhri read *fatar* (in the past tense). The separation between them by a whole clause does no harm, because the clause is not foreign to them, since it is itself governed by the governor of the qualified noun. It has also been said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for the noun of majesty, and Abu Hayyan preferred this on the ground that separation is easier in that case. It was also read in the nominative and accusative as a mode of praise, meaning: "He is the Originator," or "I praise the Originator." It is permissible that the accusative be a substitute for *waliyyan* and not a qualifier, because *waliyyan* is definite. Yes, according to al-Zuhri's reading, it is permissible for the clause to be a qualifier of the Name.

﴿While He feeds but is not fed﴾: that is, He provides sustenance and is not provided for, as Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from al-Suddi. Thus the "food" (*al-mat'am*) means sustenance (*al-rizq*) in its lexical sense, which is everything from which one benefits. The evidence for this is that it is contrasted with it in His saying: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they feed Me.﴾ The particular is used to express the general figuratively, because food is its greatest and most abundant form, owing to the great need for it. It is also possible that mention of it has been sufficient in place of mention of the rest, because the negation of everything else is understood from it, so it is literal. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial (*hal*) clause.

It is transmitted from Abu Amr, al-A'mash and Ikrimah that they read *wa-la yat'am* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *'ayn*, meaning *wa-la ya'kul* ("and does not eat"), and the pronoun refers to Allah Most High. Similar is the reading of Ablah with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *'ayn*. Ya'qub read the opposite of the first reading, namely the first verb in the passive and the second in the active, and the pronouns in both verbs then refer to other than Allah Most High, meaning: "Shall I take as a protector one who is himself provided for and does not provide?" Although the speech is addressed to idol-worshippers, it has regard to the generality of "other than Allah Most High," and it gives precedence to rational beings, such as Jesus, peace be upon him. This is because it includes denying that idols are fit for divinity, *a fortiori*. It may be said that the statement is a metonymy for its being created and not a creator, as in His saying, Most High: ﴿They create nothing, while they themselves are created.﴾ The verb is taken in the sense of benefit, that nothing returns benefit at all.

Al-Ashhab read ﴿wa-Huwa yut'imu wa-la yut'amu﴾ with both verbs in the active voice. It has been explained in two ways: either *af'ala* is in the sense of *istaf'ala*, as Al-Azhari mentioned, meaning "He feeds and does not seek food," that is, He does not request food and take it from another; or the meaning is "He feeds at one time and does not feed at another," like His saying, glory be to Him and Most High: ﴿He withholds and extends.﴾ Both pronouns refer to Allah Most High. Returning the second pronoun to other than Allah Most High is a strained reading that requires supposition.

﴿Say﴾, after explaining that taking other than Him as a protector is something that the self-evident judgment of intellects proves to be false: ﴿I have been commanded﴾ from the presence of the Protector, may His majesty be exalted, ﴿to be the first to submit﴾, turning his face to Allah, glory be to Him and Most High, sincerely devoted to Him. This is because the Prophet, peace be upon him, is commanded to do what has been legislated, except what is among his particular privileges, peace be upon him. He is the leader of his community and their exemplar. It is fitting for every commander to be the first to act on what he commands, so that it is more likely to be obeyed. Among this is what Allah Most High related about Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Glory be to You, I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers.﴾

It has also been said that what has been mentioned is for encouragement, as a king commands his subjects to do something and then says, "I am the first to do that," so as to move them to obey. Otherwise, no refusal of that ever came from him (ﷺ) that would require him to be commanded to it. There is room for scrutiny in this. ﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾

41

- That is, in a matter of the affairs of religion. In the sentence there is an implied statement: "And it was said to me: Do not be..." They said that *min* here (of "min al-mushrikin") is for quotation, and it is conjoined (*'atifah*) to the implied statement upon *umirtu*. The overall meaning is: "I have been commanded to submit, and forbidden from associating partners." It has also been said that it is conjoined to the content of what is said (*maqul*).

[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 6, verse 15]

﴿Say﴾ is in the accusative according to the sense, since it has the meaning of: "Say: Indeed I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims, and do not be [among those who associate partners]." So the waw is part of the reported speech (*al-mahkiy*). It has also been said that it is conjoined to (*qul*). [Page 111] According to the sense, that is, that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was commanded to say such and such and forbidden from such and such. This has been objected to on the ground that the smoothness of the composition (*salasat al-nazm*) rejects separating the successive proclamations (*al-khitabat al-tabligiyya*) from one another by an address that is not part of them. It has been permitted that it be conjoined to (*inni umirtu*), being within the scope of (*qul*), with the address being to each of the polytheists. The strain and forcedness of this are not hidden. The impossibility of conjoining it to (*akun*) is evident, since there is no reason for a shift (*iltifat*) and no sense in saying "You have been commanded that you not be [among them]."

﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾, that is, by opposing His command and prohibition, whatever disobedience it may be. Thus what has been mentioned enters into it by primary inclusion. As for His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾,

- that is, the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Its greatness is due to the greatness of what occurs in it. It is the object of (*akhafu*). The conditional clause is parenthetical between them, and the answer of the condition is omitted obligatorily. What precedes the particle is similar to it, and it is evidence for it, but it is not identical to it, according to the more correct view, contrary to the Kufans and al-Mubarrad. The estimate is: "If I disobey, I will be lighter [in punishment]" or "I fear the punishment of..." etc. It has been said: "I have become deserving of the punishment of that day."

There is another emphasis in the speech, with regard to what is understood from what came before concerning cutting off their hopes, and an allusion that they are disobedient and deserving of punishment, in that what is known to be impossible is attributed to the speaker's pronoun. [It is combined with] (*anna*), which indicates doubt, and the past tense is used to present it in the form of something realized, as a supposition. The meaning ultimately returns to frightening them over the occurrence of that act from them. So there is no indication in the speech that he (peace and blessings be upon him) feared for his sacred self disbelief and disobedience, although it is not so, because of his infallibility (*ismah*) (ﷺ). Some have raised the indication of the verse for what has been mentioned as a question, and then said: it has been answered that the fear is connected to disobedience that is impossible by customary impossibility, so it indicates only that he (peace and blessings be upon him) would fear if it proceeded from him, and far be it from him [to commit] disbelief and disobedience, and this does not indicate the occurrence of fear. You know that what we have presented suffices without that. It is understood from the words of some of them that the fear of the infallible from disobedience does not contradict infallibility, because he knows that God, glorified and exalted, is the doer of what He wills, and that nothing is obligatory upon Him. In some reports it is related that He, mighty is His affair, said to Moses (peace be upon him): "O Moses, do not feel secure from My plan until you cross the bridge (*sirat*)."

It has come in more than one report that when the wind blew strongly, his blessed face would turn yellow, and he would say: "I fear that the Hour may be established," even though God informed him that before it there will be the appearance of the Mahdi and Jesus (peace be upon them both), the emergence of the Dajjal (Antichrist), the rising of the sun from its west, and other signs which had not appeared at that time and had not yet been realized. It is authentically reported that he (peace and blessings be upon him) apologized for not going out to the *tarawih* prayer (voluntary night prayers in Ramadan) after he had prayed it the first night of Ramadan and people gathered eagerly for it, by saying: "I feared that it would be made obligatory upon you." Even though what occurred on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), when the prayers were made obligatory, indicates that He, exalted, does not make obligatory more than the five [prayers]. All of this indicates that God, exalted, may do what He wills. The most that follows in such cases, were He to do so, is a change in the connection of an attribute (*taghayyur ta'alluq al-sifa*), and this does not necessitate a change in the attribute itself, such that it would entail createdness (*huduth*) and the subsistence of contingent events in Him, exalted is His affair. This is a discussion of long tail, and perhaps the opportunity will lead to its verification, God willing, exalted.

[Page 112 begins within this passage.]

Whoever is spared it on that Day: that is, whoever is spared the punishment. The deputy subject (*nā'ib al-fā'il*, the grammatical element standing in for the subject of a passive verb) is the pronoun referring to the punishment, and the pronoun in *"'anhu"* (from him) refers back to *"man"* (whoever). It is also permitted for the reverse to be the case, meaning: whoever is spared from the punishment. In both readings, *"man"* is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is the conditional clause (*shart*) or the response clause (*jawab*), or both, according to the differing views. The adverbial phrase *"yawma'idhin"* (on that Day) either depends on the verb, or on the punishment, or on an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun.

It is also permitted for it to be the deputy subject. Does it then require an implied genitive construction (*mudaf*), meaning "the punishment of that Day," or not? There is a difference of opinion on this. It has been said that it is necessary, because an incomplete adverb (*zarf ghayr al-tamm*, that is, one cut off from its genitive, like *qablu* and *ba'du*) cannot be made to stand in for the subject except by means of an implied *mudaf*, and *"yawma'idhin"* has the same rule. In *ad-Durr al-Masun*, it is said that there is no need for it, because the nunation (*tanwin*, the "-in" ending), by being a substitute (*'iwad*), is treated as though the thing it replaces had been mentioned. This is contrary to al-Akhfash. Al-Ujhuri mentioned that the nunation here is a substitute for an omitted clause that the preceding speech implies, and the original would be: "the Day when the recompense will be," and the like. The sentence is then a new, independent statement (*mustu'nafa*) that emphasizes the terror of the punishment. It is also permitted for it to be an attribute (*sifa*) of *"'adhab"* (punishment).

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr (from 'Asim) read *"man yasrif"* (whoever He spares), on the understanding that the pronoun in it refers to God, may He be exalted. Ubayy read *"man yasrifi Allahu"* (whoever God spares), with the subject stated explicitly, and the object is omitted: that is, the punishment, or *"yawma'idhin"* with an omitted genitive, or the Day is taken as an expression for what takes place in it. In this reading, *"man"* is a subject.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be placed in the accusative position by an omitted verb whose implied form is: *"man yukram yasrif Allahu al-'adhab 'anhu"* (whoever is honored, God spares him the punishment), so that *"yasrif"* serves as an explanation of the omitted element. He also permitted that it be made accusative by *"yasrif"* itself, with the pronoun in *"'anhu"* referring to the punishment, meaning: whatever person God, may He be exalted, spares from the punishment, **then He has had mercy on him** (*faqad rahimahu*). That is, the great mercy, which is salvation. This is like your saying: "If you feed Zayd from his hunger, you have done him a kindness," meaning: "then you have completed the kindness to him." On this view the statement belongs to the type of: "Whoever attains the pasture of security has attained [his goal]," and the type of: "Whoever's emigration was to God, may He be exalted, [his emigration is to God and His Messenger]" (the predicate being omitted). It also belongs to the type of restricting the general to the complete.

It has also been said that the intended meaning is: then He has admitted him into the Garden. The necessitating cause is mentioned, but the necessitated result is intended, because entry into the Garden is a necessary consequence of mercy, since it is the abode of the reward that necessarily follows the abandonment of punishment.

This has been challenged with the People of the Heights (*ashab al-a'raf*). It is answered that the words of God, may He be exalted, **"That is the manifest triumph"** (*wa dhalika al-fawz al-mubin*) are a qualifying circumstantial clause for what precedes it, and the manifest triumph is only through entering the Garden, according to God's words, may He be exalted: **"Whoever is distanced from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has indeed triumphed"** (*faman zuhzih 'ani al-nari wa udkhila al-jannata faqad faz*). You know that if we say that al-A'raf is a hill in the Garden, on which the elite of the believers stand, as is one of the opinions, this does not refute the challenge. This will come, God willing, with its verification later. What has been mentioned as the answer is based on something whose remoteness is not hidden. What motivates the interpretation is the unity of the condition and the response, which they regard as impermissible.

One of the perfected scholars said: what is in this noble arrangement is similar to the words of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: **"A child will never repay his father unless he finds him enslaved, buys him, and frees him."** He means by the mentioned purchase [the buying of the father], and that the difference in the wording is sufficient for the validity of the sequence and the consequence. You may say: mercy is a cause for the averting, which precedes it, as the perfect past tense and imperfect forms suggest, and the sequence is with respect to the reports. Al-Shihab criticized this, saying it is a forced interpretation, because the cause and the effect must differ in meaning. As for the mentioned hadith, some have taken it at face value, and others have interpreted it to mean that he will not repay him at all, and this is subtle, because it is a conditional tied to the impossible. As for the response being past in form and meaning, there is a difference of opinion on this, to the point that some have prohibited it except with *kana* (was), because of its deep-rootedness in the past. End of quote. So let it be understood.

The demonstrative (*al-ishara*) is either to the averting that is contained in *"yusraf"* (is spared), or to the mercy. It is mentioned in order to interpret the verbal noun (*masdar*) as an infinitive with *"an"* and the verb. Some have taken *"ar-ruhm"* (the womb, in the sense of mercy) with a single *damma* and sukun, or with two dammas, and this, according to the *Qamus* (the dictionary), means mercy. The sense of distance is to indicate the high rank of what is pointed to. *"Al-fawz"* means attaining the desired goal. The definite article (*al-*) in *"al-fawz al-mubin"* serves to restrict the predicate to the subject (*li qasrihi 'ala al-musnad ilayhi*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 17:

﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, i.e., with an affliction such as sickness or need, ﴿there is no remover﴾, i.e., no one who removes or relieves it ﴿for you except Him﴾. The meaning is that none is able to remove it other than Allah, glorified and exalted is He, not the idols or anything else. ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾, such as health and wealth, ﴿then He is over all things competent﴾.

[Page 113]

Among that (all things) is this, so He, majestic is His affair, is able over it, so He holds it fast for you and preserves it for you, without anyone being able to repel or lift it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So there is no repeller of His bounty﴾. From this it appears that the answer (jaza') is connected to the condition (shart).

It has been said: the answer is omitted, its estimate being "then there is no repeller of it except Him, exalted is He," and what is mentioned is an emphasis for both answers, because His power over every thing, of good and of evil, emphasizes that He, glorified and exalted is He, is the remover of harm and the preserver of blessings and the one who perpetuates them. The claim that it has no connection to the first answer, but rather is the cause ('illa) of the second answer, is evidently false, since power over every thing emphasizes the removal of harm without doubt, and denying that is obstinacy. The root meaning of touching (mass), as Abu Hayyan said, is the meeting of two bodies, and what is meant here is reaching/afflicting.

Many have made the ba' in (bi-durrin) and in (bi-khayrin) a particle of transitivity (lil-ta'diya), even though the verb is already transitive, as if it were said: "And if Allah touches you the harm." They interpreted ad-durr with a damma as bad condition in the body, and others with a fatha as the opposite of benefit. He turned away from ash-shar, which is the counterpart of khayr, to ad-durr, according to what is in al-Bahr, because ash-shar is more general, so the more specific term was used alongside khayr, which is general, out of regard for the aspect of mercy. Ibn Atiyya said: the pairing of khayr with durr, although its counterpart is shar, which is more specific than it, is of the hidden eloquence, by deviating from the rule of baseness and casting off the garment of artificiality, which is that it be paired with a more specific term of its opposite or the like, because it is more fitting to the meaning and more closely attached to the context, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein or go naked﴾ ﴿and that you will not thirst therein or be exposed to the sun﴾. Here hunger was mentioned with nakedness and thirst with exposure to the sun, whereas the apparent expectation was otherwise. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

As if I had not ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,
nor poured out the wine-jar of the fine wine, nor said to my horses, "Turn back, a return after the rout."

Its clarification: in the verse he paired hunger, which is emptiness of the inner, with nakedness, which is emptiness of the outer, and thirst, in which there is heat of the inner, with the sun, in which there is heat of the outer. Likewise Imru' al-Qays paired his elevation on the steed with his elevation over the maiden, because both are pleasures of mounting, and the spending of wealth on buying wine with the risking of souls in combat, because in the first there is the joy of merriment and in the second the joy of victory. Similarly here, harm (ad-durr) was preferred for its suitability to what precedes it of warning, for the vengeance of the Great is great. Then, when He mentioned beneficence, He brought what embraces its kinds. The verse is of the type of al-laff wa al-nashr (an arrangement in which items are first listed and then matched to what they correspond to, gloss), for the touching of harm refers to His saying, ﴿Indeed I fear﴾ etc., and the touching of good refers to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever is averted from it﴾ etc. It is said that this (verse) falls within the scope of (qul, "say") and the address is general to everyone who reads it, or to the master of those addressed, ﷺ. The (la) is the negating la of the genus, (kashifa) is its noun, and (lahu) is its predicate. The detached pronoun is a substitute (badal) for the place of (la kashifa), or for the pronoun in the adverbial phrase. Abu al-Baqa' said it is not permissible for it to be in the nominative governed by (kashif), nor a substitute for the pronoun in it, because in both cases you would be applying the noun of la, and whenever you apply it to a noun you make it indefinite with tanwin. In this noble verse there is a refutation of those who hope for the removal of harm from other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, and who place their hope in anyone besides Him.

In Futuh al-Ghayb of the divine pole (al-Qutb al-Rabbani), my master Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, may Allah sanctify his secret, there is a long discourse: whoever wishes safety in this world and the Hereafter, let him adhere to patience, contentment, abandoning complaint to His creation, lowering his needs to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, adherence to His obedience, awaiting relief from Him, glorified and exalted is He, and devotion to Him. For His withholding is a gift, His punishment is a blessing, His trial is a remedy, His promise is binding, His word is action, and all His acts are good, wise and beneficial. But He, the Mighty and Majestic, concealed the knowledge of the benefits from His servants and kept it to Himself, so there is nothing but occupation with servitude, through fulfilling the commands, avoiding the prohibitions, and submission in destiny, and abandoning the occupation with lordship, and stillness regarding "why," "how," and "when?"

[Page 114]

This discourse is supported by the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: "While I was riding behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: 'O boy, guard Allah and He will guard you. Guard Allah and you will find Him before you. If you ask, ask Allah; and if you seek help, seek help from Allah. The pen has dried with what is to be. If the people were to strive to benefit you with anything Allah has not decreed for you, they would not be able to do it; and if they strove to harm you with anything Allah has not decreed against you, they would not be able to do it. So if you are able to act for Allah with sincerity in certainty, then act; but if you are not able, then in patience upon what you dislike there is much good. And know that victory is with patience, relief is with distress, and with hardship is ease.'" Therefore every believer should make this hadith the mirror of his heart, his inner garment and outer garment, and his speech, and act upon it in his movements and stillness, until he is safe in this world and the Hereafter and finds honor through the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿وهُوَ القاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبادِهِ﴾ ["And He is the Subduer over His servants"]. It has been said that this is a metaphorical expression (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*, an extended metaphor) depicting His glory, exalted is He, and His elevation, may His dignity be great, through dominance and power. It has also been permitted that the metaphor is in the adverb, by likening dominance to a tangible place. It has also been said that it is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for subjugation and elevation through dominance and power. It has further been said that *fawq* ("above") is superfluous (*za'idah*). The author affirmed its superfluity, although it is a noun, on the basis that it means *'ala* ("upon"). And this, as you see, is weak. The reason for adopting all of this is that the apparent meaning of the verse requires the affirmation of a direction (*jihah*), whereas God, exalted is He, is exempt from it, because direction is a created thing, brought into being by the creation of the world and its bringing from non-existence into existence. It would also follow from His, exalted is He, being in a direction that there are evident corruptions. You know that the position of the early pious predecessors (*al-Salaf*) is the affirmation of *fawqiyyah* (being above) for God, exalted is He, as the Imam al-Tahawi and others have explicitly stated, and they argued for this with about a thousand proofs. The Imam Ahmad has related, in the hadith of the mountain goats (*al-Awa'il*), from al-'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Throne is above that, and God, exalted is He, is above all of that." Abu Dawud related from Jubayr ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, from his grandfather, that [the Prophet's] saying (ﷺ) to the man who sought intercession with God against him: "Woe to you! Do you know what God is? Indeed God, exalted is He, is above His Throne, and His Throne is above His heavens," and he gestured with his fingers like a dome, "and indeed it creaks over Him like the creaking of a new saddle under its rider."

Al-Umawi related in his *Maghazi* from a sound hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Sa'd on the day he judged concerning the Banu Qurayzah: "You have judged among them with the judgment of the King from above the seven heavens." Ibn Majah related it as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet), saying: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, so they raise their heads toward it, and behold, the Almighty, majestic is His majesty, has looked down upon them from above them, and He says: 'O people of Paradise, peace be upon you.'" Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿سَلامٌ قَوْلا مِن رَبٍّ رَحِيمٍ﴾ ["Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful"]. "So He looks at them and they look at Him, and they do not turn to anything of the bliss so long as they are looking at Him."

It is also established that 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah recited, in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his verses in which he alluded to abstaining from intercourse with his wife when she accused him concerning his slave-girl, and they are:

"I bear witness that the promise of God is true, and that the Fire is the abode of the disbelievers,
and that the Throne is above the water, floating, and above the Throne is the Lord of the worlds,
and carried by mighty angels, the angels of God, marked [by their rank]."

The Prophet (ﷺ) approved of what he said and laughed at it. Likewise, Hassan ibn Thabit, may God be pleased with him, recited his saying:

"I bear witness by the permission of God that Muhammad is the Messenger of the One who is above the heavens on high,
and that Abu Yahya and Yahya, both of them, have a deed from their Lord that is accepted,
and that He who opposed the Jews is the son of Mary, a messenger who came from the One of the Throne, sent,
and that the brother of the 'Ahqaf (Hud), when he stood among them, stood with God's essence among them and was just."

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And I bear witness."

'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, concerning His saying, exalted is He, quoting Iblis: ﴿ثُمَّ لآتِيَنَّهم مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ وعَنْ أيْمانِهِمْ وعَنْ شَمائِلِهِمْ﴾ ["Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left"], that he said: "He could not say 'and from above them,' because he knew that God, exalted is He, is above them."

The verses and reports that explicitly state what indicates *fawqiyyah* are very numerous, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿تَنْزِيلُ الكِتابِ مِنَ اللَّهِ العَزِيزِ الحَكِيمِ﴾ ["The revelation of the Book is from God, the Almighty, the Wise"], and ﴿إلَيْهِ يَصْعَدُ الكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ﴾ ["To Him ascends the good word"], and ﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾ ["Rather, God raised him to Himself"], and ﴿تَعْرُجُ المَلائِكَةُ والرُّوحُ إلَيْهِ﴾ ["The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him"], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in what Muslim related: "(And You are the Outward, so there is nothing above You)." Likewise are the words of the early predecessors on this matter. Among them is what Shaykh al-Islam Abu Isma'il al-Ansari related in his book *al-Faruq*, with his chain of transmission, to Abu Muti' al-Balkhi, that he asked Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with him, about one who said: "I do not know whether my Lord, exalted is He, is in the heaven or in the earth." He said: "He has disbelieved, because God, exalted is He, says: ﴿الرَّحْمَنُ عَلَى العَرْشِ اسْتَوَى﴾ ['The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne'], and His Throne is above the seven heavens." I said: "What if he says, 'He is upon the Throne, but I do not know whether the Throne is in the heaven or in the earth'?" He, may God be pleased with him, said: "He is a disbeliever, because he has denied a verse concerning the heaven, and whoever denies a verse concerning the heaven has disbelieved." Another added: "Because God is in the highest of the 'Illiyyun, and He is called upon from above, not from below." End of quote.

The affirmation of *fawqiyyah* is also supported by the argument that when God created the creation, He did not create them within His sacred essence, exalted is He above that, for He is the One, the Eternal Refuge, who has not begotten nor been begotten. Thus it is established that He created them outside His essence. And if He, exalted is He, were not characterized by the *fawqiyyat al-dhat* (essential above-ness), while being self-subsisting and not mixed with the world, He would be characterized by its opposite, because whatever is receptive to a thing is not free of it or of its opposite. The opposite of *fawqiyyah* is *suful* (lowness), which is blameworthy absolutely. The claim that "we do not concede that He is receptive to *fawqiyyah* so that the denial of it would require the affirmation of its opposite" is refuted by the argument that if He, exalted is He, were not receptive to elevation and above-ness, He would have no real existence subsisting by itself. Therefore, once it is conceded that He, may His dignity be exalted, is a self-subsisting essence not mixed with the world, and that He exists externally, not merely mentally, but existing outside the minds with certainty, and since all sane people know by necessity that whatever exists in this manner is either inside the world or outside it, and denying this is denying the clearest of self-evident truths, then no proof is needed for this except that the knowledge of separation (*mubayanah*, distinctness from creation) is clearer and more manifest than it. And since the attribute of *fawqiyyah* is an attribute of perfection with no deficiency in it, and affirming it entails no contradiction of the Book, the Sunnah, or consensus, its denial is pure falsehood, especially since human natures are innately disposed to direct themselves toward the direction of height when supplicating to God, exalted is He.

Muhammad ibn Tahir al-Maqdisi mentioned that Shaykh Abu Ja'far al-Hamadani attended the assembly of Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) while he was speaking on denying the attribute of *'uluww* (height), saying: "God was, and there was no Throne, and He is now as He was." Shaykh Abu Ja'far said: "Inform us, O Ustadh, about this necessity that we find in our hearts, for no knower has ever said 'O God' except that he finds in his heart a necessity seeking height, not turning right or left. How, then, will you repel this necessity from ourselves?" He said: "So the Imam struck his head and descended," and I think he said, "and wept, and said: 'Al-Hamadani has bewildered me.'"

Some have strained to answer this by saying that this orientation upward is only because the sky is the *qiblah* of supplication, just as the Ka'bah is the *qiblah* of prayer. But this too is refuted by placing the forehead on the ground, even though He, exalted is He, is not in the direction of the earth. And it is not hidden that this is false. As for the first point: the sky being the *qiblah* of supplication has not been said by any of the early predecessors of this community, nor has God sent down any authority for it. What is established is that the *qiblah* of supplication is the *qiblah* of prayer, and they have explicitly stated that it is recommended for the supplicant to face the *qiblah*, and the Prophet (ﷺ) faced the Ka'bah in his supplication on many occasions. So whoever says that supplication has a *qiblah* other than the *qiblah* of prayer has innovated in the religion and opposed the community of the Muslims. As for the second point: the *qiblah* is that which the supplicant faces with his face, as the Ka'bah is faced in prayer. What a person aligns with his head or his hands, for example, is not called a *qiblah* at all. So if the sky were the *qiblah* of supplication, it would be prescribed for the supplicant to turn his face toward it, and this is not established in any Law whatsoever. As for the refutation by placing the forehead [on the ground], how corrupt is this refutation! The one placing his forehead intends only submission to one who is above him, through humility, not that he inclines toward Him as though He were beneath him. Rather, this does not occur to the heart of one prostrating. Yes, it has been heard of Bishr al-Marisi that he used to say: "Glory be to my Lord the Lowest!" God, exalted is He, is far above what the deniers and the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

Some have interpreted every text that attributes *fawqiyyah* to Him, exalted is He, as meaning that *fawq* there means "better" and "more excellent," as one says: "The Amir is above the vizier" and "The dinar is above the dirham." You know that this is among the things that sound intellects recoil from and sound hearts abhor, for the statement of one who says at the outset: "God, exalted is He, is better than His servants," or "better than His Throne," is of the same kind as saying: "Ice is cold, fire is hot, the sun is brighter than the lamp, and the sky is higher than the ceiling of the house," and the like. There is also no glorification or exaltation of God, exalted is He, in that. Rather, it is among the most base of speech. How, then, is it fitting to read the glorious Speech in this way, which, if mankind and the jinn gathered to produce its like, they could not produce its like, even if they were helpers of one another? Moreover, in that there is a diminishment of God, exalted is His dignity. As the proverb goes:

"Do you not see that the sword's worth diminishes
when it is said that the sword is better than the staff?"

Yes, when the context requires it, such as when it is an argument against an adversary, as in the saying of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him: ﴿أأرْبابٌ مُتَفَرِّقُونَ خَيْرٌ أمِ اللَّهُ الواحِدُ القَهّارُ﴾ ["Are scattered lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?"], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿آللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ ["Is God better, or what they associate?"], and ﴿واللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وأبْقى﴾ ["And God is better and more enduring"]. This is a matter with no objection to it, and no arrows of criticism are aimed at it. And *fawqiyyah* in the sense of superiority in excellence is among what the early predecessors affirm for God, exalted is He, too, and it is realized within absolute *fawqiyyah*. Likewise they affirm *fawqiyyat al-qahr wa al-ghalabah* (above-ness of subjugation and dominance) just as they affirm *fawqiyyat al-dhat* (above-ness of essence). They believe in all of that in the manner befitting the majesty of His essence and the perfection of His attributes, exalted is He, declaring Him far above whatever would necessarily follow from it that is impossible for Him, majestic is His dignity. They do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, nor do they deviate from the legal terms, neither negating nor affirming, lest they affirm a corrupt meaning or negate a sound meaning. So they affirm *fawqiyyah* as God, exalted is He, affirmed it for Himself.

As for the term *jihah* (direction), it may be used to mean something existent, and it may be used to mean something non-existent. And it is known that there is no existent except the Creator and the created. So if by *jihah* is meant an existent thing other than God, exalted is He, then it is created, and God, exalted is He, is not confined by anything nor encompassed by anything of the creatures, exalted is He above that. And if by *jihah* is meant a non-existent matter, which is what is above the world, then there is nothing there but God alone. So when it is said that He, exalted is He, is in a direction in this sense, it is correct according to them, and its meaning is that He is above the world, and there is nothing there but God alone. So when it is said that He, exalted is He, is in a direction in this sense, it is correct according to them, and its meaning is that He is above the world, at the point where created things end.

As for those who deny the term *jihah*, intending by that the denial of height, they cite among their proofs that all directions are created, that He, exalted is He, existed before the directions, that whoever says He, exalted is He, is in a direction necessitates saying that some part of the world is eternal, and that He, majestic is His dignity, was independent of direction and then came to be in it. These expressions and the like are to be understood as meaning that He, mighty is His name, is not in anything of the creatures, whether it is called a direction or not. This is a true statement. But direction is not an existent matter; rather, it is a notional, conventional matter, and there is no prohibition in that. In sum, it is obligatory to declare God free of resemblance to created beings, to entrust knowledge of what has come of the ambiguous (*mutashabihat*) matters to Him, mighty is His dignity, to believe in them in the manner in which they came, and to interpret them in the sense that is close to the mind.

Page 117

Among the matters commonly found in the speech of the Arabs, there is nothing objectionable in my view, provided that some verses are such that both the earlier generations (al-salaf) and later scholars (al-khalaf) agreed on their interpretation, while Allah the Exalted knows best His intended meaning. ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, i.e., possessor of perfect wisdom (al-hikmah al-balighah), which is knowledge of things as they truly are and the performance of actions as they ought to be; or, He is the one who is most thorough in perfecting (al-mubaligh fi al-ihkam), which is the mastery of arrangement (itqan al-tadbir) and excellence of measuring (ihsan al-taqdir). ﴿The All-Aware﴾

- i.e., the one who knows what is subtle of the states of the servants and what is hidden of their affairs. The lam here, and in what preceded, is for restriction (li-al-qasr).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 19: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ Al-Kalbi narrated: "The disbelievers of Makkah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'O Muhammad, has Allah not found a messenger other than you? We do not see anyone who confirms what you say. We have asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that you have no mention among them. So show us someone who testifies that you are the Messenger of Allah.' Then this was revealed." And Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "al-Nahhham ibn Zayd, Qardam ibn Ka'b and Bahri ibn 'Amr came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know of any god with Allah other than Him?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no god but Allah; with this I was sent, and to this I call.' Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse." The first report is more suited to the beginning of the verse, and the second to its end. So "ayyu" (أيّ) is the subject (mubtada'), "akbaru" (أكبر) its predicate (khabar), and "shahadatan" (شهادة) a specifier (tamyiz). In the language, "shay'" (الشيء, thing) is that which may be known and spoken of. Sibawayh mentioned it in the chapter he titled "the paths of the final endings of words," and the feminine only arises from the masculine: do you not see that "shay'" applies to everything about which information is given, before one knows whether it is male or female, while "shay'" is masculine? End of quote. Is it applied to Allah the Exalted or not? There is a difference of opinion. The position of the majority is that it is applied to Him, glory be to Him, saying: "a thing unlike other things." They argued for this with the question and answer occurring in this verse, and with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾, where He made an exception from "everything" of "the Face," which in their view means the Essence, and because it is the most general of terms, encompassing the necessary and the possible. Al-Imam reported that Jahm denied the validity of this application, citing the saying of the Exalted: ﴿To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾, and said: it is not applied to Him, glory be to Him, except for what indicates an attribute of perfection, and "thing" is not like that. In "al-Mawaqif" and its commentary: "thing," according to the Ash'aris, is applied only to the existent; so for them every thing is existent and every existent is a thing. Then the positions of people on it were set out in both works. Then it was said: the dispute is verbal, concerning the word "thing" and what it is applied to; and the truth is what language and transmission support, since there is no room for reason in establishing languages. The evident position is with us, for the people of language in every age apply the word "thing" to the existent, so that if it were said in their presence "the existent is a thing," they would accept it, and if it were said "it is not a thing," they would reject it. Like His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And I had created you before, when you were nothing﴾, which negates its application in the literal sense to the non-existent, because the literal sense does not apply to it. End of quote. In "Sharh al-Maqasid": the question of whether the non-existent is literally a thing is a linguistic one, to be referred to transmission and usage, and there have been differences regarding it in light of usages. Our position is that it is a name for the existent, because we find it commonly used in this sense, and there is no dispute about its use for the non-existent in a figurative sense. Then he said: what is reported from Abu al-'Abbas, that it is a name for the eternal, and from the Jahmiyya that it is a name for the originated, and from Hisham that it is a name for a body, is very far-fetched, since the people of language do not accept it. End of quote. In all of this there is discussion, for the claim of the Ash'aris that "thing" and "existent" are equal in language, or synonymous, as is understood from the two universal propositions mentioned earlier, has no proof on which one may rely. Their saying "the people of language in every age, etc." only indicates that every existent is a thing; as for whether every term applied to it as "thing" is literally existent, there is no indication of that, for it does not follow from the fact that the word "thing" is applied to the existent and not to "no-thing" that "thing" is linguistically restricted to the existent, since it is permissible that "thing" be applied linguistically and literally to both the non-existent and the existent
page 118 while the existent is specifically associated with applying "thing" and not "no-thing." And the people of language's denial of one who says "the existent is not a thing" is because it is a negation of the more general from the more specific, and this is not valid because the two are synonymous or equal. It has been applied to the external non-existent in the Book and the Sunnah: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And never say of anything, "I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. Al-Tabarani reported: "from Umm Salamah that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when a man asked him: 'I speak to myself about a matter which, if I spoke it, would nullify my reward.' He said: 'Such speech is encountered only by a believer.'" A similar report is from Mu'adh ibn Jabal. The basis in application is the literal sense, so one does not turn from it except when a diverting indication is found. Widespread usage cannot serve as a diverting indication after the soundness of the transmission from Sibawayh. Perhaps the reason for that prevalence is that the purpose in discourse is more closely tied to the conditions of existent things, not because "thing" is linguistically restricted to the existent. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I had created you before, when you were nothing﴾, it only necessitates negating its application in the literal sense to the non-existent, and that would harm us if the claim were restricting the linguistic application of "thing," but it is not so. For the verification in our view is that "thing," in the sense of "that which is willed," is knowledge of it and information about it, a universal concept that applies to the existent and the non-existent, the necessary and the possible; and restricting its application to some of its instances when a indication exists does not preclude its encompassing all its instances literally in the linguistic sense when no restricting indication is present. Otherwise, its encompassing both the non-existent and the existent together in His saying, the Exalted: (and Allah is Knowing of all things) would be a combination of literal and figurative senses, and that is a disputed question. There is no dispute about deriving from this verse the general scope of His knowledge over things absolutely; so it is evidence that its encompassing both the non-existent and the existent together is a literal linguistic sense. Some eminent scholars, after asserting the restriction of "thing" to the existent, mentioned that it originally is a verbal noun used in the sense of "willed" (shaa) or "that which is willed" (mashii'); if it means "willed," its application to Him, the Exalted, is valid, otherwise not. You know that, according to the verification we have mentioned, there is no barrier to applying "thing" to Him, the Exalted, without need for this detailed distinction, since it means "that which is willed," knowledge of it and information about it; so applying "thing" in this sense to Him, Mighty and Majestic, is like applying "the known" for example. The meaning of ﴿greatest in testimony﴾ is "greatest and most truthful." ﴿Say: "Allah"﴾ is a command to him (ﷺ) to answer the question himself, by himself, peace and blessings be upon him, as has passed shortly. The noble name is a mubtada' whose khabar is omitted, i.e., "Allah is greatest in testimony," and the reverse has been permitted. According to Sibawayh's position, when the indefinite is an interrogative noun or a superlative (af'al al-tafdil), it stands as a mubtada' about which a definite is predicated. His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Witness﴾ (shahid) is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', i.e., "He, glory be to Him, is a witness" ﴿between me and you﴾, so it is the beginning of a statement. It is also permitted that it be the khabar of "Allah," and the whole, according to what al-Zamakhshari held, is the answer, since it indicates that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, being the witness between him and them, the greatest thing in testimony is a witness for him. It is reported in "al-Kashf" that if the complete answer is taken to end at His saying, glory be to Him, "Allah," then it is a step from establishing monotheism to establishing prophethood: this witness, than whom none is more truthful, has testified for me through the revelation of this Qur'an. And if the whole utterance is taken as the answer, it is from the wise style, because the mind does not go to the idea that this witness might be other than Him, the Exalted; rather the discussion is about whether He testifies to his prophethood or not. So let this be understood. ﴿And it has been revealed to me﴾ from Him, the Exalted, ﴿this Qur'an﴾, the great one, which witnesses to the soundness of my mission, ﴿that I may warn you by it﴾, with what it contains of threat. Mention of warning was sufficient without mention of good news, because it is
page 119 appropriate to the context. It was said: the speech is with the disbelievers, among whom there was no one to give good news. In "al-Durr al-Masun": the speech is in the manner of ﴿garments that protect you from heat﴾, and ﴿and whoever it reaches﴾ is a conjunction upon the pronoun of the addressees, i.e., "that I may warn you by it, O people of Makkah, and all whom the Qur'an reaches and attains, of black and red, or of the two weighty groups (jinn and humankind)"; or "that I may warn you by it, you who exist and whoever will exist until the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Jarir said: whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he had seen Muhammad (ﷺ). Abu Nu'aym and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if I had spoken to him face to face." The verse has been used as evidence that the rulings of the Qur'an encompass those who existed at the time of its revelation and whoever will exist after them until Allah inherits the earth and whatever is upon it. There is a difference about this: is it by way of expression (ibarah) for all, or by consensus for those not existing and those not obligated? The Hanabila took the first view, and the Hanafiyya the second; its verification is in the books of usul. And that whoever the Qur'an has not reached is not held accountable for abandoning the legal rulings. This is supported by what Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Prisoners were brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to them: 'Were you invited to Islam?' They said: 'No.' So he released them, then recited ﴿And it has been revealed to me﴾ the verse." This is based on the view of conceptual implication (mafhum), as the Shafi'iyya held. It was objected that the verse provides no indication of this in any way, because its implication is the negation of warning by the Qur'an of one who has not been reached by it, and that is not the same as the negation of accountability, which is evident, nor does it necessarily entail it, especially for those who hold the doctrine of good and evil by reason, unless His saying, the Exalted, is taken into account: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾. In reply: the non-necessity of the negation of warning by the Qur'an entailing the negation of accountability is disputed; and the rational goodness and evil have been dismissed. It was permitted that "whoever" be a conjunction upon the implicit subject in "I warn you," by separation through the object, i.e., "that I may warn you by it, and whoever the Qur'an has reached will warn you by it too." Al-Tabarsi reported what implies this from al-'Ayyashi, from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both; but it is not hidden that this is contrary to what comes to mind. ﴿Do you indeed testify that with Allah there are other gods?﴾ This is a new sentence or is included in the speech. The interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir) or for denial; it was said it is both, and in that is a combination of figurative meanings. "Ukhra" (أخرى, other) is an adjective of "alihah" (gods). The adjective of a plural of non-rational things, as Abu Hayyan said, is like the adjective of a feminine singular, as in ﴿other needs (ma'arib ukhra)﴾. ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾ Since the gods were stones and wood, for example, they were treated in this way to belittle them. Say to them: "I do not bear witness to that, even if you bear witness to it, for it is pure falsehood." ﴿Say﴾ is a repetition of the command for emphasis. ﴿Indeed, He is but one God﴾, i.e., rather, I only testify that He, the Exalted, there is no god but Him; and "ma" (ما) is a kafza (a particle that cancels the governing effect). Abu al-Baqa' permitted, and claimed it is the most fitting with what precedes it, that "ma" be a relative (mawsulah); but its being a relative weakens this, and on it "wahid" would be the khabar, which is contrary to the apparent sense. ﴿And indeed I am free of what you associate﴾ 91 - of idols, or of your associating (others with Allah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 20:

﴿Those whom We have given the Book﴾ is a response to what was mentioned earlier in the first narration, in their saying: "We asked the Jews and the Christians," and so on. It was delayed from specifying the witness, in order to hasten to answer their arbitrary demand by their saying: "Show us the one who testifies for you." So what is meant by the relative pronoun is what encompasses both categories, the Jews and the Christians. By "the Book" is meant its genus, which applies to the Torah and the Gospel. Their being described by the bestowal of the Book serves to signal the basis of what is attributed to them in the words of the Exalted: ﴿They recognize him﴾, meaning they recognize the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by his features and attributes mentioned in both. In this there is a shift (iltifat) [of pronoun]. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Book, and Abu al-Baqa' chose this view, but the first is what the reports support, as you will come to know. ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾,
(page 120)
by their characteristics, such that they have no doubt about that at all. Abu Hamza and others narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Abdullah ibn Salam: "Allah the Exalted revealed to His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, that the People of the Book recognize him as they recognize their sons. So what is this recognition?" Ibn Salam said: "We recognize the Prophet of Allah ﷺ by the description with which Allah the Exalted described him. When we see him among you, we recognize him just as one of us recognizes his son when he sees him among the boys. By Allah, by whom Ibn Salam swears, we know Muhammad better than I know my son, because I do not know what his mother has done." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You have been granted success and you have spoken truly."

Some have claimed that what is meant by recognition here is that which comes through reflection and inference, because whatever relates to the details of his ﷺ features either remained intact at the time the verse was revealed or was not, but was altered and changed. The first is false, and it would not be possible for them to conceal it, because concealing what has spread throughout the regions is impossible. The second is likewise, because at that time they were not acquainted with his noble features ﷺ in the way they know the features of their sons.

It is answered that concealment is explicitly mentioned in the Qur'an, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿You make it into parchments, displaying them and concealing much﴾. Their concealment was not concealment of the texts themselves, but through interpreting them and by their saying that he is another man who will come forth. This is the meaning of the words of the Glorified: ﴿They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾.
