﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾, from among the People of the Two Books and the polytheists, ﴿they do not believe﴾
- in what must be believed in. The discussion of this construction has already been mentioned just above.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 21:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾, by his claim that He, exalted is His majesty, has a partner, and by his saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and ﴿these are our intercessors with Allah﴾. Among this is also counted the description of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, promised in the two Scriptures, contrary to his (true) attributes. The interrogative is for declaring something to be great in a claimed (exaggerated) manner. The commonly held view is that the intended meaning is the denial that anyone could be more unjust than one who did that, or equal to him in injustice. The construction, although it does not by its lexical form indicate the denial of equality, as the Allamah al-Thani said in his commentary on al-Maqasid and in the glosses on al-Kashshaf, does indicate it through usage. So when you say, "There is no one more excellent in the city than Zayd," its meaning is that he is more excellent than everyone, according to common usage. The secret behind this is that a relation between two things is generally conceived only in terms of difference, whether greater or lesser, especially in the matter of comparison by degrees. So if neither of the two is greater, a deficiency necessarily follows.

Some later scholars claimed that a fine and graceful point occurred to them in explaining this, which is this: two things that are equal, or even close to one another, in reality, are not safe from each being judged as surpassed by the other. For every person is unable to assess everything at its true worth, and every human being is unable to know every matter as it truly is. Understandings differ when confronted with illusions, and minds differ in repelling doubts. So if some people judge two things to be equal in reality, others may judge one of them to be superior according to the limits of their understanding, the extent of their intellects, and the reach of their perception. Thus, for everything that has someone equal to it in reality, there is someone who surpasses it according to the beliefs of people. Indeed, whenever there is someone close to it, there is someone who exceeds it in the assumptions of the common people. By the contrapositive, this reduces to our statement: whenever there is no one who surpasses it, there is no one who equals it, but rather no one even close to it, which is what is sought. In sum, the affirmation of an equal necessarily entails the affirmation of a superior one, so the negation of the superior necessarily entails the negation of the equal, because negating the necessary consequence entails negating what it necessitates, just as affirming what necessitates entails affirming the consequence. Reflect on this.

Some verifying scholars claimed that the construction's indication of the negation of equality is by conventional meaning, because whatever is not more excellent is either equal or lesser, so the expression is used for one of its two instances. Ibn al-Sa'igh said in the issue of kohl: "I have not seen a man whose eye is more beautified by kohl than Zayd's eye," and although it is explicit in negating excess, it applies to both excess and deficiency. But the intended meaning is the latter, from restricting a thing to some of its instances, like "the beast"; end of quote. You know that this too is according to convention.

﴿Or denies His signs﴾, such as denying the Qur'an, whose whole content includes the verse stating that the People of the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons, or denying the other miracles with which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was supported, by calling them magic. Among this is also counted the distortion of the Book and the alteration of the descriptions of him ﷺ that Allah the Exalted mentioned in it. He said "or" (أوْ) and not "and," though they combined both matters, to indicate that each one of them alone reaches the utmost extreme of excess in wronging oneself. It was also said: the word "or" draws attention to the fact that they combined two contradictory matters, meaning that they affirmed what is negated and negated what is affirmed. The intended meaning by "contradictory" is two matters whose nature is that they cannot be combined by convention. Or it is said: negating what is established by proof entails negating what has not been established by it, and likewise at the other extreme, so combining them is combining contradictories from this aspect.

Some claimed that the aspect of contradiction indicated by this conjunction is that fabricating against Allah the Exalted is a claim that what is attributed to Him must be accepted without any proof, while denying the signs is a claim that what is attributed to Him must not be accepted even if evidence is established for it, and that one must deny the admonition and persist in obstinacy, on the basis that the Messenger must be an angel.

It is not hidden that in the claim of contradiction there is some obscurity, and these explanations do not remove it. ﴿Indeed, it﴾, that is, the matter, meaning that this grave matter is what is intended, namely ﴿the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾, that is, they will not attain what they seek nor be saved from what they dislike ﴿the wrongdoers﴾.

12

- From the standpoint that they are wrongdoers, how will the most unjust succeed from the standpoint that he is the most unjust?

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 6, verse 22]**

﴿And the Day We will gather them all together﴾ is in the accusative as a time adverb (*zarf*) governed by a suppressed verb that is to be understood as following. The pronoun in *nahshuruhum* ("We gather them") refers either to all creatures, or to the worshippers of the false gods together with the things they worshipped. *Jami'an* ("all together") is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of that pronoun. The meaning is: "And the Day We gather all creation, or the disbelievers and their gods, altogether, then We will say to them what We will say, such and such." The verb of speech is omitted from the discourse so that it stays vague, since vagueness is more effective in causing fear and awe. The verb is supposed to be in the past tense, to indicate certainty, and this makes it appropriate for *thumma lam takun* ("then there was not") and what follows to be conjoined to it. It is also permitted to read the word in the accusative as an object (*maf'ul bihi*) of a suppressed verb, meaning: "And mention to them, for the sake of warning and admonition, the Day We gather them." Abu al-Baqa' preferred this reading. It has also been said that the implied sense is: "So that they may guard themselves, or so that they may beware, the Day We gather them..." and then "We will say," for rebuke and reproach before the witnesses, to those who associated partners with Allah, the Exalted, that for which He has sent down no authority: ﴿Where are your partners?﴾ That is, where are your gods which you made partners with Allah, may His name be glorified? The annexation (*idafah*) here is of the loosest kind of connection. *Ayna* ("where") is used to ask about something that is not present. The apparent sense of His words, exalted be He, ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses and what they used to worship﴾ and other verses, requires that these partners be present with them at the place of gathering. So either it may be said that this question is put when they are prevented from them after they have seen them, so that they may witness their disappointment, as it has been said: "As a cloud flashed for thirsty people, but when they saw it, it dispersed and vanished." Or it may be said that the question is put while they are seeing them, but because the partners do not benefit them, they are treated as absent, just as you say of someone who made another his supporter, to help him in hardships, when that person has not helped him and has fallen into trouble in his presence: "Where is Zayd?" You treat him as absent because of his lack of benefit, even though he is present, just as the absent person is. Or the speech contains an elided noun, meaning: "Where is their benefit and their use?" Some have insisted that they are absent because of the apparent sense of the question. As for His words, exalted be He, ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors, those whom﴾ up to His words, glorified be He, ﴿and what you used to claim has vanished from you﴾, it has been answered that this refers to another station, in order to reconcile the verses, or the meaning is: "We do not see the intercession of your intercessors."

Shaykh al-Islam said: This question, which indicates the absence of the partners despite their being gathered in general, in accordance with the verses that show this, occurs only after what has taken place between them and the worshippers of mutual disavowal from both sides and the severing of the ties that were between them, as His words, glorified be He, express: ﴿So We will separate them﴾ and so on. This is either because the partners are not truly present at that time, having been removed from that position, or because their absence in the capacity of partnership and intercession is considered as their absence in reality, since the question is not about them as partners, as the relative-clause description indicates. There is no doubt that the absence of the attribute necessitates the absence of the one described insofar as he is described. So they, insofar as they are partners, are necessarily absent, even though they are present insofar as their own essences, whether they were idols at first.

As for what is said, that they are prevented from them at the time of rebuke so that they lose them at the very hour in which they had placed their hope, so that they see the place of their grief and regret, this may suggest that they have not realized the true state, and that the cords of their hope have not yet been severed from them. But you know that they had witnessed them before that, and the handle of their desires had been completely cut, and moreover they had known them since the moment of death and the trial of punishment in the barzakh (intermediate state). What actually occurs at the gathering is the clear uncovering and the strong certainty that results from the confrontation and the dialogue. End of quotation.

Mawlana al-Shihab (al-Alusi) criticized this by saying: It is an imagining with no basis, because rebuke is intended in all aspects, and rebuke cannot then be conceived except after the contrary has been established. Moreover, that this occurs after the disavowal in another station is not indicated by the wording of the verse, and such a claim cannot be asserted without transmission, because it is possible that this is the station of disavowal. The implication mentioned does not hold, even though it is a rebuke. As for the addition with which his statement was supplemented, it is also open to objection, since the punishment of the barzakh does not require that they intercede for them afterwards, for many a person punished in his grave is interceded for. End of quotation.

You know that if their punishment was because of their belief that these gods benefit them and their hope for their intercession, then those who are punished for that reason... so His words, "because the punishment of the barzakh does not require..." are not in their proper place. Likewise, His words, "for many a person punished in his grave is interceded for," if by it he means that many a person punished in his grave for some sin is interceded for by someone who intercedes for him, then this is granted, but it does not prove the point. And if he means that many a person punished in his grave because of the worship of something is interceded for by that very thing, then the prohibition of this is clear, as is not hidden. So reflect.

Ya'qub read *yahshuruhum* ("He gathers them") and *thumma yaqulu* ("then He says") with the letter *ya* in both places, and the pronoun in both refers to Allah, the Exalted.

His words, exalted and glorified be He, to the polytheists: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾

**22**

- Either through an intermediary or without an intermediary. The speech that is negated in His words, "and He will not speak to them" and so on, is speech of honour and benefit, not speech in every sense. Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, was indeed spoken to, with what He spoke. The word *za'm* (claim) is used for what is true, as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Jibril (peace be upon him) claimed..." and in the hadith of Dimam ibn Tha'laba, may Allah be pleased with him: "Your messenger claimed..." and the words of Sibawayh in matters he approved: "al-Khalil claimed..." It is also used for what is false and untrue, as in this verse.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "Every *za'm* in the Qur'an means falsehood." It is often used for a strange thing whose responsibility remains upon the one who says it. Here it is transitive to two objects, both of which are omitted because they are understood from the context, meaning: "you claim them to be partners."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 23:

﴿Then their fitnah (trial, temptation) was not but that they said﴾ The original meaning of fitnah (trial, tempering), as verified by al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), is the placing of gold in fire in order to know its quality from its inferiority. Then it was used in meanings such as punishment, testing, affliction, calamity, disbelief, sin, misguidance
Page 123
and excuse. The sense intended here has been disputed. It is said: it means shirk (associating partners with God). Al-Zajjaj chose this view, and ʿAtaʾ related it from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both. The expression of shirk as fitnah seems to be because it is that by which one is tempted and which pleases you, and they were pleased with their disbelief and proud of it. The statement, in this case, is either by omission of an annexed term, as the apparent sense of some scholars' words requires, or by treating the outcome of a thing as the thing itself by claim, which is sweeter in taste and more far-reaching in meaning. The restriction (ḥaṣr) is relative to the class of statements, or claimed. As for the words of God Most High: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾

32

- this is a metaphor for disavowing shirk and the absence of adhering to it, meaning: then the outcome of their shirk was nothing but their disowning it. Al-Zajjaj stated that the like of what is in the verse is that you see a person who loves a misguided one, and when he falls into ruin he disowns him, so it is said to him: "Your love for so-and-so was nothing but that you disowned him." That is not of the type of "your complaint is the sword," nor of the omission of an annexed term, although that is valid here, and it is a fine, subtle meaning which none knows except one who knows the speech of the Arabs. It is also said: the intended meaning is excuse, and it is used in this sense because, as mentioned earlier, it is a means of extricating oneself from deceit, and excuse extricates one from sin, so it was borrowed for it.

This is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu ʿAbd Allah, Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, may God be pleased with them. It is also said: the answer given is something false. The reason for the use of the term is that it is the cause of the trial, so it is figuratively applied to it, using the effect for the cause. It may also be that there is a metaphor, because the answer also saves them, like an excuse. It is said: the restriction under these two views is real, and the oath-sentence is in its apparent sense. The reading of "takun" (was) with the feminine ta, and "fitnatuhum" (their trial) in the nominative, is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs from ʿAsim. Hamzah and al-Kisai read "yakun" with the masculine ya, and "fatanatuhum" in the accusative. Likewise they read "rabbana" in the accusative, as a vocative or as a laudatory address. It is also read in the irregular readings as "rabbu" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, serving as a preface to the denial of their associating partners; its purpose is to remove the suspicion that the denial of shirk would be by denying divinity to Him, exalted and high. The remaining readers read with the feminine ta and also the accusative of "fitnatuhum". The readings of the first group were explained on the basis that "fitnatuhum" is the subject of "takun", the feminine verb being due to its being attributed to a feminine noun, and "an qalu" is its predicate.

Hamzah and al-Kisai (read) on the basis that "an qalu" is the subject, and the verb is not feminine because it is attributed to a masculine noun, and "fitnatuhum" is the predicate.

The reading of the rest is similar to this, except that the feminine marking in it is based on the school of the Kufans, for they permit in the latitude of speech the feminization of the subject of "kana" when it is a masculine verbal noun and the predicate is feminine and placed first, as in his saying:

"And he has failed whose inner nature was treachery."

They cite this reading as evidence for that. The Basrans held that this is a necessity of poetry. It is said: the feminine marking is in accordance with the meaning of the saying, and it is of the type of "his letter came to him" meaning "my message." It is not hidden that this is rare in their speech. Al-Zamakhshari said, and it was transmitted verbatim from Abu ʿAli: this is of the type of "whose mother was you." It was disputed with what is of no benefit. Some claimed that the last two readings are more eloquent than the first, because in them the more definite is made the predicate and the less definite the subject, since "an qalu" resembles the pronoun, and the pronoun is the most definite of definites; this is contrary to the common and well-known usage, rather than the two others. There is a point to consider here, for it does not follow that the resemblance of one thing to another entails its resemblance in all rulings. The sentence, in all the readings, is coordinated with the omitted verb governing "the day We gather them" etc., as the reference to it has passed. Many have made it coordinated with the sentence before it, and "thumma" (then) is either in its apparent sense, based on the first view, or for remoteness in rank, based on the last two views, because their excuse or this answer of theirs is greater than the earlier rebuke.

You know that there is no necessity to depart from the apparent sense, since it is possible that there is a lapse of time there, based on the fact that the standing is great; so it may be said: when they witnessed the terror of that day and the manifestation of the Mighty King, may His majesty be exalted, upon them with the attribute of majesty, as the preceding sentence indicates,
Page 124
they were bewildered and astonished, and so they could not answer except after a time. Among what indicates their astonishment and bewilderment is that they lied and swore in this speech of theirs. Had they not been bewildered and astonished, they would not have said what they said, because realities are uncovered on the Day of Resurrection; when its people are made to see them and to see that they are not hidden from Him, glory be to Him, and that there is no benefit for them in such a thing, its issuing from them becomes impossible.

Because of their neglect of the matter's being built upon astonishment and bewilderment, al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi and those who agree with them denied the permissibility of lying to the people of the Resurrection, citing what we have mentioned. They answered regarding the verse that the meaning is "we were not polytheists" in our belief and our assumptions, because they used to believe about themselves that they were monotheists, far removed from shirk; and they objected against themselves that on this reckoning they would be truthful in what they reported, so why did He, glory be to Him, say:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 24:

﴿Look how they lied﴾ i.e., in their saying ﴿"By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾. Some have answered that the meaning is not that they lied in the Hereafter, but rather that the meaning is: look how they lied against themselves in the world. This has been rejected: the verse does not indicate this meaning in any way, nor does it fit it, because it concerns their loss and their state in the Hereafter, not in the world. Rather, it stands in utter opposition to it, since the beginning and end of the noble discourse are about that. Inserting an account of their state in the world between them disrupts it, and it is an extreme forced interpretation. What the majority hold is also supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when Allah will raise them all up, and they will swear to Him as they swear to you, and they will think that they stand on something. Unquestionably, they are the liars.﴾ This comes after His words, glorified is He: ﴿and they swear upon a lie while they know﴾, where He likened their lying in the Hereafter to their lying in the world. The command to look also points to this comparison, as is not hidden from one who reflects.

Ibn al-Munir mentioned that the verse is clear evidence that informing about a thing contrary to what it is, is a lie, even if the informer does not know that his report contradicts reality. Do you not see that He, glorified is He, made their report and disavowal a lie, even though He, exalted is His majesty, informed about them with His words, the Exalted: ﴿And what they used to invent has vanished from them﴾?

42

- That is, they were deprived of its knowledge at that time through bewilderment and confusion, so this does not remove the description of lying from them. You know that interpreting this clause in the manner mentioned is not apparent. What is related from al-Hasan is that (ma) is a relative pronoun, and what is meant by it is the idols they used to worship and say about them: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾, or something similar. The use of "invent" (iftira') upon them, although in reality it falls upon their states, is for emphasis regarding their matter, as if they themselves were the thing invented: that is, their idols have departed and gone from them, the ones about which they used to invent what they invented, so they did not avail them anything against Allah. It has also been said that (ma) is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), meaning: their invention went astray, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿their effort went astray﴾, meaning it did not benefit them. The clause is said to be a new independent sentence; it was also said, and Shaykh al-Islam preferred, that it is coordinated (ʿatf) upon (kadhabu, "they lied") and included with it under the sense of wonder, since the preceding interrogative (istifham) is suspended (mu'allaq) and has no bearing on this. The meaning, on the possibility of the relative and the verbal-source readings, is: look how they lied with the brazen, emphatic oath against themselves, by denying that what proceeded from them had proceeded; and how their invention went astray, that is, departed and vanished, or what they used to invent of associating partners, until they denied its occurrence from them entirely and disowned it utterly.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 25:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you.﴾ This is a statement brought in to relate what issued in the world from some of the polytheists by way of the rulings of disbelief, and then to explain what will issue from them on the Day of Gathering, as a confirmation of what preceded it and a verification of its content. The pronoun in (minhum) refers to those who associated partners (with God). Al-istima' (listening) means al-isgha' (attentive hearing); it is intransitive and is made transitive with the preposition (li), as the lexicographers have explicitly stated. It has also been said that it is implicitly containing the meaning of al-isgha', and its object is understood, namely the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him and his father), in the narration of Abu Salih, said: "Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, Umayya and Ubayy ibn Khalaf listened to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)
Page 125
while he was reciting the Qur'an. They said to al-Nadr: 'O Abu Qutayla, what does Muhammad say?' He said: 'By Him who made it (the Ka'ba) His house, I do not know what he says except that I see the movement of his lips as he speaks something; he says nothing but the fables of the ancients, like what I used to tell you about the past generations.' al-Nadr used to narrate much about the earlier generations, and he would tell the Quraysh, and they found his narration pleasing. So God revealed this verse."

The pronoun of (man) is singular in (yastami'u) and plural in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, looking to its wording and then to its meaning. Al-Karkhi said: The reason it says (yastami'u) here and (yastami'una) in Yunus is that what is here concerns a few people, so they are treated as one; while what is there concerns a multitude of disbelievers, so the plural suits it. The reason it is not pluralized in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ is that what is meant is looking that entails witnessing the proofs of truthfulness and the signs of prophethood, and those who look in this way are fewer than those who listen to the Qur'an. (Al-ja'l) here carries the sense of (al-inshã', creating/placing). (Akinna) is the plural of (kinan), like (ghita'; aghiya), in wording and meaning, because the pattern fa'al, with fatha or kasra on the first letter, takes the plural af'ila in the paucity plurals, like ahmira and aqdhila, and the plural fu'l in the abundance plurals, like humr; except when it is doubled or has a weak final radical, in which case its plural is necessarily af'ila, like akinna and akhbiya, except rarely. The verb (kanna) is triliteral, and there is also a form with the prefix, (akanna); al-Tabarsi and others mention that both are used, and al-Raghib distinguished between them, saying: (akannatu) is used for what is concealed in the soul, while the triliteral is for other things. The tanwin is for emphasis; the waw is for conjunction; and the sentence is conjoined to the sentence before it, a verbal sentence conjoined to a nominal one. It has also been said that the waw is for the circumstantial, meaning "and We have placed." And ﴿over their hearts﴾ is connected to the verb before it.

Abu Hayyan claimed that if (ja'l) means (alqa, to cast), then the adverbial phrase is connected to it, and if it means (sayyara, to make), then it is connected to an omitted element, since it occupies the position of the second object. The meaning according to what we have mentioned is: "We created over their hearts coverings in great number, whose quantity cannot be measured," ﴿lest they understand it﴾, i.e., out of aversion that they should comprehend what they hear of the Qur'an, which is indicated by the mention of listening. So the speech is on the assumption of an elided noun. Some have assumed (la) (not) before it, i.e., lest they not understand it, and they do likewise in similar cases. It is also permitted that it be an object of what is indicated by His words, exalted be He: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, i.e., We prevented them from understanding it; or of what is indicated by (akinna) alone from that. ﴿And in their ears is a deafness﴾, i.e., deafness and heaviness in hearing that prevents them from hearing it as it ought to be heard. According to more than one scholar, the statement is an image expressing the completeness of their ignorance of the affairs of the Prophet (ﷺ), the extreme remoteness of their hearts from understanding the noble Qur'an, and the rejection of their ears, may God make them deaf. It is also permitted that there be here a clear metaphor, or an implicit metaphor, or an allusion-by-association. You have already had in al-Baqara what will benefit you here, so recall it.

Talha read (wiqran) with a kasra, and it is, as Zajjaj explicitly stated, the load of a mule or the like. Its accusative on both readings is by conjunction to (akinna), as Abu al-Baqa' said. ﴿And if they see﴾, i.e., witness and perceive, ﴿every sign﴾, i.e., a miracle indicating the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), according to what is transmitted from Zajjaj, and this is what the words of Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him and his father) require, such as the splitting of the moon, the water gushing between his noble fingers, the multiplication of a little food, and what resembles these. ﴿They will not believe in it﴾, because of the extremity of their obstinacy and the firm entrenchment of imitation in them. The statement is of the type of generality of negation, like "all of that did not happen," not of the type of negation of generality.

What is meant is censure of them for not benefiting from the sense of sight, after He, glory be to Him, mentioned their not benefiting by their intellects and their hearing. It is reported from some of them that it is necessary to restrict the verse to other than compelling signs, to avoid contradiction between this and His words, exalted be He: ﴿If We will, We shall send down upon them from the heaven a sign, and their necks will remain humbly subjected to it﴾. Some were content with taking faith to mean faith by choice, and distinguished between it and the subjection of the necks; so let this be understood. Shaykh al-Islam restricted the verse to those signs that were Qur'anic, i.e., "and if they see something of that," by their seeing it through hearing it, "they will not believe in it." Perhaps what we have put forward is sweeter to the sound taste.

﴿Until, when they come to you, they dispute with you﴾, i.e., they contend with you and quarrel with you. (Hatta) here is the one after which sentences occur; it is called the initial (hatta al-ibtida'iyya), and the sentence following it has no place in i'rab; this differs from al-Zajjaj and Ibn Darastawayh, who claimed that it is in the place of a genitive by (hatta). This is refuted by the fact that prepositions are not disconnected from governing; they only enter upon a singular noun or what is in its interpretation. The sentence here is His words: ﴿when they come to you﴾ together with the answer of the conditional, namely His words, glory be to Him and exalted be He: ﴿those who disbelieve say﴾, and what lies between them is a circumstantial clause from the subject of (jã'ū). The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the personal pronoun to censure them through what is in the scope of the relative clause and to indicate the cause of the ruling. (Idha) is in the accusative place as an adverb of time, governed by the conditional or by the answer, according to the well-known disagreement on this. It has been objected that making (yujadilunaka) in the position of a circumstantial clause and (yaqulu al-ladhina) the answer leads to making the speech void, since disputing is itself this saying, unless disputing is interpreted as intending it.

This is not hidden in its problem, for disputing is absolute contention, and it is so called because of the severity in it, or because each of the two disputants wishes to throw his companion down onto the jadala, i.e., the ground. The said saying is one instance of it, so the statement conveys a more eloquent meaning, like your saying: "If Zayd insults you, he curses you." Some grammarians mention that when (idha) follows (hatta), it may be taken to mean (fa, then), and it may be taken to mean (ila, until); the limit is considered in both cases, meaning: they have gone so far in denial and obstinacy that when they come to you disputing with you, they do not suffice with mere non-belief, but say: "(in hadha) — i.e., this is not — ﴿except the fables of the ancients﴾."

52

— i.e., their written tales on which no one relies. Qatada said: their lies and their falsehood.

The sum of what has been mentioned is that their denial reached its extreme by what has been stated, because it is the complete instance. Similar to this is: "The people died, until the prophets [died]." It has also been permitted that (hatta) be the genitive particle, and ﴿when they come to you﴾ be in the place of a genitive; this is the view of al-Akhfash, followed by Ibn Malik in al-Tashil, and Abu Hayyan refuted it in his commentary. In that case (idha) is outside of the adverbial sense, as they have stated, and outside of the conditional sense as well, so there is no answer for it; then it says at that point: an explanation of (layujadilunaka), and it too is in the place of a circumstantial clause. The asatir, according to al-Akhfash, is a plural without a singular, like ababil and madhakir; some said it has a singular. In the Qamus it is the plural of isţar and isţir (with kasra on both) and ustur, and with the ta' marbuta in all of them; it has also been said it is the plural of asţar, with fatha on the hamza, the plural of satr with two fathas, like sabab and asbab, so it is a plural of a plural. The root sațr means a line.

[Page 127]

﴿They forbid others from it﴾. The pronoun in "they" refers to the polytheists, and the pronoun in "from it" refers to the Qur'an. That is, they are not satisfied with merely denying it and calling it a tale of myths. Rather, they forbid people from listening to it, lest they come to recognize its truth and believe in it. ﴿And they keep away from it﴾, that is, they distance themselves from it personally, to show the extent of their aversion and to reinforce their prohibition. The one who avoids what he forbids others from is completing the prohibition. Perhaps this is what Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam, a title of the jurist and scholar) meant when he said: "This is the secret behind placing the keeping away after the forbidding." This is the interpretation that Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "from it" refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: they forbid people from believing in him, peace and blessings be upon him, and they keep away from him. This is the interpretation that Abna' Jarir (Ibn Jarir), al-Mundhir, Abu Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ibn Jarir also transmitted it through al-Awfi. This is also reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "they" refers to Abu Talib and his followers or his like, while the pronoun in "from it" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: they forbid people from harming him, peace and blessings be upon him, and they do not believe in him.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Hilal that he said: "The verse was revealed concerning the uncles of the Prophet (ﷺ), who were ten in number. They were the most supportive of him openly, and the most hostile to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in private."

It has also been said that the plural pronoun refers to Abu Talib alone, and it is expressed in the plural to magnify his action, as if it were something no single person could accomplish. It has also been said that it was revealed in the manner of multiple actions, and so it is like the saying: "Stop at al-Mazini." Its distance is not hidden. This view was also transmitted by a group from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

It is reported from Muqatil that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with Abu Talib, calling him to Islam. Then the Quraysh gathered before him, intending evil against the Prophet (ﷺ). So he recited in verse:

By Allah, they will never reach you with their gathering
until I am laid in the dust, buried.

So proclaim your command, for you have no shame in it,
and rejoice, and let your eyes be refreshed by it.

You called me, and you claimed that you were a sincere advisor,
and you have indeed spoken the truth, and you were a trustworthy one there.

You presented a religion which is, without doubt,
among the best religions of mankind.

Were it not for the blame, or my fear of a disgraceful reproach,
you would have found me gladly accepting it, clearly."

Then this verse was revealed. According to this view and the one before it, there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person). Al-Imam (al-Razi) rejected the last view on the grounds that all the preceding verses condemn the action of the polytheists, so mention of forbidding harm to him, peace and blessings be upon him, does not fit here, and that is not blameworthy. This has been challenged on the grounds that the blame applies to the collective as a collective. Based on this verse, on this narration, some who claimed that Abu Talib did not believe in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) have argued for it. The detailed investigation of this matter will come, Allah willing, in its proper place.

Keeping away (al-na'y) is an intransitive verb that takes the particle "ʿan" when transitive, as in the verse. It is reported from al-Wahidi that he heard it used transitively without a particle from al-Mubarrad, and he recited: "I rebuke him if he becomes an echo in a distant desert; my visitor and my kinsman have kept away from me." Some have explained this as an omission and conjunction. There is no hiding the beautiful paronomasia (tajnis, a figure of speech in which words look alike but differ in meaning) in "yanhawna" and "yan'awna." It has also been read as "wayanawna" from it.

﴿And they destroy only themselves﴾, that is, they do not destroy anything except themselves, by exposing themselves to the most severe and dreadful punishment, which is the punishment of misguidance and of leading others astray. ﴿And they are not aware﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "they destroy", meaning they limit the destruction to themselves, while they are unaware, neither of their own destruction nor of their destruction being limited to themselves, and that they do not harm the Qur'an or the Prophet (ﷺ) in any way. The destruction is expressed in this way, although what is denied of harm to others is absolute harm, to indicate that what befalls them is destruction, not mere harm. Moreover, their aim was not merely to hinder what they mentioned, but they sought to plot evils against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is the thread that holds together the string of the pearls of the Qur'anic verses.

It is also permissible that the destruction is considered in relation to those whom they lead astray by forbidding. Then restricting it to themselves, while it includes both groups, is based on treating the punishment of misguidance as equivalent to the punishment of leading others astray as if it were nothing. The denial of awareness (shu'ur), according to al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), is more emphatic than the denial of knowledge ('ilm), as if it were said: "They do not perceive that at all."

[p. 128]

﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾: this begins a report of what will issue from them on the Day of Resurrection, namely speech that contradicts the vile deeds that proceeded from them in the world, and that speech is itself false. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, or to everyone who is fit for it, aiming to show how evil their condition is and how far its heinousness reaches, such that no beholder is singled out from another. The *law* (لَوْ, "if") is conditional in its original sense, and its answer is omitted so that the listener's mind may go every way, which makes it more effective in conveying awe. A parallel to this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"By your grandfather, if something had come to us, its messenger other than you, we would not have found for you a means of repelling it."*

And their saying: "If a woman with bracelets had slapped me." The verb *tara* (تَرى, "you see") is visual, and its object is omitted because what follows in the adverbial clause indicates it. The word *al-iqaf* (الإيقاف, "being made to stand") may derive from the well-known meaning of standing (*al-wuquf*), or from the sense of knowing (*al-ma'rifah*), as one says "awqaftuhu 'ala kadha" when one has made him understand and recognize something. Al-Zajjaj preferred this second meaning, i.e. "if you could see their condition when they are made to stand over the Fire, until they witness it, or are raised onto its bridge while it is beneath them and they look at it, or enter it and come to know the measure of its punishment, you would see what the frame of expression cannot encompass." The use of the past form indicates certainty.

It has been said that *law* (لَوْ) here means *inna* (إنَّ, "indeed"). Some permitted that *tara* be cognitive (عِلْمِيَّة), but this is as you see. It is read *waqafu* (وَقَفُوا) with the active form from *waqafa 'alayhi*, the intransitive verb, whose verbal noun is generally *al-wuquf*. The verb *waqafa* is also used transitively, with verbal noun *al-waqf*, and *uqifa* is heard in it as a rare dialect form.

It has been said that by analogy the verb (*faqalu*, "and they will say") is used because of the magnitude of what they have realized. *Ya layta-na nuradd* (﴿يا لَيْتَنا نُرَدُّ﴾, "Would that we were returned"), meaning to the world. The *ya* (يا) is either for alerting or for calling, and the one called is omitted, i.e. "O our people," for example. ﴿And not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, meaning the Qur'an, as we used to deny before and say: "tales of the ancients." Some explained "the signs" as including that and the miracles. Shaykh al-Islam said: it may be that by them is meant the signs that speak of the states of the Fire and its terrors, enjoining the avoidance of it, on the basis that these are what then come to their minds, and they grieve over what they neglected regarding them. It may also be that by them is meant all the signs comprised in those signs in an initial sense of inclusion ﴿and be among the believers﴾ — meaning, so that we would not see this terrifying station, just as the believers did not see it.

The nasb (نَصْب, "accusative mood") of the two verbs — according to what al-Zamakhshari said, and which al-Halabi says al-Zajjaj preceded him in — is by the implied *an* (أنْ) in answer to the wish (التَّمَنِّي, "wishing"). The meaning: if we are returned, we will not deny and we will be among the believers. Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that the accusative after the *wa* (وَاو, "and") is not in the sense of answering, because it does not occur in the answer of a conditional, so no conditional-answer relation is formed with what precedes or follows it; rather the *wa* is a conjunctive particle that links what follows to the presumed verbal noun before it, and as a conjunction, with the accusative, one of its three senses is fixed, namely concomitance (المَعِيَّة, "accompaniment"), and it is distinguished from the *fa* (فاء, "then") by the validity of its occupying the place of *fa* or of the circumstantial (الحال, "adverbial state"). The basis of the one who said it is an answer is that they take the accusative in the places where *fa* takes it, so one imagines it is an answer. What makes clear it is not is that *fa* alone is dropped without it: when *fa* is removed, the verb after it is jussive due to what precedes it, because of the conditional sense it contains. It is answered that *wa* is here treated in the manner of *fa*. Ibn al-Anbari made it a substitute for it. What supports this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Ishaq: (فَلا نُكَذِّبَ, "then we would not deny"). Also objected to is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned about the sense of conditional answer, that their being returned would not be a cause of their not denying. It is answered that causation suffices if it is in their supposition. It is rejected that mere return is not fit for this, so there must be a qualification that what is meant is the return that occurs after what compelled them to it, since the realities of things have become manifest to them. Because of this subtlety, whoever preferred the conjunction with a presumed verbal noun before it did so, as if it were said: "Would that we had a return, and the absence of denial, and being among the believers."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read both verbs in the nominative (رَفْع), and it is interpreted as the beginning of a speech of theirs, not conjoined to what precedes it, with the *wa* being like a superfluous particle; like the saying of a sinner to one who harms him for what has issued from him: "Leave me, and I will not return," meaning "I will not return; you leave me, or you do not leave me." Of this, according to what Imam Abd al-Qahir said, is his verse:

*"Today is two days since you were absent from my sight — my soul be your ransom — what is my sin, that I should make excuse?"*

It seems that what calls for this arrangement in this line is to convey the exaggeration suited to the context of amorous dalliance. Some preferred that it be a beginning of speech in the sense that it is cut off from what is within the scope of the wish, while being conjoined to it as a conjunction of report upon a directive (إنشاء). Some grammarians permitted this absolutely, and Abu Hayyan transmitted it from Sibawayh. It is also permitted that it be included under the ruling of the wish, on the basis that it is conjoined to (نُرَدُّ, "we are returned") or is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in it. So the meaning, as al-Shihab said, is upon the wish for the combination of the two matters: the return and the absence of denial, that is, the assent that results after return to the world, because return is not intended for its own sake here. That it is a wish is evident, since it is not attained at the time of the wish; even if the wish is directed at faith and assent, their wish is for what benefits them, since what is attained now does not benefit them, because they are not in a house of obligation. So they wish for a faith that would benefit them, and that comes only after an impossible return, and what depends on the impossible is impossible. Ibn 'Amir read the first in the nominative and the second in the accusative, according to what you have just learned; and the answer-relation is either with respect to the whole or with respect to the second, and non-denial of the signs is distinct from faith and assent, so there is no unity.

It is read anomalously in the reverse of this reading.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 28:**

﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before.﴾ This is an *idrab* (a turning away, i.e. a shift in meaning) from what their wish, namely the promise to affirm the signs and believe in them, would imply. That is, this is not from a sound resolve arising from a desire for faith and a longing to attain it and to be characterized by it. Rather, it is because there became apparent and manifest to them, in that standing of theirs, what they used to conceal in the world, namely *thalithat al-athafi* (the third of the three stones of a cooking hearth) and *al-dahya' al-dahyā'* (the great calamity). Because of the severity of the terror of that and their great distress from it, they said what they said. So what is meant by the relative pronoun is the Fire, as the context requires. By their concealing it is meant concealing its reality, and that is by denying its occurrence and not believing in its existence at all. It is as if it were said: "Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to deny in the world and reject as real."

Why Allah, glory be to Him, did not explicitly say "denied," as in His saying, *"This is Hell, which the criminals used to deny"* (52:14), and His saying, *"This is the Fire which you used to deny"* (52:14, in another form), even though that would be more fitting to what precedes it, namely their saying, *"And that we would not deny the signs of our Lord"*, is that it observes what corresponds to it, which is the appearing in general, together with the hidden allusion that their denial was not in its place at all, due to the strength of the evidence. It has also been said: what is meant by what they used to conceal is their abominations other than shirk, which they used to hide from people, so that they appear in their records and through the testimony of their limbs against them. It has also been said: what is meant by it is the shirk which they denied at some stations of the Resurrection, by their saying, *"By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"* (6:23). It has also been said: what is meant by it is the matter of the Resurrection and the Rising, and the pronoun in the nominative refers to the leaders of the disbelievers, while the pronoun in the genitive refers to their followers. That is, there became apparent to the followers what the leaders, who were followed, used to conceal from them in the world, concerning the matter of the Resurrection and the Rising. This is attributed to al-Hasan, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

It has also been said: the verse concerns the hypocrites. The pronoun in the nominative refers to them and the pronoun in the genitive refers to the believers, and what is meant by the relative pronoun is disbelief. That is, there became apparent to the believers what the hypocrites used to conceal of disbelief and hide from them in the world. It has also been said: it concerns the People of the Book absolutely, or their scholars. What they concealed is the prophethood of the Seal of the Messengers (ﷺ), and the two pronouns, the nominative and the genitive, refer to them and to the believers, or to the elite and the common people. All of this has been criticized on the ground that, even after overlooking what it contains of forcing meanings, there is no way to it here, because the sequence of the majestic composition is for magnifying the matter of the Fire and depicting the terrible condition of its people. Their standing before it has been mentioned, and it has been indicated that there came upon them at that point such fear, dread, bewilderment and astonishment that no description can encompass. He linked their aforementioned wish to them with the *fa'* (so) that implies causation of what precedes for what follows. Thus the removal of the Fire after that is part of the causal connection, while the Fire itself is the greatest of calamities and the most forceful of deterrents. To relate the removal to something less than it in this respect, together with the fact that its mention does not occur there, is a matter that the sanctity of the revelation should be exalted above.

It is related from al-Mubarrad that the speech is by elision of a modifier, that is, "there became apparent to them the consequence (*wabal*) of what they used to conceal." What is in this is not hidden either, so consider it carefully.

﴿And even if they were returned﴾ from that standing of theirs to the world ﴿they would surely return to what they were forbidden﴾ of disbelief and denial, or of what is more general than that, which includes what has been mentioned by primary inclusion, and its excellence is not hidden. The basis of the necessary connection in this conditional is the prior decree of Allah the Exalted concerning them with that, which follows from the corruption of their nature, the impurity of their constitution and the evil of their readiness. For this reason, witnessing what they witnessed will not benefit them. It has also been said that what is meant is that if they were returned to their former state of lack of knowledge and of witnessing, they would return. It is not hidden that this does not suit the context of censuring them for their excessiveness in disbelief and persistence, and that this is a response to their aforementioned wish. Some people have mentioned, in explaining why witnessing does not benefit them in the Hereafter, regarding its terrors which follow from sins after being returned to the world, that at that point it is like the report of the Prophet (ﷺ), supported by clear miracles. Since they did not benefit from it, and what prevented them prevented them, they will not benefit from what is like it, and what prevents them will also prevent them.

You know that this, after granting that witnessing after the return is like the report of the truthful one, returns in the Hereafter to what we have pointed to of the prior decree and the evil of readiness. And whoever is created for wretchedness, and Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the refuge, is for wretchedness, so ﴿indeed they are liars﴾.

- That is, they are indeed liars in what their wish contains of the report that this is what they desire. It may be that this is the beginning of a declaration from Him, exalted, that the habit and the constant practice of these people is lying. On both possibilities, the lying is not directed at the wish itself, because it is an *insha'* (performative, non-declarative speech), and performative speech does not admit of truth or falsehood. Al-Rab'i said: there is no harm in directing falsehood at the wish, because it admits of truth and falsehood in itself. He argued for this with the line: *"If your wish is true, it is the best of wishes; and if not, we have lived by it a pleasant while."* For the word *haqq* (true) means truthfulness, which is the opposite of falsehood and lying. The weakness of this is not hidden, and even if it is granted, it is also a *majaz* (figurative usage). It has been said that the implicit report here is the promise of faith and of not denying. It was objected that a promise, like a threat, belongs to the category of performative speech, as has been verified in its place, so truth and falsehood do not apply to it, just as they do not apply to performative speech in general. It was answered that this is one of two opinions on the question, the second being that promise and threat belong to the category of declarative speech and not performative. This opinion is based on the possibility that what is meant by the lying directed at the promise is failure to fulfil it, not its failure to correspond to reality, as al-Raghib mentioned.

[p. 131]

﴿And they said﴾ is conjoined to (ʿādū) as the majority hold. Ibn al-Kamal objected to this, arguing that ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾ would then have to be placed after the conjoined element, or before the element it is conjoined to. It is answered that its placement in the middle is because it is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) brought to confirm what the conditional clause conveys about their specific lying. Had it been placed later, it would have given the impression that the intended meaning is their being called liars for denying resurrection. It is also permitted that it be conjoined to (innahum la-kādhibūn), or to the predicate of (inna), or to (nuhū), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "they said it." It may also be a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), mentioning what they said in the world: ﴿It is not but our worldly life﴾, meaning, "it is nothing but our worldly life." The pronoun refers to the life mentioned after it, as in the words of al-Mutanabbi:

"He is the grandeur, until the eye surpasses its sister,
and until the day becomes the master of the day."

They have stated that it is valid for a pronoun to refer to something that comes later both in wording and in rank, in various cases, among them when the predicate of the pronoun explains it, as here. Some of them made it the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn). This cannot apply according to the view of the majority, because they stipulated that its predicate must be a sentence. The Kufans differed with them on this. It is reported from them that its predicate may be a single word, either absolutely or on condition that the single word functions as a verb, such as an active participle, as in: "Indeed he is standing, Zayd," on the basis that it then takes the place of a sentence. It has also been said, though this is remote, that the mentioned pronoun may be an expression of what is in the mind, which is life, and the meaning would be: "There is no life but our life in which we are." This is what is meant by their saying "the world," not the one that is near to perish, nor the lowly one, nor the one that comes before the Hereafter, as the believers say. All of these are contrary to the apparent meaning, especially the last. ﴿And we are not to be resurrected﴾ 92

- That is, if this life departs from us at all.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 6, verse 30:**

﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ is an allegorical representation (*tamthil*) of their being detained for questioning and rebuke. Alternatively, it is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for that, according to those who do not require that the literal meaning be possible. It is also permissible to consider the figurative usage (*tajawwuz*) to apply to the single word, although the preferred view among them is that it applies to the whole sentence. It has also been said that *wuquf* here means *ittila'* (being informed of or having knowledge of), which takes *ʿala* as well. In the statement there is an omitted noun (*mudaf muqaddar*), meaning "they were made to stand over the decree of their Lord or His recompense." There is no need for *tadmin* (implying one verb in the sense of another) or for treating it as an inversion (*qalb*), as has been supposed. It has also been said that it means *ittila'* without the need to posit an omitted noun, in the sense of "they knew Him, glorified and exalted be He, with the knowledge that is due to Him." However, knowing Him as He is due to be known does not necessarily mean knowing Him with the full knowledge that is due, so as to ask, "How is this, when it has been said: 'We have not known You as You are truly to be known'?" Some of the Zahiriyya (literalist school) used this verse as evidence that the people of the Resurrection will stand close to God, may He be exalted, at the place of reckoning, but what this entails is not hidden.

He said: This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) arising from the preceding speech, as if it were asked: "What did their Lord, glorified and exalted be He, say to them at that time?" And the answer was given: "He said..." It is also permissible that it occupy the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "saying": ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾, that is, the Resurrection and what follows it are real, not false, as you claimed. It has been said that the demonstrative refers to the punishment alone, but this is not correct. Nor is there any indication in ﴿So taste﴾ according to the people of spiritual experience (*arbab al-dhawq*, the Sufis) that this is the case. The interrogative particle *hamza* is for rebuke over their denial. They said it is a resumptive sentence, as has already been mentioned. ﴿Yes﴾ is the truth, ﴿by our Lord﴾. They confirmed their acknowledgment with an oath, to show the perfection of their certainty of its truth, and to indicate that this was said by them willingly and eagerly, hoping that it would benefit them. But how far-fetched that is!

﴿He said: Taste the punishment﴾ which you denied before and rejected, ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾.

3

That is: because of your persistent disbelief, or in exchange for it, or in return for it, or because of that which you used to disbelieve in. Here *ma* is either a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyya*) or a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), and the first is preferable. Perhaps this rebuke and reproach, as has been said, occurs only after they have been made to stand over the Fire and have said what they said, since the more evident view is that after this matter nothing remains but punishment. The reverse is also possible, and the matter of ordering is easy.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 31:

﴿Indeed, those who denied the meeting with Allah have lost﴾. They are the disbelievers whose circumstances have been related. However, placing the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) in the position of the pronoun is to indicate that their loss is caused by what is contained in the relative clause, namely denying the meeting with Allah the Exalted and persisting in it. What is meant by "the meeting" is the meeting with what He, glorified and exalted, has promised, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them. Some have explicitly stated that a noun has been omitted, meaning "the meeting of the recompense with Allah the Exalted." Others have explicitly stated that "the meeting with Allah the Exalted" is a metaphorical figure of speech (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) for the Resurrection and what follows it. ﴿Until, when the Hour comes upon them﴾: that is, the specific time, which is the Day of Resurrection. The origin of as-sa'ah (the Hour) is a portion of time, but it became predominant for the appointed time, like the Pleiades being called "the star" (al-najm). It is called "sa'ah" (hour) because of its brevity in relation to what follows it of eternity, or because of the swiftness of the reckoning in it by the Creator, may His name be exalted. Some have interpreted it here as the time of death, and the stated end-point applies to the denial.

It is permitted that it be an end-point for the loss as well, but in the commonly understood sense, and the speech then is in the manner of His saying, the Exalted:
Page 132
﴿And indeed upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment﴾, meaning: you are blameworthy and cursed upon until that day. So when the day comes, you will meet what makes you forget the curse with it. It is as if it were said: "Those who denied will lose, until the Day of the Establishment of the Hour, with various kinds of trials and afflictions. Then when the Hour is established, they will fall into what makes them forget this loss." That is the manifest loss. ﴿Suddenly﴾: that is, abruptly and suddenly; *bagtatan* with a vowel on the first letter is similar to it, and *bagatahu* like *mana'ahu* means he came upon him suddenly, i.e., came upon him without his awareness. Its accusative case is that it is a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the subject of (jā'atHum): meaning "surprisingly," or from its object, meaning "taken by surprise." It is permitted that it be in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of (jā'atHum), in the manner of "he returned backwards," or of a verb implied from the wording or from elsewhere. His saying, the Glorified and Exalted: ﴿They say﴾ is the answer of "idha" (when). ﴿Alas for us!﴾ is a vocative address to regret (hasrah), which is intense remorse, as if it were said: "O regret of ours, come, for this is your time." It was said: although this lamenting occurs to them at death, since death is among the precursors of the Hereafter, it is treated as being of the kind of the Hour and is named by its name; hence the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has come." Or the coming of the Hour is placed after death because of its swiftness, as if it were occurring without interval. Abu al-Baqa' said: the estimated meaning is "O regret, be present, this is your time," and it is a figurative address whose meaning is alerting their souls to recall the causes of regret, because regret itself is not requested and its arrival cannot be obtained; rather the meaning is hyperbole in this, as if they were so bewildered that they called out to it. Similar to this is the address of "woe" (waylun) and the like, and its beauty is not hidden.

﴿Over what we neglected﴾: that is, over our neglect (tafrit), so *ma* is verbal (masdariyyah). Tafrit is negligence in what one was able to do. Abu 'Ubaydah said its meaning is "wasting." Ibn Bahr said its meaning is "precedence," from which comes *al-farit* for one who precedes; and the meaning of *farrata* is that he left the precedence to others, so the doubling in it is for privation, like *jallattu al-ba'ir* (I removed the camel's hide), meaning I removed its skin and stripped it. (Concerning) *fiha*: that is, in the worldly life, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both; or in the Hour, as is related from al-Hasan. What is meant by neglect regarding the Hour is negligence in observing its right and preparing for it through faith and righteous deeds. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Paradise, meaning over what we neglected in seeking it. This is attributed to as-Suddi, but its remoteness is not hidden. As for al-Tabarsi's statement that what 'Abd al-A'mash related from Abu Salih from Abu Sa'id from the Prophet ﷺ supports it, that he said regarding this verse: "The people of the Fire see their places in Paradise and say: 'Alas for us!'" etc., it does not escape scrutiny, since the possibility remains, and it undermines the argument. And from Muhammad ibn Jarir: that the pronoun returns to the attribute, because the loss indicates it; this is also remote. Similar to this is what was said: that *ma* is a relative pronoun meaning "those which" (allati), and what is meant by it is the deeds, and the pronoun refers back to them, as if it were said: "Alas for us over the righteous deeds in which we fell short." Indeed, the referent of the pronoun on this view is mentioned in their speech, unlike on the previous opinions, where it is not mentioned in it, nor in His speech in narrating the state of these speakers according to the first opinion of some. So reflect. ﴿While they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾: this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (qalu), and it is a concomitant or anticipated circumstance. *Wizr* originally means a heavy load, and it is also said to mean sin, which is what is meant here: that they carry their sins and misdeeds, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The mention of "backs" is because the usual and most common way of carrying is upon them, as in ﴿what your hands have earned﴾, since earning is mostly by the hands. This also indicates the great heaviness of what is carried. Making sins and wrongs carried upon the back is a metaphorical figure of speech (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), and the purpose is to explain the evil of their state and the severity of the hardship, pain and great punishments they experience because of their sins. It was also said: carrying them upon the back is literal, and they are embodied. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from as-Suddi that he said: There is no wrongdoing man who dies and enters his grave but there comes to him a man of ugly face, black in color, foul of smell, wearing filthy clothes, until he enters the grave with him. When he sees him he says: "How ugly is your face!" He says: "Thus was your deed ugly." He says: "How foul is your smell!" He says: "Thus was your deed foul." He says: "How filthy are your clothes!" He says: "Your deed was filthy." He says: "Who are you?" He says: "I am your deed." So he remains with him in his grave. When he is raised on the Day of Resurrection, he says to him: "I used to carry you in the world with pleasures and desires, and today you carry me," so he mounts upon his back and drives him until he enters him into the Fire. And they related from 'Amr ibn Qays that he said: When the believer comes out of his grave, his deed meets him in the most beautiful form and the most fragrant scent, and says to him: "Do you know me?" He says: "No, except that Allah has made your scent fragrant and your form beautiful." He says: "Thus were you in the world; I am your righteous deed. You used to ride me in the world, so ride me today," and he recited ﴿The Day We gather the God-fearing to the Merciful as a delegation﴾. And if the disbeliever, his deed meets him in the ugliest form and foulest scent, and says: "Do you know me?" He says: "No, except that Allah has made your form ugly and your scent foul." He says: "Thus were you in the world; I am your evil deed. You used to ride me in the world, so today I ride you," and he recited ﴿while they carry their burdens﴾, the verse.

Some make all that is related in this matter a figurative expression too, and there is no obstacle to taking it literally and keeping the speech on its apparent sense. Many of the people of the Sunnah have indeed affirmed the embodiment of deeds in that abode, and this is what the apparent meaning of the weight requires.

﴿Surely evil is what they bear﴾

13

This is a concluding statement that confirms what precedes it and completes it. *Sa'a* (evil is) as stated here may have three aspects. The first is that it is the transitive, inflected form with the pattern *fa'ala* with a fatha on the middle letter, and the meaning is "Surely evil is what they bear," where *ma* is relative, verbal, or an indefinite qualifying noun, as the subject of it, and the statement is informative. The second is that it was transformed into the intransitive form with a damma on the middle letter and imbued with the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub), and the meaning is "How evil is that which they bear," or "How evil is their burden." The third is that it was also transformed for emphasis in censure, so it equals "bi'sa" (how wretched) in meaning and in its firmness.

﴿Wa-ma al-hayat al-dunya illa la'ibun wa-lahw﴾ (And the life of this world is nothing but play and amusement). Since He, glory be to Him, had established earlier that behind the life of this world there is another life, in which they will encounter such calamities as they will encounter, He—majestic is His majesty—clarified the condition of those two lives in themselves. Some of the commentators took this as a response to their saying: ﴿in hiya illa hayatuna al-dunya﴾ (There is nothing but our life of this world). This is a distant interpretation. Whatever the case, the meaning is: the deeds of the life of this world that are specific to it are nothing but like play and amusement in their lack of benefit and permanence. By this estimation, as many commentators have said, the righteous deeds in it are excluded, such as worship and what is done out of necessity for livelihood. The statement is an eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh), even if no genitive noun (mudaf) is assumed to be omitted, and the world itself was made to be play and amusement as hyperbole, as in his saying:

"Indeed it is only advance and retreat"

This is sound. Play (la'ib) and amusement (lahw), according to Durrat al-Tanzil (Pearl of Revelation), share the quality of being occupation with what does not concern the rational person or matter to him, whether it is of desire and delight, whether it is forbidden or not. A distinction is made between them: play is what is intended to hasten pleasure and relaxation through it, while amusement is everything that preoccupies one with desire and delight even if it is not intended for that. When amusement is mentioned without qualification, it means, as has been said, the pursuit of pleasure through women, as in his saying:

"Did not Basbasa claim today that I have grown old and that no one like me is fit for amusement?"

Qatada said: in the dialect of Yemen, lahw means "the woman." It has also been said: play is seeking pleasure and joy in what it is not becoming to seek, while amusement is diverting worry with what is not fit to divert it. It has also been said: every occupation to which one devotes oneself necessitates turning away from everything else, because the one whom no matter preoccupies from another matter is God, exalted is He. So when one devotes oneself to falsehood, one must turn away from the truth; devotion to falsehood is play, and turning away from the truth is amusement. It has also been said: the rational person occupied with something must prefer it and give it precedence over others; if he gives it precedence without abandoning the other, it is play, but if he abandons the other and forgets it because of it, it is amusement.

After recounting these sayings, the author of Durrat al-Tanzil explained the secret of placing play before amusement where they are combined, as here, and placing it after amusement as in al-'Ankabut, saying: since this discourse is directed as a refutation of the disbelievers in what they claim of denying the Hereafter, and the restriction mentioned earlier, and since in their belief, due to their ignorance, there is nothing but the joy that is hastened through the adornment of the perishing world, He placed play first, which indicates this, and completed it with amusement. Or, since they sought joy in it, and that was the goal of their gaze, while diverting worry is necessary and follows from it, He placed what He placed first. Or, since they devoted themselves to falsehood in most of their sayings and deeds, He placed what indicates that first. Or, since devotion precedes abandonment and forgetting, He placed play before amusement in observance of the external order. As for al-'Ankabut, the context is mentioning the shortness of the duration of the life of this world in comparison with the Hereafter and belittling it in relation to it. For this reason the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) that implies belittling is mentioned, and He followed this with His saying, glory be to Him and exalted is He: ﴿Wa-inna al-dar al-akhirah lahiya al-hayawan﴾ (And indeed the abode of the Hereafter—that is the true life). Occupation with amusement is among what shortens time, and it is more inclusive of it than play, and of days of happiness; so they became as he said:

"And a night among the bright nights was not but twilight and dawn."

These aspects of the distinction apply on this basis, and its detail is in Durrat al-Tanzil. Our master Shihab al-Din said this, so let it be understood.

﴿Wa-la-dar al-akhirah﴾ (And the abode of the Hereafter), which is the place of the other life, ﴿khayrun lilladhina yattaqun﴾ (is better for those who are mindful of God), that is, who guard against disbelief and sins, because its benefits are pure of harms and pains, and its pleasures are safe from ending. ﴿Afala ta'qilun﴾ (Will you not then reason?)

[23]

That is, so that you may guard against the disbelief and disobedience in which you are. The fa' (then) is a conjunction (li-l-'atf) on an omitted element, meaning: "Will you then be heedless, or will you not reflect? Will you not then reason?" The apparent expression would have been, as al-Tibi said, "And the Hereafter is nothing but earnest and truth," in accordance with the context. However, He placed ﴿khayrun lilladhina yattaqun﴾ in the place of that, establishing the cause in place of the effect (iqamat al-musabbab maqam al-sabab). Al-Kashshaf said: this is evidence that everything other than the deeds of the God-fearing is play and amusement, because when He made the Hereafter the counterpart of the life of this world, and judged the corresponding deeds to be play and amusement, it is known that the two deeds correspond according to the correspondence of what they are attributed to, namely the world and the Hereafter. So when He restricted goodness to the God-fearing, it follows that what is other than their deeds is not from the deeds of the Hereafter at all, and so it is play and amusement that yields no benefit.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿wa-la-dar al-akhirah﴾ with the genitive construction (idafah), which is an attribution of the adjective to the noun it describes. The Kufans permitted this, and whoever does not permit it interprets it as meaning "wa-la-dar al-nash'ah al-akhirah" (the abode of the final creation), or as treating the adjective as if it were a noun. Ibn Kathir and others read ﴿ya'qilun﴾ (they reason) with the letter ya' (third person). The pronoun refers to the disbelievers who said ﴿in hiya illa hayatuna al-dunya﴾. It has also been said that it refers to the God-fearing. The interrogative is for admonition and urging reflection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 33:

﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for the grief that befalls him, peace be upon him, because of what is related of the disbelievers: their persistence in denial and their exaggeration. The word qad here is for abundance (takthir). This, as al-Halabi said in answer to the objection of Abu Hayyan, refers to the objects of knowledge and not to the knowing itself, since the attribute of the Eternal does not admit increase or multiplication; otherwise it would entail its being originated, which would necessitate the origination of the one in whom it subsists, glory be to Him and exalted.

Al-Safaqusi said: Multiplicity may be valid with regard to the things known, and what falls within the scope of knowledge here is abundant, on the basis that the verb mentioned indicates continuous renewal. They cited for its indication of this the verse of the Hudhali:

"Qad atruku al-qirn musfarran anamiluhu
ka'anna athwabahu mujjat bi-firsad"

Abu Hayyan claimed that its indication of abundance is an opinion not well known among the grammarians, even though some of them held it. The words of Sibawayh, where he said: "qad is in the position of rubba," are not explicit on that, and what they cited as evidence for their claim only understands abundance from the context of the speech.

Among them is the verse, for abundance is only understood in it because pride arises only from the frequency of occurrence of what one is proud of. Some verifiers mentioned that the truth is what Ibn Malik said: that Sibawayh's unrestricted statement that it is in the position of rubba requires equating the two in diminution and in turning toward the past, and the verse is evidence for this, for pride occurs through the brave man leaving his opponent (qirn) while his garments have been stained with his blood at some times.

Abu Hayyan's statement that pride arises only from abundance, etc., is not accepted in its unrestricted form; rather it applies to what frequently occurs. As for what is rare, one is proud of its occurrence being rare, because if the brave man's opponent were often to overcome him, he would not be his opponent, since the qirn (with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ra) is the equal who opposes.

In the Qamus: the qirn is your equal in bravery or more general. Its wording requires, by precise consideration, that he overcomes him only rarely, otherwise he would not be a qirn; and the beginning and end of the speech contradict each other. Al-Tibi claimed that the word qad is for diminution, and it may sometimes be intended to mean its opposite, and this is of the type of using one of two opposites for the other.
