The point here is to make the Messenger of God (ﷺ) patient under the harm of his people and their denial, meaning: it is your right, as lord of the steadfast messengers (ulu al-azm), not to complain much of the harm of your people, and that God Most High should not know of your showing of complaint except a little; and that it may be a mockery of the deniers and a rebuke to them.

Some stated that qad here is for diminution, in the sense that what they are engaged in is the least of what He knows, may He be exalted. The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the matter (al-sha'n), and it is the subject of inna, and its predicate is the sentence explaining it. The relative pronoun is the subject of yahzunuka, and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "that which they say," which is what is related of them: "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients"; or it is that and what includes it and other than it of their raving. The clause "innahu..." takes the place of the two objects of "ya'lamu."

Nafi' read "liyuhzinuka" from ahzana, transitive from hazana, intransitive. His saying, glory be to Him: "fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka" is a causal clause for what the preceding speech implies, of the prohibition against being concerned with what they said, by way of consolation through what it conveys of the Prophet (ﷺ) reaching in the greatness of rank and elevation of station an end beyond which there is no end, in that He negated their denial of him, may God Most High fight them concerning him, and affirmed it of His signs, Most High, in the manner of His saying, glory be to Him and exalted: "Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God" (48:10), as an announcement of the complete nearness and dissolution of his affairs (ﷺ) in the matter of God, Mighty and Majestic. And in it also is an exaltation of their crime, which indicates the greatness of their punishment, as if it were said: do not be concerned with it, and leave it to God Most High, for they, in that denial of theirs, do not really deny you.

﴿But the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾

- That is: rather they deny His signs, Most High. He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, to record against them the firm rootedness in wrongdoing, of which this denial is one of its forms. It was said: if by wrongdoing is meant its absolute sense, then the placement is to indicate that this is their custom and habit, and that it is the cause of the denial, because attaching the judgment to a derived noun indicates the causality of the basis; and if by it is meant the specific wrongdoing, then it is identical with the denial and occurs by it, as in: "You have wronged yourselves by your taking the calf" (2:54), so the subject indicates the aspect by which the predicate is built, like his saying:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and taller."

It was said: that "al" in "al-zalimin," if it is a relative and the active participle is in the sense of occurrence, the speech conveys that denial is the cause of wrongdoing; and if it is the article of definition and the active participle is in the sense of permanence, it conveys that wrongdoing is the cause of denial. What is in this is not hidden. The turning to the noble Name is to cultivate awe and to exalt what they have undertaken. The mention of denial in the place of deny is to announce that His signs, glory be to Him, are of such clarity that every person witnesses their truth, and that whoever denies them does so by way of jahd; and jahd is like the denial of what is firmly held in the heart, or the affirming of what is held in the heart to be negated. The ba' is connected to "yajhadun." Jahd transitively takes itself and the ba', so one says jahadahu haqqahu and bi-haqqihi, and this is what the apparent speech of al-Jawhari and al-Raghib requires. It was said: it takes itself and the ba' only here, by its being made to include the meaning of denial. In either case, the fronting of the prepositional phrase is either for the sake of the rhyme endings (ru'us al-ay) or for restriction (al-qasr). Al-Tabrisi reported from Abu 'Ali that the prepositional phrase is connected to "al-zalimin," and in this there is obscurity. What was mentioned, that the fa' is for the causal explanation of what the speech implies, is what some verifiers established. It was said that it is a causal explanation of His saying, glory be to Him, "We certainly know," etc., on the basis that its meaning is "do not grieve," as is said in a context of prohibition and restraint: "We know what you do." So it is as if it were said: do not grieve at what they say, for the denial is in reality directed at Me, and I am the Forbearing, the Patient; so be of my character. It may be that the meaning is: what they say grieves you because it is a denial of Me, so you did not grieve for yourself but for what is more important and greater. This is not hidden to be contrary to what is obvious. It was said: the meaning of the verse is that they do not deny you in their hearts, but they deny with their tongues. This is related from Qatadah and others, and what al-Suddi related supports it: that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq met Abu Jahl, and al-Akhnas said to Abu Jahl: "O Abu al-Hakam, tell me about Muhammad (ﷺ): is he truthful or a liar? For there is no one here who hears your speech except me." Abu Jahl said: "By God, Muhammad (ﷺ) is truthful, and Muhammad has never lied at all. But when the sons of Qusayy take the banner, the water-drawing, the chamberlainship, the council-house and prophethood, what then remains for the rest of Quraysh?" So God Most High revealed this verse. Likewise is what al-Wahidi reported from Muqatil, who said: al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy ibn Kilab used to deny the Prophet (ﷺ) openly, but when he was alone with his household he said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) is not of the people of lying, and I do not reckon him other than truthful." So God Most High revealed the verse. It was said: the meaning is that their intention is not to deny you, for you are marked among them with truthfulness, but they intend to deny Me and to deny My signs. This is attributed to al-Kisa'i, and it is supported by what al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim reported and declared sound from Ali, may God honour his face, that Abu Jahl used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We do not deny you, and you are truthful with us, but we deny what you have brought," and so it was revealed. Likewise al-Wahidi reported it from Abu Maysara. Al-Radi objected to this view, saying: it is not permissible that they affirm him (ﷺ) in himself and deny what he brought, for it is known that he, peace be upon him, used to bear witness to the soundness and truthfulness of what he brought, and that it is the upright religion and the truth from which it is not permissible to deviate. How then is it permissible that he be truthful in his report while what he brought is corrupt? Rather, if he is truthful, then what he brought is correct; and if what he brought is corrupt, then he must be lying in it. Mawlana Sinan said: the sum of the meaning is that they do not deny you in reality, for they say you are truthful, but they suppose that some kind of disorder has seized your intellect, and far be it from you; so it appeared to you that you are a prophet, and the matter is not so, and what you brought is not true. Al-Tibi said: their intention is that you do not lie, for you are the truthful, trustworthy one, but what you brought is magic. From this answer to the objection of al-Radi this may be known, so reflect. It was said: the meaning of the verse is that they do not deny you in what agrees with their scriptures, though they deny you in other matters. It was said: the meaning is that not all of them deny you, though some of them deny you, and they are the wrongdoers mentioned in this verse; and on this view the mention of the wrongdoers is not placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun. Other things have been said, and what is more fitting to the grandeur of the revelation is not hidden.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash from Abu Bakr read "la yukdhibunaka" from al-ikdhab, and this is the reading of Ali, may God honour his face, and it is also related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him. The majority said: both are with the same meaning, as akthara and kathura, and anzala and nazala. It was said: the meaning of akdhabtuhu is that I found him a liar, as ahmadtuhu means I found him praiseworthy. Ahmad ibn Yahya related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say: "kadhdhabta" with shaddah when you attribute lying to him, and "akdhabtahu" when you attribute lying to what he brought, without him.

The utterance of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And messengers before you were indeed denied﴾ is consolation following consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for the generality of an affliction sometimes makes it easier to bear, to some degree.

In it there is guidance for him, upon whom be prayers and peace, to follow the noble messengers before him in patience under harm, and an implicit promise of the like of the victory that they were granted. The opening of the speech with an oath is to emphasize the consolation. The tanwin on *rusul* (messengers) is for magnification and multiplicity. *Min* (from) is connected to *takdhib* (denial). It was also permitted that it be connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of *rusul*, but Abu al-Baqa' rejected this on the grounds that a jinn cannot be described by time, though there is clear objection to this. The meaning is: By God, indeed messengers were denied before your denial, who were of great stature and great numbers; or, messengers were denied who existed in a time before your time.

﴿So they were patient over what they were denied﴾: *ma* is a verbal-source particle (*ma masdariyyah*, a particle that turns the following clause into a verbal noun). The phrase *wa-udhu* ("and they were harmed") is coordinated (*'atf*) with *kudhdhibu* ("they were denied") and falls within its ruling. The verbal noun of *kudhdhiba* is *takdhib*. For *adha* (to harm), the verbal nouns are *adhan*, *adhah*, and *adhiyyah*, as in the Qamus, and *iza'* as established by al-Raghib and others. The statement of the author of the Qamus, "Do not say *iza'*, it is an error," was caused by al-Jawhari's and others' omission of it. He and the rest of the lexicographers do not mention the analogical verbal nouns, because there is no need to mention them. The two verbal nouns here are from the passive form, and this is clear, meaning: so they were patient over the denial of their people toward them and their harming of them. So follow their example and be patient over what has befallen you from your people. By their harm is meant either the very denial itself, or what accompanies it of various kinds of harm. Al-Tabarsi chose this but did not state it explicitly, relying on the fact that denial generally entails it. In it is emphasis of the consolation. It was permitted that the coordination be upon *kudhdhibat* or upon *sabaru*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that this be a new independent sentence (*isti'naf*), but then preferred the first.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿until Our help came to them﴾ is a limit (*ghayah*) for the patience. In it is an indication of the promise of help for those who are patient. It was permitted that it be a limit for the harming, and this is based on the possibility of the independent sentence. The shift to the first-person plural "We" (*nun al-'azamah*, the royal "we") indicates concern with the matter of the help.

﴿And none can alter the words of God﴾ is an affirmation of the content of what precedes it, namely the coming of His help to them. By His words, exalted is He, as al-Kalbi and Qatadah said, is meant the verses in which He promised the help of His prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, which also indicate the help of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has decreed: "I shall surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ and His saying, mighty is His majesty: ﴿Indeed they are the ones who will be helped﴾ and ﴿Indeed, Our soldiers – they are the victorious﴾.

It was permitted that by them be meant all of His words, glorified is He, of which the verses containing the noble promises are a part, and the promises revealed concerning him (ﷺ) enter into it as a primary inclusion. The shift to the majestic Name (Allah) is, as it has been said, to indicate the cause of the ruling, for divinity necessitates that none can overpower Him, glorified is He, in any action, and that no contradiction occur from Him, exalted is His majesty, in any statement.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that no one other than Him, exalted is He, is able to alter the words of God, mighty and majestic is He, in the sense of doing what contradicts what they indicate and of preventing God, mighty is His name, from achieving that. As for whether He Himself does not alter them, the verse does not indicate this. What the texts do indicate is that He, glorified is He, may alter a threat but does not alter a promise. ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾.

Affirmation: an affirmation indeed of what they were granted of help, and an emphasis on what the speech implied of the promise to the Messenger of God (ﷺ); or an affirmation of all that has been mentioned of the denial of the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, and their harming and their being helped. *Naba'* (news) is like *qasas* (narrative) in its wording and meaning.

In the Qamus: *naba'* – with vowel on the second letter – is news, its plural is *anba'*, and some have restricted it; its indication has already passed with what is significant about it. According to al-Akhfash, who permits the addition of *min* in affirmative statements and before the definite, differing in this from Sibawayh, the subject of *ja'a* (came) is a hidden pronoun, and he corrected that the subject is a pronoun whose estimate is *huwa*, i.e., the news or the clarification. The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of it. It has been said – and the words of al-Rummani point to it – that it is omitted and the prepositional phrase is its qualifier, meaning: and there has certainly come to you a news existing from the news of the messengers. In this there is the objection that omitting the subject is not permitted here. Abu Hayyan said: What appears to me is that the subject is a pronoun referring to what the meaning of the preceding clause indicates, i.e., and there has certainly come to you this report of the denial and what follows it.

It has been said – and the words of the Kashshaf perhaps indicate it – that *min* itself is the subject, and what is meant is some of their reports.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if their turning away has been grievous to you﴾, i.e., has been burdensome and great. The verb (kāna, "has been") is used, as has been said, so that the conditional remains in the past tense and is not turned into the future. This is because (kāna), by its strong indication of the past, is not altered by (in, "if") into the future, unlike other verbs. This is the view of al-Mubarrad. The grammarians interpret it as equivalent to "and if it becomes clear and evident," meaning that their turning away ﴿has been grievous to you﴾, i.e., the turning away of the unbelievers from faith in you and in what you brought of the glorious Qur'an. This is shown by their saying about it, "fables of the ancients" (al-Anfal 8:31; al-An'am 6:25), and is indicated by their actions of keeping far away and forbidding others. Perhaps the expression "turning away" is used instead of "denial," although the consolation, as indicated by the statement of the Exalted, ﴿And messengers were denied before you﴾ (6:34), was about it, in order to magnify the matter of denial, which is the agent of (kaburа, "was grievous"). The prepositional phrase is fronted for the reason already mentioned many times. The sentence is the predicate of (kāna), explaining its subject, which is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). There is no need to estimate (qad, "indeed") before it. It has also been said that the subject of (kāna) is (i'rāḍuhum, "their turning away"), and (kaburа) together with its implied agent, which refers back to the noun, is its predicate, placed before its subject. The statement is a resumption, brought to confirm the obligation of patience derived from the consolation, by showing that this is a matter from which there is no escape at all.

It is related in some reports that al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a gathering of Quraysh and they said: "O Muhammad, bring us a sign from Allah, as the prophets used to do, and we will believe you." Allah, the Exalted, refused to bring them any sign of what they proposed. They turned away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that was grievous to him, peace and blessings be upon him, because he (ﷺ) was extremely eager for the faith of his people. So whenever they asked him for a sign, he wished that Allah, the Exalted, would send it down, hoping for their faith. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿So if you are able﴾, i.e., if you have the power and it is within your reach, ﴿to seek﴾, i.e., to look for, ﴿a passage (nafaq) in the earth﴾, which is a tunnel in it that leads to a place, as in the Qamus. Its original meaning is the burrow of the jerboa, and from it comes (nāfiqā', "the escape hole"), one of its exits. It is called (nuffaqa), like (humaza), which is the one it conceals while showing another. When it is attacked from the (qāṣi'ā', "the outer exit"), it strikes it with its head and escapes. From it the word hypocrisy (nifāq) is derived. The prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element that falls as a qualifier of ﴿passage﴾. The statement is in the mode of abstraction (tajrīd) according to one opinion. It is also permitted that it be attached to ﴿seek﴾, or to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial qualifier of its implied pronoun, meaning: a passage existing in the earth, or seek in the earth, or seek, while you are in the earth. ﴿Or a ladder into the sky﴾, i.e., a stairway in it, taken from safety (salāmah). Al-Zajjaj said: "Because it delivers you (yusallimuka) to your ascent." It is masculine, as al-Farra' said. They cited as evidence for its masculinity the Exalted's words: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen?﴾ (al-Tur 52:38). Then he said: "I recited a verse in its feminine form which you forgot." End of quotation.

Al-Ghadairi said: The verse that al-Farra' forgot is the verse of Aws, which is: "For us is a ladder in glory; they cannot climb it, and they have no ladder in the glory of the (glorious) house." They also cited, in its masculine form: "Poetry is difficult, and its ladder is long; whoever climbs in it, he who does not know it..." He means: he wants to parse it, and so he makes it foreign (yu'jimahu). The (in the sky) has parallel possibilities to those of the preposition before it. ﴿Then you bring them﴾, i.e., from it, ﴿a sign﴾ of what they proposed of the signs. The (fa, "then") at the beginning of this conditional is a responsive particle, and the response of the condition is omitted. Its estimated form may be: "you have come," in the form of a report, or "then do," as an imperative verb, and the clause is the response of the first condition. The meaning is: if their turning away from faith is grievous to you, and you loved to answer them concerning what they asked as a proposal so that they might believe, then if you are able to do such and such, then bring them a sign, do it. In this there is an indication of the extreme eagerness of the Messenger (ﷺ) for the faith of his people and the attainment of what they seek and propose, along with a hint of rebuking the people. Or the meaning is: if their turning away is grievous to you, then even if you were able to bring the impossible, you would bring it. The intended purpose is to show that he (ﷺ) reached in his eagerness for their faith such a limit. There is in it an indication of how far their faith is from the circle of existence, as is not hidden from one who reflects. The choice of seeking (ibtighā') rather than taking (ittikhādh) and similar words is to signal that what is mentioned, the passage and the ladder, are things he cannot seek, so how could he take them?

It is also permitted that the seeking of those two matters, namely the very passing through the earth and the ascent into the sky, be itself a sign. In that case the (fa, "then") in (fa-ta'tiyahum) is explanatory, and the indefiniteness of (āyah, "sign") is for magnification. The meaning according to this is: if you are able to seek those two, then you would make that a sign for them, and you would have done it.

Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying: This is apparent from the outward wording, for if it were so the construction would have been "then bring them with that a sign, what a sign." Also, what sign is there in entering a tunnel into the earth? Even if it may be valid that the ascent to the sky is a sign, what we have mentioned, that bringing a sign from both is the apparent meaning that comes to minds, is the most evident. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat transmitted it from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It has also been said that the intended meaning is: ﴿then bring them a sign from the sky﴾, and that the seeking of the passage is for escape. This is supported by what al-Tasti transmitted from Nafi' ibn al-Azraq, who said to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Inform me about His saying, ﴿So if you are able to seek a passage in the earth﴾." He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "A tunnel in the earth, so that you may go fleeing (haraban)." But this is remote. The report of Ibn al-Azraq has had what has been said about it.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾, i.e., if Allah, the Exalted, had willed to gather them upon the guidance you are upon, He would have gathered them upon it by granting them success in faith, so they would have believed along with you. But He did not will that, glorified be He, because of the badness of their choice, as Allah, the Exalted, knew of them from the beginning of all beginnings. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) said: The intended meaning is that if He, glorified be He, had willed to gather them upon guidance, He would have done so by bringing a sign that compels them to it. But He, exalted be His majesty, did not do that because it departs from wisdom. The truth is what the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox community) hold. ﴿So never be among the ignorant﴾.

53

That is, if you know that He, glorified be He, did not will their guidance and faith, then do not be, through extreme eagerness for their Islam or inclination toward the descent of their proposals, of those who are ascribed to ignorance of the fine details of His affairs, the Exalted. It is also permitted that by "the ignorant" is meant, according to what is transmitted from the Mu'tazilah, those who propose. The prohibition is intended to forbid him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, from assisting them in their proposals, describing them with the title of ignorance rather than unbelief, because the criterion of the prohibition is fulfilled.

Al-Jubba'i said: The intended meaning is: do not be impatient in the place of patience, so that your state approaches the state of the ignorant by following their path. The first is preferable. In His addressing His Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, with this address rather than with what Noah, peace be upon him, was addressed with, when He, glorified be He, said to him: ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ (Hud 11:46), there is an indication of the greater tenderness toward him (ﷺ) and of the intensity of his eagerness, peace and blessings be upon him. So understand this.

* * *

Among the allusive interpretations (bāb al-ishārah) of the verses is: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾ (6:13). It is possible that the night and the day are an allusion to the heart of the unbeliever and the heart of the believer, and what dwells in them of unbelief and faith. The meaning of that belonging to Him, glorified be He, is that it is one of the effects of His majesty and beauty. It is also possible that it is an allusion to the heart of the gnostic in the two states of contraction (qabḍ) and expansion (basṭ). So it is as if it were said: "And to Him belongs what dwells in the hearts of the gnostics, the contracted and the expanded, of the effects of the manifestations (tajalliyāt). So do not turn, in the two states, to anything other than Him, exalted be His affair."

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ (6:13). He hears their evil and good thoughts and knows their evil and good. Or He hears their moaning in their longing and knows their pouring forth (inisāb), or the like of that.

﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector (walī)?﴾ (6:14), i.e., as a helper and assistant, ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., the one who brings them into being. So they are His possession, glorified be He, and the relation of the owned to the Owner is the relation of nothing to a thing. ﴿And He feeds, and is not fed﴾ (6:14). He is the absolutely Self-Sufficient, and all others, exalted be His majesty, are pure need. To seek sustenance from one in need is folly in its judgment and misguidance from its intellect. ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to be the first to submit (aslama)﴾ (6:14), i.e., to submit himself to his Lord, exalted be His majesty. The command in this is the command of creation (al-amr al-kawnī), i.e., say: "It has been said to me: Be the first to submit, and I was." That was before the appearance of these determinations (ta'yīnāt). To this is the allusion in what has spread from his saying (ﷺ): "I was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay." So the first spirit that ran in the field of submission, obedience and love was the spirit of our Prophet (ﷺ), who submitted himself to his Master without intermediary, and all his brother prophets, peace be upon them, submitted their souls only through his intermediary (ﷺ). So he (ﷺ) is the one sent to the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, in the world of spirits, and all of them are his community, and they are his deputies in the world of witnessing. This does not contradict his command (ﷺ) to follow some of them in the bodily creation, because that is merely to attract those who believe in those particular ones in the best manner. ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ (6:14), i.e., and it was said to me: Do not be among those who associate with Allah, the Exalted, anyone or anything whatsoever.

﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ (6:18), by annihilating them and disposing of them as He wills. ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, i.e., the One who does what He does with His servants by wisdom. ﴿The All-Aware﴾, the One who is informed of hidden states and degrees of worthiness.

﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah is witness between me and you﴾ (6:19), by manifesting miracles. And greater than that, for the gnostics, is the manifestation of the lights of Allah, the Exalted, in the mirror of the noble face of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book know him as they know their sons﴾ (6:20). This is through the attributes they found in their Book, not through the light gleaming on the pages of that noble face. ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ by affirming the existence of other than Him, the Exalted, ﴿or denies His signs﴾ by manifesting the attributes of his own self. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed﴾, because they are veiled by what they have placed in the position of the Essence of Allah, the Exalted, and His attributes, exalted and high be He.

﴿And the Day We shall gather them all﴾ (6:22), and that is the Great Day of Resurrection and the very essence of gathering. ﴿Then We shall say to those who associated partners (with Allah)﴾ by affirming others. ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim﴾ (6:22), that they were partners and that they had existence? ﴿Then their trial will be only that they will say: By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (6:23), because the existence of any thing that they could associate is impossible. ﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ (6:24) by denying association from themselves while that belief was firmly rooted in them. (And it strayed) i.e., was lost to them, ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾, so they did not find it.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ (6:25), from where you are, ﴿and We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ according to what their readiness required, ﴿lest they understand it﴾, and these are the darknesses of the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammārah). ﴿And in their ears is deafness﴾, which is the deafness of misguidance. ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, because over their eyes is the veil of arrogance and ignorance. ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾, which is the Fire of deprivation (ḥirmān), ﴿and they say: Would that we could be returned and not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, from the manifestations of His attributes, ﴿and be among the believers﴾, i.e., the monotheists. ﴿Rather, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾ (6:28), within themselves, of the wretched dispositions, the dark conditions and the destructive qualities. ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden﴾ (6:28), because that is firmly rooted in them. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, in this world and the Hereafter, because lying is a habit (malakah) in them. ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ (6:30), the verse. Some of the interpreters said: This depiction of their state is in veiling and distance, even though they are in the very totality of the absolute gathering. Standing before a thing is not the same as standing with it, for the first is only in unwillingness, while the second is in willingness and desire. So the one who stands with Allah, glorified be He, through monotheism is not made to stand for reckoning. To this is the allusion in the Exalted's saying:

[p. 141]

﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face﴾, ﴿you are not accountable for their reckoning in any way﴾. This one is rewarded with kinds of bliss in all the gardens. Whoever stops with other than God through associating partners is made to stand before the Lord, the Exalted, and is punished with kinds of torment, because associating partners is a great wrong. Whoever stops with the human realm (nasut) through love of desires is made to stand before the realm of sovereignty (malakut), and is punished with fires of deprivation, and the angels of the dark states are set over him, and he is joined with the devils of the destructive passions. Whoever stops with the acts is made to stand before the realm of power (jabarut), and is punished with the fire of greed and hope, and is returned to the station of the realm of sovereignty. Whoever stops with the attributes is made to stand before the essences, and is punished with the fire of longing and separation. This is not the standing before the Lord, because in it there is the veil of the mere existent thing (al-aniyah). In standing before the Essence is the knowledge of the Lord described by the attributes of gentleness. The polytheist is first made to stand before the Lord, so he is veiled by repulsion and expulsion: ﴿Be driven away into it, and do not speak to Me﴾. Then he is made to stand before the realm of power, so he is driven away with wrath and curse, and He will not speak to them nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection. Then he is made to stand before the realm of sovereignty, so he is repelled with anger and curse: ﴿It is said: Enter the gates of Hell﴾. Then he is made to stand before the Fire: ﴿they will be kindled in it﴾, so he is tormented with kinds of fires forever. His standing before the Fire is therefore later than his standing before the Lord, the Exalted, being caused by it. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment for what they used to disbelieve﴾. As for the one who stops with the human realm, he is made to stand for reckoning before the realm of sovereignty, then before the Fire, and perhaps he will be saved if there is no wrath, and perhaps he will not be saved if it exists. The one who stops with the acts is not made to stand before the Fire at all; rather he is reckoned and enters the Garden. As for the one who stops with the attributes, he is among those with whom God, the Exalted, is pleased and who are pleased with Him. End of quote. So reflect on it. ﴿Those who denied the meeting with God have certainly lost, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾. It is the Lesser Resurrection, I mean death. It is related from one of the great scholars that it was said to him: "So-and-so died suddenly." He said: "No wonder, for whoever does not die suddenly falls ill suddenly and then dies." ﴿They say: Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it﴾, that is, concerning the right of that hour, by abandoning beneficial deeds. ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾ is a depiction of their condition. ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and amusement﴾, that is, the sensible life, for the sensible is lower and closer than the intelligible. ﴿Having no root or reality, swiftly passing and ending﴾. ﴿And the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful﴾, that is, the world of spiritual things, ﴿and they are those who strip themselves of the garments of human attributes and bodily pleasures﴾. ﴿We know that what they say grieves you﴾, according to the requirement of humanity, ﴿but it is not you they deny in truth﴾, ﴿rather the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾ by which He manifests Himself, ﴿and they reject﴾, so He, glorified be He, takes vengeance upon them. ﴿Messengers before you were denied, and they were patient over what they were denied and harmed, until Our help came to them﴾. So take them as a model and await the outcome. ﴿And none can alter the words of God﴾ by which He manifests Himself to His servants, so let your heart be at peace, and do not be among the ignorant who do not perceive the wisdom in the differences of readiness, so that you would grieve over the veiling of whoever is veiled and the denial of whoever denies. And God, the Exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.

[Page 142]

﴿Only those who listen respond﴾ confirms what the preceding discourse implies, namely that they believe. *Al-istijabah* (responding) means *al-ijabah*. Often *istaf'ala* is used in the sense of *af'ala*, as *istakhlasa* means *akhlasa* and *istawqada* means *awqada*, among other examples. From this is the verse of al-Ghanawi:

*A caller called, "O you who answer the summons to the gathering," but no answerer answered him at that time.*

This is indicated by his saying *mujib* (answerer) and not *musta'jib*. Some distinguished between *istajaba* and *ajaba*, holding that *istajaba* indicates acceptance. The intended hearing is the complete kind, which is the hearing of understanding and reflection, treating anything else as no hearing at all. That is: only those who hear what is conveyed to them with understanding and reflection respond to your call to faith, unlike the dead, of whom these (disbelievers) are some, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ (*al-mawta*, "the dead"), meaning the disbelievers, as al-Hasan said, and many others narrated it. ﴿God will raise them﴾ from their graves to the gathering. It was said that their being raised means their guidance to faith, but this is not correct. ﴿Then to Him they will be returned﴾ for recompense, and then they will hear. Before that, there is no way to make them hear, since over their hearts are coverings and in their ears is deafness.

Applying "the dead" to disbelievers is a metaphor of the subsidiary type (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*), based on likening their disbelief and ignorance to death, as it is said: *Let not the ignorant man impress you with his attire; that one is dead, and his garments are a shroud.*

It was also said that "the dead" is literal, and the speech is an allegory (*tamthil*) for His exclusive power to grant those disbelievers success in faith, by analogy with His exclusive power to resurrect the dead whose bones have decayed in their graves. This contains an indication that he (ﷺ) cannot guide them, because guiding them is like raising the dead. It has been objected that on this view His saying ﴿then to Him they will be returned﴾ has no great role in the allegory, unless it is meant as an indication of the effects that follow from faith.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of *al-mawta*, there are two possibilities. The first is that it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. The second is that it is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted and explained by what follows it; Abu al-Baqa' preferred this. It is understood from the words of Mujahid that it is in the nominative by coordination with the relative pronoun, and the clause after it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*). The apparent meaning, however, is contrary to this.

It is also read ﴿yarji'un﴾ (they return) in the active voice, from *raja'a* (to return). The widely transmitted reading is more fitting to the context, because it informs that their return is to Him, the Exalted, by way of necessity.

63

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 37:

﴿And they say﴾ — that is, the leaders of Quraysh, whose ignorance and misguidance had reached the point that they were not content with the signs they had witnessed, signs before which the solid mountains would crumble, and did not count them as anything. ﴿Why has not⁠﴾ — that is, ﴿why has not⁠﴾ ﴿there been sent down⁠﴾ — that is, sent down ﴿upon him a sign from his Lord⁠﴾ compelling faith? ﴿Say⁠﴾ — O Muhammad — ﴿Indeed, Allah is Able to send down a sign⁠﴾ of the compelling kind ﴿but most of them do not know⁠﴾.

They do not realize that the non-sending of such a sign, despite His power, is because sending it would uproot the foundation of moral responsibility (taklif), which is built upon the principle of free choice (ikhtiyar), or because it would entirely destroy them, since that follows from denying a compelling sign.

It is also permissible that they did not actually request a compelling sign, and that not counting what they had witnessed does not necessarily imply that they requested it. Rather, it is possible that they requested something other than what had occurred, something that would not be compelling, out of obstinacy and stubborn opposition. In that case, the answer concerning the compelling sign would be from the style of the wise (uslub al-hakim), or it would be an answer that implies their request in a stronger and more eloquent way.

﴿Min⁠﴾ indicates the starting point of the end (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), and the prepositional phrase may be connected to ﴿nuzzila⁠﴾, or to an omitted word that serves as a descriptor of ﴿ayah⁠﴾. What is implied by mentioning the title of His lordship (ruboobiyyah) over him, upon him be prayers and peace, of indicating causation, is only by way of sarcastic allusion on their part. Limiting the answer to demonstrating His power, glorified and exalted, to send down a sign, although it is not in the realm of denial, serves to indicate that His non-sending of a sign despite His power over it is due to a profound wisdom that must be known, and they are heedless of it, as the particle of correction (al-istidrak) indicates. Mentioning the Majestic Name serves to cultivate awe, along with indicating causation. The object of ﴿ya'lamun⁠﴾ is either entirely omitted, meaning they are not among the people of knowledge, or it is omitted and indicated by the context, meaning they know nothing.

The restriction of the lack of knowledge to most of them is because some of them are aware of the reality of the situation, and they act as they do only out of arrogance and obstinacy. Ibn Kathir recited ﴿yanzila⁠﴾ with lightening (takhfif), and the meaning here, as has been said, is one, because the gradual and non-gradual aspects were not considered.

[Page 143]

The words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿There is no creature (dabbah) on the earth﴾ form a new, independent sentence, brought (as al-Tabarsi and others say) to demonstrate the perfection of His power, may He be glorified and exalted, the excellence of His management, His wisdom, and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, glory be to Him and exalted. It is therefore like evidence that He, exalted is He, is able to send down (the signs), and that He does not send them down only out of preservation of the dazzling wisdoms. It has also been said that it is evidence that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is able to resurrect and gather (the creatures). The first is more appropriate. The particle (min) ("from") has been added to make explicit the (idea of) comprehensiveness (istighraq, the inclusion of every member of a category). A dabbah is any living creature that crawls on the earth, and its root is from dabba, yadibbu, dabiban, meaning to walk with short steps close together. The prepositional phrase (the jar and majrur, "on the earth") is connected to an omitted element, or is in the genitive or nominative case, and occurs as a qualifier of dabbah. It is described in this way to intensify the generality, as if it were said: "There is no single individual among the individual creatures that dwell in any region of the regions of the earth, on its surface or in its interior." The same applies to the qualifier in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾, also to intensify the generality, meaning: nor any single individual of the birds that flies in any direction of the sky with its two wings. It has also been said that it is to remove the figurative sense of speed (majaz al-sur'ah), since the word "flying" has been used for that, as in the verse: "A people who, when evil bares its molars, fly toward it in groups and singly." Likewise the word "bird" has been used figuratively for deeds and portion (of fate), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And every person's bird We have fastened to his neck﴾. The possibility of a figurative extension alongside this, which would make it a supporting element (tarshih) for the figurative usage, is remote and is not to be considered without an indicator. Some of the later scholars chose that the purpose of the qualifier is to depict that strange state which indicates complete strength and power. It has been objected to the two previous views that if it were said: "nor any bird in the sky," it would be shorter and would more clearly convey those two matters, along with maintaining the correspondence between the two parallel expressions by mentioning the direction of height in one and the direction of lowness in the other. It has been answered, as al-Shihab said, that if it were said "in the sky, flying with its two wings," it would not include most birds, since they do not settle in the sky. Furthermore, intending depiction does not contradict the removal of the figurative sense, since there is no barrier to intending both together, as is not hidden. Then, since the purpose of mentioning these two matters is to show the perfection of His power, may He be glorified and exalted, by explaining what they know and see of these two kinds, and the comprehensiveness of His power and knowledge over them, glory be to Him, other than these two was not intended in the explanation. Thus the objection that the likes of the fish of the sea are outside these two is answered by the claim that they are included in the first category, because "the earth" in it means the direction of lowness. This is not worth considering. Ibn Abi Ablah read (wa-la ta'irun, "nor any bird," in the nominative) as a coordination with the position (mahall) of the prepositional phrase, as if it were said: "There is no creature nor bird" ﴿except that they are communities﴾, that is, distinct groups ﴿like you﴾ in that their affairs are preserved, their matters are attended to, their interests are maintained, proceeding according to the paths of rectitude, arranged within the thread of the divine decrees and the lordly governances. The plural (umam, "communities") was used in view of construing the sense of collectivity derived from the generality, as one of the scholars chose. This implies that it would be permissible to say: "No men are standing," and analogy, as has been said, does not forbid it, but it has only been used together with a separation. Al-Sayyid al-Sanad stated that the indefinite noun here is taken as referring to the group as a group. Perhaps his meaning is that the indefinite noun mentioned, in terms of the predication made about it, is treated as referring to the whole group, not that it is intended as such. So there is no objection that the judgment in His words, glory be to Him and exalted, ﴿except communities﴾ rules out that the indefiniteness earlier, according to what was indicated, is for individuality, because the individual is not a group. Likewise it rules out that it is for the sense of kinds, because the individual is not groups, which is clear. As for what has been said, that the kind includes varieties, and each variety is a community, or that the community is every group at a time, this is refuted by the description of communities as "like you," since the address with "you" (kum) is to the species of mankind. So the appropriate comparison is of a kind to a kind in being preserved in their states, not comparing a variety to a kind, or comparing a group at a time to a kind. Indeed, al-Sakkaki said in al-Miftah that the mention of "on the earth" with dabbah, and "flies with its two wings" with bird, is to show that the intention behind the words dabbah and tair is toward the two kinds, and toward establishing them. On this basis there is no difficulty in the validity of the predication, since each of the two kinds includes many species, each of which is a community, like mankind. So it is as if it were said: "No kind among these two kinds exists except that they are communities," and so on. This is like saying: "No man among these two men is other than such and such." His meaning is that the words dabbah and tair carry the notion of kind and unity. So to show that the intention behind each of them is toward the kind as such, not toward unity or multiplicity, and it is described by a quality necessary to the kind as such, that is, without the condition of any of the two, and the comprehensiveness derived from the word (min) is with regard to the two kinds. By this, the claim that al-Sakkaki's statement must be interpreted and returned to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in this context is refuted. On this basis, the qualifier cannot be conceived as giving the sense of further generality and encompassment, because the kind as such, that is, not conditioned by anything, is one concept, as is not hidden.

It has also been objected to the view of generality that how can it be valid, given that the thing compared to (the mushabbah bihi) must necessarily be excluded from it? It has been answered that the primary intention is toward the general, and the thing compared to is in the position of the excepted, by the indication of the comparison, as if it were said: "There is no single individual of the individuals of these two kinds, in their entirety, other than you, except that they are communities like you." And you may claim that every individual of the addressees enters, by the necessary implication that he has two aspects: the aspect that he is the thing compared, and the aspect that he is the thing compared to. So reflect on all of this. ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book of any thing.﴾ Tafrit means falling short, and its origin is that it is followed by (fi, "in"). Here it has implicitly conveyed the sense of neglecting and abandoning (tadmin, that is, one verb is used with the sense of another). So (min shay'in, "of any thing") is in the position of the direct object, and (min) is an added particle for comprehensiveness. It is unlikely to make it partitive, meaning "we have not neglected in the Book any part of a thing," although some have allowed it. The intended meaning of "the Book" is the Qur'an, and this was chosen by al-Balkhi and a group, for he mentioned in it everything needed of the matters of religion and the world, and beyond that, either in detail or in summary. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "No event happens to anyone in religion except that in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, there is guidance regarding it." Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "May Allah, exalted is He, curse the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, those who pluck their facial hair, and those who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah." A woman said to him concerning this: ... He said: "Why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is (mentioned) in the Book of Allah?" She said to him: "I have read what is between the two covers, and I did not find in it what you say." He said: "If you have read it, you have found it. Have you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then he (peace be upon him) has forbidden it." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, once said at Mecca: "Ask me about whatever you wish, and I will inform you of it from the Book of Allah." He was asked: "What do you say about a person in the state of ihram who kills a wasp?" He answered that he should kill it, and he derived this evidence in a manner similar to Ibn Mas'ud's proof, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "In this Qur'an every knowledge has been sent down, and every thing has been made clear to us in it, but our knowledge falls short of what has been made clear to us in the Qur'an." Abu al-Shaykh narrated in Kitab al-'Azamah from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, were to neglect anything, He would neglect the atom, the mustard seed, and the gnat." Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "If the cord of a camel were lost from me, I would find it in the Book of Allah, the Exalted." Al-Mursi said: "The Qur'an has gathered the sciences of the first and the last, in such a way that no one truly comprehends them except the One who spoke it, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), except what Allah, the Exalted, has reserved for Himself." I have heard from some people, and the responsibility for it is upon him, that the greatest shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-Arabi, may Allah sanctify his secret, once fell from his donkey and his leg was dislocated. They came to carry him, but he said: "Give me time." They gave him a short while, then he permitted them, and they carried him. He was asked about that, and he said: "I consulted the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and I found in it the report of this incident; it was mentioned in al-Fatihah." This is a matter that our minds cannot reach. Similar to this is the extraction by some people from al-Fatihah also of the names of the sultans of the house of Uthman, their conditions, and the duration of their sultanate until whatever time Allah wills. And there is no wonder in that, for it is the Mother of the Book and gives birth to every marvelous matter. Accordingly, there is no need to restrict the word "thing" to what is needed of the proofs of tawhid and the obligations.

Abu al-Baqa' said: The word "thing" here stands in the position of a verbal noun, meaning "neglect." It cannot be a direct object, because "we have neglected" does not transitively take its object directly but by means of a preposition, and it has already been made transitive by "fi" to "the Book," so it cannot be transitive by another preposition. Many others followed him in this, and they took what is understood from the Qamus, where it says: "faratta al-shay'a wa-farrata fihi tafriran: he neglected it, and he showed weakness and fell short in it, from what is unique to him, in comparison with one who has a longer reach than him," to be a case of this verb being transitive by itself. But it is possible that its transitivity mentioned there is not a basic one, but figurative, or by way of the implicit conveyance (tadmin) that was indicated earlier. On this view, as Abu al-Baqa' said, the verse remains evidence for one who thinks that the Book contains mention of every thing. The statement in that case is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Their plot will not harm you in the least﴾, that is, harm. It was objected to this that it is not as stated, because if the negation applies to the verbal noun, it becomes negated in a general sense, and this entails negating all kinds of the verbal noun, which implies negating all its individual instances. This is not a valid objection, because the meaning in that case is that all kinds of neglect are negated from the Qur'an, and this is undoubted, and it does not entail that every thing is mentioned in it, as it did on the other view. Either way, the clause is parenthetical, confirming the content of what precedes it, because among the things is that He, exalted is He, takes care of the interests of all His creatures as is fitting. It is related from al-Hasan and Qatada that the intended "Book" is the Book that is with Allah, the Exalted, and it includes everything that has been and will be, namely the Preserved Tablet. The purpose of the parenthetical clause in that case is to indicate that the conditions of the communities are fully recorded there, not limited to this brief summary. It is related from Abu Muslim that the intended meaning is the term (ajal), that is, there is no thing except that We have appointed for it a term which it will reach. Its remoteness is not hidden.

Alqama read (ma faratna) with a light (unshaddad) pronunciation, and it has the same meaning as the heavy form. Abu al-Abbas said: The meaning of the light form faratna is "we delayed," as they say: "Allah, exalted is He, delayed the illness from you," meaning He removed it. ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾.

83

The pronoun refers to the communities in general, and the plural form is used by way of predominance (taghlib), that is, to the Lord of their affairs and no other, they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection. He will then requite them and do justice between them, to such a degree that, glory be to Him and exalted, He will take from the hornless sheep the right of the horned one, as has come in a sound hadith narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

[p. 146]

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the gathering (ḥashr) of the animals is their death. According to what has been said, his meaning, may Allah be pleased with him, is that the Exalted's words ﴿then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ are a metaphor, used as an illustration of death, as occurs in the hadith: "Whoever dies, his Resurrection has come" (man māta faqad qāmat qiyāmatuh). Therefore it is not objected that gathering (ḥashr) means being moved from one place to another, and that its construction with "to" (ilā) is an explicit statement that death is not what is meant. For death too involves a transfer from this world to the Hereafter. Yet what the group has mentioned is more fitting to the context of magnifying the matter and expressing the gravity of the situation.

Moreover, in Risalat al-Maʿad by Abu ʿAli (Ibn Sina), he says: those who acknowledge the Sharia among the adherents of tanasukh (transmigration of souls) said: this verse is evidence for it, because He, glorified is He, said ﴿there is no creature﴾ etc. In it is the judgment that non-rational animals are like us, and they are not actually like us; so it is necessary that they be like us in potential, because this judgment must be true and there is no intermediary between actuality and potentiality. In that case it is necessary to say that the human soul inheres in some of those animals, and this is the transmigration (tanasukh) that is sought.

[p. 147]

It should not be hidden that this is a worthless argument for a corrupt doctrine. Some people have made it evidence that all animals have rational souls just as individual humans do, and this is the view of the Sufis and some Islamic philosophers. Al-Shaʿrani, in al-Jawahir wa'l-Durar, cited for this purpose other proofs besides those mentioned. Among them: when the Prophet (ﷺ) emigrated and each of the Ansar seized the bridle of his she-camel, he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "Leave her, for she is commanded." The basis of the inference is that he (ﷺ) informed that the she-camel is commanded, and only one who has a rational soul understands command. If it is established that the she-camel has such a soul, it is established for the rest as well, since there is no one who makes a distinction. Among them is what is observed in the bee and its craft of making honeycomb cells, the spiders and their cunning in catching flies, and the ant and its storing of its food in a way that what it stores does not spoil. Some have also cited as evidence the ant that spoke to Solomon, upon him be prayer and peace, in the manner Allah related about it, which only those who know can comprehend. And the sheep's fear of a wolf, though it had never seen the wolf's act before, for that cannot occur except through inference, which is the way of those with rational souls. And the trained lion's not preying on its master, for example, is evidence of belief in benefit and knowledge of the good, which is a characteristic of those with souls.

More strange than this is the claim of the Sufis, which al-Shaʿrani transmitted from his shaykh ʿAli al-Khawwas, may Allah sanctify his secret: that animals are addressed and charged by Allah, Exalted is He, in a way that those veiled do not perceive. Then he said: "This is confirmed by the Exalted's words ﴿and there is no nation but a warner has passed among them﴾, where He, glorified is He, mentioned 'nation' and 'warner', and they are among the nations."

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he used to say: "Everything that is in the nations is in us, to the point that among them is an Ibn ʿAbbas like me." It is mentioned in al-Ajwiba al-Mardiyya that among them there are prophets. In al-Jawahir it is said that the warner may be from among themselves, and may be from outside them, of their kind. His shaykh related from some of them that he said: "The Exalted's comparison of those who go astray among His servants with cattle, in His words ﴿they are only like cattle﴾, is not a deficiency in them; it is only to show the perfection of their rank in knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, to the point that they were bewildered in Him. So the comparison is in truth with bewilderment, not with the one bewildered in Him. There is no one more bewildered than the knowers of Allah, Exalted is He. The highest that the knowers reach of their Lord, glorified is He, is the origin of the beasts, which they have not moved away from, that is, from their origin, though they move in their states through the movement of the divine affairs, for these do not remain in one state. Therefore those of this people whom Allah, mighty and majestic, described were more astray in path than the cattle, because they want to leave bewilderment through their thought and reflection, and this is not possible for them. The beasts knew this, stopped at it, and did not seek to leave it, and that is because of their intense knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He." End of quotation.

Al-Shihab related from Ibn al-Munir that whoever holds that beasts and creeping things are charged, and have messengers of their own kind, is among the heretics (malāḥida) on whom no reliance is placed, like al-Jahiz and others. Many jurists have stated the takfir (declaring unbeliever) of one who says this. The recompense that will be on the Day of Resurrection for animals, in their view, is not the recompense of obligation (taklif). Moreover, some of them held that animals will not be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, and they interpreted the apparent texts indicating this. What is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, has no basis.

The "likeness" (mithliyya) in the verse does not indicate any of what has been mentioned. The strangest of the strange, according to the Sufis of the outward (ahl al-zāhir), may Allah sanctify their secrets, is that they made everything in existence living and perceptive, understanding address and feeling pain as an animal feels pain, and that animals differ from inanimate things only by appetite. They rely on immediate witnessing (shuhūd) for this. Sometimes they cite the Exalted's words ﴿and there is nothing but it glorifies with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ and similar verses and reports.

The view of the majority of scholars is that glorification (tasbīḥ) is by state, not by speech. A parallel to this is the line:

"My camel complained to me of the length of the journey,
and the trough filled up and said, 'Enough!'"

What comes from some inanimate things of glorification, such as the glorification of the pebbles in the blessed hand of the Prophet (ﷺ), for example, is only by a creation of perception at that time. As for the amazing crafts observed in some animals, they are not, as the Shaykh al-Ra'is said, something issuing from deduction and analogy, but from inspiration and subjection. That is why they do not differ and do not vary. The objection from the celestial motion does not apply according to our principles. The lion's not preying on its trained master, for example, is not from belief, but there is another disposition of the soul, which is that every animal naturally loves what gives it pleasure, and the person who feeds it is beloved to it, so this becomes a preventer of its preying on him. This accident may also occur from a divine inspiration, like each animal's love for its young. On this pattern comes, for example, the fear that afflicts some animals.

They have spoken at length on this subject. I see no obstacle to saying that animals have rational souls, varying in perception according to their variation among individual humans. Yet with all that, however they may be, they do not reach in their perception and action the extent reached by humans. The evidences for this are many, and there is no definitive text opposing them that requires interpreting them. More than one scholar has stated that they know their Lord, may His majesty be exalted. As for their having messengers of their own kind, I do not say this, nor do I pronounce unbelief upon one who says it. As for the inanimate things being living and perceptive, this is a matter beyond the scope of my intellect. And Allah is Powerful over all things, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 39:

﴿Those who denied Our signs﴾: that is, the Qur'an or all the other proofs. It enters into this primarily. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") refers to the two groups known from His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾, and so on. Alternatively, it is more general than those. The discourse is connected either to His, glorified is He, words ﴿We have neglected nothing﴾ and so on, or to the words of One whose majesty is exalted: ﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾. The waw is for resumption (isti'naf), and what follows it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is (deaf, dumb). It is also permissible that this be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: some of them are deaf and some of them are dumb. The sentence is the predicate of the subject, and the first view is preferable. This is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), according to the most correct view regarding such expressions. That is, they are like the deaf and like the dumb. So they do not hear the signs in a way that moves their souls, and they are unable to speak the truth. For this reason they do not respond, and they say about the signs what they say.

His, glorified is He, words ﴿in darknesses﴾: that is, in the darknesses of disbelief and its kinds, or in the darkness of ignorance, the darkness of obstinacy, and the darkness of blind imitation in falsehood. This phrase is either a predicate following a predicate for the relative pronoun, on the basis that it stands in the place of (blind), as in His, exalted is He, words: ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾. The reason for omitting the conjunction here, rather than in what preceded it, is to indicate that this alone is sufficient for censure and for turning away from the truth. The conjunction was chosen in what preceded for the sake of mutual implication (talazum). It may be omitted for the sake of another point. Or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun hidden in the predicate, as if it were said: astray, wandering, or existing in darknesses. The circumstantial reading is preferred because it is more eloquent, since it is then understood that their deafness and dumbness are restricted to the state of being in the darknesses of disbelief, or ignorance and its two companions, so that if they were brought out of them, they would hear and speak. On this reading, there is no need to explain the reason for omitting the conjunction.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are in the darknesses. He also permitted that it be an attribute of (dumb), or an adverbial complement of it, or of (deaf), or of the verbal element that stands in for them. It is reported from Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i that the darknesses are meant literally as the darknesses of the Hereafter, meaning that they will be so on the Day of Resurrection as punishment for their disbelief in this world. The discourse on this view is connected to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the nations in general. This is far-fetched.

His, glorified is He, words: ﴿Whomever God wills, He leads astray﴾ are a confirmation of the truth and an affirmation of what came before concerning their state, by explaining that they belong to those sealed by nature, from whom faith is not possible at all. So (whomever) is a subject whose predicate is what follows it, and the object of (wills) is omitted, meaning: His leading him astray. (Whomever) cannot be a fronted object of it, because the meaning would be corrupted. The intended meaning is: whoever He, glorified is He, wills to create in him straying from the truth, He creates it in him according to his choice, which arises from his readiness. Some have permitted that (whomever) is in the accusative position, governed by an omitted verb after it that is explained by what follows it, meaning: whoever He wills to make hard or to punish, He wills to lead him astray. ﴿And whomever He wills, He places on a straight path﴾.

This is coordinated with what came before, and the discussion of it is like the discussion of that. The verse is evidence for the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox majority) that disbelief and faith are by His will, glorified is He, and that the will does not fail to achieve what is willed. Al-Zamakhshari, when he saw the tearing of his corrupt creed, sought to mend it as is his habit, and said: the meaning of ﴿He leads him astray﴾ is that He forsakes him and does not show him kindness, and ﴿He places him﴾ means He shows him kindness. Others said: the intended meaning is whoever He wills to lead astray from the path of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection, He leads astray; and whoever He wills, He places on the path that the believers take to Paradise. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

It was said that the apparent expression would have been: "and whoever He wills, He guides him." However, it was changed from that because His guidance, glorified is He, which is directing him to the right path, is not restricted to some and not others. For this reason it was said, in explaining (He places him) and so on: that is, He guides him to the right path and carries him toward it.

"Say: Tell Me (qul ara'aytakum)" — an command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to rebuke them and silence them with proof they cannot deny. As for the ta', according to what Abu al-Baqa' said, it is the pronoun of the subject, and what follows it (kum) is a particle of address (harf khitab) brought in for emphasis, not a noun. For if it were a noun, it would have to be either genitive, and there is no governing particle here, or nominative, and it is not one of the nominative pronouns, nor is there any requirement for it to be so; or accusative, which is invalid for three reasons.

The first: this verb is of the heart (qalbi), meaning "to know" (bi-ma'na 'alima), and it transitively takes two objects, as in your saying: "Ara'ayta Zaydan ma fa'ala" (Have you seen Zayd, what he did?). So if the mentioned element were made an object, it would be a third object.

The second: if it were made an object, it would be the doer in meaning, but the meaning is not that, since the purpose is not "Have you seen yourself," but rather "Have you seen others." That is why you say: "Ara'aytaka Zaydan," and Zayd is not the addressee, nor is he an apposition (badal) of it.

The third: if it were so, the signs of the dual, plural and feminine would appear on the ta', so you would say: "Ara'aytuma kuma," "Ara'aytumuka-kum," and "Ara'aytunna," and this is the view of the Basrans.

As for the two objects in this verse, it has been said: the first of them is omitted, its estimate being "Ara'aytukum iyyahu aw iyyaha," i.e., the punishment or the Hour, which are the two mentioned in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If the punishment of God comes upon you﴾, i.e., the worldly punishment, as it came upon those before you, ﴿or the Hour comes upon you﴾, i.e., its terror, as what follows indicates, because the sentence is of the type of tanazu' (contention of verbs), in which ara'a and ata both govern one single object, which is ﴿the punishment of God﴾ and "the Hour." The second was made to govern, and the pronoun was omitted in the first. The second of them is the interrogative clause, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Other than God do you call upon?﴾ and the connecting pronoun to the first object is omitted, i.e., "Other than God do you call upon to remove that?" It has been said: there is no tanazu', and the estimate is "Ara'aytukum 'ibadatakum lil-asnam aw al-asnam allati ta'budunaha hal tanfa'ukum" (Have you seen your worship of idols, or the idols you worship, whether they benefit you?). It has been said: the interrogative clause takes the place of the two objects.

Al-Radi, following others, held that (ra'a) here is of sight (basariyya), and it has been said it is of the heart, meaning "to recognize" ('arafa); on both views it is transitive to one object. The original sense of the expression is an interrogation about knowledge, recognition or sight, except that it has come to be used figuratively in the sense of "inform me," and it is not used except when enquiring about a strange state of affairs concerning something. In this, according to what al-Kirmani and others said, there are two figurative usages: the use of "seeing" to mean "informing," because seeing, in whatever sense, is a cause of it; and the use of interrogation in the sense of command, by the common element of demand. As for the statement of some of them that the interrogation is for amazement, this does not contradict that it means "inform me," since that is considered in relation to the original sense of the speech. It is related from Abu Hayyan that al-Akhfash said: the Arabs removed this expression entirely from its meaning, so they said "Ara'aytuka" and "Ara'aytuka" with the second hamza deleted when it means "akhbartu" (I informed), and when it means "absartu" (I saw), its hamza is not deleted, and they also obligated the addressing in this sense.

Page 149

So you never say: "Ara'ani Zayd 'Amran ma sana'a hadha" in the sense of "a'lam" (inform me). They also removed it entirely from its original meaning to a meaning of "ima" (either/or), as evidence of the particle fa' entering after it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen when we took refuge at the rock﴾ and the verse. The fa' only entered after it had been removed to the meaning of "ama" (as for), and the meaning is: as for when we took refuge at the rock, then the matter is thus and thus. They have also removed it to the meaning of "inform me," as we have mentioned, and when it has this meaning, there must be after it the name of the one informed about, and the sentence must follow the interrogation. It may also come in this meaning followed by a conditional particle or a time adverb. End of quote. But he was not agreed with in all of that.

Al-Kisa'i, the shaykh of the people of Kufa, held that the ta' is the pronoun of the subject and the particle of address attached is in the position of the first object. Al-Farra' held that the ta' is a particle of address and the suffixes after it are in the nominative position as subject, being accusative pronouns used in the manner of nominative pronouns. The discussion of this is elaborated in its proper place. The preferred view of many verifiers is what the Basrans held, namely that (kum) here, and likewise all the suffixes, are particles of address, and the object of enquiry for them, and the point of rebuke, is His saying ﴿Other than God?﴾ etc., and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If you are truthful﴾.

[4]

It is connected to "ara'aytakum," confirming the rebuke and revealing their falsehood. The answer to the condition is omitted, relying on what is mentioned indicating it. The estimate, as has been said, is: "If you are truthful that your idols are gods, or that your worship of them benefits, or if you are a people whose nature is truthfulness, then inform me: do you call upon other than God the Exalted if the punishment of God comes upon you," etc., for their truthfulness is among the requirements of their informing about calling upon other than Him, glorified is He.

It has been said: the answer is what His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Other than God do you call upon?﴾, i.e., then call upon Him, with the pronoun referring to other than God. This was objected to, as it impairs the eloquence of the noble composition, how not, when what is required from them is only the information of their calling upon other than Him, glorified is His majesty, at the time of the coming of what comes, not the calling itself. Others allowed that the object of the enquiry is omitted, its estimate being: "Inform me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, whom do you call upon," and they made His saying, glorified is He: "Other than God?" etc., a resumption for the rebuke, in the sense of "Do you single out your gods with calling, as is your custom when harm befalls you, or do you call upon God the Exalted apart from them?" Accordingly, the fronting of the object is for specification.

Some of them made its fronting because the denial is connected to it, and denied its connection to specification. Yes, the fronting in His saying, exalted is He:

[Page 150]

﴿Rather, it is Him alone that you call upon.﴾ (*bal*) is for restriction, meaning: rather, you restrict the calling to Him, glorified is He, and this is not for the sake of the rhyme endings (*fawasil*). The restriction is derived from what follows, and it is a conjunction with a negative clause understood from the preceding speech, as if it were said: "It is not other than God that you call upon, but rather it is Him that you call upon." Al-Zamakhshari (author of *al-Kashshaf*) made it a conjunction with ﴿Is it other than God that you call upon?﴾. Al-Zamakhshari raised an objection to the view that ﴿other than God that you call upon﴾ is the object of the interrogation: that His saying, ﴿so that He may remove that for which you call upon Him﴾, meaning "that which you call upon Him to remove," together with His saying, ﴿or the Hour comes upon you﴾, contradicts it, since the calamities of the Hour are not removed from the polytheists. He answered that He has made the removal conditional on will by His saying, ﴿if He wills﴾, and He, mighty and majestic, does not will the removal of those calamities from them. The objection was specifically raised in this way, according to what is in *al-Kashshaf*, because the two conditions there are connected to His saying, glorified is He: "Is it other than...", and ﴿Rather, it is Him alone...﴾ and so on is a conjunction with it, as a turning away from it. What is conjoined has the same ruling as what it is conjoined to, so both conditions must be connected to it also. Since removal follows calling and is derived from it, the two must also be connected to it, and so the question arose that the calamities of the Hour are not removed. As for the other way, since ("Is it other than...") and so on, being an independent statement, is not connected to the two conditions verbally, it is permissible that they be presumed, or that the apparent reading holds if the meaning supports it. And either one of them may be presumed according to what the context demands. That is because He, glorified and exalted, rebuked them for their habit of calling upon Him alone in distress. Do you not see His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out imploringly﴾? So there is no barrier to mentioning two matters and directing the reproach at one of them without the other, especially when it is specific to the reproach. End of quotation.

It may be said that the removal of worldly and otherworldly calamities, whether through the supplication of a believer or a polytheist, and indeed the acceptance of supplication in general, is conditional on will. By this, the verses ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ and ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I answer the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ are qualified. But the absence of will is realized in some cases, as in His acceptance of the supplication of the disbelievers for the removal of the calamities of the Hour and what they meet of evil recompense for their disbelief, and the removal of some of the terrors from them, such as the distress of the long standing, when intercession is granted to the Messenger (ﷺ) and he intercedes in the judgment among the creatures on that Day.
