This is not at all from the category of answering their supplication.

Moreover, the distress of the long standing, which they leave behind, is a blessing in comparison with what they will meet afterward, even though they did not know it before. Thus the calamities encompass them on that Day and never leave them at all; they only move among them from the severe to the more severe. Therefore, the saying of some of them after the words of al-Zamakhshari, "For the calamities of the Hour are not removed from the polytheists," is in my view the better: the terror of the Resurrection is also removed, as is the distress of the Standing when it is prolonged, as has been reported in the hadith of the Great Intercession. However, al-Zamakhshari did not mention this because the Mu'tazila (a theological school that denies intercession) hold the denial of intercession, and whoever followed him has been unaware of this, speaking words devoid of verification. According to *Majma' al-Bahrayn*, the Mu'tazila do not deny intercession in the judgment and separation, but they deny intercession for the people of major sins and disbelievers in deliverance from the Fire.

This is all. The exegetes differed concerning the response of the first condition. It was said that it is omitted, its estimate being: "then whom do you call upon?" It was said, and Abu al-Baqa held this, that its estimate is: "you have called upon God Most High." It was said that it is mentioned, and it is ﴿Tell me﴾ (*ara'aytakum*). It was said, and it is attributed to al-Radi, that it is the clause containing the interrogation after it, and this seems almost certain according to some opinions. Al-Damamini refuted this, saying that such a clause does not occur as the response of a condition without a *fa'* (the particle of consequence).

Al-Shihab investigated this in his glosses on al-Radi's commentary on *al-Kafiya*. Abu Hayyan said, and many followed him: "What I hold is that the response is omitted, the indication of it being ﴿Tell me﴾, its estimate being: 'If the punishment of God comes upon you, then tell me about it: do you call upon other than God Most High to remove it?' As you say, 'Tell me about Zayd, if he comes to you, what will you do with him?' For the estimate is: 'If he comes to you, then tell me,' so the response is omitted, the indication of it being 'tell me'. A parallel to this is: 'You are a wrongdoer if you do it.'" End of quotation. So understand this and do not be heedless.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you forget what you associate﴾.

Conjunction with ("you call upon"). The forgetting is a metaphor for abandonment, as was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. That is: you abandon what you associate with God Most High of idols, with complete abandonment. It was also said: it is possible that it is in its literal sense, for because of the intensity of the terror they actually forget that, and it does not occur to them at all. It does not then follow that they forget God Most High, because it is customary in hardships to cling to the remembrance of Him Most High and to forget everything other than Him, glorified is He. He placed the removal before the forgetting, though it comes later, just as it comes later than the calling, to show the full care for its matter and to indicate that it follows from the calling specifically.

14

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 42:

﴿And We certainly sent (messengers) to communities before you﴾ This is a resumptive statement, brought to explain that among the polytheists are those who do not call upon Allah Most High when the punishment comes, because of their persistence in misguidance and error, and they are not affected by the warnings of creation (al-zawajir al-takwiniyyah) just as they are not affected by the warnings of revelation (al-zawajir al-tanziliyyah). It was also said: it is brought to console the Prophet (ﷺ). The opening of the sentence with an oath serves to show greater concern with its content, and the object is omitted because the context requires describing the condition of those to whom the messengers were sent, not the condition of the messengers. The tanwin on (umam) is for magnification, and (min) is either for the beginning of the limit (ibtida'iyyah), or means (fi) "in", or is extra (za'idah), based on the permissibility of its extra use in affirmative speech, though this is considered weak. That is: by Allah, We certainly sent messengers to many communities that existed from a time, or in a time, before your time. ﴿Then We seized them﴾ meaning: they denied, so We punished them ﴿with adversity and affliction﴾

Page 151

That is, with hardship and harm.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "Fear of the ruler and high prices." It was also said: al-ba'sa' is famine and hunger, and al-darra' is illness and loss of lives and property. These two are feminine forms with no masculine counterpart on the pattern af'al, like ahmar / hamra', as is the rule; for it is not said ad arr and ab'as as adjectives, but rather they are used for comparison (al-tafdil). ﴿So that they might humble themselves﴾

24

- That is, so that they would become humbled, and so call upon Allah and repent of their disbelief.

34

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 43:

﴿Why then, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ That is, they did not humble themselves at that time, although the cause (al-muqtada) was present and the impediment (al-mani') by which they might have been excused was absent. ("Lawla") according to al-Harawi is a true negation, and he took as an example of this the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Jonah?﴾ Most scholars, however, understood it as reproach and censure (al-tawbikh wa'l-tandim), which indicates abandonment and non-occurrence. For this reason the contrast (al-istidrak) and the conjunction appear in His saying: ﴿But their hearts hardened.﴾ "Lawla" here is not an exhortative (tahdid) particle, as some have supposed, because the exhortative is specific to the present/future verb. Some have preferred the view of al-Harawi. Since humbling oneself arises from softness of heart, its negation is the negation of that softness, as if it were said: "Why did their hearts not soften? Rather, they hardened." It has also been said: the expected form would have been "But it was incumbent upon them to humble themselves," but he turned to what was mentioned because the hardness of heart, which is the impediment, indicates that what was mentioned is incumbent upon them. The meaning of "qasat" (hardened) is that they remained in the hardness they were in, or that their hardness increased. ﴿And Satan made what they used to do seem fair to them.﴾

- of unbelief and sins. So they did not bring to mind that what afflicted them of hardship and adversity had come upon them only because of these. Adornment (al-tazyin) for this has several meanings. The first is bringing a thing into being as fair and adorned in reality, as in His saying: ﴿And We adorned the nearest heaven﴾. The second is making it adorned without bringing it into being, like the hairdresser (al-masheta) adorning the bride. The third is making it beloved to the soul and desired by the disposition, even if it is not so in itself. This is either in the sense of creating inclination in the soul and disposition, or in the sense of embellishing and decorating it with speech and the like, such as whispering and enticement. On this basis the matter of its attribution is determined. It occurs in the noble text sometimes attributed to Satan, as in this verse; sometimes attributed to Him, glory be to Him, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Thus We made fair to every community their deeds﴾; and sometimes to humans, as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Their partners made fair to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾. If it is in the first sense, its attribution to God the Exalted is literal, and likewise if it is in the third sense on the basis of what is meant by it first. If it is in the second or third sense on the basis of what is meant by it secondly, then its attribution to Satan or to humans is literal, and it is not possible to attribute what occurs through seduction and whispering to Him, glory be to Him, in that way. It also occurs without a mentioned agent, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿It was made fair to the transgressors﴾. In that case, whatever is fitting is to be supplied in each place. What pertains to this discussion has already passed for you, so remember it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 44:

﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ — that is, they abandoned what the Messengers, peace be upon them, called them to and rejected it, and did not take heed from it, as related from Ibn Jurayj. It has also been said that the meaning is that they immersed themselves in their sins and did not take heed from what afflictions and adversities had befallen them. So when they did not take heed, ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ — of the abundant blessings, such as ease and abundance of provision — as a deception against them and a gradual drawing-on (istidraj) of them.

For Ahmad, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related, from the hadith of Uqba ibn Amir, raised to the Prophet: "When you see Allah, exalted is He, giving a servant in this world while he persists in his sins, then it is only istidraj." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "So when they forgot..." and what follows. It is also related from al-Hasan that when he heard this verse he said: "The people have been deceived, by the Lord of the Ka'bah. They were given what they wanted, and then they were seized." It has also been said that the meaning is that We opened for them those things as a means of establishing the proof against them and removing any excuse, and the apparent view is that (fatahna, "We opened") is the response (jawab) to (ma, "what"), because it carries the meaning of a conditional, whether it is taken as a particle or as a noun.

This has been raised as an objection: it is not evident how forgetting causes the opening of gates of good. It is answered that forgetting is the cause of the istidraj, which depends on the opening of the gates of good, and the causation of one thing for another entails its causation of what it depends upon. Or it may be said that the response is what has been mentioned in terms of its outcome and its substance, namely "We established the proof against them" and the like, and its being caused by it is evident. It has also been said that it is caused by it in terms of its end, which is seizing them suddenly. Abu Ja'far and Ibn Amir read (fattahna) with shadda, for intensification.

﴿Until, when they rejoiced﴾ — the rejoicing of insolence — ﴿in what they had been given﴾ — of blessings — and did not fulfil the rights of the Bestower, exalted is His majesty, ﴿We seized them﴾ — We punished them and sent down torment upon them — ﴿suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, so that it would be more severe upon them and more dreadful in its terror. It is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject or the object, meaning "surprising" or "surprised", or as a verbal noun, meaning "We surprised them with a surprise." ﴿Then, behold, they were despairing﴾.

44

— That is, despairing of salvation and mercy, as related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Al-Balkhi said: humbled and submissive. From al-Suddi: iblas is the change of the face, and from it Iblis was named, because Allah, exalted is He, overturned his face and altered it. From Mujahid: it means dejection (ikti'ab).

In the Shihabi glosses on the lexical meanings of al-Iblas, there are three meanings in the language: sorrow, grief (hasrah), and despair, and these are closely related meanings. Al-Raghib said: it is a sorrow that arises from intense despair. And since one who is ablas often falls silent and forgets what concerns him, it is said: ablasa fulan when he fell silent and when his argument was cut off. And (idha) is the sudden (fuja'iyyah) particle, and it is an adverb of place, as Abu al-Baqa' stated explicitly. From a group it is related that it is an adverb of time, and the view of the Kufans is that it is a particle. According to the first two views, the element governing it is the predicate of the subject, meaning: they were despairing in the place where they dwelt, or in the time of it.

﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾, i.e., their last ones, as more than one scholar has said. It derives from *dubur* (the back), when one follows another, as if he is at his back, i.e., behind him. From the same root comes the saying: "Indeed, among people is he who does not come to the prayer except *dubura* (at the back)," i.e., at the end of the time.

Al-Asma'i (al-Asma'i, a noted philologist) said: *al-dabir* means the origin, and from it comes the expression *qata'a Allahu dabirahu*, i.e., God cut off his origin. Whichever meaning is intended, the point is that they were completely uprooted by the punishment, and none of them remained. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate the reason for the ruling.

﴿And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾

54

for what befell them of punishment and destruction. The destruction of disbelievers and sinners, insofar as it is a deliverance for the people of the earth from the evil of their corrupt beliefs and their wicked deeds, is a great blessing deserving to be praised for. Thus this is a teaching from Him, exalted is He, to His servants that they should praise Him for the like of this. Al-Tabarsi chose that He, mighty is His name, praised Himself for that act.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 46:

﴿Say﴾ O Muhammad, in a manner of rebuke and reproach as well: ﴿Tell me, if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight﴾, that is, make you deaf and blind. Thus, "taking" them is a metaphor for what has been mentioned, because it is a necessary consequence of it. And using this verse as evidence for the persistence of an accident (ʿaraḍ) over two durations (zamānayn) is open to scrutiny.

﴿And seal over your hearts﴾ by covering them with something such that no understanding or comprehension at all remains for you. It has also been said: it is permissible for the sealing (khatm) to be an explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf tafsīrī) for the taking, since sight and hearing are two pathways to the heart through which it receives what it receives of perceptions; so taking them is a complete closing of its door. This is the secret in placing the taking of them before the sealing over the hearts. It has been objected that perceptions include those that depend on hearing and sight; for this reason, more than one scholar has said that faith in Allah the Exalted is obligatory upon one who was born blind and deaf and has reached the age of legal responsibility. It has also been said regarding the ordering that it is of the type of placing what relates to the outward before what relates to the inward. The reason for placing hearing first and using it in the singular has already been indicated.

﴿Who is a god other than Allah who could bring it to you?﴾ That is, bring it (that), with the pronoun being used in place of the singular demonstrative, because it is the one that has become common in usage to refer to several things by it. As for the singular pronoun, it has been said to carry this as well, and it has been reported from al-Zajjaj that the pronoun refers to what was taken and what was sealed over, as implied in what preceded, that is, what has been removed from you. Or it refers to hearing, with what follows it included together with it in the intent. Its remoteness is not hidden.

It is also permissible that it refers to one of these mentioned things. "Man" (who) is the subject, "ilāh" (god) is its predicate, "ghayr" (other than) is an attribute of the predicate, and "yatīkum" (could bring to you) is another attribute. The clause, as more than one scholar has said, is the object of the seeing, and the locus of the questioning, that is: tell me, if Allah the Exalted removes your faculties, who is a god other than Him, glorified is He, who could bring them to you? The address particle (kāf al-khiṭāb) is omitted here. It has been said: this is because the warning in it is lighter than what preceded and what follows.

It has also been said: it is a sufficiency with what precedes and what follows, since this address lies between them. It has also been said: since this is of the kind that the people cannot remain fit for address with, the particle has been dropped entirely, as a sign of this and in observance of a hidden correspondence.

﴿Look how We vary the signs﴾, that is, We repeat them in various modes. From this is the variation of the winds. The intended "signs," according to what al-Kalbi related, are the Qur'anic verses. Whether they are meant absolutely, or what has been mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to here, or what has been mentioned before this, are sayings; the closest of them in my view is the closest. Included in them is what indicates the existence of the Creator and His unity, and what contains encouragement and warning, admonition and reminder. This is a wonderment directed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It has also been said: it is directed to whoever is fit for address, regarding their failure to be affected by the striking signs that have passed.

﴿Yet still they turn away﴾

- That is, they turn aside from that. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited for this meaning the verse of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith:

"I marvel at Allah's judgment concerning us, when He has shown us turning away from every revealed truth."

Some have mentioned that one says: "ṣadafa ʿan al-shay' ṣudūfan" when one inclines away from something, and its root is from "al-ṣadf," meaning side and direction; similar to it is "al-ṣadafa," which is applied to every elevated structure. It is reported in a narration that the Prophet ﷺ passed by an inclined ṣadaf and hurried on.

The clause is coordinated with "tasrīf" (variation), included with it in its ruling, and it is the core of the wonderment. "Thumma" (yet/then) indicates remoteness: that is, after that variation which necessitates turning to Allah and faith, they still deny and disbelieve.

﴿Say: Tell me﴾ is another rebuke to them, forcing them to acknowledge that the punishment is specific to them. ﴿If the punishment of God comes upon you﴾, that is, the swift punishment that is specific to you, as it came upon peoples like you before you, ﴿suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, without any sign or warning appearing. Because by this meaning *baghtah* (sudden) includes the sense of being unaware that *khufyah* (secret) has, it is correct to contrast it with His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿or openly﴾. It is mentioned first because it is more deterrent than the open (form). He did not say *khufyah* (secretly) because concealment is not fitting for His majesty, exalted be He.

Some have claimed that *baghtah* is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for *khufyah*, based on its being contrasted with *jahrah* (openly), and that it is an implicit metaphor (*makniyyah*) without an imaginative element (*takhyiliyyah*). It should not be hidden that, apart from its being forced (*ta'assuf*), this is unnecessary, for contrasting a thing with something close to its opposite is common in eloquent speech, and among examples of it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give good news and do not repel." It is reported from al-Hasan that *baghtah* means that He comes to them at night, and *jahrah* means that He comes to them by day. It is also read as *baghatan aw jaharatan* with fatḥah on the ghayn and the hā', as both are verbal nouns (*masdar*), like *ghalabah* (overpowering), meaning: a coming suddenly, or a coming openly. In *al-Muhtasab* by Ibn Jinni, the position of our companions (the Basrans) is that every guttural consonant that is quiescent after a fatḥah is not vocalized except as a dialectal variant of it, such as *al-nahr* and *al-nahar*, *al-sha'r* and *al-sha'ar*, *al-halb* and *al-halab*, *al-tard* and *al-tarad*. The position of the Kufans is that it is permissible to vocalize the second consonant, since it is a guttural letter, as a regular analogical rule, such as *al-bahr* and *al-bahar*. I do not see the truth except with them. I likewise heard it from the common people of ʿAqil. I also heard al-Shajari say: "Anā maḥmūm" with fatḥah on the ḥā', and there is no *maf'ūl* with fatḥah on the fā' in Arab speech. They also said *al-laḥam* meaning *al-laḥm* (meat). I heard him say: *tagaddū* meaning *taghdū*, and there is no *mafal* with fatḥah on the fā' in their speech. They also said *sāra nahawahu* with fatḥah on the ḥā'. If the vowel were original, the lām would never have been sound at all. End of quotation. As al-Shihab said, this is a point that should be memorised. It is also read as *baghtatan wa jahratan* with the connecting wāw.

﴿Will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾

- That is, except you. The apparent noun is placed in the position of their pronoun, to record their wrongdoing against them and to make known that the cause of their destruction is their wrongdoing, and their placing disbelief in the place of faith and turning away in the place of turning towards. As the scholars said, the object of the interrogation and the question here is for affirmation: that is, say, affirming for them that destruction is specific to them: tell me, if His punishment, exalted be His majesty, comes upon you as you deserve, will any be destroyed by that punishment except you? That is, will anyone other than you be destroyed, one who does not deserve it? It was also said: the intended meaning of "the wrongdoing people" is the class, and they are included in it in the primary sense. This was objected to on the grounds that the specification of the coming to them rules this out. It was also said: the interrogation carries the meaning of negation, because the exception is *mufrigh* (incomplete), and the original form of it is negation. The object of the enquiry in this case is omitted, as if it were said: tell me, if His punishment, exalted and glorious be He, comes upon you suddenly or openly, what will be the state? Then it was said, as an explanation of that: what will be destroyed is ﴿only the wrongdoing people﴾, that is, by that punishment specific to you, none will be destroyed except you.

Al-Tabarsi and others restricted the destruction to destruction by punishment and wrath, to direct the restriction (*hasr*), since someone other than a wrongdoer may be destroyed; but that is a mercy from Him, exalted be He, to that person, so that He may give him the full reward for his trial. Perhaps this is a digression into what does not concern (the matter). It is also read *yuhlak* with fatḥah on the yā'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 48:

﴿And We do not send the messengers﴾ to the nations ﴿except as bringers of good news﴾ to whoever of them obeys, with reward, ﴿and warners﴾ to whoever of them disobeys, with punishment. Some of them restricted it to Paradise and the Fire, because they are the greatest of what is given as good news and what is warned of. The two words conjoined (mubashshirin and mundhirin) are in the accusative because they are circumstantial clauses (hal) that are anticipated (muqaddarah) and convey the reason (li-l-ta'lil). The form of the present tense (sigha al-mudari') is to indicate (li-l-i'dhan) that this is a continuous matter, to which the divine custom (al-'adah al-ilahiyyah) has been applied. The verse is connected to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ That is: We do not send the messengers except so that they may give good news to their people of reward for obedience and warn them of punishment for disobedience, and We did not send them so that they might be asked for signs or be mocked.

﴿So whoever believes﴾ in what belief in it is obligatory ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ of what it is obligatory to set right and to perform in accordance with the Sharia. The fa' (fa, "so") is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes. ("Man," "whoever") is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and because the relative pronoun resembles a conditional (shart), the fa' entered in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿there is no fear for them﴾ of the punishment with which the messengers warned ﴿nor will they grieve﴾

84

- due to the loss of the reward with which they were given good news. The discussion of this verse has already been presented more than once. The plural of the three pronouns referring back to (man) is according to its meaning, just as the singular of the two preceding pronouns is according to its wording.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 49:

﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, that is, the signs which the Messengers, upon them be peace, conveyed at the time of giving glad tidings and warning. It was also said: what is meant by them is our Prophet ﷺ and his miracles. The first view is the apparent one, and the relative pronoun (alladhina) is the subject (mubtada'). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the punishment will touch them﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and the sentence is coordinated with (man amana) and so on. What is meant by "the punishment" is the punishment with which they were warned, whether in this world or in the next, or the reality of punishment and its genus, which includes that in an initial way. In making it "touching" there is an indication that it is treated as a living agent that does what it wills, so there is, according to what has been said, a metaphor by implication (isti'arah makniyyah).

Al-Tibi allowed that the touching may be a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) without any metaphor in "the punishment." The apparent meaning is that what has been mentioned is based on touching being one of the特 properties of living beings. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said that it implies choice. Some scholars rejected this. Isam al-Millah claimed that by "touching" it is indicated that the punishment does not seize them in a way that annihilates them, so that they might escape through destruction. There is a basis for this view. ﴿because they used to transgress﴾.

- That is, because of their transgression.

Indeed, Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) related from Ibn Zayd that every instance of fisq (transgression) in the Qur'an means lying (kadhib). Perhaps this applies within the context of prohibition and their continuous departure from the enclosure of faith and obedience. It may also be said that the fasiq is one who departs from adherence to some rulings, but this is not appropriate here.

Say, O Messenger, bearer of glad tidings and warner, to the disbelievers who propose to you what they propose:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 50:

﴿I do not tell you that I have the treasures of Allah﴾, i.e., His decrees (maqdurat), plural of khazina, khizana or khazna, which originally means that in which precious things are kept. It is used figuratively in the sense mentioned. Al-Jubba'i and others held this view. He did not say, "I am not able to do what Allah is able to do." It was said: this is because it is more eloquent in indicating that, due to the strength of His power, His decrees are as though stored and present with Him. It was also said: "treasures" is a metaphor for provisions, by the figure of speech of mentioning the location for what is located, or the necessary for what necessitates it. It was also said: the statement contains an omitted modifier, i.e., the treasures of Allah's provision, or His decrees. The meaning is: I do not claim that those treasures have been entrusted to me, that I dispose of them as I wish, independently or by request, so that you would propose to me the descent of signs, or the sending down of punishment, or the turning of mountains into gold, or other things that do not befit my station.

﴿And I do not know the unseen﴾ is coordinated with the place of ﴿with me are the treasures of Allah﴾, so it is also a saying of "I say." Al-Halabi objected to this, since it would lead to the meaning becoming: "And I do not tell you, I do not know the unseen," which is not correct. It is answered that the intended meaning is: "And I do not tell you, I know the unseen," with the verb "I say" implied between "la" and "a'lamu," not between the "wa" (and) and "la." It was also said: the "la" in "la a'lamu" is an extra emphatic negation.

Abu Hayyan said: the apparent meaning is that it is coordinated with "I do not tell you," with no governed element of its own. He was commanded to inform about himself with these sentences, so they are governed by the command, which is "Say." This was criticized on the grounds that there is no benefit in informing that "I do not know the unseen." The benefit lies only in informing that "I do not say that," so as to negate the claim to the two matters that are specific to divinity, so that the meaning would be: I do not claim divinity.

﴿And I do not tell you that I am an angel﴾, i.e., I do not claim angelhood. The repetition of "I do not tell you" is a sign of this meaning. Some researchers said: since my being in possession of Allah's treasures and my being an angel are known to people, there is no need to negate them; the need is only to negate the claim to them, disavowing false claims. The meaning of "I do not know the unseen," since it was not known, needed negation here. So the claim that there is no benefit in informing of that is open to scrutiny. What our master Shaykh al-Islam chose is the first view, and that the meaning is: "And I do not also claim that I know the unseen of His actions, the Mighty and Majestic, so that you ask me about the time of the Hour, or the time of the sending down of punishment, or the like."

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, restricted the unseen to the outcome to which they will come, i.e., I do not claim that. And I do not also claim angelhood, so that you demand of me extraordinary acts beyond human capacity, such as ascending into the sky and the like, or count my not having their attributes as a flaw in my affair, as their saying indicates: ﴿What is the matter with this Messenger? He eats food and walks in the markets﴾. On this view, there is no evidence in the verse for the preference of angels over prophets, peace be upon them, which is the point of dispute, as Al-Jubba'i claimed, because it was revealed only as a rebuttal of the unbelievers in their saying ﴿What is the matter with this Messenger﴾, etc., and their demanding of him, peace be upon him, such things as ascending into the sky. We do not claim that prophets are distinguished over angels, peace be upon them, in not eating, for example, or in the power to perform extraordinary acts such as ascending and the like, nor that they are equal to them in that; rather, that angels are distinguished over them, peace be upon them, in that is something agreed upon by both the agreeing and the disagreeing, and that does not necessitate agreement that angels are superior to them in the disputed sense; otherwise many animals would be superior to humans, and no one claims that except an inanimate object.

This answer is more evident than what is reported from al-Qadi Zakariya, that this statement from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was by way of humility and displaying servanthood, like his saying, peace be upon him: "Do not prefer me over the son of Matta," in one opinion. Rather, that is nothing, as is not hidden. It was also said: the superiority is according to the assumption of the addressees, and this is from narrowness of mind. It was also said: since the meaning of the verse is "I do not claim divinity or angelhood," there is no ascent from the lower to the higher in it; rather it is then evidently descending. By this, the rule used by al-Zamakhshari in his argument from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The Messiah will not disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels brought near﴾ for the preference of angels over humans is destroyed, since ascent from divinity to what is higher than it cannot be conceived, as there is nothing higher to ascend to. It is objected that this does not destroy it, given the repetition of "I do not tell you," which he made an independent command, like a turning away, since the meaning is: "I do not claim divinity, but neither angelhood"; and therefore he repeated "I do not tell you."

Some said in distinguishing the two situations: in the situation of negating disdain, the later item should be higher, so that its mention is not void; and in the situation of negating claim, it is the reverse, since whoever does not dare to claim angelhood first would not dare to claim divinity, which is more remote. Yes, there is a question about whether the intended meaning of the first is negating the claim to divinity and disavowing it; otherwise it would have said, "I do not tell you that I am God," as it said, "And I do not tell you that I am an angel." Also, in the allusion to divinity by "with me are the treasures of Allah," there is an indecency that is not hidden, and the attribution of the treasures to Him, exalted, is incompatible with it. He answered the incompatibility by saying that the claim to divinity is not a claim that he himself is Allah, exalted, but that he be a partner to Him, Mighty is His name, in divinity. In this there is a question, because the attribution of the treasures to Him, exalted, is exclusive, and so it contradicts partnership, unless it means "treasures like the treasures" or they are attributed to him, and that is, as you see, far-fetched. From here Shaykh al-Islam said: making that a disavowal of the claim to divinity is something that has no basis at all.

﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾, i.e., I do nothing except follow what is revealed to me, without there being for me any part, in any way, in the revelation or in what is revealed, whether by request or in any other way at all. The summary of it is: I am a servant who obeys the command of his Master and follows what He has revealed, and I do not claim any of those things, so that you propose to me what are among their effects and rulings, and make my not responding to that a proof of the invalidity of what I claim of messengerhood. It is not hidden that this is more eloquent than "I am a prophet or a messenger," and therefore he turned to it.

There is no evidence in this for those who deny analogy, nor for the meanings of the permissibility of his, peace be upon him, exercising independent judgment, as is not hidden. Some went to the view that the purpose of this statement is a rebuttal of the disbelievers, as if it were said: "This is a claim, and it is not something unlikely; what is unlikely is the claim to divinity or angelhood, and I do not claim them." You already know what is in the claim that the purpose of what preceded was negating the claim to divinity and angelhood.

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾, i.e., the astray and the guided, in absolute terms, as many have said.

The interrogation is one of denial, and the intended meaning is denial that those who do not know the aforementioned realities are equal to those who know them, with an indication of the full clarity of those realities, a warning against error, and an encouragement to guidance. The repetition of the command is to fix the rebuke and to emphasize the obligation: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾

Some mentioned that in "the blind and the seeing" there are three possibilities: either they are an example of the astray and the guided, or an example of the ignorant and the knowing, or an example of one who claims the impossible, like divinity or angelhood, and one who claims the upright, like prophethood. The meaning is that these two categories are not equal. ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ on that, so that you be guided, i.e., so that you distinguish between the claim of truth and the claim of falsehood, or so that you know that following revelation is something from which there is no escape. The sentence is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to what has passed, either from the beginning of the surah until here, or to His, glorified be He, saying ﴿If I follow﴾ etc., or to His, Mighty is His affair, saying "I do not tell you." Al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf preferred the first, then the second. The remoteness of this preference is not hidden.

The view that angelhood is impossible was objected to on the ground that it is one of the possible things, since substances are alike, and accidents subsisting in some of them may subsist in all of them.

It was answered, after granting what is in it, that a human, while being human, cannot be an angel, because the two are distinguished by mutually exclusive accidents, without disagreement. And Adam's proceeding, peace be upon him, to eat after hearing ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree except that you become angels or become among the eternal﴾ was not a desire for angelhood while in human state. Moreover, it may be said that he did not desire angelhood at all, but desired immortality, and so he ate.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 51:

﴿And warn﴾, i.e., admonish and frighten, O Muhammad, with it, meaning with what is revealed, or with the Qur'an, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, and al-Zajjaj. It was also said: i.e., with God Most High. This was narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥak.

This is a command from Him, glory be to Him, to His Prophet (ﷺ), after He, glory be to Him, had told him that among the disbelievers are those who do not heed admonition and are not affected by it. They have joined the dead and been placed in the row of inanimate things, so the remedy of warning has no effect on them, and admonition and reminder benefit them not. Warning is given to those from whom benefit is expected in general, and from whom acceptance and listening are hoped for. They are the ones indicated by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾. So the intended meaning of the relative clause is those who consider the gathering possible in the manner that will come, whether they were certain of its occurrence, like the People of the Book and some of the polytheists who acknowledged resurrection but doubted the intercession of their forefathers, the prophets, as the earlier ones did, or doubted the intercession of the idols, as the later ones did, or doubted both together, like some disbelievers whose condition indicates that when they hear his speech they fear that it may be true. As for those who deny the gathering altogether, and those who affirm it but firmly believe in the intercession of their forefathers or of the idols, they are excluded from those who were commanded to be warned. Thus said Shaykh al-Islam.

It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with them, that the intended meaning of the relative clause is the believers, and many have endorsed this, except that they restricted it to those who are negligent, because that is what suits warning and the hope of piety. Shaykh [al-Islam] objected to this, saying that it is something that neither the preceding context (siyaq al-sibaq) nor the immediate context (siyaq) supports; rather, there is in it what decides against its soundness, and he explained this shortly, God willing. It was also said: the intended meaning is both the believers and the disbelievers. al-Imam al-Razi gave as the reason that there is no rational person who does not fear the gathering, whether he is certain of its occurrence or doubtful about it, since by consensus it is not known to be necessarily false, so this fear exists in regard to all. And [he gave as a reason] that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent to all, so he was commanded to convey to all. The defect in this is not hidden. The second object of "warn" is either the otherworldly punishment indicated by what is within the relative clause, or the punishment in general which the threat has mentioned. The mention of the title of Lordship (al-rubbubiyyah) in establishing the fear is either because the nurturing implied by it requires the opposite of what they feared the gathering for, or because it indicates absolute ownership and comprehensive control, as has been said. The intended meaning of the gathering to Him, glory be to Him, is the gathering to the place which He, mighty and majestic, made a site for their assembly and for the judgment upon them. Therefore the verse is not a proof for the anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah).

His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿They will have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (yuḥsharuː) [they are gathered], and the governing element in it is its verb. al-Imam narrated from al-Zajjaj that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (yakhafūna) [they fear], but the first is more appropriate. The phrase (man dūnahu) [besides Him] is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the subject of (laysa) [there is not], because originally it is an adjective of it, and when it was placed before it, it took the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The first circumstantial clause is to exclude the gathering that was not qualified by it from the sphere of fear, and to establish that the thing on which the fear depends is that state, not the gathering however it may be, since those who acknowledge it while firmly believing in the support of other than Him are in the same position as those who deny it regarding the absence of the fear on which the matter of warning depends. The second circumstantial clause is to establish the basis of their fear, which is the loss of what they attached their hope to, and that is none other than Him, glory be to Him, as in His saying, majestic is His affair: ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of God will not escape on earth, and will have no protectors besides Him﴾. It is not for excluding a protector who was not qualified by it from the sphere of negation, because that would imply the establishment of His guardianship over them, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides God﴾, and that is false. The meaning is: warn with it those who fear their gathering while they are not helped by their helpers in their own assumption. Thus said Shaykh al-Islam. Then he said: From this it has become clear that there is no way for the fearful to mean the negligent among the believers, since they have no protector or intercessor, whether [the protector is] other than Him, mighty and majestic, so that they might fear the gathering without His support. Rather, what they fear is the gathering without His support, glory be to Him. End of quotation. This is a verification I have not seen from anyone else, and what is in the Tafsir al-Kabir becomes small beside it. Perhaps what was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with them, is not authentically established from them, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 52:

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to warn those mentioned so that they might be included among the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), he (ﷺ) was forbidden from doing so in a way that would lead to driving them away. Some reports imply that the two verses were revealed together, while other reports do not imply this. Ahmad, al-Tabarani and others related from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The chiefs of Quraysh passed by the Prophet (ﷺ) while with him were Suhayb, Ammar, Bilal, Khabbab and others of the weak among the Muslims. They said: 'O Muhammad, are you content with these people from among your folk? Are these the ones on whom God has bestowed favour from among us? Shall we be followers of these? Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and others related from Khabbab, may God be pleased with him, who said: "al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi and Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari came and found the Prophet (ﷺ) with Bilal, Suhayb, Ammar and Khabbab, along with some weak believers. They said: 'We would like you to make for us a gathering apart from them, one by which the Arabs will recognise our virtue, for the delegations of the Arabs come to you, and we are ashamed that they should see us sitting with these slaves. He called for the parchment and called Ali, may God ennoble his face, to write it, while we were sitting in a corner. Then Gabriel descended with this verse: ﴿And do not drive away those who﴾ and so on. Then he called us and we came to him, and he was saying: ﴿Peace be upon you.
