Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And thus We tried some of them by means of others﴾, etc. When it was revealed, ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) came and apologised for his statement, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you﴾, etc. "Al-Ghadāh" (the morning) – its origin is ghadwah; the waw was changed to an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open. The origin of "al-ʿashiyy" (the evening) is ʿashawiyy; the waw was changed to a yā', and the yā' was assimilated into the (following) yā', in observance of the rule. The apparent reading is that it is singular, like al-ʿashiyyah, and its plural is ʿashāyā and ʿashiyyāt. It has been said that it is a plural of ʿashiyyah, but this is far-fetched. The meaning of the first, linguistically, is the early part of the day, or what lies between the dawn prayer and sunrise; the meaning of the second is the end of the day. Here, the intended sense of both is continuity, as one says: "He did it morning and evening" when he persisted in it. By "supplication" is meant its literal sense, or prayer, or remembrance, or recitation of the Qur'an – these are the opinions.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that the two are an expression for the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer, because time is often mentioned while what occurs in it is intended, as one says "he prayed the dawn" meaning his prayer. It may also be reversed, so that by "the prayer" its time is meant, as in "the prayer has drawn near," i.e. its time; and it may be meant by its place, as has been said regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, that the intended meaning of "the prayer" is the mosques. The two were singled out for mention because of their excellence. The opinions on "supplication" run along this view, except the second. Ibn ʿĀmir read here and in al-Kahf "al-Ghadwah" with a waw, and this is the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Raja' al-ʿAtaridi and others. Abu ʿUbayd claimed that whoever reads with a waw has erred, because "Ghadwah" is a proper noun of a genus which does not take the definite article "al-". The source of his error is that he followed the orthography, since "al-ghadāh" is written with a waw like "al-ṣalāh" and "al-zakāh". But he erred in this criticism too, because although the well-known usage of "ghadwah" is what he mentioned, its occurrence as a common noun, indefinite and declinable, has also been heard, so that "al" may enter it then. Sibawayh transmitted this from al-Khalil, and prefacing it with "he claims" does not indicate its weakness, as the words of al-Imam al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim indicate, and a great multitude of the people of language mentioned it.

Al-Mubarrad also related from the Arabs the indefinite form "ghadwah", its declension, and the entry of the article upon it when it is not intended to denote a particular day's morning. The affirmative is given precedence over the negative, and one who memorised is proof against one who did not; and its occurrence in the mutawatir recitation suffices as proof. So there is no need – as has been said – to insist that it is a proper noun but was made indefinite and thus took "al-", because making a proper noun indefinite and adding "al-" to it is a very rare occurrence in their speech. Nor is there need to insist that it is definite and that the "al-" entered it for the sake of harmonisation with "al-ʿashiyy", as "Yazid" took the article for the sake of harmonisation with "al-Walid" in the verse:

"I saw al-Walid ibn Yazid blessed, his shoulder heavy with the burdens of the caliphate,"

because this type of harmonisation, true harmonisation, is also rare, and the common form of harmonisation is figurative. There is no indication in the verse that the Prophet ﷺ ever drove them away in order to scratch the face of infallibility. What the reports convey is that he, upon him be prayer and peace, intended to make those righteous callers one occasion and the nobles of Quraysh another occasion, so that they might become friendly and he might lead them to faith; and those (companions), may Allah be pleased with them, knew what the Prophet ﷺ intended, so no humiliation or heartbreak befell them from him, upon him be prayer and peace.

﴿Desiring His Face﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "yad'ūna" (they call). Regarding the meaning of "the Face" according to the interpreters there is disagreement. It has been said – and this is the well-known view – that it is the Essence, meaning those desiring His Essence. The meaning of desiring the Essence, as has been said, is sincerity towards it, based on the impossibility of Allah being desired for His own Essence, since will is an attribute that is only related to contingent things, for it entails the preponderance of one of two sides of the object willed over the other, and that is not conceivable except in contingent things. That is: they call upon their Lord sincerely devoted to Him. This qualification was added to emphasise its being the cause of the prohibition, for sincerity is among the strongest causes of honour, which is the opposite of driving away. It has also been said that by it is meant the direction and the path, and the meaning is: desiring the path which He, great is His majesty, commanded them to desire; and this is what the words of al-Zajjaj imply. It has been said that it is a metaphor for love and seeking good pleasure, because whoever loves a person loves to see his face; so seeing the face is among the necessary consequences of love, and for this reason it was made a metaphor for it, as related by the Imam (al-Razi). And that is, as you see, far-fetched.

It has also been allowed that the mention of the Face is for glorification, as one says: "this is the face of the opinion" and "this is its face," the evidence, and the meaning is: they desire Him.

﴿Nothing of their reckoning is upon you at all﴾: the plural pronoun refers to the preceding relative pronoun, as transmitted from ʿAṭāʾ and most of the exegetes.

It has been allowed regarding "mā" that it may be Tamīmī and Ḥijāzī, and regarding "shayʾ" that it may be the subject of the adverbial phrase relying on the negation, and "min ḥisābihim" is its qualifier, which was placed first and thus became a circumstantial clause; and that it may be in the position of nominative by inception, with the preceding adverbial phrase related to an omitted element occurring as the predicate placed before it, and "min" being superfluous for totality. The speech of al-Zamakhshari points to his choice of this. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the prohibition and its answer, confirming it and averting what might be suspected of its being a justification for driving away the righteous, from the calumnies of those who slander their religion, like the conduct of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, when they said: ﴿We do not see you followed except by those who are our lowest, of immature judgement﴾. The meaning is: nothing is upon you at all of the reckoning of their faith and their false deeds, as the polytheists claim, so that you would take it upon yourself and build upon that the rulings you see. Your duty, as is the nature of the office of messengership, is only to look at the outward aspects of affairs, to apply rulings according to their requirements, and to entrust the inner realities and their reckoning to the Subtle, the All-Aware. And their outward state is calling upon their Lord at dawn and evening. It is related from Ibn Zayd that the meaning is: nothing is upon you of the reckoning of their provision, that is their poverty; and the intent is that their poverty does not harm you at all, so that it may be valid for you to proceed with what the polytheists wanted from you regarding them.

﴿And nothing of your reckoning is upon them at all﴾: it is coordinated with what precedes it, and it was brought although the answer was already complete with that, for emphasis in showing that the negation of their reckoning upon him, upon him be prayer and peace, is placed in a line with what is beyond doubt entirely, namely the negation of his reckoning being upon them. So it is in the manner of His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay an hour nor advance it﴾, according to one opinion.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the two sentences are in the sense of one sentence fulfilling the function of ﴿and no bearer bears the burden of another﴾, as if it were said: you are not held to account for the reckoning of his companion, nor are they; and then both sentences are needed. It was objected that this is not worthy of the majesty of the revelation, and the address to him, may the best of blessings and the most excellent peace be upon him, was placed in both positions – it was said – for his honour. Otherwise the apparent form would have been "wa-mā ʿalayhim min ḥisābika min shayʾ," with "ʿalā" and its object placed first, as in the first. It was also said that placing "ʿalayka" first in the first sentence is for the purpose of directing the negation to the restriction of their reckoning to him, upon him be prayer and peace, since it is he who is prompted to take upon himself their reckoning.

Some exegetes went to the view that the plural pronoun refers to the polytheists, and this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The meaning is: you are not held to account for their reckoning, so that their faith should concern you and eagerness for it should move you to drive away the believers. The pronoun in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾ refers to the believers in every case. The verb is in the subjunctive as the answer to the negation, and the intended meaning is the negation of driving away, not the negation of their reckoning being upon him, upon him be prayer and peace, because the effect is negated when its cause is negated. It is as if it were said: such a thing does not occur from you, so how would driving away occur from you? This is one of two meanings in this type of construction; the second is impossible here. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is an answer to the prohibition. Al-Imam and al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be coordinated with ﴿so that you drive them away﴾ in the sense of causation, because being a wrongdoer is an effect of driving them away and a consequence of it. It was objected that conjunction in the subjunctive requires sharing the cause of the subjunctive, which is that the second depends upon the first, such that the absence of the first entails the absence of the second; and being among the wrongdoers is absent whether it is considered in its beginning or in the remote sequence of its consequence upon driving away; and making it a consequence of driving away without considering that it is a consequence of the negated thing, and negated by its negation, nullifies the existence of the causal connection of the conjunction. It was answered that wrongdoing by driving away is dependent for its negation upon the negation of driving away, just as its existence is not dependent upon its existence; and the negation of driving away is dependent upon the negation of their reckoning being upon him, upon him be prayer and peace; so the negation of wrongdoing by driving away is also dependent upon that, and so the negation entails the negation, and sharing in the cause of the subjunctive is realised, which is evident, and denying it is obstinacy. It was also objected that the conjunction indicates that the absence of wrongdoing is due to the absence of his being entrusted with the reckoning, so it is understood from it that if their reckoning were upon him, upon him be prayer and peace, and he drove them away, it would be wrongdoing, and this is not so, because wrongdoing is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It was answered that it is in the manner of: "what a servant Suhayb is; had he not feared Allah, he would not have disobeyed Him." As for the Kashf, in clarifying the intent of the author of the Kashshaf, it says that he meant that driving away is a cause of wrongdoing, so it was said: "what is upon you of their reckoning, so that you drive them away and thereby wrong them." It is understood from this that if their reckoning were upon him, his driving them away would not be wrongdoing; this is because driving away was made a cause of wrongdoing on the assumption that he does not possess their reckoning, and on this basis there is no need to make it in the manner of "what a servant" etc.; rather that is a departure from the matter. Some allowed that the first be an answer to the prohibition just as it may be an answer to the negation. It was transmitted from ad-Durr al-Masun, and he said: the speech on it according to its outward form is "do not drive them away and so you drive them away," and this is as you see. Some made the coincidence of those two preceding negations, as regards this answer, a case of contention (tanazuʿ), except that it is impossible for the answer to the second to be in any way at all, for the meaning would then imply that if some of his reckoning were upon them, his driving them away would be good; and this is an absurdity which the Qur'an may not be interpreted to bear. There is no departure here from the preference of the Basrans regarding the operation of the second, because their condition is that the meaning be sound in both; if it is not sound, the first is operative by consensus, as in the verse: "were it that what I strive for gave me a little wealth sufficient for a meagre livelihood – and I did not seek –". And you, when you know why the second sentence was brought, you will know what is in this speech, so understand. In any case, the intended meaning is "so that you would be among the wrongdoers" to themselves, or to those believers, or "so that you would be of those characterised by the attribute of wrong."

﴿And thus We tried﴾, i.e. We tested and examined some of them by means of others, and the intended meaning is that We dealt with them in the manner of one being examined. That is an indication of the trial mentioned in the noble text, and it was expressed

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 6, verse 53 (part 2 of 2):

By this he signals its magnificence, like your saying: "I struck that blow" (*darabtu dhalika al-darb*). The *kaf* (in *dhalika*) is an inserted particle (*iqham*), meaning that resemblance is not the intended purpose of it. Rather, what is intended is its implied concomitant meaning, either metaphorical or metonymic, which is certainty and establishment. This is a regularly occurring insertion (*iqham mutta'rid*), and it is not superfluous as some have supposed. The meaning is: "Like that great and marvelous trial, We tried some of the people by means of others, in that We placed the latter ahead of the former in matters of religion, though the former were ahead of them in worldly affairs." It leads to the sense that this great matter is established from Us. Whoever thinks that resemblance is the intended purpose does not allow that this refers to what was mentioned, because that would involve likening a thing to itself. So he strains to find a basis for resemblance and difference, by making the likened-to (*mushabbah bihi*) the matter established in minds, and the likened (*mushabbah*) what the speech indicates of an external matter. It was also said: the meaning is "like how We tried the disbelievers through their wealth and the poverty of the believers, to the point that they humiliated them, contrary to their own situation in worldly causes; so We tried them according to the believers' precedence in faith and the others' lagging behind it, to the point that they envied them, and said what they said because of the difference in their religions." It is not hidden that the first is more subtle in its reasoning, or higher in standing. Some of this has already passed in discussion of this matter.

﴿لِيَقُولُوا﴾ — that is, some of the first (ones), pointing to the latter ones in contempt of them: ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ — by His guiding them to the truth and to success in what makes them happy with Him, glorified is He. ﴿From among us﴾ — that is, "from apart from us," while we are the foremost and the chiefs, and they are the slaves and the poor. Their aim in this is to deny the favour altogether, in the manner of their saying: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ It is not a belittling of those upon whom the favour was bestowed while acknowledging its occurrence, by way of objection against Him, glorified is He.

The Imam mentioned that He, glorified and exalted is He, made clear in this verse that each of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, is tested through the other. Those disbelieving chiefs, the wealthy, used to envy the poor Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, for their being foremost in Islam and quick to accept it. So they said: "If we entered Islam, we would be obliged to submit to these poor people, and that would be hard for us." A parallel to this is His saying: (Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?) and ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ As for the poor Companions, they saw those disbelievers in ease, joy, abundance and plenty, and they used to say: "How did these conditions come to these disbelievers, when we are in hardship, constriction and scarcity?" But the true verifiers, the rightly-guided, are those who know that everything Allah, the Exalted, does is true, right, wise and correct, and that there is no objection to it, either by the rule of ownership (*al-malikiyyah*), as we say, or by the standard of benefit (*al-maslahah*), as the Mu'tazilah say (*al-Mu'tazilah*, a rationalist theological school). End of the Imam's words. But there is room for scrutiny in this, because the beginning of his speech is explicit that the disbelievers acknowledge the occurrence of the favour being referred to, and envy them for its occurrence. That contradicts his comparison with their saying: ﴿Had it been good...﴾ etc. Also, his speech is almost explicit that the poor believers envied the disbelievers for their worldly life, and objected against Allah, glorified is He, by pampering His enemies and constricting His beloved ones. That is something even the lowest of believers would be too exalted to do, so how could those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, do so? Also, setting the poor Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, against "the true verifiers, the rightly-guided," indicates that they, and far be it from them, were not like that, which is self-evidently false according to the true verifiers. So reflect.

The lam here is clearly the lam of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), and it is connected to (*fatannā*, "We tried"), and what follows it is its cause. The predecessors, as our shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani said, and the Qadi al-Qudat Taqi al-Din Muhammad al-Tanukhi and others, affirmed causation (*ta'lil*) in Allah's acts, citing about ten thousand proofs for that. Those who deny it argued with arguments, the second of which was examined in *al-Mukhtabar*. The first mentioned in *Maslak al-Sidad* contains what makes clear its refutation. This is a topic that has been finished with and its carpet folded up. Many others said: it is the lam of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*, the lam of outcome). But something quoted from *Sharh al-Maqasid* rejects that. It says: the lam of consequence occurs only where the agent has no awareness of the outcome at the time of the act or before it, so it is done for a purpose, which does not actually result. Rather, the opposite results, and so it is treated as if he did the act for that corrupt purpose, to draw attention to his error. This cannot be conceived in the speech of the All-Knowing of the unseen, with regard to His own acts, although it may occur with regard to the acts of others, glorified is He, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might be to them an enemy and a grief﴾, since the consequences of His acts being based on them rest on perfect knowledge. Yes, Ibn Hisham and many grammarians did not take this condition into account. They said: it is a lam that indicates becoming and outcome absolutely, so it may occur in the speech of Allah in such a manner that there is no corruption in it. Some people said: it is for causation, in contrast to which it stands as the possibility of outcome, on the basis that *fatannā* includes the meaning of *khadhalnā* ("We forsook"), or on the basis that "the trial" is meant as forsaking, by using the cause to mean the effect.

It was objected that causation here does not have its literal meaning, on the basis that the acts of Allah are exempt from causes. So it is a metaphor for mere sequence, and in reality that is the meaning of the lam of consequence, so there is no basis for contrasting them. It was answered that they differ in terms of perspective. If the sequence is considered as analogous to causation, it is a lam of causation. If it is not considered that way, it is a lam of consequence. It was objected that consequence is a metaphor (*isti'arah*), so this distinction only holds on the view that it has a literal meaning, and on the opposing view a different distinction is needed. It may be said in distinguishing them: in the causation that contrasts with consequence there is causal relation and necessitation, while in consequence there is mere sequence and leading to. In literal causation, the impulse toward the act is taken into account. This is what is meant by those who say: "The acts of Allah are not caused." In that case it is valid to say: the lam, on the assumption that *fatannā* includes the meaning of *khadhalnā*, or that "the trial" is meant as forsaking, is for causation metaphorically, because there is causal relation and necessitation only, without impulse at all. And on the assumption of not saying that there is inclusion of meaning, and keeping the wording to what is understood from it, it is the lam of consequence, which is also a metaphorical causation. But it contains only the sense of resulting in, because the testing of some of them by others results in envy, and envy results in the saying mentioned, and there is no causal relation or impulse at all. The conclusion is that each of consequence and the causation that contrasts with it is a metaphor for literal causation, except that the contrasting causation is closer to it than consequence is. The source of this closeness is the distinguishing feature. The investigation still needs reflection, so reflect. When it is opened to you, give thanks to Allah, glorified is He.

﴿Is not Allah most knowing of the thankful?﴾
35

— This is a rebuttal of their saying that, and an indication that the basis for deserving that favour is knowing the status of the blessing and acknowledging the right of the Benefactor. The interrogative is for affirmation, with His complete knowledge of that. The first *ba'* is the "sword of the orator" (*sayf khatib*), an emphatic particle, and the second is connected to (*a'lam*, "most knowing"). The superlative form suffices to govern the object in such a case. In *al-Durr al-Masun*: knowledge is transitive with *ba'* because it includes the meaning of encompassing, and this is common in people's speech, as in "he knew of such and such" and "he has knowledge of it." The meaning is: "Is not Allah, exalted is He, knowing in the most perfect way, His knowledge encompassing the thankful for His blessings, so that they consider it unlikely that He, mighty and majestic is He, would bestow His favour upon them?" There is also in it an indication that those weak ones are aware of the right of Allah's blessings upon them, such as guidance to faith, precedence to it, and other things, and are thankful for it. Along with it is an allusion that those who are speaking [contemptuously] are, in the wilderness of error, far removed from all of that, which is not hidden.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 6, verse 54]**

﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you﴾. They are, as narrated from Ikrimah, those whom the Prophet ﷺ was forbidden to drive away. By "the signs" is meant the Qur'anic verses, or proofs in general. It is permitted that the *ba'* (the preposition "bi") be a complement of *al-iman* (belief, *silah*, the complement of a word), or that it be causal, meaning: they believe in everything that must be believed in, because of the descent of the verses or because of reflecting upon them and deriving proof from them. Describing those noble people as believers after describing them with what Allah, glorified is He, described them with, is an indication that they possess the two virtues of knowledge and action. The mention of this description last, although it is almost the source of the previous description, is because the basis of the promise of mercy is belief, just as the basis of the prohibition against driving them away, mentioned earlier, is persistence in worship. In the narration of Ibn al-Mundhir from Ikrimah there is what indicates that it was revealed concerning 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). That is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). The matter of the plural form is clear according to this.

Abd ibn Humayd and Musaddad in his Musnad, and Ibn Jarir and others, narrated from Maahan who said: "A people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'We have committed great sins.' The blessing and peace of Allah be upon him did not respond to them with anything, so they departed. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse, so he ﷺ called them and recited it to them." A similar narration is reported from Anas. It has also been said that it was not revealed concerning specific people, but rather it is to be understood in its general sense, and the Imam chose this view. The well-known view is the first, and the context of the verse favors what is narrated from Maahan.

﴿Say: "Peace be upon you."﴾ This is a command from Him, exalted is He, to His Prophet ﷺ that he should initiate greeting them with peace in a place where there is no initiation of greeting, as an honour to them specifically, as narrated from Ikrimah, and al-Jubba'i chose it. It has also been said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to convey to them His greeting, exalted is His majesty, and this is narrated from al-Hasan. And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them): the meaning is: accept their excuse and their confession, and give them good news of safety from what they apologized for. According to this, *al-salam* (peace) does not mean greeting. This too is based on the occasion of revelation according to him (may Allah be pleased with him). Some have chosen that it also has this meaning, on the assumption that what is meant by the relative clause is what is narrated from Ikrimah. Then the statement is a command to him, upon him be blessing and peace, to give them good news of peace from every disliked thing after warning their opponents.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has decreed mercy upon Himself﴾, meaning: He made it obligatory upon His Holy Essence, out of grace and goodness, by Himself, without any intermediary at all. In this there is another possibility already mentioned. It is good news for them of the vastness of the mercy of Allah, exalted is He. The sentence is not conjoined to the sentence of peace, although it is also reported by the saying. It has been said that this is because the first is supplicatory and performative. It has also been said that it is an indication of the independence of each of the two sentences' meanings, which are safety from disliked things and attaining desired aims through glad tidings. The mention of the title of Lordship together with the pronoun referring to them shows kindness to them and indicates the reason for the ruling. The full discussion of the verse has passed shortly before.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that whoever among you does evil﴾, with the *hamza* vowelled with a fatha, as Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub recited it, is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for "the mercy" (accusative), as Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and others said. It has been said that it is the object of "decreed" (*kataba*), and "the mercy" is an object of cause (*maf'ul lahu*). It has been said that it is on the assumption of the *lam* (of causation). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is omitted, meaning: upon Him, glorified is He, is that He... and what precedes it indicates this.

The rest recited *innahu* (with the *hamza* vowelled with a kasra), as a resumptive syntactic statement (*al-istinaf al-nahwi al-bayani*), as if it were said: "And what is this mercy?" The pronoun refers to the matter (*al-shan*). *Man* (whoever) is either a relative or conditional, and its position is a subject, and *minkum* (among you) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the subject pronoun. His saying, glorified is He: *bi-jahalatin* (out of ignorance) is also a circumstantial phrase according to the most apparent view, meaning: whoever does a sin while being ignorant, that is, doing the act of the ignorant, because whoever does what leads to harm in the end while knowing it, or while supposing it, is among the people of ignorance and foolishness, not among the people of wisdom and planning. Or it means: ignorant of what is connected to it of disliked things and harm.

And from al-Hasan: everyone who commits an act of disobedience is ignorant. ﴿Then repents﴾ from that, ﴿after it﴾, meaning after the act or the evil, ﴿and makes amends﴾, meaning in his repentance, by fulfilling its conditions, which are making up for what he can and resolving never to return to it, ever. ﴿Then indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

45

- Meaning: so His matter, glorified is He, is one of exceeding forgiveness and mercy toward him. The *fa'* (then) with *inna* and what follows it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is the predicate of *man*, or the response of the condition. The predicate in that case is according to the difference of opinion. Some estimated: "so for him is that..." or "so upon Him is that...," and in that case it is permissible to read it in the nominative as a subject, or in the nominative as an agent. It has been said that what is formed by *anna* is in the accusative position with an omitted verb, meaning: "let him know that..." It has been said that this is a repetition of what preceded because of the distance of the reference. It has been said that it is a substitute for it. Abu al-Baqa' said: both are weak for two reasons.

[p. 165]

The first: a substitute does not take a particle of meaning, unless the *fa'* is made superfluous, and this is weak. The second: that leads to there being left for *man* neither a predicate nor a response, on the assumption that it is conditional, and the commitment to omission is far-fetched. The opening of the *hamza* here is the reading of those who opened it there other than Nafi', for he, like the rest of the readers, recited it with a kasra.

Al-Zajjaj permitted a kasra on the first and a fatha on the second. This is the reading of al-A'raj, al-Zuhri and Abu 'Amr al-Dani. Abu Shama (may Allah have mercy on him), it is said, was not aware of this, so he said: "It is a possible grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), even if no one recited it," and it is not as he said. Some people said: this verse strengthens the view of the Mu'tazila, since Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in explaining the vastness of His mercy that the evil act, when it is accompanied by ignorance, repentance and making amends, is forgiven. For this reason it has been said that it was revealed concerning 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when he said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "If you had responded to them with what they said, perhaps Allah, exalted is He, would bring them [to you]." He did not know the harm. Then he repented and made amends, to the point that he wept, and said in apology: "I only intended good." It is objected to this that it is established that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the cause, so its revelation concerning 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) does not remove the problem.

It is answered that the intent of the one who responds is that the wording is not general, and the address of "among you" is to those who were in that consultation, and the one who did it among them was 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), so there is no problem. You know that building the answer on this narration is not of great strength, for the opponent may say: "We do not accept that narration." So perhaps the better answer is that what is mentioned in the verse is only the obligatory forgiveness according to the obligation of mercy in the beginning of the verse. Restricting that to what has preceded does not necessitate restricting absolute forgiveness to it. Then it is possible to say: Allah, exalted is He, may forgive one who has not repented, for example, but He, glorified is He, did not write that upon His own Self, exalted is His majesty. So understand it, for it is subtle.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 55:**

﴿And thus do We detail﴾, that is, always, ﴿the signs﴾, that is, the Qur'anic verses, concerning the attributes of the people of obedience and of the people of sin, both those who persist in it and those who turn back in repentance (*awwabin*). The comparison here is like the one mentioned earlier. ﴿And that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾.

**55**

It is read with the verb feminine, in agreement with the feminine subject (*sabil*, "way"). This is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Hafs from 'Asim. It is coordinated (*'atf*) with a deleted cause (*'illa mahdhufa*) for the verb mentioned above, whose causation is not intended specifically by that cause alone. Rather, it is intended to indicate that the detailing has many benefits, of which the one mentioned is one. Or it is the cause of a supposed verb, which is a reference to what was mentioned, as Abu al-Baqa' indicates. Thus it is a new sentence, meaning: "And that their way may become clear, We do what We do of detailing."

Nafi' read it with the *ta'* (feminine prefix) and put *al-sabil* in the accusative, considering the verb transitive, meaning: "And that you, O Muhammad, may make clear the way of the criminals, so that you may deal with them in the manner befitting them." The rest read it with the *ya'* (masculine prefix) and *al-sabil* in the nominative, considering the verb attributed to the masculine. Both the feminine and masculine treatment of *al-sabil* are two well-known usages.

* * *

This is "and from the category of allusion in the verses" (*ishara*, a mystical/allusive interpretation). ﴿Only those who hear respond, and the dead—God will raise them, then to Him they will be returned﴾. Ibn 'Ata' said: By this verse, He, glorified is He, informed that the people of hearing are the living, and they are the people of address and response; and He informed that the others are the dead. Others said: The meaning is that none responds except one whom God, glorified is He, has opened the hearing of his heart through original guidance, and granted him real life through the purity of predisposition (*isti'dad*) and the light of primordial nature (*fitra*), not the dead of ignorance whose faculties have died through compound ignorance, or through innate veils. Or they have no predisposition according to their nature, for they are deaf to hearing and it is not possible for them; rather God, exalted is He, will raise them to Himself in the second creation, then they will return to Him, glorified is He, in the very essence of absolute gathering for recompense and reward, while they remain veiled. It was said: The verse is an allusion to the people of sobriety (*sahw*) and the people of effacement (*mahw*).

﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies on its wings, but they are communities like you﴾, in that they were created upon monotheism and disposed to knowledge (*ma'rifa*), and they have drinking-places from the sea of God's address, branches from the trees of the gardens of His words, glorified is He, longing towards Him, mighty and majestic, and chirping His name, mighty is His name.

It was said: Sam'un the lover, when he spoke of love, the bird would fall from the air. And it is narrated in some reports that the lizard (*dabb*), after it spoke with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and bore witness to his prophethood, began to recite:

*"Unquestionably, O Messenger of God, you are truthful,*
*so you are blessed as one guided, and blessed as a guide.*
*And blessed in the evenings, living and dead,*
*and blessed as one born, and blessed as one who grows."*

Among them, too, are those who are veiled, those who commit vices, and other such things. The discussion of this topic has been detailed earlier.

﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾, that is, the Book of their deeds, ﴿of anything. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾, in the very essence of gathering.

﴿And those who denied﴾, because they are veiled by the coverings of the attributes of their souls, ﴿Our signs﴾, which are the manifestations of the attributes, ﴿are deaf﴾, so they do not hear with the ears of the hearts, ﴿and dumb﴾, so they do not speak with the tongues of the intellects, ﴿in darknesses﴾, which are the darknesses of nature and the abysses of ignorance. ﴿Whomever God wills, He leads astray﴾, by letting down the veils of His majesty; ﴿and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path﴾, by the shining of the rays of His beauty.

﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you﴾, from sickness and all kinds of hardships, ﴿or the Hour comes upon you﴾, the minor or the major, ﴿would you call upon other than God﴾, to remove what touches you? ﴿If you are truthful﴾. ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾, to remove that. Some of the knowers said: The return of the elite to the Truth, exalted is His affair, is from the very beginning of the commencement; and the return of the common people to Him, glorified is He, is after despair from the creation. This was in the time of this knower. As for our time, we see the common people, when constriction closes upon them, abandon calling upon the King, the Creator, and call upon the dwellers of the dust and those who neither hear nor see.

﴿And We had certainly sent to nations before you, and We seized them with misfortune and adversity, that perhaps they might humble themselves﴾, that is, that they might obey, emerge from the veil, and submit humbly, by the manifestation of the attribute of subjugation. ﴿But their hearts were hardened﴾, that is, they did not humble themselves because of the hardness of their hearts, by the density of the veil and the dominance of the covering of desire and love of the world. The root of all of that is evil predisposition.

﴿Say: Tell me, if God takes away your hearing﴾, so that you do not hear His address, ﴿and your sight﴾, so that you do not witness the wonders of His power and the secrets of His craftsmanship, ﴿and seals your hearts﴾, so that nothing of His knowledge enters them, glorified is He; ﴿what god other than God could bring it back to you?﴾, that is, can anyone other than Him, exalted is His power, open one of these doors? No indeed! Rather He is the Capable, the Doer of what He wills.

﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasures of God﴾, that is, from my own standpoint, ﴿the treasuries of God﴾, that is, His capabilities; ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾, that is, from my own standpoint too; ﴿nor do I tell you that I am an angel﴾, that is, a pure spirit that has no need of food or drink; ﴿I only follow﴾, that is, from that standpoint, ﴿what is revealed to me﴾ from God, exalted is He.

For him (ﷺ) there is a station: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾. And: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they only pledge allegiance to God; the hand of God is over their hands﴾. And the bird of intellect has no flight in that air.

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike?﴾, the blind being one who is blind to the light of God, exalted is He, and to His encompassing every atom from the Throne to the earth, and His manifestation as He wills according to wisdom, and His, glorified is He, not being bound by any of the manifestations; ﴿and the seeing﴾, one who sees this, so he speaks in every station with the appropriate speech.

﴿And do not drive away﴾, that is, for the sake of training, refinement, and testing, ﴿those who call upon their Lord﴾, who brought them, wherever He brought them, up the ladders of perfection; ﴿at dawn﴾, that is, the time of the manifestation of beauty, ﴿and at dusk﴾, that is, the time of the manifestation of greatness and majesty; ﴿desiring His face﴾, that is, they desire Him, glorified is He, in His essence and attributes, and seek His manifestation, mighty and majestic, for their hearts. ﴿You are not accountable for their account﴾, that is, the account of their inner deeds, ﴿in anything﴾, because God, exalted is He, has taken charge of guarding their hearts, and has rained upon them the clouds of His care, so they have stirred, swelled, and grown forth every lovely pair.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor are you accountable for their account in anything﴾ is a coordination (*'atf*) with what precedes, brought for emphasis, as mentioned in the expression. It may be intended: Do not drive away the wayfarers for the sake of the veiled; so you are not accountable for the account of the wayfarers or of the veiled in anything. The meaning of this is known with slight reflection. ﴿So that you would drive them away﴾ from sitting with you, ﴿and thus be among the wrongdoers﴾ toward them, by diminishing their rights and not attending to their condition.

Among the interpreters are those who said: The verse concerns the people of unity (*wahda*), meaning: Do not restrain the arrived perfect ones, and do not warn them, for warning, as it does not benefit those whose hearts are hardened, does not benefit those who have been overwhelmed and dissolved in God, exalted is He, and they are those who single Him out for worship constantly, with presence of heart and not witnessing anything other than Him, even their own selves. ﴿You are not accountable for their account﴾ regarding what they do, ﴿in anything﴾, since there is no intermediary between them and their Lord. ﴿Nor are you accountable for their account in anything﴾, that is, they do not engage in the affairs of your call with help and support, because they are occupied with Him, glorified is He, from whatever else, and with their constant presence with Him. ﴿So that you would drive them away﴾ from what they are upon of constant presence, by your call to them for a religious task, ﴿and thus be among the wrongdoers﴾, for your disturbing their times.

And God, exalted is He, knows best the reality of His speech.

﴿And thus We have tested some of them by means of others﴾, that is, the people, who are the veiled, by means of others, who are the knowers, ﴿so that they say﴾, that is, the veiled, pointing to the knowers and belittling them, since they only saw in them their outward condition and poverty, and did not see their rank, their standing, and the excellence of their inner state. What deluded them was what they had of wealth, status, luxury, and comfortable living: ﴿Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favor from among us?﴾, by guidance and knowledge. They meant that He, glorified is He, had not bestowed favor upon them. ﴿Is not God more knowing of the grateful?﴾, that is, those who thank Him with due gratitude, so He bestows upon them His great generosity.

﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you﴾, that is, through them, ﴿say﴾ to them, you, O intermediary: ﴿Peace be upon you.﴾ And this is because they are in the station of intermediaries; even if they reached the level of the people of contemplation, He, glorified is He, would have granted them His peace, as He, mighty is His affair, said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. The rest of the verse is clear.

Imam al-Razi said: His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when they come to you﴾, etc., contains lofty secrets. That is because whatever is other than God, exalted is He, is a sign of God's existence, and signs of His attributes of majesty and generosity, and signs of His oneness. And what is other than Him, glorified is He, has no limit, so there is no path for the intellect to comprehend it in complete detail. But what is possible is that one may come to know some of the signs, and use knowledge of them as a means to knowledge of God, exalted is He, and then believe in the rest in summary. Then he will be, throughout his life, like one swimming in those seas and like one wandering in those deserts. Since there is no limit to them, likewise there is no limit to the servant's ascent in the ladders of those signs. This is a general explanation whose details have no limit. Then, when the servant becomes described by this attribute, God, exalted is He, commands His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to them: "Peace be upon you," so this greeting is glad tidings of attaining safety. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ is glad tidings of attaining honor after that safety. As for safety, it is through deliverance from the sea of the world of darknesses, the seat of corporeal things, the mine of calamities and fears, and the place of changes and transformations. As for honor, it is through arrival at the enduring good deeds, the sacred immaterial beings, and reaching the expanse of the world of lights, and ascending to the ladders of the pavilions of majesty. End.

Another said: The allusion is to a type of wayfarers, meaning: when those who believe in Our signs come to you, by effacing their attributes in Our attributes, ﴿then say: Peace be upon you﴾, for your transcendence above the defects of your attributes and your being stripped of their garments. ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾, that is, He obligated His holy essence to the mercy of replacing your attributes with His attributes for you, because in God, glorified is He, there is a substitute for everything that has passed away. ﴿That whoever of you does evil in ignorance﴾, that is, there appeared upon him, in his changing states, an attribute of his attributes through absence or heedlessness; ﴿then repents after it﴾, that is, after the appearance of that attribute, by turning back from his change, returning to presence; ﴿and makes amends﴾, that is, what appeared from him, by humility and supplication before Him, glorified is He, and by discipline.

﴿Then indeed He is Forgiving﴾, He covers it from him, ﴿Merciful﴾, He shows mercy to him by granting establishment and the blessing of uprightness.

﴿And thus We detail the signs﴾, that is, like that clarification which We have explained to these believers, We clarify to you Our attributes; ﴿and that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾, and they are the veiled by their attributes, who do what they do on account of that.

And God, exalted is He, is the Granter of success to what is right.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 56:

﴿Say: Indeed I have been forbidden﴾ is a command to him (ﷺ) to return to addressing those who persist in polytheism, following the command to deal with others in the manner befitting their condition. That is: say to them, cutting off their empty hopes of your inclining towards them, and making clear that what they are upon is pure caprice and sheer misguidance: indeed I have been diverted and prevented, by the decisive proofs and the Qur'anic signs, ﴿from worshipping those whom﴾, that is, from worshipping the deities, ﴿you call﴾, that is, you worship or name as deities, ﴿besides Allah﴾, whether they are rational beings or not.

It may be said that what is meant by them are the idols, but it was expressed with the form used for rational beings, in accordance with their assumption.

﴿Say: I will not follow your desires﴾. The repetition of the command, although the time since the previous one is short, is to give attention to the importance of what is commanded, and to signal the difference between the two statements: the first is a report of what came earlier from Him, exalted is He, of the prohibition, and the second is of what comes from him (ﷺ), upon whom be blessings and peace, namely, ceasing to worship what they worship. In this statement there is a declaring of them to be ignorant, and an explicit affirmation that they, in what they are engaged in of worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted, are following vain desires, and are not upon anything of what the religion applies to at all, and an indication of what necessitates the prohibition and the ceasing. And in it, as has been said, there is an indication that mere imitation (taqlid) is not sufficient in matters of this kind. It has also been said, and this is very far-fetched, that what is meant is: I will not follow your desires in driving away the believers.

﴿Then indeed I would have gone astray﴾, that is: if I were to follow your desires, then I would have gone astray. This is a resumptive clause emphasizing his (ﷺ) cessation from what he was forbidden, establishing that this would be the utmost of misguidance.

Yahya ibn Wathhab recited (ḍaliltu) with a kasra on the lam, and this is a dialect form of it; the fatha, as Abu Ubayda said, is the prevalent one.

﴿And I am not of the rightly guided﴾.

It is coordinated with what precedes it, and the shift to the nominal form is to indicate permanence and continuity, that is, the permanence and continuation of the negation, not the negation of permanence and continuity. The intended meaning, as has been said, is: and I would not then be in any part of guidance, so as to be counted among them. In it there is an allusion that those addressed are likewise.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 57:**

﴿Say: "Indeed I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾ is a clarification of the truth upon which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stands, and an explanation of his following it, after refuting the falsehood in which the disbelievers are immersed, and an explanation that he (peace be upon him) never followed their (falsehood) at any time. As al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, *bayyinah* (clear evidence) means a manifest proof, from *bana yabinu* (to become evident) when it appears, or a decisive argument distinguishing truth from falsehood, on the basis that it derives from *al-baynunah*, meaning separation. Whichever it is, what is meant by it is the Qur'an, as al-Jubba'i said. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that what is meant is "I am upon certainty." And it is related from al-Hasan that what is meant by it is prophethood, but this is not apparent, just as interpreting it as rational proofs, or whatever includes them, is not apparent. The tanwin (indefinite nunation) on *bayyinah* is for exaltation, meaning that the *bayyinah* is of great status. ﴿From my Lord﴾ means originating from His side, glorified is He. He described it thus to emphasize what the tanwin conveyed.

It is permissible that *min* (from) be for connection (ittisaliyyah), and that there is an omitted noun in the sentence, meaning: "a bayyinah connected to the knowledge of my Lord." It has also been said that it is a causal (ajaliyyah) *min* connected to what the predicate is connected to, and the omitted noun is also to be supposed, meaning: "I am upon a bayyinah for the sake of knowing my Lord." The first is more apparent. In mentioning the title of Lordship (*rububiyyah*) with its attachment to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is an honour and elevation of station that is not hidden.

As for the words of the Glorified One: ﴿And you have denied it﴾, as Abu al-Baqa' said, it is a sentence that is either a resumptive sentence (isti'nafiyyah) or a circumstantial clause (haliyyah), with *qad* supposed according to the well-known view. It was brought to denounce its content and to make its occurrence seem remote, despite the existence of what necessitates its non-occurrence; or to differentiate between him (peace be upon him) and them. The pronoun refers to the *bayyinah*, and the masculine form is used with regard to the intended meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: because it has the meaning of *bayan* (clarification). It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to my Lord, in the sense of: "I have affirmed Him and declared Him one, while you have denied Him and associated partners with Him."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿What you are hastening for is not with me﴾ is a resumptive sentence clarifying their error regarding what they made the basis of their denial of the Qur'an, namely the non-arrival of the punishment it promised, which they were hastening for by saying, mockingly or as a challenge according to their claim: ﴿When is this promise, if you should be truthful?﴾ Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: he (peace be upon him) used to warn them of the descent of punishment upon them because of this polytheism, and the people, due to their persistence in disbelief, were hastening its descent, so He said to them: ﴿What is with me﴾, and so on. It seems that the statement also clarifies their error regarding what they made the basis of not paying attention to the Messenger's (ﷺ) prohibition against it and his report of the descent of punishment because of it. That is: "What they hasten for, of the promised punishment, is not with me, and you make its delay a pretext to deny the Qur'an," or "not paying attention to the prohibition against it and the threat upon it is not within my command and power, such that I could bring it." That is: "its command is not entrusted to me." ﴿The decision is not but for God﴾, that is, the judgment concerning delaying it belongs to God alone, without anyone other than Him having any involvement in it in any way whatsoever.

Some scholars chose generality regarding the object of the judgment, meaning: "the judgment concerning that, whether delay or hastening, or the judgment regarding all things," so that what was mentioned enters it by primary inclusion. The first was preferred on the basis that the intended meaning of the Glorified One's words ﴿The decision is not but for God﴾ and so on is to express regret over the occurrence of the opposite of what is desired, as the contexts of its usage attest, and this regards only the delay. ﴿He relates the truth (yaqussu al-haqq)﴾, that is, He follows the truth and wisdom in what He decides and ordains, whatever it may be, or He clarifies it with a sufficient clarification, from *qassa al-athar* (to follow a trail) or *qass al-khabar* (to relate a report). This belongs to the category of completing the specific with a general matter, according to what we have chosen, by following it with a general statement, such as the words of the Exalted: ﴿In His hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent﴾. Al-Kisa'i and others read ﴿yaqdi (He decides)﴾ from *al-qada'* (decision), and the *ya'* is omitted in the script following its omission in pronunciation due to the meeting of two sukuns. Its original usage is to be transitive with *ba'*, not directly, so *al-haqq* is put in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun that has taken its place, meaning "He decides the decision that is true," or as a direct object. *Yaqdi* then implies the meaning of "He executes," or it is transitive from *qada al-dir'a* (to make a coat of mail), meaning "He fashions the truth and arranges it," as in the saying of al-Hudhali: "two woven coats which Dawud fashioned." In the statement according to this reading there is a subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah). Mujahid argued for the first reading by the absence of the *ya'* that is needed in the second, but you know its invalidity.

Abu 'Amr argued for the second reading by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And He is the best of deciders (khayr al-fasilin)﴾. Decision (fasl) occurs only in judgment, not in narration, and if that were the case in the verse it would have said: "the best of narrators (qassin)." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi answered that *qasas* here means speech, and *fasl* has come in that sense: the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word (qawlun fasl)﴾; ﴿A Book whose verses have been perfected and then detailed (fussilat)﴾; ﴿And We detail the verses (nufassilu al-ayat)﴾. Moreover, you know with the slightest reflection that *al-qass* here may without strain or remoteness be interpreted as meaning *al-qada'* (decision). In *Irshad al-Aql al-Salim* it is said: the origin of *qada'* is decisive settlement of a matter completely, and the origin of *hukm* (judgment) is prevention. It is as if it prevents falsehood from opposing truth, or prevents the opponent from transgressing against his counterpart. The sentence ﴿And He is the best of deciders﴾ and so on is a concluding clause (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it, indicating that the relating of truth here is by a particular method, namely the separation between truth and falsehood. So understand.

Some of the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) argued by the words ﴿The decision is not but for God﴾ and so on, because it indicates restriction (hasr), that a servant is not able to do anything of things except when God the Exalted has decreed it. Thus the act of disbelief is impossible for him unless God the Exalted has decreed and judged it, and likewise in all actions. The Mu'tazilah said: the words of the Glorified One "He decides the truth" mean that everything He decides is the truth, and this requires that He does not will disbelief from the disbeliever or disobedience from the disobedient, because that is not truth. There is no hiding what is in this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 58:

﴿Say: "If I had within my power﴾ i.e., within my capability and ability ﴿that which you seek to hasten﴾ of the punishment ﴿the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾ i.e., by it descending upon you immediately after your seeking to hasten it. And in the passive construction of the verb there is an indication (al-iwdhan) of the determination of the agent, who is Allah, exalted is His majesty, and of the magnitude of the matter, and of observing good manners, which is not hidden.

Al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him said: The meaning is: If that were within my power, I would have destroyed you quickly, out of anger for my Lord, mighty and majestic, and indignation at your denial of Him, and I would have rid myself of you swiftly. The context does not support this, and in the same way he understood (ma yasta'jiluna bihi) as referring to the miraculous signs that were demanded, and the decision of the matter as referring to the establishment of the Hour. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ i.e., of their condition, and that they deserve to be given respite by way of gradual leading on (istidraj) in order to intensify the punishment. For this reason He did not entrust the matter to me, and did not decree the hastening of the punishment. This sentence confirms what the negative conditional sentence conveyed, namely that the matter of the punishment is not entrusted to him, upon him be blessings and peace, which entails the absence of the decision of the matter, and it is also a reason for it.

It has been said: it carries the sense of a contrasting exception (istidrak), as if it were said: "If I were able, I would have destroyed you, but Allah, exalted is He, knows best who among others to destroy, and He has wisdom in not enabling me to do so." In any case, there is no need to posit an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf), though some claimed that, and the estimated reading is "at the time of the punishment of the wrongdoers," which, as you see, is not right. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 59 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen.﴾ That is, its keys, as it has been recited. It is the plural of miftah (key), with a kasra on the mim, and it is like miftah, an instrument for opening. It has also been said that it is the plural of miftah, as it has been said of the plural of mihrab being mahareb. The discourse is figurative (isti'arah, metaphor), in that the unseen is likened to things secured with locks. He attributed keys to it by imaginative suggestion (takhyil), and they remain in their literal meaning. Taking "keys" to mean "knowledge" as the indicator (qarinah) of the implicit metaphor (makniyyah), on the basis that it need not be literal, is far-fetched, and even more far-fetched is the strained use of a parable. It has been said that the more appropriate view is to consider here an explicit actual metaphor (tasrihiyyah tahqiqiyyah), in which "knowledge" is borrowed for "keys" and the indicator is the addition to the unseen. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi that the intended meaning of "keys" is "treasuries," so that the word is then the plural of mafsah (with a fatha on the mim), which means a store.

Al-Wahidi allowed that it may be a verbal noun meaning "opening," but this is not the immediate sense. In the sentence there is an implicit imaginative metaphor (makniyyah takhyiliyyah), and the placing of the predicate first serves to express restriction (hasr). By "the unseen" is meant the unseen things in the sense of comprehensiveness, and the purpose, on every interpretation, is that He, glorified is He, is the One who knows all the unseen things, as they are at their beginning. ﴿No one knows them except Him.﴾ This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿keys﴾. The element governing it, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is what the adverbial phrase depends on, or the word itself if you take it as the subject. It may also be an emphasis of the content of what precedes it. The discourse is either given to explain that the unseen matters of power belong exclusively to Him, glorified is He, in respect of knowledge, following the explanation that all of them belong to Him, exalted is He, in respect of power; the meaning being: what you seek to hasten of punishment is not within my power, so that I could compel you to hasten it, nor is it known to me, so that I could inform you of the time of its descent. Rather, it is among the things that belong exclusively to Him, exalted is His majesty, in power and knowledge, so He sends it down as His will, which is founded on wisdom, requires. Or it is given to establish His general knowledge, glorified is He, which is His knowledge of everything, after establishing the specific knowledge, which is His knowledge of the wrongdoers.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned that if "keys" is taken to mean "treasuries," the meaning of the verse is that He, glorified is He, is able over all possible things, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries.﴾ Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "The keys of the unseen are five," and he recited ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾, the verse. Something similar is related from Ibn Mas'ud. Ahmad, al-Bukhari and others transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, a similar report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Perhaps taking it in the sense of comprehensiveness is preferable, and what is in the reports is to be understood as an explanation of an important part, not as a claim of restriction, since there is no doubt that the unseen things beyond these five are also known to none but Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea.﴾ This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿And with Him are the keys﴾ and so on, or with the clause before it, which is clear if that clause is taken as circumstantial. As for taking it as an emphasis, some have prohibited it, because what is conjoined is not fit for emphasis, even if His knowledge, glorified is He, of the unseen things, according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin), is in the way of detail and exclusivity, since the knowledge of the unseen and of the witnessed are different, so one does not emphasise the other. Yes, it has been said that whoever did not take it as emphatic allowed conjoining it to that clause, so that the two clauses are resumptive, to detail His knowledge, glorified is He, and its comprehensiveness, and nothing more. It is also allowed that the whole is an emphasis, because it includes the content of what precedes it, since this is not technical emphasis. The purpose of this clause, as more than one has said, is to explain the connection of His knowledge to the witnessed things after explaining its connection to the unseen, as a completion of it and an alert that all things are equal in relation to His encompassing knowledge. By "the land" (al-barr) is meant the desert, and by "the sea" (al-bahr) its opposite. In al-Qamus it is said that it is abundant water, or salt only, and its plural is abhur, buhur and bihar, and its diminutive is ubayhir, not buhayr. From Mujahid it is related that by "the land" is meant the deserts, and by "the sea" every town that has water, which is contrary to the apparent sense. Whichever is the case, the meaning is that He knows the existents in them in detail, according to the differences of their kinds and types and the multiplicity of their individuals.

﴿And not a leaf falls but that He knows it.﴾ That is, and no leaf falls from any tree but that He is knowing of it. So "from" (min) is additional in the subject, and the clause after "but" (illa) is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to it. A circumstantial clause came from an indefinite noun because it depends on negation, and the exclusive form in the circumstantial position is common and permissible. It has been allowed that it may be in the position of a qualifier to the indefinite noun, and the discourse, as it has been said, is given to explain the connection of His knowledge to the conditions of the changing witnessed things after explaining its connection to their essences. For the specification of the condition of falling by mention is only by way of emphasising it over the mention of all other conditions. Likewise, the mention of the conditions of the leaf and what is conjoined with it specifically, and not the conditions of all other existents in the land and the sea, which cannot be encompassed by the bounds of enumeration, is on the basis that it is a model for the conditions of all the rest. It has been said: perhaps the sufficiency with the condition of falling, and not with other conditions, is because it is strongly suited to what will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, in the verse of death (al-tawaffi), and because change in it is more evident, so it is more fitting to what the verse was brought for. It has also been said: because knowledge of falling, being one of the conditions that are neglected, entails knowledge of other conditions that are attended to, so reflect. As if it were said: no leaf changes from one state to another but that He knows it. ﴿Nor a grain﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿leaf﴾.

﴿In the darknesses of the earth﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier to ﴿grain﴾, expressing the perfection of the manifestation of His knowledge, exalted is He. By "the darknesses of the earth" is meant its interiors, and he used darkness as a metaphor for the interior, because nothing is perceived in it, as nothing is perceived in darkness. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the meaning is the darknesses of the earth, that which is beneath the rock in the lowest of the seven earths, or beneath a stone or a thing. ﴿Nor anything fresh or dry﴾ is also a conjunction with ﴿leaf﴾, being included with it in its ruling. By "the fresh and the dry" is meant the fresh and the dry that by nature fall, such as fruits for example, since the conjunction requires that. ﴿Except that it is in a clear record﴾ is as a repetition of His saying, glorified is He, ﴿except that He knows it﴾, because the meaning is one in the end, whether by "the clear record" is meant His knowledge, or the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), which is the place of His knowable things, glorified is He. Al-Zamakhshari went to this view. He intended, as al-Sa'd said, that it is a repetition in meaning, while in wording it is a qualifier to the things mentioned, just as ﴿except that He knows it﴾ is a qualifier to a leaf. It was objected to this that how can the qualifier of one thing be a repetition in meaning of the qualifier of another thing? It was answered that this is not a valid objection, because the leaf is included in the fresh and the dry, so there is no difference in meaning, and what was stated is correct. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first exception, a substitution of the whole if the record is interpreted as knowledge, and a substitution of inclusion if it is interpreted as the tablet, and in this there is room for reflection. It is also read ﴿nor a grain, nor anything fresh, nor anything dry﴾ with the nominative, on the basis of conjunction with the position of ﴿leaf﴾. Some restricted this reading to the last two.

It is also allowed that the nominative is on the basis of an inceptive subject, with the predicate being ﴿except in a clear record﴾. It has been said: this is the most suitable to the context, since the fresh and the dry then include what by nature does not fall. Many have taken them as including all things, since all bodies are either fresh or dry, and this includes the hot and the cold. What is meant by "all" is its linguistic meaning, not the technical term of physicians, as is not hidden. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, it is related that by "the fresh" is meant what grows, and by "the dry" what does not grow. In another report from him, the first is water and the second is moist earth. Abu al-Shaykh related from him what implies generality, and perhaps it is the more acceptable. It has also been said: the fresh is the living and the dry is the dead.

The Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'ah) related from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The leaf is the miscarriage, the grain is the child, the darknesses of the earth are the womb, the fresh is what lives, and the dry is what ebbs away." I hold Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, too highly to be spoken of with this interpretation, since it is very contrary to the apparent sense. Similar to it in not being immediately understood is what Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Muhammad ibn Juhadah, that he said: "Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, has a tree beneath the Throne, on which there is no creature but that it has a leaf in it. When its leaf falls, its soul departs from its body." This is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And not a leaf falls.﴾

Moreover, the interpretation of the record as the tablet is what a group of exegetes followed, among them al-Zajjaj, who said: "He, exalted is He, established the knowable things in a record before He created creation," as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿except that it is in a record before We bring it into being.﴾ In a narration of Muslim: "Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, wrote the decrees of creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth." The benefit of this is several matters. The first is the consideration by the angels, peace be upon them, that the newly-occurring things agree with the divine knowable things. The second, on which al-Hasan relied alone, is to alert the responsible persons not to neglect their conditions, which contain reward and punishment, since he mentioned that the leaf and the grain are in the record. The third is that the existents do not change from the prior order in the record, and for this reason came "the pen has dried with what is to be until the Day of Resurrection." This record is called the Preserved Tablet, for its being preserved from alteration and from the reach of the devils, or from erasure and affirmation, on the basis that these occur only in the scrolls of the angels and not in it. Al-Balkhi chose the view that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in a clear record﴾ is that it is guarded and not forgotten or neglected, as a speaker says to another: "What you are doing is written and recorded with me," for he only means that he is keeping it, intending to requite him for it. He recited for this:

"Indeed, with us there is a register for Salma."

Here al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned what he called a subtle point, which is that purely rational propositions are difficult to know fully and completely except for perfected intellects who have accustomed themselves to turning away from propositions of sense and imagination and have grown used to recalling purely intelligible things. They are like red sulphur. ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ is among those propositions. And since it is intended to convey them to every intellect, because the Qur'an was sent down so that all creatures might benefit from it, he mentioned an example from sensible matters that fall under that universal rational proposition, so that this intelligible matter, with the aid of this sensible example, becomes understood by everyone. So he mentioned ﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾ in order to reveal through it the reality of the admonition of the intelligible, and the land is mentioned first because a human being has witnessed its conditions and the abundance of what is in it. As for the sea, the intellect's comprehension of its conditions is less, except that the senses indicate that the wonders of the seas in general are more, their length and breadth are greater, and what is in them of animals and kinds of creatures is more marvellous. So when the imagination recalls the knowable things of the land and the sea and realises that their whole is insignificant compared with what entered the circle of generality, ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾, that becomes strengthening and completing the greatness contained under that. Then He, glorified is He, revealed the greatness of the land and the sea by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And not a leaf falls but that He knows it.﴾ That is because the intellect recalls all that is on the earth of cities, villages, deserts and perils, then it recalls how many stars and trees there are in it, then it recalls that the condition of a leaf does not change but that the Truth knows it. Then He mentioned an example even more awe-inspiring, which is ﴿nor a grain﴾, and so on.

That is because the grain is extremely small, and in the darkness of the earth the largest and greatest of bodies can remain hidden. So when a rational person hears that this small grain, lying in the darknesses of the earth despite its vastness and greatness, does not escape His knowledge, glory be to Him, he becomes intensely attentive and gains from the whole of this the greatest share of the meaning indicated at the beginning of the verse. Then, when that purely intellectual, abstract principle was reinforced by mention of these sensible particulars, He, exalted is His name, returned to mention that matter in another expression, which is His saying: ﴿Nor is anything fresh or dry but it is in a clear record﴾. For it specifies what was previously mentioned. This is based on one of the interpretations of the verse, so do not overlook it. In it there is evidence that God, exalted is He, has knowledge of particulars.

Opposition on this matter has been attributed to the philosophers, but the truth is that they do not deny this; rather, they deny His knowledge of them in a particular (partial) manner. This is a lengthy discussion. Likewise is the discussion of His knowledge, exalted is He, considered in itself. Treatises have been written on it, and it has become the battleground of the minds of the later and earlier scholars. Glory be to Him, whose true measure no one but Him can know.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 60:

﴿It is He Who takes your souls by night⦆ That is, He puts you to sleep therein, as has been related from al-Zajjaj and al-Jubba'i. In it there is a metaphor of the subsequent kind (isti'arah tab'iyyah), in that the term "tawaffi" (taking in full) is borrowed from death for sleep, because of the shared quality between them of the cessation of the perception of the outer senses and of discernment; it has been said [that it includes] the inner senses also. Its original meaning is seizing a thing in its entirety, and it is said: "tawaffaytu al-shay'" and "istawfaytuhu" have the same meaning. ﴿And He knows what you have committed (jaraḥtum) by day﴾ That is, what you have earned and done of sin therein, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Qatadah; and this is what the context of the verse requires, for it is a threat and a rebuke. For this reason "yatawaffakum" was preferred over "yunimukum" and the like. "Jaraḥtum" is used in place of "kasabtum" to include the disbelieving addressees within the category of the limbs of birds of prey and beasts [that hunt and wound]. Some scholars make the address general, and what is meant by night and day is the genus realised in each individual of them, since by the taking [of souls] and the raising [from sleep] occurring in them, the fulfilment of the specified term that is consequent upon them is realised. The preposition "bi" in the two places has the same meaning, as we have indicated.

The meaning of His knowledge (may He be glorified) of that, as has been said, is His knowledge before the wounding, as the mention of it before the raising hints; that is, He knows what you commit. The past form is used to indicate certainty, and the specification of taking [souls] with night and wounding with day is in accordance with the customary course, although it may sometimes be reversed. ﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾ That is, He awakens you during the day. Is this literally applied to this meaning or metaphorically? There are two opinions. What is understood from it in the terminology of the Shari'ah is the revival of the dead in the Hereafter, and they considered it a tarshih (nurturing complement) of the tawaffi, and this is quite evident according to what is understood in the Shari'ah terminology, because it is specific to the comparandum (al-mushabbah bihi). It has been said by others that it is not required for the tarshih to be specific to the comparandum, but only that it be more particularly associated with it in some respect, as they established in the line:

"For him is a mane, his nails not trimmed."
