Raising from the dead is stronger, because the absence of perception in it is of this kind, so its removal is more intense. They have also explicitly stated that the tarshih may remain upon its literal meaning, following the metaphor, and is intended only to strengthen it.

It is also permissible that it be borrowed from the matching element of the borrowed-from term to the matching element of the borrowed-to term. The clause is coordinated with "yatawaffakum", and the insertion of "and He knows" etc. between them serves to explain the great benefit to you in your being raised, by drawing attention to the fact that what they earn of sin, although it deserves that they be left to be taken [in death] or even destroyed outright, He (may His glory be exalted) bestows life upon them and grants them respite, as the word "thumma" (then), which indicates delay, suggests. It is as if it were said: "It is He who takes your souls during the category of nights, then raises you during the category of days, with His knowledge (may His majesty be exalted) of what you commit therein." ﴿That a term appointed be fulfilled﴾ specified for each individual, and it is the term of their remaining in this world.

Al-Zamakhshari, in interpreting the verse, went to great lengths: he made the pronoun "fihi" (in it) operate as a demonstrative referring to the content of their being taken [in sleep] and earning [sin], and "fi" in the sense of the causal "li" as in your saying "fima da'awtani" (why did you call me), and the specified term is being in the graves, that is: then He raises you from the graves regarding that for which you have spent your lives, sleeping by night and earning sins by day, and for it, so that the term He has named and set for the raising of the dead and their recompense for their deeds may be fulfilled. What we have mentioned is what al-Zajjaj, al-Jubba'i and most of the exegetes adopted, and it is free from the artificiality for which there is no need.

As for the claim of some that the motive for it is that His saying, "and He knows what you have committed by day," indicates the state of wakefulness and their earning in it, while the word "thumma" requires the raising to be delayed after it, which is why al-Zamakhshari turned to what he turned to; and some verifiers have said: His saying (glorified be He), "and He knows" etc., is an indication of what they earned during the day preceding that night, and the "waw" is for the circumstantial state, and there is no indication in it of awakening from this taking, nor that the awakening is later than the taking; and our saying that He does that taking so that the lifespan decreed may be fulfilled is a discourse arranged in the utmost order. It is not hidden that there is artificiality in this too, together with the fact that the waw of circumstance does not enter upon the present tense except rarely or by necessity, according to the well-known view. Sinan explained the delay conveyed by "thumma" by saying that the real death in the night is realised at its beginning, and the awakening is delayed from it, even if it is not delayed from its whole duration.

It was objected that in that case there is no reason for the insertion of "and He knows" etc. between them; but there is room for consideration, which is known from what we have mentioned. ﴿Then to Him﴾ (may He be glorified) alone, not to any other at all, ﴿is your return﴾ That is, your coming back and your destination through death. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾

60

- Through recompense
for your deeds which you used to persist in doing in the world.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 61:]

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾, so none of them can overpower Him, and nothing stands between Him, glorified be He, and what He wills concerning them. The word (fawqa, "above") is in the accusative of place (zarfiyyah, adverbial accusative) and is either a circumstantial qualifier (hal, circumstantial accusative) or a second predicate after the first. The discussion of what the scholars have said about this verse has already been given at length. ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ from among the angels, and they are the noble scribes mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers﴾ [82:10–11]. Or they are the successive angels (mu'aqqibat) mentioned in His words, glorified be He: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of God﴾ [13:11]. It has also been said that the intended meaning includes both categories, and that what is guarded is taken to be the deeds, the souls, or the more general category. It is reported from Qatadah that they guard the deed, the provision, and the term of life.

What most exegetes have followed is the first meaning for the guardians. According to some of them, they record all acts of obedience, acts of disobedience, and permissible acts alike, as His words indicate: ﴿What is this Book that leaves out no small matter nor great, but has numbered them all?﴾ [18:49]. It has been transmitted that the "small" refers to smiling and the "great" to laughing, and [they record] ﴿every word he utters, but with him is a watchful observer, ready﴾ [50:18]. Others said: they do not record permissible acts, since no consequence follows from them.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that with every person are two angels, one on his right and the other on his left. When the person speaks a good word, the one on the right records it; when he speaks an evil word, the one on the right says to the one on the left: "Hold off, perhaps he will repent of it." If he does not repent, it is recorded against him. The well-known view is that the two are on the shoulders; it has also been said that they are on the chin, or that they are in the mouth, one on its right and one on its left. What is obligatory is to believe in the two without specifying their location or inquiring into how they write. The apparent meaning of the verses indicates that these guardians are aware of words and deeds, as in His words: ﴿every word he utters﴾ etc., and His words, glorified be He: ﴿they know what you do﴾ [82:12]. As for the states of the heart, such as faith and disbelief, there is nothing in the apparent meaning that indicates the guardians' awareness of them. Some reports indicate awareness, such as the report: "When the servant intends a good deed but does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him," for intention is one of the acts of the heart, like faith and disbelief. Other reports indicate lack of awareness, such as the report: "On the Day of Resurrection, the deeds will be brought in sealed scrolls, and God, exalted is He, will say: 'Accept this and reject that.' The angels will say: 'By Your might, we recorded only what he did.' Then He, glorified be He, will say: 'Indeed his deed was for other than Me, and today I accept only what was done for My Face.'" In a transmission of Ibn al-Mubarak, transmitted without its full chain (mursal), it says: "Indeed the angels raise the deeds of a servant among God's servants; they consider them abundant and commend them, until they reach with them wherever God wills of His dominion. Then God reveals to them: 'You are guardians of the deeds of My servant, and I am the Watcher over what is in his soul. Indeed this servant of Mine did not sincerely intend in his deed, so place him in Sijjin' [83:7]." (This is the hadith in full.) Whoever holds that they record only outward deeds says that the meaning of "was recorded" in the hadith about intending a good deed is that it is established and realized with Us, not that it was written in the scrolls of the angels.

Whoever holds that they record inner deeds makes an exception for showing off (riya'). They record the deed but not the showing off, and God, exalted is He, hides this from them so that He may nullify the deed of the show-off after it has been recorded, either in the Hereafter or in this world, as an increase in his punishment and a horrifying of his condition. Perhaps this is like what is done with him on the Day of Resurrection: he is returned to the Fire after being brought near to Paradise.

Abu Nu'aym, al-Bayhaqi, Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn al-Najjar reported: "On the Day of Resurrection, a people will be ordered toward Paradise, until when they draw near to it, smell its fragrance, and look at its palaces and at what God, exalted is He, has prepared for its people, they will be called: 'Turn them away from it; they have no share in it.' So they will return with a regret that the first and the last have not returned with its like. They will say: 'Our Lord, if You had sent us into the Fire before You showed us what You showed us of Your reward and what You have prepared therein for Your friends, it would have been easier for us.' He will say: 'That is what I wanted for you, O wretched ones. When you were alone, you defied Me with great sins; when you met people, you met them humbly. You showed people your deeds, contrary to what you give Me from your hearts. You feared people and did not fear Me; you venerated people and did not venerate Me; you abandoned [your deeds] for people and did not abandon them for Me. Today I shall make you taste the punishment for what you were deprived of of reward.'" All of this is possible in my view, and there is no certainty, so reflect.

The scholars differed over whether the guardians are renewed every day and night or not. It has been said that they are renewed, and that the angels of the night are different from the angels of the day, permanently, until death. It has been said that the angels of the night depart and the angels of the day come; then when night comes, they depart and the first angels of the night descend, not others, and so on. It has been said that the angels of the good deeds are renewed while the angels of the evil deeds are not, and this is what the good opinion of God, exalted is He, requires. They also differed about where they reside after the death of the accountable person. It has been said that they return in every case to their places of worship in heaven. It has been said that they remain at the grave of the believer, seeking forgiveness for him until he rises from his grave. Many have affirmed that the recorder of good deeds is not limited to one, based on the hadith: "I saw such and such, and they were hastening to it, each of them wanting to record it first." The wisdom behind these guardians is that when the accountable person knows that his deeds are kept against him and presented before the heads of witnesses, that deters him more from engaging in sins and vices. And if he trusts in his master's kindness and relies on His concealment and pardon, he will not be as modest before Him as he is before his servants who are watching him. The statement of the Imam: "It is possible that the benefit of recording is that these scrolls will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, since weighing the deeds is not possible, unlike weighing the scrolls, which is possible," is nothing, as is clear. The view that the scrolls themselves are weighed is the view of some of them. This is (﴿and He sends﴾) either a new sentence or a conjunction with (﴿the Subduer﴾), because it means "the one who subdues." Its conjunction, as Abu al-Baqa claimed, with (﴿He causes you to die﴾) and the present-tense verbs after it, is nothing, just as the possibility of making it a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in (﴿the Subduer﴾) or of the adverb is nothing, because the circumstantial waw, as we have indicated above, does not enter upon the present tense. Positing an omitted subject does not remove it from being anomalous according to the sound view. (﴿Over you﴾) is related to (﴿sends﴾) because of the meaning of control within it. Placing it before the direct object is for the reason mentioned more than once: attention to what is placed first and arousing anticipation for what comes later. It has also been said that it is related to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial qualifier of ﴿guardians﴾, since if it were postponed it would be a qualifier, meaning: being over you. It has been said that it is related to ﴿guardians﴾, which is the plural of guardian (hafiz), like scribes (katabah) and writer (katib). The (﴿until﴾) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿until when death comes to one of you﴾ [6:61] is the particle with which a sentence begins, and yet it makes what follows it of the conditional sentence an endpoint of what precedes it, as if it were said: "And He sends over you guardians who guard what they guard of you for the duration of your lives, until the term of one of you ends and the causes and beginnings of death arrive: ﴿our messengers take him﴾ [6:61]." The others to whom this is delegated are the ones in charge, and the function of the guardians ends there. The "messengers," according to what Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, are the assistants of the Angel of Death. Similar to this is what we have transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "The Angel of Death has messengers who directly seize the souls, and then they hand them over to the Angel of Death."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Kalbi that the Angel of Death is the one who is in charge of that, and then he hands over the soul, if it is a believer's, to the angels of mercy, and if it is a disbeliever's, to the angels of punishment. Most scholars hold that the one who directly does it is the Angel of Death, and he has assistants from among the angels. Attributing the verb to both the direct agent and the assistant together is a metaphor, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so killed a man," and the killer is one of them. The verb has been attributed to the Angel of Death alone, in view of his being the direct agent, and to God, exalted is He, in view of His being the true commander. We have indicated above that some of the Sufis, may God sanctify their secrets, said: the one who causes death sometimes is God Himself without an intermediary, sometimes the angel, sometimes the messengers and others, and this varies according to the states of the one who dies. It is reported from al-Zajjaj, and it is strange, that the intended meaning of "the messengers" here is the guardians, so the meaning is: He sends them to guard during life, and to cause death when death arrives. Hamzah read (﴿tawaffahu﴾) with a long alif and imalah (a vowel shift toward i). It is also read, as an irregular reading (shadhdh), (﴿tatawaffahu﴾). ﴿And they﴾, that is, the messengers, ﴿do not fail﴾ [6:61]:

[16]

- by delaying or postponing.

Al-A'raj read (﴿yufrituna﴾) with a lightened form, from excess (ifrat), which is going beyond the limit, and this can be by addition or by deficiency; that is, they do not go beyond what is prescribed for them by addition or by deficiency. The clause is a circumstantial qualifier of (﴿Our messengers﴾). It has been said that it is a new sentence, brought to explain their care for what they were commanded.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 62:

﴿Then they are returned﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿He takes him⁠﻿ (tawaffathu)﴾, and the pronoun, as has been said, refers to all of them, which is indicated by one of them. This is the secret behind its coming by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). The singular comes first and the plural last, because the taking (tawaffi) occurs individually while the return occurs collectively.

Some of the researchers (muhaqqiqun) held that there is an iltifat here from address (khitab) to the third person (ghayba), and from the first-person speaker to it, because the third person clearly suits the return, even though the return is not literal, since they did not leave the grip of His judgment, glorified is He, for the blink of an eye. The Imam related the view that the pronoun returns to the messengers, meaning that they die as the children of Adam die. The first view is the one on which most of the exegetes (mufassirun) rely. The intended meaning of ﴿Then they are returned﴾ is after the resurrection and gathering, or from the barzakh, ﴿to God﴾, that is, to His judgment and His recompense, or to the place of presentation and questioning, ﴿their Mawla (Mawla)﴾, that is, their Owner who manages their affairs absolutely. This does not contradict His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the disbelievers have no Mawla﴾, because the Mawla in that verse means the helper.

Hujjat al-Islam, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned that the haqq (truth, reality) is the opposite of the batil (falsehood), and that everything about which one reports is either absolutely false, or absolutely true, or true in one respect and false in another. What is impossible in its essence is absolute falsehood, and what is necessary in its essence is absolute truth. The possible in its essence, which is necessary through another, is true in one respect and false in another. From the standpoint of its own essence it has no existence, so it is false, and from the standpoint of its other it derives existence, so it is true from the aspect that is adjacent to the bestower of existence. The meaning of absolute truth is the truly existent in its essence, from which every reality is derived, and this is none other than God, exalted is He. This is what is meant by the saying that the truth is that which is firm and lasting and has no annihilation.

In the Tafsir al-Kabir it is stated that the words mawla and wali derive from proximity, and He, glorified is He, is the Near. The word mawla is also applied to one who is manumitted (muʿtaq). This is as if to indicate that He, exalted is His majesty, freed them from punishment, and this is what is meant by His saying, glorified is He: "My mercy precedes My wrath." Also, He attributed Himself to His servants and attributed them to Himself, and this is the utmost of mercy. Also, He, exalted is His name, said: ﴿their Mawla, the Haqq﴾, and the meaning is that in this world they were under the control of false mawlas, which are the self, desire and anger, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ When a person dies, he is freed from the control of the false mawlas and passes to the control of the true Mawla. End of quote. It is as you see.

He claimed that this verse is among the strongest proofs that the human being is not merely this bodily structure, because its plain meaning indicates that death befalls the servant, and indicates that after death he is returned to God, exalted is He. The dead person, being dead, cannot be returned to God, exalted is He, because that return is not by place or direction, since He is exalted above both. Rather, it must be interpreted as his being submissive to the judgment of God, exalted is He, and obedient to His decree. This meaning cannot apply to one who is not alive. Thus it is established that here there is both death and life. As for death, it is the portion of the body, and life remains the portion of the spirit. When He, glorified is He, said ﴿Return﴾, and it is established that what is returned is the spirit, it is established that the human being is nothing but it, and this is what was sought. Likewise, it implies that the spirit existed before its attachment to the body, because the return from this world to the presence of majesty only happens if it existed in that manner. A parallel to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O self at peace, return to your Lord﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then to Him is your return﴾. The implications of this are not hidden, so reflect upon it. It was also read as al-haqq in the accusative, as a form of praise.

It is permissible that it is an adjective of the absolute object (maful mutlaq), meaning the true return, and in that case the intended referent is not God, glorified and exalted is He. The first is more apparent.

﴿Surely to Him belongs the judgment﴾ on that day, in form and in meaning, and not to anyone else in any respect. This has been used as evidence that obedience does not necessitate reward and disobedience does not necessitate punishment, since if that were established, then the obedient would have a right against God, exalted is He, namely the taking of reward, and this would contradict the restriction indicated by the verse. ﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners.﴾

26

- He reckons all creatures Himself in the swiftest and shortest time. This entails that no reckoning preoccupies Him from another reckoning, nor one matter from another. It is related in a hadith that He, exalted is He, reckons all in the time it takes to milk a sheep, and in some reports in the time of half a day. Some have held that He, exalted is He, does not reckon the creatures Himself, but commands the angels, peace be upon them, so that each one of them reckons one of the servants. Others held that He, glorified is He, reckons only the believers Himself, while the disbelievers are reckoned by the angels, because if He reckoned them He would speak with them, and that is false, due to His saying concerning them: (and He will not speak to them). The earlier scholars answered this by saying that the intended meaning is that He will not speak to them in a way that benefits them. The apparent meanings of the verses, among them what preceded in this surah, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with God: Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say: Is this not the truth? They will say: Yes, by our Lord. He will say: Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve﴾, indicate that He speaks to them on that day. Furthermore, the manner of that reckoning is among the things that the intellects of human beings, by the path of disbelief, cannot at all encompass in its details. We have nothing but faith in it, with entrusting its manner and its details to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed.

The philosophers claimed that the multiplication and repetition of actions necessitates the emergence of firm dispositions (malakat), and that each of those actions must have an effect in producing that disposition. Indeed, each part of a single action must have an effect in some way in that. Then it is said that the actions issuing from the hand are what effect the production of the particular disposition, and likewise the actions issuing from the foot. Hence the hands and feet bear witness against the human being, in the sense that those psychic effects came about in the substances of the souls through these actions issuing from these limbs. That issuing thus functions as testimony to the occurrence of those effects in the substances of the soul. As for reckoning, its purpose is to ascertain what remains of income and expenditure. Since each atom of actions has a good or bad effect according to the goodness or badness of the action, and there is no doubt that those actions were varied, necessarily some of them were counterbalanced by others. After the counterbalancing takes place, a specific measure of good disposition and another measure of blameworthy disposition remain in the soul. When the body dies, the quantity of that is manifested. This occurs in the instant that cannot be divided, which is the instant in which the soul's attachment to the body is cut off. This state is therefore expressed by the swiftness of reckoning. Whoever related this from them claimed that it is an application of prophetic wisdom to philosophical wisdom. I say: "She set out shining and you set out westward; there is a great difference between east and west."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 63:

Page 179

﴿Say: "Who rescues you from the darknesses of land and sea?"﴾ That is, say to them, as a rebuke, to establish the fall of their associates from the rank of divinity. The darknesses of land and sea are, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), their severities and terrors, which nullify the senses and bewilder the intellects. The Arabs, as al-Zajjaj said, call a day in which severe hardship befalls them "a dark day," to the point that they say: "a day with stars" (yawm dhu kawakib), meaning a day whose darkness has intensified until it became like night in its darkness. It has been recited:

"Banu Asad, do you know our trial, when there is a day with stars, grey-white?"

And among the ancient proverbs: "He saw the stars at midday" (ra'a al-kawakib zuhran), meaning his day became dark for him because of the intensity of the matter in it, until it was as if he had seen the star in daylight. From this is the saying of Tarafa:

"If you give it to him, you may also withhold it, and you show him the star running at midday."

It has also been said that what is meant is the darkness of the night, the darkness of the clouds, and the darkness of the sea. It has been said: the darkness of land is by being swallowed up by the earth in it, and the darkness of the sea is by drowning in it. The "darknesses," on the first view, as has been said, are a metaphor, and on the latter two views they are literal. Some have considered them a metonymy for being swallowed up and drowning; the discussion of metonymy is well known. Whoever permits combining the literal and the metaphorical interprets the darknesses as the darkness of night, of cloud, of the sea, of wandering, and of fear.

Ya'qub and Sahl read (yunjikum) with the lighter form, from al-injа' (to rescue), and the meaning is one. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you call upon Him﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of (yunajjikum), as Abu al-Baqa' said, and the pronoun refers to "man," meaning: "Who rescues you from them while you are calling upon Him."

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from its subject, that is: "Who rescues you from them while He is being called upon by you." ﴿In humility and in secret﴾ means openly and privately, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) and al-Hasan. So he put it in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It has been said: by removal of the preposition. "Openly" and "privately" may be understood as referring to what is with the tongue, and may be understood as referring to what is with the tongue and the heart. It is also permitted that both be accusative as circumstantial clauses from the subject of "you call," that is: "openly and privately."

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read khifyatan with a kasra on the kha', and it is a dialect form of it, like al-uswa and al-iswa (example). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Surely if You rescue us﴾ is in the accusative position as an object of an implied saying that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "you call" as well, that is: "saying: 'If You rescue us...'" The Kufans relate with what indicates the meaning of saying, like "you call," without estimation; but the correct view is estimation. It has been said that the oath clause is an explanation of the supplication, so it has no place (in i'rab).

The people of Kufa read ﴿anjana﴾ with the third-person form, in consideration of "tad'unahu" (you call upon Him), not reporting their address in the state of supplication. However, 'Asim read it with tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation), and the rest with imala (inclination). His saying, glorified is He, ﴿from this﴾ refers to what they are in, which is expressed by "darknesses." ﴿We will surely be among the grateful﴾

36

- That is, those firmly established in gratitude, persistent in it, on account of this great blessing, or on account of all the blessings of which this is one.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 64:**

﴿Say: "It is Allah who delivers you from them and from every distress."﴾ That is, from every grief that seizes the soul. What is meant by it is either that it includes what was mentioned before, and generalization after specification is common, or it refers to the various psychological and physical afflictions that befall a person, which are endless, such as illnesses and sicknesses. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to give the answer even though it was among their duties, to signal that it is evident and certain, or to humiliate them, along with the structure of His words, glorified is He: ﴿Then you associate partners with Him.﴾

46

- That is, Allah the Exalted alone delivers you from what you call upon Him to remove, and from other things. Then you, after witnessing these magnificent blessings, return to associating partners in His worship, glorified is He, and do not fulfill the covenant. He placed (you associate partners, tushrikun) in the position of (you do not give thanks, la tashkurun), which is the apparent and fitting reading given their earlier promise, referred to by His words, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely be among the grateful.﴾
180

- This serves as an admonition that whoever associates partners in the worship of Allah, the Exalted, is as if he has not worshipped Him at all, since tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) is the foundation of the matter and the basis of worship. It was also said: perhaps the intended meaning is rebuke, that they, despite their knowledge that none has delivered them but Allah the Exalted, as the fronting of the subject indicates, nevertheless associated partners with Him and did not single out Allah the Exalted for worship. So He mentioned association in its proper place. The word (thumma, "then") does not indicate temporal delay, but rather the complete distance between Allah's favor upon them and their disobedience. He did not mention the object of the association, placing it in the position of an intransitive verb, as an admonition to show that association itself is improbable.

The people of Kufa, Abu Ja'far, and Hisham on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read (yunajjikum, "delivers you") with the doubled letter (tashdid), while the rest read it without doubling (takhfif).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 65:

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers: ﴿He is the One who is able﴾, not other than Him, glorified is He, ﴿to send﴾, that is, to dispatch, ﴿upon you﴾. The phrase "upon you" is connected to "to send," and it is placed before the explicit object, which is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿a punishment﴾. This is to give it importance, to hasten to explain that what is sent is something that harms them, and to magnify the matter that is deferred. The statement is a resumption (istinaf) that serves to show that He, exalted is He, is the One able to cast them into ruin, following the explanation that He, glorified is He, is the One who rescues them from it. Within it is an implicit threat of punishment because of their associating partners, which was mentioned. The tanwin (nunation) on "punishment" is for emphasis, meaning a great punishment. ﴿From above you﴾, that is, from the direction of the heights, such as the Blast, the stones, the wind, and the sending down of the sky. ﴿Or from beneath your feet﴾, that is, from the direction of the lowest part, such as the earthquake, the sinking of the earth, and drowning.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "﴿From above you﴾" means from the side of your rulers and your nobles, and "﴿and from beneath your feet﴾" means from the side of your lowly ones and your slaves. In another narration from him, the first is interpreted as evil leaders and the second as evil servants. What is most apparent is what we have already mentioned, and it is what has been related from more than one of the exegetes. The prepositional phrase "from above you" and "from beneath your feet" is also connected to "to send," and it is permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word that occurs as an attribute of "punishment." The particle "or" (aw) here indicates the prevention of absence of both, not the prevention of combination, so there is no prohibition against what came from both directions together, as was done to the people of Nuh, upon him be peace.

﴿Or He will confuse you﴾, that is, He will mix up your affairs among yourselves, so there is an implied element in the speech. Confusing their affairs among them makes them people of differing desires. It was said that the intended meaning is the mixing of people in fighting, some with others, so there is no implied element. Upon this is the saying of al-Sulami:

"And a battalion I mixed with a battalion, until, when they were confused, I shook my hand over them."

It is read as "﴿yulbisakum﴾" with a damma on the ya', and it is coordinated with "yab'atha" (to send). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in sects (shiya'an)﴾ is the plural of shi'ah, like sidrah and sidar, and they are people who have gathered upon a matter. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal). It was also said that it is an infinitive in the accusative, governed by ﴿yalbisakum﴾ but from a different root. On this basis, it is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial, meaning differing. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and make some of you taste the violence of others﴾ is coordinated with "yab'atha," as was transmitted from al-Samin. It is understood from the words of some that it is coordinated with "yalbisa," and this is of the type of explanatory coordination, or of coordination of the cause with the effect (the result following from the cause).

It is read as "nudhiqa" with the plural of majesty, following the style of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) for the magnifying of the matter and for exaggeration in warning. The first "some" is, as it has been said, the disbeliever, and the second is the believers. In that case there is a promise and a threat. It was also said that both "some" are from among the disbelievers, meaning We make each one taste the violence of the other. It was said that both "some" are from among the believers. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan that he said concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet﴾: "This is for the polytheists," and concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or He will confuse you in sects and make taste﴾ etc.: "This is for the Muslims." It is not hidden that this is a dismantling of the noble structure of the verse. Perhaps what al-Hasan intended is that this occurs among the Muslims and befalls them, but not the first.

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him that he said: "When this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ stood, performed ablution, and asked his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that He not send upon them a punishment from above them or from beneath their feet, and that He not confuse his ummah in sects and make some of them taste the violence of others, as He made the Children of Israel taste it. Then Jibril, upon him be peace, descended to him ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, you asked your Lord for four things; He gave you two and withheld two from you. It will not come to them, a punishment from above them or from beneath their feet that will uproot them, for these are two punishments for every nation that unites in denying its prophet and rejecting the Book of its Lord. But they will be confused in sects, and some of them will make others taste violence. These two are punishments for the people who acknowledge the books and affirm the prophets, upon them be peace.'"

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and the wording is his, narrated from Thawban that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Indeed my Lord gathered the earth for me until I saw its easts and its wests, and He gave me the two treasures, the red and the white. Indeed the dominion of my ummah will reach what was gathered for me of it. And I asked my Lord for my ummah that He not destroy it by a general famine, and He gave it to me. And I asked Him that He not give power over them to an enemy from other than themselves, and He gave it to me. And I asked Him that He not make some of them taste the violence of others, and He withheld it from me. He said: 'O Muhammad, indeed when I decree a decree it is not turned back. Indeed I have given you for your ummah that I will not destroy it by a general famine, and I will not let an enemy from other than them prevail over them so that he destroys them completely, even if all who are between its regions gather against them, until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive.'" The hadith...

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, and others narrated from Abu Basra al-Ghifari, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "I asked my Lord for four things. He gave me three and withheld one. I asked Allah, exalted is He, that He not unite my ummah upon misguidance, and He gave it to me. I asked Allah, exalted is He, that He not let an enemy from other than them prevail over them, and He gave it to me. I asked Allah, exalted is He, that He not destroy them by years of famine as the nations were destroyed, and He gave it to me. I asked Allah, exalted is He, that He not confuse them in sects and make some of them taste the violence of others, and He withheld it from me."

The reports on this meaning are numerous. In some of them there is an indication that confusion and making taste are counted as one matter, and in some there is an indication that they are counted as two. From this arose the earlier disagreement concerning the coordination. Some have supported the coordination with "yalbisa" rather than with "yab'atha," because it uses "wa" (and) and not "aw" (or).

What was narrated from al-Hasan, that the first two do not occur in this ummah, is not contradicted by what Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning this verse: "As for them, they are existent, but their interpretation has not yet come." Likewise, what the former narrated in his Musnad through the route of Abu al-'Aliyah from Ibn Ka'b, that he said concerning the verse: "They are four, and all of them will certainly occur." This is because by occurrence may be meant an occurrence not in the manner of total extermination, and by non-occurrence may be meant non-occurrence in the manner of total extermination. The statement of al-Hasan is almost explicit in this, so understand.

﴿Observe how We vary the signs﴾, that is, We turn them from one type to another of the types of speech, to confirm the meaning and to bring it closer to understanding, or We vary them with promise and threat. ﴿That perhaps they may understand﴾

56

That is, so that they may know the clear reality of the matter and turn back from what they are upon of obstinacy and stubbornness. Some of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority) used the verse as evidence that Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator of good and evil. Some of the Hashwiyya (a term for literalist, unreflective traditionalists) and the Muqallida (those who follow authority without independent examination) said: it is among the strongest proofs for prohibiting reflection and inference, because in that is the opening of the door of division and disagreement, which is blameworthy by the ruling of the verse. This is not a valid point, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 66:

﴿But your people denied it﴾, that is, the Qur'an, as al-Azhari said, and this was related from al-Hasan. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the variation of the signs (taṣrīf al-āyāt), a view chosen by al-Jubba'i and al-Balkhi. It was also said that it refers to the punishment, a view chosen by most of the exegetes. ﴿Your people﴾, that is, the Quraysh; it was also said that they include the rest of the Arabs. In any case, what is meant is their obstinate ones, and it was said:

Page 182

Perhaps the mention of them under this designation is to announce the complete evil of their state, for their denial of it, despite being from his own people (peace be upon him), indicates the utmost of their defiance and stubbornness. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the subject is for the reason already mentioned many times.

﴿And it is the truth﴾, that is, the Book that is true in everything it states, free of doubt, or whose indication is firmly established, or that will certainly come to pass. The waw is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), and the sentence following it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in the genitive. It was also said that the waw is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah) and the sentence after it is a new sentence. In any case, this indicates the magnitude of their crime and the extreme ugliness of it. ﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾

66

- That is, not one entrusted with your affairs, who guards your deeds in order to requite you for them. ﴿I am only a warner﴾, and I have not spared any effort in warning, while Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who requites; so said al-Hasan.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that I have not been commanded to fight you or to prevent you from denying. Something similar to this meaning was transmitted from al-Jubba'i. The verse, according to what was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, has been abrogated by the verse of fighting, and there is no difficulty in this on the second meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 67:

﴿For every news there is a time of establishment﴾ That is, for every matter that is announced, from among the news of which your punishment is a part, or for every report from among the reports of which the report of its coming is a part. ﴿A time of establishment﴾ means a time of settling and of definite occurrence, or the time of its settling by the occurrence of what it signifies. It is not a mimi verbal noun (mustaqarr is not a mīmī maṣdar here).

﴿And you will soon know﴾

76

- That is, the state of your news, in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both together. And sawfa (soon) is for emphasis.

﴿And when you see those who engage in [discourse about] Our verses﴾ with denial, mockery, and disparagement of them, as is the habit and practice of the Quraysh in their assemblies, and they are the intended referents of the relative clause. According to Mujahid, it also refers to the People of the Book, since their practice is likewise of this kind. For this reason the particle ﴿إذا﴾ (idha, "when"), which indicates certainty, is used. This is in contrast to the forgetting mentioned later. The root meaning of khawd (immersion, engaging in discourse) comes from "khada al-qawm fi al-hadith" (the people plunged into the speech) and "takhawadu" (they conversed about it). al-Tabarsi said: khawd is confused engagement in conversation, in the manner of frivolity and play, without understanding or clarification. Some scholars of verification said: the original meaning of khawd is crossing water, which has been borrowed for discussing matters. Most of its occurrences in the Qur'an are in a pejorative sense. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, leave them and do not sit with them, ﴿until they engage in another discourse﴾, that is, speech other than it, that is, other than Our verses. The masculine form (ghayrihi) is used with reference to it being a discourse (hadith), for describing the verses as differing from it indicates considering them under the heading of discourse. It has also been said that the masculine is used with reference to their being the Qur'an. The khawd here means conversation in general, not restricted to denial and mockery. Some have claimed that the meaning is "until they occupy themselves with a discourse other than it," and that the mention of "yakhudu" (they engage) is for mushakala (rhetorical correspondence of wording). They preferred that the pronoun refers to khawd. Some scholars have used this verse to show that ﴿idha﴾ implies repetition, because it is forbidden to sit with one who engages in discourse whenever he engages in it. This was objected to on the grounds that repetition does not come from ﴿idha﴾ but from the attachment of the ruling to the derivational source of the word.

As for the reliance of some of the Hashwiyya (a term for certain literalist extremists) on this verse to prohibit argument and debate about the essence of God and His attributes, claiming that this is "engaging in the verses of God," which should not be given any attention: ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾ by distracting you so that you forget the command to turn away from them, and thus sit with them, whether at the outset or continuing. This is hypothetical, since it has not occurred, and how could Satan have any way to distract the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? For this reason the conditional ﴿in﴾ (in) is used, with the particle ﴿ma﴾ attached after it for emphasis.

Some scholars of verification held that the address here and in what precedes is to the chief of those addressed, peace be upon him, but what is meant is others. It was also said that it is addressed to others initially, meaning: "if you see, O listener, and if he makes you forget, O listener." The well-known view among the Rafidah (a name for certain Shi'i groups) is that the Prophet (ﷺ) is free from forgetfulness, based on the words of God, ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾. Others held that it is permissible. The attribution of the first view to them was explicitly stated by the author of al-Ahkam, al-Jubba'i and others. The latter said: this verse is evidence of the falsity of their claim. What I have found in the authoritative books of their scholars is that they do not allow forgetfulness, nor inadvertence (sahw), concerning the Prophet (ﷺ), nor concerning all the other prophets, peace be upon them, in what they convey from God of the Qur'an and revelation. As for anything else, they allow that he, peace be upon him, may forget it, provided it does not lead to a breach in the religion.

I do not see that the locus of disagreement is forgetfulness whose origin is not the preoccupation of the heart with satanic whisperings and thoughts, for no believer doubts the impossibility of that for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The detailed discussion of this, according to what is in the authoritative books of our own scholars, is that the view of the majority of scholars is that forgetfulness is permissible for him (ﷺ) concerning the rulings of the Shari'ah, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the hadiths. However, they agreed that he, peace be upon him, is not left to persist in it, but God informs him of it. Then most of them said it is a condition that he be alerted to it immediately, linked to the incident, without any delay. A group permitted delay for the duration of his life (ﷺ), and this was chosen by Imam al-Haramayn. Another group of scholars prohibited this regarding acts of conveying the message and acts of worship, just as they agreed on prohibiting and deeming impossible for him (ﷺ) forgetfulness in the verbal statements of conveying the message. They answered the apparent texts that appear on this matter. Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini inclined to this view. al-Nawawi affirmed the first view, for that does not contradict prophethood. If he is not left to persist in it, no harm results from it, and it does not contradict the command to follow him, rather benefit results from it, which is explaining the rulings for the forgetful and establishing the rulings.

The judge (al-Qadi) mentioned that they differed concerning the permissibility of inadvertence on his part (ﷺ) in matters not related to conveying the message and explaining the rulings of the Shari'ah, such as his actions, customs, and the remembrances of his heart. The majority permitted it. As for inadvertence in verbal statements of conveying the message, they agreed on prohibiting it, just as they agreed on the impossibility of deliberately doing it. As for inadvertence in worldly speech and in matters that are not part of conveying, speech not related to rulings, nor to reports of the Resurrection and what pertains to it, and not ascribed to revelation, a group permitted it, since there is no harm in it. Then he said: the truth beyond any doubt is preferring the view of the one who said: it is impossible for the prophets, peace be upon them, in every report of the reports, just as it is not permissible for them to contradict a report, neither deliberately nor by inadvertence, neither in health nor in sickness, neither in contentment nor in anger. It is sufficient in this regard that his biographies, speech, and actions have been collected and are cared for over the passage of time, and both the agreeing and the opposing, the believer and the doubter, have taken them up. In none of them has there come a correction of an error in a statement, nor an acknowledgment of a mistake in a word. Had it been so, it would have been transmitted just as his inadvertence in prayer was transmitted, and his sleeping through it, peace be upon him, and his reconsideration of his opinion about pollination of date palms, and his descent to the nearest water of Badr, and other such matters. As for the permissibility of inadvertence in beliefs concerning worldly matters, it is not impossible. The completion of the discussion of this topic, God willing, will come when interpreting His words, ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾, the verse...

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿yunassiyannaka﴾ with the shadda on the sin, and "nassa" has the meaning of "ansa" (to cause to forget). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "nassa" is more intensive than "ansa." The nun in both readings is doubled, and it is the nun of emphasis. The well-known view is that it is obligatory in a verb following the conditional ﴿in﴾ accompanied by the extra ﴿ma﴾. It was also said that it is not obligatory in this case, and on this is the verse of Ibn Duraid:

Do you not see my head, its color imitating the streak of dawn beneath the trailing skirts of the night?

﴿So do not sit, after the remembrance﴾, that is, after remembering the command to turn away, as the majority of commentators hold. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is after you have reminded them by your calling them to the religion and your forbidding them from engaging in the verses, and this is nothing (not correct).

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "al-dhikra" (the remembrance) means God's reminding him, and that the meaning is: even if Satan causes you to forget, before the prohibition, the ugliness of sitting with the mockers, since it is something the intellects reject; so do not sit after We have reminded you of its ugliness and alerted you to it. It is not hidden that this is a distant interpretation, based on the principle of ugliness and goodness, which the hammers of the thoughts of the mature scholars have demolished. Furthermore, we do not grant that sitting with the mockers is something the intellects reject absolutely. Ibn al-Munir mentioned that what fits what he said is "in" (if) without the "ma," and "in anSAka" rather than "imma yunsiyannaka," since Satan's causing forgetfulness, if valid, is more easily attributed to the hearing (i.e., to scripture). This is not the first engagement by al-Zamakhshari in interpreting the verses; rather, that is his habit with the wrongdoing people.

[Page 86]

That is, with them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to censure them, that by that engaging they are wrongdoers, placing denial and mockery in the place of affirmation and reverence, and persisting in that. In the verse, as many have said, is an indication that the forgetful person is not charged with the obligation. These are the questions disputed among them, and they have titled them "the question of charging the heedless," and they counted the forgetful among them. Al-Ash'ari had two views on it, and he preferred that there is no charge, since there is no benefit in it at all, unlike charging with the impossible.

Ibn Burhan in al-Awsat transmitted from the jurists the view that charging him is valid, in the sense of the act being established upon the responsibility, while from the theologians there is prohibition, since that is not conceivable to them. It may be thought that al-Shafi'i, because of his explicit statement on charging the intoxicated, is taken to hold the charging of the heedless, but this is among some misconceptions, for he only charged the intoxicated as a punishment for him, since he caused himself to commit something forbidden by his own choice; hence the hadd punishment is obligatory upon him, unlike the heedless. It has been objected to the view of impossibility that the servant is charged with knowing God, without knowing the command, because the command to know Him is indeed given. It cannot be that it is given after its attainment, since attaining what is already attained is impossible, so it is given before it. Thus it is impossible to apply this to the command, because knowing His command without knowing Him is impossible, so he has been charged with knowing God while heedless of that charge.

It has been answered: general knowledge suffices to remove heedlessness, and the thing charged is detailed knowledge. Or: the condition of charge is only the charged person's understanding of it, namely that he understands the address to the extent that compliance depends upon it, not that he assents to his being charged, otherwise there would be circularity, and the non-charging of the disbelievers would follow. Here he has understood it, even if he does not assent to it. The author of al-Minhaj, following the author of al-Hasil, answered that the charge of knowing God is an exception to the principle by consensus. The full discussion is sought in the books of legal theory (usul).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 69:

﴿And there is nothing upon those who are mindful of God﴾ Abu Ja'far (may God have mercy on him) said: When [the verse] ﴿So do not sit, after the reminder﴾ and so on was revealed, the Muslims said: "If we were to stand up every time the polytheists mocked the Qur'an, we would be unable to sit in the Sacred Mosque or circumambulate the House." So [the verse] was revealed. That is: nothing is incumbent upon those who are mindful of God (al-muttaqun) regarding the ugly deeds and states of those who engage in such discourse.

﴿of their reckoning﴾ That is, of what the wrongdoers who engage in such discourse will be held accountable for from their sins. ﴿anything﴾ That is, anything at all. [The word] "min" is extra (za'idah), for the sake of comprehensiveness (istighraq), and "shay'" (thing) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'). The "ma" is Tamimi (i.e., it does not govern the predicate), or it is its noun, and it is Hijazi (i.e., it governs the predicate). And ﴿of their reckoning﴾, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, because when the qualifier of an indefinite noun is placed before it, it is parsed as a circumstantial clause. "Min" does not mean "until" (ajal), contrary to those who forced that meaning.

﴿upon those who are mindful of God﴾ is attached to a omitted element in the nominative position, which functions as the predicate of the subject, or of the Hijazi "ma" according to the view of those who do not permit its governing a fronted predicate in any case; or it is in the accusative position, functioning as the predicate of "ma" according to the view of those who permit its governing a fronted predicate when that predicate is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase.

﴿But it is a reminder﴾ is a corrective conjunction (istidrak) from the preceding negation. That is: rather, it is incumbent upon them to remind those [engaged in such discourse], to restrain them from the ugly deeds they are involved in, by whatever admonition and reminding is possible, and to show them their disapproval and condemnation. According to many of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun), the grammatical position of "dhikra" (reminder) is either the accusative, as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for an omitted verb, meaning: it is incumbent upon them to remind them with reminding; or the nominative, as a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: but upon them is a reminder. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted the accusative and the nominative, though he estimated in the first case "nudhakkiruhum dhikra" (we remind them a reminder) with the royal "we," and in the second case "hadhihi dhikra" (this is a reminder). The statement of al-Balkhi points to this. Al-Zamakhshari did not permit its being conjoined to the position of "min shay'" because "min hisabihim" (of their reckoning) rejects it, since the meaning would become: "but a reminder of their reckoning." And that, as you see, is untenable.

It has been objected that conjoining to a qualified element does not necessarily require that the qualifier be considered in the conjoined element. The second scholar (al-'Allama al-Thani) says: when a single noun is conjoined to a single noun, especially with the corrective particle, the qualifiers that apply to the first conjoined element (the preceding one, in the reminder) definitely apply to the conjoined element by usage. You say: "No man came to me on Friday, or in the house, or riding, or from these people, but a woman [came]," and so it necessarily follows that the woman came on Friday, in the house, in the manner of riding, and was definitely from those people. Usage has not come otherwise, and nothing other than this is understood from the speech, unlike "A man of the Arabs came to me, but a woman," for there it is not unlikely that the woman is from non-Arabs. They said: the secret of this is that the prior occurrence of the qualifiers indicates that they are a settled, established matter, and that they are a qualifier of the governing element extending over all its complements. This rule is restricted to single nouns for this reason. As for sentences, a qualifier, if it is considered part of the conjoined-to element, even if it precedes, is not shared by the conjoined element, as in the verse of God, exalted is He: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾, according to what is in the commentary on the Miftah (Sharh al-Miftah). This holds when no indicator (qarinah) contradicts it, as in your saying: "A man of Tamim came to me, and a woman of Quraysh."

The restriction of this rule to the prior occurrence of the qualifier, and the claim that it is consistently applied, as mentioned by some verifying scholars, is what taste (dhawq) requires. Among them are those who generalized it, as al-Halabi said: the people of the language and the jurists (usuliyyun) say that conjunction (ataf) is for sharing in the apparent sense, so if the conjoined-to element has a qualifier, the apparent [meaning] is that the conjoined element is qualified by that same qualifier, unless a diverting indicator comes, in which case the matter is referred to it. So if you say: "I struck Zayd on Friday, and 'Amr," the apparent [meaning] is that Zayd and 'Amr shared in the striking, qualified by Friday. And if you say: "and 'Amr on Saturday," he did not share in its qualifier. The verse is of the first kind, so the apparent [meaning] is that it (the conjoined element) shares its qualifier, and this suffices for the prohibition. Al-Saffaqusi and others discussed this. So reflect.

And whoever prohibited conjoining to the position of "min shay'" for the reason mentioned above, also prohibited conjoining to "shay'" for the same reason, and also because "min" cannot be assumed to be governing after an affirmative [clause], since if it governed, it would be in the force of the stated and extra [particle], and it is not made extra in an affirmative [clause] except with adverbial phrases, or absolutely according to the majority.

﴿so that they may be mindful of God﴾ (la'allahum yattaqun)

69

- That is, they abstain from engaging in such discourse out of shame or out of aversion to their (the wrongdoers') offense. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to "those who are mindful of God," meaning: but the mindful ones should remind those engaged in discourse, so that the mindful ones may remain steadfast in their piety and not sin by abandoning what was obligatory upon them of forbidding wrong, or so that they may increase in piety thereby. This verse, as al-Nahhas reported from Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), and Abu al-Shaykh from al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr, is abrogated by the verse of God, exalted is He, revealed at Medina: ﴿And He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the signs of God being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them﴾, and so on. Al-Balkhi and al-Jubba'i adopted this view. In *al-Tawd al-Rasikh fi al-Mansukh wa al-Nasikh* [it is stated that] there is no abrogation according to the verifying scholars in this matter, because His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And there is nothing upon those who﴾ and so on is a report (khabar), and there is no abrogation in reports. So understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 70:

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion﴾ — the religion that was imposed upon them, that they were charged with and commanded to uphold its duties, which is Islam — ﴿as amusement and play﴾, in that they mocked it and ridiculed it. It is also permissible that the meaning is: they took the religion that was obligatory as something of the kind of play and amusement, such as the worship of idols and the prohibition of the baheera and the sa'iba and the like. Or: they took that which they adhere to and profess, in the position of religion for the people of the (other) religions, as something of play and amusement. The summary of it is that they took play and amusement as a religion. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "religion" is the festival (ʿid), which returns at every known time, in the manner that Allah the Exalted has legislated, like the festival of the Muslims, or in the manner that has not been legislated, of play and amusement, like the festivals of the disbelievers; for the original meaning of din is custom ('adah), and the festival is customary every year. This is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. The meaning according to all the other statements is: do not concern yourself with these people, and proceed with what you have been commanded.

Ibn Jarir and others have reported that the meaning is by way of threat, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ and ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the command to refrain from them and to leave off confronting them. According to this view the verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, and this is narrated from Qatadah. ﴿Amusement﴾ is in the accusative as a second object of (they took), and this is the preference of al-Safaqusi. It is understood from the apparent speech of some that it is the first object and (their religion) the second, and in this there is the informing about an indefinite noun by a definite one. It is understood from the words of the Imam that it is an object of purpose (for which), and (took) is transitive to one object, for he said after enumerating the aspects of the interpretation of the verse: "The fifth, and it is the closest, is that the one who is right regarding religion is the one who supports religion because there is proof that it is true, sincere and correct. As for those who support it in order to use it as a means to obtain positions and leadership, to overpower the opponent and to gather wealth, they have supported religion for the sake of the world; and Allah the Exalted has judged these things in the other verses to be play and amusement. So the intended meaning of His words, glorified is He: ﴿And leave those who have taken﴾ etc. is the indication to the one who uses his religion as a means to his worldly life." And if you reflect on the state of most of creation, you will find them described by this attribute and included under this verse. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that this is further than the 'Ayyuq (a distant star), so do not be deceived by it, however exalted its speaker. ﴿And the life of this world has deceived them﴾, meaning it deceived them and made them desire by falsehood, to the point that they denied the resurrection and claimed there is no life after it, and they mocked the signs of Allah the Exalted. Some have made gharra from gharr, which is filling the mouth, meaning its pleasures satiated them until they forgot the Hereafter. Upon this is the saying of the poet: "When we met in the evening, its goodness deceived me until I came out intoxicated." ﴿And remind with it﴾, meaning with the Qur'an. It has been stated explicitly in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, and the Qur'an explains part of itself by part. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to their reckoning. It has also been said: it is a pronoun explained by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿lest a soul be delivered up for what it has earned﴾, so that it is a substitute for it, and Abu Hayyan preferred this. According to the other aspects, it is an object of purpose, meaning lest it be delivered up, or for fear, or out of dislike that it be delivered up. Some have made it a direct object of (remind), and the meaning of ﴿tubsal﴾ is "be detained", as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. He recited the verse of Zuhayr:

"And she parted from you with a pledge that has no ransom, on the day of parting, while my heart was detained and clung."

In the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim from him it is "be handed over" (tusallam). This is also narrated from al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi, and it was preferred by al-Jubba'i and al-Farra'. In the narration of Ibn Jarir and others it is "be disgraced". Al-Raghib said: ﴿tubsal﴾ here means "be deprived of reward". Many have mentioned that al-Ibsal and al-Basl originally mean prevention, and from it comes "asad basil" (a lion who is brave), because its prey does not escape from it, or because it defends itself; and al-basil is the brave one, for his refusal to be overcome by his opponent. Al-Basl has also come with the meaning of forbidden. Al-Raghib distinguished between them: "forbidden" is general to what is prevented by a rule or by force, while al-basl is what is prevented by force. And "basal" may mean "yes" and "indeed", and as a verb-name it means "hold back". The indefiniteness of "soul" (nafs) is for generality, like it in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾, meaning: lest every soul be detained and held in pledge for destruction, or for the Fire, or be handed over to that, or be disgraced, or be deprived of reward because of its evil deed, or (remind) with detention or the detention of every soul by this. The indefinite has been taken as general although it is in an affirmative context, because the context requires it. It has been said that here it has the sense of negation. In what Abu Hayyan chose there is magnification and added emphasis, which is not hidden. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿there will not be for it﴾, meaning the soul, ﴿besides Allah any protector or intercessor﴾, is either a resumption informing of this, or in the position of a raised attribute of (soul), or in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of (earned) or from (soul), for it is in the sense of "a disbelieving soul" or "many souls". Some have preferred the circumstantial reading. (Besides Allah) is attached to a deleted element that is a circumstantial clause of (protector), and it has been said it is a predicate of (there is not), and (for it) then is attached to a deleted element as an explanation; and whoever made (min) additional did not attach it to anything. The meaning is that there will not come between it and Allah the Exalted, by repelling His punishment from it, any protector or intercessor. ﴿And if it offers every ransom﴾, meaning if that soul ransoms every ransom, and (every) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because it follows what it is attached to, not as an object. It has been said that it is an attribute of a deleted noun meaning "complete", like your saying: "he is a man, every man", meaning complete in manhood, and the estimate is "a complete ransom". This was refuted on the grounds that "kull" in this sense requires being a follower and being attached to a noun like the one it follows as an adjective, not as an emphasis, as in al-Tashil, and that its qualified noun may not be deleted. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿it will not be taken from it﴾ is the answer of the condition, and the verb is attributed to the prepositional phrase, like "a journey from the city", not to the pronoun of the ransom, because ransom, as you know, is a verbal noun and is not "taken"; unlike His saying, the Exalted: ﴿nor will ransom be accepted from it﴾, for there it means "that which is ransomed with". It has been permitted that the attribution is to its pronoun, intending by it the ransom, by way of istikhdam (a double usage), but there is no need for this, given the soundness of attributing it to the prepositional phrase; and by this one also dispenses with the view that it refers to the substitute that is taken from the context.

It has been said: the meaning of the verse is "and if that soul gives every equitable payment on that day, it will not be accepted from it, because repentance there is not accepted, and it is only accepted in this world." ﴿Those﴾, meaning those who take their religion as amusement and play, who are deceived by the life of this world, ﴿are those who have been delivered up﴾, meaning they were deprived of reward and handed over to punishment, or by one of the remaining meanings of ibsal, ﴿for what they earned﴾, meaning because of their evil deeds and deviant beliefs. The demonstrative is the subject, and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the remoteness of the rank of those pointed to in evil state; its predicate is the relative clause after it, and the sentence is a resumption that was brought after the warning against those from the aforementioned ibsal, to explain that they are the ones afflicted with it.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿For them is a drink of boiling water﴾ is another resumption explaining the manner of the aforementioned ibsal, built upon a question arising from the speech, as if it were said: "What will be for them when they are delivered up?" So it is said: "For them is a drink of boiling water", meaning hot water that gushes and circulates in their bellies and by which their intestines are cut to pieces. ﴿And a painful punishment﴾, by a fire that blazes in their bodies, as is the most apparent sense of punishment, ﴿for what they used to disbelieve﴾.

70

- That is, because of their persistent disbelief in the world. The word hamim is applied to cold water, so it is an antonym, as in the Qamus. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the clause ﴿for them is a drink﴾ be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of ﴿were delivered up﴾, and that it be the predicate of the demonstrative, with (those who) being an attribute of it or a substitute for it, or that it be a second predicate. He preferred, as his words indicate, that the demonstrative refer to the souls indicated by (soul), and the clause was made to explain the consequence of the ibsal. Many of the verifiers preferred what we have indicated.

The ordering of the two punishments mentioned upon their disbelief, although they are also punished for their other sins, as His saying, glorified is He, ﴿for what they earned﴾ indicates, is because it is the principal cause of punishment and the most important in the matter of warning; or it is meant, as has been said, by their disbelief that which is more general than it and what follows from it of sins.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 71:

﴿Say: "Shall we call upon, apart from Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us?"﴾ Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi that the polytheists said to the believers: "Follow our way and abandon the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So Allah the Exalted said: "Say..." and so on.

It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) when his son 'Abd al-Rahman invited him to worship idols. In directing the command to the Prophet (ﷺ), there is what is not hidden of the exaltation of the status of the believers, or of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). That is: "Shall we worship, going beyond the worship of Allah the Exalted, who possesses all the attributes of divinity, among which is the power to benefit and to harm, that which has no power to benefit us if we worship it, nor to harm us if we abandon it? And the lowest rank of being worthy of worship is the power to do that." The doer of "nad'u" (we call upon), and likewise what is conjoined to it in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾, is general to the master of those addressed (ﷺ) and to others, and it is not specific to al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), based on the view that he was the cause of revelation. In the verse there is a figure of speech by which the whole is meant to include the part, since turning back on one's heels cannot be conceived of for the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sense intended, which is returning to polytheism. The meaning is more fitting for us, the community of Muslims, regarding that.

"A'qab" is the plural of "'aqib," which is the back part of the foot. One says "raja'a 'ala 'aqibihi" (he returned on his heels) when he turned back returning. It is used metaphorically, as has been said, for departing without seeing the place of the foot, and this is departure without knowledge, unlike departure with advancing. It has also been said that "al-radd 'ala al-a'qab" means returning to misguidance and ignorance, whether polytheism or otherwise. The majority hold the first view. The expression of returning to polytheism as "al-radd 'ala al-a'qab," as Shaykh al-Islam said, serves to intensify its ugliness by depicting it in the form of that which is a byword for ugliness, together with the indication that polytheism is a state that has been abandoned and cast behind the back. The choice of "nuradd" (we are returned) over "nartadd" (we apostatize) is to direct the denial to apostasy by means of being turned back by another, explicitly opposing the misguiders and cutting off their empty hopes, and as a declaration that apostasy without one who turns one back is not within the realm of possibility, so that it would need to be negated and denied. ﴿after Allah has guided us﴾, that is, to monotheism and Islam, or to all that results in success in the Hereafter, as has been said. The temporal clause is connected to "nuradd" and is brought to emphasize the rejection, not merely to establish the meaning of turning back and depict it; otherwise it would have sufficed to say "after we were guided." It is as if it were said: "Shall we be returned to that, after Allah, whom there is no guide besides, has guided us, by the misguidance of the misguider?" The verse is apparently not of the category of grammatical contention (tanazu'), nor is the clause "nuradd" in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "nad'u," meaning "while we are being returned." Abu al-Baqa' permitted this.

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed﴾ is an adjectival qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "Shall we be returned a return like the return of one whom the devils have enticed..." Al-Tabarsi estimated: "Shall we call upon a call like the call of one who..." and this is not correct, as is not hidden. It has also been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the doer of "nuradd," meaning: "Shall we be turned back on our heels, being made like that?" Sahib al-Fara'id objected to this, saying that the essence of the circumstantial sense is "we are returned in a state of resembling," like your saying "Zayd came riding," meaning in a state of riding, whereas the return is not in a state of resembling, just as coming is not in a state of riding. Al-Tibi answered him that the circumstantial clause is emphatic, like His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿then you turned back fleeing﴾, so this entails nothing of that. It is not hidden that this is open to dispute.

"Istihwa'" is an "istif'al" form from "hawa fi al-ard yahwi" when he went away, as is known in the language, as if they sought its descent and were eager for it, meaning: like one whom the satanic jinn have carried off into deserts and wastelands. The discourse concerns a compound intellectual construction, or it is of the category of simile, in which one who was freed from polytheism and then reverted on his heels is likened to one whom the devils carried off into the wilderness and led astray after he had been on the straight path. This is not based on the claims of the Arabs, as one who was enticed by devils claimed. Some have asserted that "istahwa" is from "hawa" meaning "fell," as one says "hawa yahwi hawiyyan" with a fatha on the ha, when he falls from a height to a lower place, and the intended meaning is to liken the state of this misguided person to the state of one who fell from a high place into a deep, low pit, since he is in extreme confusion, weakness and bewilderment. A parallel to this is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And whoever associates with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾. This is far-fetched, although al-Imam said it is better than the first meaning, though this depends on the istif'al form from "hawa" being attested with this meaning. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "alladhi" be singular, meaning "like the man or like the group who..." and that it be a collective noun, the intended meaning being "alladhina" (those who).

Hamza read "istahwahu" with an imala-inflected alif and with the masculine form. "Fi al-ard" means in its kind (of land), and the prepositional phrase is connected to "istahwat-hu" or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from its object, meaning: being in the land. Likewise His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿bewildered﴾ is also a circumstantial clause from it, either as a substitute for the first, or as a second circumstantial clause according to those who permit that, or from "alladhi," or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the prepositional phrase be a circumstantial clause from "hayran," which is diptote, and its feminine is "hayra," meaning: wandering, astray from the road, not knowing what to do.

﴿to him﴾, that is, to the one enticed, ﴿are companions﴾, I consider them a company, ﴿who call him to guidance﴾, that is, to the straight path, which is applied to it as hyperbole, on the pattern of "Zayd is justice." The first prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a predicate preceding its subject, and "companions" is the subject.
