The clause is either in the accusative position as a qualifier of "bewildered," or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in it, or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, or a substitute for the preceding circumstantial clause; or it has no position, being resumptive. The clause "yad'unahu" (they call him) is a qualifier of "companions." His, glorified is He, saying: "Come to us" is one in which a verb of saying is presumed, so that it is a substitute for "yad'unahu," or a circumstantial clause from its doer. It has been said that it is quoted speech because calling means saying. This is based on the disagreement between the Basrans and Kufans concerning such cases, though the well-known estimate is "he says: come to us." In this there is an indication that they are rightly guided, firm upon the straight path, and that the one they call is not among those who know the way so as to be invited to come, but merely perceives the bearing of the caller and the direction of the summons.

Ibn Mas'ud read, as related by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari from Abu Ishaq, "ta'ti" (come) as a circumstantial clause from "al-huda," meaning: clear. Say to these disbelievers: the guidance of Allah, by which He guided us, which is Islam, is the guidance, meaning alone, as the definiteness of both terms or the pronoun of separation indicates, and whatever is other than it is pure misguidance and sheer error. The repetition of the command is either for the sake of emphasis on the matter commanded, or because what preceded was for the restraint from polytheism, while this is an urging toward Islam and a preparation for what follows, for the exclusivity of guidance to His guidance is what necessitates obedience to the commands after it. ﴿And we have been commanded﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾, included with it under "say." The lam in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿to submit﴾ is causal, and the second object of "umirna" is omitted, meaning: we have been commanded with sincerity so that we may submit and surrender ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾.

71

- It has been said that it is in the sense of "bi" (with), meaning: we have been commanded with Islam. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying it is strange and unknown to the grammarians. It has been said that it is superfluous, meaning: we have been commanded that we submit, with the "bi" omitted. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and whoever follows them said: the verb in this and in such constructions as ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ is interpreted as a verbal noun, and it is the subject, while the lam and what follows it is its predicate, meaning: we have been commanded for submission. This is like the proverb "you hear of the Mu'ayyadi, better than that you see him." Its remoteness is not hidden.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' held that the lam is a verbal particle with the sense of "an" (that), specifically after "aradtu" (I wished) and "umirtu" (I was commanded), so it is as if it were said: "And we were commanded that we submit." The mention of His lordship over the worlds serves to give the reason for the command and to emphasize the obligation of obeying it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 72:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that you establish the prayer and fear Him﴾, i.e., the Lord, by disobeying His command, exalted is He, with the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) being implied. It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the preceding prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa-l-majrūr). Sibawayh and a group [of grammarians] explicitly stated that (an) al-maṣdariyyah (the "that" which introduces a verbal noun clause) may enter upon an imperative. It was also permitted that ﴿an aqimu﴾ be conjoined to the position (mawḍiʿ) of li-nuslima, as if it were said: "We were commanded that we submit and that you establish [the prayer]." It was also said that the conjunction is upon the implied object of the command (maf'ul al-amr al-muqaddar), i.e., "We were commanded to believe and to establish the prayer." It was also said that it is upon His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah..." etc., i.e., say to them: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance, and that you establish [the prayer]." It was also said: upon [the phrase] "ituna" (come to us). And other than that has been said.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned that the apparent form would have been to say: "We were commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds, and to establish the prayer," but it was altered to what has been mentioned, to signal that the disbeliever, as long as he remains a disbeliever, is like an absent stranger, so he is addressed with the address used for an absent party. When he embraces Islam and enters the company of the believers, he becomes like a near, present person, so he is addressed with the address used for those who are present.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One to whom you will be gathered﴾.

It is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustaʾnafah) that makes compliance with what He, exalted is He, has commanded regarding the three matters obligatory. The fronting of the object (taqdim al-maʿmul) serves to indicate restriction (al-ḥaṣr), while observing the rhyme endings (al-fawasil): i.e., to Him, exalted is He, and not to other than Him, will you be gathered on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 6, verse 73 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, these two great things. Perhaps by their creation is also meant the creation of what is in them, and the absence of explicit mention of this is because it is evident that they encompass all the higher and lower beings. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿with truth﴾, is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the agent of "created": that is, "existing with truth." The meaning of the verse in this case, as has been said, is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of the object, meaning "clothed with truth," and that it be an attribute of the verbal noun of the emphasized verb, meaning "a creation clothed with truth."

﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is, His word is the truth﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) for what preceded. The *waw* is for resumption (*li-l-istinaf*). "The day" (*al-yawm*) in the sense of "the time" is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a fronted predicate. "His word" is the subject, and "the truth" is its attribute. What is meant by "the word" is the verbal sense, that is, the decree, the correct judgment that proceeds in accordance with wisdom. Hence it is valid to predicate it with a time expression. The meaning is: His decree, glorified is He, which is known for its truthfulness, exists at the moment He says to any of the things "Be," and it is. The fronting of the predicate is for emphasis on the generality of the time, as has been said. Al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) denied that this is for restriction, because it is not appropriate, and he took the fronting to be because it is the common usage. It has been objected that the common usage is the fronting of an adverbial predicate when the subject is indefinite and unqualified, or indefinite and qualified; but if the subject is definite, no one has said it. It has also been said that ﴿His word is the truth﴾ is a subject and predicate, and "the day" (*yawm*) is an adverbial complement for the content of the sentence. The *waw* in meaning is attached to it. The fronting is for attention to it, in that it is the locus of truthfulness. The omission of mention of what is said is because of confidence in its being most evident. What is meant by "the word" is the phrase "Be" (*kun*), either literally or figuratively. The meaning is: His command, glorified is He, which relates to everything He wills to bring into existence among things, at the moment He relates it to it, and not before it or after it among the instances of times, is the truth, that is, what is witnessed to as truth. It has also been said that the *waw* is for conjunction, and "the day" is either conjoined to "the heavens," in which case it is an object of "created" similarly, and what is meant by it is the Day of Gathering, that is: He is the one who brought into existence the heavens, the earth, and what is in them, and brought into existence the Day of Gathering and the Return. Or it is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿fear Him﴾, in which case it is also an object similarly, and the statement contains an omitted modifier, that is: fear God, exalted is He, and fear the terror of that day, its punishment, and its horror. Or it is connected to an omitted element indicated by "with truth," that is: He establishes with truth on the day, etc. This is a strained grammatical analysis, as Abu Hayyan said. It has also been said that it is conjoined to "with truth" and is an adverbial complement of "created," that is: He created the heavens and the earth in their greatness at the time He said "Be" and it was. The expression in the past tense is to bring the marvelous matter into presence. In this there is an objection, that it depends on the validity of conjoining an adverbial complement to a circumstantial clause, based on the view that a circumstantial clause is adverbial in meaning, and that is a strained view. ﴿His word is the truth﴾ is a subject and predicate, or the subject of a verb that carries a meaning; and "when He says" is for "His word, the truth," that is, for "His decree": "Be," and it is. What is meant by it is at the time He brings things into being and originates them; or at the time the Resurrection is established, so that the bringing into being is the revivifying of the dead for the Gathering. Others have said other than this, so reflect.

﴿And His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾, that is, dominion becomes firmly His on that day in form and in meaning, through the severing of the metaphorical ties that exist in this world and that justify ownership in a general sense, so none other claims it in any way. The *Sur* is a horn into which one blows, as has been established in the hadiths. God, exalted is He, knows its reality best. Its conditions have been explained in the books of the Sunnah. Its keeper is Israfil, peace be upon him, according to the well-known view. Al-Bazzar and al-Hakim narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet: "Two angels appointed over the trumpets await when they will be ordered, and then they blow."

Qatadah read *fi al-suwar* (in the forms), the plural of *sura*, and by it is meant the bodies that rise after the spirit is breathed into them. ﴿To the Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that is, of every unseen and every witnessed thing. ﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in everything He does, ﴿the Aware﴾

73
of all matters, hidden and manifest. The sentence is a concluding phrase for what preceded, and it contains *laff wa-nashr* (a structure of enumerated pairing) arranged here in order.

* * *

From the esoteric indications (*al-isharah*) in the verses: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾. Know that some of our Sufi masters, may God sanctify their secrets, mentioned that the unseen has levels. The first is the unseen of the unseens, which is God's knowledge, called the First Providence. The second is the unseen of the world of spirits, which is the imprinting of the form of everything that has existed or will exist from pre-eternity to eternity in the first, intellectual world, which is the spirit of the cosmos, called the Mother of the Book, in a universal manner; this is the prior decree. The third is the unseen of the world of hearts, which is that same imprinting itself, detailed in a scientific manner, both universal and particular, in the world of the universal soul, which is the heart of the cosmos, called the Preserved Tablet. The fourth is the unseen of the world of imagination, which is the imprinting of all existents in the particular celestial souls, impressed upon their bodies, specified and individualized, coinciding with their times, as they occur exactly. That world is what is expressed as the lowest heaven, since it is the nearest of the levels of the unseen to the world of witnessing, and the Tablet of Destiny, which is the detailing of His decree, glorified is He. They mentioned that God's knowledge, which is the First Providence, is an expression of His, glorified is He, encompassing of all things by presence; thus the treasuries that comprise all the unseens are present to His essence, and there is nothing additional, and none knows them but He, glorified is He. Likewise the doors of those treasuries are closed, and their keys are in the hand of God, exalted is He; none apart from Him, mighty and majestic, looks into what is in them, though He opens from them what He wills for whom He wills.

It may be said: many of those firmly grounded in knowledge have verified that the realities and quiddities of things are established in pre-eternity, and in their establishment they are not made, and only the existential forms are made. These do not change, do not alter, and are not subject to annihilation at all, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Everything perishes except His face﴾, on the basis that the pronoun returns to "thing." The "face" is interpreted as the reality, and God's knowledge of them is by presence. They are like mirrors for their originated forms. Thus those forms are witnessed by God, exalted is He, from pre-eternity, even though they are nonexistent in themselves, mentally and externally. They have explained that knowledge of them is folded into knowledge of the Essence, with all its considerations, among which is that He, glorified is He, is the origin for the bestowal of their existences upon them according to wisdom. Thus it can be said that the keys, in the sense of treasuries, are an allusion to those eternal quiddities, which are like mirrors for what is hidden from us of forms. Those are present with Him, exalted is He, from pre-eternity, and none knows them by presential knowledge, not needing a shadowy form, but He, majestic and exalted. This is evident to whom the care has taken by the hand. ﴿And He knows what is on the land﴾, that is, the land of souls, with its varieties of desires and their levels; ﴿and the sea﴾, that is, the sea of hearts, with the pearls of wisdom and the coral of gnosis; ﴿and not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾, from the leaves of the trees of gentleness and majesty, on the course of the soul and the adversary of the heart, ﴿in all its states﴾; ﴿nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth﴾, which is the world of natures and bodies; ﴿nor anything fresh or dry﴾, from the inspirations that come upon the heart gently without disturbance, and from the dry whisperings and passing thoughts that the soul flees from when they come upon it; ﴿but it is in a clear book﴾, which is His comprehensive knowledge. Some did not interpret any of the matters mentioned and explained "the Book" as the lowest heaven, since these particulars are specified in it. It is possible to say that the Book is an allusion to the quiddities of things, which are called the fixed entities, and their being in it means what we pointed to: that those entities are like mirrors for these external existents. ﴿And He it is who takes you in sleep at night﴾, that is, He puts you to sleep. It has also been said: He takes you in sleep by the flight of your spirits in the kingdom and their journey in the gardens of the divine presences.

It has been said: the meaning may be, "He it is who constricts you until your spirits nearly leave you in the night of overpowering and the manifestation of majesty." ﴿And He knows what you have earned﴾, that is, what you have acquired by day of actions in general; it has been said: of hard actions upon the soul that pain it, such as acts of worship. It has also been said: it is possible that the meaning is: and He knows what you have acquired in the day of gracious manifestation, of intimacy or the fleeting gnosis. ﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾, that is, in what you have earned, the forms of your deeds and your good and bad gains. It has been said: the good; it has been said: what you acquired in the day of manifestation. The first of these sayings here and in what preceded is better. ﴿That a term named may be fulfilled﴾, that is, specified with Him. ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ in the very totality of the absolute gathering. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ by manifesting the forms of your deeds to you and recompensing you by them. ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾, because He is the absolute existence, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness; for Him is manifestation as wisdom requires, and the manifestations do not confine Him. ﴿And God is encompassing them from behind﴾.

﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾, which are the faculties in which good and evil are imprinted and become a disposition or a faculty, and which appear at the separation of the spirit and take on a fitting form; or the celestial faculties in which particular forms are imprinted and which leave nothing small or great unrecorded. ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him﴾. It has been said: they are those same guardians, and God has deposited in them the power to take. ﴿Then they are returned to God﴾ in the very totality of the absolute gathering, ﴿their true Master﴾, that is, their Owner who attends to all their conditions, since there is no existence for them except through Him, ﴿the Truth﴾, and all else besides Him is falsehood. Some people of allusion mentioned that this is the most hopeful verse in the Book of God, exalted is He, on the basis that God, exalted is He, informed of the servant's return to Him, glorified is He, and his exit from the prison of the world and the hands of the recording angels, describing Himself to him as his true Master. This implies that other than Him, glorified is He, is not truly considered a master. There is no doubt that there is nothing more honorable for the servant than that his return be to his Master. ﴿Unquestionably, His is the judgment, and He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾, since the manifestation of deeds in appropriate forms occurs at the moment the spirit separates from the body.

﴿Say: Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land﴾, which are the psychic veils, and the sea, which are the veils of the heart's attributes? ﴿You call upon Him﴾ to remove them ﴿humbly﴾ within your souls ﴿and secretly﴾ within your inmost secrets: ﴿If He delivers us from these﴾ veils and screens, ﴿we will surely be among the thankful﴾ for the blessing of deliverance, through uprightness and establishment. ﴿Say: God delivers you from them﴾ by the lights of the manifestations of His attributes, ﴿and from every distress﴾ other than that, by

[Page 193]

He bestows upon you through annihilation. ﴿Then you﴾, after your knowledge of His power over that, ﴿associate partners﴾ with Him, namely your souls and your desires, worshipping them. ﴿Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you﴾, by veiling you from contemplating the malakut (the unseen, spiritual dominion), or by subduing you through your being veiled by intelligibles and spiritual veils. ﴿Or from beneath your feet﴾, by not facilitating for you the standing at the door of lordship, in the manner of servanthood and seeking union, or by veiling you with natural veils. ﴿Or confuse you into factions﴾, separate groups, each group following a power of the powers that opposes the other group. Or He makes your souls differ in their beliefs, each group following a false messiah (dajjal). ﴿And make some of you taste the violence of others﴾, through disputes and contentions, according to what difference requires. ﴿For every news﴾, that is, what is reported of, ﴿there is a fixed place﴾, that is, a place of occurrence and settlement. ﴿And you will know﴾ when He uncovers from you the veils of your bodies. ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs﴾, by displaying the attributes of their souls and affirming knowledge and power for them, ﴿turn away from them﴾, because they are veiled and associators. ﴿Nor is anything of their reckoning incumbent upon those who are god-fearing﴾, who are those stripped of their attributes, ﴿from their account﴾, that is, from the account of these veiled ones, ﴿anything; but a reminder﴾, that is, let them remind them with rebuke and deterrence, ﴿that perhaps they may fear God﴾, guarding themselves against engaging in vain talk.

It is also permitted that the meaning is: those who are stripped bare are not veiled through mingling with the veiled ones; but We remind them, perhaps they will increase in God-consciousness.

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾, that is, leave those whose habit is play and amusement, etc., for they have been veiled by what has become firmly rooted in them of hearing the warning and its effect upon them. ﴿And remind with it﴾, that is, with the Qur'an, lest ﴿a soul be given over to destruction for what it has earned﴾, that is, be veiled by its earning, so that a habitual state (malakah) comes to it. That is: remind the one whose religion is not play and amusement, lest his religion become that. As for one who has reached that limit, the reminder will not benefit him. ﴿Those are the ones who are given over to destruction for what they earned; for them is a drink of scalding water﴾, which is the intensity of longing for perfection, ﴿and a painful punishment﴾, which is deprivation from it because of being veiled by what they earned.

﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides God, that which neither benefits us nor harms us﴾, that is: shall we worship one who has no power over anything at all, since he has no real existence? ﴿And be turned back on our heels﴾ into polytheism, ﴿after God had guided us﴾ to true monotheism (tawhid haqiqi), ﴿like one whom the devils have lured away﴾ through illusion and imagination into the earth, that is, the earth of nature and the deserts of the self, ﴿bewildered﴾, not knowing where to go, ﴿having companions﴾ of thought and rational faculties, ﴿who call him to guidance﴾, the true guidance, saying, ﴿Come to us!﴾, for the true path is with us, but he does not listen. ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God﴾, which is the path of tawhid, ﴿is the guidance﴾, and other than it is other than it. ﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾, by erasing our attributes, ﴿and to establish prayer﴾, the true prayer, which is the presence of the heart (hudur qalbi). ﴿And fear Him﴾, that is, make Him a shield by freeing yourselves from your existence. ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾, by passing away (fana') in Him, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Ata' said: establishing prayer is guarding it with God, Exalted, through the secrets.

﴿And it is He who created the heavens﴾, that is, the heavens of the spirits, ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, the earth of the body, ﴿in truth﴾, that is, standing upon justice, which is what the requirement of His essence demands. ﴿And the day He says, "Be," and it is﴾, which is the time of the connection of His eternal will to manifestation in the specific determinations. ﴿His word is the truth﴾, because it requires what it required in the best order, and there is no possibility more wondrous than what has been. ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the trumpet is blown﴾, which is the time of bestowing spirits upon the forms of the hidden things which are dead in themselves, rather they have no existence and no life.

﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, that is, the realities of the world of spirits, which is called malakut, ﴿and the visible﴾, that is, the forms of the world of bodies, which is called mulk (the dominion of the visible). ﴿And He is the Wise﴾, who bestows upon the receptive capacities according to their readiness, ﴿the All-Aware﴾ of their conditions and the measure of their receptivities. There is no wise one other than Him, and no all-aware one besides Him.

[p. 194]

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ is, according to some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), in the accusative as the object (maf'ul bihi) of a suppressed verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. It is coordinated with ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon..."﴾, not with "Establish" (aqimu), because that would corrupt the meaning. The sense is: "And mention, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers, after you have denounced their worship of what can neither benefit nor harm, and have affirmed that guidance is the guidance of God Almighty and what follows from His attributes, the time when Abraham, peace be upon him, said, reproaching ﴿his father Azar﴾ for worshipping idols, while they claim to follow his creed. This is something that will shame them and expose the corruption of their way."

Azar is on the pattern of Adam. It is a non-Arabic proper name (a'jami) belonging to the father of Abraham, peace be upon him, and he was from a village in the countryside of Kufa. It is either a substitute (badal) for "Abraham" or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) to it. Al-Zajjaj said: "There is no disagreement among the genealogists that the name of Abraham's father, peace be upon him, is Tarah, with a ta' with two dots above, followed by an alif, then a ra' (unpointed), fatha-vowelled, and a ha' (unpointed)." It is also narrated with a khaʾ with a dot.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted with a sound chain from Ibn Jurayj that his name was Tayrah or Tarah. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the name of Abraham's father, peace be upon him, was Yazar, and the name of his mother was Muthla.

Those who held that Azar is not his name include Mujahid, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others. Those who held this differed: some said Azar is a title (laqab) of his father, peace be upon him; some said it is the name of his grandfather; some said it is the name of his paternal uncle, and both uncle and grandfather are called "father" metaphorically (majazan); and some said it is the name of an idol, a view reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Mujahid, may God be pleased with them. Others said it is a descriptive term (wasf) in their language, meaning "the one who errs." It is reported from Sulayman al-Taymi that he said: "I was told that its meaning is 'the crooked one.'" And it is reported from some that it means "the aged old man" in Khwarazmian.

On the view that it is descriptive, its being diptote (mana' sarf) is due to its being modelled on the pattern (mawazin) of fa'al with a fatha on the 'ayn, for this pattern is commonly diptote in non-Arabic proper names. It was said that the better view is that it became dominant as a name and was therefore assimilated to proper nouns (ʿalam). Some make it a derived adjective (na't mushtaqq) from al-azr, meaning strength, or al-wizr, meaning sin. In that case it is diptote because of descriptiveness and the form of the verb, as it is on the pattern af'al.

On the view that it means "idol," the expression involves an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf) with the modified noun replaced by the noun it modifies, that is, "worshipper of Azar."

Ya'qub read ﴿Azaru﴾ with a damma, as a vocative (nida'). This was used as evidence that it is a proper noun, on the basis that the vocative is only elided with proper nouns, and eliding it with descriptive nouns is anomalous. That is, "O Azar!" ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ That is, "Do you make them gods for yourself?" The denial is directed at adopting the class (jins) without considering plurality, and the form of the class is intended with regard to its occurrence. It was read ﴿a-azaran﴾ with two hamzas, the first interrogative and fatha-vowelled, and the second fatha-vowelled and kasra-vowelled; the second is either original or substituted from a waw. Whoever reads this way reads ﴿tattakhidu﴾ without the hamza. Then it is an object (maf'ul bihi) of a suppressed verb, meaning "Do you worship Azar?" on the view that it is the name of an idol, and ﴿tattakhidu...﴾ is an explanation and confirmation of that, and it falls under the denial. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) on the view that it means "power," meaning "For the sake of power do you take idols as gods?" The utterance is a denial of his seeking strength through them, in the manner of God's words: ﴿Do they seek honour with them?﴾ It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial (hal) or a second object of ﴿tattakhidu﴾.

Some grammarians parsed ﴿Azar﴾ on the reading of the majority as an object of a suppressed verb, also meaning an idol: "Do you worship Azar?" They made His words ﴿Do you take...﴾ an explanation and confirmation, meaning that it is an indicator of the elision and not an explanation in the technical sense of the construction of preoccupation (ishtighal), because what follows the hamza does not govern what precedes it, and what does not govern cannot explain a governing element, as is established among them.

What the great majority of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) rely on is that Azar was not the father of Abraham, peace be upon him. They claim that none of the ancestors of the Prophet ﷺ was a disbeliever at all, based on his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I was never transferred from the loins of the pure men to the wombs of the pure women, and the polytheists are impure." Restricting purity to purity from fornication has no proof that can be relied upon, and the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording and not from the specificity of the occasion.

They have written treatises on this subject and argued for it with what they argued. The claim that this is the view of the Shi'a, as al-Imam al-Razi asserted, arises from lack of thorough investigation. Most of these hold that Azar is the name of Abraham's paternal uncle, peace be upon him. The use of "father" for an uncle occurs in God's words: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac."﴾ In this there is also the use of "father" for a grandfather.

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: "The maternal uncle is a parent (wali-d) and the paternal uncle is a parent," and he recited this verse. In a report: "Return my father Abbas to me." Some supported the claim that the true father of Abraham, peace be upon him, was not a disbeliever, and that the disbeliever was only his uncle, by what Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted in his Tafsir with a sound chain from Sulayman ibn Surad, who said: "When they wanted to throw Abraham, peace be upon him, into the fire, they began gathering firewood, until an old woman would gather firewood. When he realized this, he said, 'God is sufficient for us and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' When they threw him, God Almighty said: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham.﴾ So it was. His uncle then said, 'It was for my sake that he was protected.' So God sent upon him a spark of fire which fell upon his foot and burned it."

And by what is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others: that Abraham, peace be upon him, kept asking forgiveness for his father until he died. When he died, it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, so he did not ask forgiveness for him. Then he emigrated after his death and the episode of the fire to Syria, then he entered Egypt, and what happened to him with the tyrant happened, then he returned to Syria with Hajar. Then God commanded him to transfer her and her son Ishmael to Mecca, and he did so. There he prayed and said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley near Your Sacred House...﴾ up to His words: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the reckoning takes place.﴾ From this it is inferred that the one mentioned in the Qur'an as a disbeliever is his uncle, since it is stated in the first report that the one who perished before the emigration was his uncle, and the second report shows that the asking of forgiveness for his parents took place a long time after the death of his father. Had the one who perished been his true father, this asking of forgiveness for him would not have been valid at all. So what appears is that the one who perished was the disbelieving uncle, expressed metaphorically as "father," and he did not ask forgiveness for him after death. The one he asked forgiveness for was the true father, who was not Azar. The use of "parent" (walid) in the verse of forgiveness and "father" (ab) elsewhere indicates a distinction.

Some people argued that Azar was not the father of Abraham, peace be upon him, on the ground that this indicates that he, peace be upon him, spoke to him with harshness and roughness, as in God's words: ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾, meaning those who follow you in their worship, ﴿in manifest error﴾, a great deviation from the truth, ﴿clear﴾.

That is, plainly, without any ambiguity at all. Addressing a father with roughness is not permissible, because it involves causing him harm. The verse of "uff" (ta'fif), by its implication, covers all kinds of harm, as its generality includes both the disbelieving and the believing father. Also, when God Almighty sent Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh, He commanded him to be gentle with him and to speak to him with gentle words, in observance of the right of upbringing, which is greatest in the case of a parent. Also, calling with gentleness is more effective, for harshness produces aversion, so it is not fitting from anyone other than Abraham, peace be upon him, even with strangers, so how could it be fitting from him with his father, who was "the compassionate, the forbearing"?

It is answered that this is not harm that is forbidden in any way, and nothing other than that is required by the situation. We do not concede that the motive for ordering Moses, peace be upon him, to be gentle with Pharaoh is merely the observance of the right of upbringing. A person may sometimes be harsh with someone for his benefit, as Abu Tammam said:

*So he was harsh that they might be restrained, and whoever is resolute, let him be harsh at times toward one he loves.*

Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri said:

*Strike your child and guide him to right conduct, and do not say, "He is a child who has not reached maturity."*
*For many a split in the head brings benefit, so measure by the split of the head of the arrow and the pen.*

Abu Khafaja al-Andalusi said:

*Alert your child from his youth by reproaching him, for perhaps his intelligence lies dormant there.*
*And rebuke him until tears flow down his cheeks and his insides burn.*
*For the sword does not gleam in your hand until its fire is kindled, until water runs down its two sides.*

47

Gentleness being more effective is not accepted without qualification, since circumstances differ. This is shown by the words of the Exalted to His Prophet, peace be upon him, at one time: ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾, and at another: ﴿And be harsh with them﴾. Yes, if it were claimed that what has been mentioned supports the view that Azar was not the true father of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, that might have been accepted. But since it is claimed to be proof for that view, it is not accepted, so reflect.

"Seeing" (al-ru'yah) is either cognitive, in which case the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is its second object, or visual, in which case it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object. The sentence serves as the reason for the rebuke and censure.

The origin of the error of the idol-worshippers, as can be understood from the words of Abu Ma'shar Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Munajjim al-Balkhi in some of his books, is the belief that God, exalted is He, is a body. The Imam reported from him that he said: Many people of China and India used to affirm God and the angels, but they believed that He, glorified be He, is a body with a form, like the most beautiful of forms, and that the angels also have beautiful forms. However, they all are veiled by the heavens, in their view. Therefore, they took images and statues of elegant appearance, pleasing in shape and structure, and made the most beautiful of them the form of God, and what is below Him the form of the angel. They persisted in worshipping these, intending nearness to God and to the angels.

The Imam himself mentioned, regarding the origin of idol-worship, that people saw the changes in the states of this lower world tied to the changes in the states of the stars, so they assumed that happiness and misfortune are linked to the manner in which they occur at the rising of the ascendants. Then the opinion of most people came to prevail that the source of the occurrence of events in this world is the celestial connections and the astral correspondences. So they exaggerated in venerating the stars. Then some of them believed that the stars exist necessarily by their own essence, and some believed that they are created and brought into being by the Supreme God, but they said that, even so, they are the ones who govern the affairs of the world. Under both assumptions, they busied themselves with worshipping them. When they saw that the stars disappear from sight, they made for each star an idol from the substance attributed to it in their claim, and devoted themselves to worshipping it, their aim being the worship of those stars and seeking nearness to them.

For this reason, the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, established proofs that the stars have absolutely no influence on the states of this world, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾, after He had explained that the stars are subjugated. Also, if it were supposed that an action proceeded from them and an influence in this world, they would not be free of signs of having come into being and of being created. Therefore, worshipping the branch rather than the root would be pure error.

What indicates that the substance of the religion of the idol-worshippers is what has been mentioned is that He, glorified be He, after relating Ibrahim's rebuke of his father for taking them, established the proof that neither the stars nor the moon is fit for divinity. And I say: Perhaps this was a cause of the worship of idols at first.

Page 197

As for the cause of the Arabs' worship of them, it was different from this. Ibn Hisham said: Some people of knowledge told me that Amr ibn Luhayy, who was the first to change the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, went out from Makkah to Syria on one of his journeys. When he arrived at the land of al-Balqa, where the Amaliqah, the descendants of Imlaq, were living at that time, and it is said Imliq ibn Wudd ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him, he saw them worshipping idols. He said to them: What are these that I see you worshipping? They said: These are idols we worship, and we seek rain through them, so they send us rain, and we seek victory through them, so they give us victory. He said to them: Will you not give me one of them, so that I may take it to the land of the Arabs and they may worship it? So they gave him an idol called Hubal. He came with it to Makkah, set it up, and commanded the people to worship it.

Ibn Ishaq said: They claim that the first worship of stones among the children of Isma'il, peace be upon him, was this: whenever one of them traveled from Makkah, when it became confining for them and they sought wider space in the lands, he would carry with him a stone from the stones of the Haram, out of veneration for the Haram. Wherever they alighted, they would place it and circle around it as they circled the Ka'bah, until a later generation succeeded them, forgot what they had been upon, exchanged the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, for another, worshipped idols, and became like the nations before them in their errors. The completion of the discussion on this will come, God willing, later.

This act of showing (*ira'ah*) is derived from sight (*ru'yah basariyyah*), used figuratively as a lexical metaphor (*isti'arah lughawiyyah*) for knowledge, by mentioning the cause and meaning the effect. That is, "We made him know and gave him insight." The apparent wording would have been "We showed" (*arayna*) in the past tense, but it shifts to the present form as a narration of a past state, to bring its image to mind so that it seems present and witnessed. It has also been said that the use of the future form is because the object of the showing has no limit, so its significance cannot be grasped except gradually. This is not valid. The demonstrative refers to the verbal noun of ﴿nuri﴾ (We show), and not to another showing understood from His saying ﴿Indi ara-ka﴾ (I see you), nor to what he warned his father about and what he led his people astray with, in terms of knowledge and insight. Both have been permitted. It has also been said that the object of comparison may be the making-to-see in the sense that it occurs, and the thing compared to it may be the making-to-see in the sense that it is the signified meaning of the word. A parallel to this is the description of a statement as conforming to reality, when the statement is identical to the reality. It has also been permitted that the *kaf* (like) means *lam* (for), and that the demonstrative refers to the preceding statement. You know what is more eloquent and preferable among what has been mentioned before in its parallels, and it is none other than the first, that is, that marvelous making-to-see, by which We made him see, peace be upon him, ﴿the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, His lordship and His ownership of them, not some other, lesser showing than it. *Malakut* is a verbal noun like *raghabut* and *rahamut*, as Ibn Malik and other lexicographers have said, and its *ta'* is an augmentation for emphasis. Therefore it has been interpreted as great dominion and overpowering authority. It is, as al-Raghib said, specific to God Most High, contrary to some others. It is related from Mujahid that what is meant by *malakut* is the signs. It has also been said: the wonders that are in the heavens and the earth. He, peace be upon him, had the seven heavens opened for him, so he looked at what was in them until his sight reached the Throne, and the seven earths were opened for him, so he looked at what was in them.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Ibrahim saw the malakut of the heavens and the earth, he came upon a man committing one of the sins of Allah, and he invoked against him, and he died. Then he came upon another committing one of the sins of Allah, and he invoked against him, and he died. Then he came upon another, and he went to invoke against him, and Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'O Ibrahim, you are a man whose supplication is answered, so do not invoke against My servants, for they are with Me in one of three states: either the sinner repents and I will accept his repentance, or I will bring forth from his loins a soul that will fill the earth with glorification, or I will take him to Me, and if I wish I will pardon, and if I wish I will punish.'"

Something similar has been related, both as a statement of a Companion and as a statement traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), through various routes, and there is no dispute regarding it, because rational proofs support it, contrary to one who imagined otherwise. It has also been said that the malakut of the heavens is the sun, the moon and the stars, and the malakut of the earth is the mountains, the trees and the seas.

صفحة 198
These statements, as has been said, require that the showing be visual, since what is meant by showing the aforementioned sensory matters is not merely enabling him, peace be upon him, to see them and witness them in themselves. Rather, it is his, peace be upon him, being informed of their realities and their being made known to him in respect of their indication of the affairs of the Mighty and Majestic. There is no doubt that this is not something perceived by the senses, as the preceding comparison indicates.

It has been read as *turi* (with a *ta'*), with the verb attributed to the malakut, meaning: it makes him, peace be upon him, see the indications of lordship. ﴿And that he might be among the certain (al-muqinin)﴾.

75

That is, among the company of those firmly established in certainty, who have reached the rank of *ayn al-yaqin* (the certainty of direct vision) regarding the knowledge of God Most High. This does not imply that doubt preceded it, as is clear. The *lam* is connected to a deleted element placed later, and the clause is an interpolated parenthesis confirming what precedes it, meaning: and so that it would be thus, We did what We did of the marvelous making-to-see mentioned. The restriction is in view of the fact that this result is the primary intended purpose of that making-to-see, and that guiding the creation and establishing the proof against the unbelievers are among its consequences. Some did not take this into account and therefore estimated the verb as preceding, because the cause is not restricted to what has been mentioned.

It has been said: it is connected to the preceding verb, and the clause is conjoined to an estimated cause that the discourse extends over, meaning: so that he would reason, and so that he would be. It was objected that reasoning, apart from its being a cause for turning, cannot be a cause for the showing, so how can it be conjoined to it by repeating the *lam*? This is not valid. Some claimed that on this basis the malakut of the heavens and the earth should mean their marvels and signs, because reasoning is one of the ends of showing them, not the end of showing the lordship itself. You know that the seeing of lordship is only through seeing its proofs and traces. Some people have permitted that the *waw* is extra and that the *lam* is connected to what was said, and this is far-fetched, although they mentioned it as a view like the first two in every instance of this kind in the Qur'an.

[Page 199]

The Most High's words, ﴿When the night covered him﴾, may be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with ﴿And when Abraham said﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) that affirms what came before and what follows. His peace be upon him, recognising the lordship (rubūbiyyah) and sovereignty (mālikiyyah) of the Most High over the heavens and the earth and all that is in them, and that all things are subdued under His dominion (malakūt), in need of Him in all their states, glorified is His majesty, and his being among those firmly grounded in knowledge who reached the summit of certainty of sight (ʿayn al-yaqīn), requires that he judge the impossibility of the divinity of anything other than Him, glorified is He, such as the idols and the stars that his people worshipped. Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) chose this view. It may also be that the verse is a detailed explanation of what was mentioned about the showing of the malakūt, and a clarification of how he reasoned (istidlāl) to it and reached the rank of firm conviction (īqān). The sequence is mentioned for the reason that the detail comes later than the summary in the mention.

The meaning of ﴿When the night covered him﴾ is that it concealed him with its darkness. This root, in its derivations, indicates concealment. From al-Rāghib: the basic meaning of *janna* is concealment from the senses. It is said: *janna-hu al-layl* and *ajanna-hu* and *janna ʿalayhi*, meaning it concealed him, and *ajanna-hu* means he provided for him something that conceals him.

The Most High's words, ﴿he saw a star﴾, are the response (jawāb) to *lammā* (when). The seeing of it is usually realised only when the light of the sun is removed from the senses. As Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said, this is clearly indicative that it was not at the beginning of its rising, but after it had disappeared from the senses through being dimmed by the light of the sun. His verified view is that it was near setting. The indication of the reason for that will come, God willing, later. By the star, according to what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, is Jupiter. Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Qatādah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that it was Venus." ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) built upon a question arising from the preceding speech. This statement from him, peace be upon him, was by way of supposition and giving rein, in accommodation to his father and his people who worshipped idols and stars, for the one who argues against a position he relates and then refutes it turns against it with invalidation, and this is the truth most deserving of acceptance.

[Page 199 continued / 200]

It has been said that there is an implied rhetorical question of denial (istifhām inkārī) in the speech; and the omission of the interrogative particle is frequent in their speech. From it is the line: "Then they said, 'Do you love her?' I said, 'Exceedingly.'" And the line: "I said, and I denied the faces: 'They are they!'" It was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the Most High's words ﴿But he did not attempt the steep ascent﴾ that the meaning is: "Did he not attempt?" And from this is taken the Most High's words ﴿And is it a favour of which you remind me, that you have enslaved the children of Israel?﴾. It has also been said that it is spoken by way of mockery, as one says to a humble man who has become leader of a people: "This is your master," in mockery. It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, intended to invalidate their claim of the lordship of the stars, but he, peace be upon him, knew from their adherence to their forefathers and their distance in disposition from accepting proofs that if he openly called to God, the Most High, they would not accept and would not pay attention. So he turned to a method that would lead them on to listen to the argument, by mentioning a statement that gives the impression that he was assisting them in their doctrine, while his heart was at peace with faith. His aim from this was that he might be able to mention the proof for its invalidation, even if they did not accept. The Imam (al-Rāzī) established this: when he, peace be upon him, did not find any way to the call except this way, and he was commanded to call to God, the Most High, he was in the position of one compelled to utter the word of disbelief. It is known that under compulsion it is permissible to utter a word of disbelief with the tongue. If that is permissible for the preservation of one person, then it is more fitting to be permissible for the rescue of a world of rational beings from disbelief and everlasting punishment. Thus Abraham's speech, peace be upon him, was of the kind of outward agreement with the people, so that when he presented to them the proof that invalidated their statement, their acceptance of it would be more complete and their benefit from hearing it more perfect. Then he said: What strengthens this view is that the Most High related a similar method from him in another place, which is His words ﴿So he glanced at the stars﴾ ﴿and said, "I am indeed sick"﴾. That is because the people used to infer the occurrence of future events by the science of the stars; so he agreed with them outwardly, while he was innocent of it inwardly, in order to thereby reach the breaking of the idols. So if agreement is permissible for this purpose, why would it not be permissible in our question for a similar reason? It has also been said that while the people were calling him, peace be upon him, to the worship of the stars, and the debate between them was standing firm, a star rose, and he said, "This is my lord," meaning: "This is the lord to which you call me." It has been said: all of these views are nothing before the verifiers, especially what the Imam established. All those views are founded on the basis that this statement occurred after his maturity and his calling his people to monotheism, and the context and the sequence of the verse are two just witnesses to that.

Some have claimed that it occurred before maturity, and there is no necessity of a doubt arising that leads to disbelief, because when he believed in the unseen, he wished to confirm what he was resolute about, by saying that if God, the Most High, were not God and what his people worship were such and such, then the whole of it would not be valid for that; so it is necessary that God, the Most High, is God, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the context and the sequence reject it, as is not hidden. It has been claimed that he, peace be upon him, said what he said because he did not yet know his Lord, glorified is He; and ignorance during childhood before the establishment of proof does no harm, and that is not counted as disbelief, which is not to be paid attention to at all. The verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqūn al-muḥiqqūn) have said: it is not permissible that there be a messenger of God, the Most High, upon whom there comes a time at which he is not a monotheist of God, the Most High, nor knowing of Him, and free from every object of worship other than Him. The Most High has related from the state of Abraham, peace be upon him, especially in his childhood, what makes no trace of anything contrary to that conceivable, so the first view alone is correct. Perhaps the adoption of that method in explaining the impossibility of the lordship of the star, rather than explaining the impossibility of the divinity of the idols, as has been said, is because its invalidity and impossibility is more hidden than the first; so if he had declared the truth from the outset, as he did concerning the worship of the idols, they would have persisted in obstinacy and hostility and insisted in their rebellion, wandering blindly. And the priority of the invalidity of the divinity of the idols over what was mentioned is from the sequence of ascending from the hidden

[Page 200]

to the more hidden. It has been said: the people used to worship the stars, so they made for each star an idol of the metals attributed to it, such as gold for the sun and silver for the moon, to draw near to them through them; so the idol became like a qibla for them. He therefore first denied their worship of the idols on the outward level, then invalidated their being originated and what they were attributed to among the stars, by the non-entitlement of them to that as well. Perhaps they believed their influence to be independent, not the influence of the idols; and for this reason he addressed the invalidity of divinity in the idols and of lordship in them.

Abū ʿAmr and Warsh, through the route of al-Bukhārī, read ﴿*ra'ā*﴾ (رَإي) with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and a kasrah on the hamzah wherever it occurs. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf and Yaḥyā, from Abū Bakr, read (رِئِي) with a kasrah on the rāʾ and the hamzah. ﴿So when it set﴾, that is, it went down, ﴿he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾

67

That is, the lords that move from place to place, that change from state to state. The negation of love has been said to be an indication of the negation of belief in lordship. Some have used the absence of love as a metonymy, since its negation necessarily entails the negation of the thing itself by a stronger means. Some have supposed an omitted noun in the statement, that is, "I do not love the worship of those that set." Whichever is the case, the derivation of the attribute is the cause of the ruling, because setting and concealment are both transitions, and each of them contradicts the entitlement to lordship and divinity, which are among the requirements of lordship, since that setting entails the two impossible attributes of origination (ḥudūth) and contingency (imkān) for the eternal Lord who is worshipped.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 77:

﴿Then when he saw the moon rising﴾ — that is, beginning to rise and spreading its light. Perhaps, as al-Azhari said, it is derived from al-bazgh (بَزْغ), which means "a split," as if by its light it splits the darkness apart. It is said: bazaghat al-naab (بَزَغَ النَّابُ) when the tooth appears; and bazaghat al-baytar al-dabbata (بَزَغَ البَيْطارُ الدّابَّةَ) when the farrier draws the animal's blood; and it is said: bazagha al-dam (بَزَغَ الدَّمُ), meaning the blood flowed. On this basis, it is possible that the rising of the moon is likened to these things, and the words of al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) are explicit in this. The apparent meaning of the verse is that this sighting was after the stars had set.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is the answer to (lamma) (لَمّا, "when"), and it is in the same manner of speech as before. ﴿Then when it set﴾ as the star set, ﴿he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾ — to His true path, from which there is no deviation.

Indeed, nothing of what he saw is fit for lordship. This is an exaggeration on his part, peace be upon him, in fairness. In it, as al-Zamakhshari said, there is an alert to his people that whoever takes the moon as a god, which is similar to the stars in setting, is astray. The allusion to their misguidance here, as Ibn al-Munir said, is clearer and stronger than his earlier statement, "I do not love those that set." He, peace be upon him, progressed to this because the opponents had already been confronted with the first argument as proof, so they became familiar with criticism of their belief. Had this been said at the beginning, they might have recoiled and not listened to the argument. Peace be upon him did not present to them that they were in error until he was confident of their attention to the full purpose and their listening to it to the end. The evidence for this is that, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, he progressed in the third round to explicitly declaring his disassociation from them and explicitly stating that they were in polytheism, once the proof had been established against them, the truth had become manifest, and it had reached its utmost clarity.

In this sentence there is evidence in more than one respect that his, peace be upon him, argument was not for himself but was a debate with his people, and likewise what will come.

Interpreting this as meaning that he, peace be upon him, made himself seem incapable and sought help from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, in attaining the truth, and that what follows is an indication of the attainment of certainty from the evidence, is very much contrary to the apparent meaning. Moreover, it has been said that the attainment of certainty from the evidence does not contradict debating with the people. Then, the apparent meaning, according to Shaykh al-Islam, is that he, peace be upon him, was at that time in a place which had on its western side a towering mountain behind which the star and the moon would be hidden at around midday or shortly after. The star was close to him, and its eastern horizon was initially exposed; otherwise, the rising of the moon after the setting of the star and then its setting before sunrise, as indicated by it,

صفحة 201
(Page 201)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he saw the sun rising﴾, meaning: just beginning to rise, in a manner that is hardly conceivable. Another said: the moon was not, when he saw it, at the beginning of its rising, but was behind a mountain and then rose from it, or in another direction he could not see; otherwise there is no possibility that the moon rises from its place of rising after the setting of the star and then sets before the sun rises. Ended.

You know that the claim of the existence of a mountain in the west or the east is contrary to the apparent meaning, especially according to the view of Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam), because this argument took place in the regions of Babylon, as the words of historians and the people of transmitted reports indicate. There is today no lofty mountain such that a star would be hidden behind it at midday or shortly after. The possibility that it existed at that time, and did not remain through the passing of years, is not remote. Likewise it is said according to the view commonly held among people today that the event of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) took place near Aleppo, because there is also no towering mountain there, as the Shaykh says. Moreover, what is understood from rising and setting is rising from the true horizon of that place and setting from it, not rising and setting in general.

Al-Shihab said: what compelled them to the above is the sequence indicated by the particle fa (fa), and it may be a customary sequence, like "he married and then a child was born to him," indicating that no days or nights passed between them, whether it was an inference or a conjecture or a leading-on. It is not specific to the second, as it is imagined. Moreover, we do not accept what has been mentioned if it is a specific star; it would only be refuted if the whole of the stars were intended, or one unspecified star, so reflect. Ended.

It is not hidden that the view of customary sequence, and the commitment that this argument did not occur in one night and its morning, is what the heart inclines to. The claim that it is possible for the moon to rise after the setting of the star in reality, and before the rising of the sun and its setting before its rising, is not asserted by anyone knowledgeable of astronomy in these climates in which we are, because the impossibility of that is customary. And if a specific star were meant, it is an evident matter, especially according to what came from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the sighting of the moon was at the end of the month. Yes, that may be possible in some zodiac signs at specific latitudes, but between us and them are vast deserts; perhaps for this reason he ordered reflection, so reflect.

(He said) i.e., in the same manner as before: ﴿This is my lord﴾, a reference to the observed body as such, not as named by one of the names, let alone in the respect of its being named "the sun." For this reason the demonstrative was mentioned.

Abu Hayyan said: It may be said that most of the languages of the non-Arabs do not distinguish in pronouns or in demonstratives between masculine and feminine, and they have no sign of feminine gender; rather, the feminine and masculine are alike for them. So in the verse the feminine was referred to with what is used for the masculine when relating the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and when Allah, glorified is He, reported about the feminine with "rising" and "setting" (the feminine forms), He used the feminine according to the requirement of Arabic, since that is not a quotation.

It was objected that this would only be apparent if their speech were quoted exactly in their language; but if it is expressed in the language of the Arabs, the ruling of Arabic is what is taken into account. Several have stated explicitly that the criterion for masculine and feminine is the quotation, not the quoted. Do you not see that if someone said: "the daytime star rose," and you related it by its meaning, saying "the sun rose," you would not be able to leave the feminine without a justification, because of what occurred in his expression. And if you examine what occurs in the noble text, you will see that only the quotation is observed in it. Moreover, the view that the dialogue of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was in Persian and not Arabic is based on the premise that Isma'il (peace be upon him) was the first to speak Arabic, and the correct view is the opposite.

It was also said: the masculine is for the masculine predicate, and they have stated regarding the pronoun and the demonstrative likewise that observing the predicate there is better than observing the referent, because it is the locus of the benefit in speech, and what has passed is gone. In the Kashshaf, after making the masculine for the masculine predicate:
Page 202
And adopting this method was necessary to safeguard the Lord from the suspicion of femininity. It was objected to this that this is granted regarding the true Lord, and what is here is not so. It was answered that this is apparent on the supposition that he was being guided, and the intent on the other path is to show the Lord's protection in order to lead them on, for if He were belittled in any way it would be a cause for their not listening. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is greater﴾, is an emphasis on what he (peace and blessings be upon him) aimed at of showing fairness, together with a subtle indication, as is said, to the corruption of their religion from another angle, by showing that the greater is more worthy of lordship than the lesser. That the sun is greater than what preceded it is beyond doubt, and the reports differ regarding the measure of its body. What the investigators of the science of astronomy hold is that it is one hundred and sixty-six times, and a quarter and an eighth, the size of the earth, and six thousand six hundred and forty-four times, and two-thirds of a unit, of the moon. They mentioned that the earth is thirty-nine times, and a fifth and a tenth of a unit, of the moon. The verification of that is in the commentary on the Mukhtasar al-Hay'a of al-Burjandi.

﴿Then when it set﴾, as the preceding one set (he said) to his people, proclaiming the truth among them: ﴿O my people, I am innocent of what you associate﴾.

78

- i.e., of your associating, or of what you associate of the bodies which are created, changing from state to state, subjected to their Creator. He (peace be upon him) argued by the setting rather than the rising, though rising is also a movement; it was said that this is because its indication is multiple: movement with concealment, and the first is motion, which is originated, so the originatedness of its locus follows; the second is disappearance, which entails the possibility of its subject. The rising is not like that, for although it is movement with emergence, the second has no role in the inference. It was objected that rising is also movement with concealment, because concealment is subsequent in the first and prior in the second. As for his (peace be upon him) seeing the star they worship in the middle of the sky, as is said, without witnessing its rising, it becomes a point only in the star and not in the moon or the sun, unless it is said that setting is preferred by its generality, unlike rising.

The better view is what has been said: that the arrangement of this ruling and its two counterparts upon setting rather than rising and appearance is a necessary requirement of driving the argument in this wise manner, for each of them, though in itself a movement incompatible with entitlement in general, was made to bear the first ruling, namely "This is my lord," in the aforementioned way; and since the second is a condition necessitating the effacement of traces and the nullification of rulings, which are both clearly incompatible with the said entitlement, a clear incompatibility of which nearly every stubborn obstinate denier would acknowledge, he made the ruling follow from it. Ended.

Akin to this is what the Imam (al-Razi) said regarding the manner of the inference from setting: that its indication of the intended meaning is evident, known to everyone. For the setting one's dominion ceases at the time of setting. It is related from some of the investigators that the descent into the lowest point of possibility is a setting. The best speech is that in which there is a share for the elite, a share for the middling, and a share for the common people. The elite understand from setting possibility, and everything possible is in need, and what is in need cannot be a cutter of need, so there must be an ending at what is exalted above possibility, so that needs are cut off by its existence, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾. As for the middling, they understand from setting absolute motion, and everything in motion is originated, and everything originated is in need of the Eternal, Capable; so the one that sets is not a god, rather the God is He to whom that setting one is in need. As for the common people, they understand from setting going down, and they witness that every star draws near to setting and going down, its light vanishes, its brightness diminishes, its dominion goes, and it becomes like one deposed; and whoever is like that is not fit for divinity. Then he said: so the word ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾ comprises the portion of the near ones, the people of the right hand, and the people of the left hand, so it became the most complete of proofs and the most excellent of demonstrations. Here there is also another subtle point: that he (peace be upon him) was only disputing with them, and they were astrologers. The doctrine of the people of astrology is that when a star is in the eastern quadrant and rising toward the middle of the sky, it is strong and of great influence; but when it is western and near to setting, it is weak of effect and little in power. So by this subtle point he alerted that the God is He whose power does not change into incapacity and whose perfection does not change into deficiency; and your doctrine is that the star, when in the western quadrant, is weak in power, deficient in effect, incapable of governance, and that indicates a defect in its divinity.

It appears from this that setting, according to the astrologers, has a greater particularity in being a cause of impugning its divinity. It is not hidden that understanding the descent into the lowest point of possibility from ﴿when it set﴾ in this verse is hardly sound. As for the meaning being: "when its possibility was established, the signs of that being evident, such as corporeality and spatiality, for example, he said..." etc., there is no hidden problem with it. Yes, understanding this meaning from ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾ may perhaps be allowed, though remotely. It is related from the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali, that he took the star to be the animal soul which every star has, the moon to be the rational soul which every sphere has, and the sun to be the pure intellect which every sphere has. And from some of them that he took the star to be the sense, the moon the imagination and the estimative faculty, and the sun the intellect. The meaning is that these perceptive faculties are deficient, finitely powerful; and the Manager of the world has dominion over them, conquering them. This too is contrary to the apparent meaning, and something similar will come, God willing, in the chapter on allusion.

He (peace be upon him) did not confine himself, in arguing against his people, to the setting of the sun, though it follows from the impossibility of the attribute of lordship in it that it is impossible in other things a fortiori. Also in it is observing brevity and conciseness, ascending from the lower to the higher, emphasizing the establishment and clarity as is fitting for that situation; and he did not argue against them by corporeality and spatiality and the like, which the beholder perceives upon sight in the signs of originatedness and possibility, choosing what is clearer in indication and more complete.

Then, when he (peace be upon him) disavowed what they disavowed, he turned toward the Originator of these created things and their Bringer-into-being, and said: ﴿Indeed I have turned my face toward He who created (faṭara)﴾, meaning brought into being and produced, ﴿the heavens﴾, of which these celestial bodies are parts, ﴿and the earth﴾, of which those idols are parts, ﴿as a ḥanīf﴾, meaning inclining away from all false religions and deviant beliefs, ﴿and I am not of the polytheists﴾.

79

—fundamentally, in anything of the sayings and actions. The meaning of turning the face toward He who created, and so on, is directing one's intention in worship to Him, glorified is He.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The meaning is "I have directed my worship and obedience." The reason this usage is permitted is that whoever obeys someone else and submits to his command turns his face toward him, so the turning of the face toward him became a metonymy (kināya) for obedience. Apparently the lām (in the phrase) is the complement of waja-ha (he directed). In al-Ṣiḥāḥ (of al-Jawharī): "I directed my face to Allah" and "I turned toward you and to you." Its apparent implication is a distinction between waja-ha and tawajja-ha, by using the first with lām and the second with ilā. Based on this, the use of lām here rather than ilā is evidently clear. There is nothing in al-Qāmūs (of al-Fīrūzābādī) addressing this distinction.

Al-Imam claimed that since the meaning is directing the face of the heart toward His service and obedience for the sake of worshipping Him, and not the heart's turning toward Him, exalted is His majesty, because He is transcendent above place (ḥayyiz) and direction (jiha), the word ilā was dropped and lām was suffice, so he omitted it. The sufficiency with lām here is clear evidence that the object of worship is transcendent above place and direction. Yet there is something in the heart about this.

If it is said: At most, what the proof indicates is that the star, the sun, and the moon are not fit for lordship and divinity, and from this degree alone it does not follow the negation of polytheism absolutely and the affirmation of monotheism. Why, then, did he (peace be upon him) affirm monotheism and negate polytheism with certainty after establishing that proof?

The answer: the people agreed on negating all other partners, and they only disputed this particular specific form. When it was established by proof that these things are neither lords nor gods, and the negation of others was established by consensus, there arose necessarily certainty in negating partners in general.

Then, it is well known that this argument is from the first mood of the second figure (al-shakl al-thānī, the second figure of the syllogism). The individual (shakhṣiyya) is in the status of the universal (kulliyya) according to them, as if it were said: "This, or the moon, or this, has set. And no god is one who sets (lā shay'a min al-ilāh bi-āfil). Or: My Lord does not set. It produces: This, or the moon, or this, is not a god, or is not my Lord."

As for the minor premise, it is as if expressed in His words, exalted is He: (When it set) in both places, and His words, glorified is He: ﴿When it set﴾ in the last. As for the major premise, it is taken from His words, exalted is He: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, because it points to a syllogism, which is: every one that sets does not deserve worship; and everyone who does not deserve worship is not a god. It produces from the first: every one that sets is not a god. It requires: "No one of the setting ones is a god," by the implication of the affirmative-indefinite (al-mūjiba al-ma'dūla) converted into the resulting negative. And it is valid to make the major premise a negative from the beginning, so it produces what was mentioned and converts to "no one of the gods is setting," which is one of the two major premises. From this, with slight attention, the manner of deriving the second major premise is known.

Al-Malawī said: It is better to say that His words, exalted is He, ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, contain a proposition, namely: no one of the setting ones deserves worship. This is made a major premise for a necessary minor premise, namely: the god who deserves worship. It produces: no one of the gods is setting. When this conclusion is added to the earlier proposition, namely "this is setting" and the like, it produces from the second figure: "this is not a god," or "no one of the moon is a god." And if you add its converse, the equivalent (al-mustawī), to it, it produces from the first figure the very desired conclusion. So the second is not specified in the verse; rather the first is also taken from it. End of quote. So reflect on it, and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 80:

﴿His people argued with him﴾, meaning they disputed with him, as al-Rabi' said, or they began to overpower him in the matter of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), at times by presenting corrupt proofs rooted in taqlid (blind imitation), and at other times by intimidation and threats. ﴿He said﴾, denouncing their arguing with him, (peace be upon him), despite their inferiority to that rank, the difficulty of the aim, the strength of the opponent and the clarity of the truth: ﴿Do you argue with me about God?﴾, that is, about His affair, may He be exalted, and His oneness, glory be to Him. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, read it with the nun lightened, so there is the omission of one of the two nuns.

It is disputed which of the two is the omitted one. It is said that it is the nun of the nominative (nun al-raf'), which is the view of Sibawayh, and he preferred it on the grounds that the need arose for a nun with a kasra because of the ya', whereas the nun of the nominative is not given a kasra. Also, its omission has occurred, as in the line: "Each has an intention in hating his companion / by God's blessing, you annoy us and we annoy you," where he intended tuqlunana (you annoy us). The second nun here is not a protective nun (nun al-wiqaya), but is part of the pronoun, and omitting part of a pronoun is not permissible. Also, it stands in place of the damma, and the damma may be omitted for lightness, as in the reading of Abu 'Amr: yansurukum, yush'irukum, ya'murukum.

It is also said that it is the protective nun (nun al-wiqaya), which is the view of al-Akhfash, and he preferred it on the grounds that it is the added nun by which the heaviness was produced.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He has guided me﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the speaker, emphasising the denial. For his being, (peace be upon him), guided by God, may He be exalted, and supported by Him, glory be to Him, is something that necessitates restraint from arguing with him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and disregarding such arguments and not paying attention to them when they arise. It is said: the meaning of ﴿and He has guided me﴾ is to the establishment of the proof against you of His oneness, exalted is His majesty. It is also said: "He has guided me" to the truth after I had followed your way, by supposition and assumption, and its falsity had become entirely clear, as you have witnessed. On both views, it does not imply that he, (peace be upon him), had previously been in error or ignorant of the knowledge of his Lord, may He be majestic and exalted. And "(هْدانِ)" is written, as al-Ajhuri said, without a ya'.
