﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾: this is a response, as is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, to what they frightened him with, namely that some harm might befall him from their false deity, just as the people of Hud said to him: ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ (11:54). This intimidation is said to have been about abandoning worship of what they worship; it is also said that it was rather about belittling it and treating it with contempt, such as breaking and disparaging it. It is also said: perhaps that was when he did to their gods what he did, which God has related to us. In some reports it is mentioned that when he (peace be upon him) grew up and matured, Azar began making idols and giving them to him to sell. He would go and call out to whoever would buy what harms and does not benefit. No one would buy them, so when they became worn out, he would take them to the river, dip their heads in it and say to them, "Drink!", mocking his people, until his mockery spread among them. Then they argued with him and threatened him.

The "(ما)" is a relative noun, and its returning pronoun has been omitted. The pronoun in the genitive refers to God, may He be exalted, meaning: I do not fear that which you associate with Him, glory be to Him. It is also permitted that it refers back to the relative noun, with the "ba'" being causal, meaning: that by means of which you associate. It is also permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun, and that it be a verbal noun (masdariyya).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except that my Lord should will something﴾, with the estimate of "time" according to more than one, is an exception from the most general of times, a "reduced" (mufarragh) exception. Some have said that the verbal noun is in the accusative of the adverbial sense (zarfiyya) without estimating a time. Ibn al-Anbari prohibited that, distinguishing between the explicit verbal noun, which he permits to be accusative in the adverbial sense, and the non-explicit, which he does not permit. Ibn Jinni does not distinguish between the explicit and the other, and permits it in both equally. The exception is connected (muttasil) in one view. "(شَيْئًا)" is an object, or an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: I do not fear what you associate with Him at any time except at the time of His will, may He be exalted, that something of harm should befall me from them; or something of His will of harm befalling me from them, and that comes only from Him, may He be exalted, without any part of your gods in its bringing about and its origination. It is also permitted that the exception is disconnected (munqati'), in the sense of: "but I fear, if my Lord wills, my fear of what you have associated with Him." In mentioning the title of lordship (rububiyya) together with the attachment to his (peace be upon him) pronoun, there is an indication that His will, if it occurs, is not devoid of a benefit returning to him through nurture, or a manifestation from him (peace be upon him) of submission to His judgement, glory be to Him and exalted, and surrender to His command, and acknowledgement that he is under His dominion and lordship, may He be exalted.

﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: it is as if it were a reason for the exception, meaning: He has encompassed everything in knowledge. So it is not far-fetched that in His knowledge, glory be to Him, is the infliction of harm upon me from them by means of some cause among the causes. "(عِلْمًا)" is put in the accusative as a transferred specification (tamyiz) from the subject, and it is also permitted that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun for "encompassed" without its own word. In the explicit mention in place of the pronoun there is emphasis on the meaning mentioned, and delight in mentioning Him, may He be exalted: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾

80

- That is: will you turn away after I have made it clear to you, instead of reflecting on the fact that your gods are entirely incapable of any benefit or harm? Then you do not remember that they are unable to harm me. The use of "remember" (tadhakkur) rather than "reflect" (tafakkur) or the like indicates that the matter of their gods is fixed in minds and requires only reminding.

[Page 206]

﴿And how should I fear what you associate (with Allah)﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), as Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) said. It is brought to negate fear from him, peace be upon him, according to the claim of the disbelievers, by way of argument *ad hominem* (*iljami*), after negating it from him in reality and in fact. The interrogative is for denial of the occurrence and its total negation. In directing the denial toward the manner of fear, there is an emphasis that is not present in directing it toward the fear itself, by saying: "Do I fear something?" Because every existent has some manner (*kayfiyyah*), so when its existence is negated from all aspects, this is by demonstrative argument (*burhani*). *Kayfa* (how) is an adverbial of state (*hal*), and the governing element of it is *akhafu* (I fear). *Ma* is either a relative pronoun or an indefinite qualifying noun, with the returning pronoun omitted. It is also permitted that it be a verbal-masdar particle (*masdariyyah*).

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿and you do not fear that you have associated with Allah﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *akhafu*, with an implied subject (*mubtada'*) because of the *waw*. It was said: there is no need for the implied subject, because the negated present tense may be joined with *fa'* (the particle of connection). There is no need here for a pronoun returning to the subject of the state, because the *waw* suffices for the linkage. This (clause) confirms the denial of fear and its negation from him, peace be upon him, and it indicates their acknowledgment of that. For since they did not fear in the place of fear, it is more fitting and more appropriate that he should not fear in the place of security. That is: how should I fear, I, what is not within the realm of fear at all, while you do not fear the peril of what is the greatest and most terrifying of things that cause fear, which is your associating others with Allah, the One who originated the heavens and the earth, what is among His creatures? He expressed this by His, the Glorified's, saying ﴿for which He has sent down to you no authority﴾, that is, no proof, by way of mockery. It was said that this is with the notification that religious matters are not to be relied upon except on proof sent down from Allah, the Exalted. The pronoun in *bihi* (by it) returns to the relative pronoun, and the speech is by omission of a modifier, that is: by His associating. It is also permitted that it returns to the associating restricted by its connection to the relative pronoun. No returning pronoun is needed, and this, as it has been said, is based on the opinion of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat, a grammarian) that linkage may be achieved by the return of the pronoun to what is connected to its companion, and the mention of the object of association, which is the Glorious Name, is in the circumstantial clause, not in the first clause. It was said: because what is intended in the circumstantial clause is to magnify the matter, and mentioning what is associated is included in that.

Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) said: the apparent thing is that one should say, regarding the reason for mentioning it in the second and omitting it in the first, that when it was said shortly before this (﴿and I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾), what is here was like a repetition of it, so brevity was appropriate. And that he, peace be upon him, omitted it as an indication of the remoteness of His Oneness from association, so it is not fitting in his presence to attribute it to Allah, the Exalted, nor to mention it along with Him. And when the condition of the polytheists who do not declare Him, Glorified, free of that was mentioned, it was made explicit. It was also said: the mention of the Glorious Name in the second clause is so that the pronoun in ﴿what He has not sent down﴾ may return to it. But this is nothing, because mentioning it earlier in the sentence suffices. It was also said: because what is intended is his, peace be upon him, denial of their not fearing their associating with Allah, the Exalted, since that is the denied and improbable thing to a sound intellect, not merely the general act of denial. This is not so in the first clause, for what is intended there is the denial that he, peace be upon him, should fear other than Allah, the Exalted, whether or not it is something the disbelievers associate. But this is also nothing, because the second clause is not included with the first in the ruling of denial except according to the one who claims coordination (*'atf*), and that is something with no way to it at all, because it leads to the corruption of the meaning, decisively, since it has been established earlier that denial in the sense of total negation, so the meaning reverts to negating fear from him, peace be upon him, and negating his negation from them, and this is clearly corrupt. Also, how does ﴿what you associate﴾ indicate what is other than Allah, the Exalted, which is not a partner? ﴿This is indeed a marvel﴾. Then, the verse is explicit that association is among what Allah has not sent down any authority for. Whether it is rationally impossible for authority to exist for that or not: the apparent sense of some scholars' words, and in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) there is what supports it in general for the second part. But what I choose is the first. And the Imam's (al-Razi's) statement that it is not rationally impossible to be commanded to take those images and figures as a direction for supplication is not within the place of disagreement, as is not hidden from the examiner. So consider.

﴿So which of the two parties has more right to security?﴾ is a statement arranged upon the denial of his, peace be upon him, fear in the place of security, together with the certainty of their not fearing in the place of fear. It is brought to compel them to acknowledge his deserving of it because of the security he is in, and their not deserving what they are in. By this it is known what is wrong with the claim that the denial in the first clause is for negating occurrence, and in the second is for deeming the occurrence improbable. The comparative form (*sigha al-tafdil*), which indicates that they deserve it in some respect, was used only to bring them down from the rank of obstinacy and stubbornness, by directing the speech according to the course of fairness. By "the two parties" is meant the party secure in a place of security and the party secure in a place of fear. So the choice of what is in the noble arrangement, as has been said, over saying "which of us has more right to security, I or you?" is to emphasize the compulsion toward the answer by alerting to the cause of the ruling, and to avoid explicitly declaring them in error, which may prompt obstinacy and stubbornness. Along with this, the arrangement indicates that the right to security is not exclusive to him, peace be upon him, but includes every monotheist, as encouragement for them toward monotheism. ﴿If you know﴾.

81

That is: who is more deserving of that, or of any of the things, or: if you are among the people of knowledge, then inform me of that. It is read ﴿*sultanan*﴾ with a *damma* on the *lam*, and this is a dialect in which the *damma* is made to follow the *damma*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 82:

﴿Those who believe﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), which may be from His part, the Exalted, explaining the true answer from which there is no escape.

This is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Ibn Zayd and al-Jubba'i. It may also be from the part of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. This is narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. The resumptive character of the clause has been questioned on the grounds that it cannot be taken as an explanation (bayan), because it is not an answer to a presumed question, whereas this is an answer to an actual question; nor can it be taken as a grammatical resumption (istinaf nahwi), since Ibn Hisham said: the grammatical resumption is that which occurs at the beginning of speech and is cut off from what precedes it, whereas this is connected to what precedes it by the necessary link between answer and question, and there is nothing else in our view besides these two.

It has been answered by choosing that it is grammatical, and the meaning of its being cut off from what precedes it is that it is not conjoined to it and is not linked to it in terms of i'rab (grammatical case-structure), even if it is connected in another respect. It has also been said: what is meant by the beginning of speech is its beginning either actually or presumptively, i.e. the group of those who believed in what must be believed in. ﴿And did not mix﴾, i.e. did not confound, ﴿their belief﴾ with that ﴿with wrongdoing﴾, i.e. with shirk, as the group of polytheists do, who claim that they believe in Allah, the Exalted, and that their worship of others besides Him, glory be to Him, is among the completions of their faith and its rulings, because it is for the sake of drawing near and intercession, as their saying indicates: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, Ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, Mujahid and most of the exegetes held that wrongdoing here means shirk, and what supports this is that the verse came as an answer concerning the condition of both groups.

This is indicated by what al-Shaykhan, Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and they said: Which of us has not wronged himself? So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: It is not as you think; rather it is what Luqman, peace be upon him, said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate others with Allah; indeed, shirk is a great wrong﴾."

It cannot be said that his saying ﴿indeed shirk﴾ etc. does not imply that other than shirk is not wrongdoing, because they have said: the tanwin in (bi-zulmin) is for magnification, so it is as if it were said: they did not mix their faith with a great wrong. And when it became clear that shirk is a great wrong, it was known that what is meant is that they did not mix their faith with shirk; or that what is immediately understood from the unqualified term is its most complete instance. It has also been said that what is meant is disobedience (ma'siyah), and this is reported from al-Jubba'i and al-Balkhi, and al-Zamakhshari approved it following the majority of the Mu'tazilah.

They used the verse as evidence that the perpetrator of a major sin has no security and no salvation from punishment, since by placing ﴿for them﴾ (lahum) before what follows, it restricts security to those who did not mix their faith with wrongdoing, i.e. with sin (fisq). They claimed that interpreting it as shirk is contradicted by the mention of mixing (labs), i.e. confounding, since it does not coexist with faith because of their opposition, and it only coexists with sins. And the hadith is a solitary report (khabar wahid), so it is not acted upon against a definitive proof. As for the claim that sin also does not coexist with faith according to them, so the argument does not hold for them, because faith is the name for performing acts of obedience and avoiding evil deeds, to the extent that the sinner is not a believer just as he is not a disbeliever, it is rebutted, as has been said, by the fact that faith is often used for mere assent (tasdiq) itself; indeed, from the verb only this meaning is almost understood, to the extent that deeds of righteousness are conjoined to it, as occurs in more than one verse. It has been answered that faith is meant as the assent of the heart, and that may coexist with shirk, such as one who assents to the existence of the Creator but not to His oneness, as we have indicated above. Among this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah without being associators﴾. Likewise, if it is meant as unqualified assent, whether by the tongue or otherwise, then coexistence in this sense is more evident, as in the case of the hypocrite. And if it is meant as assent to everything that must be assented to, such that one is outside disbelief, it is said that mixing faith with shirk does not necessarily entail combining them such that one is truly described as both believer and associator; rather, it is that disbelief covers it and makes it overcome and extinguished, or that one is described by faith, then disbelief, then faith, then disbelief, repeatedly. And after granting all that has been mentioned, we say: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is security﴾, only indicates that security is restricted to other than the disobedient, and this does not require that the disobedient are definitely punished, but rather that they are fearful of that, admitting the possibility and the preponderance of the likelihood of occurrence. It has been said that what is meant by security is security from eternal punishment, not security from punishment absolutely. The relative pronoun is the subject, and the demonstrative is a second subject, and the reference to the relative pronoun is in terms of its being described by what is in its relative clause; and in referring to it with what has the sense of distance after describing it with what was mentioned, there is what is not hidden. The clause "for them is security" is from the fronted predicate and the delayed subject, and it is the predicate of the second subject, and the clause is the predicate of the first. It is permitted that "those" be a substitute for the relative pronoun or an appositive to it, with "for them" as the predicate and "security" as the agent of the adverbial phrase because it depends on the subject; and that "for them" be a fronted predicate and "security" a delayed subject; or that the clause be the predicate of the relative. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the relative be the predicate of an elided subject, and said: the estimate is "they are those who". It is not free from distance, and most hold the first view. ﴿And they are guided﴾

82

- to the truth, and others are in manifest error. Some have estimated: to a path that entails security from eternal punishment.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 83:**

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the argument that Abraham (peace be upon him) made by the words of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿When the night covered him﴾ etc. It is also said to refer to His words, ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ up to ﴿while they are guided﴾. Composing a formal argument (ḥujja iṣṭilāḥiyya) from it requires reflection. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is for the glorification of the one indicated. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿Our argument﴾, are its predicate (khabar). The addition of it to the "we" of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama) contains an evident glorification. His words, exalted is He, ﴿We gave it to Abraham﴾, mean: We guided him to it, or taught it to him. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to "argument," and its operator is the sense of the demonstrative. Or it is in the nominative position, as a second predicate, or it is the predicate and "Our argument" is an apposition (badal) or explanation (bayān) for the subject. It is permitted that the clause "We gave" etc. be a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) or an explanatory clause (tafsīriyya), but its remoteness is evident. ﴿Abraham﴾ is the first object of "We gave," placed before the second because it is a pronoun.

His words, glorified is He, ﴿against his people﴾, are connected to "Our argument" if it is taken as the predicate of "That," or to a deleted element if it is taken as an apposition, so that there is no intervening foreign element between the parts of the apposition. That is: We gave it to Abraham as an argument against his people. Abū al-Baqāʾ did not permit its connection to "Our argument" at all, because of the verbal-noun status (maṣdariyya) and the separation. Perhaps the one who permits it does not regard the verbal-noun status as preventing the adverbial phrase from connecting, and treats the separation as tolerated. It has also been said that it is valid to connect it to "We gave" (ātaynā), because it includes the meaning of prevailing.

Page 209

His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿We raise by degrees﴾, mean: lofty ranks of great status in knowledge and wisdom. It is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnaf) with no place in the grammatical structure, confirming what precedes it. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "We gave," meaning: while We are raising. The accusative of ﴿degrees﴾ is either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) by interpretation as "elevations," or as an adverb of place (ẓarf), or by removal of the preposition, meaning "to degrees," or as a specification (tamyīz). The object of "We raise" is His words, ﴿whom We will﴾. Its postponement in the last three possibilities is, as has been mentioned more than once, for the sake of giving attention to what is fronted and stimulating interest in what is delayed. The object of the will is deleted, meaning: whom We will to raise, according to what wisdom requires and what the public interest demands. The choice of the imperfect form indicates that this is a continuous practice among the righteous, not specific to Abraham (peace be upon him). It was read as ﴿He raises﴾ with the letter yāʾ, by way of iltifāt (shift of person), and likewise ﴿We will﴾ [as ﴿He wills﴾]. More than one of the seven readers read ﴿degrees of whom﴾ with the genitive construction, so that it is the object of "We raise," and raising the degrees of a person is raising him. Some permitted making it an object also in the reading with tanwīn, and taking "whom" as "for whom," but this is remote.

His words, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise﴾, meaning: in everything He does of raising and lowering, ﴿Knowing﴾.

38

That is, [He is Knowing] of the condition of the one He raises and his readiness for it, at varying levels. If you wish, you may generalize, and then what has been mentioned enters primarily. It is a causal explanation of what precedes. In placing "Lord" as an annexed noun to his pronoun, upon him be blessings and peace, in the position of the nūn of majesty, by way of iltifāt, in the midst of explaining Abraham's condition (peace be upon him), there is what is not hidden of showing increased kindness and care toward him (ﷺ).

Here, al-Imam [al-Razi] mentioned in these Abrahamic verses a number of rulings. The first: His words, glorified is He, ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, indicate that He, mighty and majestic, is not a body, for if He were a body He would be absent from us, and so He would be setting, and setting contradicts lordship. It should not be unnoticed that counting that supposed absence as setting is not free of difficulty, because setting is concealment together with movement, and that supposed absence was not like that; rather it is merely concealment in what appears. Yes, it does contradict lordship too, but the discussion concerns whether it is setting, for the argument from the verse to be complete. It may not be said that the hadith of the Night Journey mentions a veil, so how can it be valid to say that concealment contradicts lordship? For we say: the veil mentioned is, as al-Qadi ʿIyad said, only with respect to the servants, not with respect to Him, exalted is He. They are the ones veiled, and the Creator, glorified is His name, is exalted above what veils Him, since a veil only surrounds a measurable, perceptible thing. More than one scholar stated that mentioning the veil for Him, exalted is He, is a figure of speech for His preventing creation from seeing Him. Al-Sayyid al-Naqib said in al-Durar wa-l-Ghurar: The Arabs use "veil" to mean hiddenness and non-manifestness. One of them says to another when he finds his understanding difficult: "Between me and you is a veil." They say of something whose path is difficult: "Between me and it are such-and-such veils, barriers, and coverings," and the like. The apparent meaning, on this basis, is that there is a metaphor in the single term there. So reflect. The second: this verse indicates that it is impossible for Him, exalted is He, to be in such a way that He descends from the Throne to the heaven at one time and ascends from the heaven to the Throne at another time, for otherwise the meaning of setting would result. You know that those who describe their Lord, glorified is His majesty, with the attribute of descent, having heard His sound hadith from their Messenger (ﷺ), do not say that it is motion and transition as is the case with bodies. Rather they entrust the determination of its intended meaning to Allah, exalted is He, after declaring Him free of resemblance to created things. In that case it is not objected that it has the meaning of setting, which is impossible for the Lord, majestic is His majesty.

Page 210

The third: it indicates that He, exalted is His majesty, is not a locus for originated attributes, as the Karramiyya say, for otherwise He would be changeable, and then the meaning of setting would result, which is evident. The fourth: what has been mentioned indicates that religion must be based on proof and not on imitation (taqlīd), for otherwise the argument would have no benefit whatsoever. The fifth: it indicates that the knowledge of the prophets of their Lord is acquired by reasoning and not innate, for otherwise Abraham (peace be upon him) would not have needed to reason. The sixth: it indicates that there is no path to attaining knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, except by contemplation and reasoning about the conditions of His creatures, for if its attainment were possible by another path, he (peace be upon him) would not have turned to this method. What is in these last two is not hidden from you. The seventh: His words, glorified is He, ﴿And that is Our argument﴾ etc., indicate that this argument came to exist in Abraham's intellect (peace be upon him) by the giving of Allah, exalted is He, and by the manifestation of it in his intellect. That indicates that faith and disbelief do not come about except by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, and this is reinforced by His words, ﴿We raise by degrees﴾ etc. The eighth: His words, glorified is He, ﴿We raise﴾ etc., indicate the invalidity of the criticism of the Hashwiyya against speculation, the establishment of argument, and the presentation of proof. There are other rulings in it that are not hidden from one who reflects.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishārī) interpretations of it: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾, when he saw him veiled by the outward appearances of the world of dominion (mulk) from the realities of the realm of divine sovereignty (malakūt) and His lordship, exalted is He, over things, believing in the influence of created beings and bodies, heedless of the malakūt, majestic is His majesty: ﴿Do you take idols﴾, that is, forms empty in their essences of life, ﴿as gods﴾, so that you believe in their influence? ﴿Indeed I see you and your people in clear error﴾, evident to one from whose eye the veil has been removed. ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the malakūt of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, We made him stand upon the spiritual powers by which We manage the affairs of the upper and lower worlds, or We made him stand upon their reality. ﴿And that he might be among the certain﴾, that is, among the people of certainty, who know that there is no influence except for Allah, exalted is He, who manages the affair by His names, glorified is He. ﴿When the night covered him﴾, that is, the night of the world of corporeal nature became dark over him. This, according to the Sufis, occurred in his childhood and early youth: he saw a star, which is the star of the soul called the animal spirit, appearing in the malakūt of the human frame. When he saw its overflow, its life, and its nurturing from that, he said by the language of state: ﴿This is my lord﴾. At that time Allah, exalted is He, was showing him through His name the Giver of Life. ﴿Then when it set﴾, by the rising of the light of the heart, ﴿he said: I do not love those that set﴾. ﴿Then when he saw the moon﴾, that is, the moon of the heart rising from the horizon of the soul, and he found its overflow through the unveilings of realities and knowledge, and its nurturing from that, ﴿he said: This is my lord﴾. At that time Allah, exalted is He, was showing him through His name the Knowing and the Wise. ﴿Then when it set, he said: If my Lord does not guide me﴾ to the light of His face, ﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾, those veiled by the inward things from Him, glorified is He. ﴿Then when he saw the sun﴾, that is, the sun of the spirit rising and manifesting upon him, he said, having found its overflow, its witnessing, and its nurturing from it: ﴿This is my lord﴾. At that time He, glorified is He, was showing him through His name the Witness and the Most High, the Mighty: ﴿This is greater﴾ than the first two. ﴿Then when it set﴾, by the manifestation of the lights of the Truth and the radiance of the veils of the Face, ﴿he said: O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾, since there is no existence except by Him, glorified is He. ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾, that is, I have submitted my essence and my existence ﴿to Him who originated﴾, that is, brought into being, ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, the heavens of the spirits and the earth of the soul, ﴿as one inclining﴾, turning away from all that is other than Him, even from my existence and my inclination, through annihilation (fanāʾ) in Him, majestic is His majesty. ﴿And I am not of those who associate﴾ anything with Him. ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ concerning abandoning the straight way. ﴿He said: Do you argue with me about Allah when He has guided me﴾ to His true existence and His unity? ﴿Those who have believed﴾ with true faith, ﴿and have not mixed their faith with injustice﴾, from the appearance of a soul or a heart or the existence of a remnant, ﴿for them is security﴾ in truth, ﴿and they are guided﴾ in reality to the Truth.

Al-Nisaburi said: It may occur to the mind that Abraham (peace be upon him) was overtaken by the night of doubt and its darkness, so he first looked into the world of bodies, found them setting on the horizon of change, and so did not see them fit for divinity. He ascended from them to the world of souls that manage bodies, and saw them setting on the horizon of perfection, so their judgment was the judgment of what is below them. He ascended from them to the world of pure intellects and found them setting on the horizon of possibility, so nothing remained but the Necessary Existent. It has also been said other than this. What has been mentioned is based on the premise that the argument was with his own self (peace be upon him), and this is what some exegetes adopted, and they narrated about it a long report that is mentioned in many books and is well known among the common people. But the preferred view with me is what you have learned, and Allah, exalted is He, speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 84:

﴿And We gave him﴾, i.e., Ibrahim (peace be upon him), ﴿Ishaq﴾, who was his son by Sarah; he lived one hundred and eighty years. In Nadim al-Farid it is stated that the meaning of Ishaq in Arabic is "the one who laughs" (al-Dahhak). ﴿And Ya'qub﴾, who was the son of Ishaq; he lived one hundred and forty-seven years. The sentence is coordinated with His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ etc. The coordination of a verbal sentence with a nominal one is something on which there is no dispute regarding its permissibility. It is also permissible, though remotely, that it be coordinated with the clause (ataynā) [We gave], on the basis that it has no place in i'rab (grammatical case), as is one of the possibilities. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿each﴾ is an object of what follows it, and its being placed before it is for restriction (qasr), not in relation to others than the two of them, but in relation to one of them, meaning each one of them ﴿We guided﴾, not one of them without the other. It was said: the intended meaning is each of the three, and al-Tabarsi held this view. Many of the researchers (muhaqqiqun) preferred the first view, because the guidance of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is definitely understood from the speech, and the mention of the one guided to him was omitted because it is evident that he is the one who was given to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), for both of them are devoted to it.

Al-Jubba'i said: the intended meaning is that We guided them to attaining reward and noble rank. ﴿And Nuh﴾. The Shaykh al-Islam said: it is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb that is explained by ﴿We guided before﴾. Perhaps he did not make it a preposed object of the mentioned verb in order to avoid separating the conjunction from what it conjoins with something, or so that the preposing would not be empty of the earlier benefit, namely restriction; and this is not free from reflection. That is, before Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Nuh, as al-Jawaliqi said, is a non-Arabic word that takes inflection (mu'rab). Al-Kirmani added that its meaning in Syriac is "the one who rests." Al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak: he was named Nuh because of his much weeping over himself, and his name was Abd al-Ghaffar; but the first view is more established in my opinion. Most of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, held, as al-Hakim said, that he (peace be upon him) was before Idris (peace be upon him). The genealogists mention that he was the son of Lamak (with a fathah on the lam and a sukun on the mim followed by a kaf), son of Matushalakh (with a fathah on the mim, a shaddah on the ta' with a damma after it, followed by a silent waw, and a fathah on the shin with the lam and the khaʼ), son of Akhnukh (with a fathah on the letter with dots and a damma on the light nun, followed by a silent waw, then a letter with dots), and he is Idris, as it is said. Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who was the first of the prophets? He said: Adam (peace be upon him). I said: Then who? He said: Nuh (peace be upon him). Between them were ten generations." This is apparent in that Idris (peace be upon him) was not before him.

Ibn Jarir mentioned that his birth (peace be upon him) was one hundred and twenty-six years after the death of Adam (peace be upon him). He, glorified is He, mentioned him here; it was said that because when He, glorified is He, mentioned His favour upon His friend through the branch, He followed it with mention of His favour upon him through the root, for the nobility of the father passes to the son. It was also said: He, glorified is He, mentioned him because his people worshipped idols, so He mentioned him so that he would have an example in him. As for the claim that he was mentioned for what has passed, there is no indication of the bond of fatherhood so that it may be accepted, and the indication of "before" (min qablu) for that is not apparent. Some were content with its being well known without this.

﴿And from his offspring﴾. The pronoun, according to a group, refers to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), because the context of the sublime arrangement is to explain his affairs, and what Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon him of giving the argument, raising of ranks, granting of prophet-sons, and preserving this honour in his progeny; all of that is to obligate those who belong to his religion among the polytheists and the Jews. Others preferred that it refers to Nuh (peace be upon him), because it is closer, and because He mentioned in the sequence Lut (peace be upon him), who was not of the offspring of Ibrahim but was his nephew, as will come, Allah willing; he believed in him and migrated with him to Syria, and Allah, exalted is He, sent him to the people of Sodom. Likewise Yunus (peace be upon him) was not of his offspring, according to what Muhyi al-Sunnah mentioned. So if the pronoun were for him, it would be restricted to those counted in this verse and the one after it. As for those mentioned in the third verse, they are coordinated upon Nuh, and it is not necessary that what is a condition in the coordinated be considered in the coordinating. The mention of Isma'il there does no harm, even though he was of the offspring of Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, because silence about including him in the offspring does not imply that he is not among them; and he was not counted, as some researchers said, in the gift like Ishaq, because the gift of Ishaq came in his old age and the old age of his wife, so it was in extreme strangeness. Ya'qub was mentioned because the continuation of prophethood from generation to generation is the utmost of blessing. And he did not coordinate ﴿each We guided﴾ because it emphasizes that it is a blessing.

Some people claimed that Yunus (peace be upon him) was of the offspring of Ibrahim, and it is stated in Jami' al-Usul that he was among the tribes in the time of Sha'ya; and then Lut alone remains outside, and there is no room for returning the pronoun to Ibrahim. He made it specific to those counted in the three verses, because since he was the nephew of Ibrahim, who believed in him and migrated with him, it was possible to make him of his offspring by way of predominance, as al-Tibi said. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that all these prophets, peace be upon them, are attributed to the offspring of Ibrahim, even though some of them were not joined to him by birth from either a mother or a father, because Lut is the son of the brother of Ibrahim, and the Arabs call the paternal uncle a father; as Allah, exalted is He, told of the sons of Ya'qub that they said: ﴿We worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, although Isma'il was the paternal uncle of Ya'qub. The prepositional phrase is connected to a hidden verb understood from what precedes it, and it was said: it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of those mentioned in the verse; the first was chosen, meaning: and We guided from his offspring ﴿Dawud﴾. He, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, is the son of Iysha (with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the dotted ya' below, and the letter with a dot on the shin), son of 'Awbar (with an unpointed letter and a single dot, on the pattern of Ja'far), son of 'Abir (with a single dot and an unpointed letter with a fathah), son of Salmun, son of Yakhitun, son of 'Amiyy, son of Yarib (with a dotted ya' below and ending in a single-dotted ba'), son of Ram, son of Hadramawt (with an unpointed letter then a dotted letter), son of Faris (with a fa' and ending in an unpointed letter), son of Yahudha, son of Ya'qub.

Ka'b said: he had a reddish face, smooth hair, a white body, a long beard with some curl in it, and a good voice and form; and prophethood and kingship were combined for him. Al-Nawawi reported from the historians that he lived one hundred years, and the period of his kingship was forty of them, and he had twelve sons. ﴿And Sulayman﴾, his son. Ka'b said: he was white, large, handsome, bright, beautiful, humble and modest, and his father used to consult him in many of his affairs in his young age, for the abundance of his intellect and knowledge. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he ruled the earth. The historians said that he was made king at the age of thirteen, and began building the Bayt al-Maqdis four years after his kingship, and died at the age of fifty-three. The preposing of the explicit object is for concern for his matter, along with the fact that among objects there is a kind of length, which delay might perhaps disturb the harmony of the noble arrangement. ﴿And Ayyub﴾. Ibn Jarir said: he is the son of Mus, son of Rum, son of 'Is, son of Ishaq; it was said: son of Mus, son of Tarakh, son of Rum, etc. Ibn 'Asakir related that his mother was a daughter of Lut (peace be upon him), and that his father was among those who believed in Ibrahim, so he was before Musa (peace be upon him). Ibn Jarir said: he was after Shu'ayb. Ibn Abi Khaythamah said he was after Sulayman. Al-Tabarani narrated that the period of his life was ninety-three years. ﴿And Yusuf﴾, who, according to the correct well-known view, is the son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, and what Ibn Hibban included in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet, supports this: "The noble son of the noble son of the noble son is Yusuf, son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, who lived one hundred and twenty years." In it there are six dialect forms, with the sin vowelled in three ways together with the ya' and the hamza. The correct view is that it is non-Arabic and has no derivation. ﴿And Musa﴾, who is the son of 'Imran, son of Yashhar, son of Mahith, son of Lawi, son of Ya'qub, and there is no disagreement about his lineage; and it is a Syriac name.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Musa was only named so because he was placed between a tree and water; so water in Coptic is mu and tree is sha. In the Sahih his description is that he was of brown complexion, tall, with curly hair, as if he were one of the men of Shanu'ah. He lived, as al-Tha'labi said, one hundred and twenty years. ﴿And Harun﴾, his brother and full brother; it was said: on his mother's side; it was said: on his father's side only. Al-Kirmani mentioned both in his Ajaib. He died before Musa, peace be upon them both, and had been born a year before him. In some hadiths of the Night Journey: "I ascended to the fifth heaven, and behold, there was Harun, half of his beard white and half of it black, nearly striking his navel because of its length. I said: O Jibril, who is this? He said: the beloved among his people, Harun son of 'Imran." Some mentioned that the meaning of Harun in Hebrew is "the beloved."

﴿And thus do We reward the good-doers﴾.

84

- It was said: that is, We reward them like what We gave Ibrahim (peace be upon him): raising his ranks, multiplying his offspring, and prophethood among them. The intended meaning is absolute resemblance in return for goodness with goodness, and proportion between deeds and rewards without diminishing, not sameness in every respect, because the singling out of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with the abundance of prophethood among his descendants is a well-known matter.

Some researchers preferred that the comparison is in the manner of what passed in His saying: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ and its like. The definite article in ﴿al-muhsinin﴾ is for the known (al-'ahd), and the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for praise of them for goodness, which is an expression for performing deeds in the fitting manner, which is their descriptive goodness accompanying their essential goodness. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it by saying: "To worship Allah as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." The sentence is a parenthetical clause confirming what came before it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 85:

﴿Wa-Zakariyya﴾ is the son of Azn ibn Barkiya. He was of the progeny of Sulayman, upon them both be peace, and he was killed after the killing of his son. On the day he was given the good news of him, he was ninety-two years old; it is said ninety-nine, and it is said a hundred and twenty years. It is a non-Arabic name, and it has five dialects, the most famous of which is with the long vowel (al-madd), and the second is with the short vowel (al-qasr). Both have been read in the seven canonical readings. Also read Zakariyyi with a shadda on the yaʾ and without it, and Zakar, like qalam.

(Wa-Yahya) his son, and it is a non-Arabic name. It is said to be Arabic. On both views, as al-Wahidi said, it is not inflected (la yanṣarif). He was named by this on the second view because he was given life (ḥayiya) by it through the womb of his mother. It is also said to be other than that. And ʿIsa ibn Maryam, and it is a Hebrew or Syriac name. In the Sahih it is reported that "he was of medium build, reddish, as if he had just come out of a bathhouse." In his mention, upon him be peace, there is evidence that dhurriyya includes the children of daughters, because his ascription is only through his mother. It has been objected that since he has no father, his attribution cannot be traced to himself through the mother, so the analogy of others to him in being the progeny of his maternal grandfather does not clearly hold.

It has been answered that the implication of his having no father would be that he should not be mentioned within the scope of dhurriyya, and this is a clear objection. The matter is disputed, and those who hold that a daughter's son enters the progeny cite this verse. Musa al-Kazim, may Allah be pleased with him, argued with it, according to what some have related from al-Rashid. In al-Tafsir al-Kabir, Abu Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with him, cited it before al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, [citing] the verse of mubahala, when "the Prophet ﷺ called al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, after the revelation of ﴿Come, let us call our sons and your sons﴾."

Some claimed that this is among his special features, ﷺ. The fatwas of our companions have differed on this question, and what I incline to is the view of inclusion. And Ilyas: Ibn Ishaq said in al-Mubtada': he is the son of Yasin ibn Finhas ibn al-ʿIzar ibn Harun, brother of Musa ibn ʿImran, upon them be peace. al-Qutabi related that he was from the tribe (sibt) of Yushaʿ. It is also said that he was of the descendants of Isma'il, upon him be peace. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that he is Idris, and he, according to what Ibn Ishaq said, is the son of Yarid ibn Mihlayil ibn Anush ibn Qaynan ibn Shith ibn Adam, and he is the grandfather of Nuh, as we have indicated. This was related from Wahb ibn Munabbih. In al-Mustadrak it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that there was a thousand years between Nuh and Idris. On the view that he was before Nuh, the explanation (al-bayan) would be specific to those in the first verse. Al-Shihab stated that the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Zakariyya﴾ and what follows it, then, is coordinated (maʿtufan) upon the whole preceding discourse, ﴿kull﴾, i.e., each one of those mentioned, ﴿of the righteous﴾.

- That is, those perfect in righteousness (al-ṣalah), which is an expression for doing what is fitting and guarding against what is not fitting, and it is predicated by gradation (bi-l-tashkik), so it is described by what is of the highest ranks of the prophets, upon them be peace. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ), brought in to praise them by its content.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 86:

﴿And Isma'il﴾ is, as al-Nawawi said, the eldest son of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. It is said, as is related from al-Jawaliqi, that it is pronounced with a nun at its end, and it is said that its meaning is "obedient to Allah." ﴿And al-Yasa'﴾: Ibn Jarir said he is the son of Akhtub ibn al-'Ajuz. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (al-Laysa') on the pattern of Daygham. It is a non-Arabic name, to which the definite article (al-) was attached contrary to analogy, and it coincided with the transfer (naql) so the sign of arabization was applied to it, as stated by al-Tibrizi. He explicitly stated that using it without the article is an error that people overlook. It is therefore not like Yazid in the saying:

I saw al-Walid ibn Yazid, blessed, whose shoulders were heavy with the burdens of the caliphate,

in every respect. On the first reading it is also non-Arabic. It is also said that it is an arabized form of Yusha', and it is said that it is Arabic, transferred from "yasa'," the present tense of "wasi'a." ﴿And Yunus﴾: he is the son of Matta, with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the taa' with a final letter taa', a maqsur noun like Hatta. It is also said Matta with the letters unjoined (Matta), and it is the name of his father, as stated by Ibn Hajar and other hadith masters. It occurs in the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq that it is the name of his mother, but this is rejected. We have not found, as others have not, a confirmed connection of his lineage, peace be upon him, and what is in Jami' al-Usul has already passed. It is also said that he lived in the time of the Parthian kings of the Persians. The nun may be pronounced with three vowels and may be hamzated.

Abu Talha read (Yunis) with a kasra on the nun. It is said he intended to make it an Arabic word from "anisa," but this is anomalous. ﴿And Lut﴾: Ibn Ishaq said he is the son of Haran ibn Azar. In al-Mustadrak it is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he was the son of the brother of Ibrahim, and his father's name is not stated explicitly. ﴿And each﴾, that is, each one of these mentioned, not some of them to the exclusion of others. ﴿We preferred﴾ through prophethood ﴿over the worlds﴾

86

- That is, over the worlds of their age. The sentence is a parenthetical clause, like its companions, and in it is evidence that the prophets are superior to the angels.

﴿And from their fathers and their offspring and their brothers﴾ may be taken, as has been said, to be connected to what is connected to (from his descendants) (ﷺ is not applicable here), with the ﴿min﴾ (مِن) being *ibtidā'iyyah* (indicating origin or starting point). The object is then omitted, meaning: "And We guided from their fathers, their sons, and their brothers many groups." Alternatively, it is coordinated with (each We preferred) (كُلًّا فَضَّلْنا), and the ﴿min﴾ is *tab'īḍiyyah* (partitive, indicating a part), meaning: "We preferred some of their fathers," and so on.

Page 215

Some have taken it as coordinated with (Noah) (نُوحًا), with the ﴿min﴾ standing in the position of the direct object, interpreted as "some." The reason for the partitive sense is that some of them were neither prophets nor rightly guided, it has been said. This applies to others than the fathers, because the fathers of all the prophets were rightly guided monotheists. You know that this is disputed with regard to the fathers of our Prophet (ﷺ), and many people hold the opposite view. So what do you think about the fathers of the other prophets, peace be upon them?

It is not hidden that attributing the fathers, sons, and brothers to their pronoun does not require that each of them had a father, son, or brother. So do not overlook this. ﴿And We chose them﴾ is coordinated with (We preferred them) (فَضَّلْناهُمْ), meaning: We selected them. ﴿And We guided them to a straight path﴾.

87

This is a repetition for emphasis and a preface to explaining what they were guided to. The secret in mentioning these great prophets, upon whom be the best of God's blessings and the most complete peace, in this style, which includes mentioning the superior before the more excellent and the later in time before the earlier, has not become clear to me. Likewise, the secret in the affirmation first with His words, ﴿And thus do We reward﴾, etc., and second with His words, glorified is He, ﴿each of the righteous﴾. And God knows best the secrets of His speech.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the guidance to the straight path, or what is understood from the noble wording concerning the sources of the verbs mentioned, or what they adhered to. What is in "that" of the meaning of distance is as has passed many times. ﴿The guidance of Allah﴾: the *idafa* (genitive construction, ilafa) is for honour. ﴿He guides by it whom He wills﴾: His guidance of those of His servants who are prepared for it. In attaching the guidance to the *mawsul* (relative pronoun) there is an indication that the content of the *silah* (relative clause) is the cause, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, bestows guidance by His grace. ﴿And if they had associated﴾, i.e., those mentioned, ﴿it would have been void﴾, i.e., would have been nullified and fallen away ﴿from them﴾, despite their merit and their exalted rank, ﴿what they used to do﴾.

– i.e., the reward of their righteous deeds. So how about those other than them, when they are who they are and their deeds are their deeds?

**[p. 216]**

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ ("those") refers to the eighteen prophets mentioned, and to those joined with them in the text, peace be upon them, on account of their being characterized by what was mentioned of guidance and other sublime attributes, as has been said. The Imam (al-Razi) restricted it to the prophets mentioned. And from Ibn Bashir, who said: "I heard a man ask al-Hasan about (*Ulā'ika*), and he said to him: 'Who is at the beginning of the verse?'" It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning the genus of it. What is meant by giving it is the complete imparting of understanding of the realities contained in it, and the empowering of comprehension of its sublime and subtle matters. This is more general than whether that occurs by revelation at the outset or by inheritance thereafter, for among those mentioned there are some upon whom no specific scripture was sent. ﴿And the judgement﴾, meaning the decisive settling of matters among people with truth, or wisdom, which is knowledge of the realities of things. ﴿And prophethood﴾: some of them explained it as messengership (*risalah*). It has been given as a reason that those mentioned here are messengers. However, in *al-Muhakamat* by our master Ahmad ibn Haydar al-Safawi, it is stated that Dawud, peace be upon him, is not a messenger, even though he had a Book; but I have not found an explicit text on this. Some scholars held that Yusuf ibn Ya'qub, peace be upon him, is also not a messenger. (And Yusuf) in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And Yusuf came to you before with clear proofs﴾ is not Yusuf ibn Ya'qub, peace be upon them both, but rather Yusuf ibn Ifrathim ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub, and this is a strange view. More strange than it is the claim that he was a messenger to the jinn. Al-Shihab said: It may be said that the more general term was used in the noble composition because some of those included within the generality of their fathers and offspring were not messengers. ﴿If they disbelieve in them﴾, meaning in these three (judgement, Book and prophethood), or in the prophethood which encompasses the rest; ﴿these people﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, as related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and Qatadah, in accordance with the indication of the demonstrative and the context, as has been said. It was also said that what is meant by them is the disbelievers who denied the prophethood of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, in general. In either case, their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and in what was revealed to him of the Qur'an, entails their disbelief in what confirms all of it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the agent (*fa'il*) is for the reason mentioned more than once. ﴿Then We have entrusted with them﴾, meaning We have commanded them to uphold them, and granted them success in believing in them and in fulfilling their rights, ﴿a people﴾ (*qawman*), magnificent, ﴿who are not disbelievers in them﴾

89

- at any time, but rather who persistently believe in them. What is meant by them, as related by Ibn Jarir and others from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and by Abd ibn Humayd from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, are the people of Madinah among the Ansar. It was also said that they are the companions of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, in general; it was also said that they are every believer among the children of Adam, peace be upon him; and it was said that they are the Persians. For each of these groups is granted success in believing in the prophets and in the scriptures sent down to them, and acting upon what is in them of the foundations of the sharia and its branches which remain in our sharia. It is related from Qatadah that they are the prophets, peace be upon them, the ones mentioned. In that case, what is meant by entrustment is the command with what is more general than implementing their rulings, as is their practice regarding their own Book, and from believing in its truth, as is their practice regarding all the other Books whose light the Qur'an has gathered. Al-Zajjaj preferred and chose this view. Al-Zamakhshari preferred it on two grounds. The first: that the verse following refers to the prophets mentioned, peace be upon them; so if those entrusted were not them, a separation by a foreign element would result. The second: that it is connected with the particle *fa* (then) to what precedes it, which requires this. Some scholars found this unlikely, for the apparent meaning is that the one who affirms prophethood and the one who denies it are different from those to whom it was given.

Ibn Humayd and others related from Abu Raja' al-Attaridi that they are the angels. In that case, entrustment is the command to bring them down, preserve them, and believe in their truth. The Imam found this unlikely, because the word *qawm* (people) is rarely applied to other than the children of Adam. In any case, the tanwin on *qawman* is for magnification (*tafkhim*), as we have indicated. It is the object (*maf'ul*) of *wakkalna* (We have entrusted), and *bihā* (with them) before it is related to what follows it. Its being fronted before the explicit object is for the reason already mentioned, and because it is lengthy, and placing it later might disrupt the harmony of the noble composition or separate the adjective from the noun it qualifies. The *ba'* that comes after the relative clause of *bikafirin* (disbelievers) was fronted in order to preserve the verse endings (*fawasil*), and the one after it is for emphasizing the negation. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, indicated by the clause *faqad wakkalna* (then We have entrusted) and so on; that is: if these people disbelieve in them, then it counts for nothing at all, for We have granted success in believing to a people who persistently believe in them and act upon what is in them. Thus in their faith there is sufficiency in place of the faith of these people. From this it is known that the preferable view, as the Shaykh al-Islam said, is to interpret "the people" as one of the groups other than the prophets and the angels, peace be upon them, since by their believing in the Qur'an and acting upon its rulings, sufficiency is achieved from the faith of the disbelievers in it and their acting upon its rulings; this is not the case with the faith of the prophets and angels, peace be upon them.

[Page 217]

﴿Those﴾, i.e., the prophets mentioned, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and from al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. It has also been said that the reference is to the believers who were entrusted (with the message). This was related from al-Hasan and Qatada, but what it entails is not hidden. It is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿whom Allah has guided﴾, i.e., We guided them to the truth and the straight path. The shift to the Glorious Name (Allah) serves to indicate the cause of the guidance and to protect the one guided, relying on the extreme clarity of that guidance. ﴿So follow their guidance﴾, i.e., make their guidance singular in being followed, and make the following restricted to it. What is meant by "their guidance" is, according to the majority, their path in faith in Allah, the Exalted, His unity, and the fundamentals of religion, not the laws (shara'i') that are susceptible to abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation), for after abrogation they no longer remain guidance. Moreover, they differ regarding them, so it is not possible to take all of them as models. The meaning of God's command to Him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to follow that guidance is to take hold of it, not because it is the path of those exalted ones, but because it is the path of reason and revelation. In this there is an honouring of them, since their path is the truth that agrees with the evidence of reason and transmitted proof.

[Page 218]

With this, al-'Allama al-Thani answered an objection: that what is obligatory in beliefs and the fundamentals of religion is to follow the proof from reason and transmission, so it is not permissible, especially for the Prophet ﷺ, to imitate another; so what is the meaning of his being commanded to follow (them)? It was objected to this that his, peace and blessings be upon him, belief at that time was not on account of their belief but on account of the proof, so there is no meaning to his being commanded to follow that. It was also objected that taking up the fundamentals of religion was already attained by him before the revelation of the verse, so there is no sense in commanding the taking of what has already been taken; unless it is understood as a command to remain steadfast upon it. Al-Qutb al-Razi, in his glosses on the Kashshaf, verified that the following commanded here is only in noble characters and perfect attributes, such as forbearance, patience, asceticism, abundant gratitude, humble supplication, and the like. In the verse there is evidence that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is definitely superior to them, since it includes that Allah guided those prophets, peace be upon them, to the virtues of character and the attributes of perfection. And since the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to follow their guidance all together, it is impossible, given his infallibility, to say that he did not comply; so it must be said that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did comply and attained all of that and acquired those noble characters found in all of them. Thus there gathered in him the qualities of perfection that were scattered among them, and in that case he is definitely superior to all of them, just as he is superior to each one of them. This is a fine deduction.

Some have cited it as evidence that he ﷺ was obliged to follow the law of those before him, but this is nothing (of substance). In His command to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to follow them, rather than to follow them in a different way, there is an allusion, not hidden, to the exaltedness of his station ﷺ in the view of the people of spiritual taste.

The ha' in (iqtadih) is the ha' al-sakt (the silent ha', added in pause), which is also added while silent to make the connected reading resemble the pause. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim recited with it. Hamza and al-Kisa'i omit the ha' in connected speech only. Ibn 'Amir recited (iqtadihi) with a kasra on the ha' without elongation (ishba'); this is what the readers call ikhtilas, and it is the transmission of Hisham from him. Others transmitted its elongation, which is its kasra with its connection to a ya'. Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid claimed that the reading of Ibn 'Amir is an error, giving as reason that the ha' is the ha' of pause, so it is never moved in any circumstance; it is mentioned only so that the vowel of what precedes it may be shown by it. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi refuted him by saying that the ha' is the pronoun of the verbal noun, not the ha' of pause; that is, "follow the following" (iqtada al-iqtida'). Like it, as Abu al-Baqa said, is the verse: "This is Suraqa, reciting the Qur'an, and the man, at the time of the wolf's approach, if he meets her, is a wolf," for the ha' in it is the pronoun of the study (darsu), not an object, because "yadrusu" has already transitively reached "al-Qur'an." Some have said that the ha' of pause may be moved, likening it to the pronominal ha', and the Arabs often give a thing the rule of what resembles it and treat it accordingly. The verse of Abu al-Tayyib has been transmitted: "Woe to my two hearts, from what my heart is—shabm," with the ha' vowelled with a damma and with a kasra, on the basis that it is the ha' of pause, likened to the pronominal ha' and therefore moved. The author of al-Durr al-Masun preferred to take the kasra as due to the meeting of two sukun (unvowelled letters), not due to the likeness to the pronoun, because its ha' is not vowelled with a kasra after an alif, so how could what resembles it be (so vowelled)? Al-Imam claimed that the affirmation of the ha' in connected speech is for following the Imam, and one may not follow him in that, because it implies that the recitation is without transmission (naql), following the script, and this is an error.

﴿Say: I do not ask you﴾, i.e., I do not seek from you, ﴿for it﴾, i.e., for the Qur'an, or for the conveying (of the message), for the context of the speech indicates both, even though neither has been mentioned, ﴿any wage (ajran)﴾, i.e., any reward, whether little or much, just as the prophets before me, peace be upon them, did not ask their peoples for it. It has been said: this is among what we were commanded to follow from their guidance, peace be upon them. This is clear according to what al-Qutb said, because refraining from taking a wage in exchange for a kindness is among the noble characters and fine deeds. As for the view of those who restricted the earlier guidance to the fundamentals, it has been said that there is a conflict between saying this and saying that restriction. It was answered that deriving the following of the fundamentals from the first command does not preclude his, peace and blessings be upon him, being commanded to follow another matter, such as conveying (the message). The placing of the complement there (before the verb) is only to negate following the way of others in another matter.

The verse has been cited as evidence that it is permissible to take a wage for teaching and for conveying rulings; on this there is a lengthy and well-known discussion among the jurists, which is not in need of exposition.

﴿It is only (in huwa)﴾, i.e., the Qur'an is nothing but ﴿a reminder (dhikra)﴾, i.e., an admonition, so it is a verbal noun; treating it as referring to the Qur'an is for emphasis, and there is no need to interpret it as masculine ﴿to the worlds﴾,

90

— universally, so that no people is singled out with it to the exclusion of others. The verse has been cited as evidence for the universality of his mission, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾ When Exalted is He related about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he mentioned the proof of monotheism (tawhid) and the refutation of polytheism (shirk), and Majestic is His glory, having established that proof in the clearest manner, He, Glorified is He, then began to establish the matter of prophethood. This is because the core of the Qur'an's concern rests on establishing monotheism, prophethood, and the Return (ma'ad). Thus the verse is connected to what precedes it, as the Imam (al-Razi) said. More preferable than this is what has been said: that He, Glorified is He, is speaking of the Noble Qur'an and that it is a magnificent blessing from Him, exalted is He, upon all nations, as indicated by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. He follows this with an explanation of their disdain for it and their disbelief in it, in a manner that extends to disbelief in all the divine books.

The root of qadr is knowing the measure of a thing through testing (sabr), and then it was used for knowing a thing in the most complete manner until it became a true meaning of it. Al-Wahidi said: it is said "qadara al-shay'" when one tests it and wants to know its measure; one measures it (yaqduruhu) with a damma, qadran. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If it is obscured from you, then estimate (faqduru) for it," meaning, seek to know it. Then it is said of one who knows a thing that he "measures its measure" (yaqduru qadrahu), and if he does not know it by its attributes, that he does not measure its measure.

The interpretation differs here. From al-Akhfash, the meaning is: they did not know God with His true measure, that is, His true knowledge. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they did not magnify God with His true magnification. Abu al-'Aliyah said: they did not describe Him with His true description. All of these are possible.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) chose what al-Akhfash held, because it is the most suitable to the context, meaning: they did not know Him, Glorified is He, with the true knowledge of His kindness to His servants and His mercy upon them, and did not observe His rights in that, rather they neglected them with great neglect, when they said, denying the sending of messengers, peace be upon them, and the sending down of books, disbelieving in His magnificent blessings in both: or, they did not know Him, Majestic is His glory, with the true knowledge of His wrath against the disbelievers and the severity of His seizure of them, when they dared to deny that by their saying: ﴿God did not send down anything upon a human being﴾, that is, anything at all, so "min" is for emphasis. The accusative of "haqqa" is as an adverbial object (masdar). It is, as Abu al-Baqa' said, originally an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning "their true measure"; when it was made genitive construct with its qualified noun, it took the case it would have taken. "Idh" is an adverb of time, "the time." Whether it carries the meaning of cause here or not is two possibilities. Abu al-Baqa' links it to "qadaru," and it is not definite. It was also read "qadarihi" with a fatha on the dal.

It has been disputed who said that shocking statement. Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that they were the polytheists of Quraysh, but the majority hold that they were the Jews, and their aim in that was to disparage the prophethood of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, by way of exaggeration. So it was said to them by way of a binding argument: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought﴾, for the meaning is that God, exalted is He, had sent down the Torah upon Moses, peace be upon him, and you have no way to deny that. So why do you not allow the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ)? By this, the difficulty for the majority view is resolved, namely that the Jews say the Torah is the Book of God, sent down upon Moses, peace be upon him; how then could they say: ﴿God did not send down anything upon a human being﴾? The summary of this is that they presented the sending down of the Qur'an upon him, peace be upon him, in the form of impossibilities, until they exaggerated in denying it, so they were bound to affirm it. It has also been said that the utterance of this statement came from anger and forgetfulness of its reality. Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that "Malik ibn al-Sayf, one of the rabbis of the Jews, said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): I adjure you by Allah, who sent down the Torah upon Moses, do you find in it that Allah, exalted is He, hates the fat rabbi? You are the fat rabbi, you have grown fat from the wealth which the Jews feed you. The people laughed, and he became angry, and he turned to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: ﴿God did not send down anything upon a human being﴾. His people said to him: What is this which has reached us from you? He said: It angered me. So they removed him and put Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf in his place, and Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse." It was objected that this does not suit the binding argument from the sending down of the Torah upon Moses, peace be upon him, since the speaker has acknowledged that it came from him out of anger, so let this be understood. It is not an objection that this surah is Meccan, while the debates that occurred between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Jews were all Medinan, so it is not feasible to say the verse was revealed concerning the Jews; for Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan and al-Kalbi that this verse is Medinan. The saying of Mujahid was also objected to: that the polytheists of Quraysh, just as they deny the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), deny the prophethood of all the other prophets, peace be upon them, so how is it fitting to direct this binding argument at them? It is answered that, since the sending down of the Torah was among the well-known and widespread matters, and for that reason they used to say: ﴿If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them﴾, the binding argument with what has been mentioned was apt. Nevertheless, what the majority held is more worthy of acceptance. Among the people is one who claimed that in the verse there is a proof of the third figure (shakl), namely: Moses is a human being, and Moses had a book sent down to him, which produces that some human being had a book sent down to him; the minor premise is taken from the strength of the verse, and the major from its explicit wording; the conclusion is a particular affirmative which contradicts the universal negative that the Jews asserted, namely: no human being had a book sent down to him; this is taken from their saying: ﴿God did not send down anything upon a human being﴾. These two particular propositions were produced, although the condition of the third figure is that one of the two premises be universal, because the particular proposition, in their view, has the status of the universal.

The Imam said: Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may mercy be upon him, philosophized and said: this verse is built upon the second figure of the logical figures, because its outcome returns to this: Moses, upon whom God sent down something; and one of the human beings upon whom God did not send down anything, produces that Moses was not a human being, and this is an absurd impossibility. This impossibility is neither according to the form of the syllogism nor according to the soundness of the first premise, so there remains only that it follows from supposing the soundness of the second premise, namely their saying: ﴿God did not send down...﴾ etc., so it is necessary to say that it is false. In that there is room for reflection, so let it be reflected upon.

Then, the description of the Book as having reached them is for increasing the establishment and intensifying the rebuke; likewise with His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿as a light and guidance﴾, for its being clear in itself and making clear for others is among what emphasizes the binding argument to the utmost degree. Its accusative is in the adverbial state (hal) from "al-Kitab," and the governing element is "anzala," or from the pronoun in "bihi" with the governing element "ja'a." The apparent
(page 220)
view is that the adverbial phrase is related to "ja'a." It is also permitted that it be related to an implied element that functions as an adverbial state of the subject. The "li" in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿for the people﴾ is either related to "huda" or to an implied element that functions as a qualifier of it, meaning: guidance existing for the people. By them are meant the Children of Israel. It has been said: they and others besides them. The meaning of it being guidance for them is that it guides whoever comes upon it, directly or indirectly, to what saves him from faith in God and His Messenger, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you make it into scrolls﴾ is a resumptive clause with no place in the grammatical structure, brought to deny what they did of distortion and alteration. It is also permitted that it be in an accusative position as an adverbial state, as previously mentioned, meaning: you place it into scattered scrolls and separated pages, with the preposition deleted, based on treating "qaraTis" as an indefinite adverb of place, as has been said.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the meaning is "you make it into scrolls possessing" (dha qaraTis). Many have permitted omitting the implied element, in the sense of: you make it the very scrolls, and in this is additional reproach for them for their evil conduct, as though they had removed it from the category of Book and reduced it to the status of blank scrolls devoid of writing. On the first reading, the purpose is not to rebuke them merely for placing it in scrolls, since every book must be put into scrolls; rather the purpose is the rebuke for making it into scrolls described by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿you show them and hide much﴾. So the conjoined clause and that to which it is conjoined are in the position of a qualifier of "qaraTis." The returning pronoun to the qualified noun from the conjoined clause is deleted, meaning: much of them. By "much" is meant the attributes of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, and the rest of what they concealed of the rulings of the Torah, such as stoning the married adulterer. This is undoubtedly addressed to the Jews, and they used to do that with their common people, conspiring together in it. This is evident on the assumption that the preceding answer was to them, for addressing them with it requires addressing them; and whoever holds that what preceded was for the polytheists takes this as a shift (iltifat) to addressing the Jews, since their mention has occurred. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the three verbs with the third-person yā' and a plural pronoun referring to the Jews as well, except that it shifted away from addressing them, distancing them because of their commission of the ugly act, from the arena of direct address. For this reason He addressed them when He attributed goodness to them in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew﴾. This is better, as has been said, than the shift on the first view, because in it there is a transition from speech with one group, the polytheists, to speech with another group, the Jews, before completing the first speech, since its completion is by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Say: God﴾ etc. This is unlike the shift on the second view. The clause, according to what Abu al-Baqa' said, is in the position of an adverbial state from the subject of "taj'alunahu" with the implied "qad" or without it, according to the difference of opinion.
