In light of this, as Shaykh al-Islam said, "ma" should be taken as a reference to what they took from the Book of sciences and laws, so that the restriction by the adverbial state serves to emphasize the rebuke and intensify the censure, not as what they received from the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, in addition to what is in the Torah, and as a clarification of what was obscure to them and to their fathers of its difficulties, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ﴾. For their receiving that is not among what restrains them from what they did with the Torah, so the clause would be devoid of emphasis of rebuke and would not deserve to occupy the position of an adverbial state. Rather, the proper course then is that it be a resumptive clause confirming what preceded concerning the coming of the Book, by way of completion, digression, and preparation for what follows concerning the coming of the Qur'an. There is no way, as he said, to make "ma" a reference to what they concealed of the rulings of the Torah, as His saying, Exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿There has certainly come to you Our messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾. For its appearance, although it is a deterrent to them from concealment for fear of exposure, and a correction for the clause's occupying the position of an adverbial state, yet that is something the concealers know with certainty.

It is also permitted that the clause be conjoined to ﴿who sent down the Book﴾ in meaning, meaning: say, who sent down the Book, and who
(page 221)
taught you what you did not know? This is far-fetched. Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that this is addressed to the Muslims, and it is related from him that he recited "And you were taught, O assembly of the Arabs, what you did not" etc. According to some, this is an interjected clause for the sake of favor upon the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, and his followers, by guiding them to dispute in the best manner. Some have said: the people in what precedes is general, including the Muslims and the Jews; "and you were taught" is conjoined to "you make it," and the address in it is to the people with regard to the Jews, and in "you were taught" it is to them with regard to the Muslims. It is not hidden that this is an overreach.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 91 (part 2 of 2):

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say: "Allah"﴾ is a command to His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer the preceding question on their behalf, indicating that they deny the truth out of obstinacy, and signalling that the answer is determined, and announcing that they have been silenced and were not able to speak at all. The noble Name (Allah) is either the subject of an implied verb, meaning "Allah sent it down," or the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is an implied clause, meaning "Allah, the Exalted, sent it down." The disagreement over the more preferred of the two possibilities is well known. ﴿Then leave them﴾, that is, let them be, ﴿in their plunging﴾, that is, their falsehood, so there is no burden on you after the establishment of the proof and the silencing of the objector. ﴿Playing﴾.

It (the adverbial phrase "in their plunging") occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the first (hum, "them"). The adverbial phrase is either a complement of (dharhum, "leave them") or of (yalʿabūna, "playing"), or a circumstantial clause relative to the object of (dharhum), or relative to the subject of (yalʿabūna).

It is also permitted that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause relative to the second (hum). In meaning, this is the subject of the verbal noun to which it is attached. The adverbial phrase is connected to what precedes it, either as a superfluous element or as a circumstantial clause relative to (hum). In that case it is not permissible to connect it to (yalʿabūna), either as a circumstantial clause or as a superfluous element, because it would then be a dependent that comes after its governor in structure and meaning, while also preceding it in structure, since the governing element of a circumstantial clause governs its referent, which would result in circularity and corruption of meaning. According to some, the verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword. The Imam (al-Razi) chose that it is not abrogated, because it comes in the form of a threat, and a threat does not contradict the occurrence of fighting; therefore the revelation of the verse that indicates its obligation does not remove the meaning, so abrogation does not take place regarding it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 92:

﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down﴾. This confirms the sending down of the noble Qur'an after establishing the sending down of what it refers to, namely the Torah, and it refutes their foul saying immediately after it. The word (kitab, "Book") is indefinite for glorification (li-l-tafkhim), and the clause (anzalnahu, "We have sent it down") is in the place of the nominative as a description of it.

As for His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿blessed﴾, meaning abundant in benefit and good, because it includes the benefits of both abodes and the knowledge of the first and the last, as a description following another description. The Imam said: "It is the way of Allah the Exalted that whoever investigates this Book and holds fast to it, through it he attains the honour of this world and the happiness of the Hereafter. We have witnessed, and praise be to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the fruit of our service to it in this world. So we ask Him not to deprive us of the happiness of the Hereafter, for He is the Benevolent, the Merciful."

As for His saying, Majestic and Exalted is He: ﴿confirming that which is before it﴾, this is another description. The idafah (annexation, construction) here, as stated by Abu al-Baqa, is not a pure (mahdah) idafah. The relative pronoun (al-ladhi) may refer either to the Torah, because it is the greatest Book sent down before it and because the address is to the Jews, or to what includes it and other heavenly books. This was narrated from al-Hasan. The relative pronoun is masculine in agreement with the Book, or with "the sent down," or something similar. The meaning of its being "before its hands" is that it precedes it, for everything that is "between the two hands" is like that. Its confirmation of all of them lies in establishing monotheism, commanding it, negating association with Allah, and forbidding it, and in all the fundamental principles of the laws that are not abrogated.

﴿And that you may warn the Mother of Villages﴾. It has been said: it is coordinated with what the description of the Book indicates, as if it were said: We sent it down for blessings, for confirming what came before it, and for warning. The Allamah (al-Alusi's reference to the second scholar) chose that it is coordinated with the explicit description, meaning: a blessed Book which is also for warning. It is claimed that with this there is no need for that strained interpretation, for coordinating an adverbial phrase with a single word in the case of predicates and descriptions is common. The claim that what calls for it is the removal of those previous descriptions from the conjunction particle and the juxtaposition of this with it, requiring that descriptions, when multiplied and the first of them is not conjoined, become impermissible or reprehensible, while the reality is otherwise, is answered as follows: the better view is that the verbal and semantic context requires it. As for the meaning, warning is the cause of its being sent down, as indicated by ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you by it﴾. If it were conjoined, it would be conjoined to the first of the descriptions, according to the preferred view of conjunction when there are multiple items. It is not good to conjoin a cause to what it is the cause of, nor a prepositional phrase to a verbal clause, for this is like the saying: "A man stood with me and to serve me," and that is, as you see, unsuitable. From this the verbal motive becomes known.

It has also been permitted that it be a cause for an elided element to be estimated either after or before it, meaning: "And that you may warn, We sent it down," or "And We sent it down that you may warn." The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for emphasis or for restricted specification relative to something else. It may also be coordinated with an estimated element, meaning: "that he may give good news and that he may warn." In any case, there is an elided annexed word in the speech, meaning: the people of the Mother of Villages. By it is meant Mecca the Honoured, and it was so named because it is the qiblah (direction of prayer) and pilgrimage destination of the people of the villages, and they gather around it as children gather around a compassionate mother, and they also venerate it with the veneration of a mother. This is reported from al-Zajjaj and al-Jubba'i. It is also said because it is the greatest of the villages in status, so the others follow it as a branch follows its root. It has also been said: because the earth was spread out from beneath it, so it is as if it emerged from beneath it as children emerge from beneath the mother; or because it is the site of the first House placed for mankind. This was reported from al-Suddi.

Abu Bakr, reading from Asim, recited (liyundhira, "that he may warn") with the yā' (the third person masculine), on the basis of metaphorical attribution to the Book, because it warns by means of it. ﴿And whoever is around it﴾, of the people of the settled areas (al-madar) and the people of the tents (al-wabar), in the east and the west, because of the universality of his mission, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the one who proclaimed the Qur'an in them in more than one verse. The wording does not reject this interpretation. There is therefore no basis in this verse for a group of Jews who claimed that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent only to the Arabs. Moreover, it is possible to say that those people were singled out for mention because they have the greatest right to his warning, peace be upon him, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾. For this reason, the Book of every Messenger was sent in the language of his people. ﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter﴾ and in what it contains of reward and punishment. Whoever restricts himself to the second (i.e., the Hereafter) in the explanation takes into account the priority of warning. ﴿They believe in it﴾, meaning in the Book. It has been said: or in Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because they fear the punishment and desire the reward, and this continually moves them to reflect and contemplate until they believe in him. ﴿And they are over their prayer they guard﴾.

92

- It is possible that by "prayer" is meant general obedience, metaphorically, or that it is restricted to part of it which is the pillar of religion and the sign of faith. For this reason, faith was metaphorically applied to that, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Allah would never let your faith be lost﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 93:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah,﴾ like those who said, ﴿"Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being,"﴾ ﴿or said, "It has been revealed to me,"﴾ from His side, exalted is He, ﴿while nothing has been revealed to him﴾, i.e. while in fact nothing had been revealed to him, like Musaylima and al-Aswad al-Ansi. ﴿And one who says, "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down,"﴾ i.e. "I am capable of composing the like of that discourse," like those who said, ﴿"If we wished, we could say the like of this."﴾ The explanation of the first with what we have mentioned, we have not found for anyone else. The explanation of the second was adopted by al-Zamakhshari and others, and the explanation of the third was adopted by al-Zajjaj and those who agreed with him. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that His saying, ﴿"And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' while nothing has been revealed to him"﴾, was revealed concerning Musaylima the Liar, and the last part was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. Some, on this basis, made the conjunction of the first "or said" with "invented" and so on a conjunction of explanation (atf al-tafsir).

This was objected to, on the grounds that it cannot be with "or." It was then deemed good that it is a conjunction of different things, considering the description (al-'unwan), and that "or" is for classification (lil-tanwi'), meaning that at times he claimed that Allah had sent him as a prophet and at other times that Allah had revealed to him, although in reality prophethood entails revelation and revelation entails prophethood. It is understood from the practice of some of them that "or" means "and." As for Ibn Abi Sarh, he did not explicitly claim the capacity, but his speech may imply it, as is understood from some narrations. Some explained the second by Abd Allah and his claim as being made in the manner of alternation (al-tardid), for it is narrated that Abd Allah ibn Sa'd had professed Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called him one day and wrote something for him. When the verse, ﴿"And We created man from an extract of clay,"﴾ was revealed concerning the believers, he dictated it to him, and when he reached His saying, ﴿"Then We produced him as another creation,"﴾ Abd Allah was amazed at the detail of the creation of man and said, ﴿"Blessed be Allah, the best of creators!"﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Thus was it revealed to me." Then he doubted at that moment and said, "If Muhammad is truthful, then it has been revealed to me, and if he is lying, then I have said as he said."

Taking the second part to mean a claim of the capacity to produce the like is valid, and the explanation of the second and third with it is valid only if the title of the relative clause in the last is taken as a matter of courtesy (min bab al-mumashat), for instance, as is not hidden. The Imam (al-Razi) considered the general sense of fabricating lies against Allah and made the conjoined element one of the kinds of things described as fabrication. Then he said: The difference between this statement and what precedes it is that in the first he was claiming that revelation came to him regarding what he lied about, and he did not deny the descent of revelation upon the Prophet (ﷺ). In the second, he affirmed revelation for himself and negated it from him, upon him be blessings and peace, so it combined two great lies: affirming what does not exist, and negating what exists. End of quote. In this there is a departure from the apparent sense, in that he made the pronoun in "ilayhi" refer to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the waw in "wa lam yuha" a conjunction, with the two conjoined elements being the object of the saying. What comes to mind is making the pronoun refer to "man" (man) and the waw a waw of circumstance, and what follows it is His speech, exalted is He. Perhaps it may be said that, setting aside the occasion of revelation, the intended by "one who invents a lie against Allah" is one who associates anyone with Allah, by applying the invention of lies to its greatest instance, which is shirk. Many verses proclaim this meaning. By "one who says, 'It has been revealed to me,' while nothing has been revealed to him" is intended the claimant to prophethood who is lying, and by "one who says, 'I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down'" is intended the one who attacks the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ). So it is as if it were said: Who is more unjust than one who associates others with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or who falsely claims prophethood, or who attacks the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ)? The discussion of similar interrogative sentences has already preceded, so reflect and ponder.

﴿And if you could see﴾, i.e. could witness. Its object is omitted, indicated by the adverbial phrase in His saying, ﴿when the wrongdoers﴾. Once the object was omitted, the adverbial phrase took its place. The original is: "If you saw the wrongdoers when they are." ﴿When﴾ (idh) is an adverb for "see," "the wrongdoers" is the subject, and His saying, ﴿in the agonies of death﴾, is its predicate, and "when" is an adverb for "see." The restriction of the seeing to this time is to convey that the intent is not mere seeing, but seeing them in a dreadful state, in the eyes of every beholder. It was said that the object is "when," and the intent is to emphasize the terror of this time because of the severity of what occurs in it. The answer to the condition is omitted, i.e. you would see a dreadful, appalling matter. By "the wrongdoers" is intended what includes the three types of fabrication, the last two sayings, and the ghamra (overwhelming). As al-Shihab said in the original: ghamra is the single instance from "ghamara al-ma'" (the water covered him). It was then borrowed for intensity and became so widespread that it became like a literal meaning. From it is the verse of al-Mutanabbi:

"A swift swimmer aids me through overwhelming after overwhelming,
for she has witnesses in it, from it, and upon it."

Here, what is intended is the agonies of death, as reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. ﴿And the angels﴾, who seize their souls, and they are the helpers of the Angel of Death, ﴿stretching out their hands﴾, i.e. with punishment. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they strike their faces and their backs, saying to them, ﴿"Bring forth your souls,"﴾ i.e. free them from what you are in of punishment. The command is for rebuke and to show their incapacity. Some held that this is a depiction of the angels' action in seizing the souls of wrongdoers, by analogy with the action of an insistent creditor who stretches out his hand to one who owes him a debt, harasses him in demanding it, grants no respite, and says: "Pay me what you owe me this instant, and I will not leave my place until I pull it out from your eyelids." In al-Kashshaf it is stated that it is a metaphor for harshness in the drive, insistence and severity in taking life without respite or delay, and that there is no literal speech there. Ibn al-Munir preferred that they actually do these things to them in the forms described, and when the literal sense can be maintained, there is no departure from it.

﴿Today﴾: what is intended is absolute time, not the conventionally understood day. It is either the time of death, or what includes it and what follows it. ﴿You will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, i.e. the punishment that contains humiliation and severity. The construction (idafa), as in "a bad man," indicates that he is firmly established in that quality, because the specification conveyed by the idafa is stronger than that conveyed by a descriptive attribute. It was also permitted that the idafa be taken in its apparent sense, since punishment may be for discipline and not only for humiliation and disgrace. Some explained "the agonies of death" as the severe punishments of the Fire. Although these are in reality more severe than the agonies of death, the term was used for them to bring the matter closer to understanding. The angels' stretching out their hands is by striking the wrongdoers in the Fire with iron maces, the "bringing forth" is by bringing them out of the Fire and its punishment, and "today" is the known Day. ﴿For what you used to say﴾ of fabrication ﴿against Allah other than the truth﴾, such as denying that He sent anything down to a human being and claiming revelation, or ascribing partners to Him, or falsely claiming prophethood and denying it of one who truly possessed it, or the like. The expression "other than the truth" for falsehood is not hidden. It is the object of "you used to say." It was also permitted that it be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e. "a saying other than the truth." ﴿And you used to be arrogant toward His signs.﴾

93

- i.e. you turn away from them, so you do not reflect upon them, and you do not believe.
