[p. 224]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 94:**

﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone﴾ for reckoning. ﴿Alone﴾ means separated from the helpers and the idols that you claimed were your intercessors, or separated from the wealth, children, and all the other things of this world that you preferred. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others narrated from Ikrimah, who said: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said, "Al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me," so this verse was revealed. According to what some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) held, the clause is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) within the words of Allah, the Exalted, and it does not contradict His saying ﴿(and He will not speak to them)﴾, because what is meant is the negation of speaking to them in a way that benefits them, or because it is a metaphor for anger. It has also been said that it is conjoined to the words of the angels, "Bring them out" etc., and is part of their speech. But this is remote, even though the Imam thought it preferable and stronger.

﴿Alone﴾ (furada) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a grammatical term meaning a descriptive state of the subject or object) of the subject pronoun. It is the plural of fard contrary to analogy, as if it were the plural of fardan, like sakran, according to what is in al-Sihah (a lexicon by al-Jawhari). The alif is for the feminine, as in kusala. According to the author of al-Durr al-Masun (al-Samin al-Halabi), the rāʾ in its singular form is vocalized with a fatha, and its sukun has been reported with the tamrid (hedging) form. It is related from al-Raghib that it is the plural of fariid, like asir and usara. In al-Qamus (a lexicon by al-Fayruzabadi) it is said: they came as afrad, furad, furada, farad, furad, and fardā, meaning one after another. The singular is fard, fard, fariid, and fardan. Fard is not permitted in this meaning. Perhaps this is far from the intended meaning in the verse. It has also been read as furadan, like rukhal with a damma on the rāʾ, and furada, like uhad and rubaʾ, being a modified (maʿdulah) attributive form. It is not objected that the coming of this modified pattern is restricted to numerals; rather it occurs with some of its words, as al-Farra' and others stated, so it is not restricted. Yes, it is common in what has been mentioned. Furadā, like sakrā, is the feminine of fardan, and the feminine form is for the plural of the one who has the state.

﴿As We created you the first time﴾ is a substitute (badal, a grammatical term meaning a noun that replaces the preceding noun in its grammatical role) for ﴿furada﴾, a substitute of the whole, because what is meant is resemblance in the aforementioned state of being alone. The kaf is a noun meaning "like," that is, like the condition in which you were born, in being alone. It is also permissible for it to be a second circumstantial state, according to the view of those who permit multiple circumstantial states without conjunction, and this is the correct view. Or it may be a circumstantial state of the pronoun in ﴿furada﴾, so it is a synonymous or nested circumstantial state. The comparison is also in being alone. It is possible that it is with regard to the beginning of creation, that is, you are compared to the state of the beginning of your creation, barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised. It was also permitted that it be an attribute of the verbal noun of ﴿you have come﴾, that is, a coming like Our creating you.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated, and he declared it sound, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she recited this verse and said: "O Messenger of Allah, alas for our shame! Men and women will be gathered together, and some will look at the private parts of others." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Each one of them on that day will have a matter that occupies him, so men will not look at women, nor women at men, being preoccupied with one another."

﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, that is, what We gave you in the world of wealth and servants. It contains a rebuke, that is, you were occupied with it instead of the Hereafter. ﴿Behind your backs﴾ means you did not send ahead anything of it for your souls. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "A son of Adam will be brought on the Day of Resurrection as if he were a bundle of sticks, and the Blessed and Exalted One will say to him: 'Where is what you gathered?' He will say: 'O Lord, I gathered it and left it at its greatest abundance.' He will say: 'Where is what you sent ahead for yourself?' He will not see that he sent anything ahead." And he recited this verse. The clause is said to be a new sentence, or a circumstantial state with qad implied.

﴿And We do not see﴾, that is, We do not perceive. According to what Abu al-Baqa' stated, it is a narration of a state (hikayat hal), and to it relates His saying, ﴿with you﴾. It is not a circumstantial state of the object of ﴿We see﴾, meaning His saying, ﴿your intercessors﴾, nor a second object. The seeing is cognitive, and the attribution of the intercessors to the pronoun of the addressees is with regard to their claim, as His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He, reveals: ﴿whom you claimed﴾ in the world ﴿that they are among you partners﴾, that is, partners of Allah, the Exalted, in your lordship and in the right to your worship. The word "claimed" here is explicit for falsehood, though its use for truth has also occurred, as the reference to it was previously mentioned. Among that is the poet's verse:

*"You say, 'We are ruined if he is ruined,' yet provision for the servants is only from Allah, as he claimed."*

﴿Your bonds have been severed among you﴾, with the nasb (accusative) of "bayna" (between). This is the reading of ʿAsim, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim. Its analysis has been disputed. It was said: the statement implies an omitted subject, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: the matter or the connection between you has been severed. It was said: the subject is the pronoun of the verbal noun. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying it is not correct, because the condition for the benefit of the predication is missing in it, namely the difference between the judgment and the one judged upon. For this reason it is not permitted to say "stood" or "sat" while you mean "stood he" (that is, the standing) or "sat he" (that is, the sitting).

It was answered that it is heard in "bada bada'an" (it appeared, an appearance), and they have estimated in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it appeared to them after they had seen the signs that they should imprison him﴾, that "bada" (appeared) is the "bada'" (appearance).

Al-Saffaqsi said: whoever makes the subject the pronoun of the verbal noun says that what is meant, that the severing and separation occurred, is achieved by this consideration. Even if it is granted, the severing considered as the referent is defined by the generic article, while "taqatta'a" is indefinite, so how can it be said that the judgment and the one judged are identical?

It is not hidden that the interpretation is necessary according to this estimation, because if the severing was severed, the connection came into being, which is the opposite of the intended meaning.

It was said: "bayna" itself is the subject, and it remained in its accusative state, treating it according to its most common condition. This is the position of al-Akhfash. It was said that it was built (mabni) because it was attributed to a built word. Other things have been said.

Abu Hayyan chose that the statement is of the type of tanazuʿ (grammatical contention, in which two verbs compete for one noun), in which it is governed by "what you used to claim" and "was severed," and "was lost from you." He made the second verb, "dalla" (was lost), operative, and supplied its pronoun in "taqatta'a." What is meant by this is the idols. The meaning is: "What you used to claim has been severed between you, and they were lost from you," as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and the means were severed from them﴾, that is, no connection remained between you and what you used to claim were partners, so you worshipped them.

The rest of the seven readers read "baynukum" with the rafʿ (nominative) as the subject. It is one of the words with opposite meanings, like "qurʾ" (which means both purity and menstruation), used for joining and separation. What is meant here is joining: your connection was severed and your union scattered. Ibn ʿAtiyyah criticized this, saying that it has not been heard from the Arabs that "bayn" means connection, and that it was only derived from this verse. It was answered that it is a metaphorical meaning and does not depend on hearing, because "bayn" is used for two things that are connected, as in "between me and you there is kinship, friendship, and partnership," so it came to mean a bond. Moreover, even if it is said that it is literal in that sense, it is not far-fetched, for Abu ʿAmr, Abu ʿUbaydah, Ibn Jinni, al-Zajjaj, and others among the imams of the language transmitted it, and they are sufficient as an authority for it. Thus its being derived from this verse is not accepted. On this basis it is a verbal noun (masdar), not an adverb of place. It was also said that "bayn" here is an adverb of place, but the verb was attributed to it by way of extension (ittisaʿ).

ʿAbd Allah read: ﴿Certainly that which was between you has been severed﴾, where "ma" is either descriptive or relative. ﴿And lost from you﴾ means was wasted and perished. ﴿What you used to claim﴾.

**94**

- That they are your intercessors; or that they are partners of Allah, the Exalted, in you; or that there is no resurrection and no recompense.

Verse 95 (Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone): ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ This begins a description of some of His wondrous acts, which point to the perfection of His knowledge, power, subtle craftsmanship and wisdom, following the establishment of the proofs for tawhid (Divine unity). This indicates that the goal of all rational and transmitted discussions and all legal matters is only the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, in His essence, attributes and actions.

Al-faliq (the splitter) means the originator and the innovator, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Dahhak. Al-habb (the grain) is well known. Al-nawa is the plural of nawat al-tamr (date-stone), as stated in al-Qamus (the lexicon) and elsewhere. It may be feminine or masculine, and its plurals are anwa' and nawan, with the nun vowelled either with a damma or a kasra. The Imam explained it as "the thing found inside the fruit," with a thaa' (ث), which is more general than date-stone with a ta' (ت) and others. It is well known that when al-nawa is used without qualification, what is meant is what is in al-Qamus. When another meaning is intended, it is qualified, so one says: nawa al-khawkh (peach stone), nawa al-ijas (plum stone), and similar. The root of al-falq is splitting (al-shaqq), and the application of al-faliq to the originator is based on the consideration that the intellect imagines non-existence as an unbroken darkness with no opening and no cleft. Therefore, whenever He brings a thing into existence, the mind imagines that He has split that non-existence and cleft it, and brought that innovated thing out of it.

According to al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi, the meaning is: the splitter of the dry grain, bringing out the plant from it, and the splitter of the date-stone, bringing out the palm tree and trees from it. Most of the exegetes follow this, and it is perhaps the preferred view.

In this there is an indication of the perfection of power, because of the wonders it contains, whose birds sing on the branches of wisdom, and whose rivers overflow in the gardens of generosity. From Mujahid and Abu Malik: the meaning of al-falq is the split that occurs in the grains, and by al-nawa is meant that He, exalted is He, is the creator of both in this manner, as in your saying: "He narrowed the mouth of the well and widened its bottom." This was criticized on the grounds that it does not indicate the perfection of power, as in the previous view.

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, meaning He brings forth what grows from animals, plants and trees, from what does not grow, such as the sperm drop, the grain and the date-stone. The clause is a fresh (resumptive) sentence explaining what precedes it, according to the majority view, and for this reason the conjunction was omitted. It was also said that it is a second predicate, and was not conjoined, to signal its independence in indicating the greatness of Allah, exalted is He. ﴿And He brings the dead out of the living﴾, such as the sperm drop and its counterparts, ﴿out of the living﴾, such as animals and their counterparts. According to some, this is conjoined to ﴿splits﴾ and not to ﴿brings the living out﴾ etc., because, as you know, the latter is an explanation of what precedes it, and this cannot serve as an explanation, even if it is valid to conjoin a derived noun (ism mushtaq) to a verb and vice versa.

Ibn al-Munir preferred that it be conjoined to (brings out). He said: "Both have appeared frequently in the present tense, and this is evidence that they are twins linked together, and it makes the separation (qita') unlikely. So the correct view, and Allah knows best, is to say: the original form was to use the form of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), in line with its counterparts in the verse, except that He turned away from that in this attribute alone, in order to make the bringing forth of the living from the dead conceivable and present in the hearer's mind. This can only be achieved by the present tense, not by the active participle or the past tense." Consider ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green?﴾ How He turned away from the past tense matching (anzala) for this reason. And the saying: "Indeed I have met the ghoul, as she runs, a long stretch like a sheet, flat as a plain, so I take her and strike her, and she falls prostrate on her hands and her side," where he turned to the present tense to depict his bravery and to bring to the hearer's mind what cannot be counted in number. Such a shift is made where care is greater. There is no doubt that the bringing forth of the living from the dead is more evident in power than its reverse, and it is also the first of the two states, since looking comes first, and then the other category is secondary to it. So the first is more worthy of being depicted and emphasized in the soul, and for this reason it is always placed first before the other category in mention, according to their order in reality. What made the conjoining of the noun to the verb easy and good is that the active participle has the meaning of the present tense, and each of them can be understood as the other, so there is no fault in conjoining one to the other."

The Imam said regarding the reason for this difference: the verbal form indicates that the agent is attentive to the act at every moment and time, whereas the nominal form does not indicate renewal and continuous attention moment by moment. What supports this is what Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir mentioned in Dala'il al-I'jaz (Proofs of Inimitability): that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky?﴾ mentions the provision with a verbal form, because it indicates that He provides for them moment by moment and instant by instant. And His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿And their dog stretches forth its forelegs at the threshold﴾ mentions the nominal form to indicate that it remains in that state. Given that this is established, it is said: since the living is more noble than the dead, the attention to bringing the living out of the dead must be greater than the attention to bringing the dead out of the living. Therefore the first category is expressed in the verbal form and the second in the nominal form, as a reminder that the attention to producing the living from the dead is greater and more complete than the attention to producing the dead from the living. Then, the conjunction is used because the sentence contains an additional meaning, and this does not harm the clause being an explanation of what came before, just as the inclusion of the living and the dead in the conjoined clause for animals and plants does not harm it.

Whatever the case, it is necessary to say either that the metaphor is general or that the literal and the figurative meanings are combined, according to the view of those who consider this valid. If we say that "living" is literally applied to whoever is characterized by life, which is an attribute that makes perception and power possible, and "dead" literally applies to whoever has lost that attribute or something similar, then applying them to things such as plants, growing trees and the date-stone is metaphorical. The words of the Imam hint at this, for he took what was reported from al-Zajjaj, that the meaning is: He brings forth the fresh, tender plant from the dry grain, and brings the dry grain out of the living, growing plant, as one of the figurative senses, like what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the meaning is: He brings the believer out of the disbeliever and the disbeliever out of the believer.

﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ (dhalikum): the Mighty One, the Exalted in majesty, the Shining in proof, is (Allah), the Essence, the Necessarily Existent, the One deserving worship alone. ﴿So how are you deluded?﴾

95

How are you turned away from worshipping Him and associate with Him those who have no power over anything? There is no way to that at all. Al-Sahib ibn 'Abbad used this to argue that the act of the servant is not created by Allah, exalted is He, because if He created the lie (ifk) in them, it would not befit Him, exalted is His majesty, to say: ﴿So how are you deluded?﴾ We have already given the answer to that in the fullest way, so reflect on it.

[Page 227]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 96 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Fāliq al-Iṣbāḥ﴾ (the Splitter of the dawn) is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is the Splitter," or it is another predicate of *inna* (indeed). *Al-Iṣbāḥ*, with a kasra on the hamza, is a verbal noun that has been used as a name for the dawn (*al-Ṣubḥ*). Imru' al-Qays said:

[Page 228]

*Alā ayyuhā al-laylu al-ṭawīlu alā injalī bi-ṣubḥin wa-mā al-iṣbāḥu minka bi-amthali*

("Ah, O long night, will you not clear away with a dawn? The dawn is not better than you.")

al-Ḥasan (al-Basri) read it with a fatha (*al-Fataḥ*), taking it as the plural of *ṣubḥ*, like *qufl* and *aqfāl* (lock and locks). He also cited the verse:

*Afnā riyāḥan wa-banī riyāḥin ∗∗∗ tanāsukha al-amsā'i wa-al-aṣbāḥi*

With a kasra and with a fatha, the word may be a verbal noun, and it may be the plural of *masy* and *ṣubḥ*.

*Al-Fāliq* means *al-Khāliq* (the Creator), as narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and from Qatadah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Many others said it means *al-Shāqq* (the Splitter, the one who cleaves).

An objection arises: it appears that darkness is what splits open to produce the dawn. The answer is that there are two kinds of dawn. The true dawn (*al-ṣubḥ al-ṣādiq*) is the one whose light spreads across the horizon in a band. The false dawn (*al-ṣubḥ al-kādhib*) is the one that appears as an elongated column, whose upper part is brighter than the rest, and which is followed by darkness. On the first reading, the meaning is that He splits it from the whiteness of the day. Alternatively, a noun is understood to be omitted in the sentence, so the meaning is "the Splitter of the darkness of the dawn by the dawn." This is because the horizon on the western and southern sides is filled with darkness, while the light has only appeared on the eastern side. It is as though the horizon were a sea filled with darkness, and He, glorified is He, cleaved that dark sea by sending a stream of light through it.

On the second reading, the objection is that He, glorified is He, splits the dawn from the darkness at the end of the night and cleaves it off from it. The division of dawn into true and false, which has been mentioned, is something that observation attests to, and no two people dispute it. However, there is a discussion by the astronomers (*Ahl al-Hay'ah*) about its cause, the essence of which is that the dawn, and likewise the twilight (*al-shafaq*), is an illumination in the sphere of vapour (*kurat al-bukhār*), due to the closeness of the sun to the eastern horizon and its distance from the western horizon.

It has been established that the sphere of vapour is a condensed air containing the earthly and watery particles that rise from the two spheres (of earth and water) through the heating of the sun and other things. The shape of this air is that of a sphere surrounding the earth, centred on its centre, with a surface parallel to the earth's surface, at a maximum height from the earth's centre in all directions. This entails that it is spherical. Its density varies, because what is closer to the earth is denser than what is farther away, since the finer parts rise and move farther away more than the denser parts. However, the condensation does not reach the point of blocking what lies behind it. This sphere ends at a limit it does not exceed, which is about fifty-one miles from the surface of the earth. The earth has a shadow in the form of a cone whose base is a circle upon it, nearly great in size, facing the sun, with its apex opposite to it. The earth is divided by this base into two parts: one larger, illuminated, facing the sun, and the other dark, opposite to it. Light and darkness move across the surface of the earth, in a day and its night, one full revolution, like two opposite banners, one white and the other black.

The rays of the sun surround the cone of shadow from all its sides and are diffused throughout all the celestial spheres, except for a small portion of the sphere of the moon and the sphere of Mercury that falls within the cone of the earth's shadow. But since the spheres are extremely transparent, the rays pass through them and are not reflected from them, which is why we do not see them as luminous. Likewise, the clear air that surrounds the sphere of vapour does not receive light.

As for the sphere of vapour, its density varies, because what is closer to the earth is denser than what is farther away, and the denser is more receptive to illumination. The dense and coarse part, through the mixing of the many forms from the surface of the cone of shadow, is receptive to light. The day is the duration of this cone's being below the horizon, and the night is the duration of its being above it. When all this has been established, it is said: when the sun draws closer to the eastern side of the horizon, the inclination of the cone towards its western side increases, and this continues until the ray surrounding it is seen. The first thing seen is what is closest to the observer's place, which is a line that extends from his eye in the plane of a azimuth circle passing through the centre of the sun, perpendicular to the line tangent to the sun and the earth. This is the line that lies in the plane of the common section between the ray and the shadow. Light is therefore first seen rising above the horizon at the point where the perpendicular falls, elongated like a straight line. What lies between it and the horizon appears dark because of its distance, even though it is in reality illuminated.

Because the air near the horizon is dense, this has a role in it, and this is the false dawn. Then, when it draws close to the eastern horizon, light is seen spreading across it, increasing moment by moment, and the first light is obliterated by this strong illumination, just as the light of lamps and stars is obliterated in the light of the sun. Thus it seems as though the first has ceased to exist, and this is the true dawn.

To clarify what has been mentioned, according to *al-Tadhkirah* and the commentary of *Sayyid al-Muhaqqiqin* (al-Jurjani): it is imagined, for the sake of explanation, that there is a plane passing through the centre of the sun, the earth, the axis of the cone, and the centre of its base. This produces a triangle with acute angles, whose base lies on the horizon and whose two sides lie on the surface of the cone. As for the formation of the triangle, this is because it is established that when a flat plane passes through the axis of the cone and the centre of its base, it produces a triangle within it. As for the acuteness of the angles, this is because the apex of the cone, at midnight, lies on the meridian circle above the earth. At that time, either the cone stands upright on the plane of the horizon, which is the case when the sun is directly over the head, or it inclines to the north or south with its distance from the east and west being equal, which is the case when the sun is not directly overhead.

In any case, that assumed plane extends between the two horizons. In the first assumption, this is obvious. In the second, it is because the distance of the apex of the cone from the eastern and western sides is equal, so the two base angles of the triangle are acute, since it is necessary for them to be equal, and a triangle cannot have two right angles or two obtuse angles. When the apex of the cone inclines away from the midnight meridian above the earth, because the sun moves away from it to the eastern side beneath the earth, the eastern angle of that triangle becomes narrower, becoming less than what it was, and the western angle widens until it becomes obtuse. But the point in question does not change, and there is no doubt that the closer of the side that faces the sun to the observer is the place where the perpendicular that exits from the sight falls on that side, not the point where the side joins the horizon. This is because if a perpendicular exits from the eye to the eastern side, it cannot fall on the point where this side joins the horizon, otherwise the right angle would coincide with part of an acute angle. Nor can it fall beneath the horizon, by cutting the base of the triangle and reaching the said side after extending beneath it, otherwise it would entail in the triangle formed beneath the horizon that part of the extracted portion and part of the perpendicular would be a right angle and an obtuse angle. Nor can it fall in the direction of the apex of the triangle, at the point where one of its sides joins the other, nor outside it in that direction, for the same reasons we have mentioned. Therefore it must fall inside the triangle, between the two ends of the eastern side. It has been made clear that its place is closer to the observer than its point of junction with the horizon. There is no doubt that what falls of this side within the condensed part of the sphere of vapour is entirely illuminated when the sun is close to the eastern horizon. However, what is nearer to the observer appears more truly, and this is the place of the perpendicular. From here, the true and false dawn are established. That is the end of their discussion.

Imam al-Razi denied that the false dawn is an effect of the disc of the sun. Rather, it is by the direct creation of Allah, exalted is He. He said: because when the centre of the sun reaches the circle of midnight, the place whose horizon is that circle has already seen the sun rise from their east, and at that place the light has illuminated half the sphere of the earth. This means that light has appeared in the eastern quarter of our land, and that light would be spreading and dispersing through all parts of the atmosphere, and it must increase moment by moment. In that case, it is impossible for the first dawn to be an elongated line. Since it is not so, it is known that it is not from the influence of the disc of the sun, nor of the same kind as its light. It is also understood from his words that the second dawn is like the first, and is only by the creation of the Chooser, and it is impossible for it to be from the influence of the disc of the sun.

[Page 229]

Between that, it is one of the premises agreed upon that a luminous body, whether it is the sun or something else, does not cast its light except upon the body opposite to it, not upon what is not opposite. At the rising of dawn, the sun is not yet elevated above the horizon, so the body of the sun is not opposite any part of the surface of the earth, and therefore it is impossible for the light of the sun to fall upon the surface of the earth. When that is impossible, it is impossible for the light of dawn to be from the influence of the disc of the sun.

He then said: If they say, why should it not be possible to say that the sun, while beneath the earth, causes the illumination of that air which is opposite to it, and that air is opposite the air standing above the earth, so the light of the air standing beneath the earth becomes a cause for the light of the air standing above the earth? Then that light continues to travel from another air adjacent to it until it reaches the air that surrounds us.

[Page 230]

This passage has been translated as faithfully and completely as possible, preserving the text as it stands, with the Qur'anic quotation within ﴿ ﴾ markers, the Arabic verse of Imru' al-Qays and the verse cited by al-Ḥasan rendered in transliteration with English meaning, and the technical terms glossed.

[p. 231]

Abu 'Ali ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) in *al-Manazir* (*Optics*) also relied on this view. The answer is that this is false for two reasons.

The first is that the air is transparent and colourless, so in itself it does not receive light or colour. What is like this cannot reflect light onward to something else, so its light cannot become the cause of the light of another air facing it. If they say, "Why could it not be said that dense particles of vapours and smoke have collected on the horizon, and because of their density they receive light from the disc of the sun, and then it overflows onto the air facing them?" we reply: If that were so, then whenever there were more vapours and smoke on the horizon, the light of dawn should be stronger. But the matter is not like that; it is the opposite.

The second is that the circle which is the horizon for us is exactly the circle of midday (noon) for another people. If that is so, then the circle which is midday in our land must be the horizon for those peoples. Once this is established, we say: when the centre of the sun reaches the circle of midnight and passes beyond it, the sun has risen over those peoples, and half the world is illuminated there, and the quarter of the sphere which is the eastern quarter for the people of our land is then a western quarter with respect to that town. If that is so, then when the centre of the sun passes beyond the circle of midnight, its body has come opposite the air of the quarter which is the eastern quarter of our town. So if the air received the quality of light from the sun, the light would have to appear in this eastern quarter of our town after midnight, and the air of this quarter would have to become extremely bright at that time. Since this is not the case, we know that the air does not receive the quality of light in itself. And if this is refuted, the excuse which Ibn al-Haytham mentioned is refuted. End of what is meant from him.

I do not think he has brought anything by which the dawn of this question is made to shine, as will not be hidden from one who has comprehensive knowledge of what we have previously presented.

The most eminent of the later scholars, the allama Ahmad ibn Hajar al-Haytami, mentioned that the astronomers (ahl al-hay'a, the people of astronomy) have a long discussion on verifying the false dawn (al-subh al-kadhib), based on conjecture founded on the false principles of the philosophers, such as their denial of rupture and joining (in the heavens). Moreover, it does not explain the cause of its upper part being luminous, although it is further from its source, which is the sun, than its lower part; nor does it explain the cause of its complete disappearance, after which darkness follows, as the imams have stated, and they fixed its duration at one hour. The apparent meaning is that by this they mean a general period of time, because it sometimes lengthens and sometimes shortens, and this is the nature of the seasonal (unequal) hours, called the "crooked" hours, which are contrasted with the equal hours, each of which is always fifteen degrees.

Some astronomers claimed that it does not disappear, but gradually diminishes until it is submerged in the true dawn. This has already been mentioned to you in what we transmitted from them, and perhaps this is by calculation rather than by sensory observation.

In the report of Muslim: "Do not let the call to prayer of Bilal, nor this spreading light (al-'arid li-'amud al-subh) deceive you, until it spreads (hatta yastatir)." That is, that column spreads out across the regions of the horizon. From calling the second one "a spreading light" (*'arid*), two things are derived. One of them is that it appears (ya'riḍu) to the ray that originates from it, which is the dawn. The second is a restriction (inhibition) near its appearance, as the word "breathing" (tanaffus) in His, the Glorified's, saying indicates: ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. At that restriction, something breathes out from it like a small window (kuwwa). In what is restricted, when part of it comes out at once, what is observed is that its first part is greater than its last part. This is because the speech of the Truthful (the Prophet) may indicate this, and because it informs about the cause of its length, the brightness of its upper part, the difference in its duration, and its complete disappearance, which agrees with sensory observation, and is better than what the astronomers mentioned, which falls short of this.

The second thing is that the Prophet (ﷺ) by the term "spreading light" indicated that the intended thing in essence is the true dawn, and that the false dawn is intended only incidentally, so as to alert people to the nearness of the true dawn, so that they might wake up to attain the virtue of the beginning of the time, since they are occupied with sleep, which, were it not for this sign, would prevent them from attaining the beginning of the time. The summary is that it is a light which Allah the Exalted brings forth from that ray, or creates at that time as a sign of the nearness of dawn, and differing from it in form, so that the distinction may occur and the sign appearing from the one who sets the sign may become clear, the intended purpose. So reflect on this, for it is rare and important.

In a report in Ahmad: "The white dawn which extends (al-mustatil) on the horizon is not the dawn; rather, the dawn is the red one which spreads across (al-mu'tarid)." In it there is evidence for what was mentioned in another place.

Among the things that support what I have pointed to regarding the window is what many have reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the sun has three hundred windows, rising each day from one window. So it is no wonder that when it comes near that window, its ray is restricted and then breathes out, as already explained.

Al-Qarafi the Maliki and others, like al-Asbahi of the Shafi'is, have a discussion on this which clarifies it, explains the correctness of what has been mentioned about the windows, and agrees with the difficulty that it appears and then disappears. Its summary, though there is some length to it, the need for it is felt: it is a whiteness that rises before dawn and then goes away for most eyes, but not for the diligent observer with a strong gaze.

Ibn Bashir al-Maliki mentioned that it is from the light of the sun when it comes near the horizon; when it appears, the eyes become accustomed to it, so it seems to them that it has set, which is not the case. Al-Asbahi reported that some of them mentioned that it goes away after rising and returns to its place at night, and this is the view of many Shafi'is. And that Abu Ja'far al-Basri, after defining it as being present for about two hours, said that it rises elongated towards about a quarter of the sky, like a column, and may not be seen when the air is clear in winter, and it is most visible when the air is turbid in summer. Its upper part is thin and its lower part is wide. This does not contradict what was mentioned earlier, that its upper part is brighter, because that is at the first rising, and this is at its greatest nearness to the true dawn. Beneath it is blackness, and then whiteness that covers all of that. Then he raised an objection to it, saying that he observed it for about fifty years and never saw it set; rather, it descends so that it meets the one that is extended in the blackness and they become one dawn.

The claim of its disappearance and then return is a delusion, or he saw it varying with the seasons and thought it went away. Some of the timekeepers say: it is the Milky Way when the dawn is with the Pleiades (su'ud), and this would require that it is not found except for about two months in the year.

Al-Qarafi said: Others said it is a ray that comes out from the layers of the Mount Qaf. Then he refuted this by saying that Mount Qaf does not exist, and he proved this by something that refutes it: what came from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, through many chains which the hadith scholars transmitted, and a group of those who committed themselves to transmitting only the authentic. The statement of a Companion on such a matter, and similar things which have no room for opinion, has the ruling of a report traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ). Among them: that behind our land there is an encircling sea, then a mountain called Qaf, then land, then a sea, then a mountain, and so on until he counted seven of each. And some of those transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah that it is a mountain of emerald (dumurrud) encircling the world, on which are the two shoulders of the heaven. And similarly from Mujahid. Just as his saying "it does not exist" was refuted by this, so too his following statement was refuted: "It is not permissible to believe in what has no evidence," because if by "evidence" he means any indication whatsoever, then there are indications for this; or if he means rational indication, then this is something for which conjecture suffices, as is clear.

Then it was reported from al-Qarafi, from the astronomers, that it appears and then is hidden permanently. Then he raised a difficulty about it and extended his answer with things that are not made clear

[p. 232]

except to one who has mastered the two sciences of geometry and optics. So it is more fitting that it varies with the variation of the view, because it varies with the variation of the seasons and the conditions that affect its place. For it may become so fine in some of these states that it is not seen at all. In that case, this is the excuse of those who said that it disappears and then darkness follows it.

This, and it is not hidden, that the claim that the light of dawn arises merely by the creation of Allah the Exalted, not from an ordinary cause, as the words of the Imam indicate, is easier than the claim that it is from a ray coming out of the layers of Mount Qaf. And the claim that the ray comes out from this layer is easier than the claim that it comes out from the sun, which, according to what has been determined regarding the sizes of celestial bodies, is one hundred and sixty-six times the size of the earth with a fraction previously mentioned, according to what is well known; or three hundred and twenty-six times its size, according to what Ghiyath al-Din Jamshid al-Kashi said in his treatise "The Ladder of the Heaven"; or something close to that, according to what is in some narrations of a window in a mountain surrounding the earth.

As for the report on this matter, if it is authentic and we say that it has the ruling of a report traced back to the Prophet, then it should be interpreted, and the door of interpretation is wider than that window. For many people have crossed the circle of the earth along the tropic of Cancer several times and have not found any trace of this encircling, towering mountain. And establishing seven mountains and seven seas in the aforementioned manner is also something whose problems are not hidden. That Allah the Exalted cannot be incapacitated by anything is something no one doubts except an atheist. But the discussion is about whether what has been mentioned exists in external reality. And what the hearts of many people incline towards regarding the matter of dawn is what the astronomers have mentioned.

Aristukhus (Aristarchus) explained in the second proposition of his book *On the Sizes and Distances of the Two Luminaries* that when a sphere borrows light from a larger sphere, the illuminated part of it is greater than half of it. He also explained in the first proposition of that same book that for any two spheres of different sizes, a right circular cone can be drawn enclosing both of them, with its apex on the side of the smaller one, and the cone touches each of them along the circumference of a circle. There is no doubt that a cone formed of radial lines encloses the sun and the earth, with its apex on the side of the earth. So this cone is tangent to the earth along a circle separating its illuminated and dark parts, and this is a small circle, because the illuminated part of the earth is smaller.

They have also verified that the illuminated part of the air is the sphere of vapour, apart from what has entered the shadow of the earth's cone. And it is always illuminated because of its density and the surrounding of the rays of the sun upon it, but it is not seen at night because of its distance from sight. And the apex of the cone is always opposite the body of the sun, as we have indicated. So at midnight it lies on the circle of midday, and after that it inclines towards the side of setting, moment by moment, until whiteness is seen on the side of the east, as has been explained in detail before.

On this basis, it does not follow, in the case which the Imam mentioned, that when the centre of the sun passes the circle of midnight it rises over those peoples. The illumination of half the world for them is the illumination of the eastern quarter for us, because of the difference in position, as will not be hidden from one who reflects.

To accept the claim of sphericity, the cone, and similar things which the astronomers mentioned is not objectionable. Yes, believing in the truth of what they say, where it is known to contradict religion by necessity or is known by definitive evidence to be false, is disbelief or misguidance. So reflect.

And it has been read as (*fāliqa*) in the accusative as a form of praise.

Al-Nakha'i read (*faliqa al-isbah*) ("He splits the dawn"). ﴿And He made the night a rest﴾: that is, one in whom is at rest (yaskunu ilayhi) whoever is wearied by the day, and who finds comfort in it and relief in its repose. Everything to which a man is at rest, finding comfort and tranquillity in it, and relief in its company, whether a spouse or a beloved, is called *sakan*. From this it was said of fire, "*sakan*", because one finds comfort in it, and for this reason they called it "the comforting one" (mu'nisa).

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada that the meaning is that every bird and animal rests in it. Something similar was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

[p. 233]

رَضِيَ اللَّهُ تَعالى عَنْهُمْ [may God Most High be pleased with them]. The meaning then is: He made the night a place of rest, taking the word *maskūnan* from *al-sukūn*, which means calm and settledness, as in His saying ﴿that you may rest therein﴾. All of the Seven readers except the Kufans read *jāʿilu* (the active participle, "Who makes") in the nominative, and it is read irregularly in the accusative. In both readings *al-layli* (the night) is in the genitive through the construction of annexation (*iḍāfa*). According to many scholars, the accusative of *sakanan* (as a direct object) is governed by a verb implied by this descriptive word, not by the word itself. The reason is that the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) must refer to the present or the future in order to govern an object, and here it refers to the past, as the reading *jaʿala* (the perfect verb "He made") shows.

Al-Kisāʾī and some Kufan scholars permitted its governing an object in the past tense without restriction, treating it as analogous to the verb whose meaning it contains. Some permitted this only when the word takes the definite article *al-*. Others permitted it in the second case when the word is annexed to the first, because it resembles the definite word with *al-*. According to this view and the first view, there is no need to assume an implied verb; rather, the governing element is the descriptive word itself. Some scholars chose that it governs the object as well, but on the understanding that the meaning is a continuous making across different times, not only the past. On this view it does not function like the resembling adjective (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*), because that, as the verifiers (*al-muḥaqqiqūn*) said, when intended to express continuity, is conditional on the attribute being well known and widely used in that sense. In our reading, *sakanan* in the accusative is the second object (*mafʿūl thānī*) of *jaʿala*.

It is permitted that *jaʿala* means "brought into being" (*aḥdatha*), which takes one object only. Then *sakanan* is accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). *Wa al-shamsa wa al-qamara* (and the sun and the moon) are conjoined to *al-layl*. On the reading in which *al-layl* is genitive, their accusative is governed by the implied *jaʿala* that governs *sakanan*, or by another similar verb. It is also said that they are conjoined to the position (*maḥall*) of *al-layl* in the genitive, since the annexation of the descriptive word to it is not literal when the past is not intended. The word is read in the genitive, which is clear. It is read in the nominative as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the predicate omitted, meaning "they are made" (*majʿūlān*). ﴿Ḥusbānan﴾, that is, arranged in different cycles by which the times are reckoned, when acts of worship and transactions are tied to them. Or it means "they are reckoned" (*maḥsūbān*) as a reckoning.

*Al-ḥusbān* with a *ḍamma* is the verbal noun of *ḥasiba* with a *fatḥa*, just as *al-ḥisbān* with a *kasra* is the verbal noun of *ḥasiba* with a *kasra*. This is the original attested form for words like this, and anything else is irregular, as has been said. It is reported from Abu al-Haytham that *ḥusbān* is the plural of *ḥisāb*, like *rukbān* and *rikāb*, and *shuhbān* and *shihāb*. Its use here after *dhālika* (that) is an indication that the sun and moon are made in this way.

Al-Ṭabarsī said: "*Dhālika* refers to what has preceded: the splitting of the dawn, the making of the night as a place of rest, and the sun and moon as a reckoning." The majority hold the first view, and it is the apparent one. The sense of distance in *dhālika* serves to indicate the high rank of what is referred to and the remoteness of its station, meaning: that arrangement, wondrous in its nature, is ﴿the decree of the Mighty﴾, that is, the Overpowering, the Compelling, whom nothing in creation can resist, and among those things is the arranging of these two in the specific manner, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾,

96
— the one who is exceedingly knowing of all the things known, among which are the worldly and otherworldly benefits contained in that arrangement.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 97:

﴿And it is He who has made﴾ i.e., created or made ﴿for you﴾ i.e., for your sake ﴿the stars﴾. It has been said: what is meant by them is other than the two luminaries (the sun and the moon), because they are the ones by which guidance (al-ihtida', mentioned below) takes place, and because the word "najm" (star) in common usage is restricted to what is other than those two. It is also permissible that the two be included among them, so that this would be an explanation of their general benefit following the explanation of their specific benefit. The astrologers (al-munajjimun) divide the stars into fixed stars (thawabit) and wandering stars (sayyarat). The wandering stars are seven by the consensus of the earlier scholars, and eight with the addition of Herschel (Hirshil) according to the astrologers today. The fixed stars, none knows their number except God Most High. The number observed of them, as ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sufi said, is one thousand and twenty-five, including the Pleiades (al-Dafira). Whoever excludes it says: they are one thousand and twenty-two. They have arranged the fixed stars into six magnitudes (aqdar), and they called them magnitudes increasing by a sixth each time, and they made each magnitude into three ranks: greater, middle, and smaller. They have other divisions for them based on other considerations, upon which they have built what they have built, and it is hardly accepted from them except what does not entail a prohibited matter in the religion.

﴿That you may be guided by them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (lakum) by repeating the governing particle, a substitution of part (badal ishtimal); as if it were said: He made the stars for your guidance ﴿in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾, i.e., in the darkness of the night on land and sea. Its attribution to them both is for association (lil-mulaabasa), or [it means] in the confusing paths, and he called them "darknesses" by metaphor. This is singling out some of their benefits for mention according to what the context requires; otherwise they are more beneficial than the scattering of the staff, and they, in all that results from them, are like the other customary causes: they have no influence in themselves. There is no harm in learning the science of the stars and knowing the zodiacal signs, the mansions (manazil), the positions and the like, of what is used to reach a religious benefit.

The great scholar Ibn Hajar, may God have mercy on him, said: What is forbidden of the science of the stars is what its practitioners claim of knowing future events in the time to come, such as the coming of rain, the falling of snow, the blowing of wind, the change of prices, and the like; they claim that they perceive this through the movement of the planets by their conjunction and separation. This is a knowledge which God Most High has reserved for Himself, and no one knows it besides Him; so whoever claims knowledge of it is a sinner, and it may even lead him to disbelief. As for one who says: the conjunction or separation which is such-and-such, God Most High has made it a sign, according to what His divine custom has consistently established, for the occurrence of such-and-such, though it may sometimes fail to occur, then there is no sin on him for that. Likewise is the reporting of what is perceived through direct observation from the science of the stars, by which one knows the zenith (zawal), the direction of the qibla, and how much of the time has passed and how much remains; there is no sin in it, rather it is a communal obligation (fard kifaya). As for what is in the hadith of the two Sahihs from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, led us in the dawn prayer after rain (ma') that had fallen during the night. When he finished, he turned to us and said: Do you know what your Lord has said? They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: 'Some of My servants have awakened as believers and some as disbelievers. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by the grace of God, that is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the stars; and the one who said: We have been given rain by the such-and-such star (nawʾ), that is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the stars.'" The scholars have said: this is to be understood as when he says it intending that the star is the originator; but if he says it in the sense that the star is a sign of the descent of rain, while the one who sends it down is God alone, then he does not disbelieve, but it is disliked for him to say it, because it is among the expressions of disbelief. End of quote.

I say: Reports are abundant prohibiting the science of the stars and looking into them. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever acquires a branch of knowledge from the stars has acquired a branch of magic, increasing as much as he increases." Al-Khatib reported from Maymun ibn Mihran who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, "Advise me." He said: "I advise you to fear God, and beware of the science of the stars, for it leads to soothsaying (kihana)." It was also reported from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade me from looking into the stars." And similarly from Abu Hurayra and ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with them both. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The one who learns the letters of Abu Jadur (abjad) in the stars has no portion with God on the Day of Resurrection." Abu al-Khatib reported from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Learn from the stars what you are guided by in the darknesses of land and sea, then stop." And other reports besides these. Perhaps what they indicate of prohibition on learning is by way of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i), because that knowledge may lead to what is forbidden in the law, as the report of Ibn Mihran indicates. Likewise the prohibition on looking into them is to be understood as the looking that soothsayers (kahana) used to do, who claim that the stars themselves have influence, and who decide with certainty, by their trine, quartile, conjunction, and opposition for instance, the judgments they indicate in such a way that they never fail with certainty. Moreover, knowing all that God Most High has deposited in each star is impossible for anyone other than the Knower of the unseen, and knowing some or all of some of it does not benefit nor yield more than conjecture; the one who clings to it is like one clinging to the ropes of the moon, and the one who grasps it is like one grasping the rays of the sun. Yes, some events in the world of generation and corruption have customarily been produced by God Most High, for the most part, at the rising of a star, its setting, or its conjunction with another star; and what is observed at the disappearance and rising of the Pleiades and the rising of Canopus is evidence for what we have mentioned. It is not far-fetched that this is among the customary causes, and their effects may fail to follow them, whether we say that the influence is with them, as is well known from the Ash'aris, or we say they are the influencers by God's permission, as is the view preferred by the earlier scholars (al-salaf). This is indicated by the words of the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali regarding causation. So whenever an experienced observer reports something of that kind in this manner, there is no harm in it. As for what al-Khatib reported from ʿIkrima, that he asked a man about the calculation of the stars, and the man hesitated to inform him, so ʿIkrima said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, say: "It is a knowledge that people are unable to attain, and I wished I knew it."

And what al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Hafs, who said: The Arabs were specialized in several qualities: soothsaying (kihana), physiognomy (qiyafa), augury (iyafa), the stars, and calculation; Islam demolished soothsaying and confirmed the rest after that. And the saying of al-Hasan ibn Salih: I heard from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said about the stars: "That is a knowledge the people have neglected." So perhaps that, if it is authentic, is to be understood in line with what we have said. After all this I say: it is a knowledge that does not benefit, and ignorance of it does not harm; what God Most High wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be.

﴿We have detailed the signs﴾ i.e., we have made clear the recited signs mentioned for His blessings, of which this blessing is part, or the created signs indicating His Majesty's affairs, Most High, in detail, detail by detail, ﴿for a people who know﴾.

97

- The meaning of the signs mentioned is that they act in accordance with what they require, or that they reflect upon the created signs and thus know the true state of affairs. The specification of the detailing to them, despite its generality to all, is because they are the ones who benefit from it.

[Page 236]

98

﴿And He it is who produced you from one soul﴾, that is, Adam, peace be upon him. This is a reminder of another blessing, for the return of the multitude to a single origin is closer to affection and compassion. It also indicates the great power of Him, glory be to Him and exalted, ﴿So there is a place of lodging and a place of storage﴾. That is, for you there is a lodging in the loins or upon the earth, and a storage in the wombs, or in the grave, or the place of lodging and storage is among what has been mentioned. The loins are made the lodging of the seed and the womb its storage, because the seed comes into being in the loins not from another person, and in the womb from the father's side. So it resembles a deposit, as if the man had deposited with it what was with him. The surface of the earth is made a lodging and its interior a storage, because of their settling upon the first and their taking dwellings and houses on it, and the absence of any of that in the second. It was also said: the expression for their being in the loins or upon the earth as "lodging" is because these are their natural abode, just as the expression for their being in the wombs or in the grave as "storage" is because neither of these is their natural abode.

Jamaʿa (a group of narrators), including al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the lodging is the womb and the storage is the loins. It is reported in another narration that a scholar (ḥabr) of Taymāʾ wrote to him asking him, may Allah be pleased with him, about this, and he answered him with what has been mentioned.

The interpretation of the lodging as the womb is supported by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will﴾. As for the interpretation of the storage as the loins, Shaykh al-Islam said: it is not clear, and it is not as he said. For the Imam, after distinguishing between lodging and storage, mentioned that lodging is closer to permanence than storage. Among what indicates the strength of this view, meaning what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is that a single drop of seed does not remain in the father's loins for a long time, whereas the fetus remains for a long time. Since staying in the womb is longer than staying in the father's loins, it is more fitting to take lodging to mean staying in the womb. It follows from this that taking storage to mean staying in the loins is more fitting.

I say: perhaps the storage is taken to mean the loins on the basis that Allah, exalted is He, after bringing forth from the backs of the children of Adam, peace be upon him, their offspring on the Day of the Covenant, and made them witness against themselves, and what happened happened, returned them to where He had brought them out from. So they are as a deposit there, which will come forth when Allah, exalted is He, wills. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, also clearly applied the name "deposit" to what is in the loins. ʿAbd al-Razzaq related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn ʿAbbas said to me, "Have you married?" I said, "No, and that is not on my mind today." He said, "If there is a deposit in your loins, it will come forth."

The interpretation of the storage as the world and the lodging as the grave is reported from al-Hasan, and he used to say: "O son of Adam, you are a deposit in your family, and you are about to join your companion." And he recited the verse of Labid:

*"Wealth and family are but a deposit, and the deposits must surely be returned one day."*

Sulayman ibn Zayd al-ʿAdawi said on this meaning:

*"The beloved were bereaved by beloveds before us, so people are bereaved by it and bereave; the one who is deposited is a stranger, and the one who is settled in his place is visited."*

It is related from Abu Muslim al-Isfahani that the lodging is the male, because the seed is only generated in his loins, and the storage is the female, because her womb resembles a storage for that seed. So it is as if it were said: "He it is who created you from one soul; so among you is a male and among you is a female."

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read (fa-mustaqirrun) with a kasra on the qaf, and then it is an ism fāʿil (active participle) meaning "settled." ﴿And storage﴾ is an ism mafʿūl (passive participle). The meaning is: among you is one who settles and among you is one who is stored. The reason the first is active and the second passive is that settling here is the opposite of being stored. The two conjoined nouns in the first reading are either masdars (verbal nouns) or ism makān (nouns of place), and the first cannot be an ism mafʿūl, because "istaqarra" is intransitive, and likewise the second, so that it may be like the first. ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾, which clarify the details of the creation of humankind, and among them is this verse. ﴿For a people who understand﴾.

- Regarding the reason for this, it was said: it is mentioned with the mention of the stars as ﴿know﴾, and with the mention of the production of the children of Adam as ﴿understand﴾, because the production from one soul and their transformation through their varied states is more subtle, finer in craftsmanship and management. So the mention of fiqh (deep understanding, the use of insight and precise reflection) corresponds to it. This is based on the view that fiqh is more eloquent than ʿilm (knowledge). It was also said: the two have the same meaning, except that when it was intended to close each verse with a closing phrase, to indicate that each of them stands independently with respect to the purpose of the proof, and it was disliked to close with two identical closing phrases in wording, due to repetition, a different closing phrase was adopted to beautify the composition and to show variety in eloquence.

Ibn al-Munir mentioned another reason for assigning the first to knowledge and the second to understanding. He said: since the intended purpose was to rebuke those who do not reflect on the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and do not take lesson from His creatures, and the signs mentioned first were external to the observers themselves, since the stars and contemplating them and the knowledge of the divine wisdom in arranging them are matters external to the one who observes, whereas contemplating the production of humans from one soul and their turning through different stages and varying states is not like that. It is a contemplation that does not exceed the observer himself or go beyond him. When this is established, a person's ignorance of himself and his states, and his failure to reflect and contemplate on them, is more shameful than his ignorance of external matters such as the stars, the spheres, and the measures of their movement and their changes. Since fiqh is the lowest degree of knowledge, as it is an expression for comprehension, it was negated, by way of rebuke, from the more shameful of the two groups in ignorance, namely those who do not look insightfully into themselves. And negating the lower is more shameful than negating the higher, so it was applied to the worse of the two groups in condition. Here ﴿yafqahūn﴾ is the present tense of faqiha the thing, with a kasra on the qaf, when one understands it even at the lowest level of understanding. It is not from fuqiha with a damma, because that is a high rank and means "became a faqīh (jurist)." He then mentioned that if it is said, "So-and-so does not understand anything (lā yafqahu shay'an)," this is more blameworthy in common usage than your saying, "So-and-so does not know anything (lā yaʿlamu shay'an)." The meaning of your saying "he does not understand anything" is that he lacks the capacity for understanding even if he understands; but as for your saying "he does not know anything," its extent is that knowledge has not been acquired by him, and he may have the capacity for understanding and knowledge if he were to learn. The argument that the one who abandons reflection on himself is more ignorant and in a worse state than the one who abandons reflection on others is drawn from His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾. ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ So He singled out seeing within the self after its inclusion among the signs on the earth, and He rebuked those who do not look insightfully into themselves with a new, independent rebuke. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His speech.
