Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 99 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky﴾ is a reminder of another of His magnificent blessings, which reveal the perfection of His power, exalted and majestic is He, and the vastness of His mercy. By "water" is meant rain, and by "the sky" is meant the clouds, or the phrase is elliptical, meaning "from the direction of the sky." It has also been said that the phrase is to be taken literally. Sending down from the sky, in the literal sense, means sending down to the clouds and then from them to the earth. This is the view chosen by al-Jubba'i (d. 303 AH), who argued against the view of those who say that large quantities of vapour gather in the depths of the earth, then rise and ascend into the air, where clouds form from them, and they drip as water, which is the rain that is sent down. He gave several arguments:

First: hail sometimes occurs in hot weather, indeed in the height of summer, whereas rain is found in the coldest weather and falls unfrozen. This refutes what was mentioned.

Second: when vapours rise and ascend, they disperse, and when they disperse, drops of water are not formed from them. Vapour only gathers when it meets a smooth ceiling, as in some bathhouses. If this is not the case, no considerable amount of water flows from it. Therefore, if vapours ascend into the air with no smooth surface above them to which they can attach, then nothing of water should result from them.

Third: if the formation of rain came from the rising of vapours, these would be constantly rising from the seas, and so rain should constantly fall there. Since this is not the case, we know that that view is false.

Then he said: "These people (the philosophers) only needed this view because they believed that bodies are eternal, and therefore increase and decrease cannot enter them. In that case there is no meaning to the occurrence of events except the attribution of a new attribute to those essences after they had been characterised by another attribute. For this reason they needed to explain the creation of everything from a specific material. As for the Muslims, since they believe that bodies are originated, and that the Creator of the world is a free, choosing agent, capable of creating bodies however and whenever He wills, there is no need here to devise these artificial explanations. Since the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that water is sent down from the sky, and there is no proof that this apparent meaning is impossible, it is necessary to take it in that sense." End of quotation.

It is not hidden from anyone who consults the books of these people that they answered all of those arguments. What led them to this view was not merely what was mentioned, but also their view that the rending and rejoining of the heavens is impossible, the existence of a sphere of fire beneath the sky, the cessation of the world of the elements at that point, and the observation of someone on a lofty mountain seeing a cloud raining while no water is seen descending from the sky to him, along with other things. Although some of this has been shown to be false by the revealed law, and some of it has not been established as false by the revealed law and the law does not testify to its soundness, nevertheless the observation of the one on the mountain and similar things requires the soundness of their view in general. I see no harm in it.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "There is no drop that falls except that with it is an angel." This, according to most scholars, is to be taken in its apparent sense. The philosophers interpret this angel as the nature inherent in that corporeal substance which necessitates that descent. It has also been said that it is a pure light, detached from matter, subsisting by itself, governing the drop and preserving it. Plato affirms this pure light for every kind of celestial sphere, star, simple element, and their compounds, according to what the master of Illumination (Suhrawardi) held, and it is one of the views concerning the Platonic Forms. The words of Shaykh Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi in his commentary on al-Fatiha point to something similar.

﴿Water﴾ is in the accusative as the object of ﴿sent down﴾. The direct object which is not explicit is placed before it, as has been noted many times before. ﴿So We brought forth with it﴾, that is, by means of the water. The fa' (so) indicates sequence, and the sequence of each thing is according to its nature. ﴿We brought forth﴾ is coordinated with ﴿sent down﴾. The shift to the first-person plural (iltifat, a shift of grammatical person) shows complete care for the matter for which the water was sent down. Some scholars have mentioned a special point for this shift other than what has been stated, namely that He, glory be to Him, when He mentioned earlier what alerts you that He is the Creator, required that attention be directed toward Him so that He might be addressed. The choice of the pronoun of majesty ("We") rather than the singular pronoun is to show complete care. That is: "So We brought forth, by Our majesty, with that water, though it is one, ﴿the plants of every kind﴾," that is, every category of the various types of plants, differing in quantity, quality, properties, and effects, in varying degrees of increase and decrease, as His words, glory be to Him, make clear: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾.

"Plant" (nabat) is like "growth" (nabt). According to al-Raghib (al-Isfahani), it is what comes out of the earth among growing things, whether it has a stalk like a tree or has no stalk like a star-plant (najm). However, in common usage it has come to be restricted to what has no stalk, and among the common people it is restricted to what animals eat. When the real meanings are considered, it is used for everything that grows, whether plant, animal, or human. According to some, the meaning here is the first one.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿So We brought forth from it green [shoots]﴾, are taken as the beginning of the detailed explanation of what was stated in general terms about the bringing forth. He began with the detailed state of the star-plant (najm). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the plant. ﴿Khadir﴾ (green) is in the sense of ﴿akhdar﴾ (green), like a'war and awar (one-eyed). "Khadir" is used most often of what has green colour by nature. The basic meaning of greenness is a colour between white and black, closer to black; for this reason green is called black and vice versa. The meaning is: "So We brought forth from the plant that has no stalk something tender and green," namely what branches off from the root of the plant emerging from the seed.

It is also permitted for the pronoun to refer to the water, with "from" (min) being causal. Abu al-Baqa' considered this sentence in that case a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿We brought forth﴾. Some verifying scholars mentioned that, if the pronoun refers to the water, the verse contains a wonderful meaning, since it includes an indication that He, exalted is He, brought forth from the sweet, white water, in appearance, kinds of plants and fruits differing in tastes and colours. To this the poet alluded when describing rain: "It stretches over the horizons its white threads, and from them weaves green for the dry earth around it." His words, exalted is He, ﴿We bring forth from it﴾, are an attribute of ﴿green﴾. The present tense is used to make the scene present with all its strangeness. It is also permitted that the clause be independent: "We bring forth from that green a grain piled up," that is, some of it above others, as in the ear of grain (sunbul). It has been read as ﴿There comes forth from it grain piled up﴾.

﴿And from the palm trees﴾: "palm trees" is the plural of "palm" (nakhl), as al-Raghib said. "Palm" is well known and is used for both singular and plural. This is the beginning of the detailed explanation of the state of the trees, following the explanation of the state of the star-plant according to some. The prepositional phrase is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam). His words, glory be to Him, ﴿from its spathes﴾ are a substitute for it, a partial substitute (badal ba'd min kull) with the governing verb repeated. His words, glory be to Him, ﴿clusters﴾ are the subject (mubtada'), and the sense is: "from the spathes of the palm there are clusters." It is also permitted that the predicate be omitted, the implied element being ("We brought forth"), a verb of general existence, to which the prepositional phrase is attached. The estimate is: "and We bring forth from its spathes clusters." According to the reading mentioned above, ﴿clusters﴾ is coordinated with ﴿grain﴾. It has also been said that the meaning is: "We brought forth from the palm trees a palm whose spathes are clusters, and from the palm trees something of its spathes are clusters." "Qinwan" is the plural of "qinw," meaning a bunch (idhq), which for dates is like the cluster for grapes. Its dual is also "qinwan," and nothing distinguishes the dual from the plural except the case endings. There are no singular nouns whose dual and plural are the same except three: hadha, sinw and sinwan, ri'd and ri'dan, meaning "like," as Ibn Khalawayh said. Sibawayh recorded shiqd and shiqdan, and hushsh and hushshan, meaning "garden." This was transmitted by al-Jalal al-Suyuti in al-Muzhir. It has been read with the qaf vowelled with a damma and with a fatha, as a collective noun (ism jam'), because fi'lan is not among the patterns of broken plurals.

﴿Hanging low﴾ (daniya) means near to the one reaching for it, as al-Zajjaj said. Mention of its opposite is omitted because the opposite is indicated by it, and because of the added favour in it. It has been said that the meaning is "near to the earth" due to the abundance of its fruit and the heaviness of its load. Nearness, according to both views, is literal. It is possible that it means ease of reaching its fruit, metaphorically.

﴿And gardens of grapes﴾ is coordinated with ﴿the plants of every kind﴾. That is: "And We brought forth with it gardens consisting of grapes." Al-Wahidi made it coordinated with ﴿green﴾. Al-Tibi said: "The more apparent view is that it is coordinated with ﴿grain﴾, because His words, glory be to Him, ﴿the plants of every kind﴾ are an explanation, since it includes every kind of growing thing. The growing things are grain, seeds, and the like. His words, glory be to Him, ﴿So We brought forth from it green [shoots]﴾ and what follows are an explanation of that plant, and it is a substitute for the first ﴿So We brought forth﴾, a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal)." It has been said: "This is based on the view that the plant means the general sense, and in that case it is not good to coordinate it with it, because it is included in it. If what has no stalk is meant, it is necessarily coordinated with it, because it is not included in it, and it is necessary to supply another verb for His words, glory be to Him, ﴿and from the palm trees﴾, as has been indicated. So reflect."

Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī, may God ennoble his countenance, and Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ﴿and gardens﴾ in the nominative, as the subject: "and for you" or "then there are gardens" or something similar. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be coordinated with ﴿clusters﴾. In al-Taqrib he said: "In this there is an issue, because if it is coordinated with that, then ﴿of grapes﴾ is either an attribute of ﴿gardens﴾, which corrupts the meaning, since the meaning becomes 'and from the palm trees, there are gardens produced from grapes,' or it is the predicate of ﴿gardens﴾, which is not correct, because it would be a coordination of a singular with a sentence, and the subject would be indefinite, which is not correct." In al-Kashf it says that the second is far from what is understood from al-Zamakhshari's wording, although the answer is possible that coordinating with what is specified is itself specified, as Ibn Malik said, citing the verse: "With me is patience, and complaint is with my slayer; so has anyone heard of a stranger thing than this?" The more apparent view is the first, but it coordinates a sentence with a sentence. It is estimated as "and something produced from green, or from vine, or the result is gardens from grapes," without its complement, because restriction is necessary, as has been verified in coordinating a single noun alone. It is not hidden that this is an unnecessary strain. Perhaps the mention of "gardens" here, as has been said, without being satisfied with the generic noun as in what precedes and what follows, is because benefit from this kind is generally not obtained except when a group of its members gather together.

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate﴾ is in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas), because these two kinds are particularly esteemed among them. Or it is in the accusative as coordinated with ﴿plant﴾.

His words, glory be to Him, ﴿resembling one another and not resembling﴾ are either a circumstantial clause (hal) of ﴿the olive﴾, since it precedes, and the circumstance of what is coordinated with it is omitted in favour of it. The estimate is: "and the olive resembling and not resembling, and the pomegranate likewise." Or it is a circumstantial clause of ﴿the pomegranate﴾, since it is nearer, and the first is supplied like it. In either case there is an implied addition, which is "some of it": "some of that resembling and some of it not resembling," in shape, quantity, colour, taste, and other attributes that indicate the perfection of the power of its Maker and the wisdom of its Originator and Creator, exalted is His majesty. Otherwise the meaning would be "all of it resembling and all of it not resembling," which is not valid. Some have permitted that it be a circumstance of both, with the requirement of an interpretation. Here the verb-forms ifta'ala and tafa'ala have the same meaning, as in istawa and tasawa (both meaning "to be equal"). It has been read as ﴿resembling one another and not resembling﴾.

﴿Look﴾ is a look of consideration and insight. ﴿At its fruit﴾, that is, the fruit of that, namely the olive and the pomegranate, and what is meant is their trees. Previously, the fruit itself was meant, so there is a double usage (istikhdam, a rhetorical device in which one word carries two meanings). According to al-Farra', the meaning in the first is the olive tree and the pomegranate tree, and in that case there is no double usage. In any case, the pronoun refers back to them by interpreting them as a demonstrative. Its reference to each one of them separately, as alternatives, is far-fetched and has no parallel in leaving the reference of the pronoun unspecified.

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 99 (part 2 of 2):

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to everything mentioned earlier, under the interpretation stated above, so as to include the palm and other fruit-bearing things. ﴿When it bears fruit﴾, that is, when it brings forth its fruit: how it brings it forth meagre, hardly fit to be benefited from. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (ثُمُرِهِ) with a dammah on the thaa', which is the plural of thamarah, like khashabah and khushub, or the plural of thimar, like kitab and kutub. ﴿And its ripening﴾, that is, to the state of its ripeness or its ripe condition: how it returns large, of great benefit and complete delight. Originally it is a verbal noun of yana'a, said of fruit when it has ripened. It has also been said to be the plural of yani', like tajir and tujur. It was read with a dammah, which is a dialect form of it. Ibn Muhaysin read (ويانِعِهِ). It is not hidden that restricting the statement to ﴿when it bears fruit﴾, as we have indicated, carries an implication that the fruit-bearing tree at that stage is weak and not beneficial, thus contrasting with the state of ripeness. The complete difference points to complete power. It is related from al-Zamakhshari that he said: If you ask, why was it not said "to its tender fruit and its ripening"? I say: this style has a benefit, namely that ripening is coordinated with fruit in a manner of special emphasis, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and Jibril and Mika'il﴾, to indicate that ripening is preferable to tenderness. It has a sound aspect, even if it is hidden from some observers.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ is a reference to what they were commanded to look upon. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is as has passed more than once. ﴿Are signs﴾, great or numerous, indicating the existence of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, and His oneness. ﴿For a people who believe﴾.

99
- That is, they seek faith in Allah, the Exalted, as al-Qadi said, or they are believers in actuality. Their specific mention is because they are the ones who benefited from this, not others, as it has been said. The way the aforementioned indicates the existence of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, and His oneness is that the coming into being of those diverse kinds and branching types from a single root, and their transition from state to state in a wondrous pattern, must be through the origination of a Maker who knows their details, prefers among the possible options what His wisdom requires over others, and is not obstructed by an opposing rival or a competing equal,

[p. 241]

Then, after He (glorified be He) had mentioned these magnificent blessings, which indicate His oneness, He rebuked those who associated others with Him, and He answered them with His words, exalted is His majesty: ﴿And they made﴾ in their belief ﴿for Allah﴾, whose state is what He detailed within these verses, ﴿partners﴾ in divinity (ulūhiyya) or lordship (rubūbiyya), ﴿the jinn﴾, that is, the angels, since they worshipped them and said: they are the daughters of Allah, glorified be He. Their being named "jinn" is metaphorical, due to their being concealed (ijtinān) and hidden (istitār) from the eyes, like the jinn. In describing them by this, there is a belittling of their rank in relation to the station of divinity.

This is narrated from Qatada and al-Suddi. Some of the speakers' statements imply that the jinn literally include the angels. It was also said that the intended meaning is the devils (shayāṭīn), narrated from al-Hasan. The meaning of "making them partners" is that they obeyed them as Allah, exalted is He, is obeyed, or that they worshipped the idols through their enticement and incitement.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the verse was revealed concerning the zindīqs (heretics) who said: Allah, exalted is He, is the creator of people, livestock, animals and beasts, while Iblis is the creator of predators, snakes, scorpions and evils. So, by "the jinn" is meant Iblis and his followers, who commit evils and cast evil whisperings into human souls. These are the Magians, who hold to light and darkness, and they have in this matter statements that hearing rejects and souls recoil from.

The Imam asserted that this is the best of the interpretations mentioned for the verse. As for the two objects of (ja'ala, "made"): it was said they are (lillāh, "for Allah") and (shurakā'a, "partners"), and (al-jinn, "the jinn") is either in the accusative governed by an implied verb, which came as an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: whom did they make partners? So it was said: the jinn. Or it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for (shurakā'a), and the substituted element is not entirely dropped. The second object is placed first because it is the locus of denial, and because the first object is an indefinite (munkar) that deserves to be delayed. It was also said that the two are (shurakā'a) and (al-jinn), and placing the second before the first is to magnify the idea that a partner of any kind should be taken for Allah, glorified be He. And (lillāh) is related to (shurakā'a), and placing it before it is for the same rhetorical point mentioned, as chosen by al-Zamakhshari.

(al-Jinnu) was read in the nominative, as if it were said: who are they? So it was said: the jinn. And in the genitive, as an idāfa of specification (al-idāfa allatī hiya li-l-tabyīn): ﴿and He created them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hāl) from the subject of (ja'alū, "they made"), with or without the particle (qad), depending on the two opinions, emphasizing the monstrousness and falsehood of their making such, in view of their knowledge of its content, that is: while they knew that Allah, exalted is He, alone created them. It was also said the pronoun refers to the jinn, meaning: and the situation is that He, exalted is He, created the jinn; so how can they make His creation a partner to Him? The first view was preferred because it is free from scattering of pronouns. The Imam preferred the second, because returning a pronoun to the nearest mentioned item is obligatory, and because when the pronoun returns to this nearest item, the single word becomes a decisive, complete and perfect proof in refuting the false doctrine.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (wa-khalqahum), in the form of a verbal noun (maṣdar), in coordination with (al-jinn), meaning: and what they fashion of idols. Or in coordination with (shurakā'a), meaning: and they made for Him their fabrication of abominations, attributing them to Him, glorified be He, and saying: Allah commanded us with them.

﴿And they invented falsehood for Him﴾, that is, they fabricated and forged for Him, glorified be He. Al-Farra' said: it is said: khalaqa al-ifk, ikhtalaqahu, kharaqahu and ikhtarahu, with the same meaning. It is related from al-Hasan that he was asked about this and said: it is an Arabic expression that the Arabs used to say; when a man told a lie in the assembly of a people, one of them would say to him: "he has invented it, by Allah."

al-Raghib said: the root of kharq is cutting something in a corrupt manner without reflection or deliberation, and from it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Did you sink it to drown its people?﴾ It is the opposite of khalq (creating), which is doing something with measure and gentleness, whereas kharq is without measure. The Exalted said: ﴿and they invented for Him﴾, meaning they judged this in the manner of kharq and in the sense of cutting.

Nafi' read (wa-kharraqū), with the doubling of the rā' for intensification. Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, read (wa-harrafū), from tahrīf (distortion), meaning: and they falsely attributed to Him ﴿sons and daughters﴾. The Jews said: Uzayr is the son of Allah; the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah; the Arabs said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. Allah, glorified be He, is exalted above what they say, without knowledge of its reality, whether through error or correctness, and without thought or deliberation concerning it; rather they said it out of blindness and ignorance, or ﴿without knowledge﴾ of the rank of what they said and of how far it is from the bounds of propriety.

In any case, the prepositional phrase is related to an implied verb which came as a circumstantial clause from the waw (of "they"), or as a qualifier of an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: they invented falsehood while being in a state of ignorance, or an invention existing without knowledge. The aim, according to both views, is to blame them for ignorance. It was also said that this is a metaphor (kināya) for the negation of what they said, since what has no basis cannot be known, nor can evidence be established for it, and there is no need for it, because its negation is known from calling it fabrication and forgery, and from the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they describe﴾

100

[from what they attribute to Him, that He, exalted is His majesty, has a partner or a son. The discussion of (subḥān, "glory be") and what it conveys of hyperbole in declaring Allah free of imperfection has already preceded. (Ta'ālā, "exalted") is coordinated with the implied verb that governs (subḥān) in the accusative.]

The Imam distinguished between tasbīḥ (glorification) and ta'ālī (exaltation) in that the former relates to the statements of those who glorify, while the latter relates to His essential attributes which belong to His own essence, glorified be He, and not to anything else. What is meant by "sons" in what preceded is more than one, or it is that whoever permits one permits many.

[p. 242]

**Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, commentary on surah 6, verse 101:**

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, the one who originates them and brings them into existence without an instrument, without matter, without time, and without place. This is what al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said. Just as *badi'* applies to the one who originates, it also applies to the thing originated, in the sense of the passive participle (*ism maf'ul*, passive participle). From this comes the expression *rikun badi'* (a fine, novel thing). Likewise, *al-bid'* with a kasra on the *ba'* is said of both.

It has also been said that it is the idafa (construct phrase, the attributing of a noun to a following noun) of a *sifa mushabbaha* (resembling adjective) to its agent, lightened after its nasb (accusative), by likening it to the active participle, as is well known. That is, [the meaning is] "originator of His heavens and His earth," from *bada'a*, when something is of a wondrous pattern, an extraordinary form, and a delightful beauty. Or it is an idafa to a zarf (adverbial of place or time), as in the saying of people, "Fulan is *thabt al-ghadar*," meaning "steadfast in treachery." Here *ghadar* is with a dotted *ghayn*, and the *dal* and *ra'* are unpointed, and it means a place full of stones and cracks. They say this when a man is steadfast in fighting or in speech. The intended meaning of "originator of the heavens and the earth" is that He, glorified is He, has no counterpart in them.

The meaning of this, according to what some verifiers said, is that His origination of them has no parallel, because they are the greatest of the visible creations. So it is not objected that negating a counterpart in them does not require negating it absolutely. There is no need for the strained reading that the verse is given as a rebuttal of the polytheists according to their claim that there is no existent outside of them. Many have preferred the first interpretation, and the meaning according to it is that He, exalted is He, is the originator of the two realms of the upper and lower world without any agent matter at all, exalted absolutely above being affected. The begetter is the source of the offspring and is affected by the transfer of its matter from itself. So how could it be possible for Him to have a child?

It has been read *badi'a* with a fatha, as a praise, and with a kasra, as a *badal* (substitute) of the glorious Name or of the pronoun in the genitive in "Glorified is He," according to the view of those who permit it. Its nominative in the well-known reading has three possibilities, as Abu al-Baqa said. The first is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject. The second is that it is the agent of *ta'ala* (exalted is He), and its being stated explicitly in place of the pronoun is to give a reason for the ruling, and the placing of the zarf between it and the verb is for the sake of emphasis on its explanation. The third is that it is the subject, whose predicate is the saying of Him, glorified is He: "How can He have a child?" On the first two, it is an independent sentence, brought in just as the preceding one was, to show the impossibility of what they attributed to Him, exalted is He, and to affirm His transcendence above it, majestic is His station.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has no consort﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) confirming the impossibility mentioned, since a child cannot exist without a mother at all, even if its existence without a father is possible. That is: from where and how could He have a child when He has no consort from whom the child would come?

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read *lam yakun* with a masculine verb, and this is permitted despite the nominative being feminine, because of the separation, as in the verse:

*"Indeed the mother of evil bore al-Akhtal, on the nape of whose rump are a hard lump and a mole."*

Ibn Jinni said: verbs are made feminine to match the feminine nature of their agent, because the two act as one word, since each is not independent of its partner. So when they are separated, it is permitted to make the verb masculine, and this is easier in the case of *kana* (to be), because if you omit it, what follows it stands on its own.

It has also been said that the subject of *yakun* is a pronoun referring to Him, exalted is He, and the predicate is the zarf, with *sahiba* (consort) raised by it as its agent, because it depends on the subject; the zarf is the predicate placed before, and *sahiba* is the subject, and the clause is the predicate of *yakun*. On this view the noun may be a pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), since the clause is then suitable to explain the pronoun. It is not so on the first view, because, as is explained in its proper place, it is only explained by an explicit clause. The objection that, if the main element of the explaining clause is feminine, the implied pronoun is that of the story and not of the matter, so the question returns, is not a valid one, as there is no necessity; and some have imagined otherwise.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He created every thing﴾ is either a resumption to establish the impossibility mentioned, or another circumstantial clause confirming it, that is: how can He have a child when He has created every thing among the existents, among which is what they called a child? So how can the created be imagined to be a child of its Creator?

From the Tafsir al-Kabir (al-Tafsir al-Kabir, the great commentary of al-Razi) it is understood that whoever claims that God, exalted is His state, has a child, if he means that He brought him into being by way of origination without a prior drop of seed, for example, is answered: His creation of the heavens and the earth is of this same kind, so they would necessarily be His children, which is false by consensus. If he means what is known of begetting among animals, he is answered first: He has no consort, and that is a necessary thing in what is known. Second: obtaining a child in that way is only valid for one who is not able to create, originate, and bring into being all at once. But one who is the creator of all possibilities and capable of all originated things, when He wills something, says to it "Be," and it is: so the bringing into being of a person by way of begetting is impossible for Him. If he means a third concept, then it is not conceivable.

﴿And He is Knower of all things﴾: it is of His nature that every thing is known, whether it is created or uncreated, as the replacement of the pronoun by the explicit noun indicates. ﴿Knower (*alim*)﴾ is intensive in knowledge, pre-eternally and everlastingly, as the shift to the nominal sentence indicates. Accordingly, the child is either eternal or originated. It is impossible that it be eternal, because the eternal must be necessarily existent in itself (*wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi*, existing necessarily by its own essence), and whatever is like that is independent of other than itself, so it is impossible for it to be a child of another. Thus it is necessarily originated. There is no doubt that He, exalted is He, knows all things; so either He knows that in obtaining the child there is for Him a perfection or a benefit, or He knows that there is not. If the first, then no time can be supposed but that the motive for bringing this child into being was already present before it, and that would necessitate its being eternal, which is impossible. If the second, then it is necessary that it never comes into being at any time whatsoever.

The Imam (al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him) established the refutation through this sentence in another way as well. Some made this sentence, together with what precedes it, comprise one of the aspects of the refutation. The sentence is either circumstantial or a resumption. Some confined themselves to the second, and said: it is a resumption confirming the content of what precedes it of the decisive proofs against their hideous doctrine, which they dared to hold without knowledge. The apparent meaning of this is that what is in the verse is decisive proofs against the falsehood of what the fabricators claimed. The words of the Imam, after establishing the aspects, are: "If the first and the last came together to mention in this question a speech equal to it," that is, equal to what the verse indicates in strength and perfection, "they would be unable to produce it." Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) claimed that what is understood from it is persuasive proofs. Perhaps the better view is to say that some of it is decisive and some of it persuasive. So reflect.

﴿Dhalikum﴾ (That is) refers to the one described by the sublime attributes mentioned, and the distance implied in it is as explained many times before. The address is to the particular polytheists already known, by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person).

Al-Tabarsi held that it addresses all people. [He read it as] the subject (*mubtada'*), and the words of God, the Exalted, ﴿Allah, your Lord; there is no god but Him, the Creator of all things﴾ are four synonymous predicates (*akhbar*). That is: that One described by those magnificent attributes is Allah, the one deserving worship exclusively, the Owner of your affairs, with no partner whatsoever, the Creator of all things that have existed and will exist. The matter regarded in the subject, as the demonstrative indicates, is only His creation of what has already existed, as the past tense form indicates. It has been permitted that the majestic Name be an apposition (*badal*) to the demonstrative, with ﴿your Lord﴾ as its adjective and what follows as the predicate; or that the majestic Name be the predicate and what follows be an apposition to it; or that it be an apposition while the rest are predicates; or that a subject be assumed for each of the three predicates; or that the whole be treated as a single noun; or that ﴿Creator of all things﴾ be an apposition to the pronoun. Other possibilities have also been permitted.

As for the words of God, the Exalted, ﴿So worship Him﴾, it is a consequence (*musabbab*) of the meaning of the whole sentence, for whoever combines these attributes is, as He is, the one deserving worship exclusively. Some have claimed that the worship commanded is the utmost submission, which cannot be realized together with associating partners; therefore it was not necessary to say, "So do not worship except Him." From this it is understood that the mere concept of worship (*'ibadah*) itself conveys exclusivity. And the claim that placing the object first in ﴿Iyyaka na'budu﴾ (You alone we worship) conveys exclusivity does not contradict this, because conveying restriction in two ways (*hasr*) is prevented from being so, as in *lillahi al-hamd* (praise be to Allah) and the like.

God, the Exalted, said here, ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; there is no god but Him, the Creator of all things; so worship Him﴾, while in Surat al-Mu'min He said: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no god but Him; so how are you turned away?﴾ Here He placed ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ before ﴿Creator of all things﴾, and there it was reversed. Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) said: this verse came after His words, ﴿They attributed to Allah partners, the jinn﴾, etc. So when He said, majestic is His affair, ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾, He followed it with what removes association, saying, mighty is He in speech, ﴿there is no god but He﴾, then ﴿Creator of all things﴾. That verse, however, came after His words, glorified is He: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people, but most people do not know﴾. So the discourse there was about establishing and affirming the creation of people, not about negating a partner from Him, majestic is His affair, as was the case in the first verse. Therefore placing ﴿Creator of all things﴾ first there is more fitting. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best the secrets of His speech.

﴿And He is Disposer (*wakil*) over all things﴾

102

- This is a conjunction (*'atf*) to the preceding sentence, meaning: He, along with those sublime attributes, is the one who manages all matters, worldly and otherworldly. It follows from this that no affair should be entrusted to anyone other than Him, from among those who do not manage affairs.

It has been permitted that this sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) and a qualifier (*qayd*) of the worship, and the meaning is interpreted as: He, the Exalted, together with what has preceded, is the manager of your affairs; so entrust them to Him, and seek nearness through His worship to the attainment of your aims. Some explained *wakil* as "watcher" (*raqib*), that is, He, the Exalted, is watchful over your deeds and will reward you for them. Our companions (the Ash'ari theologians) used the generality of ﴿Creator of all things﴾ as evidence that He, the Exalted, is the creator of the actions of servants.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school) said: here there are things that exclude the actions of servants from the scope. The first: the placing of that generality before His words, ﴿So worship Him﴾, for if the actions of servants were included there, the sense of the verse would be: "We created your actions, so do them again in their very same form"; its corruption is obvious. The second: ﴿Creator of all things﴾ is mentioned in the context of praise and commendation, and one is not praised for creating adultery, sodomy, theft, or disbelief, for example. The third: He, the Exalted, said afterward: ﴿Indeed there have come to you insights from your Lord; so whoever sees, it is for his own self, and whoever is blind, it is against it﴾, which is an explicit statement that the servant is independent in doing and abstaining, and that there is no impediment for him. The fourth: this verse came after: ﴿And they attributed to Allah partners, the jinn﴾, and what is meant by it, as reported from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas), is a refutation of the Magians (*Majus*) in affirming two gods. Therefore ﴿Creator of all things﴾ must be understood as negating that, and this is only the case if we say that He, the Exalted, is the creator of what exists in this world of beasts, pains, and the like. If it is understood in that way, the actions of servants are not included. What is in this of consideration is not hidden. Similar to it is their use of the verse as evidence for denying the attributes (of God) and for the createdness of the Qur'an. So reflect.

[Page 245]

﴿لا تُدْرِكُهُ الأبْصارُ﴾ *(No vision comprehends Him)*. *Absar* is the plural of *basar*, which, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is applied to the seeing organ, to the power within it, and to *basirah* (insight), which is the power of the heart that perceives. Perceiving (*idrak*) a thing is an expression for reaching its limit and encompassing it. Most of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) take *basar* here to mean the organ, since it is the seat of the power. It has also been said that it refers to that organ, and to the imaginations and the intellects, as Amir al-Mu'minin Ali (may Allah honor his face) said: "Tawhid is that you do not imagine it," and he also said: "Whatever you have perceived, He is other than it."

Al-Raghib transmitted from some people that they took it to mean *basirah*, and he mentioned that by this they alluded to what is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) in his saying: "O You whose ultimate knowledge is the inability to know Him! If the knowledge of You is that You know things, then know that He is not like any of them; rather He is the Originator of everything you have perceived."

The Mu'tazilah (*Mu'tazilah*, the rationalist school that denied the vision of Allah) used this verse as evidence that Allah, Exalted, cannot be seen. The explanation of this, as in *al-Mawaqif* and its commentary, is that the *idrak* attributed to the sight is in fact vision (*ru'yah*), and there is no difference between "I perceived it with my eye" and "I saw it," except in wording; or the two are mutually implicating, such that the negation of one cannot be valid together with the affirmation of the other. So it is not permissible to say "I saw Him" while denying "I perceived Him with my eye," nor the reverse. Therefore the verse negates that the eyes see Him, and this encompasses all eyes through the *lam* of the genus (*al-lam al-jinsiyyah*) in a context of emphasis, at all times. For your saying "So-and-so is perceived by the eyes" does not convey the generality of all times, so it must be conveyed by what opposes it. Thus no eye sees Him, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, for the reason mentioned. Also, Allah, Exalted, is praised by being unseen, since He mentioned it amid praises. And whatever attribute's absence is a praise, its presence would be a deficiency, from which Allah, Exalted, must be declared free. It is therefore clear that His vision, glory be to Him, is impossible. The phrase "from among the attributes" is said to exclude acts such as pardoning and retribution, for the former is grace and the latter is justice, and both are perfection. End of quotation. Its summary is that by *idrak* is meant absolute vision, not vision in the manner of encompassment; and that "the eyes do not perceive Him" is a universal negative, perpetual. This is the strongest of their transmitted proofs on this question, as our teacher, the Shaykh al-Kurani (may his secret be sanctified), mentioned.

The response to this is in several respects. First: *idrak* is not absolute vision, even if al-Amidi, Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, chose it according to what he transmitted; rather it is vision in the manner of encompassing the sides of the seen object, as Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) explained it in one of his two interpretations. In *al-Durr al-Manthur* it is recorded that Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding "No vision comprehends Him": no one's sight encompasses Allah, Exalted. End of quotation. Much of the linguists and others went this way. Vision qualified by the modality of encompassment is more specific, absolutely, than absolute vision, and the negation of the more specific does not necessitate the negation of the more general. Thus it is valid to say "I saw Him" while "what my eye perceived" means "what encompassed it from its sides," even though the converse is not valid.

Second: "No vision comprehends Him" may be understood in such a way that the negation is first applied and then the *lam* comes, so it is a universal negative in the style of His saying, Exalted: "And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants" (Qur'an 3:108). This is then for the generality of the negation. Likewise it may be understood that generality is considered first and then the negation applies to it, so it is a particular negative, as in: "Not all the slaves stood up," and "I did not take all the dirhams." This is for negating the generality. Whenever negating the generality is possible, it is not explicit for the universality of the negation, although universality of the negation is most common in such cases. And whenever this is so, no proof remains in it against the impossibility of vision absolutely, which is evident. This is when the *alif-lam* in *al-absar* is for comprehensiveness (*al-istighraq*). If it is for the genus, then "No vision comprehends Him" is an indefinite negative (*salbiyah muhmalah*), which is in the force of a particular proposition, so the meaning becomes "Some vision does not comprehend Him," and this is agreed upon.

Third: Even if we grant that *idrak* is absolute vision, and that the *alif-lam* is for comprehensiveness, and that the speech is for the generality of the negation, we do not grant its generality in states and times, that is, we do not grant that it is perpetual. For it is possible that what is meant is the negation of vision in this world, as the restriction of it to that is narrated from al-Hasan and others.

What indicates this is what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi recorded in *Nawadir al-Usul* and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, *'My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look at You'* (Qur'an 7:143), and then said: Allah, Exalted, said: O Musa, indeed no living thing sees Me but dies, no dry thing but crumbles, and no moist thing but disperses; and only the people of Paradise see Me, those whose eyes do not die and whose bodies do not decay."

The response of those who say that it is perpetual, because your saying "So-and-so is perceived by the eyes" does not convey the generality of times, so what opposes it must convey it, is: this does not hold unless it is necessary that the opposition be from Allah, Exalted, to "Is perceived by the eyes," and "No vision comprehends Him" is a contradictory opposition. There is no requirement for that, neither rationally, nor linguistically, nor legally. As for the first (the rational): when we find an absolute affirmative proposition, it is possible that a perpetual absolute negative opposes it, and a perpetual negative opposes it; the true perpetual is not fixed except if the absolute is false with certainty. But the falsity of the absolute here is the very beginning of the investigation and the exact point in dispute. So it is not permissible to base the perpetuity of "No vision comprehends Him" on the falsity of this absolute proposition, namely "Allah is perceived by the eyes," meaning by it the eyes of the believers in Paradise and at the Standing; for that would be begging the question, which entails circularity.

As for the second: a proposition, whether affirmative or negative, is used according to the contexts, sometimes for the absolute and sometimes for the perpetual. It is not necessary in the language that, when we find an affirmative proposition used in some context in the sense of the absolute, its opposing proposition must be used in the sense of perpetuity, definitively. Rather it varies according to contexts and the intention of those who use them, and this is quite evident.

As for the third: the aforementioned absolute, in the earlier sense, is the very point of dispute between us and the Mu'tazilah legally. We say it is true legally, and we argue for it by reason and by transmitted evidence from the Book and the Sunnah. Whenever this is so, "No vision comprehends Him" must not be perpetual, to avoid contradiction. It will be either an absolute general proposition or a temporal absolute proposition. On either assumption there is no contradiction, since the unity of time is absent. So it is true that: Allah is perceived by the eyes, that is, the eyes of the believers on the Day of Resurrection, for example, or at the time of His manifestation in His light that does not leave the eyes intact. And: Allah is not perceived by the eyes, that is, in this world, with the qualification indicated earlier, or at the time of His manifestation in His light that overwhelms the eyes, which is the blazing light mentioned in the hadith in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere: "The veils of His face would burn away whatever His sight reaches." To this qualification the second of Ibn Abbas's two interpretations, the first of which was mentioned, points.

It is narrated that he said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord." Ikrimah said to him: "Does not Allah say, *'No vision comprehends Him'*?" He said: "Woe to you! That is His light, which is His light; when He manifests with His light, nothing can perceive Him." The hadith continues. By affirming these two lights, his two answers, peace be upon him, to Abu Dharr are reconciled, when he asked him: "Have you seen your Lord?" He said in one of his answers: "A light; how could I see Him?" And in the other answer: "I saw a light." It is said that the light whose seeing He negated in the rhetorical interrogation indicated by *anna* (how?) is His light, that is, the light that overwhelms the eyes and before which no sight can stand. And the light whose seeing He affirmed is the light that does not overwhelm the eyes.

Likewise it is possible to interpret the saying of Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her): "Whoever claims that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord, glory be to Him, has greatly slandered Allah, Mighty and Majestic," and her citing this verse as evidence for it, as follows: she meant, whoever claims that Muhammad, peace be upon him, saw his Lord, glory be to Him, in His light which is the light that overwhelms the eyes, has greatly slandered Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The citing of the verse is then in accordance with what is narrated from Ibn Abbas in his second interpretation. In that case the Mu'tazilah's claim that "Tudriku-hu al-absar" (*the eyes perceive Him*) is perpetual cannot hold, unless that absolute proposition is false legally, which is the very point in dispute, as you have understood. So they have no evidence at all for the claim of perpetuity.

It may also be said that what is meant is the negation of vision at the time when Allah, Exalted, does not permit the eyes to perceive. The proof of the validity of intending this qualification is that the seeing of the eyes is an act of the servants and an acquisition of theirs, and it has been established by more than one proof that the servants are not able to do anything of the things that can be done except by His permission, will and enabling. So the eyes do not perceive Him except by His permission, and this is what was sought.

This explanation is confirmed and its pillars strengthened by the fact that "No vision comprehends Him" comes after His saying, glory be to Him: "And He is over all things a Guardian" (Qur'an 6:102). The point of the confirmation is that Allah, Exalted, informed that He is over all things a *wakil*, that is, one who manages their affairs. It is known that the eyes are among things, and that their perceiving is among their affairs. So He, glory be to Him and Exalted, manages them and disposes of them according to His will. He bestows perception upon them and permits them when He wills, as He wills, and to the degree He wills. He withdraws perception from them, wholly or partly, at whatever time He wills, as He wills. Nothing is hidden from this, that it is the utmost of praise for might, dominance and triumph. For whoever is over all things a guardian, if the eyes do not perceive Him except by His permission, while He perceives the eyes and nothing is hidden from Him, this is the utmost in His might and dominance and in His being victorious over His command.

Some of the scholars (*al-muhaqqiqin*) held that the verse was not presented for praise, but for warning: that He, glory be to Him, is watchful from where He cannot be seen, so let one beware. This is evident according to the second interpretation of *wakil*.

Fourth of the aspects: it is permissible that what is meant by "No vision comprehends Him" is according to the customary manner of seeing sensible things, which is conditioned by the nine customary conditions, as the end of the verse indicates. It is known that negating the specific does not entail negating the general, so it does not follow from the verse, on this view, that vision is negated absolutely.

Fifth: What has been said is: even if we grant the opponent what he intends, we say that the verse only indicates that the eyes do not perceive Him, and we say this too, and we claim that those who possess eyes perceive Him. The objection that just as the eyes do not perceive Him, so likewise nothing else perceives Him, and so there is no benefit in the specification, is answered by the claim that the absence of benefit would follow only if the purpose were confined to negating the judgment of the stated part concerning the unstated part; and this is not granted. Perhaps it was specifically in response to a questioner about it, and not to others, or for another meaning.

**Sixth:** Even if we grant that the intended meaning is "the eyes of observers do not perceive Him with their eyes," the verse still does not establish the point at issue. It is possible that God is perceived by a **sixth sense** (*hassah sadisah*) distinct from these five senses. This is the view attributed to Dirar ibn 'Amr al-Kufi. It is reported of him that he used to say: "God, exalted is He, is not seen with the eye, but with a sixth sense which He will create for the Day of Resurrection." He argued from this verse, saying: "It indicates that the negation of God's being perceived is restricted to sight. Restricting a ruling to one thing implies that the case is different for other things. Therefore it is necessary that the perception of God by other than sight is possible in general. And since it has been established that none of the senses that exist now is suitable for this, it follows that God will create on the Day of Resurrection a sixth sense by which the vision and perception of God will occur." End of quotation.

Some people have used the verse to argue that comprehending the essence of God is impossible, on the basis that *al-absar* is the plural of *basar* meaning *basirah* (insight). He established this in the same way that the **Mu'tazilah** (the rationalist theological school) established their argument for the impossibility of vision, and there is much to be said about that. Indeed, the possibility of reading *al-basar* as *al-basirah* weakens the Mu'tazilite argument, as is clear. They have other textual proofs for this question, and God willing, we will discuss some of them later. They also have rational arguments, which scholars have already understood to be among the places of falsehood.

Perhaps the discussion will lead to the loosening of the reins of pens in the gardens of investigating this matter, if God, the King, the All-Knowing, wills. From Him comes success in grasping, by the eyes of understanding, the hidden secrets, and in splitting the dawn of truth with its shining lights.

﴿And He perceives the eyes﴾, that is, He sees them in the manner of encompassing them, or He encompasses them with knowledge, or with knowledge and vision, as has been said. Al-Amidi mentioned that the Basrian Mu'tazilah held that God's *idrak* (perception) means vision, while the Baghdadian Mu'tazilah held that it means knowledge and not vision. The word "eyes" here, as one of the verifying scholars has determined, refers to the light by which visible things are perceived, for that light is not perceived by any perceiver, unlike the body of the eye, which is seen. Perhaps this is the secret behind the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun. It has also been allowed that the meaning is that every eye cannot see itself. ﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾.

103

Therefore He, glory be to Him, perceives what the eyes cannot perceive. The sentence is brought to describe Him, exalted is He, with that which includes the justification of His words, glory be to Him: "(And He) etc."

Many have allowed that what has been mentioned is an instance of *al-laff* (the wrapping style, in which two attributes are mentioned and each corresponds to one of two items). The Subtle (*al-latif*) suits His being not perceived (with the vowel fatha on the verb, i.e., "not perceived"), and the All-Aware (*al-khabir*) suits His being perceiving (with kasra, i.e., "perceiving"). *Al-latif* is used metaphorically from the opposite of *al-kathif* (the dense), for that which is not perceived by the senses, the hidden aspect of a thing.

It is understood from the apparent sense of the words of al-Bahai, as al-Shihab said, that there is no metaphor in this. For he said in explaining the Beautiful Names of God: "*Al-Latif* is He who treats His servants with gentleness, and His gentle kindnesses, glory be to His majesty, have no limit, outwardly or inwardly, in this world or the next: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of God, you could not number it﴾." It has also been said: *al-Latif* is the All-Knowing of subtle and fine matters, of meanings and realities; for this reason one who is skilled in his craft is called *latif*.

It may also be that it comes from *al-lataafah* (subtlety), the opposite of *al-kathafah* (density). Although in ordinary usage this is among the attributes of bodies, absolute subtlety is not found in a body, because corporeality necessarily entails density; its subtlety is only relative. Therefore it is not far-fetched that absolute subtlety be attributed to the absolute Light, which is too exalted to be grasped by insights, let alone by eyes, too rare to be sensed by secrets, let alone by thoughts, too high to resemble forms and likenesses, and too pure to be inhabited by colours and shapes. For subtlety belongs only to one of this description, and describing others with it is not absolute but relative to what is lower than them in subtlety, and they are described as dense in relation to Him. End of quotation.

The preferred view is that applying *al-latif* in the sense of the opposite of *al-kathif*, in the way that comes to mind, to God, exalted is He, is not a true (literal) usage at all, as is clear.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 104:

﴿Indeed there have come to you clear evidences from your Lord.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) delivered on the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ), so that the implied word is "qul" (say), as some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) have said. "Basair" (clear evidences) is the plural of "basira" (insight), which for the heart is like sight for the eye. What is meant by them is either the signs (ayat) occurring here or all the signs, and what has been mentioned enters into this primarily. The "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghaya) in a metaphorical sense, and it is connected either to "ja'a" (has come) or to a deleted element that occurs as an attribute of "basa'ir." The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyya) together with its attribution to the pronoun of the addressees serves to show the fullness of kindness toward them. That is: indeed there has come to you from the direction of your Owner and the one who conveys to you your perfection, which is fitting for you, through the revelation that speaks the truth and the right, that which is like insights for hearts; or: indeed there have come to you evidences existing from your Lord. ﴿So whoever sees﴾ — that is, the truth through those evidences and believes in it — ﴿it is for his own self﴾ — that is, he sees for his own self, as is reported from al-Kalbi and followed by al-Zamakhshari; or "his seeing is for his own self," as Abu Hayyan chose, because of what you will learn shortly, God willing.

On both views, what is meant is that the benefit of that returns to him. ﴿And whoever is blind﴾ — that is, whoever does not see the truth after it has become clear to him through those evidences, a clear manifestation, and goes astray from it. The term "blindness" is used for it only to repel from it. ﴿Then upon it﴾ — blindness, or "its blindness is upon it," that is, the burden of that falls upon it. These are two views for those mentioned earlier. Abu Hayyan mentioned that estimating a verbal noun (masdar) is preferable for two reasons: first, that the deleted element is a single word and not a clause, and the prepositional phrase is a principal element and not a complement. Second, that if the estimated element were a verb, the "fa'" would not enter, whether "man" is conditional or relative, because it is prohibited in the past tense. It has been objected that estimating the verb is preferred because a verb explicitly stated precedes it, and it is stronger in signification; and also that in estimating it there is a fronting of the operand which indicates exclusivity; and also that what was mentioned in the second reason is not necessary,
Page 249
because the verb is not estimated as preceding the response particle; rather the object of the past verb is estimated as fronted, and the "fa'" must be present in it. So if you say: "Whoever honored Zayd, then for his own self he honored him," the "fa'" would be unavoidable. Yes, the verb "ʿamiya" has not been known to take "ʿala" as its complement, and that is the necessary consequence of the earlier estimate in the second clause; and it seems that for this reason some of them departed from it after agreeing on the first, to the phrase "fa-'alayha" — its burden.

﴿And I am not over you a guardian.﴾

104

Rather, I am only a warner, and God, the Exalted, is the One who watches over your deeds and recompenses you for them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 105:**

﴿And thus﴾, i.e., like that wondrous variation, ﴿We vary the verses﴾, which indicate meanings that are pure and that reveal sublime truths, not a variation lesser than that.

It has been said: the meaning is, just as We varied the verses before, We vary these verses. What is most worthy of acceptance has already been mentioned to you. The origin of *taṣrīf* (variation) is, as ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā said, the carrying out of a meaning that circulates among successive meanings, from *ṣarf*, which is the transfer of a thing from one state to another.

Al-Rāghib said: *taṣrīf* is like *ṣarf*, except that it denotes repetition, and it is most often used for turning a thing from one state to another and from one matter to another.

﴿And so that they may say: "You have studied"﴾ is a cause (*ʿillah*) for an action that has been omitted, relying on the indication of the context. The sense is: "and so that they may say, 'You have studied,' We do what We do of the variation mentioned." Some have assumed the verb to be in the past tense, and the matter in this is easy. The *lām* is the *lām* of consequence (*lām al-ʿāqibah*).

It is also permissible that it be a *lām* of causation in the true sense, because the sending down of the verses is for the misguidance of the wretched and the guidance of the fortunate. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He misguides many by it and guides many by it﴾. The *wāw* is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyyah*). It has also been said that it is conjunctive, coordinating with a deleted cause. The *lām* is connected to *nuṣarrifu* (We vary), i.e., like that variation We vary the verses so that the proof may be established against them, and so that they may say, etc. This is preferable to estimating "so that they may deny" and "so that they may say," etc. It has also been said that the *lām* is the *lām* of command (*lām al-amr*), and the reading with a sukūn on the *lām* supports it, as if it were said: "Thus We vary the verses, and let them say what they say," for they are of no concern and their words carry no weight. This is a command whose meaning is threat, intimidation, and disregard. Al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī, in *al-Durr al-Maṣūn*, rejected this, saying that what follows it refutes it, since the *lām* there is explicit that it is the *lām* of *kay* (in order that). The sukūn of the *lām* in the anomalous reading is no proof, since it may be for lightening.

The meaning of ﴿*darasta*﴾ is "you read" and "you learned." Its origin, as al-Aṣmaʿī said, is from their saying: "*darasa al-ṭaʿām yadrusuhu dirāsan*," when one threshes it (tramples it), as if the reciter tramples the speech so that it becomes light upon his tongue.

Abū al-Haytham said: one says "*darastu al-kitāb*," meaning I made it familiar through frequent reading until its memorizing became easy, from their saying "*darastu al-thawb adrusuhu darsan*," so it is "*madrūs*" and "*darīs*," i.e., I wore it out. From this the worn garment is called *darīs*, because it has become soft. *Al-dirsah* is practice, and from it comes "*darastu al-sūrah*," until I memorized it. This, as al-Wāḥidī said, is close to what al-Aṣmaʿī said, or is the same thing, since the meaning returns in it to softening and facilitating.

Al-Rāghib said: one says "*darasa al-dār*," meaning its trace remained, and the remaining of a trace requires its effacement in itself; therefore *al-durūs* is explained as effacement. Likewise "*darasa al-kitāb*" and "*darastu al-ʿilm*" mean I took up its trace through memorization, and since taking it up is by continuous reading, he expressed the continuation of reading by *al-dars*. This is far from what preceded it, as is not hidden.

Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read ﴿*dāraста*﴾ with an *alif* and a fatḥah on the *tāʾ*, and this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, meaning: "you have studied with others, O Muḥammad, from among those who know the past reports, and you have reminded them." They intended by this what they intended by their saying: ﴿Only a human is teaching him﴾. The Imam said: this reading is strengthened by His saying, relating from them: ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication he has invented, and others have helped him with it﴾.

Ibn ʿĀmir, Yaʿqūb and Sahl read ﴿*darasat*﴾ with a fatḥah on the *sīn* and a sukūn on the *tāʾ*, and it is related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with them.

The meaning is: these verses have come and have been effaced, and this is like their saying: "the myths of the ancients."

It has been read ﴿*darusta*﴾ with a *ḍammah* on the *rāʾ*, as an intensification of *darasta*, because the *fiʿl* of the *ḍammah* pattern is for natures and innate dispositions, i.e., its effacement has become intense. And ﴿*dursit*﴾ in the passive form, with the meaning "it was read" or "it was effaced." The coming of *ʿafā* transitively is established, just as its coming intransitively is. And ﴿*dārasat*﴾ with the feminine *tāʾ* as well. The pronoun is either for the Jews, because of their fame in study, i.e., the Jews studied with Muḥammad ﷺ, or for the verses, and it is in reality for their people, i.e., the people of the verses studied and conveyed them to Muḥammad, peace be upon him, and they are the People of the Book. ﴿*Dursit*﴾ is in the passive with an unspecified agent; ﴿*durisat*﴾ is in the passive with the second person feminine address and with shadda; it is attributed to Ibn Zayd. ﴿*Iddārasta*﴾ with shadda, active, is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās. In another narration from Ubayy: ﴿*darasa*﴾, with its attribution to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ or to the Book, in the sense of "was effaced" or similar. And ﴿*darasna*﴾ with the feminine plural *nūn*, lightened and with shadda. And ﴿*dārisāt*﴾, in the sense of "old" or "possessing study," or "possessing effacements," like ﴿*ʿīshatin rāḍiyah*﴾. Its nominative is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are *dārisāt*."

﴿And that We may make it clear﴾ is coordinated with ﴿so that they may say﴾, and the *lām* in it is the *lām* of causation, explained by the clarification of what indicates the benefit that results from the action, according to many of the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*). There is no doubt that clarification is a benefit that results from the variation. The disagreement over whether the actions of Allah, the Exalted, are caused by purposes is well known, and we have indicated it earlier. The pronoun refers to the verses by way of interpretation as the Book, or to the Qur'an, though it is not mentioned because it is known; or to the verbal noun of *nuṣarrifu*, as has been said; or *nubayyinu*, i.e., and We shall certainly perform the clarification ﴿for a people who know﴾.

[p. 250]

105

For they are the ones who benefit from it, and this is the reason for singling them out in mention. They are, as related from Ibn ʿAbbās, His friends whom He guided to the path of right direction. He described them with knowledge to announce the extreme ignorance of others and their being entirely devoid of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 106:

﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, i.e., persist in the religious practice of what has been revealed to you of the laws and rulings, the foundation of which is monotheism (tawhid). The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun, upon him be blessings and peace, is a manifestation of kindness toward him (ﷺ) that is not hidden. The prepositional phrase ("from your Lord") may be connected to (ūḥiya, "is revealed"); it may be a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the implicit subject pronoun in it (the passive verb's pronoun); and it may be a circumstantial phrase from its referent.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿There is no god but He﴾ may be a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) between the conjunct and the conjoined, by which the obligation of following is emphasized, especially in the matter of monotheism. Abu al-Baqa' and others permitted that it be an emphatic circumstantial phrase (ḥāl mu'akkidah) of ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: alone in divinity. ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾.

- That is, do not give weight to their false statements, among which is what was related about them just before, do not be concerned with them, and do not turn to their harm. According to this, there is no abrogation (naskh) in the verse. It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is abrogated by the verse of the sword, so that turning away is understood as encompassing refraining from them.

Verse 107 of Surah al-An'am (6): "Had Allah willed, they would not have associated others with Him" (﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ ... ﴿ما أشْرَكُوا﴾).

Al-Alusi: The words "Had Allah willed, they would not have associated" (﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما أشْرَكُوا﴾) refer to their not associating partners. This is evidence for the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) that God Most High does not will the faith of the disbeliever. However, this does not mean that God prevents him from it while directing Himself toward him; rather, it means that God does not will it from him because of his bad choice, which arises from his bad preparedness (istidad). The sentence is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) that emphasizes the turning away (i'raD). Likewise is the saying of God Most High: "We did not make you a guardian over them" (﴿وما جَعَلْناكَ عَلَيْهِمْ حَفِيظًا﴾), meaning a watchful overseer (raqib muhaymin) from Our side, who guards their deeds over them; and likewise the saying of the Glorified: "Nor are you a custodian over them" (﴿وما أنْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِوَكِيلٍ﴾).

107

- From their side, you take charge of their affairs and manage their interests. It was also said: the meaning of "We did not make you a guardian over them" is that you protect them from what harms them, and "Nor are you a custodian over them" means you bring to them what benefits them. The word "over them" (ʿalayhim) in both places is connected to what follows it, and it was placed before it either for emphasis on it (lil-ihtimam bihi) or to observe the rhyme of the verse endings (li-ri'ayat al-fawasil).

[Page 251]

﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides Allah﴾, that is, do not insult them or mention them with ugliness. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) may refer either to the polytheists, meaning: do not revile them in respect of their worship of their deities, such as saying "Ruin to you and to what you worship," for example; or to their deities. In that case the verse is explicit in forbidding reviling them. The returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is then understood, meaning: those whom you invoke.

The expression "those" (alladhina) is used for them on the basis of the polytheists' claim that they are rational beings, or by way of taghlib (prevalence of the rational), including the angels, the Messiah and 'Uzayr, peace be upon them. It has been said that reviling the deities is reviling those who worship them, just as it is said, "striking the beast is slapping its rider." ﴿Lest they revile Allah in enmity﴾, that is, transgressing from the truth into falsehood. Its accusative form is because it is a emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and that it be a verbal noun (masdar) from a source other than the verb itself. "Yasubbu" (they revile) is in the accusative as the answer to the prohibition (jawab al-nahy). It has also been said that it is in the jussive by coordination (al-'atf), like their saying: "Do not stretch it, lest you tear it."

The meaning of their reviling Allah, glorified and exalted, is that their speech leads to it, like their insulting him, ﷺ, and the one who commands him. ﴿Without knowledge﴾ has been explained in this sense, that is: they revile Allah, exalted, without knowing that they are reviling Him. Otherwise, the people used to acknowledge Allah, exalted, and His greatness, and that their deities were only worshipped so that they would be intercessors for them with Him, glorified be He. How then would they revile Him? It is possible that what is meant is their explicit reviling of Him, mighty is His name; there is no difficulty on the basis that anger and rage carry them to that. Do you not see that the Muslim may be carried by the intensity of his rage to utter disbelief?

Among what we have witnessed: some of the ignorant common folk, most of the Rafidah (Rafidites), reviled al-Shaykhayn (the two Shaykhs, Abu Bakr and 'Umar), may Allah be pleased with them both, in his presence. This greatly enraged him, so he reviled 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. He was asked about that and said: "I only intended to enrage them, and I did not find anything that enrages them like that." He was then made to repent of this great ignorance.

Al-Raghib said: their reviling of Allah, exalted, is not that they revile Him, glorified be His majesty, explicitly; rather, they delve into the mention of Allah, exalted, and persist in that through disputation, and increase in describing Him, glorified be His name, with what is far above Him. Persistence in disbelief and obstinacy may also be considered reviling, and it is a practical reviling. The poet said:

*"The fault of the Banu Malik was not that one of them reviled a youth, so he was reviled with a white [sword], notched, cutting, that cleaves the bones and peels the sinew."*

It alludes thereby to what the other said:

*"We revile with deeds, not with speech."*

It has also been said: what is meant by reviling Allah, exalted, is reviling the Messenger, ﷺ, and a similar case in this respect is His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾, and the verse.

Ya'qub read ("'udūwan") and it is said: "'adā fulān ya'dū 'adwan wa 'udūwan wa 'udwānan."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: "When Abu Talib's death drew near, Quraysh said: 'Come, let us enter upon this man and command him to forbid his nephew from us, for we are ashamed to kill him after his death, lest the Arabs say: he used to protect him.' When he died, they killed him. So Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya and Ubayy, the two sons of Khalaf, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Aswad ibn al-Bukhturi set out to Abu Talib and said: 'You are our elder and our chief, and Muhammad has harmed us and harmed our deities, so we wish you would call him and forbid him from mentioning our deities, and we will leave him and his God.' So he called him, and the Prophet, ﷺ, came. Abu Talib said to him: 'These are your people and the sons of your paternal uncle.' The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, said: 'What do you want?' They said: 'We want you to leave us and our deities, and we will leave you and your God.' Abu Talib said: 'Your people have been fair to you, so accept from them.' The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, said: 'Tell me, if I give you this, will you give me a word which, if you say it, you will rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs will submit to you by it?' Abu Jahl said: 'Yes, we will indeed give it to you, and to your father, and ten times its like. What is it?' He said: 'Say: There is no god but Allah.' They refused and recoiled. Abu Talib said: 'Say something other than it, O nephew, for your people have been alarmed by it.' He, ﷺ, said: 'O uncle, I am not one who says anything other than it, even if they brought me the sun and placed it in my hand, I would not say other than it.' They said: 'Either you cease reviling our deities, or we will revile you and revile whoever commands you.' So Allah, exalted, revealed this verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "They said: 'O Muhammad, either you desist from reviling our deities, or we will indeed revile your Lord.' So Allah, exalted, forbade them to revile their idols." In another narration from him, they said this at the revelation of the saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾, and then ﴿And do not revile﴾ was revealed, etc. This was questioned on the ground that describing their deities as the fuel of Hell, and as not harming or benefiting, is itself reviling them, so how was it forbidden in what is here? It was answered that if they intend by recitation their reviling and their rage, the prohibition regarding them is consistent, and there is nothing strange in that, just as recitation is forbidden in disliked places.

Al-Kashshaf says: the meaning on this narration is that reviling does not come from you, on the basis of what occurred in the verse, so it becomes reviling in return for their reviling. It has been said: what is in the verse does not count as reviling, because it mentioned their faults merely for the sake of belittling and humiliating them, and what is in it was only given to demonstrate their unfitness for divinity and worship. Consider this. Close to this is what has been said: the prohibition in reality is only against departing from argument into reviling, as if it were said: do not go out from calling the disbelievers and disputing with them into reviling what they worship besides Allah, exalted, for that is not part of argumentation at all, and it leads to the reviling of Allah, mighty and majestic.

The verse has been cited as evidence that when obedience leads to a greater disobedience, it is obligatory to abandon it, for what leads to evil is evil. This is in contrast to obedience in a situation where there is a disobedience that cannot be averted; the two often resemble each other. For this reason Ibn Sirin did not attend a funeral in which men and women gathered, and al-Hasan disagreed with him, saying: "If we abandoned obedience because of disobedience, that would quickly spread in our religion, for the two are distinct."

Al-Shihab quoted from al-Maqdisi in al-Ramz that the correct view among our jurists is that one does not abandon what is sought because of the concomitance of an innovation, such as abandoning accepting an invitation because of what it contains of diversions, or the funeral prayer for a wailing woman. If one is able to prevent it, he prevents it; otherwise he endures. This applies when one is not being followed; otherwise he does not sit, because in that there is a blemish upon the religion.
