As for what is related of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was tested with this, it occurred before he became an imam who is followed.

It is related from Abu Mansur that he said: "How does Allah, exalted, forbid us from reviling those who deserve reviling, lest those who do not deserve it be reviled? Yet He has commanded us to fight them, and if we fight them, they kill us, and killing a believer without right is reprehensible? Likewise He commanded the Prophet, ﷺ, to convey and recite to them, even though they denied him?" He answered that reviling the deities is permissible, not obligatory, whereas fighting them is obligatory, and likewise conveying. What is permissible is forbidden in respect of what issues from it and arises from it, and what is obligatory is not forbidden in respect of what issues from it. On this basis the distinction for Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, arises concerning one who cuts off the hand of a thief as retaliation (qisas) and he dies from it: he is liable for the blood-money (diyya), because the exacting of his right is permissible, so he is held responsible for what issues from it; whereas the imam who cuts off the hand of a thief and he dies is not liable, because it is obligatory upon him, so he is not held responsible for what issues from it. End of quotation. From here, the obedience mentioned earlier is not to be taken in its unrestricted sense.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that strong adornment, ﴿We have made attractive to every community﴾ among the nations ﴿their deeds﴾, whether good or evil, by bringing about what enables them and moves them toward it, as guidance or abandonment. It is permitted that what is meant by "every community" is the communities of disbelief, since the discourse concerns them, and by "their deeds" their evil and corruption. The thing likened is the making attractive of their reviling of Allah, exalted in majesty, for them. The verse has been cited as evidence that it is He, exalted, who made disbelief attractive to the disbeliever, just as He made faith attractive to the believer. The Mu'tazilah denied this, and "Satan made their deeds attractive to them," so they interpreted the verse in ways whose weakness is not hidden.

﴿Then to their Lord﴾, the Owner of their affair, ﴿is their return﴾, that is, their returning and their destination through resurrection after death, ﴿and He will inform them﴾ without delay ﴿of what they used to do﴾.

108

- In the world, continuously, whether good or evil; and that is by reward for the first and punishment for the second. So the sentence is for promise and threat.

[Page 253]

Some have interpreted "what" (ma) as the evil deeds made attractive to them, and said: this is a threat of recompense and punishment, like a man's saying to one he threatens: "I will inform you of what you did."

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 6, verse 109]**

﴿And they swore﴾, that is, the polytheists, ﴿by God, their most emphatic oaths﴾, that is, striving in them. So ﴿جَهْدَ﴾ (*jahda*, "most emphatic") is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*).

It is also permitted that it be in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: they swore by the most emphatic of their oaths, that is, the most binding of them. It is ﴿جَهْدَ﴾ with a *fatha* or a *damma* on the *jim* originally, meaning exertion and hardship. It has been said that with a *fatha* it means hardship and with a *damma* it means capacity. It has also been said that it is what burdens a person. The meaning here, according to al-Raghib, is that they swore and exerted themselves in the oath, to bring it to the utmost extent of their capacity, ﴿that if a sign came to them﴾ from among their proposals, or from the kind of signs. Some of the verifiers preferred this, saying it is the most fitting for their state of obstinacy and stubbornness and the extremity of their rebellion and corruption, since they did not count the overpowering miracles they were witnessing as being of the kind of signs, so they proposed other ones. ﴿they would surely believe in it﴾. Their aim was nothing but to impose conditions upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in demanding a miracle, and not to regard the clear proofs they had witnessed from him, upon him be prayer and peace. The *ba'* (ب) is the complement of *iman* (belief), and what is meant by believing in it is affirming the Prophet (ﷺ). To take it as causal, meaning "they would believe because of it," is contrary to the apparent sense.

﴿Say: Signs are only with God﴾, that is, all of them, so what they proposed enters among them by primary inclusion. ﴿with God﴾, that is, their matter is in His judgment and decree exclusively. He disposes of them according to His will, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom. No power or will of anyone is connected with them, either independently or jointly, in any way, so that I could undertake to send them down upon request. This, as you see, closes the door to proposals.

It has been said that the meaning is: signs are only with God, not with me, so how can I answer you to them, or bring them to you? Or the meaning is: He is the one able to do them, not I, so that I could bring them to you. Shaykh al-Islam objected to this, after choosing what we have mentioned, saying that it has no relevance to the context. How could it be, since their proposal is not that they come without God's power?

So reflect.

It was narrated that "the Quraysh proposed some signs, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: If I do some of what you say, will you believe me? They said: Yes. And they swore: If you do it, we will all surely believe. So the Muslims asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to send it down, hoping for their belief. So he, upon him be prayer and peace, was resolved to supplicate, and it was revealed."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad al-Qurazi, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke to the Quraysh, and they said: O Muhammad, you inform us that Moses, upon him be peace, had a staff with which he struck the rock, and that Jesus, upon him be peace, used to revive the dead, and that Thamud had a she-camel. So bring us some of those signs so that we may believe you. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: What do you want me to bring you? They said: Turn Safa into gold for us. He said: If I do, will you believe me? They said: Yes, by God, if you do, we will surely follow you all. So the Messenger of God, upon him be prayer and peace, stood and supplicated. Gabriel, upon him be peace, came to him and said: If you wish, Safa will become gold; but if they do not believe at that point, We will surely punish them. And if you wish, leave them until their repentant one repents. So he (ﷺ) said: I will leave them until their repentant one repents. So God revealed this verse up to ﴿they are ignorant﴾."

﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾

This is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*), not included under the command, coming from Him, the Exalted, to explain the wisdom in what the preceding answer implied, namely the non-coming of the signs. It is addressed to the believers, as al-Farra' and others said, either specifically by way of shifting address (*iltifat*), since they were eager for its descent in hope of their (the polytheists') conversion; or it includes the Messenger of God, upon him be prayer and peace, by way of generalization, because of what has been narrated that indicates his desire for it as well, such as his resolve to supplicate. In it is a clarification that their oaths are fraudulent, and that their belief is in the corners of non-existence, even if they were granted what they asked for.

Some permitted that it come under the command, but there is no basis for this except by assuming: "Say to the disbelievers: Signs are only with God; and to the believers: And what will make you aware..." etc. This is a forced reading for which there is no need.

From Mujahid: the address is to the polytheists, and it is included under the command, and there is an shift of address (*iltifat*). According to him, "that they" (*annaha*) etc. is an initial informative statement, as indicated by what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him.

The ﴿ما﴾ (*ma*) is interrogative with the sense of denial, according to what more than one has said. The ﴿لا﴾ (*la*) is negating, because otherwise the verb would remain without a subject. Taking the pronoun as referring to God, the Exalted, is forced or inappropriate except at a distance. It has been objected: since the polytheists proposed a sign, and the believers were wishing for its descent in hope of their conversion, it was in their assumption that they would believe if it descended. So if denial against them is intended, the fitting thing is to deny their belief, not its non-existence. It is as if they said: "Our Lord, send down a sign for the polytheists, for if it descended they would believe." Then, in denial, one would say: "What will make you know that when it comes they will believe?"

This is clarified by an example: if someone says to you: "Honour so-and-so, for he will reward you," and you know from him that he will not reward, then if you deny the one advising you to honour him, you say: "And what will make you know that if I honour him he will reward me?" You have denied him the affirmation of reward while you know it is absent. But if he says to you: "Do not honour him, for he will not reward you," while you know from him that he will reward, and you want to deny the one advising you to deprive him, you say: "And what will make you know that he will not reward me?" You have denied him the absence of reward while you know it is established.

As is not hidden, the verse is of the kind of this example. So the apparent sense, given that they assumed their belief and desired it, while God knew it would not occur from them, even if the angels were sent down to them and the dead spoke to them, would be to say: "And what will make you aware that they, when they come, will believe?"

Some answered this by saying: this interrogation carries the sense of negation, and it is an informative statement about them concerning their lack of knowledge, not a denial against them. The meaning is: the signs are with God, the Exalted; He sends them down according to what is beneficial, and He, glorified be He, knows that they will not believe, and the signs will not benefit them. You do not know what is in reality and in God's knowledge, which is that they will not believe. Therefore you expect their belief.

The conclusion: the interrogation is for denial and has two meanings, "*lam*" (not) and "*la*" (not). If it carries the sense of "*lam*," one says: "And what will make you aware that when they come they will believe?" without "*la*," meaning: why did you say that when they come they will believe, and expect that? If it carries the sense of "*la*," one says: "And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?" with "*la*" affirmed, meaning: you do not know that they will not believe, so you expect their belief and desire a sign to descend for them. This second is what is intended, and it returns to establishing an excuse for the believers in their request and their desire for it.

Others answered that the ﴿لا﴾ (*la*) is superfluous, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ and ﴿And it is forbidden for a town that We destroyed that they will not return﴾. The intended meaning is "that you prostrate" and "that they return," without "*la*." From al-Khalil: the ﴿أنَّ﴾ (*anna*) is in the sense of *la'alla* ("perhaps"), as in the saying: "Go to the market, perhaps you will buy meat," and the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*They halted at the abandoned rain-hill, for we weep for the abodes as Ibn Khidham wept,*

and the verse of another:

*Will you turn back with us, for we see the open grounds, or the traces of tents?*

This is supported by the fact that *yushʻirukum* and *yudrikum* have the same meaning, and *la'alla* often follows the verb of knowing, as in: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾. Also, in the codex of Ubayy, may God be pleased with him, it reads: "And what will make you know? Perhaps they," (*wa ma yadrika la'allaha*). The discourse on this has been completed before ﴿annaha﴾, and the second object of ﴿yush'irukum﴾ is omitted. The clause is a resumptive statement explaining the denial. Its estimate is: "What thing will inform you of their state and what will happen when that comes? Perhaps when they come they will not believe. So why do you wish for its coming? For his wish is fitting only when their belief upon its coming is certain to occur, not when its non-occurrence is expected."

Some people claimed that ﴿annaha﴾ etc. is the answer to an omitted oath, based on the view that *anna* in the answer to an oath may be opened. But its distance is not hidden.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr ibn 'Asim, and Ya'qub read ﴿أنَّها﴾ with a *kasra*, as a resumptive statement, in accordance with what has been drawn out of additional confirmation of their non-belief. Al-Kashf said: This is an answer to an assumed question, according to what Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib mentioned, as if it were said: "Why were they reproached?" And it was said: "Because when they come they will not believe." You may also build it on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾, meaning: of what will come from them, for it is an expression in the form of the possible, as if he had been asked about it by a doubting questioner. Then it was given a reason: "that when they come," definitively, with the opposing extreme, and an explanation that the interrogation is not functioning in its literal sense. In it is a denial of the believers' affirmation in a way that includes denying the truthfulness of the polytheists in what they swore to. This is a kind of rhetorical magic of subtle method. End.

Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read ﴿تُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (*tu'minun*) with the second person, and the address in the verse is then to the polytheists without disagreement.

It has been read: "And what will make you aware that when they come to them they will not believe?" So the denial returns to the polytheists' undertaking the aforementioned oath, together with their ignorance of the state of their hearts when that comes, and of it being then as it is now.

It has been read: "And what will make you aware (*yush'irkum*)" with pure sukun and with *ikhtilas* (a rapid, reduced vowel).

On all other readings, the pronoun in ﴿bihā﴾ ("in it") refers to ﴿الآية﴾ (*al-ayah*, the sign, singular), not to ﴿الآيات﴾ (*al-ayat*, the signs, plural). This is because their non-belief at the coming of what they proposed is more forceful in blame. Likewise, the use of ﴿إذا﴾ (*idha*, "when") with the past tense, rather than ﴿أنْ﴾ (*an*) with the future, is for greater condemnation of them.

Some claimed that its return to ﴿الآيات﴾ (the signs) is preferable, because of its proximity, together with the added emphasis on their distance from belief and their reaching the utmost extent of obstinacy.

[Page 254]
[Page 255]

This is a long, technical passage with specialized Sufi and Mu'tazili terminology, and I'm translating it as instructed, keeping technical terms transliterated with glosses on first use, and rendering the Qur'anic verses in plain English within their markers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 110 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away﴾ is a conjunction with (they believe) and is included in the same ruling as ﴿And what will make you realise﴾, restricted by what it is restricted by. That is: and what will make you realise that We turn their hearts away from perceiving the truth, so they do not perceive it, and their sight away from witnessing it, so they do not see it? This, according to the Imam (al-Razi), is a confirmation of what is in the first verse, that they do not believe. Shaykh al-Islam (al-Bayḍawi) mentioned that this turning is not from the turning of hearts and sights towards the truth and their readiness for it, but rather for the complete aversion of their hearts from it and their total turning away from it. For this reason He mentioned it after the mention of their not believing, to indicate their rootedness in disbelief and to close off the assumption that their not believing arises from God's turning their perceptions by way of compulsion. Its realisation, according to what our shaykh of shaykhs al-Kurani stated, is that He, glory be to Him, when He knew from eternity the evil of their readiness hidden in their quiddities, bestowed upon them what it required, and did to them what they asked of Him in the tongue of readiness, after He had encouraged and warned them, established the proof and clarified the path. To God belongs the conclusive proof, and God did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers. ﴿As they did not believe in it﴾, i.e., in what came of the signs by God; it is said: in the Qur'an; it is said: in Muhammad (ﷺ), though no mention of this has preceded; it is said: in the turning, and this, as you see, is weak.

﴿For the first time﴾, i.e., at the arrival of the preceding signs. The kaf is in the position of an adjective to a verbal noun governed by (they do not believe). And "ma" is verbal (masdariyya), i.e., they do not believe but rather disbelieve with a disbelief that is like their disbelief the first time. The placement of the turning of hearts and sights in the middle is because it is among the completions of their not believing. Abu al-Baqa said: the kaf is an adjective to an elided verbal noun, i.e., a turning like their disbelief, i.e., a punishment equal to their disobedience the first time; and what is in it is not hidden. The verse is evident that belief and disbelief are by God's decree and predestination.

Al-Ka'bi answered it by saying that what is meant by ﴿And We turn﴾ etc. is: We do not do to them what we do to the believers of benefits and kindnesses, because they removed themselves from this limit by means of their disbelief. Al-Qadi (said) that what is meant is: And We turn their hearts and their sight within the signs that appeared, so We do not find them believing in them at the end, as they did not believe in them at the beginning. Al-Jubba'i (said) that what is meant is: And We turn their hearts and their sight in Hell over the flame of the fire and its embers, so that We punish them as they did not believe in it the first time in the world. All of these are like a mirage in a desert plain which the thirsty one takes to be water, and thus is the general speech of the Mu'tazila.

﴿And We leave them﴾, i.e., We let them be, ﴿in their transgression﴾, i.e., their exceeding the limit in disobedience, ﴿wandering blindly﴾.
110
- i.e., they wander about bewildered. This is a conjunction with (they believe), restricted by what it is restricted by as well, explaining what is meant by the turning of hearts and sights, indicating that it is not on its outward sense. The preposition phrase is connected to what is before it. The clause (wandering blindly) is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the accusative in (We leave them). It has been read as (He turns, and He leaves) in the third person, with God as the subject, and al-A'mash read (are turned) in the passive, attributing it to their hearts.

* * *

Here, by way of the esoteric indications in the verses: ﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾. Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: That is, We purified them and sheltered them in Our presence, and guided them to be content with Us, sufficient of anything other than Us. ﴿That is the guidance of God; He guides by it whom He wills of His servants﴾, and they are the people of precedence who asked Him, glory be to Him, for guidance in the tongue of eternal readiness. ﴿And had they associated﴾ by inclining to other than Him, and this is the associationism of the perfect, as indicated by my master ʿUmar ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified, in his saying: "Had there come to my mind, apart from You, any desire upon my heart by inadvertence, You would have judged me an apostate." ﴿Then surely their deeds would have been voided from them﴾ because of the magnitude of what they had done; indeed, associationism is a great wrong. ﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾, and they are the veiled, ﴿then We have entrusted with them a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾, and they are the knowers of God, glory be to Him, who are the treasuries of the realities of faith.

And in a report: "A group of my community will continue standing by the command of God, the Exalted; those who forsake them will not harm them until the command of God, glory be to Him, comes, and they are upon that." ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so by their guidance﴾, which is the etiquettes of the Shariʿa, the Path and the Reality, ﴿follow﴾: a command to him (ﷺ) to take on all that was dispersed among them of that guidance. This, according to what was said, was in the stations of the intermediaries. When He anointed the eyes of his secrets with the kohl of lordship, He made him self-sufficient in his essence, upright in his state, and brought him out from the limit of will to the limit of gnosis and uprightness. For this reason, peace be upon him, He commanded him to drop the intermediaries, as His saying indicates: ﴿Say: I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord﴾, together with his saying (ﷺ): "If Moses were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me." Some of the gnostics said: there is no intermediation of intermediaries in this, because He commanded him to follow their guidance, not them. Its parallel is: ﴿Follow the creed of Abraham﴾, where He, glory be to Him, did not say: follow Abraham. ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, i.e., they did not know Him with His true knowing, ﴿when they said: God did not send down anything upon any human being﴾, i.e., He did not manifest any of His knowledge and speech, glory be to Him, to anyone; this is because of their claim of His remoteness from His servants, glory be to Him, and the impossibility of some of His attributes appearing in a human form. Had they known, they would not have denied, nor believed that there is no manifestor for the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom except the perfect human; rather, were the film removed from the eye, they would not see one as two. ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾, for what is in it of the secrets of nearness and union and of longing for beauty and loveliness; indeed, through it the Truth manifested Himself to His creation, if only they knew.

﴿Confirming what is before it﴾ of the Torah and the Gospel, for it combines the outward and the inward in the most complete way. ﴿And that you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾, which is the heart, ﴿and those around it﴾, of the faculties. ﴿And who is more wrong than one who fabricates against God a lie﴾, like one who claims perfection and arrival at tawhid and deliverance from the multiplicity of the attributes of the self, and claims that he is with God and that he is among the people of guidance, while he is not so. ﴿Or says: It has been revealed to me, when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, like one who names the fabrications of his illusion and imagination and the inventions of his intellect and thought a revelation and an outpouring from the Holy Spirit, and so claims prophecy on that basis. Or ﴿says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down﴾, like one who acted as Pharaoh and claimed divinity. ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, namely these three categories, ﴿and the angels are stretching out their hands﴾ to seize their souls.

Like an insistent creditor, they say: ﴿Bring out your souls﴾, as harshness and rebuke against them, ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ and abasement, for the presence of the attributes of your selves and their dark conditions, and the thickening of the veils of your egoism and your Pharaohism. ﴿And indeed you have come to Us alone﴾, i.e., singled out, stripped of everything, absorbed in the very unity of the Essence, ﴿as We created you the first time﴾ at the taking of the covenant.

﴿Indeed God splits the grain and the date-stone﴾, i.e., the grain of the heart by the light of the spirit from the sciences and gnoses, ﴿and the date-stone﴾, i.e., the date-stone of the self by the light of the heart from the characters and noble qualities; or: He splits the grain of eternal love in the hearts of the lovers and the sincere, and the date-stone of the tree of the lights of eternity in the heart of the gnostics, so that it bears fruit with pure deeds, noble stations and exalted states. ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, i.e., the one who knows from the ignorant; ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, i.e., the ignorant from the knowing. Or: the living heart emerges from the dead self at times by the light of the spirit taking over it, and at other times He brings forth the dead self from the living heart by its turning toward it and the passions and attributes of the self taking over it. ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾, i.e., manifester of the lights of His attributes over the surfaces of the horizons of His creatures; or splitter of the darkness of dawn by the light of dawn. That is because the sea of nonexistence was full of darkness, so He split it by letting a rivulet of His light flow into it, until the flood reached the cliff's peak. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: the splitter of the darkness of nonexistence by the dawn of origination and bringing into being; the splitter of the darkness of inanimateness by the dawn of life, reason and right guidance; the splitter of the darkness of ignorance by the dawn of perception; the splitter of the darkness of the corporeal world by freeing the holy soul into the expanse of the world of the spheres; the splitter of the darkness of preoccupation with the world of contingents by the dawn of the light of full absorption in knowing the Governor of the originated and the originating. Some gnostics said: the meaning is the splitter of the darkness of the attributes of the self from the heart by the dawn of the light of the sun of the spirit and its shining upon it. ﴿And He made the night﴾, i.e., the night of bewilderment in the pure Essence, ﴿a resting place﴾ in which the spirits of the lovers repose, as one of them said:

Increase me, through excess of love for You, in bewilderment, and have mercy on a heart burning in the flame of Your passion.

Or: making the darkness of the self a resting place of the heart, in which it rests at times for relief and repose; or a resting place in which the bodily faculties dwell and become still from agitation, as it is said. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾, i.e., the sun of the manifestation of the attributes and the moon of the manifestation of the actions, ﴿as a reckoning﴾, i.e., by the reckoning of the states, by which they are taken into account; or the sun of the spirit and the moon of the heart, counted among the noble enduring existents, reckoned by them; or by the reckoning of times and states. ﴿And it is He who set for you the stars﴾, i.e., the guides, or the stars of the senses, ﴿that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land﴾, which is the knowledge of etiquette, ﴿and of the sea﴾, which is the knowledge of realities. Or the meaning: that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land of bodies to the interests of livelihood, and the sea of knowledges by acquiring them through them. ﴿And it is He who brought you into being﴾, i.e., manifested you, ﴿from a single soul﴾, which is the universal soul, ﴿so a place of settlement﴾ in the earth of the body during manifestation, ﴿and a place of storage﴾ in the very unity of the Essence. ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky﴾, i.e., from the sky of the spirit the water of knowledge, ﴿and We brought forth with it the growth of every thing﴾, i.e., every kind of character and virtue. ﴿Then We brought forth from it﴾, i.e., from the growth, ﴿green﴾, the adornment of the self and its delight; ﴿We bring forth from it﴾, i.e., from the green, ﴿grain piled up﴾, i.e., noble consecutive deeds and sincere intentions by which the heart is strengthened; ﴿and from the palm tree﴾, i.e., the palm of reason, ﴿from its spathe﴾, i.e., from the manifestation of its attachment, ﴿are clusters﴾ of knowledges and realities, ﴿near at hand﴾, close to reach, because of their manifestation by the light of the spirit, as though self-evident; ﴿and gardens of grapes﴾, which are the grapes of states and tastes, from which the nectar of love is pressed, and in one intoxication of it, even for an hour, you see time a obedient servant and yourself the one in command; ﴿and the olive﴾, i.e., the olive of reflection; ﴿and the pomegranate﴾, i.e., the pomegranate of noble resolves and self-directed determinations; ﴿resembling﴾, as among individuals of one kind, ﴿and not resembling﴾, as two kinds and two individuals of them, for example. ﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾, i.e., observe it with vigilance at the beginning of the path and the start of the state; ﴿and its ripening﴾, which is perfection upon arrival by presence. ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾, i.e., the jinn of illusion and imagination, since they obeyed them.

And they submitted to them, ﴿and they created them and invented [falsely]﴾ and fabricated ﴿for Him sons﴾ from among the intellects, ﴿and daughters﴾ from among the souls, whom they believed to be, by virtue of their immateriality, influential like Him, ﴿without knowledge﴾ on their part, [not realizing] that they are His names and attributes, which have no influence except through Him, exalted is His majesty. ﴿Glorified is He, and exalted above what they describe﴾ [of] His being bound by what they have bound Him to, exalted is His majesty. ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾.

Al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn ʿArabi), may God sanctify his secret, said in the three hundred and twenty-first chapter [of his book, al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya]: that is, from every eye, from the eyes of faces and the eyes of hearts. For hearts see only through sight, and the eyes of faces see only through sight. Wherever sight is, perception occurs through it. So sight is called, in the intellect, "the eye of insight," and in the outward sense it is called "the sight of the eye." The eye, outwardly, is the locus of sight, and insight, inwardly, is the locus of the eye, which is the sight in the eye of the face. Thus the name differs for it, while it itself does not differ in its essence. Just as eyes do not perceive Him with their sights, insights do not perceive Him with their eyes. There is a report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "God, exalted is He, has veiled Himself from the intellects just as He has veiled Himself from sights, and the exalted assembly seeks Him just as you seek Him." So we share in the seeking with the exalted assembly, and we differ in the manner. Some of us seek Him by their thought, and the exalted assembly has intellect, and thought belongs to it. And some of us seek Him by [the intellect itself], and there is none in the exalted assembly who seeks Him by it, because the perfect one among us is in the divine form in which God created him. Therefore it is valid for one with this quality to seek God, exalted is He, by it. Whoever seeks Him by it reaches Him, for no one else reaches Him. The perfect one among us has a supererogatory [practice] beyond his obligatory ones; when the servant draws near to his Lord by it, He loves him, and when He loves him He becomes his hearing and his sight. When the Real becomes the sight of such a servant, He sees Him and perceives Him by His sight, because His sight is the Real, so he perceives Him only through it, not through himself. There is no angel who draws near to God, exalted is He, by a supererogatory act. Rather they are in the obligatory acts, and their obligatory acts have engrossed their breaths, so they have no supererogation. Thus they have no station that produces that the Real should be their sight, so that they perceive Him by it. They are servants of compulsion, and we are servants of compulsion in our obligations and servants of choice in our supererogations, to the end of what he said.

It is explicit that some sights perceive Him, but from the standpoint of removing otherness.

And in the four hundred and fourteenth chapter, after he recited [verses]:

Whoever sees the Real face to face, openly,
has only seen Him from behind a veil, though he does not know it.

And this, by it, is indeed a wondrous matter:
every seer does not see except what he is in of bliss and torment.
The form of the seer is manifested to him, and it is the very eye of the seer, indeed the eye of the veil.
So when the seer sees Him, glorified is He, face to face, he does not see Him except when the Real, majestic is His majesty, becomes his sight. Then he himself is the seer of himself by his sight, in the form of His servant. The form gives him face-to-face [vision] when it is the bearer of sight and of all the faculties, etc.

And in the four hundred and first chapter, after he recited [verses]:

The dead and the living have become equal
in that nothing they have is anything.
From me there is no light, nor darkness,
nor shadow in them, nor in their seeing of me is anything nonexistent.
Their dispersal in their existence is folded, and their understanding, if its meaning is from Him, when you verify it, is error.
Indeed every visible thing that the seer sees from Him is only [seen] according to his station and rank. So he has not seen Him, and has seen only himself. Were it not so, vision would not differ among seers, for if He were the seen, they would not differ. But since He, glorified is He, is the manifester of their seeing of themselves, for this reason they describe Him as "the one who manifests," majestic is His majesty. Yet the seer's preoccupation with seeing himself in the place of the Real veils him from seeing the Real. If the seer's own form, or the form of some existent, did not appear to him, perhaps he would see Him. We are veiled from Him only by seeing our selves in Him. So if we were to pass away from ourselves, we would see Him, for no one would remain who sees Him by our passing away. And if we do not pass away, we see nothing but our selves in Him, our forms, our measure, and our station. So in every state we have not seen Him. We may broaden [the matter] and say: we have seen Him, and we speak truly, just as if we were to say, "We have seen the human being," we would speak truly in saying that we have seen those who passed away among people, and those who remain, and those in our time, as human beings, not from the standpoint of the individual personality of each human. And since the whole world and its individuals are in the form of the Real, and we have seen the Real, then we have seen and spoken truly. And when we look at the eye of discrimination within the eye of an eye, we do not speak truly, to the end of what he said.

In this there is a precious verification of this inquiry. From it is known what is in the words of some of them: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ because of the extreme manifestness of Him, glorified is He: ﴿And He is the Subtle﴾, for there is no subtler [than Him], as al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may God sanctify his secret, said, from the identity of the becoming of the servant's eye of sight; ﴿the Aware﴾, that is, the all-knowing with the knowledge that it is the servant's sight. ﴿And God is encompassing from behind them﴾, and ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾.

And from al-Junayd, may God sanctify his secret: "The Subtle is He who illuminates your heart with guidance, nourishes your body with food, makes for you guardianship through trial, guards you while you are in the fire, and admits you to the Garden of refuge."

Another said: "The Subtle: if you call upon Him, He answers you; if you aim for Him, He shelters you; if you love Him, He brings you near; if you obey Him, He suffices you; if you anger Him, He pardons you; if you turn away from Him, He calls you; if you turn toward Him, He guides you; if you disobey Him, He keeps you." How subtle is this speech!

﴿There has come to you insights from your Lord﴾, and they are the forms of the manifestations of His attributes. Some of the knowers said: they are His words, through which He manifests Himself to the possessors of realities, and from beneath their canopies there emerge the lights of His eternal qualities.

﴿So whoever sees﴾ and is guided ﴿benefits himself﴾ by that sight, that is, its fruit returns to him. ﴿And whoever is blind﴾ and veiled from guidance ﴿it is against himself﴾, his blindness and his veiling. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾; rather God, exalted is He, is a guardian over you, for you and all your affairs exist through Him.

(And thus We vary the signs for a people who know.) Ibn ʿAta said: that is, the reality of the explanation, which is standing with Him wherever He stands, and moving with Him wherever He moves, neither advancing by one's own dominance nor lagging behind Him out of incapacity. Another said: the meaning is: they know My station and understand My address, not those who do not know the place of My address and My intention in My speech.

﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾. It was said: it is an allusion to a revelation specific to him (ﷺ) which no one else can bear, or an allusion to the revelation of monotheism; therefore He, glorified is He, described Himself by saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. Then He, majestic is His majesty, said: ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾, those veiled by multiplicity from unity. ﴿And if God had willed, they would not have associated [others with Him]﴾. Rather He, glorified is He, willed their association, because it is known to Him, majestic is His majesty, from eternity, apart from their faith, and He wills only what He knows, not what is pure non-existence which He does not know.

﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides God﴾, but rather guide them to the truth with what is best. ﴿Lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾, by reviling you, while you are His greatest manifestations. ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾, since it is He whom they sought from Us through the tongues of their eternal predisposition, and it is part of Our way not to reject a seeker. ﴿And they swore by God with their strongest oaths that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it﴾, that is, they sought supernatural customs and turned away from the clear proofs, due to their being veiled by the sensory and the sensed. ﴿Say: the signs are only with God﴾, so He brings them as wisdom requires. ﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾ because of the prior decree of wretchedness upon them. ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾ because their predisposition requires that. ﴿Just as they did not believe in it the first time﴾, when they turned away from the clear proofs, or in eternity. ﴿And We leave them in their rebellion﴾, which is theirs by the requirement of their predisposition, ﴿wandering blindly﴾, bewildered, hesitating, not knowing the way of right guidance. (And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide.)

Here ends the printing of the seventh part of the tafsir Ruh al-Ma'ani (the Spirit of the Meanings, a tafsir by ʿAllama al-Alusi), by God's power and strength, and it is followed, God willing, by the eighth part, whose beginning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had sent down...﴾, the verse.

[Page 2]

﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾: this makes explicit what His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿And what would make you aware...﴾ etc., implied, concerning the wisdom that prevents answering them in what they proposed, and it demonstrates in the most eloquent and emphatic manner that they are lying in their claim of belief. That is: even if We had not confined Ourselves to what they proposed here, but had sent down to them the angels, as they asked when they said, ﴿Why are the angels not sent down to us?﴾ and said, ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ ﴿and had the dead speak to them﴾, by reviving them so that they bore witness to the truth of faith, as they proposed when they said, ﴿then bring our forefathers﴾. ﴿And We gathered﴾, that is, assembled and drove, ﴿against them every thing face to face﴾, that is, in confrontation and direct sight, so that they would confront them, as is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Qatada. On this reading it is a verbal noun (masdar), as many have said. Ibn Zayd also held this view, and from him it is said: "I met so-and-so qubulan, muqabalatan, qublan, qibalan, and qabilan," all with one meaning, which is facing directly. Al-Raghib related that it is the plural of qabil in the sense of muqabil ("facing"), relative to their senses. It was also said that it is the plural of qabil in the sense of kafil ("guarantor"), like raghif and rughuf, and qadib and qudub. Thus it derives from your saying, "I accepted the man (qabiltu al-rajul) and took responsibility for him (tqabbaltu bihi)," when you undertake responsibility for him, and from it comes qubala, meaning a document of a covenant and a deed. This was related from al-Farra'. From Mujahid it is related that its interpretation is "the group," on the basis that it is the plural of qabila (tribe), as al-Raghib said. He also related its interpretation as "guarantor," and likewise as "direct observation and confrontation," in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, that is: if We brought before them every thing, such that guarantee and testimony to the truth of faith could come from them, not individually but in company. Or: if We gathered against them every thing in groups in one place. ﴿they would not have been believers﴾, that is: it would not have been valid or right for them to have faith. On these views, the accusative of (qubulan) is that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of (kull). This is permissible on the view that (kull) is plural, because (kull) may be treated according to its meaning or according to its form, as the grammarians (al-nuhat) have stated, and they cite as evidence the verse of Antara:

"Every abundant eye poured over him, so they left every garden like a dirham."

Since he said "taraknna" rather than "taraktu," there is no need for what has been said, that this is by consideration of its implication, which is the collective totality. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read (qibalan) with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', and it is a verbal noun in the sense of confrontation and observation, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial, as al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and many others said. From al-Mubarrad it is related that it means "direction" and "side," so its accusative is adverbial (zarfiyya), as in their saying: "I have such-and-such (li kadha) before so-and-so (qibala fulan)." It is also read (qubulan) with a damma and then a sukun.

﴿they would not have been believers﴾ is the answer to (law) ("even if"). When it is negated, the lam is not introduced, contrary to those who have erred and supposed it.

He explained this ruling by their poor predisposition, which is established eternally in God's knowledge, which relates to things as they are in reality. Some explained it by the prior decree against them of disbelief. Some eminent scholars objected to this, saying that it involves explaining events by an eternal decree, and its corruption is not hidden. He also explained it by the invalidity of their predisposition and the change of their receptive nature through their bad choice, and Shaykh al-Islam followed him in this. He explained it by their persistence in disobedience, their excess and their rebellion in tyranny, objecting to what was mentioned that it is one of the rulings that follow from the said persistence, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) responded to this, saying: "It is nothing, because what has been mentioned, according to the doctrine of al-Ash'ari, who holds that the servant's choice has no effect, even if it accompanies the act according to him, and it does not entail compulsion as is supposed, according to what the scholars of usul (legal theory) verified. There is no doubt that the eternal decree is a cause for the occurrence of events, and there is no corruption in this. As for the bad choice of the servant, it is a cause for the eternal decree. Its verification, as it has been said, is that bad choice, although it suffices for the non-occurrence of faith, is not conclusive in this, because it is possible that he chooses well by directing it to faith instead of directing it to disbelief. So his bad choice in what is still ongoing is a cause for the decree of his disbelief in eternity. Thus after the decree, what happens from him is disbelief necessarily, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.﴾" End.

I say: even if this is disapproved by the men of excess, the one who explains it by bad predisposition is the one who follows the path of rectitude. The verification of this is that many of the firmly grounded and of the perfected people of unveiling have verified that the quiddities of contingent things known to God, exalted is He, from eternity, are non-existent entities distinct in themselves with an essential distinction that is not made. This is because it has been verified that knowledge of them depends on that distinction. What is made are their existent forms, which are newly originated. They have essential predispositions which are not made, and their requirements differ. Some of them require the choice of faith and obedience, and some require the choice of disbelief and disobedience. Divine knowledge relates to them, revealing them as they are in themselves, with the difference of their predispositions, which are among the keys of the unseen that none knows but Him, and the difference of the requirements of those predispositions. When divine knowledge relates to them as they are, in what their predisposition requires of choosing one of the two possible sides, namely faith and obedience or disbelief and disobedience, the divine will relates to this which the servant chose while it was non-existent, according to his predisposition, out of bounty and mercy, not out of obligation, since He is self-sufficient above the worlds. This is what makes the choice of the servant directed to the other possible side, as He wills. Thus the will of the servants, after the relation of the divine will, becomes the will of God, exalted is He. From this it is clear that their eternal choice, according to their predisposition, is followed by the knowledge that is followed by the will, in observance of wisdom, out of bounty. Their choice in what is still ongoing follows the eternal will which relates to their choice of what they chose. So they are compelled in what is still ongoing, while in the very same choice, that is, they are driven until they do what proceeds from them by their choice, not by coercion or compulsion. From this the meaning becomes clear of the words of the Commander of the Faithful, Ali, may God ennoble his face: "God, exalted is He, is not disobeyed by being overcome, nor obeyed under compulsion, nor did He delegate ownership, nor were they compelled in their eternal choice." This is because it is prior in rank to the knowledge that precedes the relation of the will, and compulsion follows the will, which follows knowledge, which follows the known, which here is their eternal choice. So it is impossible that it should follow what is later than it by several ranks. Whoever finds good, let him praise God, exalted is He, for He bestows favor by bringing into being what they chose, and it is not obligatory for Him to observe wisdom. Whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself, for His will, majestic is His glory, has not related to the actions that proceed from them except because they chose them eternally according to their predisposition. So He, exalted is He, chose out of observance of wisdom, out of bounty. The servants are acquirers (kasibun) by God, exalted is He, for there is no acquisition except by power, and no power except by God, the Exalted, the Mighty. God, exalted is He, creates their actions through them, because He, glorified is He, informed that He creates their actions, together with the attribution of the act to them, which is understood as their proceeding from them by their choice. This entails that what is created by God, exalted is He, through the servant, is the very same as what the servant acquires by God, exalted is He. There is no contradiction between the actions being created by God, exalted is He, and their being acquired by them according to their capacity and choice. What has spread from al-Ash'ari, that the servant's power has no effect at all, but is only concomitant with the act, and the act is purely by the power of God, exalted is He, is something that is hardly accepted among the verifying and rightly guided scholars. The servant's power, according to them, is effective by the permission of God, exalted is He, not independently as the Mu'tazila claim, nor ineffective as is attributed to al-Ash'ari, nor completely negated as the Jabriyya say. This is a settled matter, and we have indicated it at the beginning of the commentary. And our purpose here is nothing other than to verify that the non-belief of the disbelievers is only because of their eternal poor predisposition, which is not made, which is followed by knowledge, which is followed by the will, so that what is in the words of al-Shihab and others may be known. This has been accomplished by His grace, exalted is He, for whoever reflects and is fair.

﴿unless God wills﴾: this is an exception from the most general of states. If it is considered that all their states include the state of the relation of the will to them, then it is a connected exception (muttasil). If it is not considered, because the state of willing is not one of their states, then it is a disconnected exception (munqati'), that is: but if God, exalted is He, wills, they will believe. Abu Hayyan considered this remote. It was also said that it is an exception from the most general of times, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The turn to the majestic name is to cultivate awe and to introduce dread. That is: they would not have believed, after the gathering of the aforementioned matters that necessitate faith, in any state, except in the state of His will, exalted is He, that they believe. The intended meaning is to show the impossibility of their faith occurring, on the basis that the occurrence of the will is impossible, as the context and what follows indicate. ﴿but most of them are ignorant﴾ (111): this is an exception from the content of the conditional clause, after the occurrence of the exception. The pronoun of plurality refers either to the Muslims or to those who swore. The meaning is: their state is as explained, but most Muslims are ignorant that they will not believe when the signs come, because they are ignorant that God, exalted is He, does not will their faith at that time. So they swear by God, exalted is He, with their most emphatic oaths, to what almost never exists at all. So the sentence, on the first reading, as some verifiers have said, confirms the content of His saying, ﴿And what would make you aware...﴾ etc., according to the well-known reading. On the second reading it is an explanation of the source of the error of those who swear and the ground of their oath according to that reading as well, and a confirmation of it on the reading ﴿you do not believe﴾ with the second person, and likewise on the reading ﴿And what would make them aware that when they come they will not believe﴾.

The people of the Sunna used this verse to show that God, exalted is He, wills the disbelief of the disbeliever from him. They confirmed this by saying that when He, glorified is He, mentioned that they will not believe unless God, exalted is He, wills their faith, this indicated that He, majestic is His glory, did not will their faith, but rather their disbelief.

The Mu'tazila answered this by saying that what is meant is "unless He wills by compulsion and coercion," and their non-belief entails the absence of compulsory will, which does not entail the absence of will absolutely. Al-Jubba'i used this to show that God's will, exalted is He, is newly originated, otherwise it would entail the eternity of what the senses show to be newly originated. The people of the Sunna escaped this by claiming that its relation to bringing that newly originated thing into being at the present moment is a newly originated relation. So consider all of this carefully.

[p. 5]

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾ is an independent statement, brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the enmity he witnesses from the Quraysh and for the sayings and deeds they built upon it. "Thus" (dhalika) points to what is understood from what came before. The kaf (ka-) is in the accusative position, as an adjective of an emphatic verbal noun (masdar) that follows it. The fronting of the object serves restriction (qasr), which conveys exaggeration. The word ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾ (enemy) is in the sense of ʿaduww (enemies), as in the poet's words:

"When I do not benefit my friend with my affection,
then my enemy does not harm them with my hatred."

That is, just as We made that appointment concerning you, when We appointed for you enemies besides you who do not believe, who plot evil against you and strive to nullify your cause, so too We appointed for every prophet before you enemies who did with them what your enemies did with you, not an appointment lesser than it.

Imam ʿAli (ʿalayhi al-salam) read it in this sense, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the meaning of what preceded in the discourse. It is likely that he did not intend the technical conjunction (al-ʿatf al-istilahi). It was also permitted that it be connected to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every community their deeds﴾, meaning: just as We did that, We appointed for every prophet an enemy. But this is far-fetched.

Whatever the case, the verse is clear in support of what the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the Sunni school) hold: that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of evil just as He is the Creator of good. To interpret it as meaning "And just as We left you and your enemies free, so We did with those before you of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their enemies," [p. 5 continues:]

We did not prevent them from enmity, because of the trial (imtihan) in it, which is the cause of the manifestation of steadfastness, patience, and the abundance of reward and recompense. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. Similar to it is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Asamm, that this appointment is by way of causation (tasabbub), in that He, exalted is He, sent the prophets, peace be upon them, and singled them out with miracles, so whoever envied them envied them, and that became a cause of strong enmity. A parallel to this is the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

"It is you who made them envious."

It has also been said: the meaning is that just as We commanded you to oppose your people of the polytheists, so too We commanded the prophets before you to oppose their like; or just as We informed you of the enmity of the polytheists and decreed it, We informed the prophets of the enmity of their enemies and decreed it. But all of these are nothing, and such is the general run of the interpretations of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist theological school).

﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾: that is, the rebellious ones of both kinds, as reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid, with the idafa (genitive construction) in the sense of the explanatory min (min al-bayaniyya, "namely"). It has also been said that it is an idafa of attribute to the qualified noun, the original being "the mankind and the jinn who are devils." It has also been said that it has the sense of the lam (of possession or benefit), i.e., devils belonging to/for mankind and jinn. The tafsir of al-Kalbi, from Ibn ʿAbbas, supports this, for it is reported from him that he said: Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, divided his troops into two groups: he sent one group to mankind and another group to the jinn. In another report from him, the jinn are the jinn, and they are not devils of the devils. Iblis was born of them, and they do not die except together with him, while the jinn die, and among them are believers and disbelievers.

The phrase is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾. The verb "appointed" (jaʿala) is transitive to one object or to two objects, and the first object is the one that was fronted; the second was placed before it in haste to explain the enmity. The lam, in both cases, is connected either to "appointed" or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾; it was placed before it because the latter is indefinite. It was also permitted that it be connected to it, and it was placed before it for emphasis. It is also possible that ﴿shayatin﴾ is in the accusative by an omitted verb.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Some of them inspire to others﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) brought to explain the rulings of their enmity, or it is a circumstantial qualifier of "devils," or an adjective of "enemy." The pronoun is pluralized in accordance with the meaning, as in the previous line of poetry. The root meaning of wahy (inspiration), as al-Raghib said, is rapid indication. Because of the rapidity implied, it is said "a matter of wahy." That occurs by speech in the manner of allusion and insinuation, and it may occur by a bare sound without composition, by indication with some limbs, and by writing as well. The meaning here: the devils of the jinn whisper and insinuate to the devils of mankind, or some of each of the two groups to the other.

﴿The embellished speech﴾: that is, the adorned falsehood of speech. The root of zukhruf is decorative adornment, and from it the gold is called zukhruf. Some have said: the original meaning of zukhruf is gold, and since it is pleasing to the eyes, every adornment is called zakhrafa, though it may be specific to falsehood.

﴿Deception﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), i.e., so that they may deceive; or it is a masdar in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, i.e., deceiving; or it is a masdar of an omitted verb that is a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of "inspire," i.e., they deceive with deception. Al-Zamakhshari explained ghurur as deceit and seizing unawares. Al-Raghib is reported to have said: it is said "gharrahu ghurura," as if he folded him over while unaware, i.e., its first folding.

[p. 6]

﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾: this is a return, as has been said, to the explanation of the affairs occurring between him, peace be upon him, and his people, understood from relating what happened between the prophets, peace be upon them, and their nations. This is indicated by the shift of address and the mention of the attribute of lordship together with the attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, which expresses complete gentleness in consolation. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿they did it﴾ refers to their enmity toward him (ﷺ). The inspiration of some of them to others, the embellished false sayings concerning his matter, peace be upon him, are understood as included in what precedes; and the matter of singularity is easy. It has also been said that it refers to what was mentioned of the enmity of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the inspiration of embellishments is more general, whether it concerns his matter (ﷺ) or the matters of his brother prophets, peace be upon them. In this view, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ (112) is nearly explicit that by them is meant the disbelievers contemporary with him, peace be upon him. It has also been said that it refers to the inspiration, or the embellishment, or the deception, and in taking that as general or specific there are two possibilities, the better of which is not hidden.

The object of the will is omitted, i.e., the non-occurrence of what was mentioned. There is no difficulty in making the specific non-occurrence the object of the will, and some have estimated it as their faith.

It was objected that the established principle is that the object of the will, when it occurs as a conditional, is the content of the consequent, as in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿani), and here it is ﴿they did it﴾. It was answered that here He mentioned the will earlier attached to something, namely faith, as was indicated, then it was mentioned in the conditional clause without an attachment. So it is apparent that it is permissible to estimate an attachment for the content of the consequent, and also to estimate what the verb of will was attached to earlier. There is no harm in observing each of the two according to what the situation requires. What is mentioned in the books of rhetoric pertains only to cases where the verb of will is not repeated and there is no indication other than the consequent. So know this, for it is subtle. In my view, the better course is to take the content of the consequent absolutely.

He, glorified is He, said here: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾, and later: ﴿And had Allah willed, they would not have done it﴾. He varied between the two names in the two places for what some have mentioned: that what precedes this verse of their enmity toward him, peace be upon him, like the enmity of the other prophets, peace be upon them, which if He willed He could have prevented them from it so that they would not reach harm at all, requires mention of Him, may His majesty be great, under this title, indicating that He is his Nurturer (murabbi), in the protection of His safeguarding. And the reason He, glorified is He, did not do that is a matter His wisdom required. As for the other verse, it mentions before it their associating partners, so mentioning His name, may it be exalted, under the title of Divinity, which requires the absence of partnership, is fitting. It is as if it were said here: since what they did are among the rulings of your enmity, of the varieties of corruption, by the will of your Lord, may His majesty be great, Who you have not ceased to be in the protection of His safeguarding and the shade of His nurturing, then leave them and their fabrication, or what they fabricate of kinds of plots, and do not concern yourself with it, for for them in that are severe punishments, and for you are praiseworthy consequences, because His will, glorified is He, is founded upon utterly profound wisdom.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 6, verse 113:**

﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾, that is, to the ornamented speech (zukhruf al-qawl). It has been said that the pronoun refers to the revelation (wahy), or to the deception (ghurur), or to the enmity (ʿadawa), since it means "hostility" (al-ʿadi). The wāw is for coordination (ʿatf), and what follows it is coordinated with ﴿deception﴾, on the basis that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). In that case it is another cause (ʿilla) for the inspiring (al-iyha'). What lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ). It is not in the accusative because the condition for the accusative is absent: the deception is the act of the one who inspires, while the inclination of the hearts is the act of the one to whom it is inspired. On the last two interpretations, it is a cause for a deleted verb which the context requires, meaning: "And so that this may happen, We made what We made."

The root of ṣaghw, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is inclination. One says: "The sun and the stars inclined (ṣaghat) toward setting," and "I tilted (ṣughtu) the vessel and inclined it (asghaytuhu)," and "I inclined (asghaytu) toward so-and-so, I turned my hearing toward him." It is related that one says: "ṣaghawtu ilayhi aṣghū and uṣghī ṣaghwan and ṣaghyan." It has also been said: "ṣaghaytu uṣghī and asghaytu uṣghī." In the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit), "ṣagha yaṣghū and yuṣghī ṣaghwan, and ṣaghā yuṣghī ṣaghan and ṣaghyan" means "he inclined." Some learned scholars have mentioned that this verb comes both from the wāw root and the yāʾ root: it is said yaṣghū and yuṣghī. Its verbal noun is said to be ṣaghyan with fatḥ and kasr, and al-Farra' (al-Farra', the grammarian) added ṣaghiyyan and ṣaghuwwan with doubled yāʾ and wāw. It is also said: "an uṣghiya" like it.

Here the meaning is: "and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it." ﴿Who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, that is, in the required manner. The specification of their not believing in the Hereafter, rather than in the other matters that must be believed, is because they disbelieve in it. Our master Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Suʿud) said, indicating ([Page 7]) what is the basis of the inclination of their hearts toward what is cast to them: the pleasures of the Hereafter in this present life are surrounded by hardships, and its pains are adorned with desires. Those who believe in it and in the states of what is in it do not know that behind those hardships are pleasures, and beneath those desires are pains. They look only at what appears to them in this world at first sight. Thus they are compelled to love the desires, among which are ornamented words and deceptive falsehoods. As for those who believe in it, since they are standing upon the reality of the situation and looking at the outcomes of matters, it is not conceivable that they would incline toward those ornaments, because they know their falsity and the evil of their consequences. The verse is a proof against the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist theological school) in one respect. Al-Kaʿbi (Abu al-Qasim al-Kaʿbi) answered that the lam is for consequence (al-ʿaqiba) and not for causation in any way, but that is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Another said: it is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), vowelled with kasra because the verb was not emphasized with the nun. It has been objected that the nun and the lam of oath remain on their fatḥa, as in his saying:

*"If your houses have grown narrow upon me, surely my Lord knows that my house is spacious."*

with fatḥa on the lam of *layaʿlamu*. Indeed, it is reported from some Arabs that the lam of the answer to an oath, when it enters a present-tense verb, is vowelled with kasra, as in his saying:

*"That you may be sufficient for me, you and your entire vessel."*

This is also not agreed upon, for some people denied it and made the lam in the line a lam of causation, with the answer deleted, meaning: "you will surely drink, so that you may be sufficient for me." Al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) cited the line as evidence for the answering of an oath with the lam of purpose.

Al-Radi (Radi al-Din al-Astarabadi) said: according to the Basrans (the grammarians of Basra), it is not permissible, in the answer to an oath, to suffice with the lam of the answer instead of the nun of emphasis, except in poetic necessity. From al-Jubba'i (Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i) it is reported that the lam here is the lam of command, and what is meant by it is threat or abandonment. The use of the imperative for that is common.

It has been objected that if it were the lam of command, the letter of causation would be deleted. It was answered that the letter of causation may indeed remain in such a case, as it was explained concerning the reading *"Send him with us tomorrow, that he may graze and play"* and *"Indeed, whoever fears God and endures..."*, so let this be like that. What supports that it is the lam of command is that it was read with the letter of causation deleted.

Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) read with sukun on the lam in this and in the two verbs after it. So the claim that the weakness of its being for command is more evident than the weakness of the first two interpretations is not clear.

Our companions (the Ashʿari theologians) used the attribution of inclination to the hearts as evidence that bodily structure is not a condition for life. Thus, the living, according to them, is the part in which life subsists, and the world is the part in which knowledge subsists. The Mu'tazila said: the living and the world are the whole, not that part, and the attribution is metaphorical.

﴿And that they may be pleased with it﴾, for themselves, after their hearts have inclined toward it. ﴿And that they may commit﴾, that is, that they may acquire. Al-Raghib said: the origin of *qarf* and *iqtiraf* is the stripping of bark from a tree, or the scab from a wound, and what is taken from it is called *qarf*. *Iqtiraf* was borrowed for acquiring, whether good or evil, but it is used more for wrongdoing. For this reason it is said: "Confession removes commission (al-iʿtiraf yuzil al-iqtiraf)." It is also said: "I accused so-and-so of such-and-such," meaning I blamed and charged him with it. This has been applied to what is here, but it is far-fetched. Similar is what is reported from al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) that the meaning here is: "and that they may fabricate, and that they may lie." ﴿What they are committing﴾ (113), that is, the abominations they commit, which it is not fitting to mention. It is permitted that *ma* be a relative pronoun with a deleted returning pronoun, and that it be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), in which case there is no need to posit a returning pronoun.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 114:**

﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ This is a resumed statement, with the words "say" implied. The hamzah (interrogative particle) is for denial, and the fa' (connective particle) couples it to an implied antecedent that the context requires. The meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad: Shall I incline toward the adornments of the devils, or deviate from the straight path, so that I seek a judge other than God Most High, who would judge between me and you and distinguish the one who is in the right from the one who is in the wrong?" It has been said that the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Appoint between us and you a judge from among the rabbis of the Jews or the bishops of the Christians, who will inform us about you from what is in their Book concerning your affair." So the verse was revealed. The attribution of this denounced seeking to his noble self (ﷺ), and not to the polytheists, is as in His saying: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of God?﴾ (3:83), although they are the ones seeking it, in order to show complete fairness, or in consideration of their saying "appoint between us and you a judge."

The word *ghayra* (غَيْرَ, "other than") is the object of *abtaghi* (أَبْتَغِي, "I seek"), and *hakaman* (حَكَمًا, "a judge") is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of it. It has also been said that *hakaman* is a specifying accusative (tamyīz) for the indefiniteness in *ghayra*, like the saying "We have camels other than them." It has also been said that it is an accusative of purpose (maf‘ūl lahu). The hamzah of interrogation has priority over the verb as the first element of the sentence, because the denial concerns seeking a judge other than God Most High, not seeking in general, so it deserved to be placed first and given prominence. It has been said that its placement is for restriction, and it is understood to mean that the purpose is to restrict the denial, not to deny the restriction. It has also been said that its placement hints at the obligation of restricting the seeking to Him, and of being content with His being the judge.

It is also permitted that *ghayra* be a circumstantial accusative of *hakaman*, and that *hakaman* be the object of *abtaghi*, with the placement being because it is the focus of the denial. *Ḥakam* (حَكَم, "judge") is used for the singular and the plural, as al-Raghib said. He and others stated explicitly that it is more emphatic than *ḥākim* (حَاكِم, "judge"), and not equivalent to it, as al-Wahidi transmitted from the lexicographers. He gave the reason that it is an adjectival form (ṣifah mushabbahah) indicating the permanence of its meaning, which is why it is applied only to a just person or to one who repeatedly issues judgments.

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause that reinforces the denial. The attribution of the sending down to them specifically, although the requirement of the matter would be to show that the relation of the Book to the disputants is equal, is for the purpose of inclining them toward the revealed Book and drawing them down to accept its judgment, by implying the strength of its relation to them. It has also been said that this is because it better suits the opening of the verse, on the basis that its purpose is to denounce them. And although the phrase is in the form of "what is worshipped" (i.e., *ma* rather than *man*), this is to show fairness. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who created me, and to Him you will be returned?﴾ (36:22).

According to some verifiers, the meaning of the verse is: "Shall I seek a judge other than Him, while He is the One who has sent down to you the Book, and you are an unlettered people who do not know what you are doing, and who do not know the Qur'an, which speaks the truth and the right, and which deserves to be named by the name 'Book'?"

﴿Detailed﴾ means: in which truth and falsehood, the lawful and the unlawful, and the other rulings are made clear, to the extent that nothing of the confusion and ambiguity remains in the affair of the religion. So what need is there, after this, for a judge? Then he said: "This, as you see, is clear that the noble Qur'an is sufficient in the affair of the religion, self-sufficient apart from anything else by its explanation and detailing. As for whether its inimitability (i‘jaz, "the miraculous inimitability of the Qur'an") entered into this, as has been said, then no." End of quotation.

It is not hidden that considering the i'jaz is a desirable matter if the verse is connected in meaning to His saying: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths...﴾ (6:109). The explanation of that, as mentioned by the Imam (al-Razi), is that when God Most High related of the disbelievers that they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them they would believe in it, He answered them, may His majesty be exalted, that there is no benefit in showing those signs, because if He showed them they would remain persistent in their disbelief. Then He made clear in this verse that the proof indicating his prophethood, peace be upon him, has already been established and perfected, so what they request is a request for more, which is not something that must be attended to. Then He drew attention to the presence of the proof from this verse by two aspects. The first is that He sent down to him the detailed, clarified Book, containing many sciences and complete eloquence, which creation has been unable to match. Therefore the manifestation of this miraculous inimitable matter is a proof that He has judged in favour of his prophethood. The meaning of the verse, then, is: "Say, O Muhammad: You are making arbitrary demands in seeking all the other miracles. Is it rationally permissible to seek other than God, glory be to Him, as a judge? Everyone says that this is not permissible. Then say: He, Most High, has judged the validity of my prophethood, since He has singled me out with a Book like this, complete and detailed, reaching the level of inimitability." The second aspect is that it contains, in the Torah and the Gospel, the signs indicating that he (ﷺ) is a true messenger and that the Qur'an is a true Book from God Most High. This is what is meant by the verse, in addition. End of quotation. And some have explained the relevance of the i'jaz as follows:

Its inclusion is because the obligation (of the argument) cannot be completed except by knowledge that the revealed matter is from God Most High, and this depends on the i'jaz, such that one dispenses with any other sign indicating the truth of his claim, peace be upon him, that it is from God Most High. However, he (al-Razi) said that in the indication of the noble text upon this there is obscurity, unless it is said that the nominal circumstantial clause indicates it, because it contains a sense of the affirmation and establishment of that in itself, or the Book is taken to mean the known one whose i'jaz is recognized. He mentioned that this is due to a failure to reflect upon the verse, since the meaning is: "I do not seek a judge concerning my affair or the affair of others except God, glory be to Him, who sent down the Book for that purpose, and He judges in favour of him (ﷺ) regarding the truth of his claim by the i'jaz. When they attacked his prophethood, peace be upon him, and swore that if a sign came to them they would believe, God made clear that they were sealed upon their hearts, and He commanded him to rebuke them and denounce them by His saying: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ etc., i.e., 'Shall I deviate from the straight path, so that I single out another for judgment, when He is the One who has sent down this miraculous Book which has silenced you and laid the proof upon you? So God is sufficient as a judge between me and you by sending down this detailed Book with clear signs, of monotheism, prophethood, and other matters, which has rendered you incapable, all of you.'" This returns to the meaning that he (ﷺ) answered them by saying what is required by their claim, since they had attacked his miracles, so he defeated them in the best manner, and added to it the knowledge of the People of the Book. On this basis, its being miraculous is derived from its being sufficient in itself, and in the affair of others, as has been indicated. This has some closeness to what the Imam mentioned, and to what he pointed to concerning the connection of the verse in meaning with what preceded, His saying: ﴿And they swore by God...﴾. It is not without merit. However, the claim that the indication of the noble text upon the i'jaz is obscure is one whose soundness I do not find hidden. Nothing that was mentioned has clarified that obscurity, and that the context of the verse points to considering this is not far from the line of reasoning you have heard, so reflect. Some people have said: It may be that the Book means the Torah, i.e., that God has judged between me and you by what He sent down in it in detail, since He informed you of my prophethood and detailed in it my signs. But this, as you see, is not the truth; the truth is what came before.
