﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ is a resumed statement, not included under the implied "say," but directed from Him, Most High, to establish the truth of the Book upon which the matter of judgment was made to depend by its sending down, and to affirm that it has been sent down from His presence, mighty and majestic. The purpose is not to argue for the establishment of his prophethood (ﷺ), as appears from al-Razi's speech. The Book here means the Torah and the Gospel, and the expression of them by this name is to indicate the kinship between them and the Qur'an, which requires that they share in truth and in being sent down from God Most High, along with the brevity it contains. The relative pronoun (those to whom We gave the Book) may mean the scholars of the Jews and Christians, or both groups in general, with the scholars included first and foremost. The giving (*ītāʼ*, إيتاء) in the first case means conveying it actively, and in the second case is more general, including both that and conveying it potentially. The mention of the two groups under the heading "given the Book" is to announce that they knew what they knew from their Book. It has also been said that the relative pronoun means the believers among the People of the Book.

From ‘Aṭā’ it is transmitted that the Book means the Qur'an, and the relative pronoun refers to the senior Companions and the people of Badr, may God be pleased with them all. It is not hidden that this is farther than the Pleiades. The expression of the title of Lordship (*rubūbiyyah*), with its attachment to his pronoun (ﷺ), is to honour him, with the implication that his being sent down is one of the effects of Lordship. The particle *min* (مِن, "from") is for the starting point of the ending, metaphorically, and it is connected to *munazzal* (مُنَزَّل, "sent down"). The particle *bi* (بِ, "with") is for accompaniment, and it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial accusative of the pronoun hidden within *munazzal*, meaning: "accompanied by the truth." Most of the seven readers recited *munzal* (مُنْزَل) with the light form, from *inzāl* (إنزال, "sending down"). The distinction between *anzala* (أنزل) and *nazzala* (نزّل) has been pointed out earlier: the first is sudden, the second is gradual, and the second is more frequent. Reciting with either of them indicates setting aside the distinction, and it is not an indication of the two meanings in respect of his sending down to the lowest heaven and then his sending down to the earth, because his being sent down all at once to the heaven, as has been said, is not known to the People of the Book.

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ (114). That is, those who hesitate as to whether they know that, because they do not see from them the traces of knowledge and the rulings of recognition. So the fa' (فَ) is for the consequence of the prohibition upon the report of the knowledge of the People of the Book, or upon the statement that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth. The prohibition is not intended as a literal prohibition to him (ﷺ) from doubting this, but rather as encouragement and incitement to him, peace be upon him, as in His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ (6:14). It is possible that the address is in reality to the community, by way of allusion, even though it has a form directed to him, peace be upon him. It is also possible that it is addressed to everyone who could conceivably doubt, on the basis that the original form of address is with a specific individual, and it may be left for others, as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when the criminals...﴾ (32:12). The fa' in these views is for the consequence of the prohibition upon their very knowledge of the state of the Qur'an.

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. This begins an explanation of the perfection of the Qur'an in itself, following the explanation of its perfection in terms of its being ascribed to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, by virtue of its being sent down from Him, glorified is He, with truth. The confirmation of this is by the knowledge of the People of the Two Books concerning it. The perfection of a thing, as al-Raghib said, is its reaching a limit beyond which it needs nothing outside itself. By "the word" (al-kalimah) is meant "the speech" (al-kalam), and it is meant, as Qatadah and others said, the Qur'an. Applying it to the Qur'an is either by way of metonymy (majaz mursal) or metaphor (isti'arah). Its relation (ʿalaqah) precludes applying "word" (kalimah) to a sentence that does not convey a complete meaning, and its relation is not that; yet this usage is not found in their speech. This expression was chosen for the subtlety in it, which is not hidden from one who examines closely. Some said: because "word" is the basis of being described as truthful and just, and through it the effects of judgment become apparent. From Abu Muslim: the intended meaning of "the word" is the religion of God, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and the word of God is the highest﴾.

It was said: what is meant by it is His, the Mighty and Majestic, proof against His creation. The first is the apparent one. ʿAsim, Hamzah, ʿAli, Khalaf, Sahl and Yaʿqub read it in the singular, "word" (kalimah). The rest read "words" (kalimat) of your Lord.

﴿Truthfully and justly﴾: two verbal nouns (maṣdarān) placed in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥal) of "your Lord" or of "word", as Abu ʿAli al-Farisi held. Abu al-Baqa' permitted their being in the accusative as specification (tamyiz) and as purpose (ʿillah). Truthfulness applies to reports and promises, as is well known, and justice applies to rulings and judgments.

﴿There is no changer of His words﴾: a resumptive clause (istinaf) explaining their superiority over others, following the explanation of their superiority in themselves.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: when He, glorified is He, informed of the completion of His word, and completion is generally followed by deficiency, as it has been said:

When a matter is completed, its deficiency appears; expect its decline once it is said to be complete.

He mentioned this as a precaution and clarification, because the completion of His word is not like the completion of others. It was permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of ﴿has been fulfilled﴾, on the basis that the apparent noun suffices without a linking pronoun. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial qualifier of "your Lord", lest a stranger element separate the circumstantial qualifier from its referent, namely ﴿truthfully and justly﴾, unless both are made circumstantial qualifiers of it also.

The meaning is: no one changes any of His words for something more truthful and more just than it, nor for something like it. How then can one conceive of seeking the judgment of other than Him, exalted is He? By "more truthful" is meant clearer and more manifest in truthfulness. So it is not objected that truthfulness does not admit increase or decrease, for if a statement corresponds to reality it is truth, and otherwise it is falsehood.

Al-Karmani mentioned, regarding the hadith "the most truthful of speech" (aṣdaq al-ḥadith), etc., that the speech was treated as a speaker, so it was described with it, as one says "Zayd is more truthful than others", and a speaker admits increase and decrease in that. It was also said: the meaning is that no one can alter it openly, as was done to the Torah. So this is a guarantee from Him, glorified is He, of its preservation, like His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾. Or: there is no prophet and no book after it that would change it or abrogate its rulings, and ʿIsa, peace be upon him, will act by it after his descent without abrogating anything, as has been established in its proper place.

It was said: the meaning is that the rulings of God, exalted is He, do not admit change or cessation, because they are eternal (azaliyyah), and the eternal does not cease. The Imam claimed that the verse, on this reading, is one of the strong foundations for affirming predestinarian compulsion (jabr), because when He, exalted is He, judged Zayd to happiness and ʿAmr to wretchedness, then said ﴿there is no changer of His words﴾, it follows that the happy one cannot become wretched and the wretched one cannot become happy. So the happy one is he who was happy in his mother's womb, and the wretched one is he who was wretched in his mother's womb. I say: it is not hidden that the wretched one in (divine) knowledge is not happy, and the happy one in it is not wretched at all, because knowledge relates only to what the known is in itself, and His judgment, exalted is He, follows that knowledge, and likewise His bringing things into being according to the pattern of that knowledge. There is no conceiving of compulsion in that in any way, because He, the Mighty of Majesty, did not bestow upon the receptive recipients (qawabil) except what they requested from Him, exalted, through the tongue of their readiness (istiʿdad), as His saying indicates, glorified is He: ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾. Yes, compulsion would be conceivable if the recipients requested one thing and He, the Mighty of Majesty, bestowed its opposite upon them; but God, glorified is He, is greater and higher than that. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of everything that the hearer relates to, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ (115) of everything that can be known, so that there enters into that the statements of those who litigate and their outward and inward conditions, entering primarily.

Then, He, exalted is He, according to what the Imam mentioned, when He answered the doubts of the disbelievers and demonstrated by proof the validity of prophethood, guided that after the removal of doubt and the manifestation of proof, the intelligent person should not turn toward the words of the ignorant. So He, glorified is He, said:

[page 11]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 116:

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah.﴾ Shaykh al-Islam said: When it was established that Allah, exalted is He, alone has the right to judge, because He is independent in what necessitates this, namely the sending down of the Book that distinguishes truth from falsehood, the complete truthfulness of His speech, the perfection of His justice in His rulings, the impossibility of anyone altering any part of them, and His, glorified is He, complete encompassing knowledge of all that is heard and all that is known, He then followed this with a statement that the disbelievers are characterised by deficiencies opposed to those perfections, namely misguidance, leading others astray, following corrupt conjectures that arise from ignorance, and lying about Allah, exalted is He. This clarifies that their state is contrary to what they are accused of, and warns against relying on them and acting on their opinions. So He, glorified is He, said what He said. It may also be that this is a guidance towards following the Qur'an and holding fast to it, after explaining its perfection in the most complete manner. It is addressed to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and to his community.

It has also been said: He, upon him be peace, was addressed, but others were intended. By "those on earth" is meant people, and by "most of them" is meant the disbelievers. It has also been said: it includes them and others, such as the ignorant and those who follow their desires. It has also been said: the people of Makkah are meant, and "the earth" is their land, and most of its people were disbelievers at that time.

Some people claim that this is, in meaning, a prohibition against following anyone other than the prophets, peace be upon them, since they and the noble ones are few, the fewest of people in number. Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾. This is, as you see, weak. Similar to it is the possibility that it is a prohibition against following anyone other than Allah, glorified is He, because if most of those on earth were obeyed, they would mislead, let alone obeying a few or one of them. The meaning is: if you obey any of the disbelievers by opposing what He has legislated for you and placed in His words sent down to you from Him, they will mislead you from the truth; or, if you obey the disbelievers by making some of them judges, they will mislead you from the path that leads to it, or from the law He has prescribed for His servants. ﴿They follow only﴾, that is, they follow in what they are upon of polytheism and misguidance, ﴿nothing but conjecture﴾. Conjecture regarding what relates to Allah, exalted is He, does not avail anything of the truth, and nothing suffices there except knowledge, and how could they have it? This differs from the rest of the rulings and their causes. For example, knowledge is not a condition for them, otherwise most of the worldly and otherworldly benefits would be lost. The difference between them, as stated by al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam in his
صفحة 12
*al-Qawa'id al-Kubra*, is that the one who conjectures allows the opposite of what he conjectures. So if he conjectures an attribute of the Deity, mighty is His majesty, then its opposite is permissible, and that is a deficiency, while deficiency is not permissible for Allah, glorified is He. This differs from rulings: if one conjectures that the lawful is unlawful or the unlawful is lawful, there is no permitting of deficiency upon the Lord, majestic is His majesty, because if He, glorified is He, made the unlawful lawful and the lawful unlawful, that would not be a deficiency for Him, mighty and majestic is He. So the permissibility of it lies between two matters, each of which is a perfection, unlike the attributes. Other than one scholar said: the meaning is that they follow nothing but their conjecture that their forefathers were upon the truth, and their ignorance and their false opinions. By "conjecture" is meant what is opposite to knowledge, that is, ignorance. So there is no evidence in the verse that acting on conjecture is absolutely impermissible. Therefore, those who deny analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy) have no proof from it. The Imam, after establishing the basis of their argument, said: The answer: why could it not be said that conjecture is an expression for a dominant belief when it is not based on an indicator, and it is like the conjecture of the disbelievers? As for when the dominant belief is based on an indicator, it is not called conjecture. But this is, as you see, ﴿And if they are﴾, that is, and they are not, ﴿except guessing﴾ (116), that is, they lie. The root of *kharṣ* is speaking on the basis of conjecture and the saying of one who is not certain and does not verify, as al-Azhari said. From this comes *kharṣ al-nakhl* (estimating the date palms), with the *kha'* vowelled with a fatha, and the thing estimated is *khirṣ* with a kasra, that is, *makhrūṣah*. The meaning is that the habit of these people is lying, and they continue to renew it from time to time, together with what they are upon of following conjecture regarding their Creator, mighty is His majesty.

The Imam also said: The meaning is that these disbelievers who dispute with you concerning your religion and your way are not certain of the soundness of their doctrines; rather, they follow nothing but conjecture, and they are guessers and liars in claiming certainty. The restriction of lying to the claim of certainty is far-fetched, and it is not hidden. Other than one scholar said: The meaning is that they lie about Allah, exalted is He, regarding what they attribute to Him, majestic is His majesty, such as taking offspring for Him, making the worship of idols a means to Him, glorified is He, and making lawful carrion and the *bahira* (the she-camel whose ear was slit) and the like. Perhaps what we have adopted is better and more forceful in censure. It may also be that the meaning is that these disbelievers follow the conjecture of their predecessors in matters of their religion, and that their own nature is also conjecture. The outcome of this is censure of them for their corruption and the corruption of their foundations. However, this is very far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 117:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ (117) This is a confirmation, as some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said, of the content of the conditional clause and what follows it, and an emphasis on what it conveys of warning. That is: He is most knowing of the two groups, so beware lest you be among the first.

("Man") is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun in the accusative position as an object of a verb implied by ("a'lam"), as al-Farisi held, meaning: "He knows," not by it. For "af'al" (the elative form) does not govern an overt noun when it is intended as a comparative, according to the correct view, contrary to some of the Kufans, because it is weak and does not work like its verb. When it is stripped of comparison and given the meaning of the active participle, some allowed its governing an object, as stated explicitly in al-Tashil, and in that case its object is brought in the genitive with the preposition "bi" or "li." Some people claimed that the "ba'" here is implied, so that the two ends of the verse correspond. It is not permissible for "af'al" to be annexed to "man," because the meaning would be corrupted.

It is also permitted that it be an interrogative in the nominative position as a subject, with the predicate being ("yadillu"), and the clause is suspended from the implied verb. This view was held by al-Zajjaj.

What is expressed regarding the first group, in the manner in which it is expressed, and regarding the second group, as "the guided," without stating what they were guided to, is not hidden: it shows concern for the others and a greater distinction between them and the first group. It was also read as ("man yudil") with a dammah on the ya', so that "man" is an object of the implied verb mentioned, and the subject of ("yudil") is a pronoun referring to it, and its object is omitted, meaning: "He knows who misleads people." This would be an emphasis on warning against obeying the disbelievers. It was also permitted that it be genitive by annexation, meaning: "the most misleading of those who mislead," from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿whom Allah leads astray﴾, or from your saying "adlaltuhu" when you found him astray, as "ahmadtuhu" means when you found him praiseworthy. It may also be an interrogative with the verb likewise suspended, and the subject of ("yadillu") may be a pronoun for Allah, exalted is He, and "man" in the accusative by the implied verb mentioned, meaning: "He knows whom Allah, exalted is He, leads astray." It has been said: the apparent wording would have been "bil-mahdiyyin" (the guided), but the likely reason for departing from it is to indicate that guidance is an established attribute that belongs to them in themselves, as though it did not need an act of making, in line with his, upon him be blessings and peace, saying: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition)." By contrast, misguidance is something that comes upon them and that He brought about in them. So reflect.

The superiority in knowledge is either considered with respect to the objects of knowledge, since they are infinite, or with respect to the aspects of knowledge by which it can be related to them. It is also either considered in terms of the mode, which is that knowledge is necessary to Him, glorified is He, or that it is inherent in His essence and not by another.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 118:

﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned.﴾ This is a command that follows from the prohibition against following the misguiders, among whose misguidance is making lawful what is unlawful and making unlawful what is lawful. al-Wahidi has mentioned that the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, tell us about a sheep that has died: who killed it?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah the Exalted killed it." They said: "So you claim that what you and your companions kill is lawful, and what the hawk and the dog kill is lawful, but what Allah the Exalted kills is unlawful?" So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

'Ikrimah said: When Allah the Exalted revealed the prohibition of carrion, the Magians from the people of Persia wrote to the polytheists of Quraysh, who had been their allies in the Jahiliyyah, and there was correspondence between them: "Muhammad and his companions claim that they follow the command of Allah the Exalted, yet they claim that what they slaughter is lawful and what Allah the Exalted slaughters is unlawful." So some of the Muslims were troubled by this, and Allah, glorified be He, revealed the verse.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and a group [of scholars] narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Shall we eat what we kill, and not eat what Allah the Exalted kills?' So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse."

The meaning, according to what many have held, is: eat of that over which the name of Allah the Exalted has been mentioned at its slaughter, not that over which the name of another has been mentioned exclusively, or together with His name, may His name be mighty, or that which died of its own accord. The restriction, as has been said, is derived from the non-following of the misguiders and from the condition; were it not so, this statement would be addressing what is not needed and be silent about what is needed. Some have claimed that there is no restriction, and that the impermissibility of what died of its own accord is derived from the explicit wording itself, namely His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that...﴾ etc. This is contrary to what the majority hold.

﴿if you are believers in His signs﴾, among which are the verses that have come concerning this matter, ﴿believers﴾ (118). For belief in them necessitates permitting what Allah the Exalted has made lawful and avoiding what He has made unlawful. It has also been said: the meaning is, if you become knowers of the realities of matters of which this command is one, by means of your faith. It has also been said: the intended meaning is, if you are characterized by faith and certain of it, for assent varies between conjecture, imitation and verification. The prepositional phrase is connected to what follows it, and it has been placed first for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), and the answer of the conditional is omitted, the preceding context indicating it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 119:

﴿And what is it with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned?﴾ This is a denunciation of the idea that there could be anything that would cause them to abstain from eating what the name of Allah the Exalted has been mentioned over. So "mā" (what) is an interrogative of denunciation (al-istifham al-inkari), and it is not a negation as has been said. It is the subject (mubtada'), and "lakum" (for you) is the predicate (khabar). "An ta'kulu" (that you eat) has the preposition (harf al-jarr) implied before it, i.e., "an ta'kulu" (from eating), and the disagreement concerning the position (mahall) of the resulting phrase after the deletion is well known.

It has been permitted that this be a circumstantial clause (hal), but this was rejected on the grounds that the verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb does not occur as a circumstantial clause, as Sibawayh explicitly stated, because it is definite (ma'rifah), and because it is introduced by the particle of the future (harf al-istiqbal), which is incompatible with the circumstantial sense, unless it is interpreted as indefinite (bi-nakirah) or a genitive construction (mudaf) is assumed, i.e.,
Page 14
"dhawa an la ta'kulu" (possessors of not eating). The object of "ta'kulu," as Abu al-Baqa' said, is deleted, i.e., "shay'an mimma..." (something of that which...), etc. It has been said: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it is permissible to eat of that over which the name of Allah the Exalted has been mentioned and of that over which it has not been mentioned together, and "min" is not partitive (tab'idiyyah) to exclude it, but rather to exclude what is not eaten, such as dung and blood, and this is excluded by the preceding restriction (al-hasr al-sabiq), so do not be heedless. The occasion of revelation of the verse, according to what Imam Abu Mansur said, is that the Muslims used to shun eating the good things out of asceticism and renunciation, so there was revealed ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾, by His saying: ﴿Say, I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾, the verse, so what is other than that remained permissible. It has been said that it was by His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾. Imam (al-Razi) objected to this, saying that Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last of what was revealed at Medina, while this surah is Meccan, as you know, so that is not possible. As for the delay in recitation, it does not necessitate delay in revelation, so the delay of ﴿Say, I do not find﴾ ... etc. from this verse in this surah is not harmful. It has been said: the detailing is by inspiration that is not recited, and the clause is circumstantial, emphasizing the preceding denunciation.

The people of Kufa other than Hafs read ( fassala ma hurrima ) with the first verb in the active voice and the second in the passive voice. The people of Medina, Hafs, Ya'qub and Sahl read ( fassala wa harrama ), both in the active voice, and the rest read both in the passive voice.

﴿Except what you are compelled to﴾, i.e., necessity has compelled you to eat it because of the severity of hunger. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's explanation, as the second scholar (al-'Allamah al-Thani) said, requires that "ma" be a relative pronoun, so there is no alternative to taking the exception as disjunctive (munqati'), i.e., "but that which you are compelled to eat of what is forbidden to you is lawful for you in a state of necessity." It has also been permitted, according to al-Rahmah, to make it an exception from the pronoun in "harrama," with "ma" being a verbal noun in the sense of a period of time, i.e., "He has detailed for you the things that have been forbidden to you, except the time of necessity for them." It was objected that the exception from the pronoun is not valid in that case, but rather it is a truncated exception (istithna' mufarragh) from the general implied adverbial noun, as if it were said: "They have been forbidden to you every time except the time of ..." etc. Some people have raised here something which I do not think is among what is required, where he said after some discussion: "The important point in this context is explaining the benefit of ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾, and it seems that the benefit in it, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is for emphasis in the prohibition of refraining from eating: that what is forbidden becomes what is not eaten, unlike what is lawful, which does not become what is not eaten. So how could one shun what is eaten? So reflect."

﴿And indeed many﴾ of the disbelievers ﴿do lead astray﴾ people by making lawful what is unlawful and making unlawful what is lawful, like Amr ibn Luhayy and his kind, who established the bahira and the sa'ibah and permitted eating carrion. It is related from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning of this "many" are those who disputed about carrion.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿la-yudilluna﴾ with an open yā' (yuḍillūna with fatḥah), ﴿by their desires﴾ which are deviant, and their ﴿false appetites﴾, ﴿without knowledge﴾ drawn from the Shari'ah and resting upon revelation, or ﴿without any knowledge at all﴾, as has been said. This was mentioned to indicate that what they are upon is pure desire and appetite. It has been permitted that it be of the type of His saying: ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾ (119), those who exceed the truth into falsehood and the lawful into the unlawful, so He will recompense them for that. Perhaps the intended ones are this "many," and the apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun to mark them with the attribute of transgression.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 6, verse 120:

﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin﴾. That is, what is openly done and what is done in secret, as Mujahid, Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said. Or it means what is done by the limbs (*al-jawarih*, the bodily members) and what is done by the heart, as al-Jubba'i said. Or it means marrying what the fathers married and the like, and fornication with foreign women, as was reported from Ibn Jubayr. Or it means fornication in taverns and taking secret lovers (*akhdan*, sing. *khidn*), as was reported from al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. It has also been reported that the people of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period) used to hold that fornication was a sin when it was made public, but when its doer concealed it, there was no sin in it.

Al-Tibi said: "On this interpretation, it is intended by the coordination (*al-'atf*) and is caused by not following [the command]. On the first interpretation, it is a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridah*) serving as emphasis (*tawkid*) for His words, glorified is He: ﴿So eat﴾ first and ﴿do not eat﴾ second. This is the more apt reading, and perhaps the command in the view preceding it is similar to this."

﴿Indeed, those who earn sin﴾, that is, who do the sinful acts that contain sin and commit foul deeds, whether outward or inward, ﴿will be recompensed for what they used to commit﴾ (120). That is, they earn sin of whatever kind it may be, so it is necessary to avoid all of it. The sentence is an explanation (*ta'lil*, causal justification) of the command.

[Page 15]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 121:**

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, i.e., of the animals, as is the most evident meaning. The verse is apparent in prohibiting that over which the invocation (tasmiyah) has been omitted, whether deliberately or through forgetfulness. This is the view of Dawud (al-Zahiri).

From Ahmad, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and al-Jubba'i, the same is reported. Al-Shafi'i held the opposite, on the basis of what Abu Dawud and Abd ibn Humayd reported from Rashid ibn Sa'd as a mursal (a report whose chain omits the Companion) hadith: "The slaughter of a Muslim is lawful, whether the name of Allah the Exalted has been mentioned or not." From Malik, and this is the transmission relied upon by the leading scholars of his school, [it is reported] that what is left without the invocation deliberately is not eaten, whether through carelessness or otherwise. Ashhab has a rare opinion permitting what is left without invocation by one who is not careless. Some claimed that the school of Malik is like that of al-Shafi'i, and others that it is like that of Dawud and those with him. What we have mentioned is what is found in the books of the Malikis, and the people of Makkah know its valleys best.

The school of Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, distinguishes between deliberate and forgetful omission, as is the sound view within the school of Malik. The scholar al-Thani (the second scholar) said: the one who forgets, according to the school of the Greatest Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, is not one who has omitted the invocation; rather it is in his heart, according to what has been reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about that over which the invocation was left out through forgetfulness, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'Eat it, for the invocation of Allah the Exalted is in the heart of every Muslim.'" The deliberate one was not assimilated to it except because of the impossibility of specifying the Book by analogy (qiyas), even if the ratio legis is textually stated. Or it is because he omitted the invocation deliberately, so it is as if he negated what is in his heart. This was objected to: specifying a general text from which some part has already been excluded by analogy with a textually stated ratio legis is permissible by consensus; and we do not concede that one who deliberately omits is in the position of one who negates what is in his heart, since he may be confident of that and not need to mention it.

Then he said: they held that the forgetful one is excluded by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And indeed it is a transgression (fisq)﴾, since the pronoun refers to the verbal noun derived from the content of ﴿over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, namely the omission, because it is the nearest antecedent. It is known that omission through forgetfulness is not a transgression, since the forgetful one is not under obligation and is not held accountable, so the deliberate sense is determined.

This was objected to: that this being a transgression, especially in the sense of emphatic affirmation, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and no one has held it, and it does not accord with His saying: ﴿or a transgression over which something other than Allah has been invoked﴾; moreover the Qur'an explains one part by another, especially in a single ruling. And that what has not had the name of Allah mentioned over it includes carrion, while it is certain that omitting the invocation over it is not a transgression. Some returned the pronoun to what has the meaning of the slaughtered animal and made it the very transgression by way of hyperbole; but it is necessary to take into account that it is one left without invocation deliberately, since there is no transgression in forgetfulness, and then the reading does not hold either. From what has preceded, what is in it is known.

The scholar mentioned, for the Shafi'is, in claiming the permissibility of what is left without invocation, whether deliberately or through forgetfulness, and the prohibition of what is slaughtered on the stones (ansab) or dies of its own accord, several considerations. The first: the invocation is in the remembrance of the believer and in his heart as long as he is a believer, so the absence of mention is not realized from him, and therefore nothing is prohibited from his slaughter except what has been invoked over for other than Allah the Exalted.

Page 16

The second: His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed it is a transgression﴾, in the sense of emphatic affirmation, is not valid with regard to eating what the name of Allah the Exalted has not been mentioned over, whether deliberately or in error, since there is no transgression in doing what is a matter of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning). The third: this sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), since it is not good to conjoin a declarative statement to an imperative one; and the transgression has been explained by His saying, mighty is His majesty: ﴿over which something other than Allah has been invoked﴾. So the prohibition on eating is restricted to what has not had the name of Allah the Exalted mentioned over it and has been invoked over for other than Allah the Exalted. Thus what is not so is permitted, either by way of the inference of contrariety (mafhum al-mukhalafah), or by the ruling of the original state, or by the general texts that come concerning the permissibility of foods. This is the summary of what the Imam mentioned in a session of admonition (tadhkir) that the Sultan of Khwarazm convened for him, in which he spoke, in the presence of him and of some of the Hanafi imams. Accordingly, the Shafi'is have no need for an external proof to specify the verse.

It was objected: this entails that the prohibition does not cover the eating of carrion, although it was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul); and that the emphasis by "inna" and the lam entails that the sentence is not circumstantial, because it is only good where the intention is to inform of its certain realization, or to refute a denier, actually or presumptively, as is explained in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-ma'ani). The circumstantial clause occurring in commands and prohibitions is based on supposition, as if it were said: "Do not eat of it if it is a transgression," so ﴿and indeed it is a transgression﴾ is not good; rather it is "and it is a transgression." From here many held that the sentence is a new (resumptive) statement.

As to the first, it was answered that what was invoked over for other than Allah the Exalted entered into His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a transgression﴾, and by His saying, majestic is His glory: ﴿And indeed the devils﴾... etc. carrion. Thus the claim of those who say the prohibition is specified to what was invoked over for other than Allah the Exalted, or that which died of its own accord, is established.

As to the second, the scholar answered that since the meaning of transgression here is the invoking for other than Allah the Exalted, the emphasis is appropriate, as if it were said: "Do not eat of it when this type of transgression, whose ruling is established, is realized, and the polytheists deny it." Some interpreted the verse as concerning carrion, because the dispute about it is, as you will know shortly, God willing, exalted is He.

I would pick out as the pronoun's return the eating that is indicated by ﴿and do not eat﴾. What appears from the words of some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) is that what has not had the name of Allah the Exalted mentioned over it is general, covering what has been invoked over for other than Allah the Exalted, what is left without invocation deliberately or in error, and what dies of its own accord, because it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse. The verification is that an apparent general text, when it comes upon a particular occasion, is a clear statement regarding that occasion, remaining apparent in what is other than it on its apparent sense; and that a permitting exception for what is forgotten in invocation requires a specifying element, namely the report containing the question and answer. He claimed that this, on close examination, is not specification but rather a prevention, because the forgotten case is included in the generality, supported by the aforementioned hadith.

It is also supported by the fact that a general text coming upon a particular occasion, even if it is strong in covering that occasion so that its apparent sense is a clear statement regarding it, is nonetheless weak in covering what is other than it, so that it descends from the heights of its apparent sense concerning it, and suffices, in opposition, with what it would not suffice with were it not for the occasion. End of quotation.

What is in it is not hidden from one who has thorough knowledge of what the scholar mentioned before. Many of our companions mentioned that the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, contradicts consensus (ijma'), since there was no disagreement among those before him regarding the prohibition of what is left without invocation deliberately; the disagreement among them concerns what is left without it through forgetfulness. The school of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is that it is prohibited; the school of Ali, may Allah honour his face, and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is that it is permitted. They did not disagree on the prohibition of what is left without invocation deliberately. For this reason Abu Yusuf and the shaykhs, may Allah have mercy on them, said: what is left without invocation deliberately does not admit of ijtihad, and if a judge were to rule for the permissibility of its sale, the ruling would not be enforced, because it contradicts consensus. And the apparent sense of the verse requires that it includes what is left without invocation through forgetfulness, except that the Law made the forgetful one as one who remembers, by way of an excuse on his part; and in that is the removal of hardship, for man is very forgetful.

The statement of some of the Shafi'is, may Allah have mercy on them: "If the invocation were a condition for lawfulness, it would not drop out by the excuse of forgetfulness, as purity [is a condition] in the chapter of prayer," leads to equating deliberate and forgetful omission. This is familiar where the forgetful one is in a state that reminds him, such as eating during prayer or sexual intercourse while in the state of ihram; but not where there is no such reminding state, like eating while fasting. Here, if there is no state that makes forgetfulness likely, namely the change in condition that occurs to slaughtered animals when the soul of the animal departs, then it is not a reminding state that exists.

In my view, the truth is that the matter is one of ijtihad, and the establishment of consensus is not conceded. Even if al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, contravened [consensus] as was claimed, his argument for his claim, as you have heard, is not free of soundness. As for the statement of al-Asfahani, as in al-Mustasfa, that he (al-Shafi'i) was grossly wrong in contravening seven verses of the Qur'an, three of them in surah al-An'am: the first, ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾; the second, ﴿And what is it with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾; the third, ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾; and three in surah al-Hajj: the first, ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided them of the cattle﴾; the second, ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite, that they may mention the name of Allah﴾; the third, ﴿And the camels We have made for you among the symbols of Allah; for you therein is good, so mention the name of Allah over them as they stand in line﴾; and one verse in surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿So eat of what they hold for you, and mention the name of Allah over it﴾; this is gross insolence toward this Qurashi Imam, and its source is the failure to recognize his excellence, the breadth of his knowledge and the subtlety of his inquiry. In sum, the discussion of the verse has wide scope, and each of the proponents of those positions has argued from it.

It is reported from Ata' and Tawus that they both argued from its apparent sense that what is left without invocation, whether an animal or other than it, is forbidden. The occasion of revelation supports the opposite of that, as you know, and caution is not hidden.

﴿And indeed the devils﴾, i.e., Iblis and his armies, ﴿do inspire﴾, i.e., they whisper ﴿to their allies﴾, those who followed them among the polytheists. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said, and it was said: the devils here means the rebellious Magians, so their inspiring to their allies is what they conveyed to the Quraysh, as we related from Ikrimah. ﴿That they may dispute with you﴾, i.e., by satanic whisperings, or by what is transmitted of the falsehoods of the Magians. ﴿And if you obey them﴾ in making lawful what is forbidden, ﴿indeed you are polytheists﴾ (121). It is evident that whoever abandons obedience to Allah the Exalted for obedience to another, and makes lawful what is forbidden and follows him in his religion, has associated [a partner] with Him the Exalted; rather he has preferred him over Him, glorified is He.

The Imam reported from al-Ka'bi that he said: the verse is evidence that faith (iman) is a name for all acts of obedience, although its meaning in lexical usage is assent (tasdiq), just as Allah the Exalted made shirk a name for everything that is opposition to Allah, mighty and majestic, although in lexical usage it is specific to one who believes that Allah the Exalted has a partner, on the ground that He, glorified is He, called the obedience of the believers to the polytheists in the permissibility of carrion "shirk." Then he said: one may say: why should it not be that what is meant by shirk here is the belief that Allah the Exalted has a partner in ruling and obligation, and by this measure the meaning of this shirk returns to belief alone. End of quotation. The apparent sense is that the expression of this obedience as shirk is by way of intensification (taghlid), and its parallels are numerous. The discourse here, as Abu Hayyan and others said, is on the supposition of an oath with the omission of the lam of preparation, meaning: "And if you obey them, by Allah, indeed you are polytheists," and the answer of the condition is omitted because the answer of the oath has taken its place. Abu al-Baqa' and some who followed him made the aforementioned [clause] the answer of the condition, with no oath, and claimed that omitting the fa' there is good when the condition is in the past tense, as here. It was objected that this is not found in the books of Arabic grammar; rather all agree on the necessity of the fa' in the nominal sentence, and they did not permit its omission except in poetic necessity. It was answered that al-Mubarrad permitted that in ordinary usage, as al-Muradi mentioned in his commentary on al-Tashil.

[Page 18]

﴿Is he who was dead and whom We brought to life...﴾ is an allegory (tamthil) given to discourage the Muslims from obeying the polytheists, following the warning against them by pointing out that the Muslims are illuminated by the lights of divine revelation, while the polytheists are immersed in the darknesses of disbelief and transgression. How could obeying them be conceivable? So the verse, as al-Tayyibi said, is connected to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey them...﴾. The interrogative hamzah (alif of interrogation) is for denunciation, and the waw, as many have said, is for conjoining a nominal clause (jumlah ismiyyah) to a similar clause that is implied by the context. That is: "You are like them, and [is it not so with] one who was dead, then We gave him life." ﴿And We made for him﴾, in addition to that, from outside [himself], ﴿a light﴾, a great one, ﴿by which he walks﴾, i.e., by means of which, ﴿among the people﴾, i.e., among them, safe from their harm. The clause is either a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) answering a question arising from the discourse, as if it were said: "What does he do with that light?" and it is answered, "He walks..." etc.; or it is a qualifying clause (sifah) for it [the light]. The word man (who) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) serving as the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its relative clause (silah), and the predicate is the prepositional phrase in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿like one whose likeness﴾, i.e., whose attribute is wondrous, ﴿is in the darknesses, not coming out of them﴾. The man in it is also a relative pronoun, and (mathaluh) [his likeness] is the subject, and His statement, exalted is He, ﴿in the darknesses﴾, is the predicate, with a omitted (huwa) as the predicate of the subject. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿not coming out of them﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in the adverbial phrase, and this clause is the predicate of the subject, namely (mathaluh), by way of narration (hikayah), meaning: when he is described, it is said to him this. The clause (mathaluh) together with its predicate is the relative clause of the relative pronoun.

If you wish, you may make both places an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). It is not permitted that ﴿in the darknesses﴾ be a predicate of (mathaluh), because the darknesses are not a container for the likeness. The apparent sense of some scholars' words, such as Abu al-Baqa's, is that (fi al-zulumat) is the predicate and there is no omitted (huwa) there; and it does not necessarily follow, as some verifying scholars have stated, the issue of the adverbial sense (zarfiyyah), because what is meant is that his likeness is his being in the darknesses, and the intent is narration. Yes, what was mentioned first is better, because the predicate of (mathaluh) can only be a complete clause, and the adverbial phrase without an apparent agent does not fulfil that function.

It has been allowed that the clause ﴿not coming out of them﴾ be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (mathaluh), but Abu al-Baqa prevented it because of the separation. It was said that it is also because of the weakness of a circumstantial clause coming from a noun in the genitive construction (mudaf ilayh). Nafi' and Ya'qub read (mayyitan) with shaddah (doubled ya), and it is the original form of the lightened one; the omitted letter from the second ya', which was converted from a waw, was elided by deletion just as it was elided by conversion, and there is no difference between the two according to the majority.

Then, this latter [reading], as Shaykh al-Islam said, is an allegory for those who remain in misguidance such that they never leave it at all, just as the first is an allegory intended for one whom Allah created upon the natural disposition of Islam and guided by the clear signs to the path of truth, which he follows however he wishes. But not in the sense that each one of these meanings is indicated by the words that are suitable to it from the words occurring in the two allegories, by way of comparison with what corresponds to it from their meanings, for the words of an allegory remain upon their original meanings; rather, it is that from the multiple matters considered on each side of the two allegories, a distinct form has been abstracted, and from the multiple matters mentioned on each side of the two allegories, a distinct form has been abstracted, so the first two were compared with them and took their place, and what indicates the latter two was used for them by a kind of figurative extension, to the end of what he said.

Al-Qutb al-Razi stated that they are two allegories, not two metaphors (isti'arah). It was rejected, as al-Shihab said, on the grounds that the apparent meaning is that "one who was dead" and "whose likeness is in the darknesses" are of the kind of allegorical metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), since there is no explicit mention of the compared item, nor any indication that would contradict the metaphor. The first metaphor as a whole is the compared item (mushabbah), and the second is the thing compared to (mushabbah bihi). This is like what you say in the single-word metaphor: "Would the lion be like the fox?", i.e., the brave like the coward. It is among the wondrous meanings that one should pay attention to and remember.

The transmitted exegesis from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that what is meant by the dead one is the disbelieving misguided person, by the living is guidance, by the light is the Qur'an, and by the darknesses are disbelief and misguidance. According to what Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him, the verse was revealed concerning Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him,
[Page 19]
and he is the intended one by "the one whom Allah brought to life and guided," and [it was revealed concerning] Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him, and he is the intended one by "whose likeness is in the darknesses, not coming out of them." Something similar was also reported from Zayd ibn Aslam.

In another narration from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it [was revealed] concerning Hamzah and Abu Jahl; and from Ikrimah, that it [was revealed] concerning Ammar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl. Whatever the case, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not the specific cause of revelation, so everyone who submits to the command of Allah enters into it, as does everyone who remains upon his misguidance and obstinacy.

﴿Thus﴾ is a reference to the adornment mentioned, in the manner established regarding its like, or a reference to the inspiration of the devils to their allies, or to the adornment of faith for the believers. ﴿It was made attractive﴾ from Him, exalted is He, as a natural disposition, or from the side of the devils as whispering, ﴿to the disbelievers﴾, such as Abu Jahl and his likes, ﴿what they used to do﴾ (122), i.e., what they continued to do of the various forms of disbelief and sins, among which is what has been related of them of abominations.

﴿Thus﴾ (it is) said, that is, just as We placed in Mecca the greatest of its criminals to scheme therein, ﴿We have placed in every town﴾ among the rest of the towns ﴿the greatest of its criminals to scheme therein﴾. Or (it means): just as We made the deeds of the people of Mecca appear fair to them, We placed in every town... etc. Al-Razi adopted both possibilities, and many have made *ja'ala* (to make, to place) the transitive verb meaning *sayyara* (to render), which takes two objects. Opinions differ on identifying them. It is said: ﴿in every town﴾ is the second object, and ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾, in the genitive construction (*idafa*), is the first. It is also said: ﴿the greatest﴾ (*akabir*) is the first object and ﴿its criminals﴾ (*mujrimiha*) is an apposition (*badal*) to it. And it is said: ﴿the greatest﴾ is the second object and ﴿its criminals﴾ is the first object, because it is definite (*ma'rifa*), so that by the original structure it is the subject of the nominal sentence. The estimated sense is: "We placed in every town its criminals as the greatest," so that the prepositional phrase (*jar wa majrur*) is attached to the verb.

Abu Hayyan objected that making ﴿its criminals﴾ an apposition to ﴿the greatest﴾, or an object, is an error and an oversight of a grammatical rule: the elative (*af'al al-tafdil*) must be kept in the singular and masculine form when it is accompanied by *min* (than), whether expressed or implied, or when it is in construct with an indefinite noun, whether the referent is a masculine singular or otherwise. If it agrees with what it describes in feminine, dual or plural form, then one of two things must accompany it: either *al-* (the definite article) or a construct with a definite noun. In both of these analyses, *akabir* remains in the plural, is neither prefixed with *al-* nor in construct with a definite noun, and this is not permitted.

Shihab (al-Khafaji) responded to him, saying: this objection does not apply, because *akabir* and *asagir* have been treated as nouns, since they mean "chiefs," as al-Raghib explicitly stated. What he mentioned applies only when the word keeps its original meaning. This is supported by the words of Ibn 'Atiyya: it is said *akabira* (the feminine/plural form), just as one says *ahmar* (red) and *ahamira*, as the poet said:

"Indeed the three *ahamira* have been left behind (*ta'awwalat*)..."

Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that he (Shihab) did not know that any of the linguists or grammarians permitted *afadila* as a plural of *afdal*. But there is room to examine this. As for the answer that it is by deletion of a definite first term (*al-mudaf al-ma'rifa*) because it is known, that is, "the greatest of the people" or "the greatest of the people of the town," its weakness is not hidden. End of quotation. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words is that the adverbial phrase ("in every town") is a *laghw* (superfluous, not governing anything), ﴿the greatest﴾ is the first of the two objects and is in construct with ﴿its criminals﴾, and ﴿to scheme﴾ (*li-yamkuru*) is the second object.

Some have permitted *ja'ala* to be transitive to one object, on the basis that "making" here means "establishing," in the sense of settling them in a place and letting them dwell in it, and its object is ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ in construct form. It is understood from some statements that the possibility of the construct only holds on the interpretation of *ja'alnahum* as *makkannahum* (We established them). This is not free of disquiet. The later scholar (al-'Allama al-Thani), after listing a number of opinions, said: "What sound reasoning requires is that ﴿in every town﴾ is superfluous, ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ is the first object, and ﴿to scheme﴾ is the second. Its goodness is not hidden, but it is based on taking the demonstrative reference to one of the two matters mentioned earlier." Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) disputed this and claimed that the closer view is that the referent is the disbelievers previously mentioned, in terms of their being characterized by their attributes, and the singular form is in view of the group or the one mentioned. The place of the *kaf* (the "like" of ﴿thus﴾) is in the accusative, as the second object of *ja'alna*, placed before it to convey restriction, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Thus were you before﴾. The first object is ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾, and the adverbial phrase is superfluous. That is: "Like those disbelievers who are the leaders of Mecca and its criminals, We placed in every town its greatest criminals," meaning We made them characterized by the attributes mentioned: their deeds made fair to them, persisting in falsehood, disputing the truth with it, ﴿to scheme therein﴾, that is, to carry out scheming in it. End of quotation. Its remoteness is not hidden.

The singling out of the greatest is because they are the most capable of leading people and of scheming against them. It has also been read as *akbara mujrimiha* (with *akbar* in the singular). This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His words, glorified is He: ﴿And they scheme only against themselves﴾ are a parenthetical statement, by way of a promise to him (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelieving schemers: that is, the harm of their scheming reaches none but themselves. ﴿And they are not aware﴾ (123) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿they scheme﴾, meaning: they scheme only against themselves, while they are not aware of this at all, but rather they suppose that they are scheming against others.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 124 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿When a sign comes to them﴾ This returns to describing the state of the sinners of Mecca, after the state of others was described as consolation. The great sign that was related came only from them, not from all the sinners. That is, when a sign comes to them through the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿They say: "We will not believe until we are given what was given to the messengers of Allah."﴾ Shaykh al-Islam said: Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Until revelation is sent down to us and Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to us and informs us that Muhammad (ﷺ) is truthful, as they said." ﴿Or until you bring Allah and the angels as a group (qabil)﴾. It is also related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said the same. As you see, this is clear that what is dependent on being given what the messengers (peace be upon them) were given is their belief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in what was sent down to him, a true belief, as is what is understood from it when stated without qualification. However, this requires that "what the messengers of Allah were given" be understood as general revelation and the speaking of Jibril (peace be upon him) to them in general, and that the word "risalah" (mission) in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ be turned away from its apparent meaning and understood as the message of Jibril (peace be upon him) in the manner mentioned, and "placing it" be taken to mean delivering it to the one to whom it is sent, not placing it in its proper place, which is the Messenger, so that it may serve as an answer to their proposal and a rejection of it. The sense of their proposal, "We will not believe," is that the sign was sent down from Allah to the Messenger (peace be upon him), "until Jibril comes to us in person, visibly, as he comes to the messengers, and informs us of that." The sense of the rejection is: "Allah knows best whom it is fitting to send Jibril (peace be upon him) to, for some matter, signifying that they are far from deserving that honour." There is in this much far-fetching that is not hidden.

And you know that there is no far-fetching in taking "what the messengers of Allah were given" to mean general revelation. Rather, the far-fetching lies in departing from the statement "We will not believe until we are made messengers," which, in the noble arrangement of the words, carries a kind of support for this reading. Yes, turning "risalah" away from its apparent meaning and taking "placing" to mean "delivering" is not free of remoteness, but perhaps the matter there is easy. It is understood from the words of some that general revelation and the speaking of Jibril (peace be upon him) in general, even if they do not necessitate that mission, are nonetheless close to its rank, so the stated answer is suitable without need for the two described turnings and takings. But there is what there is in this.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl when he said: "The Banu Manaf have competed with us in nobility, until when we became like two horses in a race, they said: 'Among us is a prophet to whom revelation is sent. By Allah, we will never accept him or follow him until revelation comes to us as it comes to him.'"

[Continued in the next part.]

al-Dahhak said: Each one of the people asked to be singled out for the mission and revelation, as Allah, may He be exalted, informed about them in His saying: ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open﴾. The Shaykh said: It is not hidden that each of these two statements, although suitable to the mentioned rejection, nonetheless requires that by the belief dependent on being given the like of what the messengers were given is meant merely their affirmation of his mission (ﷺ) in general, without it covering all people. And that the particle "hatta" (until) in the words of the accursed one, "until revelation comes to us as it comes to him...", be a limit (ghayah) for not being content, not for not following. For this is established under both assumptions: whether revelation comes or not. The meaning is: "We will not believe in his mission at all until we ourselves are given prophethood, the like of what the messengers of Allah were given, or a giving like the giving to the messengers of Allah." It is not hidden that it is also possible for the words of the accursed one to contain a limit, with the meaning being mere agreement and doing the like of what he (ﷺ) does, namely the oneness of Allah, the exalted, and abandoning the worship of idols, not following his footsteps by obeying his command. Moreover, the accursed one only sought the coming of revelation as it comes to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that is not an explicit demand for independence which contradicts following.

Perhaps his intent, may the curse of Allah be upon him, was sharing in nobility in such a way that he would not fall entirely short of him (peace be upon him). It is also possible to claim that these unbelievers, since each of them was an Abu Jahl in what the rank of messengership requires, do not refuse that of two messengers, one may be sent to the other, and one of them must obey the command of the other and follow him, even though he shares with him in the basic messengership. So let this be understood.

It was also said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him): "If prophethood were true, I would have been more deserving of it than you, for I am older than you in years, and greater in wealth and children." So this verse was revealed. The Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, criticised this, saying that it has no connection to their rejected words unless what is meant by the belief dependent on what was mentioned is merely belief that the revealed sign is a true revelation, not belief that it was sent down to him (peace be upon him). Then the meaning would be: "When a sign sent down to the Messenger comes to them, they say: 'We will not believe in its descent from Allah until its descent is to us, not to him, because we are the ones who deserve it rather than him.'" For the summary of the meaning of his words, "If prophethood were true...", is: "If what you claim of prophethood were true, I would be the prophet, not you. And since the matter is not so, it is not true." Its outcome is making belief in the truth of prophethood dependent on his own being a prophet.

You know that the mention of "prophethood" and their saying "messengers of Allah" are not, on the apparent reading, in full harmony with each other. So the truth is that this saying should be dropped from the level of consideration, even though a similar report is related from Ibn Juraij (two of them), because of the greater care it shows in applying it to what is in the verse.

"Mithla ma utiya" (like what was given) is in the accusative, being an adjective (na't, qualifying modifier) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and "ma" is a masdariyyah (verbal particle), meaning: "until we are given it, a giving like the giving to the messengers of Allah." The attribution of "giving" to them (the messengers) is with respect to their being given it (peace be upon him). "Haythu" (where) is a object of an omitted verb, meaning "knows"; it has left the sense of place (zarfiyyah, adverbial of place) by the view that it is used in other than that sense, and no account is taken of one who denies this. The sentence after it, as stated explicitly by Abu 'Ali in the Kitab al-Shi'r, is a qualifier of it. Its being annexed to what follows it when used as a noun is a matter of debate. al-Radi said: "It is better that 'haythu' is annexed, and there is no barrier to annexing it, while it is a noun, to a sentence," and this was discussed. According to many, it is not permitted here for it to be genitive by annexation, since "af'al" (more knowing) is part of what is annexed to it, nor accusative by "af'al" as an adverb of place, because His knowledge, exalted is He, is not restricted to a place. Among those who stated this is Ibn al-Sa'igh. Some permitted the second, and what was given as a reason for prohibiting it was answered: it is permissible to make the restriction of His knowledge by the adverb of place metaphorical, in terms of what it relates to; indeed that is preferable to removing "haythu" from its adverbial sense, for that is either rare or impossible.

The sentence ﴿Allah knows best﴾ and so on is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), and the meaning is that the rank of messengership is not something attained by what they claim of abundance of wealth, aid of means and number, but is attained by soul-related virtues and a holy soul which Allah, exalted is He, bestows by pure generosity and bounty upon one whose readiness is complete. Some explicitly stated that it follows innate readiness, which does not entail the necessitation that the philosophers speak of, because He, glorified is He, if He wills, gives that, and if He wills, withholds, even if the locus is ready. And what is in al-Mawaqif, that innate readiness is not a condition for sending, but Allah, exalted is He, specially chooses by His mercy whom He wills, is to be understood as referring to necessitating innate readiness. For Allah's habit is that He sends from every people their most noble and purest in disposition. The full discussion is in its own place.

Most of the Seven readers read "risalatihi" (His messages) in the plural. It is related from some of them that it is recommended to pause on "rusul Allah" (the messengers of Allah), and that supplication is answered between the two verses. I have not found anything in this to rely upon.

﴿Those who committed crimes will suffer﴾ is another resumptive sentence, announcing against them what they will encounter of kinds of evil, after having announced against them their deprivation of what they hoped for. The particle "sa" (will) is for emphasis. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of a pronoun for greater reprehension. It was also said: to signal the causation of the content of the relative clause, meaning: it will certainly befall them in place of what they desired, and to which they attached their empty hopes, of the honour of prophethood and the nobility of messengership. ﴿Humiliation﴾, that is, great abasement and disgrace after their arrogance, ﴿with Allah﴾ on the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said: "from Allah," and most of the exegetes hold this, as al-Farra' said, but he objected to it, saying that in Arabic one may not say "I came near Zayd" while meaning "from near Zayd." It was also said: the meaning is that this is in His guarantee, glorified is He, or it is a store for them with Him, and this runs in the manner of mockery, as is not hidden. ﴿And a severe punishment﴾ in the Hereafter or in this world, ﴿for what they used to scheme﴾ (124). That is, because of their constant scheming, or in return for it. Since this was among the greatest of the material of their crimes, the cause is explicitly stated.

﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide﴾, that is, to make known to him the path of truth and enable him to believe. The Mu'tazilah said: the meaning of His guiding him is to reward (thawab), or to Paradise, or to reward him for guidance, or to increase him in that. ﴿He expands his breast for Islam﴾, so it becomes wide and spacious. This is a metaphor or a metonymy for making the soul prepared for the truth to settle in it, purified of what prevents it and opposes it, as he (ﷺ) indicated when it was said to him: "What is the expansion, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "A light cast into the breast, so it expands and widens." It was asked: "Is there a sign by which it is known, O Messenger of Allah?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Turning to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before the meeting with death."

﴿And whomever He wills to lead astray﴾, that is, He creates misguidance in him because of his bad choice. It was also said: the meaning is that He leads him astray from reward or from Paradise, or from increase of faith, or forsakes him and leaves him to what he wants. ﴿He makes his breast narrow, constricted (haraj)﴾, such that it recoils from accepting the truth, so there is scarcely any outlet for good in it. Ibn Kathir read "dayyiqan" (narrow) with lightening (tafkhif), and Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "harajan" with a kasra on the ra', meaning: intensely narrow. The rest read it with a fatha, as a descriptive adjective by the verbal noun for emphasis. The original meaning of "haraj," as al-Raghib said, is the gathering of a thing, and from it the constriction is called haraj. Some verifiers said: its original meaning is intense constriction, for the "harajah" is a thicket whose trees are so entangled that entry into it is difficult.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and others related from Abu al-Salt al-Thaqafi that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "harajan" with a fatha on the ra'. Some of what was with him among the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited "harajan" with a kasra, so 'Umar said: "Bring me a man from Kinanah and make him a shepherd, and let him be from the Mudlij tribe." So they brought him to him, and 'Umar said to him: "O young man, what is the 'harajah' among you?" He said: "The harajah among us is a tree that is among trees that neither a grazing animal nor a wild animal can reach, nor anything." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Thus is the heart of the hypocrite: nothing of good reaches it."

﴿As if he were climbing up into the sky﴾. This is a resumptive sentence, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the description, or another description. The purpose is exaggeration of the narrowness of his breast, since he is likened to one who attempts what he cannot do, for the ascent to the sky is a figure for what lies outside the sphere of capacity. In it is an indication that faith is impossible for him, just as ascending is impossible for him, and that impossibility in this is customary. From al-Zajjaj: its meaning is "as if he were ascending into the sky," turning away from the truth and fleeing far from it. The original form of "yassa'ad" is "yatasa'ad," and it has been read so, so the "ta'" was assimilated into the "sad."

Ibn Kathir read "yas'adu," and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yassa'adu," whose original form is also "yatasa'adu," and what was mentioned applied to it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 124 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Thus﴾ refers either to the placing (*ja'l*) mentioned after it, as has been explained above, or to the earlier placing, meaning: like that placing, namely the placing of the breast as constricted in the manner mentioned. ﴿Allah places defilement﴾, that is, punishment or abandonment (*khidhlan*).

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "*Rijs* (defilement) is that in which there is no good." Al-Raghib said: "*Rijs* is a filthy thing." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is the curse in this world and punishment in the Hereafter." Its root, as has been said, is from *irtijas*, which means agitation. ﴿Upon those who do not believe﴾ (125), that is, upon them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate the reason.

﴿And this﴾ refers either to what the Qur'an has brought, as transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, or to Islam, as transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, or to what has preceded of guidance and abandonment, as has been said. ﴿Is the path of your Lord﴾, that is, His way which He has approved, or His custom and the way which His wisdom requires. Nor is it hidden what there is of gentleness in mentioning the title of Lordship together with the addressing pronoun. ﴿Straight﴾, without crookedness or deviation, or just and consistent. It is either a confirming *hal* (circumstantial accusative) for its referent, with its governing verb omitted obligatorily, as in the example *hadha abuka 'atufan* ("this is your father, kind"), or a founding (new information) *hal*, and what governs it is the sense of the demonstrative or the particle *ha* used for alerting.

﴿We have detailed the signs﴾, that is, We have made them clear in detail. ﴿For a people who take heed﴾ (126), that is, who remember what is within them, and so they know that all events are by His decree and destiny, glorified is He, and that He, majestic is His state, is wise and just in all His acts. The specification of this people by the mention is because they are the ones who benefit from that detailing.

﴿For them﴾, that is, for these people, ﴿is the abode of peace﴾, that is, Paradise, as Qatada said. Al-Salam is Allah, Exalted is He, as al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said, and the attribution of the abode to Him, glorified is He, is for honour. Al-Zajjaj and al-Jubba'i said: "*Al-Salam*" means safety, i.e., the abode of safety from calamities, afflictions and all the hateful things which the people of the Fire encounter. It has also been said that it means greeting, i.e., an abode in which their greeting is peace. ﴿With their Lord﴾, that is, under His guarantee and His bounteous sponsorship, or as a store kept for them with Him, whose true nature none knows but Him. The clause is a new sentence, and it has been said that it is an attribute of "a people." ﴿And He is their Guardian﴾, that is, their lover or their helper. ﴿For what they used to do﴾ (127), that is, because of their righteous deeds, or He is their Director in recompense for them, by taking upon Himself the delivery of the reward to them.

\* \* \*

Furthermore, among the allusive (*isharah*) readings of these verses is the following: ﴿And thus We have placed for every prophet an enemy﴾. This is because of the differences in the ranks of their spirits in purity and turbidity, light and darkness, nearness and distance. From here it has been said: "The ignorant are enemies to the people of knowledge." Whenever the difference intensifies, the enmity intensifies and the harm arising from it increases. For this reason it is reported in some traditions: "No prophet has been harmed as I have been harmed." This enmity also causes greater turning toward the Truth, majestic is His state, and turning away from pleasures, and eagerness for the virtue by which the enemy is overcome, and caution against what might become a cause of reproach, and other things. ﴿And so that﴾, that is, inclines toward it, ﴿the hearts of those who do not believe﴾ incline, and they are the veiled ones, because of the existence of affinity. ﴿And so that they may be pleased with it﴾ through their love for it. ﴿And so that they may commit what they are committing﴾, from the sense of mutual support and backing.

﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah﴾ between me and you? ﴿While it is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, the inimitable, comprehensive one, detailing in it the truth and the falsehood, such that no argument remains for any speaker. So seeking anything else, which does not befit a sensible person and which no one inclines toward except the ignorant, is improper.

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾, that is, His decree in eternity has been completed by what He decreed and determined. ﴿In truth﴾, corresponding to what occurs, ﴿and in justice﴾, suited to the preparedness (*isti'dad*). It has been said: truthful in what He promised, and just in what He threatened. ﴿There is no changer of His words﴾, because they are in the pattern of what has been established in His knowledge, and reversal is impossible.

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾, that is, from the lower direction, by inclining toward the world and the world of the self (*nafs*, the carnal soul) and nature, ﴿they will lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾, because they call only to the desires that distance one from Allah, exalted is He. ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾, that is, they follow only what they follow, being veiled in the station of the self by illusions and imaginings. ﴿And they do nothing but guess﴾ by analogizing the unseen to the seen.

﴿And leave the outward of sin﴾ in the sayings and deeds that appear on the limbs, ﴿and its inward﴾ in the corrupt beliefs and false resolves.

Sahl said: "The outward of sin is disobedience in whatever form it takes, and its inward is love of it." Al-Shibli said: "The outward of sin is heedlessness, and its inward is forgetting the contemplation of what came before." Some said: "The outward of sin is seeking the world, and its inward is seeking Paradise, because both occupy one from the Truth, and whatever occupies one from Him, glorified is He, is sin." It has been said: "The outward of sin is the portions of the self, and its inward is the portions of the heart." It has been said: "The outward of sin is love of the world, and its inward is love of status." It has been said: "The outward of sin is seeing one's own deeds, and its inward is the heart's resting in one's states."
