﴿And indeed the devils﴾, who are those veiled by the outward from the inward, ﴿do inspire their allies﴾, that is, those among the deniers who befriend them, ﴿to dispute with you﴾ by means of the doubts they receive. ﴿And if you obey them﴾ and abandon what you are upon of *tawhid* (affirmation of Allah's oneness), ﴿you are indeed associators like them﴾.

﴿Is one who was dead﴾ through ignorance and the desire of the self, or through being veiled by its attributes, ﴿then We gave him life﴾ through knowledge and love of the Truth, or through the unveiling of the veils of His attributes, ﴿and made for him a light﴾ from Our guidance and Our knowledge, or a light from Our attributes. Or: one who was dead through spiritual striving (*mujahadat*), so We gave him life with the spirit of contemplations; or dead through the desires of the self, so We gave him life with the purity of the heart; or dead through seeing the reward, so We gave him life by seeing the return to the Bestower, and We made for him the light of insight (*firasa*) or of guidance.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: The meaning is: one who was dead away from Us, so We gave him life through Us and made him an imam who guides by the light of answered prayer, and misguidance returns to him. Ibn 'Ata' said: One who was alive by the life of his self and dead in his heart, so We gave him life by the mortification of his self and the life of his heart. We facilitated for him the paths of success and anointed his eyes with the lights of nearness, so he sees none but Us and turns to none other than Us.

﴿Like one whose likeness is in darkness﴾, that is, the darkness of his self, its attributes and its acts, ﴿from which he cannot come out﴾ because of the badness of his preparedness.

﴿Thus has been made attractive to the disbelievers﴾, the veiled ones, ﴿what they used to do﴾, so they are veiled by it.

﴿And thus We have placed in every town the greatest of its criminals to scheme therein﴾. This may serve as a cause for the increased perfection of the knowers, as has been explained above regarding the placing of enemies for the prophets, peace be upon them. It is also possible that it is an allusion to what is within the selves: that is, thus We placed, in every town, which is the existence of the human being that is the body, ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ from the powers of the commanding self, ﴿to scheme therein﴾ by misguiding the heart. ﴿And they scheme only against themselves﴾, because the consequence of their scheming returns to them, both outwardly and inwardly.

﴿And when a sign comes to them﴾ through the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, ﴿they say: "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah"﴾, namely the messengership sent to them. ﴿Allah knows best where He places His message﴾. This is where the treasury of preparedness is full and the self is holy.

﴿Those who committed crime will suffer humiliation before Allah﴾ through being veiled from the Truth, that is, abasement through the loss of their rank at the ruin of their bodies, ﴿and severe punishment﴾ through their deprivation of what is agreeable, and the arrival of the one who negates (*al-nafi*) upon them in the bodily resurrection.

[p. 25]

﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide﴾ to Him and to make Him known to him, ﴿He opens his breast to Islam﴾ by casting into it a light from His lights, so that he comes to know Him through it. ﴿And whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast constricted, tight﴾, so that nothing of the lights of the sun of gnosis (ʿirfan) enters it, ﴿as if he were climbing up into the sky﴾ in recoil and flight from accepting that, because it contradicts his readiness (istiʿdad). It was said: the meaning is, whomever Allah wills to guide to monotheism (tawhid), He opens his breast to accept the light of the Truth (al-Haqq) and the submission of existence to Allah, Glorified is He, by uncovering the veils of the attributes of his own self (nafs) from the face of his heart that faces the self, so that it expands to accept the light of the Truth. And whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast constricted, tight, through the self's domination over it and its pressure upon it, as if he were climbing into the sky of his spirit along with those dark bodily states; and that is an impossibility. It was said other than that. ﴿Thus Allah places the filth﴾, that is, the filth of defilement by the stench of nature, ﴿upon those who do not believe﴾, and they are those veiled from the Truth.

**﴿And this﴾**, that is, the path of *tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness), or the appointing. **﴿is the path of your Lord﴾**, that is, His way which He has chosen, or His custom which His wisdom has required. **﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who remember﴾**, meaning the cognitions and realities that are fixed in their innate capacity (*isti'dad*).

﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord﴾ It is the courtyard of His majesty, the precincts of the holiness of His attributes, and the places where the lights of His beauty descend, free from the peril of veils, the cause of troubles, and the onset of punishment. He is their Guardian in the mode of His care and the unveiling of His beauty to them; or, their Guardian preserves them from seeing others in between. It is also permissible that the meaning be: for them is the abode of safety from every fear and calamity, where the servant dwells in the shade of the Essence and the Attributes, and in the lushness of subsistence after annihilation. Most [scholars] hold that al-Salam is among His names, exalted is He; so what is your opinion of an abode attributed to Him, exalted is His station?

When Salma descends into a valley, its water is pure and sweet-flowing, and its trees are rosy-hued.

We ask God Most High to admit us into that abode, by the sanctity of His chosen Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 128:

﴿And on the Day He gathers them all together﴾ It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyyah), and its governing verb is implied: "Remember," or "Say," or "there is what is not mentioned because of its awfulness." It is also permissible that it be an object (maf'ul bihi) of an implied verb, i.e., "Remember that day." The pronoun in the accusative refers to those who are gathered from the two species (al-thaqalan, humankind and jinn). It has been said that it refers to the disbelievers. Ḥafṣ, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Rawḥ, on the authority of Yaʿqūb, read "yaḥshuru" with the letter yāʾ, while the rest read it with the nūn of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) to magnify the matter.

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn!﴾ is on the basis of an implied "saying." Al-maʿshar (assembly) is a group whose affair is one. Al-Ṭabarsī said: it is the complete group of a people, which includes the various categories of groups, and from it comes "al-ʿashara" (the ten), because it is the completion of the series. What is meant by "the jinn," or by their assembly, according to what has been said, is the devils. Some learned men mentioned that the word jinn is used in two senses: one of them is for the spiritual beings concealed from all the senses, so that the angels and the devils enter among them; and the second is for the spiritual beings other than the angels. Others said: the spiritual beings are three: good ones, who are the angels; evil ones, who are the devils; and intermediate ones, among whom are good and evil. In any case, the one addressed by the call is the evil ones who lead people astray, for they are the ones addressed by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿You have indeed led astray many of mankind﴾, i.e., you have multiplied their misguidance and their leading astray, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj said. So the speech is on the basis of an omitted modifier, or "from them," in that you made them your followers, so they were gathered together with you, just as one says: "The commander has multiplied his soldiers." This is by way of reproach and rebuke.

It has been said: the word "assembly" was mentioned with regard to the jinn rather than with regard to humankind because misguidance often requires solidarity and cooperation, and "assembly" carries a hint of this, which is not the case with "ghawā" (misguidance).

﴿And their allies from mankind said﴾, i.e., those who obeyed them and followed them, ﴿from mankind﴾, i.e., those who are of mankind, or who are existing from them. So "min" is either to explain the kind, or is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "awliyāʾ." ﴿Our Lord, some of us benefited from others﴾, i.e., mankind benefited from the jinn in that they directed them to the desires and to what leads to them, and the jinn benefited from mankind in that they took them as leaders and chiefs and followed their command, so they brought joy upon them through that.

It is reported from al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jurayj, al-Zajjaj and others that the benefit of mankind from them was that when one of them travelled and feared the jinn, he would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley." And their benefit from mankind is their acknowledgment that they are capable of protecting them and granting them refuge.

It is reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb that what is meant by some benefiting from others is the obedience of some of them to others and their agreement with them. Al-Balkhi said: it is possible that the benefit is restricted to mankind, so that some of mankind benefited from some of the jinn, but not the jinn from mankind.

﴿And we have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾, and it is the Day of Resurrection according to what many have said. It is reported from al-Ḥasan, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj that it is death; and the first is more preferable. The allies only said what they said as an acknowledgment of what they did of obeying the devils, following desire, and denying the resurrection, and to show regret over it and grief over their state, and submission to their Lord. Otherwise, the benefit of the report and its implication is not something whose realization is established.

It has been said: perhaps the restriction to relating the speech of the misguided is to indicate that the misleaders have been utterly silenced, so that they were not able to speak at all.

It is read "ājālanā" (our terms) in the plural, and "alladhī" in the masculine and singular. Abu ʿAli said: it is a generic (jins), or alladhī was placed in the position of allatī.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'nāf bayānī), as if it were said: "Then what did Allah, exalted is He, say at that time?" So it was said: He said: ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾, i.e., your dwelling place and the place of your residence, or your staying, on the basis that "mathwā" is either a noun of place or a verbal noun. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the plural, and the governing element in it is "mathwā" if it is a verbal noun, and they posited an implied governing element, i.e., "they will dwell abiding," if "mathwā" is a noun of place, because then it is not suitable to govern. Abu al-Baqa said: the governing element in the circumstantial clause on this assumption is the meaning of the annexation (iḍāfah), and they rejected it on the grounds that a relation of annexation does not govern, and it is not valid that it should put the circumstantial clause in the accusative.

﴿Except what Allah wills﴾. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that He, exalted is He, excepted a people whom it was already foreknown in His knowledge would become Muslims and would affirm the Prophet ﷺ. This is based on the view that the exception is not from what was spoken of, and that "mā" carries the meaning of "man" (who). It is not hidden that the use of "mā" for rational beings is rare, so this is far-fetched, as the inclusion of what came before in the excepted is far-fetched. It has been said: "mā" is a temporal verbal particle, according to what is apparent, and what is meant is except the time in which they are transferred to the zamharīr (extreme cold). It is reported that they enter a valley of zamharīr whose cold distinguishes between their joints, so they cry out and ask to be returned to the blazing fire. This was refuted on the grounds that it involves diverting "al-nār" (the fire) from its technical meaning, which is the abode of punishment, to its lexical meaning. It was answered that there is no harm in it when a necessity calls for it. It was objected to this: the objector does not accept any necessity other than this interpretation, along with the fact that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿your abode﴾ apparently requires what the objector maintains. It has been said: they have a time in which they go out of the abode of punishment; it is reported that the gates of Paradise are opened for them and they come out of the Fire, but when they turn to enter, they are shut in their faces, mocking them. To this is the allusion in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today those who believed among the disbelievers laugh﴾.

You know that the apparent meanings of the verses clearly indicate that the punishment of the disbelievers is not lightened after their entry into the Fire; and in their coming out there is a lightening, whatever lightening it may be, even though after it there is what makes the forelocks turn grey. Perhaps the report regarding this is not authentic. The well-known view is that the hypocrites will be brought near to Paradise until, when they smell its fragrance and see what Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for His servants in it, they will be called: "Turn them away from it; they have no share in it." The report in its entirety has been mentioned earlier, and that would be before their entry into the Fire, as is not hidden to one who consults the hadith.

It has been said: the excepted is the period of their respite before entering. As if it were said: "The Fire is your abode forever, except what He grants you respite." Abu Ḥayyan refuted this on the grounds that in exception it is required that the time of the excluded and that from which it is excluded be the same. So if you say, "The people stood except Zayd," its meaning is "except Zayd, who did not stand." It is not valid that the meaning be "except Zayd, who will not stand in the future." Likewise, "I will strike the people except Zayd" means "except Zayd, for I will not strike him in the future," and it is not valid that the meaning be "except Zayd, for I did not strike him." It was answered that this applies when the exception is not disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ). But when it is disjunctive, it is permissible, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will taste therein death, except the first death﴾, i.e., but the first death, for they have indeed tasted it. So perhaps the one who says that the excepted is the time of their respite is committed to disjunctive exception, as in this verse, and there is no objection to it when the like of it occurs in the Qur'an. There is in this an evident consideration.

Al-Zajjaj went to a subtle opinion, which becomes clear only with elaboration. He said: the meaning, and Allah knows best, is "except what Allah wills of an increase in punishment," and he did not explain the basis for the soundness of the exception, nor what is excepted according to this interpretation. Ibn al-Munir said: We will explain it, so we say: punishment, and Allah forbid, is of varying degrees. So it is as if what is meant is that they will be eternal in the kind of punishment, except what your Lord wills of an increase that reaches the utmost limit and ends at the furthest extreme, to the point that, by its reaching the end and its distinction from the kinds of punishment in severity, it is counted as outside of it, not of the kind of punishment. When a thing reaches its end according to them, they express it by its opposite, just as they expressed the abundance of an action by "rubba," and it was originally placed for the opposite of abundance, which is scarcity. This is a matter customary in the language of the Arabs. Abu al-Ṭayyib has hovered around it, saying:

"You were so generous that you almost became miserly, a barrier to the extreme; and from joy comes weeping."

So when these people are transferred to the extreme of punishment and the utmost severity, they have reached the limit which almost goes out of the name of absolute punishment, to the point that dealing with it in expression is permissible as dealing with something different. This is a good point, which is hardly understood from al-Zajjaj's words except after this elaboration. In the tafsir of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, there is something that supports it. End. It is transmitted from some of them that this exception is tied to the will of Allah, exalted is He, to lift the punishment, i.e., they will be eternal until Allah wills, if He wills. Its purpose is to manifest power and submission to the fact that their eternity was only because Allah, exalted is His majesty, willed it; and that it was rationally permissible in His will that He not punish them, and if He punished them, He would not eternalize them; and that this is not a matter obligatory upon Him, but is only the consequence of His will and His determination, exalted is He. In the verse, according to this, there is a repelling of the thoughts of the Mu'tazilah, who claim that the eternal punishment of the disbelievers is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, by the requirement of wisdom, and that it is not rationally permissible for this requirement to be otherwise. Perhaps this is the truth from which there is no escape. In its meaning is what has been said: the intent is hyperbole in eternity, in the sense that it does not cease except at the time of Allah's will, and that is something that does not occur together with its being presented in the form of exit and holding out hope to them of that, as mockery and as intensifying the matter against them. Among the eminent scholars of the modern age, the great ones, someone claimed this aspect for it, and that the ledgers are empty of it; it is mentioned in more than one place. If he does not know, that is a calamity; and if he knows, the calamity is greater. The complete discussion on that will come, Allah willing, at His saying, glorified is He: "except what your Lord wills."

﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise﴾ in punishment and reward, or in all His actions, ﴿Knowing﴾ (128) of the states of the two species and their deeds, and of the recompense befitting them, or of everything; and what has been mentioned enters it primarily.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 129:

﴿And thus﴾ — that is, like what preceded of the empowering of the jinn over humankind to lead them astray and misguide them; or like what preceded: ﴿We shall make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾ — from among humankind — ﴿some of them to others﴾ — that is, We shall place them in such a state that they take each other as allies and exercise control over one another in this world, through misguidance, leading astray, and other things. It has been used as evidence that when the subjects are wrongdoers, God Most High empowers over them a wrongdoer like them. And in a hadith: "As you are, so shall you be ruled over" (kama takunu yuwalla alaykum). Or the meaning is: We shall make some of them companions of others in punishment, just as they were so in this world when committing what leads to vile deeds, as it has been said; and the like of this is related from Qatadah. ﴿Because of what they used to earn﴾ (129) — that is, because of what they were persistently engaged in earning of disbelief and sins.

صفحة 28
of the Qur'anic verse quoted above, the commentary continues: [the passage is complete as given; no further text was supplied.]

**"O assembly of jinn and humans"**: this begins the narration of the rebuke and reproach that will be directed at the two groups for their neglect regarding their own souls. **"Did there not come to you"** in the world **"messengers"** from God, Mighty and Majestic, **"from among you"**, that is, from among your own number. This does not mean that every messenger came to every nation, nor that those messengers were of both kinds together. Rather, each nation had a messenger specific to it, and those messengers were from humankind only, since it is well known that there were no messengers or prophets among the jinn. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted be He: **"From both of them emerge the pearl and the coral"** (55:22), for these come only from the salt water, as its verification will come, God willing.

Al-Farra' (a grammarian) held that an elided noun (*mudaf*) is understood here, meaning "from among one of you." Others said: the intended sense of "messengers" includes the messengers of the messengers. It is established that the jinn listened to the Qur'an and warned their people with it, as He, glorified be He, said: **"And when We turned toward you a company of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an"** (46:29), up to His saying, Mighty and Majestic: **"They returned to their people as warners"** (46:29). It is also related from al-Dahhak and others that God sent messengers to the jinn from among themselves, and some of them stated that a messenger from among them was called Yusuf. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that messengers were sent to each of the two groups from among their own kind. Some claimed that there is a consensus (*ijma'*) that no messenger was sent to the jinn from among themselves, and that messengers were sent to them only from among humankind. As to whether this occurred before the mission of our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, or not, the view expressly stated by al-Kalbi al-Thani is: "The messengers used to be sent to humankind until Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to humankind and the jinn."

**"Who recount to you My signs"**, which I revealed to them. This clause is another attribute of "messengers," confirming what is meant by their being sent, namely conveying and warning. This has been achieved with regard to both weighty groups. **"And warn you"**, that is, they frighten you with what is contained within them of calamities **"of the meeting of this your day"**, that is, the Day of Gathering, in which they have witnessed what they have witnessed. **"They will say"**: this is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*), and its purpose is to narrate their words: how they will speak and how they will acknowledge. **"We bear witness against ourselves"**, that is, that the messengers came to them, recited to them and warned them, and that they confronted them with disbelief and denial. As for His saying, glorified be He: **"And the life of this world deceived them,"** together with what is conjoined to it, it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraDh*) explaining what led them in the world to commit the abominations they committed, and what compelled them in the Hereafter to confess to disbelief and to deserve punishment. It is also a rebuke of them for this and a dismissal of their opinion. Thus there is no repetition between the two testimonies. The meaning is: they were deceived in the world by the base life and the lowly, transient pleasures, turned away from the enduring bliss promised by the messengers, peace be upon them, and dared to commit what would drag them to the everlasting punishment about which they had been warned. **"And they will bear witness"** in the Hereafter **"against themselves that they were"** in the world **"disbelievers"** (130) in the signs and the warnings. They were forced to submit to the severest punishment. In this there is, for them, the utmost regret, and for the listeners, a warning against imitating their conduct, which needs no further elaboration.

That is a reference to the coming of the messengers, or to the question implied by "Did there not come to you" (ألم يأتكم), or to what has been related of their affair, namely their testimony against themselves of disbelief and of deserving the punishment. It may be in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "the matter is that," or as the subject of an implied predicate, or its predicate is His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿That your Lord would not destroy the towns﴾, with the preposition lam omitted, taking *an* as a verbal particle (*an masdariyyah*) or as the lightened form of *inna*, whose subject is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). It may also be in the accusative, as the object of an implied verb such as "We have made (*fa'alna*)" or something similar. It is also permitted for *an lam* (...) etc. to be a substitute (*badal*) for the demonstrative.

His words, ﴿with wrongdoing﴾, are connected either to "destroying" (*muhlik*), meaning "because of wrongdoing," or to an implied element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) describing the towns, meaning "or being associated with wrongdoing," or as a circumstantial clause describing your Lord, or describing His pronoun in *muhlik*. The intended meaning is "destroying the people of the towns," but either the attribution is figurative, or the genitive noun has been omitted and the noun in the genitive position has been placed in its stead. This is not contradicted by His words, ﴿while its people are heedless﴾ (131), because the original is "while they are heedless," and when the noun was omitted, the noun was replaced by its pronoun.

Shaykh al-Islam objected to making "with wrongdoing" a circumstantial clause of "your Lord" or of its pronoun, on the ground that the heedlessness of its people is already included in the meaning of wrongdoing and in its very reality, so it is not fitting to restrict it by a subsequent clause. It was objected to him that wrongdoing may be conceived without heedlessness, such as when it occurs in a state of alertness and while complying in a state of awareness. If what is intended here is destruction in a state of heedlessness, then the benefit of the restriction is to specify the intended meaning, and its merit is not hidden. But what is wrong with it is not hidden either.

He, may his secret be sanctified, chose among the possibilities mentioned and the modes of parsing the third demonstrative in each case. He said: The meaning is that "that" is established because of the non-existence of your Lord's being one who destroys the towns for any wrongdoing they committed before they were forbidden from it and alerted to its falsehood through messengers and a Book, and before reason would have been compelled by its own self-evident judgment, and before they were warned of the consequence of their crimes. That is, were it not for the non-existence of His, may He be exalted, being one who punishes them before the sending of the messengers and the sending down of the Books, it would not have been possible to rebuke them with what was mentioned, nor would they have testified against themselves to their disbelief and to their deserving punishment, nor would they have pleaded that no messenger came to them, as in His, may He be glorified, words: ﴿And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ He explained what was mentioned by the non-existence of worldly punishment, which is the destruction of the towns before warning. However, the closer explanation for the non-existence of punishment in general without sending messengers is more complete, according to what His words, ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾, express, according to the interpretation adopted by the people of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) regarding its meaning. This is to show His, may He be glorified, transcendence above both kinds of punishment without warning, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner.

It is not hidden that what he chose is a sound view, except that his later statement, "if that is taken as a reference to the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, and their warning, and the predicate of the subject is omitted, as the majority agreed upon, it is far removed from the requirement of the context and is rejected," and that on all the other possibilities the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) by way of shifting the address (*talwin al-khitab*). The apparent meaning is that the non-destruction before warning is not specific to humans, but jinn also are not destroyed before being warned, even though the term "people of the towns" does not commonly apply to them. This is based, in our view, on the pure grace of God, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist school) say: it is obligatory upon God, exalted is He, not to punish before warning and the establishment of proof, and they based this on the principle of rational good and evil (*al-husn wa'l-qubh al-'aqliyyan*). Our imams affirm this, but they do not make it the basis of the ruling, as the Mu'tazilah claim.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 132:

﴿And for each﴾ of the accountable beings, whether jinn or humans, ﴿there are degrees﴾, that is, ranks; so it encompasses the degrees of descent in its literal sense or by way of predominance (taghlib), ﴿according to what they did﴾, that is, according to their deeds, whether good or evil, or on account of their deeds, or as a recompense for them. Thus "min" (mi) is either ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin), or ta'lIliyyah (indicating cause), or bayaniyyah (explanatory) with an elided noun (taqdir mudaf). ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾ (132). So the deed of any doer, or the measure of what he deserves of reward or punishment, is not hidden from Him, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿taʿmalūna﴾ with the letter ta' (second person), by way of predominance of the address over the third person. If ﴿yaʿmalūna﴾ with the letter ya' were intended to include the addressee, namely if the whole creation were meant, there would be no objection to considering the predominance of the absent over the addressed, except that such a usage is not attested in their speech.
Page 30

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 133:

﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani)﴾, meaning: there is no independence from anything, whatever it may be, except for Him, glory be to Him. So He, exalted is His majesty, has no need of the servants, nor of their worship. And it is not hidden what there is in confronting the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) by using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and in attributing it to His pronoun, upon him be prayers and peace, of abundant gentleness. The sentence is a subject and predicate, and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Full of mercy (dhu al-rahmah)﴾ is another predicate. It has been permitted that it be the predicate, and ﴿al-Ghani﴾ be an attribute, i.e., the one described with general mercy, so He shows mercy to the servants by imposing obligations, perfecting them, and gives them respite in their disobedience until what He wills. In this is an indication that what was mentioned earlier of the sending (of messengers) is not for His benefit, but for His mercy upon the servants, and a preparation for His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾, meaning: He has no need of you at all. If He wills, He will take you away, O disobedient ones, or O people, by destruction. And in the shifting of the address is an intensification of the threat that is not hidden. ﴿And will make to succeed you after you whomever He wills﴾, meaning: and will bring into being, after your removal, ﴿whomever He wills﴾ from creation. The use of "ma" rather than "man" is to show the perfection of greatness and to remove them from the rank of rational beings. ﴿As He produced you from the descendants of another people﴾ (133). Meaning: from the offspring of other people who were not of your likeness, and they were the people of Noah's ark, upon him be peace. But He, glory be to Him, kept you alive out of mercy toward you. The "ma" in "kama" is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, and the place of the kaf is in the accusative, either as a masdar or as a descriptive for the masdar of the preceding verb, i.e., and He will produce a production like your production, or He will make a succession (istikhlaf) that is like your production. The "min" is for the starting point of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). It has been said that it has the meaning of substitution (badal). The conditional clause is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) confirming the content of what precedes it of self-sufficiency and mercy.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 134:

﴿Indeed, what you are promised﴾ — i.e., indeed that which you are promised of the Resurrection (al-qiyamah), the Reckoning (al-hisab), the punishment (al-iqab), the reward (al-thawab), and the differing of ranks (tafawut al-darajat wa'l-darakat). The form of the future tense (sigha al-istiqbal) is used to indicate continuity that is renewed (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi). And ﴿ma﴾ is the noun of inna (ism inna). It is not permissible for it to be the kafah (the particle that "restrains" inna from governing a noun, i.e., ma as a restrictive particle), because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿lata'tin﴾ ("is surely coming") prevents that, as Abu al-Baqa said: it is the predicate (khabar) of inna. The meaning is: indeed that is certainly going to happen. And the choice of ata'tin ("coming") over waqi' ("occurring") is to show the completeness of the swiftness of its occurrence, by depicting it in the form of a diligent seeker whom no fleeing person can escape, as is indicated by His exalted saying: ﴿and you cannot escape﴾ (134), i.e., you cannot make the one who seeks you incapable of reaching you, nor make him unable to overtake you.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning of "and you cannot escape" is "and you will not be outrunners." The choice of the active participle form over the imperfect (al-mustaqbal) serves to announce the nearness of the coming and the permanence which the shift from the verbal to the nominal sentence conveys, directed toward the negation. So the intended meaning is the continuance of the negation of inability (al-i'jaz), not a statement of the continuance of its non-existence. And there are parallels to this in the Noble Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 135:

﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your standing"﴾. This is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to confront the disbelievers with intensified threat and repeated warning, and to show them the extreme firmness he holds in the religion, the utmost reliance on his affair, and his complete disregard for them at all, after having made clear to them their state and their final end. That is, say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers: ﴿act according to your standing﴾, i.e., according to the utmost of your establishment and ability. The word makanah is a verbal noun of makkana, since tamakkana is the most emphatic form of establishment. It is also permissible for it to be a noun of place, meaning a location, like maqam and maqamah. Hence Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) explained it as "in your place," as narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from him. Those who explained it as "state" used it figuratively, meaning: act according to your state in which you are.

Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, read *makanatikum* (in the plural) throughout the Qur'an. Al-Wahidi claimed that the correct reading is the singular, but there is room for scrutiny. The meaning is: remain upon your disbelief and your hostility toward me. ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ according to my standing, i.e., I remain steadfast upon Islam and upon my endurance of you.

The command to threaten, and its presentation in the form of a command, as many have said, is for the sake of emphasis regarding the warning: it is as if the one threatening wants to punish his opponent, has gathered and resolved upon it, so he compels him by the command to what leads to it. It also indicates that the one who threatens can only produce evil, like the one commanded to do something who cannot escape from it. Al-Allamah al-Thani (al-Kafawi?) considered this to be a metaphorical allegory (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah), likening that meaning to the meaning of a commanded and obligatory act that must come from one upon whom wretchedness has been decreed.

﴿So you will come to know who will have the final outcome of the abode﴾. That is, you will certainly know this; "so" (fa-sawfa) is for emphasizing the content of the sentence. The knowledge is cognitive (irfani), so it takes one object. Man is an interrogative clause suspending the verb of knowledge; its position is nominative as the subject, and the sentence after it is its predicate, and together they fill the place of the object of knowledge.

By "the abode" is meant the worldly life, not the Abode of Peace, as has been said. By "the final outcome" is meant the good end, i.e., the outcome of good, because it is the original one, for Allah, exalted is He, made the world a field for the Hereafter and a bridge of passage to it, and He desires of His servants good deeds so that they may attain a good ending.

As for the outcome of evil, it is not to be counted, because it is among the results of the distortion of the wicked. That is, "you will come to know which of us will have the good final outcome that Allah, exalted is He, created this abode for." It is also permissible for "man" to be a relative pronoun (ma mawsulah), in which case its position is accusative as the object of ﴿you will know﴾, meaning: "you will come to know that which has the final outcome of the abode." Along with the warning derived from the threat, this contains fairness in speech and an alert to the complete confidence of the warner in his affair. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *yakunu* with the ya' (third person), because the feminine gender of "final outcome" is not real.

﴿Indeed, he﴾, i.e., the matter, ﴿the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ (135), i.e., they will not attain their objective. The word "wrongdoing" was used in place of "disbelief" because it is more general than it, and it is more beneficial, for if the wrongdoer does not succeed, then how about the disbeliever, who is characterized by the greatest forms of wrongdoing?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 136:

﴿And they assigned﴾, that is, the idolaters of the Arabs, ﴿to God a share of what He created﴾, that is, what He brought into being. Al-Raghib said: al-dhar' (creating) is God the Exalted's manifesting of what He has originated; it is said: "God dhara'a (created) the creation", meaning He brought their individual beings into existence. Al-Tabarsi said: al-dhar' is creation in the manner of innovation (ikhtira'), and its root meaning is manifestation; from it comes "mulihhun dhara'aniyyun" (a salt-whitened... ), due to the manifestness of its whiteness. The phrase "min" is connected to "ja'ala" (assigned), and "ma" is a relative pronoun, with the clause "dhara'a" as its relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿from the tilth and the cattle﴾ is connected to "dhara'a".

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "mimma" be connected to a omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a share﴾, and that ﴿from the tilth﴾ be also a circumstantial clause from "ma" or from the omitted returning pronoun. And ﴿a share﴾ in every case is the object of "ja'ala", and it is transitive to one object. It was also permitted that it be transitive to two objects, the first being ﴿of what He created﴾ on the basis that "min" is partitive, and the second being ﴿a share﴾. It was also said: the matter is the reverse.

It was objected that this does not support the soundness of the meaning. Whatever the case, this is the beginning of denouncing their monstrous states by relating their shameful sayings and deeds. Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said regarding the verse: when they tilled a field or had a produce, they set aside for God a portion of it and a portion for the idol. Whatever of the tilth or produce or of the share of the idols was kept, they preserved and counted it. If something of what was designated for the True God fell away, they returned it to what they had assigned to the idol; and if the water that was assigned to the idol overtook and irrigated something of what they had assigned to God, they assigned it to the idol; and if something fell from the tilth and produce that they had assigned to God and it was irrigated by what they had named for the idol, they left it for the idol. They used to forbid from their livestock the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham, and they would assign them to the idols, while claiming that they forbade them for God, glorified is He. It is also related that they would designate some of the tilth and offspring for God the Exalted, and would spend it on guests and the poor, and on other things for their gods, and spend from them on their servants (sadana), and slaughter at their shrines. When they saw what they had assigned to God growing and increasing, adding good to itself, they reverted and assigned it to their gods; and when what they had assigned to their gods increased, they left it, excusing themselves that God the Exalted is self-sufficient. This was only due to their extreme ignorance, in that they associated with the Creator, the Capable, a lifeless object that is powerless over anything, and then preferred it over Him, glorified is He, by assigning the increasing portion to it. Al-Zajjaj and others chose this narration.

The original structure of the noble text is: "And they assigned to God ... etc., and to their partners," so "the partners" was omitted, because, as it is said, it is a matter established among them; and its supposition was indicated by explicitly mentioning it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they say: This is for God, by their claim, and this is for our partners﴾, that is, the idols. They called them their partners because they assigned to them a portion of their wealth, so they are their partners in it. It is possible that the attribution (idafa) is for the slightest connection, since they claimed they were partners of God the Exalted. Al-Kisa'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "bi-zu'mihim" with a damma on the zay, and it is a dialect for it; the kasra is also attested, so it is triply vocalized, like "al-wudd". Its meaning has already been mentioned. The first was restricted with it to draw attention that, in reality, what is assigned to God, glorified is He, is not left unattached to any reward, like voluntary acts by which the face of God the Exalted is sought. It was also said: it is to indicate that this is something they invented, which God the Exalted did not command them. It was rebutted that this is derived from the assigning (ja'l), and for this reason the second was not restricted with it.

It is permitted that this be a preparation for what follows, on the basis that the meaning of their saying ﴿this is for God﴾ is a mere claim from them, whose necessary implication, namely its being exclusively for Him, the Exalted, they do not know. Then His saying, glorified is He: ﴿What is for their partners does not reach God, and what is for God reaches their partners﴾ is an explanation and detailing of it, that is, what they designated for their partners is not diverted to the ways in which what they designated for God the Exalted is diverted, and what they designated for God the Exalted is diverted to the ways in which what they designated for their gods is diverted. ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ (136), regarding what they did of preferring a created being, incapable of everything, over a Creator, capable of everything, and their acting upon what was not prescribed for them. "Sa'a" (evil is) functions like "bi'sa" (wretched is), so "ma", whether relative or descriptive, is the subject, and the object of the dispraise is omitted, i.e., "their judgment is this." It was also said: "sa'a" here is not the one that functions like "bi'sa", so it does not need a specified object of dispraise, but only a subject; for the subject of the one that functions like it must be definite with "al-" or be in construct in the more common usage. This was chosen by some scholars.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 137:

﴿And thus﴾ means: and in the same way as that adornment, namely the adorning of association (shirk) in the division of acts of devotion from the tilth and the livestock between Allah the Exalted and their associates; or in the same way as that eloquent adornment well known from the devils. ﴿He has made attractive to many of the polytheists﴾, i.e., the polytheists of the Arabs, ﴿the killing of their children﴾. So they would bury alive their young daughters, burying them while still alive. They were, as has been said, two groups in this: one of them said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah, may He be glorified, so attribute the daughters to Allah, the Exalted, for He has more right to them," and the other would kill them out of fear of poverty. It was also said: out of fear of that and of shame, and this is related from al-Hasan and a group. It was also said: the cause of killing daughters was that al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir raided a people and took their women captive, and among them was the daughter of Qays ibn 'Asim. Then they made peace, and every woman among them wanted her own tribe, except the daughter of Qays, for she wanted the one who had captured her. So Qays swore that no daughter would be born to him without his burying her alive, and this became a custom among them. It was also said: when one of them's sons reached ten, he would vow that one of them would be sacrificed, as 'Abd al-Muttalib did in his well-known story, and to this the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded when he said: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." The word "killing" is the object of "made attractive," and it is annexed to "their children," an annexation of the verbal noun to its object.

And His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿their associates﴾ is its subject. By "the associates" is meant either the jinn or the custodians (sadana), and they were so named because they are partners ⟨of theirs⟩ in
page 33
their wealth, as was mentioned just before, or because of their obedience to Him, as the partner of Allah, Mighty is His name, is obeyed. The meaning of their adorning that for them is making it appear good to them and urging them toward it.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿was made attractive﴾ in the passive form, with the thing passed over being the killing, the children were put in the accusative, and the associates were put in the genitive by annexing the killing to them, separated between them by its object. Al-Zamakhshari objected to this, saying: it is something that, even if it were in the place of necessities, namely poetry, would be vile and rejected, as the following line is vile:

"A watering-place which pushed the she-camel of Abi Mazada"

So how much more so in prose speech, and how much more so in the inimitable speech. Then he said: What led him to that is that he saw in some of the copies of the Qur'an ﴿their associates﴾ written with a ya', and had he read with the genitive for "the children" and "the associates", because the children are their associates, he would have found a way out from this forcing. End of quotation.

Indeed he has mounted a blind camel in this speech and wandered in a desert waste. He imagined that the Seven Imams of the readings each chose a letter and read with it by his own reasoning, not by transmission and hearing, as some ignorant people have claimed. Therefore, he says, Ibn 'Amir erred in this reading, and he began to explain the source of his error. This is a plain error which fears disbelief, we seek refuge in Allah the Exalted, for the seven readings are mutawatir in whole and in detail from the most eloquent of those who spoke the Arabic letter ḍād (ﷺ). So to disparage any of them is in the same sense as disparaging the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), indeed disparaging Allah, Mighty and Majestic; we seek refuge in Allah, Glorified is He, from that. Abu Hayyan said: How strange, for a weak non-Arab in grammar to refute a pure Arab a mutawatir reading whose parallel exists in Arabic speech in more than one line of verse, and more strange is the ill-mannered conduct of this man toward the imam readers whom this Community chose to transmit the Book of Allah, Exalted, East and West; and the Muslims have relied on their transmission because of their precision, knowledge and piety. End of quotation. Other imams also criticized him severely. Perhaps his excuse in this is his ignorance of the two sciences of readings and principles.

It may be said: there is no distinction between a governing annexed noun and other annexed nouns. The precise grammarians have distinguished between them: the second is separated by an adverbial element, while the first, when it is a verbal noun or the like, is separated by its object absolutely, because its annexation is intended to be separated and its object is postponed in rank, so its separation is as no separation. Therefore that is permissible in it and is not restricted to poetry as other cases are. Among those who explicitly stated this is Ibn Malik, who faulted al-Zamakhshari for failing to make this distinction. In his Kafiya he said: "An adverb or what resembles it may separate the two parts of an annexation, and it may be used; two separations occur in the necessity of some poets, and in choice they have annexed the verbal noun to a subject after an object that intervenes," like the saying of one of the speakers in the rajaz:

"By rubbing the grains of the husked spike ... in the valley like the rubbing of ginned cotton,"
"My reliance is the reading of Ibn 'Amir,"
"And how many a supporter and helper it has."
End of quotation. And after all this, even if we grant that Ibn 'Amir's reading contradicts the analogy of Arabic, it would still be obligatory to accept it once its transmission is established, just as things that contradicted analogy were accepted, though the soundness of their transmission falls far short of the soundness of the aforementioned reading. How fine is the saying of the Imam, as related by al-Jalal al-Suyuti: "I often see the grammarians perplexed in establishing the wording found in the Qur'an; when they cite an unknown line of verse in support of it, they rejoice in it, and I am greatly amazed at them, for if they make the occurrence of that unknown line in accordance with it a proof of its soundness, then making the occurrence of the Qur'an with it a proof of its soundness is more fitting." From what we have mentioned, what is wrong in al-Sakkaki's saying becomes known: he said that separation between the annexed and the annexed-to is permissible with other than an adverb, and similarly his saying:

"Between the forearm and the forehead of the lion"

is to be taken as the omission of the annexed-to from the first, and similarly the reading of one who read ﴿killing their children, their associates﴾, because of its reliance on trustworthy transmitters and the abundance of its parallels. Whoever wants it should consult Ibn Jinni's Khasa'is, which I take to be understood as omitting the annexed-to from the first and supplying the annexed noun in the second, as in the reading of one who read ﴿and Allah desires the Hereafter﴾ with the genitive, meaning the goods of the Hereafter. Although what I have mentioned has some distance, rejecting the trustworthy and eloquent is even further. End of quotation. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read ﴿was made attractive﴾ in the passive, with ﴿killing﴾ in the nominative, ﴿their children﴾ in the genitive, and ﴿their associates﴾ in the nominative, by supplying a verb indicated by "was made attractive," as in the saying:

"Labbayka, Yazid, a suppliant for litigation, and one who is struck by what the calamities strike."

It is as if, when it was said, "The killing of their children was made attractive to them," it was then said, "Their associates made it attractive," ﴿in order that they might ruin them﴾, i.e., destroy them by misguidance, ﴿and that they might confuse them regarding their religion﴾, i.e., mix up for them what they had of the religion of Isma'il (peace be upon him), until they slipped from it into polytheism, or their religion which they were obliged to follow. It was also said: the meaning is that they might bring them into a religion that is confused. The "lam" is for causation if the adornment is from the devils, because their aim in misguiding them is nothing but that; and for consequence if it is from the custodians, since that is not the focus of their concern, but it is a consequence. ﴿And had Allah willed﴾, i.e., had He willed that they not do that, ﴿they would not have done it﴾, i.e., the polytheists would not have done the killing they were made to find attractive, or the associates would not have done the adorning, misguidance and confusion, or both parties would not have done all of that, treating the singular pronoun as if it were a demonstrative. ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ (137). The "fa" is explanatory: meaning, since what occurred did so by the will of Allah the Exalted, leave them and their fabrication, or what they fabricate of lies, and do not concern yourself with them, for in what Allah the Exalted wills there are far-reaching wisdoms; and in it is a severity of threat that is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 138:

﴿And they say﴾: a narration concerning another kind of the disbelief of those unbelievers. It was also said that it is a continuation of what preceded. ﴿These﴾, i.e., what they had assigned to their gods; the feminine form is for the report. ﴿Cattle and tilth﴾, i.e., crops. ﴿Forbidden (ḥijr)﴾, i.e., prohibited from them. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, like "dhibḥ" (slaughter), in which the singular and plural, masculine and feminine are alike, because its origin is the verbal noun; for this reason it occurs as an attribute of "cattle" and "tilth."

Al-Ḥasan and Qatadah read ﴿ḥujr﴾ with a ḍammah on the ḥā'. He also read it with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the jīm, and with ḍammahs on both the ḥā' and the jīm together. In this reading it may be a verbal noun, like "ḥulm," or a plural, like "suquf" and "ruhun." And from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, [it is read] ﴿ḥirj﴾ with a kasrah on the ḥā' and the rā' placed before the jīm, meaning "narrow." Its origin is "ḥarij," with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and a kasrah on the rā'. It was also said that it is metathesized from "ḥajr," like "'amīq" and "mu'iq."

﴿None may eat of them﴾, i.e., consume them, ﴿except whom we will﴾. They mean, as was narrated from Ibn Zayd, men without women. It was also said: they mean that, and the servants of the idols. The sentence is another attribute of "cattle" and "tilth."

The words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿by their claim﴾ are connected to an omitted element and occur as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they say," i.e., they said that while attached to their false claim, without any proof. "Cattle" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is conjoined to the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿these are cattle﴾, i.e., they said, pointing to a portion of their cattle: "These are cattle." It was also said that the demonstrative at first refers to what had been assigned to their gods, mentioned earlier, and what lies between them is parenthetical. This [phrase] is conjoined to the earlier "cattle," its inclusion in what preceded being because what is meant by it is the sawā'ib and similar animals, which by their claim were set free and left unused for the sake of the gods. ﴿Their backs have been forbidden﴾, i.e., prevented, ﴿so they are not ridden and not carried upon.﴾
Page 35
﴿And cattle﴾, i.e., and these are cattle, as previously explained.

The words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿over which they do not mention the name of Allah﴾ are an attribute of "cattle," imposed by Him, the Exalted, to specify the qualified noun and distinguish it from others, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and their saying, "We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah"﴾ according to one opinion, not that it occurs in their reported speech like its counterparts. It is as though it were said: "And cattle that were slaughtered for the idols, for these are the ones over which the name of Allah, exalted is He, is not mentioned, and over which only the names of the idols are mentioned." Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Abu Wa'il that the meaning is: they do not perform the pilgrimage upon them, nor do they recite the talbiyah over them.

It is narrated from Mujahid: they had a portion of their cattle over which they did not mention the name of Allah, the Exalted, nor anything concerning them, neither when riding nor when milking, nor [anything else].

﴿As a fabrication against Him﴾, i.e., against Allah, glorified and exalted is He. "Fabrication" is put in the accusative as a verbal noun, either because their reported saying carries the sense of fabrication, or by implying a verb of the same root, i.e., "they fabricated a fabrication," or as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they say," i.e., fabricating, or as a causal object, i.e., for the sake of fabrication, which is remote in meaning. As for "'alayhi" (against Him), it was said that it is connected to "they say," or to the omitted "fabrication" on the first two possibilities, and to "fabrication" on the last two. The connection to "they say" is quite remote. What prevented them from connecting it to the verbal noun, according to what has been said, is that a verbal noun used as an absolute object does not govern, since it is not equivalent to "that" plus a verb. This is open to scrutiny, because interpreting it that way is not necessary for the preposition to be connected to it, for it is sufficient that it retains the scent of the verb.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to an omitted element that occurs as an attribute of "fabrication," i.e., a fabrication existing against Him.

﴿He will surely recompense them﴾ for ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾ (138), i.e., on account of it or in exchange for it. The recompense was left indefinite for magnification.

[Page 35]

﴿And they say﴾, narrating another of the forms of their disbelief: ﴿What is in the bellies of these cattle﴾. By this they mean the fetuses of the baḥā'ir and sawā'ib, as is related from Mujāhid and al-Suddī. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they meant by it the milk. The word ﴿mā﴾ is a mubtada' (grammatical subject), and its khabar (predicate) is His statement, glorified is He: ﴿exclusively for our males﴾, meaning: lawful for them alone, with no female sharing in it. The ta' in khāliṣah is either for transferring the word into the category of nouns (ism), or for emphasis, as in rāwiyat al-shiʿr (a person who narrates much poetry), meaning one who narrates it much. Or it is because khāliṣah is a maṣdar (verbal noun), as al-Farrā' said, like ʿāfiyah, and it is used in place of khāliṣ for emphasis. Or it is by implying dhū (possessor of). This is widespread in the speech of the Arabs. One says: "So-and-so is my khāliṣah," meaning "one who is exclusively mine" (dhū khulūṣī). The poet said:

You were my trusted one, and you were my khāliṣah,
and not every man is worthy of being trusted.

It has been said: the coming of a maṣdar on the pattern fāʿil and fāʿilah is rare. It has also been said that the ta' is for the feminine, on the basis that mā is an expression for the fetuses.

The masculine form in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and forbidden to our wives﴾, means: to the category of our wives, who are females, by consideration of the wording. This has been deemed unlikely, because it would mean observing the meaning first and the wording second, which is contrary to the usual practice in the Noble Book, the reverse of this. Some have claimed that the Qur'an contains parallels to it, among them His statement, exalted is He: ﴿all of that, its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾, where the pronoun of kull (all) is feminine first, in observance of the meaning, and then masculine, in accordance with the wording. It has also been said that what is here follows the usual practice of observing the wording first, because the ṣilah (relative clause) of mā is a prepositional phrase (jār wa-majrūr), and its implied complement is the verb istaqarra (masculine), not istaqarrat (feminine). But there is no basis for this, because the complement and the hidden pronoun in it are not known to be masculine or feminine, so that they could be considered in accordance with one of the two aspects. What fairness requires is that the accordance with the wording after the meaning is rare, and that anything else is preferable wherever a way to it is found.

Some have mentioned that departing from the usual practice here is not free of a subtle meaning, both semantic and verbal. As for the first: the agreement of the statement with the action, since it is customary among people of honour to console females because of their weakness. For this reason it is recommended for a man, when he gives something to his children, to begin with their females. As for the second: observing what resembles the antithesis (ṭibāq), by a relation between khāliṣah and dhukūrinā, and between muḥarram and azwājinā. But this, as you see, is [weak].

﴿And if it is a dead one﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on what is understood from the speech: that is, it is lawful for the males and forbidden to the females if it is born alive, and if it is born dead ﴿they are﴾, that is the males and females, ﴿partners in it﴾, that is in what is in the bellies of the cattle. It has been said that the pronoun refers to "dead one", but since its meaning includes both male and female, the masculine was given precedence, and so the pronoun was made masculine, as was done in what precedes it. ﴿Partners﴾ means they eat from it all together. What is mentioned in this conditional clause appears only on the first view of the interpretation of the relative pronoun. As for the second view, it does not appear, and perhaps the one who holds it reads the verse in one of the readings to follow, or interprets the pronoun differently.

Al-Aʿraj and Qatādah read khāliṣatan in the accusative, and this is explained as a maṣdar used for emphasis, and the khabar of the subject is ﴿for our males﴾. Al-Quṭb al-Rāzī said: it is permissible for it to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase that forms the ṣilah, meaning: in a state of its being free from the bellies, that is, its coming out alive. He insisted on making it a ḥāl muqaddarah (a future-determined circumstance), but this is perhaps not necessary. More than one scholar prohibited making it a ḥāl from the pronoun after it, or from dhukūrinā itself, because a ḥāl may not precede the operating element when that element is implicit, such as a prepositional phrase, a demonstrative noun, or the particle of indication (hā al-tanbīh), which operates through what it contains of verbal meaning, nor may it precede its own referent when that is in the genitive case, as is established in its proper place.

Ibn Jubayr read khāliṣan without the ta' and also in the accusative, and the discussion of it is similar to what has passed. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Aʿmash read khāliṣatu in the nominative with an idāfah (genitive construction) to the pronoun, as a substitute (badal) for mā, or as a second subject (mubtada' thānin). Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar read wa-in takun with the ta', maytatun in the nominative. Ibn Kathīr reads yakun with the yā', and maytatun in the nominative. Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim reads takun with the ta', like Ibn ʿĀmir, maytatan in the accusative.

The Imam said: the reason for Ibn ʿĀmir's reading is that he attached the feminine marker to the verb, since the word is feminine in form. The reason for Ibn Kathīr's reading is that maytatun is the subject of yakun, and its predicate is implied: that is, "if there is for them, or there is there, a dead one." It was made masculine because maytah means mayyit (dead one).

Abū ʿAlī said: the verb did not receive the feminine marker, because the feminine gender of the subject to which it is attributed is not real, and kāna does not need a predicate, since it has the meaning of waqaʿa (occurred) and ḥadatha (happened). The reason for the last reading is that the meaning is: and if the fetuses or the cattle are dead, ﴿He will surely requite them﴾, and there is no doubt, ﴿for their description﴾ of the lie against Allah, exalted is He, concerning the matter of making lawful and forbidden, from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and their tongues describe the lie﴾. This, as some of the verifiers said, is among the eloquent and wondrous forms of speech, for they say: "his speech described falsehood" when it was false; and "his eye is half magic," meaning he is a magician; and "his figure describes slenderness," meaning slender, as an exaggeration, so that whoever heard or saw him was described to him by what would explain it to him. Al-Maʿarrī said:

The lightning of al-Maʿarrah passed after a lull,
so it spent the night at Rāmah describing the glitter.

﴿Their description﴾ is in the accusative according to what al-Zajjāj held, since it occupies the position of the maṣdar of yajzihim. So the meaning is: the requital for their description, that is, the requital for their description (or: for the description). It has been said that the implied meaning is: He will requite them with punishment because of their description, that is, because of its cause. When the preposition was dropped, waṣfahum (their description) became accusative.

﴿Indeed He is Wise, Knowing﴾ (139). This is a justification for the promise of requital, for the Wise, the Knowing, who knows what proceeded from them, scarcely leaves their requital, which is among the requirements of wisdom. The verse has been used as evidence that it is not permissible to make an endowment (waqf) specifically for male children to the exclusion of females, and that such an endowment is annulled even after the death of the endower, because it is an act of the Jāhiliyyah. Some of the Mālikīs used this as evidence for the same in gifts (hibah). Al-Bukhārī in al-Tārīkh related from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "One of you intends to take wealth and make it for the males among his children. This is only as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 140:

﴿Indeed, they have lost who killed their children﴾ The ones meant are the Arabs who used to kill their children, as has passed. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of ʿIkrimah that it was revealed concerning those of Rabiʿah and Mudar who used to bury their daughters alive. That is, their souls were destroyed, since they deserved punishment for doing so; or their religion and their worldly life were lost.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿qattalū﴾ (they slew) with doubling of the letter (qaṭṭalū), for the sense of frequency: that is, they did this many times. ﴿Foolishly, without knowledge﴾: that is, due to the lightness of their intellects and their ignorance of the attributes of their Lord, glory be to Him. ﴿Foolishly﴾ (safahan) is in the accusative either as a reason (ʿillah) for ﴿qatalū﴾, or as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal) of its subject, which is supported by the reading ﴿sufahāʾ﴾ (foolish ones), or as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of a verb omitted, indicated by the context. The prepositional phrase ﴿bi-ghayri ʿilm﴾ is either a qualifier or a circumstantial phrase.

﴿And they forbade what Allah had provided for them﴾, namely the baḥīrah, the sawāʾib and the like. ﴿Fabricating against Allah﴾ is in the accusative according to one of the aforementioned possibilities. The explicit mention of the Glorious Name in place of a pronoun serves to show the completeness of their rebellion and transgression. ﴿They have certainly gone astray﴾ from the straight path. ﴿And they were not guided﴾ (140) to it, even though they were guided by various kinds of guidance; or it means they were not guided from the outset. The purpose is to emphasise the negation of guidance from them, because the form of the verb implies the occurrence of straying after it had not been, so this was followed by this state to clarify their deep-rootedness in error and that their newly arisen straying is "darkness upon darkness." Some verifiers have stated that the clause is coordinated with (ḍallū) according to the first view and is a parenthetical insertion according to the second. Ibn Razin read: ﴿qad ḍallū qabla dhālika wa-mā kānū muhtadīn﴾ (they had strayed before that, and they were not guided).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 6, verse 141:**

﴿He it is who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ is a preface to what follows concerning the detailed states of the livestock. Al-Imam said: it is a return to the original purpose, which is establishing the proofs for affirming Tawhid (the oneness of God). That is, He is the one who created and brought forth those gardens, with no partner in that in any way whatsoever. The trellised (ma'rushat) are the vines that are carried upon a trellis ('arish), which is a framework of sticks made in the shape of a roof, with the vine placed upon it. ﴿And untrellised﴾ refers to the vines lying spread on the surface of the earth. This is the view of those who say that both the trellised and the untrellised belong to the vine.

It is related from Abu Muslim that the trellised is that which needs a trellis to be built for it, on which it is carried and held up, such as the vine and what is similar to it. The untrellised is the upright tree that needs no trellis, being independent through its straightness and the strength of its trunk. In a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, the trellised is what grows in gardens and inhabited areas, of what people plant, and the untrellised is what grows in the wilderness and the mountains. It was also said: the trellised is the grape that is given a trellis, and the untrellised is everything that grows spread out over the surface of the earth, such as the gourd and the watermelon.

'Isam al-Din said: It is not far-fetched that by the trellised is meant that which is trellised by nature, like the trees that rise upward, and by the untrellised that which spreads over the surface of the earth, like the vine. His words, glorified be He: ﴿and the date palm and the crops﴾, are a specification after a generalization, and it is conjoined to ﴿gardens﴾. That is, He produced them ﴿varied﴾ in form and manner, ﴿its fruit﴾, that is, its produce which is eaten from it. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read ﴿أُكُلُهُ﴾ (ukuluhu) with a sukun on the kaf (ukuluhu → ukluhu), and this is a dialectal form of it, as indicated by the words of al-Raghib. The pronoun (in ukuluhu) may either refer to one of the two conjoined items specifically, with the ruling for the other being inferred by analogy to it, or to each one alternatively, or to both together, and the pronoun carries the sense of a demonstrative. It is related from Abu Hayyan that the pronoun may not be made singular when conjoined with a waw; so the apparent reference is to the nearest preceding mention, which is ﴿the crops﴾, and the circumstance (hal) of the date palm is then omitted, since the circumstance stated for the crops indicates it. The estimated reading is:
[p. 38]
"and the date palm, varied in its fruit, and the crops, varied in their fruit."

He also permitted another interpretation, namely that there is an elided noun (mudaf muqaddar, an implied possessed noun) in the sentence, and the pronoun refers to it, meaning: the fruit of the gardens. The circumstance indicated is, in every case, an estimated circumstance (hal muqaddarah, an anticipated circumstance), since there is no variation at the time of creation.

Abu al-Baqa' claimed that the circumstance is as such if no elided noun is estimated, meaning: the fruit of the date palm and the grain of the crops, and it is a simultaneous circumstance (hal muqarinah) if one is estimated.

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate﴾, that is, He produced both ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾, meaning that some of their individual kinds resemble one another in color, taste, or form, and some do not resemble one another. Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "similar in appearance and dissimilar in taste." The accusative (of the two words) is in the circumstantial position (hal).

﴿Eat﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibahah, a command expressing mere permissibility), as expressly stated by more than one scholar. ﴿From its fruit﴾: the discussion about the reference of the pronoun follows the patterns already mentioned just above. ﴿When it bears fruit﴾, even if it has not yet ripened or matured. The purpose of the restriction is then the permission to eat before ripeness. It was also said that its purpose is the permission for the owner to eat from it before paying God's right, and this is the view chosen by al-Jubba'i and others.

﴿And give its due﴾, that which God has made obligatory on it, ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾. According to a narration from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, this is a tenth and a half of a tenth. This was the view of al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Qatadah, Tawus, and others. The adverbial phrase (zarf) qualifies what the command indicates in its form regarding obligation, not what it indicates in its root regarding the act, since payment is not at the time of harvest, nor is the grain in its ear, as the apparent sense might suggest, but after cleaning and winnowing. 'Ali ibn 'Isa claimed that the adverbial phrase is connected to "the due," and so it requires none of the interpretation mentioned.

In another narration from the Rabbi (Ibn 'Abbas), he used to give charity on the day of harvest by way of obligation, without a specified amount; then it was abrogated (nasakh, abrogation) by the zakat. This was the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and others. It was said: the obligatory zakat cannot be meant by this, because it was prescribed in Medina, and the surah is Meccan. Al-Imam answered this by saying: we do not concede that zakat was not obligatory in Mecca, and that its verses are Medinan does not prove that. Moreover, it has been said that this verse too is Medinan. It is related from al-Sha'bi that this is a right in wealth other than zakat. Ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others related from Mujahid that he said regarding the verse: "When you harvest and the needy are present, throw some of the ears to them; when you thresh it and the needy are present, throw some to them; when you winnow it, gather it, and know its measure, set aside its zakat."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿حِصادِهِ﴾ (hisadihi) with a kasrah on the ha', and this is a dialectal form of it. He departed from ﴿حَصْدِهِ﴾ (hasdihi), which is the well-known verbal noun, to ﴿حِصادِهِ﴾ (hisadihi), because it indicates a specific harvest, namely the harvesting of the crop when its time has come, as Sibawayh expressly stated and al-Raghib alluded to.

﴿And do not be excessive﴾, that is, do not go beyond the limit, so that you extend your hands in giving in every extreme.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who cut down palm trees and said: "No one shall come today except that I feed him." He fed people until evening, and he had no fruit left. So God revealed this. A similar report is related from Abu al-'Aliyah.

Abu Muslim said that what is meant by ﴿do not be excessive﴾ is excess in eating before the harvest, lest it lead to diminishing the right of the poor. 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Ibn al-Musayyab that the meaning is: do not withhold charity, so that you disobey. Al-Zuhri said: the meaning is: do not spend in disobedience to God, and a similar report is related from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Mujahid) that he said: "If Abu Qays were gold and a man spent it in obedience to God, he would not be excessive; but if he spent a dirham in disobedience to God, he would be excessive." Muqatil said: what is meant is: do not associate idols with the tilled land and the livestock.

The address in all these views is to the owners of wealth. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam that the address is
[p. 39]
to the rulers, meaning: do not take what is not rightfully yours and harm the owners of wealth. Al-Tabrisi chose that it is an address to all of them, both the owners of wealth and the rulers, meaning: let the owner of wealth not be excessive in giving, nor the imam in taking and distributing.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the excessive﴾ (141). Rather, He is displeased with them because of their excess, and He punishes them for it if He wills, may His majesty be exalted.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 142:**

﴿And of the livestock, some for burden and some for [slaughter and] carpets.﴾ This begins an account of the condition of the livestock and a refutation of what they had fabricated against Allah, the Exalted, concerning them, by way of prohibition and permission. It is coordinated with ﴿gardens﴾, and the common element is the permission to benefit from both. The prepositional phrase ﴿of the livestock﴾ is related to a verb of bringing into being (*inshaʾ*). *Ḥamūlah* is that which is ridden or carried upon, with no singular form, like *rakūbah*.

By it is meant the animals that carry loads. By *farsh* is meant that which is spread out for slaughter, or that which is spread out, namely what is woven from their wool, hair and fleece. Abu Muslim took the first view, and it is related from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. The second view was taken by al-Jubbaʾi. It was also said: the *ḥamūlah* are the large animals suitable for carrying, and the *farsh* are the small animals close to the ground, like the carpet spread upon it. This is related from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, but he restricted it to the large and small camels. This is one of the reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. In another report, the *ḥamūlah* are camels, horses, mules, donkeys and everything that is ridden upon, and the *farsh* are sheep.

﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you.﴾ That is: eat some of what Allah, the Exalted, has provided for you, namely the lawful. Thus *min* is partitive (*tabʿīḍiyyah*).

Provision (*rizq*) includes both the lawful and the unlawful. The Muʿtazilah restricted it to the lawful, as has been mentioned at the beginning of the book, and they claimed that this verse is one of their proofs for that.
