They constructed a logical syllogism whose premises are easy to obtain. Its form is: the unlawful is not legally edible, and it is pure; and provision is that which is legally edible, by His saying, ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾. Therefore the unlawful is not provision.

You know that this would only follow if every provision that is legally edible were true, and the verse does not indicate that. As for if *min* is partitive, it is obvious. As for if it is initial (*ibtidāʾiyyah*), then there is nothing in it that indicates the inclusion of the whole. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: consider it lawful to eat of what Allah, the Exalted, has given you.

﴿And do not follow﴾ in matters of permitting and forbidding, by imitating your predecessors who speculated in this, who invented [these rulings] from themselves and fabricated against Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿the steps of Satan﴾, that is, his paths. For that from them is by his misguidance and by his leading them astray. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ (142), that is, one whose enmity is evident. He expelled Adam, peace be upon him, from the Garden and said: ﴿I will surely seize [i.e., control] his descendants, except for a few﴾. May Allah, the Exalted, protect us and the Muslims from his evil. Indeed, He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

\* \* \*

This is (and from the mode of allusive interpretation (*ishārah*) in the verses): ﴿And the day He will gather them all﴾ in the very unity of the absolute gathering, saying, ﴿O assembly of jinn﴾, that is, the psychic faculties, ﴿you have taken away much from mankind﴾, that is, from the senses and the outward organs, or from the human forms, by making them your followers through your misguiding them and adorning for them the bodily pleasures. ﴿And their allies from mankind will say: Our Lord, some of us have enjoyed others﴾, and each of us benefited from the other in the form of human collectivity. ﴿And we have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾, by death or by the return, in the most ugly states and the worst conditions. ﴿He will say: The Fire is your abode, wherein you will abide eternally, except as Allah wills﴾. And He does not will except what He knows, and Allah, glory be to Him, does not know a thing except as it is in itself. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Wise﴾, who does not punish you except according to the states of your souls, as wisdom requires, ﴿Knowing﴾ of those states, so He punishes according to them. ﴿Thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾, that is, We make some of them allies of others, or [make some] lead to others, and companions of them in punishment, ﴿for what they used to earn﴾ of sins, according to their readiness.

﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did not messengers from among you come to you?﴾ And according to many of the people of allusion, these are the intellects, and they are messengers ⟨of a⟩ special, intrinsic kind, sent to their possessors, which makes the sending of other messengers valid, and they are external messengers.

Some of the Muʿtazilah took the word "messenger" in His saying, ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾, also to mean the intellect. And these questions, according to some of the interpreters, and the answers and testimonies are all by the tongue of the state and the manifestation of the attributes. ﴿That is because your Lord would not destroy the cities﴾, that is, the bodies or the hearts, ﴿unjustly while their people are unaware﴾; rather He alerts them through reason and its guidance, establishing the proof, and for Allah is the conclusive proof. ﴿And for each are degrees﴾, ranks in nearness and distance. ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ in His essence, free of all that is other than Him, ﴿the Possessor of mercy﴾, the general, all-encompassing mercy. So He created the servants so that they might profit from Him, not so that He might profit from them. "Self-Sufficient" according to many indicates the attribute of majesty, and "Possessor of mercy" indicates the attribute of beauty. ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾ by His essential self-sufficiency from you, ﴿and make to succeed you whom He wills﴾ of the people of His obedience, by His mercy. ﴿Say: O my people, act according to your standing﴾, that is, your direction of readiness. ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ according to my standing in that. ﴿And it is He who produced﴾ in the hearts of His servants ﴿gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾, like the vine of passion and love, ﴿and untrellised﴾, and these are the spiritual attributes upon which hearts are naturally disposed, such as generosity, fidelity, chastity, forbearance and courage. ﴿And palm trees﴾, that is, the palm of faith, ﴿and crops﴾, that is, the crop of the intentions for righteous deeds, ﴿and olives﴾, that is, the olive of sincerity, ﴿and pomegranates﴾, that is, the pomegranate of the tree of inspiration. It was also said: [they are] everything else besides that, and the door of interpretation is wide. ﴿Eat of its fruit﴾, which is the witnessings and the unveilings, ﴿when it bears fruit, and give﴾ to the seekers ﴿its due﴾, which is guidance and good admonition, ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾, the time of your arrival in it at the station of establishment and steadfastness. ﴿And do not waste﴾ by concealing it from those who deserve it, or by beginning to speak at other than its time and by preaching before its time. ﴿Indeed, He does not like the wasteful﴾; He does not approve their conduct. ﴿And of the livestock﴾, that is, the powers of the human being, ﴿some for burden﴾, that which is prepared to bear the trust and the obligations of the Law, ﴿and [some for] carpets﴾, that which is prepared for the rectification of the heart and the sustaining of human nature. ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, and it varies: the provision of the heart is verification by way of proof, the provision of the spirit is love with sincere avoidance of the cosmos, and the provision of the innermost secret is the witnessing of gnosis by the glance of direct sight. ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ by inclining toward the perishing desires and by veiling oneself with what is other than Him. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾; he wants to veil you from your Master. And Allah, the Exalted, is the one who grants success in following the right path.

[Page 40]

**Verse 143 of Surah al-An'am (6)**

﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾ *(eight mates/pairs)*. *Zawj* (زوج, pair or mate) is said of each of the two partners, male and female, among animals that mate, and it is also applied to the two together. What is meant here is the first sense, since otherwise the count would be four. Presenting it with this term and this number fits the context of the discourse better. ﴿ثَمانِيَةَ﴾ is, according to what al-Farra' said and what many of the verifying scholars chose, a *badal* (substitute, apposition) for ﴿حَمُولَةً وفَرْشًا﴾ *(for burden and for carpet)*, and is in the accusative governed by what governed those two. This is evident if *ḥamūlah* and *farsh* are explained as including the eight mates. But if this is restricted to camels, there is some obscurity.

It has been permitted that the implied meaning is "and He produced eight," and that it is coordinated with *jannāt* (gardens), with the verb deleted and the conjunction altered. Abu al-Baqa' considered this weak, though its rationale is clear. It may also be an object of *kulū* (eat) which precedes it, the meaning being "eat the flesh of eight mates." ﴿ولا تَتَّبِعُوا﴾ *(and do not follow)* is a parenthetical clause. It may also be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from *mā* (what), meaning the livestock, and it is interpreted as "of various kinds" or "of many kinds," so that it serves as an explanation of the condition. This is evident according to those who require that a circumstantial clause be a derived noun or interpreted as one. Shaykh al-Islam objected to this, saying that the eloquence of the noble composition rejects it, since it is evident that the verse is arranged to clarify the state of the livestock by first dividing it into *ḥamūlah* and *farsh*, then dividing it into eight mates, which result from dividing the first into camels and cattle and dividing the second into sheep and goats, and then dividing each of the four categories into male and female. All of this is to clarify the substances about which they fabricated lies against Him, glory be to Him, concerning what is lawful and unlawful, and then to rebuke them by exposing their lying and fabrication in each of those substances, by directing denial at them in detail. End of quotation. There is clear objection to this.

His words, glory be to Him, ﴿مِنَ الضَّأْنِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ *(from the sheep, two)* mean two pairs: the ram and the ewe. *Ithnayn* (two) is in the accusative. It was said that it is a *badal* from ﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾, a partial substitute (*badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull*) or a complete substitute (*badal al-kull min al-kull*) if the coordination to it is considered, in the accusative governed by its governor, and the prepositional phrase is attached to it.

The second scholar said: The apparent view is that ﴿مِنَ الضَّأْنِ﴾ is a substitute for *al-an'ām* (the livestock), and *ithnayn* is a substitute from ﴿حَمُولَةً وفَرْشًا﴾, or from ﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾ if we permit a substitute to have a substitute. It was also permitted that the substitute be *ithnayn* as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the indefinite noun, placed before it.

It is read *ithnānī* (two) as a subject (*mubtada'*), whose predicate is the prepositional phrase, and the sentence is explanatory (*bayāniyyah*) and has no grammatical place (*lā maḥall lahā min al-i'rāb*). *Al-ḍa'n* (sheep) is a collective noun, like *al-ibil* (camels), the plural of *ḍa'īn* in the pattern of *amīr* and *'abīd*, or the plural of *ḍā'in* in the pattern of *tājir* and *tujr*. It is also read with a fatḥah on the hamzah, and this is a dialectal variant of it.

﴿ومِنَ المَعْزِ﴾ *(and from the goats)*, two pairs, ﴿اثْنَيْنِ﴾: the male goat and the female goat. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Ibn 'Amir read *al-ma'z* with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, and it is the plural of *mā'iz*, in the pattern of *ṣāḥib* and *ṣaḥb*, and *ḥāris* and *ḥars*. Ubayy read *al-mi'zā* (with the feminine ending), and it is a collective noun of *ma'z*.

These four pairs, according to what Shaykh al-Islam chose, are an elaboration of the *farsh* (carpet, i.e., the animals used for food and small load). He said: Perhaps they are mentioned first in the elaboration, though their root is mentioned later in the summary, because these two kinds are the most liable to be eaten, and eating is the main thing to which lawfulness and unlawfulness pertain. This is the secret behind limiting the command to it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿كُلُوا مِمّا رَزَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ *(eat of what God has provided for you)*, without mention of benefiting by carrying and riding, and other things they had forbidden, such as the *sā'ibah* (free-roaming camel) and its counterparts. Some of them gave as a reason for the precedence the nobility of the sheep and goats, and for this reason the prophets, peace be upon them, pastured them. This does not suit the context, as is not hidden.

﴿قُلْ﴾ *(say)*, as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of their inability to answer: ﴿آلذَّكَرَيْنِ﴾ *(is it the two males)*, the male of the sheep and the male of the goat, ﴿حَرَّمَ﴾ *(has He forbidden)*, God Most High, ﴿أمِ الأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ *(or the two females)*, meaning the females of those two kinds. *Al-dhakarayn* and *al-unthayayn* are in the accusative governed by *ḥarrama* (forbade).

﴿أمّا اشْتَمَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ أرْحامُ الأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ *(or what the wombs of the two females contain)*, meaning: or what the females of the two kinds have carried, whether male or female. ﴿نَبِّئُونِي بِعِلْمٍ﴾ *(inform me with knowledge)*, meaning: tell me of a matter known from Him, Most High, brought by the prophets, peace be upon them, which indicates that He, Most High, forbade something of what has been mentioned; or inform me with a clear proof issuing from knowledge that comes from Him. ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ *(if you are truthful)* (143) in your claim that He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, forbade it. The command is for the purpose of rebuke and to demonstrate their inability.

[p. 42]

**"And of camels, two [of them], two"**: the male and the female. This is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with His saying, glorified is He, **"Of sheep, two [of them], two."** As al-Raghib said, the word *ibil* (camels) is used for a large herd, has no singular from its own form, and is pluralised, as stated in al-Qamus, as *aabal*. Its diminutive is *ubayla*.

**"And of cattle, two [of them]"**: they are the bull and its female. **"Say"**, as a rebuke to them concerning these two kinds as well, **"Has He forbidden the two males, or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain?"** That is, of these two kinds. The meaning, as many of the eminent scholars have said, is a denial that God, exalted is He, forbade them any of these four kinds, and an exposure of their lying in this. The detailing of the males, the females, and what their wombs contain is for the sake of emphasis in refuting them, by directing the denial at every category of their fabrication. They used to forbid the males of the livestock at one time, their females at another time, and their offspring however they were at yet another time, all while attributing all of this to God, glorified is He. The interrogative particle *hamza* was not placed directly before the indefinite word, which is the prohibition (*al-tahrim*). What is customary in usage is that the word which is indefinite is placed after it, but the phrasing of the noble text is more eloquent.

Its explanation, according to what al-Kisa'i said, is that establishing a prohibition necessarily entails establishing its locus (*mahall*, the object it applies to). So when its locus is negated, namely the three sources (of the animals), it follows that the prohibition is negated, in a demonstrative manner. It is as if the speech were placed in the position of one who concedes that such a prohibition had occurred, and then they are asked to produce a locus, so that their lie becomes evident and they are exposed when confronted. God, glorified is He, mentions the matter after the four kinds by saying: "Say: Has He forbidden the males or the females, or what the wombs of the females contain?", because repetition also adds emphasis in binding them to the argument and rebuking them.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) reported from the exegetes that they said: the polytheists of the age of ignorance (*jahiliyya*) used to forbid some of the livestock. God, glorified is He, therefore argued against this by pointing out that sheep, goats, camels and cattle each have a male and a female. If God had forbidden the male of them, then all their males would have to be forbidden. If He had forbidden the female, then all their females would have to be forbidden. And if God, exalted is His state, had forbidden what the wombs of the females contain, then all the offspring would have to be forbidden, because wombs contain both males and females.

He (al-Razi) objected to this, saying it is very far-fetched, because one could say: grant that these four kinds are restricted to males and females, yet it does not follow that the cause of the prohibition of what they ruled as forbidden must be restricted to maleness and femaleness. Rather, the cause of its prohibition may be that it is a *bahira* (a she-camel whose ear was slit), or a *sa'iba* (a freed animal), or a *wasila*, or some other consideration. This is like when we say: God forbade the slaughter of some animals for food. If it is then said: if that animal was forbidden because it is a male, then every male animal must be forbidden, and if it was forbidden because it is a female, then every female animal must be forbidden, yet this statement does not necessarily follow for him. Therefore, that is the explanation which the exegetes gave. Then he mentioned two points of his own regarding the verse, but what we have mentioned suffices, so there is no need to quote them.

Some people claimed that what is meant by the "two" in sheep, goats and cattle is the domestic and the wild, and in camels the Arabian and the Bactrian. This is something that should not be paid attention to. What is reported from Layth ibn Sulaym does not indicate it. The statement of al-Tabarsi, that it is what is narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with him, is a lie without basis, and it is a habit I recognise from Akhram.

His saying, glorified is He, **"Or were you witnesses"**, is a repetition for the sake of rebuke and confounding. The particle *am* here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*, introducing a new question), and the meaning is: "Rather, were you present and observing when God commanded you and bound you to this?" The knowledge of this would come either by God, glorified is He, sending a messenger to inform you of it, or by you seeing God, exalted is He, and hearing His speech about it. The first is inconsistent with your position, since you do not believe in a messenger, so it is necessary that the seeing and hearing be from your side, and that is impossible. In this there is clear mockery of them.

**"Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God"**, attributing to Him, glorified is He, the prohibition of what He did not prohibit. What is meant by this, as reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, is Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qami'a, who slit the ears of the she-camels (*bahair*), freed the animals (*sawa'ib*), and deliberately lied against God, exalted is He. It has been said that they are their elders who established this, and it has been said that it is all of them, since they shared in the fabrication against Him, glorified is He and exalted. The meaning is: "Which group is more unjust than the one who..." etc. It has been objected that the qualifier of deliberateness is an element in the meaning of fabrication, and whoever followed Amr among the elders may have erred in imitating him, and so would not have been deliberately lying, therefore it is not appropriate to interpret the relative clause in this way. The *fa'* (so) indicates the consequence of what follows from the preceding rebuke and exposure of their lies and fabrication. **"Kadhiban"** (a lie) is in the accusative: it has been said as a direct object, and it has been said as an infinitive of a kind not derived from the verb itself. Some later scholars took it as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*, describing the state of the subject), meaning "lyingly", but this is far-fetched, not an error, contrary to the one who claimed it.

**"In order to lead people astray"**: this is connected to "fabricates". **"Without knowledge"** is connected to a deleted element occurring as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "fabricates", meaning: he fabricates against Him, glorified is He, while ignorant that the prohibition came from Him, exalted is His state. The describing of him as lacking knowledge, even though the fabricator knows that it did not come from Him, is a notification of how far beyond bounds he goes in wrongdoing. For whoever fabricates against Him, glorified is He, without knowledge that it came from Him, exalted is His majesty, while there is the possibility of it coming from Him, if he is at that extent of wrongdoing, then what should one think of the one who fabricates while knowing that it did not come from Him?

It has been permitted that it is a circumstantial accusative from the subject of "lead astray", meaning: while being clothed in ignorance of what it leads him to of the great punishment. It has been said that the meaning of the verse according to this is that he acted as one who intends to lead people astray, by calling them to what contains misguidance, even if he did not intend to lead astray, and was ignorant and not aware of that. This clearly shows that the *lam* is for consequence, and this has a valid basis. It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to a deleted element that is a circumstantial accusative from "people". But what came before is clearer and more eloquent in censure.

Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) used the verse as evidence that leading people astray from the religion is blameworthy and does not befit God, exalted is He, because if He blames leading astray which involves nothing but forbidding what is permissible, then what is greater than that is more deserving of blame. In this there is the response that not everything blameworthy among creatures is blameworthy from the Creator.

**"Indeed God does not guide the wrongdoing people"** (144): to the path of truth. It has been said: to the abode of reward, since they deserve punishment. Al-Tabarsi preferred this, and al-Qadi went in this direction based on his own school, and it is not far-fetched according to our principles either. It has been said: to what is good for them in this world and the next, and this is more complete in benefit and more fitting with the omission of the object. The negation of guidance from the wrongdoer necessitates its negation from the greater wrongdoer, all the more so.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 145 (part 1 of 2):]

﴿Say﴾ is a command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), after the polytheists have been confronted with their own inconsistency and rebuked, and after it has been made clear that what they claim about the prohibitions is pure fabrication, by stating to them what was actually forbidden to them.

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿I find not in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ ... etc. This is a metaphor (kinaya) for non-existence. It also signals that the only way to establish prohibition is explicit textual statement from God, Exalted is He, and not desire and whim. It is also, as has been said, an indication that the original state of things is permissibility. ﴿Forbidden﴾ is an attribute of an omitted noun that is indicated by what follows, and it has taken its place after being omitted. So it is the first object of ﴿find﴾, and its second object is ﴿in what has been revealed﴾, which has been placed first for emphasis, not because the first object is indefinite, since it is a general indefinite under negation, and so the fronting of the predicate with a prepositional phrase is not obligatory. The first object is not omitted, meaning: "I do not find, as I search through what has been revealed to me, whether the Qur'an or other, according to what the change of wording from 'was sent down to me' to 'was revealed to me' suggests, or what has been revealed to me of the Qur'an, any food forbidden from among the foods you have forbidden for yourselves," ﴿for an eater﴾, meaning any eater whatsoever, male or female, in response to their saying: "It is forbidden for our wives." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who eats it﴾ is in the position of an attribute of ﴿eater﴾, and it was brought in as in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿a bird that flies﴾, to remove any possibility of metaphor. It has also been read as ﴿yuṭa''imuhu﴾ with shadda and a kasra on the ʿayn, and the original form is ﴿yaṭtaʿamuhu﴾, where the tāʾ was changed to ṭāʾ and the first of the two identical letters was assimilated into the second. By "taste" (ṭaʿm) is meant the consumption of nourishment. It may also be used of drink, as was mentioned earlier in the discussion of it, but the more immediate meaning here is the first. It may also be used to mean any benefit at all, and from this is what is in the hadith about Badr: "We did not kill anyone who had any ṭaʿm (benefit)." The words ("We killed only the old men, bald-headed") mean that they killed those who had no benefit to them and no worth. Taking this meaning here is very far-fetched, and I have not seen anyone say it. Yes, it has been said: what is meant is all kinds of consumption,
[Page 44]
of eating, drinking, and other things. Perhaps including other than eating is by way of analogy. Likewise, "eater" has been interpreted as "one who finds," from the saying "a man who is a ṭāʿim," meaning one in good circumstances and provided for. Keeping ﴿eats it﴾ on its apparent sense, meaning one who finds it and eats it, the attribute then does not serve merely to add emphasis to what we have pointed to.

﴿Unless it be﴾ that food or that forbidden thing ﴿carrion (maytatan)﴾. By it is meant that which was not slaughtered in the lawful manner, and so it includes the strangled animal and similar. Ibn Kathir and Hamzah read ﴿takūna﴾ with a tāʾ, because the predicate is feminine. Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿yakūna maytatan﴾ with a yāʾ and with ﴿maytatun﴾ in the nominative. Abu Jaʿfar also reads with shadda, on the basis that kāna is the complete (tāmma) verb. ﴿Or blood﴾ is conjoined to ﴿carrion﴾, or to what is within its scope. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿poured forth (masfūḥan)﴾, meaning spilled and flowing, like blood in the veins, is an attribute of it. By it is excluded congealed blood, such as that of the liver and the spleen. In the hadith: "Two dead things were made lawful to us: fish and locusts; and two bloods: the liver and the spleen." It has also been permitted to take blood from the veins after slaughter, and many jurists have gone this way. It is reported from ʿIkrimah that he said: "Were it not for this qualification, Muslims would have followed the veins as the Jews followed them."

﴿Or the flesh of swine, for indeed it﴾, meaning the flesh, as has been said, since it is what is spoken of; or the swine, since it is the nearer in mention. The flesh is mentioned because it is the greatest thing benefited from it, so if it is forbidden then other parts are forbidden by a fortiori reasoning. It has also been said, and this is contrary to the apparent sense, that the pronoun refers to each of carrion, blood, and swine's flesh, in the sense that what is mentioned is ﴿filth﴾, meaning foul, or ﴿evil, made abominable﴾. ﴿Or a transgression (fisq)﴾ is conjoined to ﴿swine's flesh﴾, according to what many grammarians (muʿribīn) have chosen. What lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraḍ) that affirms the prohibition. ﴿That over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ is a descriptive attribute of it, clarifying it. The root meaning of ihlāl is raising the voice, and what is meant is slaughter in the name of idols. It is called "transgression" only because it goes to great lengths in transgression. It is also permitted that ﴿transgression﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu) of ﴿invoked﴾, and it is conjoined to ﴿be﴾, and ﴿by it﴾ serves as the deputy of the agent, and the pronoun refers to what the concealed pronoun in ﴿be﴾ refers to.

Abu Hayyan said: "This grammatical analysis is extremely forced, and the construction on it departs from eloquence, and it is not permissible according to the reading of whoever reads ﴿unless it be carrion﴾ with the nominative, because the pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ has nothing to refer back to, and it is not permissible to presume an omitted noun to which the pronoun refers, meaning 'a thing over which the name of other than God has been invoked,' because such a thing is permitted only in poetic necessity." End of quotation. By this, as al-Halabi said, he meant that a noun and its attribute as a whole clause may not be omitted except when the partitive particle is present in the sentence, as in "some of us stayed and some of us departed," meaning a group stayed and a group departed. If there is no partitive ﴿min﴾ in it, then it is by poetic necessity, as in his saying:

"I shoot with my palm, which was among the best shooters of humankind,"

meaning "with the two palms of a man who was ..." etc. This, as has been established in its place, is the view of some. As for others, they say: whenever evidence indicates the noun, it is omitted absolutely. Thus the one who permits this view may hold it, and he prevented it from the standpoint of the nominative of ﴿carrion﴾. As al-Saffaqsi said: "There is scrutiny in this, because the pronoun refers to what it refers to under the assumption of the accusative, and the nominative does not prevent that. Yes, the first grammatical analysis is preferable, as is not hidden."

﴿Then whoever is compelled﴾, meaning one whom dire necessity afflicts, impelling him to consume any of that, ﴿neither desiring (bāghin)﴾, meaning seeking what it is not his to seek, such as taking that from another compelled person like himself. This is the view taken by many exegetes.

Al-Hasan said: "Neither desiring," meaning not partaking for pleasure. Mujahid said: ﴿neither desiring﴾ against a leader (imām), ﴿nor transgressing (ʿādin)﴾, meaning exceeding the measure of
[Page 45]
necessity. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (145). He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy and does not hold him to account for that. This is the response (jazāʾ) of the conditional, but it is taken in terms of its necessary meaning, which is non-accountability. Some have said there is an implied response, so that this would be a reason clause for it, but there is no need for that.

﴿Neither desiring﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and likewise what is conjoined to it. The restriction by the first circumstance is not to show that if the condition in the previous sense is not met, the prohibition under investigation would be established; rather it is a warning against another forbidden act, which is taking the right of another compelled person. For whoever takes the flesh of carrion, for example, from another compelled person and eats it, its prohibition is not due to its being the flesh of carrion, but due to its being the right of the other compelled person. As for the second circumstance, it is to make certain the removal of the prohibition under investigation, for going beyond the amount that stills hunger is forbidden as far as it is the flesh of carrion.

Mention of the two attributes of forgiveness and mercy signals that sin remains, but God, Exalted is He, forgives him and has mercy on him. This has been discussed earlier, so keep it in mind and do not be heedless.

This verse has been challenged on the grounds that it restricts the forbidden foods to four: carrion, poured-forth blood, swine's flesh, and the transgression over which the name of other than God has been invoked. There is no doubt that the forbidden things are more than that. It has been answered that the meaning is: "I do not find forbidden anything of what the people of the Jahiliyya used to forbid, such as the baḥāʾir and the sawāʾib, as we have pointed out." In that case, the exception of the four from it is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: "I do not find what they forbade, but I do find the four forbidden." This carries no indication of restriction, and a disjunctive exception does not have the restrictive force of a connected one, as they have pointed out, and this is something that deserves attention.

If you say: The exception is not carrion itself, but the state of being carrion, and that is not of the kind of food, so the exception is necessarily disjunctive, and there is no need for that qualification. Al-Qutb said: "Yes, that is so, but the intent is to exclude carrion from forbidden food, meaning: I do not find any forbidden thing except carrion. Thus, without the qualification, it would in reality be a connected exception, and the problem would arise and this answer would be weakened," for several reasons. Among them: God said in Surat al-Baqara and in Surat al-Naḥl: ﴿He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, swine's flesh, and that over which other than God has been invoked﴾, and "only" (innamā) conveys restriction. He, glorified is He, also said in Surat al-Maʾida: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾, and the exegetes agreed that what is meant by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, swine's flesh, and that over which other than God has been invoked﴾. As for the strangled animal, the struck animal, and others, they are kinds of carrion, and they were mentioned again because they used to rule these as lawful. So the two verses indicate that nothing is forbidden except four things. Then it is necessary to say that this verse under discussion indicates restriction, so that it agrees with that, and there is no qualification, while the original state is no qualification.

It has been answered regarding the problem that the verse only indicates that he, upon whom be prayer and peace, did not find in what was revealed to him, up to that point, any forbidden thing other than what is stated explicitly in it. That does not contradict the descent of prohibition in some other matter. It has been said: in that case the exception is from the most general of times or the most general of states, and it is "emptied" (mufarragh), meaning: "I do not find any of the foods forbidden at any time or in any state, except at a time or in a state in which the food is one of the four, for then I do find it forbidden." Thus the verbal noun derived from ﴿that it be﴾ serves as a temporal or modal expression.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) objected to this answer, saying: the verses that indicate restriction were revealed after the Sharia had become established, so they indicate that the ruling established in the Muhammadan law from its beginning to its end is nothing but the restriction of prohibited things to these items. And since restriction of the prohibited to these four is established by that indication, this is an acknowledgment of the permissibility of everything else, and saying that a fifth thing is forbidden would be abrogation (naskh). There is no doubt that the foundation of the Sharia is that the original state is non-abrogation, because if the possibility of abrogation arising were equal to the possibility of the ruling remaining as it was, then it would be possible to use any of the texts to establish any of the rulings, on the grounds that it could be said: "It was established, but it has since been abrogated." As for what was said regarding the exception, it is objected that the verbal noun formed from "that" and the verb cannot be put in the accusative as an adverb of time, nor can it serve as a circumstantial qualifier, because it is definite. Some said, to maintain the connectedness of the exception: the implied meaning is "except the thing described as being one of the four," in which case it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿forbidden﴾. But this involves evident artificiality. It has also been said that on the reading of the nominative, the implied meaning is "except the existence of carrion," and the genitive construction there is of the type of attribute to described noun, meaning "a carrion that exists."

It has also been answered that, although the verse indicates restriction, we specify it by the report (al-ikhbar). Al-Imam also objected to this, saying: this is not a case of specification at all, but is plainly abrogation, because since its meaning is that there is no forbidden thing other than the four, establishing another forbidden thing is a claim that the matter is not so, and that is a removal of the restriction. And abrogating the Qur'an by a single report (khabar al-wahid) is not permissible. Al-Qutb al-Razi answered this by saying: there is no meaning to the restriction here except that the four are forbidden and what is other than them is not forbidden. This is a general statement, so establishing another forbidden thing is a specification of this general statement, and specifying a general statement by a single report is permissible.

Many of the early generation (salaf) argued from the apparent sense of the verse, and they permitted what is other than the things mentioned in it. Among that is the domestic donkey. Al-Bukhari reported: "From ʿAmr ibn Dinar: I said to Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: 'They claim that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys at the time of Khaybar.' He said: 'Al-Hakam ibn ʿAmr used to say that on the authority of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but that the sea (i.e., Ibn ʿAbbas) refused it.' And he recited: ﴿Say: I find not in what has been revealed to me...﴾ the verse."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 6, verse 145 (part 2 of 2):

Abu Dawud related from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he was asked about eating the porcupine (*qunfudh*), and he recited the verse. Ibn Abi Hatim and others related with a sound chain from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that whenever she was asked about every animal with a fang among beasts of prey and every bird with talons, she would say, ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it...﴾ etc. Ibn Abbas also related that he said: "There is nothing forbidden among animals except what Allah the Exalted has forbidden in His Book," then ﴿Say: I do not find...﴾ to the end of the verse.

Imam al-Razi strengthened the view of the literal meaning (*zahir*). He said, after some discussion: "Thus it is established, by the reasoning we have mentioned, that this statement is strong and this position is sound, and it is the view that Malik ibn Anas held." Then he said: "Among the difficult objections is that many jurists restricted the general application of this verse by what is related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whatever the Arabs find loathsome is forbidden.' It is known, however, that what the Arabs find loathsome is not a fixed standard. The master of the Arabs, indeed the master of all the worlds, peace be upon him, when he saw them eating the lizard (*dabb*), said: 'My nature dislikes it,' and it was not made a reason for its prohibition. As for the rest of the Arabs, among them are those who find nothing loathsome, and they may differ about some things, with one people finding them loathsome and others finding them good. It is therefore known that the matter of loathing is not fixed, but varies with the differences of persons and circumstances. How, then, is it permissible to abrogate this definitive text by that matter, which has no fixed standard nor known rule?" End of quotation. But what is in it is not hidden.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also argued from His saying, glorified is He, ﴿to an eater who eats it﴾, that what is forbidden of carrion is only its eating, and that its hide becomes pure by tanning. Ahmad and others related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "A sheep belonging to Sawda bint Zam'a died, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If only you had taken its hide.' She said: 'We would take the hide of a sheep that has died?' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah the Exalted only said, ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion﴾, and indeed you do not eat it; tan it and you may benefit from it.'"

[Page 47]

The Shafi'is argued from His saying, glorified is He, ﴿for it is filth (*rijs*)﴾, for the impurity (*najasah*) of the pig, on the basis that the pronoun returns to "pig" because it is the nearest previously mentioned noun.

﴿And to those who were Jews﴾, meaning the Jews specifically, and not those other than them among the earlier and the later peoples. ﴿We forbade every animal with a claw﴾, meaning one whose toes are not separated, like the camel, the ostrich, the goose and the duck. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jarir, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that it refers to the camel alone. Al-Jubba'i said that it includes all predators, dogs and cats, and whatever hunts with its claw. It is reported from al-Qutabi and al-Balkhi that it means the bird with talons (dhu al-mikhlab) among birds and the animal with hooves (dhu al-hafir) among quadrupeds, and that the hoof was called a "claw" (zufr) metaphorically. Al-Imam (al-Razi) found this unlikely. Perhaps the consequence of wrongdoing was the generalization of the prohibition, since some of it had been lawful before it.

It is also possible that what is meant is "every animal with a lawful claw", by the indication of the words ﴿We forbade﴾. As some have said, this is a confirmation of what preceded regarding the restriction of the prohibited things to what was detailed, by refuting the contrary slander of the Jews and their denial of this. They used to say: "We are not the first to whom it was forbidden; it was forbidden to Noah, Abraham and those after them, peace be upon them, until the prohibition ended." Some of the verifiers said that this is a completion of what came before it, because it contains a lifting of the prohibition: that Allah, exalted is He, forbade the Jews all these matters, and likewise forbade the bahirah, the sa'ibah and similar things, as a punishment against them specifically out of wrath towards them.

Al-Hasan read (ظِفْرٍ) with a kasrah on the ẓa' and a sukun on the fa'. Abu al-Simak read it with a kasrah on both. It was also read, as Abu al-Baqa' said, (ظُفْرٍ) with a dammah on the ẓa' and a sukun on the fa'.

﴿And from the cattle and the sheep We forbade them their fat﴾, not their flesh, for the flesh remains lawful. What is meant by "fat" (shuhum) is the thin fat that lies over the intestines and the paunch, and the fat of the kidneys. It has been said that this is general, and an exception is made from it in what follows. The phrase (مِنَ البَقَرِ) is connected to the verb ﴿We forbade﴾ after it. In that case it would have sufficed to say "the fat", but it was given the pronoun suffix for added connection and emphasis, as one says "I took from Zayd his property", which is common in their speech. Abu al-Baqa' allowed, and his apparent practice indicates that he preferred it although it is contrary to the apparent meaning, that (مِنَ البَقَرِ) is coordinated with ﴿every animal with a claw﴾ in the sense of "and some of the cattle", and he took ﴿We forbade them their fat﴾ as an explanation of what is forbidden from it. In that case the pronoun suffix is for the connection that is needed.

﴿Except what their backs carry﴾, meaning what adheres to their backs. The exception is either disconnected (munqati') or connected (muttasil) from "the fat". Those who held it to be disconnected include the Imam al-A'zam, may Allah be pleased with him. It is transmitted from him that if someone swears not to eat fat, he is considered to have broken his oath only by the fat of the belly. His two companions disagreed with him on this, and said he breaks his oath also by the fat of the back, since it is fat and has the property of melting in fire. They supported this with this exception, on the basis that the original state of an exception is connection. The Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, held that it is in reality flesh (lahm), because it grows out of the blood, is used like flesh in preparing food and in fried dishes, and is eaten like flesh, which is not done with fat. For this reason, if someone swears not to eat meat, he breaks his oath by eating it, and its seller is called a lahhām (meat seller), not a shahhām (fat seller). Although connection is the original state of an exception, there is here something that indicates disconnection, namely the words of the Exalted: ﴿or the (al-hawaya)﴾. It is coordinated with the excepted item, yet it is not fat. Rather, it means the (al-mabi'ir) (the intestines/entrails), as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid and others, or the (al-marabid), which is the (nabat al-laban) (the milk-plant), as narrated from Ibn Zayd, or the (al-masarin) and the intestines, as many of the lexicographers said. The one who holds connection can say that the coordination is on the basis of an omitted noun, meaning "the fat of the (al-hawaya)". Or it can be interpreted with what the (al-hawaya) carry of fat, on the basis that (al-hawaya) may be interpreted as what the intestines contain, since it derives from (hawāhu), meaning "he contained it", so it applies to the fat wrapped around the intestines.

Several have allowed that the coordination is with ﴿their backs﴾, or with ﴿their fat﴾. In that case what is mentioned is forbidden, and this was the view of some of the earlier generations. It coordinates the words of the Exalted: ﴿or what is mixed with bone﴾, which is the fat of the buttock, because it is joined to the coccyx (al-'us'us). It has been said that it is the marrow (al-mukh), and no one says it is fat, yet they say its prohibition too. The (al-hawaya) has been said to be the plural of (hawiyah), like (zawiyah) and (zawaya). Its pattern is (fawa'il), and its origin is (hawawa), so the waw which is the middle radical was changed to a hamzah, because it was the second of two weak letters enclosing the lengthening of (mafa'il). Then the kasrah hamzah was changed to a ya', then it was given a fathah because of the heaviness of the kasrah on the ya', so the last ya' was changed to an alif because it moved after a fathah, and it became (hawaya). Or the waw was changed to a fathah hamzah, then the last ya' to an alif, then the hamzah to a ya', because it fell between two alifs, as was done with (khata'ya). It has been said that it is the plural of (hawla'), like (qasi'a) and (qawasi'), its pattern is also (fawa'il), and its weakening is as you know. It has been said that it is the plural of (hawiyyah), like (zarifah) and (zara'if), its pattern is (fa'a'il), and its origin is (hawa'iy), so the hamzah was changed to a fathah ya', and the ya' which is the final radical to an alif, so it became (hawaya).

Al-Farisi allowed that it is a plural for each of these three, and it has also been heard in its singular form. The particle (أوْ) (aw, "or") is in the sense of (wa, "and").

Abu al-Baqa' said that for dividing their positions, its parallel is in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they said: "Be Jews or Christians"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is, when the coordination is with the fats, for permission, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever﴾, meaning every one of these is worthy of being disobeyed, so disobey this one or that one. The particle (أوْ) is eloquent in this meaning, because if you say "Do not obey Zayd and 'Amr", it is possible that you were forbidden from obeying both of them together, so if Zayd is obeyed on his own it is not a sin. But if you say "Do not obey Zayd or 'Amr or Khalid", the meaning is: all of these are worthy of being obeyed, so do not obey any one of them, nor obey the group. From this is "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin or al-Sha'bi". The meaning is not a command to sit with one of them, but rather that they are all worthy of sitting with, so if you sit with one of them you are right, and if you sit with the group you are right. The later scholar (al-'Allamah al-Thani) chose this. He said: the correct position is that the word (أوْ) in coordination with the excepted item is of the kind of "sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin", just as in coordination with the item from which the exception is made. That is, it is for showing equivalence in all of them, so all of them are forbidden. Its verification is that the basis of the prohibition returns to the prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not eat any one of the three", and this is the meaning of generality. This is what al-Zamakhshari intended, as transmitted from him, that the sentence has the force of a prohibition. So the reason for the coordination with the particle of choice is that it is eloquent in this meaning. Then he said: From this it becomes clear that the misunderstanding is false, which holds that on the basis of coordination with the item from which the exception is made, the meaning would be: "We forbade them their fat, or We forbade them the (al-hawaya), or We forbade them what is mixed with bone", so that they are permitted to leave whichever of them they wish and eat the other two. He claimed that the apparent meaning is that such a thing, though permissible, is not from the Shari'ah, that one indefinite item from among specified matters should be forbidden or made lawful, and that this applies only to the obligatory. This claim is strange, because the forbidden-by-choice and the permitted-by-choice are things which the jurists and all the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence have stated clearly. It requires careful reflection, so let him reflect carefully.

Al-Tibi mentioned, in summarizing the words of some verifiers regarding (أوْ) here, that if you coordinate with the fats, the three fall under the ruling of negation, so all are forbidden except what is excepted from it. If you coordinate with the excepted item, only the fats are forbidden. The (أوْ) in the first case is for permission, and in the second for classification.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the recompense or to the prohibition. On the first view it is in the accusative as an emphasizing infinitive (maṣdar) for what follows it. On the second it is in the accusative as a second object of the verb, meaning: that prohibition ﴿We recompensed them﴾. The verb (jaza) takes an object with the preposition (bi-) and directly, as al-Raghib and others mentioned. What is related from Ibn Malik, that the demonstrative pronoun does not take the accusative when pointing to a verbal noun unless it is followed by the verbal noun, as in "I stood this standing" and "I sat that sitting", but one cannot say "I stood this" or "I sat that", was refuted by Abu Hayyan and al-Jalabi, who held as correct the use of the demonstrative pointing to a verbal noun without being followed by it.

[Page 49]

It is also permitted that (ذلك) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is that", or the subject whose predicate is what follows, with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning: "We recompensed them with it". ﴿For their wrongdoing﴾, meaning because of their injustice, which is their killing of the prophets without right, their consuming of usury, which they had been forbidden, and their consuming of people's wealth falsely. Whenever they committed a sin, they were punished by the prohibition of something that had been made lawful for them, and they denied this, and claimed that these things had never been forbidden to any nation. It has also been said that what is meant by their wrongdoing is their oppression of their poor, on the basis of what 'Ali ibn Ibrahim transmitted in his tafsir: that the kings of the Children of Israel used to forbid their poor to eat the flesh of birds and fats, so Allah, exalted is He, forbade them this as a consequence of that prohibition. This also follows the principle of benefit. There is no objection to the prohibition being on the basis of the abstention from benefit for an increase in reward, or for a previous crime. ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ (146) in all Our reports, among which is the report of the prohibition and of the wrongdoing. Some of them counted among these the promise and the warning, and restricted it to them.

The Imam strengthened with this verse what Imam Malik and many of the earlier generations held, namely the view that the apparent meaning of the preceding verse requires, that what is permitted is all besides the four mentioned in it. This is because he required that the claw be understood as the talon, for the understanding of it as the hoof is far-fetched, for two reasons. The first is that the hoof is hardly called a claw. The second is that if the matter were so, it would have been necessary to say that Allah forbade them every animal with a hoof, which is false, because the verse indicates that the sheep and the cattle are permitted to them even though they have hooves. Since it is necessary to take it as the talon, and the verse indicates that the prohibition is restricted to the Jews, as we have pointed out, for two reasons: the first is that the construction indicates restriction in language, and the second is that if this were established for everyone, there would be no benefit in restricting it to them. It would also follow that predators and birds with talons would not be forbidden to Muslims, but their prohibition would be specific to the Jews. In that case, what is narrated, that "he (ﷺ) forbade every animal with fangs among the predators and every bird with talons", is weak, because it is a single report (khabar wahid) contrary to the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and so it is not accepted. Thus the view of the majority stated earlier is established. Yet there is an objection that is not hidden, so reflect carefully.

﴿Then if they deny you﴾: that is, the Jews, as Mujahid, al-Suddi and others said. This is what the apparent meaning requires, since they are the nearer antecedent, and because the polytheists are mentioned afterward under the title of association (al-ishrak). It was also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists. On the first view, the meaning is: if the Jews deny you regarding the ruling mentioned and persist in what they were upon of claims, the prohibition has been stated earlier. ﴿Then say﴾ to them: ﴿Your Lord is the Possessor of mercy﴾ that is great ﴿and vast﴾. He does not hold you accountable for every sin you commit, and He grants you respite for some of them. ﴿And His punishment will not be averted﴾, meaning His punishment will not be entirely repelled ﴿from the people who are criminals﴾ (147). So do not deny what has occurred from Him, exalted is He, of prohibiting some of the good things for you as a punishment and a severity.

On the second view: if the polytheists deny you regarding what has been detailed of the rulings on what is permitted and what is forbidden, then say to them: ﴿Your Lord is the Possessor of vast mercy﴾, and He does not treat you with punishment for your denial. So do not be deceived by that, for it is a respite, not a neglect.

It was also said: it is possible that the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, is the Possessor of vast mercy, so He shows mercy to me by abundant guidance to affirm my truthfulness, and therefore your denial does not harm me but harms you, because His punishment is not averted from the criminal deniers. Or: He will show mercy to me by taking vengeance on you, and His punishment will not be averted from you. This view is remote. It was also said: the intended meaning is that He is the Possessor of mercy toward the obedient and the Possessor of severe punishment toward the criminals, so the statement ﴿and it will not be averted﴾ etc. takes its place, because it includes an alert to the descent of punishment upon them, along with an indication that it certainly overtakes them without any preventer diverting it from them at all.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 148:**

﴿The ones who associated partners [with Allah] will say﴾: a narration of another kind of their falsehoods. The foretelling before its occurrence, and then its occurrence as it was foretold, is indicated by His words, exalted is He, at the time of its occurrence: ﴿Those who associated partners [with Allah] said: "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything."﴾ This is explicit that it is from Allah, exalted is He. Many scholars have stated explicitly that the occurrence of what Allah, exalted is He, has foretold of the unseen is one of the aspects of the inimitability (i'jaz) of His speech, even if the inimitability does not lie in this alone, as in a weak opinion: "If Allah had willed, our not associating partners [with Him] and our not prohibiting anything would have been [so]." ﴿We did not associate partners [with Allah], nor did our fathers, nor did we prohibit anything.﴾ They did not intend by this statement an excuse for committing an ugly act, since they did not believe their deeds to be ugly, and they were pleasing to them. Rather, as the verses have expressed, they are as ﴿they think they are doing good work﴾, and that they worship the idols only so that they may bring them near to Allah in closeness, and that the prohibition came only from Allah, mighty and majestic. Thus their intention by this was nothing but to argue that what they had committed is true, legitimate, and approved by Allah, exalted is He, on the basis that will and desire entail command and necessitate approval, as the Mu'tazilah claimed. The sum of their statement is therefore: what we commit of association [with Allah], prohibition, and other things, has been willed by Allah, exalted is He, and His will and desire have attached to it; and whatever His will and desire, glorified is He, attach to is legitimate and approved by Him, mighty and majestic. It follows that what we commit of association and prohibition is legitimate and approved by Allah, exalted is He.

After relating this from them, He, glorified is He, responded to them with His words, mighty is the Speaker: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like what these people lied, ﴿denied those who were before them﴾, namely their predecessors, the polytheists. The sum of this is that their statement includes a denial of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and the miracle has indicated their truthfulness. It is not hidden that the first premise contains no falsehood in itself; rather it includes the affirmation of what reason and revelation agree upon, namely that every existing thing occurs by the will of Allah, exalted is He, and that it is impossible for anything contrary to His will to occur in His dominion. The source of the denial is therefore the second premise, because the Messengers, peace be upon them, call them to monotheism and say to them: indeed Allah, exalted is He, does not approve for His servants disbelief as a religion, and does not command indecency. So their saying that what we commit is legitimate and approved by Him, exalted is He, is a denial of this statement. Since the corruption of this argument lies in consideration of the second premise, it is determined that it is not true; and then its contradictory is true, namely: not everything to which will and desire attach is legitimate and approved by Him, glorified is He, on the basis that desire does not entail command and approval, according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. For will specifies some possibilities over others, whether they are commanded or forbidden, good or ugly. On this basis there is no proof in the verse for the Mu'tazilah; rather the matter has been reversed, and the verse has become a proof for us against them, because they did not distinguish between what is commanded and what is willed, and they believed, like the polytheists, that everything willed is commanded and approved.

It is also permissible to say that the intention of the polytheists in their statement was to reject the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, and to lift the sending of messengers and the obligation of religious duties. This is what is mentioned in many books of kalam (theology). Its sum then is: whatever Allah, exalted is He, wills must happen, and whatever He does not will is impossible; and whatever is of this nature is not charged with, since it is conditional upon capacity (istita'ah). It follows that for what we commit of association and other things, we were not charged to abandon it, and no prophet was sent for it. Allah, exalted is He, responded to them that this is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, because they meant by it that the Messengers, peace be upon them, in their claim of being sent and charged, are liars; and their truthfulness has been established by definitive proofs. Because that is truth, by which falsehood was intended, Allah, exalted is He, censured them with denial. The necessity of the occurrence of what is connected to will does not contradict the truthfulness of the claim of being sent and charged, because these serve to make the proof manifest and to convey the argument. Another interpretation of the verse will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, shortly.

**[Page 50]**

﴿Our fathers﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿we associated﴾, and this is permissible according to the Basrans, even if the pronoun is not emphasized, because for them any intervening element suffices, and here it is separated by ﴿lā﴾ (not). The Kufans do not stipulate anything in this and cite what is here as evidence, and they do not accept this separation, because the conjunction particle should precede it to avoid awkwardness (hujnah); and in their view, separation between the conjoined and the conjoined-to is not sufficient. Abu 'Ali hesitated regarding the sufficiency of separation between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, even if the conjunction particle does not separate them. The Imam (al-Razi) claimed that there is an elision (taqdir) in the sentence, because negation is not directed to the persons of the fathers; rather it must be directed to an act that proceeded from them, and that is association. So the sense is: ﴿we did not associate, nor did our fathers associate﴾. Then there is no difficulty.

﴿Until they tasted Our might﴾, that is, they attained Our punishment which We sent down upon them because of their denial. It is said that there is in this, according to what has been stated, an indication that they have a punishment stored up with Allah, exalted is He, because tasting is the first perception of a thing.

﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge﴾, that is, any known matter which is valid to argue with according to your claim, ﴿so that you bring it forth﴾, that is, that you display it, ﴿to us﴾ in the most complete manner and clearest explanation. It is also said: the intention is, "Do you have a firm belief, corresponding to what you claim, that association and all else you are upon is approved by Allah, exalted is He, so that you display it to us through proof?" Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) in al-Irshad made this and what follows it an evidence that the polytheists deserved rebuke for their statement only because they used to mock the religion and seek to reject the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, since there reached their ears from the laws of the Messengers, peace be upon them, the entrusting of affairs to Him, glorified is He. So when they were asked to submit to Islam and undertake the rulings, they argued against them with what they had taken from their words, mocking them, peace and blessings be upon them. Their purpose was not to mention what their belief contains; how could it be, when faith in the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, is a branch of faith in Him, mighty is His majesty, and that is, for them, as far off as the Pleiades (al-'Ayyuq)?

﴿If you follow﴾, that is, what you follow in that, ﴿except conjecture﴾, the false conjecture which does not avail anything against the truth. Or the intention is: indeed your custom and the bulk of your affair is that you follow nothing but conjecture. ﴿And you are only guessing﴾ (148), you lie against Allah, exalted is He. The discussion of the ruling on following conjecture has already been presented in detail, so refer back to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 149:

﴿Say: "Then to God belongs the conclusive argument."﴾ That is, the clear proof that has reached the utmost firmness and strength in establishing (the truth), or by which its possessor has made his claim sound, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾. By it, according to the well-known view, is meant the Book, the Messenger, and the clarification (al-bayan). Our shaykh of shaykhs, al-Kuranī, said: ﴿the conclusive argument﴾ is an indication that knowledge follows the known, and that the will of God, exalted is He, is related to the manifestation of what the readiness (isti'dad) of the known in itself requires, out of regard for wisdom, as generosity and mercy, not as obligation. And it (hujja) is from ḥajj in the sense of intention (qasd), as though by it the establishing of the ruling and the seeking of it is intended; or in the sense of prevailing, which is the well-known view. The fa' is the answer to a deleted conditional: that is, "If it becomes clear that you have no argument, say: then to God belongs the argument." ﴿Had He willed﴾ your guidance, all of you, ﴿He would have guided you all﴾ (149) by granting you success in it and compelling you towards it. But He willed the guidance of some, those who turn their choice to following the path of truth, and the misguidance of others, who turned it to the opposite.

Al-Kuranī said: The meaning is: "But He did not will," since He did not know that you have a guidance which your readiness requires. Rather, what is known to Him is the absence of your guidance, and this is the requirement of your eternal readiness, which is not made by Him. This is a verification of the truth, and it does not contradict what is in the beginning of the verse, because of what you know of their intention in it. The benefit of sending the messengers, on the view of readiness, is stirring up the motives toward action, and abandoning (it) by the choice of the responsible person arising from that readiness, and cutting off the excuse of the wrongdoers. We have already pointed to this earlier, so reflect.

Ibn al-Munir mentioned another aspect in explaining what is in the verse, namely that the rebuttal against them was only because of their belief that they were stripped of their choice and power, and that their polytheism proceeded from them only in the manner of compulsion. They claimed that they were establishing a proof against God, exalted is He, and His Messenger, peace be upon him, by this. So God, exalted is He, rejected their claim of the non-existence of choice for themselves, and their doubt was like that of one who was deceived before them by this illusion, so he denied the messengers and associated partners with God, mighty and majestic, relying on the idea that he only does that by the will of God, exalted is He, and he intended to silence the messengers with this doubt. Then He, glorified is He, made clear that they have no argument in that, and that the conclusive argument belongs to Him, majestic and exalted, not to them. Then He, glorified is He, further clarified that every occurrence happens by His will, and that He did not will from them except what proceeded from them, and that if He, exalted is He, had willed guidance from them, they would all have been guided.

The purpose of this is that the aspect of rebuttal against them be made pure, and that the belief in the implementation of the will and the generality of its relation to every existent be freed from the rebuttal, and that the rebuttal be directed to their claim of the negation of choice for themselves, and that their establishing of the proof by this be specific to them. When you reflect on the verse, you find that its beginning repels the doctrine of the Jabriyya (compulsionists), and its ending defeats the Mu'tazila. For the first affirms that the servant has choice and power in a way that cuts off his argument and excuse in opposition and disobedience, and the second affirms the implementation of God's will in the servant, and that all his actions are in accordance with the divine will. By this the conclusive argument is established for the People of the Sunna against the Mu'tazila. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.

Al-Qutb gave the verse this interpretation: their intention was to reject the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, on the meaning that God, exalted is He, willed our polytheism and desired it from us, and you oppose His will by calling us to faith. So He, glorified is He, rebuked them with aspects, among which He counted His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then to God belongs the conclusive argument﴾, for it is by the estimation of a condition, that is: if the matter is as you claim, then to God belongs the argument.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Had He willed﴾ .. etc., is a substitute for it by way of explanation, that is: had He willed, He would have guided each of you and your opponents to His religion. So if the matter were as you claim, Islam too would be by His will, and therefore you must not prevent the Muslims from Islam, just as, by your claim, the prophets must not prevent you from polytheism. Then it would follow for you that there should be no opposition or enmity between you and the Muslims, but rather agreement and allegiance. Then he said: Perhaps this argument may be directed by saying that whatever contradicts your doctrine of sects must be true for you, since it is by the will of God, exalted is He, so this entails validating contradictory religions. But this is disputed, because validity only comes through conformity to the path of the Law, and it does not follow from making His will, exalted is He, dependent upon something that this conformity applies to it. It is not hidden that the first aspect, like this aspect, is not free from a certain unease, so reflect.

﴿Say, "Bring your witnesses"﴾: i.e., bring them forward to give testimony. *Halumma* is an *ism fi'l* (verbal noun, a word that functions as a verb without being inflected as one), and according to the people of the Hijaz it is not inflected. According to the Banu Tamim, it is treated as a verb: it takes feminine, dual, and plural forms. It is indeclinable (*mabni*) on the basis of the well-known principle that these features are characteristics of verbs.

It is related from Abu Ali al-Farisi that pronouns may attach to a word that is a particle, such as *laysa*, or an *ism fi'l*, such as *hat* ("bring"), because of its resemblance to verbs. On this view, *halumma* is an *ism fi'l* in all cases, as stated in the commentary on *al-Tashil* (Sharh al-Tashil). Al-Radi (al-Razi) also holds this view, when he said: "The Banu Tamim inflect it: they make it masculine, feminine, and plural, taking its original form into account. Its original form, according to the Basrans, is *halumma*, from *lamma*, when it means 'to come near'. The alif is deleted to indicate the sukun on the lam, because its original form is *alamma*. According to the Kufans, its original form is *hal umma*; the damma of the hamza is transferred to the lam and the hamza is deleted, as is the standard practice." This is considered unlikely, because *hal* does not precede an imperative. This objection is answered by what al-Radi transmitted from them: that the original form of *hal umma* is *hallaa umma*, and *hallaa* is an expression of urgency meaning "hurry." It was changed to *hal* to lighten the construction, and then the same changes were applied to it. It may be transitive, meaning "bring" or "come with," or intransitive, meaning "come forward," as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Bring forward to us﴾ and ﴿Those who testify that God has forbidden this﴾. Their great ones who established their misguidance will be gathered together. The purpose of bringing them is to expose and confront them, and to show that they have no basis, just as their followers have none. For this reason, the word "witnesses" is restricted by the possessive construction, and they are described in a way that indicates that they are witnesses known for testifying in their favor and supporting their creed. This refers to what they had forbidden of the livestock, as related in the preceding verses.

Mujahid said: it refers to the *bahira* and the *sa'iba* (types of livestock they declared forbidden). ﴿If they testify﴾, i.e., those witnesses known for falsehood, after they have appeared and testified that God has forbidden this, ﴿then do not testify with them﴾, i.e., do not confirm them, for it is a pure lie. Explain its corruption to them, because accepting it from them is agreement with them in false testimony. Silence may indicate approval. The meaning intended by "do not testify" (*la tashhad*) is either through metaphor by implication (*isti'ara taba'iyya*), or through the figure of speech where the cause is mentioned and the effect is meant (*majaz mursal*), since testimony is a consequence of acceptance, or through allusion (*kinaya*), or it is from the category of *mushakala* (assimilation of a word to a related word). Some people claimed that the pronoun in *shahidu* refers to the polytheists, meaning: if they do not find a witness who testifies to this, they testify for themselves, for themselves; so do not testify. This is very far-fetched, and even further than that is the view that it refers to the corruption (of their testimony) more closely. Also the view of one who claimed that the meaning is "bring your witnesses from others." If they do not find such, because non-Arabs do not forbid what was mentioned, and they testify for themselves, then do not believe them.

﴿And do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs﴾: the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to indicate that whoever denies the signs follows only his desires, and that whoever follows evidence can only believe in them. The address is said to be to everyone who is suited to it, and it is said to be addressed to the chief of those addressed, and the intended meaning is his community.

﴿And those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, like the idol-worshippers. This is conjoined to the first relative clause by way of conjoining an attribute to an attribute while the subject is the same, since whoever denies His signs does not believe in the Hereafter, and vice versa. Some people claimed that by the first relative clause is meant those who deny while acknowledging the Hereafter, such as the People of the Two Books, and by the second relative clause, those who deny while rejecting the Hereafter. What is wrong with this is not hidden. ﴿And they ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ (150): i.e., they make for Him equals, that is, partners. It is like His words: ﴿They associate others with Him﴾. It is also said: they turn away from Him by their deeds and attribute them to other than Him, Glorified and Exalted is He. It is also said: they turn away from Him by their worship. The clause is conjoined to "do not believe," and the meaning is: do not follow those who combine denial of the signs, disbelief in the Hereafter, and association of partners with their Lord, Mighty and Majestic is He. However, the prohibition is not based on the combination mentioned, but rather on the fact that those people possess these traits and are characterized by them. It is also said: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun in "do not believe."

[Page 54]

﴿Say, "Come."﴾ This is a command to him (ﷺ) after the falsity of their claims had become clear, to explain to them, in the wise manner, those forbidden things whose explanation the situation calls for. It is a notice that their duty is to abstain from these forbidden things. As for the forbidden foods, they were explained earlier. *Ta'āla* ("come") is an imperative from *ta'ālī* (rising, exalting). Its original use is for someone in a high place to call someone below him. It was then broadened by generalization and used, by way of metaphor, in the sense of an unrestricted use of a restricted term. Here it may, as has been said, retain its original sense, as a veiled reproach to them: they are at the bottom of ignorance, and if they heard what is said to them they would rise to the peak of knowledge and the summit of honor.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿I will recite﴾ (*atlu*) is the answer to the command, meaning: if you come to me, I will recite. The phrase in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾ (*mā ḥarrama rabbukum*), may be a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*) with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning: I will recite that which your Lord has forbidden, i.e., the verses containing it, that is, its prohibition. The intended sense is the verse indicating it. In both of these readings it is in a position of accusative as the object of *atlu*. It is also permissible that it be an interrogative, in which case it is in a position of accusative as the object of *ḥarrama*, and the clause is the object of *atlu*, because recitation belongs to the category of speech, so the clause may govern as an object. This is based on the Kufan school (*al-madhhab al-Kūfī*), which holds that a clause may be quoted with whatever carries the meaning of saying; other grammarians supply a verb of saying or the like in such cases.

The meaning here, on the interrogative reading, is: "Come, I will tell you and explain to you the answer to what your Lord has forbidden." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿to you﴾ (*ʿalaykum*), is related in every case to *ḥarrama*. It is also permissible for it to be related to *atlu*. The first was preferred, because it is more suitable to the context of stressing the obligation to refrain from the forbidden things mentioned. This is also the secret in mentioning the title of Lordship together with the pronoun referring to them. That the thing recited is forbidden to all does not harm this, as is not hidden.

﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾ (*an lā tushrikū bihi shay'an*): that is, of associating (*ishrāk*), or "anything of things." So *shay'an* may be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) or an object. The discussion of the grammar of *an lā* will come, God willing, exalted is He.

He, glorified is He, began with the matter of associating partners because it is the greatest of the forbidden things and the largest of the major sins.

﴿And to parents﴾ (*wa-bil-wālidayn*): that is, "Be good to them, with complete goodness, with no harm in it." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means showing kindness to them together with gentleness and humility: one should not speak harshly to them in reply, nor fix one's gaze on them, nor raise one's voice over them, but should stand before them like a servant before his master, in humility toward them. God, exalted is He, joined this obligation to the previous one because the blessing of parents is the greatest blessing upon the servant after the blessing of God, exalted is He, since the true cause of a human's existence is God, mighty and majestic, while the apparent cause is the two parents.

He, glorified is He, followed the obligation concerning parents with the obligation concerning children, for complete suitability, and said: ﴿Do not kill your children﴾ by burying them alive, ﴿out of poverty﴾ (*min imlāq*), that is, because of poverty or out of fear of it, as in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ (*khashyata imlāq*). It has been said that the address in each verse is to a different category, not a single address. The one addressed by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿out of poverty﴾ is someone who is afflicted with poverty, and the one addressed by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ is someone who has no poverty but fears its occurrence in the future. For this reason He put forward their provision here, in His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, and He put forward the provision of their children in the context of fear, so that it says: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾. This is a fine statement.

Whatever the case, the clause ﴿We﴾ ... etc. is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*), brought to explain the prohibition and to nullify the causal role of what they had taken as a cause for committing the forbidden act, and it is a guarantee from Him, exalted is He, for their provision: that is, We provide for both groups, not you, so do not proceed to what you have been forbidden on that account.
