﴿And do not approach the indecencies﴾ (*al-fawāḥish*): that is, fornication (*al-zinā*). The plural is either for emphasis, or in view of the multiplicity of those from whom it proceeds, or with intent to forbid the varieties of it. For this reason His saying, glorified is He, ﴿what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾ is substituted for it: that is, what is done openly in the shops, as is the custom of their lowly ones, and what is done secretly by taking secret lovers, as is the habit of their nobles. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī. It has been said that the intended meaning of the indecencies is all sins.

Regarding the meaning of what is apparent of them and what is hidden on this view, there are opinions whose indication has already been given. Al-Imām [al-Rāzī] and a group chose this view, and some verifiers preferred the first, because it fits better the arrangement of the coordinated terms. The reason for placing this prohibition between the prohibition on killing children and the prohibition on killing in general is that the indecencies, in this sense, while being in themselves a grave crime, are in the position of killing children, since the children of fornication are in the position of the dead. It has been narrated from him, upon him be blessings and peace, that he said concerning coitus interruptus (*al-ʿazl*): "That is a hidden burying (*wa'd khafī*)." On the other view, the placement of this general prohibition between its particular instances does not appear to make sense, and its placement between the two prohibitions would be like separating the tree from its bark. The linking of the prohibition to approaching them is either for emphasis in restraining from them, because of the strength of the motives toward them, or because approaching them leads to committing them.

﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden﴾: that is, which God has forbidden to be killed by making it inviolable through Islam or through a covenant. Thus the combatant (*ḥarbī*) is excluded and the protected non-Muslim (*dhimmī*) is included. What has been narrated from Ibn Jubayr, that the soul mentioned here means the believing soul, is not in its proper place. ﴿Except by right﴾ (*illā bil-ḥaqq*) is an exceptive clause (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*) from the most general of states: that is, do not kill it in any state except the state of being connected with the right, which is the command of the Law to kill it, as in what is narrated in the report: apostasy after belief, fornication after marriage, and killing an inviolable soul. Or it is from the most general of causes: that is, do not kill it by any cause except by a cause of right, which is among what is in the report. Or it is from the most general of verbal nouns: that is, do not kill it with a killing except a killing that is by right, which is killing by one of the mentioned causes.

﴿That﴾ (*dhālikum*): that is, what has been mentioned of the five weighty obligations, among the legal obligations. ﴿He has enjoined upon you﴾ (*waṣṣākum bihi*): that is, He demanded it of you with emphasis. The nominal clause is a resumptive sentence, brought to renew the covenant and to stress the obligation to observe what they were charged with. Al-Imām [al-Rāzī] said: it was brought to bring acceptance close to the heart, because it contains gentleness and mercy. ﴿So that you may reason﴾ (*laʿallakum taʿqilūn*): that is, that you may use your intellects, which restrain your souls and hold them back from committing the vile forbidden acts.

[Page 55]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 6, verse 152:**

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, meaning, do not meddle with it in any way, ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, meaning, by the course of action that is best for his property, such as preserving it and developing it. It has also been said: the intended meaning is, do not approach his property unless you are characterized by the trait that is best in regard to his welfare. Whoever does not find himself upon the best of traits should not approach it. But this is far-fetched. The address is to the guardians and executors, because of His words, exalted is He: ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾. For this is a limit (ghayah) to what is understood from the exception, not to the prohibition, as if it were said: Safeguard it until he reaches maturity, and when he reaches it, then hand it over to him, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment (rushdan), then hand over to them their property﴾.

As for ashudd, according to what al-Farra' said, it is a plural with no singular. Some of the Basrans said: it is a singular, like kaannaka, and no other word of this pattern has come in the singular forms besides these two. It has also been said: it is the plural of shiddah, like ni'mah and an'um, and the ha' was assumed to be added to it because of the frequency of the plural of fa'al in af'ul, like qadah and aqduh.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the plural of shudd, with the shin pronounced with a damma, like wudd and awudd. It has also been said it is the plural of shadd, with the shin pronounced with a fatha. In any case, it derives from shiddah, that is, strength, or from elevation, from shadda al-nahar (the day rose) when it rose high. From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

*"My covenant with her is at the rising of the day, as if she had dyed her fingers and her head with al-'athlam."*

The meaning of reaching ashudd according to al-Sha'bi and a group is reaching puberty (al-hulum). It has been said: that he reaches eighteen years. Al-Suddi said: that he reaches thirty. However, the verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by His words, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age (al-nikah)﴾. It has been said other than this. The disagreement concerning the time of handing over the orphan's property to him has already been discussed, and we have extensively expounded the truth in that matter, so recall it.

﴿And give full measure (awfu)﴾, meaning, complete ﴿the measure (al-kayl)﴾, meaning the measured quantity; so it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of the passive participle, ﴿and the balance (al-mizan)﴾ likewise, as Abu al-Baqa' said. It is permissible that there is an omitted genitive construction here, meaning: the measured quantity of the measure and the weighed quantity of the balance. ﴿With justice (bil-qist)﴾, meaning with fairness, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in awfu, meaning being just. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the object, meaning complete. Perhaps the bringing of this circumstantial clause is for emphasis.

In al-Tafsir al-Kabir: If it is said, the giving of full measure and balance is the very same as justice, so what is the benefit of the repetition? We say: it is the command of God, exalted is He, to the one who gives, to give the one entitled his right without deficiency, and the command to the rights-holder to take his right without seeking an increase. So reflect.

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity (wus'aha)﴾, meaning, except what is within its capacity and is not difficult for it. The sentence is a new independent clause, brought after the command to give full measure and balance with justice, as a relaxation regarding what exceeds one's ability, since observing that, as it is, involves hardship along with its frequent occurrence. So it is as if it were said: Your obligation is what is within your capacity in this matter, and what lies beyond it is pardoned for you. It is also permissible that it was brought to make light the matter of the obligations mentioned earlier, so that they would embrace them, as if it were said: everything We have obligated you with is possible and not burdensome, and We do not obligate what cannot be borne.

﴿And when you speak (qultum) a word, in a judgment or testimony or the like, ﴾ then ﴿be just (fa'dilu)﴾ in it, and speak the truth, ﴿even if it concerns (kana) one who is near of kin (dha qurba)﴾, meaning, one who is a relative of yours. ﴿And fulfill the covenant of God (bi-'ahdi Allahi awfu)﴾, meaning what He has enjoined upon you of the enumerated matters, or any covenant whatsoever, so that what has been mentioned enters into it in a primary manner; or what you have pledged to God, exalted is He, by your oaths and vows. The prepositional phrase is connected to what follows it, and its fronting is for the sake of emphasizing its importance. ﴿That (dhalikum)﴾, meaning what has been detailed of the weighty obligations, ﴿He has enjoined upon you (wassakum bihi)﴾, meaning commanded you with it as an emphatic command, ﴿that you may remember (la'allakum tadhakkarun)﴾ (152), what is within its contents, and act in accordance with its requirement. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *tadhakkarun* with the dhal lightened, while the rest read it with the dhal doubled, throughout the Qur'an. Both have the same meaning.

The first verse was concluded with His words, glorified is He: ﴿that you may understand (la'allakum ta'qilun)﴾, and this one with His words, exalted is He: ﴿that you may remember﴾, because the people were persistent in polytheism, the killing of children, approaching adultery, and the killing of a soul unlawfully, without being repelled by it or recognizing its ugliness. So He, glorified is He, forbade them, that perhaps they would understand its ugliness, so they would be repelled by it and abandon it. As for preserving the property of orphans for them, giving full measure, justice in speech, and fulfilling covenants, they were doing these and took pride in being characterized by them. So God, exalted is He, commanded them with that, that perhaps they would remember if forgetfulness overtook them. This is what al-Qutb al-Razi said. Then he said: If you say, the kindness to parents is also of the second kind, so how was it mentioned among the first? I say: the greatest of blessings upon man is the blessing of God, exalted is He, and following it is the blessing of the parents, because they are the apparent influences, and from them comes the blessing of upbringing and protection from destruction in childhood. So when He forbade disbelief in God, exalted is He, He forbade after it ingratitude toward the blessing of the two parents, as an alert that since the people did not commit ingratitude, then by way of priority they would not commit disbelief.

Al-Imam said: The reason each verse was concluded with what it was concluded with is that the five obligations mentioned in the first verse are clear and manifest, so it was necessary to understand and comprehend them. The four obligations mentioned in this verse are hidden, obscure matters in which there must be much striving and thought until one reaches the point of balance, which is remembrance. End. It is possible to say: most of the earlier obligations were expressed in the form of a prohibition, and prohibition means restriction, and a person is eager for what is forbidden. So it was appropriate that the enjoining be rationalized by something that alludes to the meaning of restraint and confinement. This differs from the other obligations, most of which were expressed in the form of a command, in which restraint is not apparent as it is in a prohibition. Thus the emphasis of the demand and the intensity in it is for him to persist in it and to remember if he forgets. So reflect.

This is Ruh al-Ma'ani, the commentary of al-Alusi, on surah 6, verse 153:

﴿And that this is My path, straight﴾. It refers to His law (*shar'*), upon him be blessings and peace, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both. The forthcoming prohibition is consistent with this. According to Mujahid (*Mujahid ibn Jabr*), it refers to the commands and prohibitions in the two verses. It has also been said that it refers to what is mentioned in the surah, for most of it concerns the affirmation of Tawhid (the Oneness of God) and Prophethood, and the explanation of the Law.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *inna* with a *kasrah*. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a *fathah* and light (non-doubled) *nun*. The rest read it with a doubled *nun*.

Ibn 'Amir read *ṣirāṭī* with a *fathah* on the *yā'*. It is also read *wa-hādhā ṣirāṭu rabbikum* and *wa-hādhā ṣirāṭu rabbika*. The attribution of the path (*ṣirāṭ*) to the Lord, glorified is He, is in respect of its origination (*waḍ'*), and its attribution to him, upon him be blessings and peace, is in respect of its following (*sulūk*) and its calling (*da'wah*).

[Page 57]

That is: this is the path that I travel and to which I call. ﴿Straight﴾, with no crookedness in it. Its accusative (*naṣb*) is as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). ﴿So follow it﴾: that is, trace its footsteps and act upon it. ﴿And do not follow the ways﴾: that is, the misguidances, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration from him, they are the differing religions, such as Judaism and Christianity. Ibn al-Mundhir, 'Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from Mujahid that they are innovations (*bid'ah*) and doubtful matters (*shubuhat*). ﴿So they will scatter you﴾: it is put in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition. The original form is *tatafarraqa*, and one of the two *tā'*s is deleted. The *bā'* is for transitivity, meaning: so it will scatter you, in the manner of its scattering, "the scattering of Saba'" (*ayādī Saba'*). Thus, as you see, it is more eloquent than "your scattering," as is said, and *dhahaba bihi* (he took it away with him) is more eloquent than *adhhabahu 'an sabīlihi* (he took it away from its way), because of what it indicates of continuance (*istiṣḥāb*). That is, the way of Allah, the Exalted, which has no crookedness and no hardship, which is the religion of Islam. It has also been said that it is following Revelation and pursuing proof. In this there is an indication that His path, peace be upon him, is the very way of Allah, the Exalted.

Ahmad and a group narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ drew a line with his hand, then said: 'This is the way of Allah, the Exalted, straight.' Then he drew lines to the right of that line and to its left, then said: 'And these are the ways; there is not one of them except that upon it is a devil calling to it.' Then he recited: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ ... to the end."

It was attributed to him, upon him be blessings and peace, first because that is more conducive to following, since by it becomes clear that it is the path of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿That﴾ refers to following the ways. ﴿He has enjoined you with it, that you may become righteous﴾ (153): the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, by persevering in doing what He commanded and continuing to refrain from what He forbade.

Abu Hayyan said: "Since the straight path comprises the obligations, and He, glorified is He, commanded following it and forbade following other paths, He concluded that with *taqwa* (God-consciousness), which is the protection from the Fire, for whoever follows His path is saved with everlasting salvation and attains everlasting felicity. Allah, glorified is He, repeated the injunction for further emphasis. What an injunction! How great its importance and how clear its proof."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as *ḥasan* (good), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Whoever would like to look at the injunction of Muhammad, peace be upon him, with his seal, let him recite these verses: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ up to ﴿that you may become righteous﴾."

Ibn Humayd, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Which of you will pledge allegiance to me upon these three verses?' Then he recited them to the end, then said: 'Whoever fulfils them, his reward is with Allah, the Exalted. Whoever falls short in any of them and Allah, the Exalted, seizes him for it in this world, that will be his punishment. Whoever has it deferred to the Hereafter, his affair is with Allah, the Exalted: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will pardon him.'"

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Adi, who said: "Ka'b heard a man reciting ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ ... to the end. He said: 'By Him in whose hand is Ka'b's soul, it is indeed the first verse in the Torah: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ to the end of the verses."' And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: these are decisive verses (*muḥkamāt*) which no other of all the Books has abrogated (*naskh*). They are forbidden to all the children of Adam. They are the Mother of the Book (*umm al-kitāb*). Whoever acts upon them enters Paradise, and whoever abandons them enters the Fire."

Now, ﴿that do not associate anything with Him﴾ in His words, glorified is He: *an* here may be either explanatory (*mufassirah*) or verbal (*maṣdariyyah*). The "second scholar" (al-'Allamah al-Thani) said: "Both possibilities involve a problem. If it is made verbal, it would be an explanation of what is forbidden, in apposition to *mā* or its omitted resumptive pronoun. Clearly, what is forbidden is association (*shirk*), not its negation. Moreover, the commands that follow are coordinated with ﴿do not associate﴾, which entails coordinating an imperative (*ṭalabī*) with a declarative (*khabarī*), and making a required, commanded act into something forbidden. This requires a strained explanation, such as making *lā* superfluous, or coordinating commands with prohibitions by considering the prohibition of their opposites, and treating a declarative as implying a demand. As for making *lā* a prohibitive particle that occupies the position of the complement of *an* (the verbal particle), as Sibawayh permitted, since the jussive operates on the verb and the accusative operates on *lā* along with it, this is no way forward here, because the superfluity of the prohibitive *lā* is something no one has said and it does not occur in speech. If *an* is made explanatory and *lā* prohibitive, and the prohibitions serve as an explanation of the recitation of the forbidden things, two problems arise. One is coordinating ﴿that this is My path, straight﴾ with ﴿that do not associate﴾, when there is no sense in coordinating it with *an* explanatory followed by a verb. The second is coordinating the commands mentioned, for they cannot serve as an explanation of the recitation of forbidden things, but rather of obligations. Al-Zamakhshari chose to make it explanatory and to coordinate the commands, because they carry the meaning of prohibitions, and there is then no way to make it verbal and relative (*mawṣūlah*) to the prohibition, for the reason you have learned."

He answered the first problem by saying that His words, glorified is He, ﴿And that this is My path﴾, are not coordinated with ﴿that do not associate﴾. Rather, it is a reason (*ta'līl*) for following, linked to ﴿follow it﴾, with the preposition *lām* omitted. The pronoun of ﴿follow it﴾ may refer back to the path, since it precedes it in wording.

If it is said: "On this view, ﴿follow it﴾ would be coordinated with ﴿do not associate﴾, and the meaning would be: so follow My path, because it is straight. This combines the two coordinating particles *wa* and *fa*, and it is not sound. If *wa* is made a resumptive and parenthetical particle..." We say: the occurrence of *wa* with *fa* when the complement is fronted, separating them, is common in speech, as in ﴿And your Lord, so magnify﴾ and ﴿And that the mosques are for Allah, so do not call upon anyone with Allah﴾. If you refuse to combine them absolutely and reject the superfluity of *fa*, then make the complement dependent on an omitted element, with what is mentioned after *fa* coordinated with it, as in "Glorify, so magnify; and call upon Allah, so do not call upon anyone with Allah," and "they preferred it, so follow it."

As for the second problem, coordinating the commands with the prohibitions that follow *an* explanatory, for the recitation of forbidden things, while it is certain that what is commanded cannot be forbidden, shows that the prohibition refers to their opposites. The meaning is that the commands are as though mentioned and their necessary implications intended, which are the prohibitions of their opposites, to the point that it is as if it were said: "I recite what is forbidden: that you should not harm your parents, nor diminish the measure and the balance, nor abandon justice, nor break the covenant." Such a construction, although not permissible in principle, may perhaps be permitted by way of coordination. As for making the pause on His words, may He be exalted, ﴿your Lord﴾, and the accusative of ﴿that do not associate﴾ by *'alaykum* (upon you), meaning "keep to abstaining," this is refuted by the coordination of the commands, unless *lā* is made prohibitive and *an* verbal, relative to the commands and prohibitions. Abu Hayyan said: "It is not necessary that all the commands be coordinated with everything that *lā* governs. It is not sound to coordinate ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾ with ﴿come﴾, with what follows it being coordinated with that."

The view that the prohibition refers to the opposites of the commands has been criticised as being very remote, an obscure riddle of meanings, and not necessary. Then he said: "As for the coordination of these commands, it may have two aspects. One is that they are coordinated not with the prohibitions before them, which would entail that the prohibition extends to them since they fall within the scope of the explanatory *an*. Rather, they are coordinated with His words, may He be exalted, ﴿I recite what your Lord has forbidden﴾. He commanded them first with a command which led to the mention of prohibitions, then He commanded them secondly with commands. This meaning is clear. The second is that the commands are coordinated with the prohibitions, falling under the ruling of the explanatory *an*. This can be sound on the assumption of an omitted element of which *an* is the explanation, both for it and for the explicit statement before it, which indicates its omission. The estimate is: 'and what He commanded you with,' which is omitted, because the meaning of 'what your Lord has forbidden you' indicates it. For the meaning of ﴿what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ is: what your Lord has prohibited you from. So the meaning is: 'Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited you from and what He has commanded you with.' When this is the estimate, it is sound for *an* to be explanatory of the verb of prohibition indicated by 'forbidden' and of the omitted verb of command. Do you not see that you may say: 'I commanded you that you should not honour an ignorant man, and honour a learned man'? And it is permitted to coordinate a command with a prohibition and a prohibition with a command, as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:"

*Do not perish in grief, and bear yourself with grace.*

"We know of no disagreement on this, unlike disparate sentences differing in declarative, interrogative and imperative form, for there is a well-known disagreement concerning the permissibility of coordinating them." End of his words. You know that coordinating with "come" is extremely remote and should not be considered. What he mentioned about the omission, and making the explanation apply to the omitted element and the explicit statement, is not without merit.

Al-Tabarsi transmitted the permissibility of ﴿that do not associate﴾ being with an estimated *lām*, in the sense: "I make clear to you the forbidden, so that you do not associate." This is because when they forbid what Allah has made lawful, they have made other than Allah, in acceptance from them, equal to Allah, glorified is He, and by that they have become polytheists. The speech of Allah, the Exalted, should not be construed in such a manner, as is not hidden.

﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾: this is a statement issuing from Him, the Exalted, confirming the injunction, establishing it, and paving the way for what follows concerning the sending down of the Glorious Qur'an, as the shift of style to the first person plural (*iltifāt* to the speaker) indicates. It is coordinated with an omitted element that the context requires and the composition demands, as if it were said after His words, glorified is He, ﴿That is what He has enjoined you with﴾, by way of resumption, confirming it and establishing its content: "We did that."

[Page 60]

﴿Then We gave﴾ ... etc. Shaykh al-Islam, may God sanctify his secret, took this view. It has also been said that it is conjoined to ﴿This He has enjoined upon you﴾. From al-Zajjaj it is reported that it is conjoined to the sense of recitation, as if it were said: "Say: Come, I shall recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you, then recite to them what God gave Moses, peace be upon him." It has also been said that it is conjoined to (qul, "say"), and there is an ellipsis in it, meaning: "Say: Come, then say: We gave Moses the Book."

From Abu Muslim, which al-Maghribi approved, it is connected to His words in the story of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾. This is because He, glorified is He, counted His blessing upon him through what He placed in his progeny of prophets, peace be upon them, and then conjoined to it the mention of what He bestowed upon him through what He gave Moses, peace be upon him, of the Book and prophethood, and Moses too was of his progeny. All of this, as you see, is weak, although its degrees differ in weakness. As for thumma (then), al-Farra' said it denotes narrative sequence (al-tartib al-ikhbari), as in the example: "It reached me what I did today, then what I did today is more wondrous." Ibn Usfur criticized this, saying it is nothing, because thumma requires that the second come after the first with an interval, and there is no interval between two narrative statements. Therefore one must return to the view that the sense of sequence has been stripped from it, or that it denotes sequence of rank (tartib rutbi), as his words "more wondrous" in the example indicate. Here it is clearly so, because the giving of the Torah, which contains rulings and abundant benefits, is greater than this well-known exhortation on people's tongues. Some have explained the narrative sequence, which requires that the second come after the first, by saying that expressions that have passed are placed in the position of the distant. It has also been said that it is due to the intervention of the clause ﴿So that you may be God-fearing﴾ between the two conjoined elements.

Some have said that (thumma) here means (waw, "and"), and this has occurred frequently in the Book. ﴿Complete﴾ (tamaman) is for honor and blessing, and it stands in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, "for the sake of"), and the omission of the preposition (lam) was permitted because it carries the sense of (itmaman, "for completion"). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a verbal noun (masdar) of ﴿We gave﴾, from its meaning, because giving the Book is a completion of the blessing, as if it were said: "We completed the blessing with a completion," and so it is like (nabatan, "growth") in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth a growth﴾. And it permitted that it be a circumstantial (hal, "state") from the Book, meaning "complete." ﴿Upon the one who did well﴾, meaning: upon the one who performed its duty well, whoever he might be, so (alladhi, "the one who") is generic. This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): (upon those who did well), and the reading of al-Hasan: (upon the doers of good). From al-Farra' it is reported that (alladhi) here is like it in his words:

"Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Fulj, they are the people, all the people, O mother of Khalid."

The statement of Mujahid is open to both interpretations, or: (upon the one who did well) means his conveying of it, and he is Moses, peace be upon him; or "complete, upon what Moses, peace be upon him, did well," meaning he performed it well in knowledge and laws, that is, in addition to his action, in the manner of perfecting. From Ibn Zayd it is reported that the intended meaning is "complete, upon God's goodness toward His prophets, peace be upon them." Its apparent meaning is that (alladhi) is a literal relative pronoun, and this has been said regarding His words: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those who engaged﴾. The pronoun in (ahsana, "did well") then refers to God, exalted is He. Similar to this is what is reported from al-Jubba'i, that the intended meaning is "upon what God, exalted is He, did well to Moses, peace be upon him, of prophethood and other things." Both are contrary to the apparent meaning. From Abu Muslim it is reported that the intended relative is Abraham, peace be upon him, and this is based on his claim that the verse connects to the story of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (ahsanu, "better") in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and (alladhi, "which") is an attribute of the religion or of the manner in which the Books are: meaning "complete, upon the religion which is the best religion and the most pleasing," or "We gave Moses the Book complete and perfect in the manner which is the best that Books can be." The superiority is relative to other than the religion of Islam and other than what the Qur'an is upon.

﴿And a detailing of everything﴾, meaning: a detailed explanation of everything that is needed in religion. There is no indication in it that there is no ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, contrary to one who claimed that. Similar wording has come in the description of the Qur'an, such as His words, exalted is He, in Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿And a detailing of every thing﴾ concerning those who are obligated. The discussion of these conjoined elements is like the discussion of the element they are conjoined to, regarding the possibilities of causality (illiyya), verbal-noun status (masdariyya), and circumstantial status (haliyya). The apparent meaning is that the Book includes detail, as God, exalted is He, has informed, to the extent that its letter qualified it.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, who said: When Moses, peace be upon him, threw down the tablets, guidance and mercy remained, and detailing departed. ﴿So that they﴾, meaning the Children of Israel, who are indicated by the mention of Moses, peace be upon him, and the giving of the Book. It is not permissible for the pronoun to return to (alladhi) based on the generic sense, or on what al-Farra' said, because it does not fit His words, glorified is He: ﴿In meeting their Lord they believe﴾ (154). Rather, the fitting phrasing in that case would have been, for example, "so that they may be shown mercy." The prepositional phrase is connected to what follows it, and it was placed first for the sake of the rhyming endings (fawasil). The meaning of "meeting" has been said to be the recompense, and it has been said: the return to the dominion of the Lord, glorified is He, and His authority, on a day when no one else possesses anything. From Ibn Abbas, the meaning is: that they may believe in the resurrection and affirm the reward and punishment.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 155]**

﴿And this﴾, which has had its commands and prohibitions recited to you, that is, the Qur'an, is a ﴿Book﴾ of great standing, whose worth cannot be measured. ﴿We have sent it down﴾ through the mediation of the Trustworthy Spirit (al-Ruh al-Amin), comprising the benefits of the religious and worldly sciences (funun), a portion of which has been detailed for you. The clause is an attributive description (sifah) of ﴿Book﴾. His statement, glorified is He: ﴿blessed﴾, meaning abundant in good in religion and in this world, is another attribute. The first attribute was placed before the second even though it is not correct (as a predicate) because the discourse is addressed to those who deny the sending down. It is also permissible that this and what precedes it be two predicates (khabar) about the demonstrative (ism al-isharah). The particle "fa" (so) in His exalted statement: ﴿so follow it﴾ indicates that what follows it results from what precedes it, for the great standing of the Book in itself and in its description necessitates following it, that is: act upon what is in it, or obey its commands, and be mindful of opposing it or its prohibitions. ﴿That you may be shown mercy﴾ (155), that is, so that you may be shown mercy as a reward for that. It has been said: the meaning is "be mindful, in hope of mercy," or "be mindful so that the purpose of piety is the mercy of God, exalted is He."

[p. 61]

﴿Lest you say﴾ is an *'illah* (causal clause) governing an implied verb, which is indicated by the stated "We have sent down" (*anzalna*). The stated verb is the governing element (*'amil*) of the clause, not the stated verb itself. This differs from the view of al-Kisa'i, so that there is no separation between the governing element and what it governs by a foreign element. According to the Kufans, the implied element is *bi-taqdir la* ("with *la* implied"), meaning "so that you do not say." According to the Basrans, it is with the elision of a noun (*hadhf al-mudaf*), meaning "out of dislike that you say." It has also been said that it may be the object of *ittaqu* ("fear"), and al-Farra' held this view. It is also possible that the implied *lam* is the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*), meaning that one of the two statements resulted from Our sending down (the Book), in the way that an end result follows from an act. This would be a rebuke to them for their distance from happiness. The more immediate meaning is what was mentioned first, namely: "lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, 'Had We not been sent down [the Book]...'"

﴿The Book was sent down﴾, the one that speaks with the rulings and is conclusive in argument, ﴿upon two groups﴾, two communities existing ﴿before us﴾. According to Ibn 'Abbas and others, they are the Jews and the Christians. The sending down is specified to their two scriptures because these two are the ones renowned among the heavenly Books for containing rulings.

﴿And indeed we were﴾: here *in* is the lightened form (*al-mukhaffafah*) of *inna*, and the *lam* that follows it distinguishes it from the negating *in*. It is inactive (*muhmalah*), following what the grammarians have established: when the lightened *an* is attached to the *lam* in one of its two parts and is followed by an abrogating element (*nasikh*), it is inactive and does not govern any noun, whether stated or pronominal, whether affirmed or elided. The meaning is "and indeed, we were..." ﴿of their study﴾, that is, their recitation, ﴿heedless﴾ (156), not paying attention. We did not know what it was, because it was not in our language, so it was not possible for us to receive from it what would bring our salvation. Perhaps they meant by this the (affirmation of) monotheism. It has also been said that the rulings meant are those mentioned in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Come...﴾ etc., because they are general to all the children of Adam and do not differ in any age of the ages. Shaykh al-Islam interpreted the verse in this way. He then said: Thus it becomes clear that their excuse, even though they were not commanded with what is in the two Books, is because these contain the rulings mentioned, which apply to all nations. Likewise, the cutting off of that excuse by the sending down of the Qur'an is because it also contains them, not only the other laws and rulings.

﴿Or you say﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you say﴾ (in the previous verse). Both have also been read with the ya' (yaqūlū), as an iltifat (shift) from address to the ﴿follow it and fear God﴾ (second-person address). The address that follows after this is also an iltifat, and its position is not hidden. Al-Qutb said: He, exalted is He, first addressed them with what He addressed them with; then, when He reached the report of their wretched statements, He turned away from them and proceeded in the third person, as if they were absent. Then, when He, glorified is He, wished to rebuke them afterwards, He addressed them again. So it is an iltifat of the utmost elegance.

﴿If the Book had been revealed to us﴾ as it was revealed to them, ﴿we would surely have been better guided than them﴾ to the truth, which is the ultimate aim, or to what it contains of rulings and laws, because our minds are sharper and our understanding keener.

﴿Now there has certainly come to you﴾ is connected to a omitted element indicated by the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasīḥah, the fa' that reveals an implied condition). It may be a cause for that, or a condition for it, meaning: do not make this excuse, for there has come to you... etc. Or: if you are truthful in what you promise of yourselves, on the assumption that the Book had been revealed to you, then what you supposed has happened, and there has come to you ﴿a clear proof﴾, a great and evident argument, which you recognise because of its manifestness and because it is in your own tongue, ﴿from your Lord﴾. The preposition here may be connected to an omitted element that serves as an attribute of ﴿a clear proof﴾, and it is also valid for it to be connected to ﴿has come to you﴾.

In any case, this indicates its relative excellence, along with an allusion to its intrinsic nobility. And in mentioning the title of Lordship together with the attribution to their pronoun, there is what is not hidden of additional emphasis on making following obligatory.

﴿And guidance and mercy﴾ are coordinated with ﴿a clear proof﴾; their tanwin is like their tanwin for glorification. The intended meaning of all of that is the Qur'an. It was expressed as ﴿a clear proof﴾ first, to signal their complete capacity to study it, and as ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ second, to draw attention to the fact that it contains what the Torah contained of guiding people and showing them mercy; rather, it is the very essence of guidance and mercy. In al-Tafsir al-Kabir: If it is said, "A clear proof and guidance are one thing, so what is the benefit of the repetition?" We say: the Qur'an is a clear proof regarding what is known by transmission, and it is guidance regarding what is known by transmission and reason. Since the benefit differs, this coordination is valid. And what is in it is not hidden.

Page 62

﴿So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God﴾. The fa' is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes, for the coming of the Qur'an, described as mentioned, necessitates the utmost injustice of whoever denies it. The relative pronoun here refers to those addressed, and it was placed in the position of their pronoun by way of iltifat, to specify explicitly their being characterised by what is in the scope of the relative clause, to indicate the cause of the ruling, and to remove them from the rank of direct address. He expressed what came to them as ﴿the signs of God﴾ to magnify the matter. It has been read ﴿kadhaba﴾ with light pronunciation. The first preposition is connected to what is "with him"; the second may be so connected, and this is the apparent reading.

It may also be that it is connected to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial clause, the meaning being: he denied while the signs of God were with him.

﴿And turns away from them﴾, i.e., turns away without reflecting upon them, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others; or he turned people away from them. Thus it combines misguidance and misleading. The verb in the first sense is intransitive, and in the second sense transitive, and the second is more common in usage.

﴿We will surely recompense those who turn away from Our signs﴾: a threat to them, by stating the recompense for their turning away or their hindering, in such a way that the recompense for their denial is understood from it. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the pronoun to establish the true basis of the recompense.

﴿With a dreadful punishment﴾, i.e., a punishment that is evil and severe, ﴿for what they used to turn away﴾ (157). I.e., because of what they were doing of turning away, repeatedly and continually. This is an explicit statement of what was indicated by applying the ruling to the relative clause, with the cause being what is in the scope of its relative clause.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 158 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Do they await﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain that faith cannot come from them through the sending down of what has been mentioned of the clear signs, guidance, and warning; it also indicates that among the signs there are some from which faith brings no benefit, as an emphasis on conveying and warning, and on removing excuses and pleading ignorance. The "hal" (هَلْ, interrogative particle) here is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari). Al-Radi denied that it comes with this meaning and said: it is for affirmation (taqrir) in affirmative statements. The majority hold the first view. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Makkah.

Al-Jubba'i claimed that it refers to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, meaning: they are not awaiting ﴿except that the angels come to them﴾ to take their souls, ﴿or that your Lord comes﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾, as He has informed and in the sense He intended. To this interpretation went Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, and Muqatil. It was also said: the coming of the angels is to bring down punishment and the earthquake upon them. It is narrated from al-Hasan that the coming of the Lord means the coming of His command with punishment. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: the command of your Lord comes concerning them with killing. It was also said: the meaning is that all of His signs come, that is, the signs of the Resurrection and total destruction, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord come﴾. You know that the well-known position of the early scholars (salaf) is not to interpret such things by supposing an omitted noun or the like, but rather to delegate the meaning to the All-Subtle, the All-Aware, while firmly holding that the apparent meaning is not intended. Among them are those who keep it upon its apparent sense, but claim that the coming attributed to Him, exalted is He, is not the coming that characterizes created things. The summary of that is that they affirm the apparent meanings, deny the necessary implications, and claim that these are implications in the case of created beings. But where is dust from the Lord of lords!

Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) permitted taking the statement in its apparent, commonly understood sense, its purpose being to report the belief and doctrine of the disbelievers. Al-Imam relied on this, but it is far-fetched or false. The intended meaning of "the signs" is, according to some, the minor signs of the Hour; these, as derived from the reports, are many. It is authentically related by way of Hudhayfah ibn Usayd, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked down on us from an upper chamber while we were discussing, and he said: 'What are you discussing?' We said: 'We are discussing the Hour.' He said: 'It will not be established until you see ten signs before it: the smoke, the Dajjal, 'Isa son of Maryam, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the beast, the rising of the sun from its west, and three earthquakes:
Page 63
an earthquake in the East, an earthquake in the West, and an earthquake in the Arabian Peninsula; and the last of that is a fire that comes out of the bottom of Aden or Yemen, driving people to the place of gathering; it rests with them when they rest, and it rests with them when they take a midday rest.'" Some say that the "some" refers to: the Dajjal, the beast, and the rising of the sun from its west. The word "some" is also meant in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before﴾. Muslim, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet ﷺ, something that is explicit in this. An objection was raised: that the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him, comes after the Dajjal, may the curse be upon him, and he, peace be upon him, calls people to faith and accepts it from them, and in his time there is much good, worldly and otherworldly. It was answered with what is free from scrutiny. The truth is that the "some" in which faith brings no benefit is the rising of the sun from its west.

For al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated: "The Hour will not be established until the sun rises from its west; when it rises and people see it, they will all believe, but that is the time when no soul will benefit from its faith," then he recited the verse. Indeed this specification has been narrated from him ﷺ in more than one sound report, and to this went the majority of the exegetes. The reports whose apparent meaning contradicts this are, on careful examination, not contradictory to it, as will be clear to the one who reflects. The reason faith brings no benefit at that time is that when the change of the upper world is witnessed, necessary knowledge is attained and faith in the unseen, which is what one is obligated to, is removed; so faith at that point is like the faith at the death rattle. The implication of the reports on this matter is that faith is never accepted after that. However, the apparent position, according to the Zawajir, is that what occurs after that is accepted provided there is no negligence, like one who was insane and then recovered, or who became Muslim by following his parents.

From al-Balqini: if the situation is delayed after the sun rises from the west and a long time passes until it is forgotten, faith is accepted, because the compelling sign has disappeared; and he has a sound basis. But al-'Iraqi's statement that the apparent position is that a long time will not pass until it is forgotten is not consistent with what al-Qurtubi narrated in his Tadhkirah from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ, and what al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar quoted in his commentary on al-Bukhari, that people will remain after the sun rises from its west for one hundred and twenty years. The discussion of how the sun rises from the west is detailed in the books of hadith. In Suq al-'Arus by Ibn al-Jawzi, it is said that the sun rises from its west for three days with their nights, then it is said to it: "Return from your rising place." The well-known view is that it rises for one day from the west, then travels to the line of midday, then returns to the west, and after that rises from the east as it did before. The report of 'Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa is explicit in this. All of it is a possible matter, and Allah, glorified is He, is powerful over all things.

Al-Bukhari in his History, and Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn 'Asakir, narrated concerning how this happens, from Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When Allah wills to make the sun rise from its west, He turns it on the pole, so its east becomes its west and its west its east." The astronomers and those who agree with them claim that the rising of the sun from the west is impossible, and they say: the sun and the other celestial bodies are simple, their properties do not differ in direction, motion, or otherwise, and no change befalls them from what they are. They have built this on something like a crumbling, unstable cliff. Al-Kirmani said: even granting their principles, there is no impossibility in it either, since they hold that the zodiac circle, called the sphere of fixed stars, may coincide with the equator, which is the midline of the greatest sphere called the Atlas sphere, so that the east becomes west and the west east. End. There is scrutiny in this, which shows the distance of explaining how coincidence occurs and what follows from it according to the books of their verifiers. So I say: al-Tadhkirah and its commentary by al-Sayyid al-Sanad say:

The total inclination, which is the extreme of distance between the two zones, the equator and the zodiac circle, as found by ancient and modern observations, is not one single thing; rather, what the ancients found was greater than what the moderns found. It may be thought that what the one who is more recent in time found was less than what the one who is more ancient in time found, although most of what they found did not reach twenty-four degrees, and the least of it did not fall below twenty-three and a half degrees.

Then the apparent view is that this difference is due only to the faultiness of the instruments in their circularity, their division, or their setting at the true midday line, not to the movement of one zone toward the other; otherwise the difference would have to follow one pattern, and it does not, as has been shown in its proper place. Yet it is possible that the origin of the difference is movement, and the lack of regularity is due to the faultiness of instruments. Since it is impossible for this approach to be caused by the movement of the equator toward the zodiac zone, for it would entail that the latitudes of lands differ from what they are and that the line of equilibrium be a different place at every time, some have held that the zodiac zone moves in latitude and so approaches the equator of the day. If this is true, there must be proven another sphere that moves the zodiac sphere in this motion. Then, if the zone moves in latitude, it is possible that the cycle is completed, and it is possible that it is not completed but moves to a certain limit and then returns; that limit may be after its coincidence with the equator zone twice, or at its second coincidence, or between the two coincidences, whether after completing half its cycle, at half of it, or before that. If it does not reach what is between the two coincidences, it either returns at its first coincidence or before that. These are eight rationally possible cases, and there is no more beyond them. In the first five cases, the two halves of the northern and southern surface of the zodiac sphere exchange, so the half of the zodiac surface that was northern of the equator becomes southern of it, and vice versa, together with what follows from the two halves of rulings: the rulings of the northern half are established for the southern half after it becomes northern, and the rulings of the southern for the northern after it becomes southern. In the first three of these, each of the two halves of the zodiac zone coincides with each of the two halves of the equator zone. In the remaining cases beyond the first five, only some of the mentioned surface is exchanged. In the first seven cases, a half of the zodiac zone coincides with the adjacent half of the equator zone. At each coincidence, night and day become equal in all regions, because the path of the sun is the equator, bisected by the horizons that intersect it, and the seasons of the year become void, because the distance of the sun from the zenith becomes one fixed thing, namely the latitude of the land. The situation continues in this way until the two zones separate by an amount that is perceptible, which occurs only over a very long period. In the second case, there is no coincidence at all, no equalization of the two poles, and no voiding of seasons, except that the altitudes and the durations of day and night for particular portions of the zodiac circle increase and decrease in a specific place. End, in summary.

It is not hidden that among the necessary consequences of what they have mentioned of the exchange arising from the coincidence twice is the coincidence of the southern pole of the zodiac with the northern pole of the world and the reverse; the zodiac signs of autumn becoming the signs of spring and the reverse; the signs of summer becoming the signs of winter and the reverse; the reversal of the order of the signs into its opposite, so that Pisces rises, then Aquarius, then Capricorn, and so on up to Aries; the agreement of the motion of what moves from west to east with the motion of the greatest sphere; and other things. But the east becoming west and the west becoming east is not a necessary consequence of the mentioned coincidence; rather, it cannot be conceived at all. Yes, if the claim were the coincidence of the equator zone with the zodiac zone, such that the motion is of the equator toward the zone, then what was mentioned could be imagined; but this is impossible according to what al-Sayyid al-Sanad explicitly stated earlier, though he assumed non-impossibility; so reflect. The "waiting" in the verse is to be taken as a figurative expression based on likening the state of
