[Page 66]

These disbelievers persist in their unbelief and stubbornly continue in their obstinacy until those awesome events come upon them, events in which faith becomes absolutely necessary for them at the moment they witness them, and they are then waiting for them. This is what the transmitted exegesis (al-tafsir al-ma'thur, interpretation based on reports from the Prophet and the Companions) requires. One should not turn away from it once the attribution of some of it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and of the rest to some of his Companions (may God be pleased with them) has been established as sound. Nothing in the noble text rejects it, nor does the context support any other reading.

It has also been said that what is meant by the coming of the angels and the coming of the Lord, may He be glorified, is what they proposed when they said: ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?﴾ and in His saying: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels before us as a group.﴾ What is meant by the coming of some of the signs, other than what was mentioned, is what they proposed when they said: ﴿Or you make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed,﴾ and similar great signs on which they conditioned their faith. It has also been permitted to take "some of the signs" in His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come,﴾ as including their proposals and other great calamities that nullify the choice on which the sphere of moral responsibility (taklif) revolves. This is a statement that is not weak in itself, but if the ḥadīth is sound, then it is a matter of a particular school of thought (madhhabī). The expression "some" is used for dread and magnification. Likewise, the attribution of the signs to the name of the Lord, which indicates total sovereignty over that, and its attribution to His pronoun (the Prophet), upon him be prayers and peace, is for honour. The indefinite form of "a soul" (nafsan) is for generality. The clause ﴿had not believed﴾ is in the accusative position as a qualifier of "a soul," and it is separated from it by the subject (al-fā'il), because it contains a pronoun referring back to the qualified noun. There is no defect in this, since it is not foreign to it, as both share the same governing element. It has also been permitted that the clause be resumptive (istinafiyya, a new independent clause), and that "the day" (yawma) be in the accusative governed by "will not benefit."

[Page 67]

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿ya'tīhim﴾ with the *yā'* (third person masculine), because the feminine marking of "the angels" is not real (ḥaqīqī). It is also read ﴿yawmu﴾ with the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is the clause, and the returning pronoun (al-'ā'id) is omitted, meaning "it will not benefit in it." Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Sirin read ﴿lā tanfa'u﴾ with the *tā'* on top. Ibn Jinni explained it as belonging to the type "some of his fingers were cut off," where the genitive construction (al-muḍāf) has acquired the feminine from the second term (al-muḍāf ilayhi), because it resembles what can be dispensed with. Abu Hayyan said that the feminine is due to interpreting "faith" as "belief" and "knowledge," like "his book came to him, so he despised it," meaning "the page."

His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿or it earned good through its faith﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "had believed," and the statement is taken as negating the disjunction, which entails generality, and which by its explicit meaning indicates that the condition for non-benefit is the absence of both matters together: the faith that came first and the good earned through it. By its implicit meaning (mafhūm), it indicates that benefit is conditioned on the realization of one of them, by way of preventing their being empty of both, not a real separation (al-infiṣāl al-ḥaqīqī). The meaning is that faith will not benefit a soul at that time if it did not previously issue from it, either in mere faith or in good earned through it. Good is therefore realized by whichever one occurs, as the noble texts indicate, from the verses and authentic ḥadīths. The Mu'tazilah say that the disjunction between the two negations intends the negation of generality, not the generality of negation. The meaning is that faith will benefit a soul at that time if it did not previously bring its faith forward, or if it brought its faith forward but did not earn good through it. This is explicit in support of what they hold, that faith unaccompanied by action is not considered and does not benefit its possessor. They did not interpret it as a general negation, as they established in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not obey any of them who is sinful or ungrateful,﴾ because that applies where no contextual or verbal indication contradicts it. Here, there is an indication that contradicts it, for if the general negation were taken, the mention of the condition of non-benefit in the absence of earning good in faith would be superfluous. This is because if faith is absent before that day, earning good in it is absent with certainty. Moreover, what necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire is the absence of faith, without the absence of earning good having any effect on that at all, so mentioning it while explaining what necessitates eternal abiding would also be meaningless speech.

Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) answered this by saying that it is based on the assumption that the intent of describing the soul with the two mentioned absences is merely to explain that each of them necessitates eternal abiding in it, and that the faith that arises does not save it from that. This is not the case. Otherwise, it would have sufficed in the explanation to say: "faith that arises will not benefit a soul." Rather, the primary intent of describing it with those two absences, in the course of the non-benefit of faith that arises, is to establish that what necessitates benefit is one of the two possessions, namely the earlier faith and the good earned through it. This is for the reason mentioned, namely the method and the encouragement to attain them within the warning against abandoning them. It cannot be said that just as the absence of the first is independently sufficient to necessitate eternal abiding in the Fire, so the absence of the second is ineffective, and therefore mentioning the second is superfluous. This is an analogy with a difference. How could it be otherwise, since eternal abiding in it is a matter in which multiple causes cannot be conceived? As for deliverance from it along with entry into Paradise, it has degrees, some of which follow from faith itself and some of which follow from its various branches, quantitatively and qualitatively.

The mention of what necessitates the basic benefit, which is earlier faith, is not restricted to it, although it is set against what does not necessitate it at all, which is the faith that arises. Rather, what necessitates additional benefit is also joined to it, as guidance toward seeking the highest and as an indication that the lesser suffices, and as a means of despairing the disbelievers of what they have attached their empty hopes to, namely the deeds of righteousness they performed in disbelief, which belong to the category of noble deeds. It also shows that faith that arises does not benefit them alone, nor do they benefit by combining it with their earlier and later deeds.

Then he said: "You may say: the intent of describing the soul with the two mentioned absences is an allusion to the state of the disbelievers in their rebellion and their neglect of each of the two obligatory matters, although the obligation of one of them is conditional on the other, as in His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed, but he denied and turned away.﴾ It is a recording against them of the completeness of their transgression, and a notification that their punishment will be multiplied, because it is established that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the law in respect of accountability, as His saying, may He be exalted, indicates: ﴿Woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat.﴾" End.

[Some] said, to avoid the charge of superfluity, something other than that. One of them answered the Mu'tazilah's reliance by saying that the verse includes what the science of rhetoric calls implicit wrapping (al-laff al-taqdīrī, where a term is omitted and understood from the other), as if it were said: "Faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, nor will its earning good through its faith benefit it if it had not earned good before." It was brief because of knowledge of this. There is obscurity in this that is not hidden. Similar to it is what some researchers grasped, even though the statement is complete with it without any wrapping or consideration of brevity: the meaning of the verse is that faith does not benefit by reason of its essence if it did not occur before, nor by reason of action if no action was performed before. Faith benefits by reason of action in that it becomes a cause for the acceptance of action. The expression does not bear this, nor is it understood from it without considering an implied element in the structure of the speech.

Our master Ibn al-Kamal said: The intended meaning of faith in the verse is the definite (al-ma'rifa) one, as the reading ﴿lā tanfa'u﴾ with the *tā'* indicates, and "earning good" means submission. We, the people of the Sunnah and the community, say what the text requires: that beneficial faith is the combination of the two matters. There is no proof in it for the opponent, because their basis is taking faith in the technical sense (al-ma'nā al-iṣṭilāḥī) that was invented after the revelation of the Qur'an, and restricting good to what is done by the limbs. Each of these contradicts the original and apparent meaning. Even if it is granted, we say: beneficial faith must involve two matters, belief in the heart and affirmation by the tongue. The first is expressed by His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿had believed,﴾ and the second by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or earned.﴾ Earning occurs through bodily instruments, among which is the tongue. So the explicit meaning of the verse, according to our school, is clear. End.

It is not hidden from you that the terms used in the speech of the Lawgiver are technical legal meanings (ḥaqā'iq shar'iyya), and what is understood from them without any indication is what is known. Faith, although it is correct that its linguistic meaning, which is the assent of the heart in general, was not transferred from it, even if it is used for specific assent, is what is understood from it primarily. In that case, the statement of this scholar is not free from scrutiny.

[Page 67, continued]

Qadi al-Baydawi, may God whiten the face of his conditions, answered that for those who consider faith unaccompanied by action and say that it benefits its possessor by delivering him from eternal abiding in the Fire, this ruling is specific to that. That is, this ruling, namely the non-benefit of bare faith to its possessor, is restricted to that day, meaning that it does not benefit him in it. It does not follow that it does not benefit him in the Hereafter at any time. It is not meant that what is judged as not benefiting is what came into being on that day of faith and deed, nor does it follow from the non-benefit of what came into being in it that earlier faith does not benefit, even if it is bare of action, as it has been said. This is because this is not a restriction of the ruling at all. Rather, it is a restriction of the object of the judgment. Its outcome may return to the verse including implicit wrapping, as we have indicated. It may be objected that this entails restricting the ruling of non-benefit to the faith that arises on that day as well, and no one holds this, since it does not benefit its possessor at any time by agreement. It may be answered that the restriction in the ruling of non-benefit is considered only with respect to bare faith and by that consideration alone, so that the meaning of the verse becomes: "On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, faith not preceding its possessor in it will not benefit, nor will faith in which good has not been earned." Although faith benefits in the Hereafter, this involves a restriction in the ruling and in what is judged. So reflect. It has also been said that the saying, may He be glorified: ﴿earned﴾ has been diverted from being coordinated with ﴿had believed﴾ to being coordinated with ﴿had not,﴾ but after making "or" mean "and," and understanding faith in ﴿will not benefit a soul its faith﴾ as the faith that arises on that day. If that does not benefit together with the good earned in it, it is understood from it that it does not benefit without it, by a stronger argument. You know that such a possibility harms the argument, and we are concerned with refuting their argument, so it does not harm us that it has a degree of remoteness.

Among the most surprising things I have come across concerning an answer by some learned men of Rum (Anatolia) is that "or" means "except," and after it is an implied present-tense verb, like it in the words of al-Hariri in the ninth assembly: "By God, my eye has not rinsed its mouth with sleep, nor has my night given birth to its day, except that I found Abu Zayd al-Sarufi." The original is "or it earned," meaning "except that it earned." What is meant by this exception is to emphasize the negation of the negation by making it contingent on something impossible, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ (4:22), and ﴿nor to combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ (4:23), in the opinion of the poet:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."*

The essential meaning in our case is this: when that (sign) comes to them, faith will not benefit a soul that had not believed before that day, unless that soul had earned some good in faith before that day. Earning good in faith before that day is impossible for a soul that had not believed before, so the benefit sought is all the more likely to be impossible. Other answers have been given to this argument as well. The sum of all of this is that the verse, because of the possibilities it contains, cannot contradict the definitive texts, which are firm in their transmission and strong in their meaning and are not affected by such doubts. These texts state that faith alone, without deeds, is sufficient for deliverance from everlasting punishment, even after the long and the short of it (i.e., after whatever delay). After all this, the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) are answered as follows: the word "good" (khayr) is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general, and it follows that faith benefits by mere good, even a single instance of it. That is not their doctrine, for in their view all righteous deeds are included in "good."

﴿Say﴾ to them, after clarifying the true state of affairs, as a warning: ﴿Wait﴾ for whatever you are waiting for, namely the coming of one of these matters. ﴿Indeed, we too are waiting﴾ (158) for that, and then we will be successful while you will be destroyed.

It has been said: in this there is a confirmation that what they are waiting for is the coming of the angels of punishment or the coming of His command, and an implicit promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers that they will witness the punishment that will befall the disbelievers. Perhaps this is what they witnessed on the day of Badr.

Page 68

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ is a resumptive statement explaining the condition of the People of the Book, following the explanation of the condition of the polytheists. This is based on what is reported from Ibn Abbas and Qatada, that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians. That is, they scattered their religion and split it into parts, so each group clung to a part of it. Ali (may Allah honour his face), Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فارقوا﴾ (*fāraqū*, "parted from") with an alif, meaning they separated themselves from it. Abandoning part of it, even while taking up another part, amounts to abandoning the whole or separating oneself from it. ﴿And they became sects (shiya')﴾: that is, groups, each group following an imam and adhering to him, or supporting him and promoting his cause. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, all of them in the Abyss except one. The Christians split into seventy-two sects, all of them in the Abyss except one. And my community will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Abyss except one."

The exception of one sect from each of the two groups of the People of the Book applies only with reference to the past era, before abrogation (*naskh*, "the abrogation of earlier law"). As for after it, all of them are in the Abyss, although the reasons for their entry differ.

Among the strange things that occurred: some of the zealous Imami Shi'a of our time, named Hamad, narrated, in place of "except one" in this report, "except one sect" (*illā firqatan*), and claimed that this contains an indication of the salvation of the Shi'a. He argued that the numerical value (*jummal*, the system of assigning numbers to letters) of the word *firqa* equals the numerical value of the word *shī'a*, so that it is as if he (peace and blessings be upon him) had said: "except the Shi'a." The best-known bearers of this title are the Imami Shi'a. After I had refuted his statement with several objections, I said to him: This kind of indication entails that a dog would be [saved], because the numerical value of *kalb* (dog) equals the numerical value of *Hamad*. So the dog was silenced with a stone.

﴿You are not of them in anything﴾: that is, you have no part in questioning them about, or investigating, their divisions, or in their punishment; or, you are free of them. It has been said that this may be a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of protection from them, meaning you are not of them in any harm. It is reported from al-Suddi that he was forbidden to engage in fighting them, and then this was abrogated by what is in Surat Bara'a. The word ﴿minhum﴾ (of them) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), because it is an indefinite qualifier placed before its noun.

﴿Their affair is only with Allah﴾: this is a justification for the preceding negation. That is, He alone takes charge of their affairs in this world and the Hereafter, and manages them as wisdom requires. It has also been said that "those who divided" are the people of innovations (*ahl al-bid'a*) from this community. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, al-Shirazi in *al-Alqab*, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying, "Indeed, those who divided..." etc.: "They are the people of innovations and whims from this community."

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, and others reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her): "O Aisha, those who parted from their religion and became sects are the people of innovations, the people of whims, and the people of misguidance from this community. They have no repentance, and I am free of them, and they are free of me."

On this reading, the statement is a resumptive explanation of the condition of the innovators, following the explanation of the condition of the polytheists, indicating that they are not far from them. The phrase ﴿Their affair is only...﴾ on this view is not a justification but a threat concerning what they did. That is, their return is to Him, the Glorified, ﴿then He will inform them﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿of what they used to do﴾ (159) in the world, with continuous punishment for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 160:

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the measures of the recompense of those who act, and it has been introduced with an explanation of the recompense of the doers of good, which is indicated by mention of their opposites. That is: whoever among the believers comes with a single trait from the traits of obedience, whatever trait it may be. It was said: it is monotheism (tawhid), and this was attributed to al-Hasan, but it is not established from al-Hasan. ﴿Then for him there is ten﴾ good deeds ﴿like it﴾, as a bounty from God, exalted is He.

Ya'qub read ("ashr) with tanwin and (amthaluha) in the nominative, as an adjective. This is the least of the multiplications promised, and the promise has come of seventy and seven hundred, and without reckoning. Therefore it was said: what is meant by "ten" is abundance, not restriction to a specific number.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, Abu al-Shaykh from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abd ibn Humayd and others from Ibn 'Umar, that the verse was revealed concerning the Bedouin (a'rab) specifically; as for the Emigrants (muhajirun), the good deed is multiplied for them seven hundredfold. The apparent meaning is generality.

The omission of the feminine ta' from ﴿ashr﴾ is because the counted noun is feminine, as we have indicated, but it has been elided and its adjective placed in its stead. It was also said: the counted noun is the one mentioned, except that it acquired the feminine gender from the noun it is annexed to. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, whoever he is among the worlds, ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾, by the ruling of the promise: one for one. And the imposition of the punishment of eternity for the disbelief of an hour is because the disbeliever intends that, were he to live forever, he would remain upon that belief forever. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ (160) by a reduction of reward or an increase of punishment, for that from Him, exalted is He, is not considered wrong, since it is for Him, glorified is He, to punish the obedient and reward the disobedient. It was said: the meaning is that they will not be diminished in good deeds from ten times their like, nor in evil deeds from their like, in the context of recompense.

Among the Mu'tazilah, some argued by this verse for the affirmation of rational good and evil (al-husn wa'l-qubh al-'aqliyyan), and its formulation was disputed. It was said: when they saw that one of the proofs of the Ash'ariyyah for negation is that the servant is not independent in originating his act, as has been explained in its proper place, reason does not judge independently that reward and punishment are ordained upon it. They said: His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾ ... etc., is explicit that the servant is independent and free in his good and bad acts, and if that is established, rational good and evil are established. This was answered: the verse does not indicate the servant's independence; at most it indicates direct performance, and they do not deny that. It was also said: the verse indicates that God, exalted is He, has a good act, and if the goodness of acts were due to their being commanded or permitted, God's act would not be good, since He is neither commanded nor permitted. Also, if knowledge of good and evil depended on the revelation of the Law, God's acts would not be good before the revelation, and that is a departure from the religion.

It was answered: as for the first, we do not claim that there is no good except what He commanded or permitted, so that it could be said that God's acts would have to be not good, since it is impossible for Him to be commanded or permitted in them. Rather, what the Lawgiver commands or permits is good, but the converse does not hold of itself; indeed an act may be good by reference to its agreement with a purpose, or by reference to its being commanded to praise its doer, and by this consideration God's act is good whether it agrees with a purpose or opposes it. As for the second, the good and evil, even if they are defined by the revelation of the Law as prohibition and permission, we do not concede that there is no goodness or evil except through the Law, so that this would be necessary for us. Rather, good and evil are more general than what has been mentioned, as is known in its place. And it does not follow from the realization of the meaning of good and evil without revelation's prohibition and permission that they are intrinsic to acts. It is not hidden from the discerning that their statement, "if the goodness of acts ... etc.," and their statement, "if knowledge of good and evil depended ... etc.," are two independent objections out of ten argumentative objections mentioned by al-Amidi in Abkar al-Afkar, and that each of the two preceding formulations is still not free from scrutiny, so reflect.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 161:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me﴾. This is a command to him (ﷺ) to declare what the true religion is, the religion that those who split (the religion into sects) claim to follow, though they have utterly abandoned it. The opening of the sentence with the particle of emphasis (*harf al-tahqiq*, the emphatic particle *inna*) serves to show the full importance of its content. The mention of the title of Lordship (*al-Rububiyyah*), together with its attribution to his pronoun (peace be upon him), is as has passed more than once. The meaning is: say, O Muhammad, to these dividers or to all people: my Lord has guided me, through revelation and through the signs set up in the horizons and in the souls, ﴿to a straight path﴾, one that leads to the truth.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿a religion﴾ (*dinan*) is a substitute (*badal*) for the position (*mahall*) of ﴿to a path﴾ (*ila sirat*), since the meaning is "He guided me to a path," similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾. Or it is an object (*maf'ul*) of an implied verb indicated by what has been mentioned, meaning: He guided me, or gave me, or made me know, a religion. It is also permitted that it be a second object (*maf'ul thani*) of the mentioned verb.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿qiyaman﴾ (*qiyaman*) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) like *al-sighar* and *al-kibar*, used as an adjective for emphasis (*mubalaghah*). It is also permitted that the underlying form be *dha qiyam* (possessing uprightness). By analogy it should be *qiwaman*, like *iwadun* and *hiwalun*, but it was made *qiyaman* in accordance with the vowel-change (*i'lal*) of its verb, *qama*, as in *al-qiyam*. Kathir read *qayyiman* (قَيِّمًا), which is *fai'al* from *qama* as well, like *sayyid* from *sada*. It is said that this form is more intensive than *mustaqim* in terms of its pattern, while *mustaqim* is more intensive than it in terms of the whole root and pattern together. It has also been said that *mustaqim* is more intensive because the *sin* (in *istaqama*) indicates a request, so it implies a demand for standing upright and its requirement. Many scholars hold there is no difference between *qayyim* and *mustaqim* in the basic meaning. They explained *qayyim* as the firm one that sustains the affairs of this life and the Hereafter, and took *mustaqim* from *istaqama al-amr* in the sense of "became firm." Otherwise what was mentioned would not be possible. It has also been said that *mustaqim* is the opposite of *mu'awwaj* (crooked), while *qayyim* is the firm one that is not abrogated.

﴿the religion of Abraham﴾ (*millata Ibrahim*) is put in the accusative by an implied verb, "I mean," or it is an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayan*) to *dinan*, based on the permissibility of the explicative apposition and what it explains differing in definiteness and indefiniteness.

﴿a hanif﴾ (*hanifan*), meaning inclining away from the false religions, or devoted sincerely to God, exalted is He, in worship. It is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of Abraham. They agreed on the permissibility of a circumstantial accusative coming from the genitive noun (*mudaf ilayhi*) when the noun in the construct (*mudaf*) is a part of it or is in the position of a part, in that its standing in for it is valid. The governing element of this circumstantial accusative is the same governing element of the construct noun. It has been said that the meaning of the construct is due to what is in it of the sense of a verb, which the preposition indicates. This meaning is strengthened here by the partness or near-partness that exists between the two terms of the construct.

It is also permitted that it be an object of an implied verb, meaning: I mean *hanifan*.

﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ (161) is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiradh*) confirming his purity (peace be upon him) from what the falsifiers are upon. It has been said that it is a conjunction (*'atf*) on what preceded, and in it is a refutation of those who claim that they are upon his religion (peace be upon him): from the people of Mecca who say, "The angels are the daughters of God," from the Jews who say, "Uzayr is the son of God," and from the Christians who say, "Jesus is the son of God."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 162:

﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer﴾ — i.e., its genus (jins), so that it encompasses the obligatory prayers and others. The command is repeated for greater emphasis (mazid al-i'tina'). It has also been said: because what is commanded here relates to the branches of the sacred laws (furu' al-shara'i'), whereas what preceded relates to their foundations (usuluha).

﴿and my sacrifice (nusuki)﴾ — i.e., all my worship, as said by al-Zajjaj and al-Jubba'i. This is the mention of the general after the specific (min 'atf al-'amm 'ala al-khass). It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Suddi that what is meant by it is the sacrificial animal slaughtered for the Hajj and the 'Umrah; and from Qatadah that it is the udhiyah (sacrificial offering on Eid al-Adha). It is joined with prayer as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, according to the well-known view. It has also been said that what is meant by it is the Hajj, i.e., "Indeed, my prayer and my Hajj."

﴿and my living and my dying﴾ — i.e., what accompanies my life and my death of faith and righteous deeds.

It has been said: it is possible that what is meant by "living and dying" is their apparent meaning, but the first is the one fitting to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (162).

Page 71

Because what is meant by it is sincerity according to the outward sense. It has also been said that what is meant by it, considering this possibility, is that all of that belongs to Him, Exalted is He, as dominion (mulk) and power (qudrah).

﴿No partner to Him﴾, that is, in my worship, or in it and in giving life and causing death. Nafi' read *maḥyāya* (مَحْيايَ) with the *yā'* unvowelled (sākin), treating the connected reading (*waṣl*, continuous recitation) as if it were a pause (*waqf*, stopping). In one narration, he read the *yā'* with a kasra. On the first reading, the meeting of two unvowelled letters (*al-sākinayn*) is permitted because the reciter intends a pause, and in pause such a meeting is allowed. Some critics objected that this involves joining two unvowelled letters, which is not permitted. That objection is misplaced. A group of transmitters related this reading from Nafi'. As for what is said, that he retracted it and that it is not lawful for anyone to transmit it from him, it is nothing.

﴿And of that﴾, that is, the saying or the sincere devotion, ﴿I have been commanded﴾, not anything other than it. ﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾ (163), that is, those who submit to carrying out what God the Exalted commanded. It was also said: those who submit to the decree and destiny of God the Exalted. The intended meaning is the Muslims of his community, as was said, and this is the case of every prophet in relation to his community. It was also said that this is an allusion to his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: «The first thing God the Exalted created was my light» (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 6, verse 164:

﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?"﴾ This is a denial of seeking other than Him, the Exalted, as a lord, not a denial of seeking the Lord. For this reason the object was placed first, and the fronting is not for restriction (ikhtisas), since the intended meaning is: "Shall I seek from other than Allah a lord, and take him as a partner to Him?" And on the assumption of restriction, it would not be associating another, but rather monotheism. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: "It is not far-fetched to say that the fronting is for restriction, and he mentioned in rejecting their call to other than Him the rejection of restriction, as an alert that associating another is seeking other than Allah, the Exalted, since He, glorified be He, has no aim except through His monotheism, mighty and majestic is He. And what is in the noble composition is more eloquent than 'Shall I worship other than Allah?' and the like, as is not hidden."

﴿And He﴾, glorified be He, ﴿is the Lord of everything﴾: a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) emphasizing the denial, i.e., while the state is that everything other than Him is a creature under His lordship, how could it be imagined that it would be a partner to Him?

﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾. It is narrated that they used to say to the Muslims: "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." So He replied to them with what has been mentioned, i.e., that what every soul has earned of sins is borne by it alone, not by another, so that your saying would be valid. On this basis, His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, i.e., a sinful soul, is an emphasis of what preceded it. It was said: their saying that may bear two meanings. The first: "Follow our way, and let what you have done of sins be written against us, not against you." The second: "Follow us, so that we may bear on the Day of Resurrection what has been written against you of sins."

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And every soul earns…﴾ etc., is a refutation of it according to the first meaning, and His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And no bearer…﴾ etc., is a refutation of it according to the second meaning. It was also said: their answer is the second, and the first is part of the answer to their call to worship their gods; that is, "If I answered you to what you called me to, I would not be excused by saying that you preceded me to it and that I did it following you and obeying you, so that would not benefit me anything, nor would it save me from Allah, the Exalted, because every person's earning and deed is upon him." Some of them preferred it over the first, on the ground that establishing a new meaning is better than emphasis.

﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾: a turning of address (talwin lil-khitab) and a directing of it to all, to affirm the promise and intensify the warning, i.e., to the Owner of your affair is your return on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Then He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾ (164): by clarifying the right course from error and distinguishing the upright from the crooked.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 6, verse 165:

﴿It is He who made you successors (khalaif) on the earth﴾, meaning: some of you succeed others. Whenever one generation passes, another comes, until the Hour is established. This could not happen except by a Knowing, Governing One. This is the view of al-Hasan. Or it means: He made you vicegerents (khulafa') of God, the Exalted, on His earth, to act freely in it, as it has been said. The address in both interpretations is general. It has also been said that the address is to this Community specifically, and this was narrated from al-Suddi. That is, He made you successors to the earlier nations. ﴿And He raised some of you above others﴾ in excellence and wealth, as narrated from Muqatil. ﴿In degrees﴾, many and varying. ﴿That He may try you through what He has given you﴾, meaning: that He may deal with you as one who tests you, to see what you do, of what pleases Him and what does not. ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾: the address is turned away to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the title "Lord" is attributed to him (peace and blessings be upon him) to show special gentleness toward him (ﷺ). ﴿Is swift in punishment﴾, meaning: His punishment in the Hereafter comes swiftly upon whoever does not observe the rights of what He has given him, because everything that is coming is near. Or it means He is swift in carrying out His will when He wills it, since He, the Exalted, is far above using means and instruments.

It is also permissible that "punishment" refers to punishment in this world, such as what follows neglect: distance from the natural disposition (fitrah), hardness of heart, veiling of the sight, deafness of the hearing, and the like. ﴿And indeed, He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (165) to whoever observes the rights of what God has given him as it should be observed.

In making the predicate of this sentence these two attributes, which are in the intensive form and emphasized with the particle of emphasis (lam), while making the predicate of the first sentence a description applied to other than its subject, there is a clear indication that He, the Exalted, is Forgiving and Merciful in His essence. His forgiveness and mercy depend on nothing, as His words in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi, a saying of God related by the Prophet) indicate: "My mercy precedes My wrath." He is intensive in this, and He inflicts punishment only incidentally, and only after a sin has come from the servant that makes him deserving of it. How graceful is the opening of this surah with praise and its closing with forgiveness and mercy. We ask God, the Exalted, to grant us the largest share of both. Indeed, He is the Bestower of favours, and to Him belongs praise at every beginning and end.

(From the path of allusion in the verses) ﴿Those who associated partners [with God]﴾, who affirmed an existence other than His existence, ﴿will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated [anything] with Him,﴾ ﴿nor would our fathers [have associated], nor would we have prohibited anything﴾ (from before us). They said this in denial of the messengers, peace be upon them. ﴿Thus did those before them deny﴾, and they said the same as what they said, ﴿until they tasted Our punishment﴾ which befell them for their denial, and it is the veil. ﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out for us through clear proof?"﴾ ﴿You follow only assumption﴾, because you are veiled in the station of the self (nafs). ﴿Say: "Then to God belongs the conclusive proof."﴾ That is: if the matter is as you say, then you have no proof; rather, the conclusive proof belongs to God against you. For He, the Exalted, wills only what He knows from eternity, and He knows nothing except as it is in itself. So if you were not, in your own selves, polytheists of bad predisposition, God would not have willed that from you. ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾, but He did not will it, because in your eternal predisposition there is no such thing.

The verse also admits of other meanings, which are perhaps not hidden: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him."﴾ For affirming an existence other than God, the Exalted, is a great wrong. ﴿And to the two parents﴾, that is, to the spirit and the heart, ﴿do good﴾, ﴿kindness﴾, by observing their rights. ﴿And do not kill﴾, that is, do not destroy ﴿your children﴾, your powers, by employing them in what they are not for ﴿out of poverty﴾, that is, out of your want of the Most Holy Overflow (al-fayd al-aqdas). ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾ by pouring upon you and upon them that by which you are nourished of the knowledges, in measure, when you turn toward Us. ﴿And do not approach the immoralities﴾, the abominable deeds, ﴿what is apparent of them﴾, like the acts of the limbs, ﴿and what is concealed﴾, like the acts of the heart. ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden﴾, the Exalted, to be killed, ﴿except by right﴾, that is, except by its cause, by intending its turning toward Him, or except a killing that is bound to that right, which is killing it when it inclines toward other than Him. ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, that is, what is prepared for the orphan of the heart, cut off from the ties of this world and the Hereafter, of the knowledges which lie beyond the realm of reason, ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, which is to affirm that generally and not deny it, ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, when he becomes strong enough to receive the various kinds of manifestations (tajalliyat). At that point it becomes right for you to approach what God, the Exalted, has prepared for him of those knowledges, because of the strength of your hearts and the sanctity of your spirits.

Some people have taken "the orphan" as an allusion to the presence of prophethood (peace be upon him), and this, as you see, is far-fetched. ﴿And give full measure﴾, that is, the measure of the Law, by observing the outward rights, ﴿and the balance﴾, that is, the balance of Reality, by observing the inward rights, ﴿with justice﴾, with fairness. ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾, that is, say nothing but the truth. ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾, which is monotheism (tawhid). ﴿And that this is My path, straight﴾, not inclining to the right or the left. ﴿So follow it﴾, that you may reach God, the Exalted. ﴿And do not follow [other] ways﴾, which those of veiling have described, ﴿lest they separate you from His way﴾, so that you go astray and do not reach Him, the Exalted. ﴿Do they await only that the angels should come to them﴾ to take their souls, ﴿or that your Lord should come﴾ in the manifestation of the form (tajalli suwari) on the Day of Resurrection, as is established in that hadith, ﴿or that some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾, which is the uncovering of the shin (kashf 'an saq). ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾, which is the uncovering mentioned, ﴿no soul will benefit from its faith﴾ at that time, because the obligation has ended.

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ into scattered desires, like those whose qualities of the self have overcome them, ﴿and became sects﴾, divided groups according to the dominance of those desires, ﴿you have nothing to do with them﴾, because they are people of division and of veiling by multiplicity, so their aspirations do not unite and their aims do not become one. ﴿Their affair is only with God﴾ regarding the recompense for their division. ﴿Then He will inform them﴾ when the forms of their varying and scattered desires become manifest ﴿of what they used to do﴾ of bad deeds and following of desire. ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. This is because the evil deed belongs to the station of the self, which is the level of units, while the good deed, at its first station, is the station of the heart, which is the level of tens, and its least rank is ten. It may be multiplied more than that when it comes from the station of the spirit or the station of the innermost secret. This is the secret of the difference in the recompense of good deeds, which the texts indicate. ﴿Say: "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path"﴾, which is the way of essential monotheism (tawhid dhati), ﴿a upright religion﴾, firm, which no creeds or sects abrogate, ﴿the religion of Abraham﴾, by which I turn away from other than Him, ﴿a hanif﴾, inclining away from every religion that contains association. ﴿Say: "Indeed, my prayer﴾, my presence and witnessing by the spirit, ﴿and my sacrifice﴾, my drawing near by the heart, ﴿and my living﴾ in truth, ﴿and my dying﴾ in the self, ﴿are for God, Lord of the worlds﴾, no share of me belongs to anyone in that, ﴿no partner is His﴾ in anything at all, since there is no existence besides Him. ﴿And with that﴾, that is, with sincerity and not seeing other than Him, ﴿I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾, those who submit to annihilation (fana') in Him, the Exalted. ﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than God?"﴾, so that I seek the impossible, ﴿while He is the Lord of all things﴾, meaning: everything other than Him, considering the details of His attributes, the Exalted, is a thing that is lord-ed. ﴿And no soul earns except against itself﴾, since the earning of the self is a form of association in His acts, the Exalted, and whoever associates, his burden is upon himself. ﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾, since the angels do not pass beyond to other than its owner. ﴿And it is He who made you successors on the earth﴾, by making you the locus of His names, ﴿and raised some of you above others in degrees﴾ in that locus-hood, because it is according to predisposition, and that varies. ﴿That He may try you through what He has given you﴾, and that His knowledge may become manifest concerning who observes the rights of what He gave and who does not. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment﴾ for whoever does not observe, ﴿and indeed, He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ to whoever does observe that. We ask God, the Exalted, to enable us to what pleases Him, and to make our future state better than our past.
